summary: A scriptural passage (cap. 3, v. 7) Atwood cites in support of the point that it is God who gives the increase.
body: Cited by Atwood, with the reference cap. 3, v. 7 given in the footnote, in support of the point that the increase comes from God: “neither he that watereth, but God, that giveth the increase” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n32].

summary: Cited for reference only.
An abbot Atwood cites as having praised the Hermetic Art and the wisdom of Arnold.
body: Cited by Atwood as one who praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom [I.1 ¶43].

summary: Named as the addressee of Aquinas' Thesaurus Alchimiae.
body: Mentioned only as the person to whom Aquinas' *Thesaurus Alchimiae* is addressed [I.1 ¶42; I.1 n49; I.1 n51].

summary: In a view attributed to Plato, the defective reasoning by negation through which Matter is apprehended, describing it only by what it is not.
body: A quoted view (Plato): Matter can be apprehended, but only by a reasoning that proceeds by negation, describing it by what it is not: “Matter is indeed to be apprehended, and that by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53].

summary: Cited through the Sepher Jezirah (Liber de Creatione) as an example of the wisely simple, and elsewhere for travelling with his asses.
body: Atwood cites the *Sepher Jezirah* (*Liber de Creatione, Authore Abraham*, cap. 1), presenting Abraham as an example of the wisely simple who subdued the will to the Law of Wisdom, and closing with a Latin injunction: “Intellige in scientia et sepias intellignetia” [II.3 ¶55; II.3 n61; II.3 ¶56; II.3 n62] (our rendering, roughly: understand in knowledge and be wise in understanding). Elsewhere he is mentioned, by way of illustration, as one who constantly travelled with his asses [III.2 ¶64].

summary: Mentioned as the one who indicated the fire and the furnace to Flamel.
body: Mentioned by Atwood as the one who indicated the fire and furnace to Flamel [III.1 ¶37].

summary: Cited for reference only.
The ultimate foundation of knowledge; philosophers dispute its conditions and difficulty, but, Atwood says, none deny that it is possible.
body: Atwood's term for the ultimate ground of knowledge. She notes that “philosophers have disputed about the conditions and difficulty of the Absolute ground” [II.1 ¶33]; the record adds that none deny its possibility.

summary: What the hypostasis bounding abstract reason proves to be when met by the inquiring light within; prior to all duality of consciousness.
body: In Atwood's account, the hypostasis that bounds abstract reason, when met by the inquiring light within, proves to be Absolute Identity, “which, before all duality of consciousness, is the fortitude and life of all” [III.2 ¶31]. She also speaks of the “incomprehensible nature of the objective contact in Identity” [III.2 ¶33].

summary: In a quoted account, the abyss where the parts of the world lay mingled and formless before the spirit's breath agitated the mass.
body: From a passage attributed to the metropolitan of Memphis: before the spirit's breath agitated the mass, the parts of the world “lay mingled and inform, brooding overwhelmed in the Abyss of Being” [III.3 ¶46].

summary: That which is without ground, fathomless or void (Boehme); for Atwood also the Kabalists' name for the Matter, called by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.
body: Quoting Boehme, the text defines it: “the Abysse, that is without ground, or fathomless or void” [III.2 ¶16]; in the same place the One Thing is spoken of as “the first divine manifestation out of the abyss” [III.2 ¶16]. Atwood elsewhere uses the word for the Matter as the Kabalists name it: “that Abyss of the Kabalists, styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60], so Abyss = Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.

summary: A name connected with dissolution, identified by Atwood with the vitriolic solvent; in Hermes and the Master, ‘our Acetum’ with which the soul or sulphurous Form is mingled.
body: Atwood names it alongside the solvent: something “becomes their vitriolic solvent and most sharp acetum” [I.2 ¶40]; the reader takes it as a name of the dissolving stage, which is an inference. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the watery soul is mingled with it to obtain the sulphurous Form: “to mingle the same with our Acetum” [I.3 ¶27]; the same words recur in a passage quoted from the Master [IV.2 ¶14]. In neither quoted passage is the Acetum itself explained.

summary: Paired principles that, by action and reaction, raise one another successively until spiritual ability is complete.
body: Atwood describes the work as “raising successively actives by passives, and, vice versa, passives by actives” [IV.1 ¶41], continuing until spiritual ability is complete. Compare agent and patient.

summary: Legal measures Atwood cites to illustrate the suppression of transmutation, which only drove its pursuit into secrecy.
body: Cited by Atwood to illustrate the legal suppression of transmutation, which in her account only drove the pursuit into secrecy [I.1 ¶55; I.1 n61].

summary: A mystical soil whose glories the prophet describes, spoken of with the winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles.
body: Atwood speaks of “that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], whose glories the prophet describes, in a context of winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles. The text as recorded gives no further plain meaning.

summary: In the Smaragdine Table of Hermes, the manner by which all things arose from the One Thing.
body: A term of the Smaragdine Table (Hermes, quoted): “so all things arose from this one thing by adaptation” [I.1 ¶9], and “Hence were all wonderful adaptations of which this is the manner.” [I.1 ¶9]. A second rendering of the Table reads “so all things proceeded from this One Thing by adaptation” [IV.2 ¶44].

summary: A true master of the Art, one who has accomplished it, sharply distinguished by Atwood from pretenders; in quoted authorities, the initiate whom the Lord illuminates and seals.
body:
Atwood's usual word for a genuine, accomplished master of the Art. The adepts are those who truly understood Geber: “They who have really understood Geber, his adept compeers” [I.1 ¶33]. They are rare and set against pretenders: “The true adepts have been rare exceptions in the world” [I.1 ¶41]; “Many usurped the title of the adepts, who had no knowledge even of the preliminaries of the Art” [I.1 ¶53]; “the pretenders to the Art were in latter times far more numerous than the true adepts” [I.1 ¶86] (said with reference to Sendivogius). The public could not tell them apart, so “even the true adepts --- for the public knew not to distinguish --- suffered equal cruelty” [I.1 ¶66]. She applies the title to individuals: Ripley “though reputed a good adept” [I.1 ¶64]; “Henry Khunrath, a pious and learned adeptest” [I.1 ¶70].

On their writing: “the adepts appear to have a directly contrary aim” [I.1 ¶82], their writing deliberately obscuring, being “so very abstruse and envious in their disguises” [IV.1 ¶18]; they caution against excitation [IV.1 ¶18]. “Aristotle is much blamed by Adepts in general” [I.1 ¶16], and of the Bononian Enigma “the adepts claim it as having exclusive reference to the occult material of their art” [I.1 ¶20]. A cited speaker says “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17]; Eirenaeus (quoted) says “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26]. “Verily, says the adept” introduces a cited speaker [III.1 ¶8], where the word is also used of those who call the fire of life Antimony.

In quoted patristic passages the adept is the initiate: Clemens Alexandrinus, “he sets his seal upon the adept whom he illuminates with his beams” [II.2 ¶5]; the Bishop of Alexandria, “He sets his seal upon the Adepts” [IV.2 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood ties the word to discovery: “The seeker, however, in this point of relation, is the adept, the discoverer, the finder.” [APP ¶23] — the seeker at the point where the Golden Fleece appears.

summary: The anonymous ‘adept’ or ‘adepts’ whose sayings Atwood cites throughout, almost always in support and sometimes explicitly endorsed, on the matter, the fire, the stages of the work and its spiritual end.
body:
Atwood frequently quotes an unnamed ‘adept’, sometimes identified only by a footnoted work (*Rosarium*, *Lumen de Lumine*, *Filium Ariadne*, *Introitus Apertus*, *Mercury’s Caducean Rod*, *Maieri Symbola Aureae Mensae*, *Fama et Confessionis, R.C.*), and the adepts collectively. The voice is used in support, and she sometimes endorses it explicitly [III.1 ¶64; III.1 ¶66]. The adept also backs her condemnation of fraudulent books [I.1 ¶53].

**The matter and gold.** “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44; I.2 n43]; “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63; I.3 n70]. The subject is despised: “It is what the world cares not for, as the adept says, but disesteems it” [II.2 ¶18]. The adepts teach that all things derive from one Spirit, gold nearest it [I.2 ¶48]; purified sulphur as seed and mercury as earth of the wise [I.3 n29; I.3 n30]; the Matter's birth is “singular and not without a miracle” [III.3 ¶62]; “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n7].

**Fire and process.** “men neither see nor do they believe there is any other fire but the common fire” [I.3 n41]; the three fires “should be quickly lighted” with a Fourth supervening [IV.2 ¶11; IV.2 n2]; “O happy gate of Blackness!” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n44]; the Seed of Spirit is “a decompounded ens, extremely heavy, shining through the darkness like a fiery star” [II.3 ¶30]; “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41] (extent of quotation unclear); “Open the compound creature; look up the elements; divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; on renewal of the powder, “if the process fails in any stage, an addition of the same will renew it” [II.1 ¶25]; Nature alone cannot enter the True Light: “she has no hands” [III.2 ¶61; III.2 n45]; the Orient Animal is stripped “not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. Also cited: the sign of returning colours and the white elixir, “now our king hath triumphed over the miseries of death” [I.3 n22]; a reading of ‘dust of the earth’ [I.3 n51]; the Preparing Spirit and cleansing of the Argent vive [IV.1 ¶10]; the guide [II.3 n37]; the Light becoming visible, “Lux manifeste et visibilis ad oculum” [III.3 ¶10], and “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North!”, glossed by Atwood as the Light arising out of the crucifixion of cerebral life [III.3 ¶15]; the purified substance's endless transformations [III.2 ¶22; III.2 n22]; the loadstone, Salt, Pole and Fire and the union of agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30; IV.2 n19]; nature's ordinary manifestation contradicting her perfect law [I.2 ¶18; I.2 ¶20]; imaginative impressures lingering in a place [III.4 ¶42].

**Spiritual end.** The Corner Stone is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise” [III.1 ¶66]; “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18; IV.2 n16], which Atwood completes and extends; the adepts' maxim “they who sow in tears shall reap in joy” she expands into the sacrifice of Self-Will [III.3 ¶20]; they say “Natus est jam Elias Artista” [IV.2 ¶12] (our rendering: Elias the Artist is now born) and concealed the three operations [IV.2 ¶3]; with Plutarch they witness to the fable's meaning [IV.2 ¶7]; God “has always revealed them to his elected children” [IV.4 ¶25]. Their analysis of man's life as a pure fire in an ethereal vapour is reported ‘as they profess’ yet presented by Atwood as shown [IV.4 ¶4].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Adepts call the Art “Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29], and reducing their ground to physical science is dismissed as twaddle [APP ¶30].

summary: A solitary adept of Alexandria, named as the master of Morienus.
body: Named by Atwood as a solitary adept of Alexandria and Morienus's master [I.1 ¶35].

summary: Bound up with sacrifice and prayer; its three terms contain all the Divine measures, and its end is where rational inquiry rests and true love is found.
body: Atwood connects adoration with sacrifice and the advantages of prayer. She speaks of “these three terms of adoration, in which, according to the authorities, all the Divine measures are contained” [III.4 ¶25]; these reconcile the warring elements of life and give three supernal benefits. “And thus the end of all adoration is attained” [III.4 ¶26] — the point at which rational inquiry rests and true love is found.

summary: In Khunrath, the starting matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed; called Saturn, the lead of the Wise.
body: From Khunrath (quoted): the matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed, called “our heart of Saturn” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives its identity: “Adrop (which in its proper tongue is called Saturn, i.e., the lead of the Wise)” [IV.1 ¶36]; so Adrop = Saturn = lead of the Wise.

summary: The externally generated form imposed on a body, to be constricted, set against the body's inner central form, to be developed into life and act.
body: Atwood contrasts two forms in a body: “the adventitious or externally generated image may be constricted utterly, and the central form contrariwise developed into life and act” [I.2 ¶20]. The work, on this account, suppresses the outward image and brings forth the inner form.

summary: The temple's interior sanctuary, entered by the Aspirant after leaving the statues behind; an image of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within.
body: Atwood uses the image of “the Aspirant entering into the interior to behold the Adytum, leaves behind him all the statues in the temple” [III.2 ¶66], as a figure of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within. She also speaks of approaching “to the gate of the first Adytum” [III.3 ¶3], whose vestibule is where the Tears of Isis are contemplated.

summary: In Proclus, the soul's innermost recess, where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.
body: Quoted from Proclus: the soul withdraws “into her interior recesses and into the Adytum of Life” [II.4 ¶29], where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.

summary: A riddling inscription, unattributed in the text, describing a thing that is none of the opposites yet all, cited after the claim that the Matter is one Identity.
body: An unattributed riddling inscription cited after Atwood's claim that the Matter is one Identity; it describes something that is none of the opposites yet all, nowhere in particular yet everywhere: “No male, nor female, nor hermaphrodite,” [III.3 ¶66].

summary: Book 6 of the Aeneid, cited for its descent to the shades, which Atwood reads as an illustration of stages of the work and of the Epopteia of Universal Nature.
body:
Atwood quotes Book 6 in Latin to illustrate the inner journey. The apparitions: “Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum” [II.3 ¶21; II.3 n16] (ours: here, trembling with sudden fear, he seizes his sword), as Aeneas draws on bodiless shades until warned. The place of shades: “Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae” [II.3 ¶26; II.3 n28] (ours: this is the place of shades, of sleep and drowsy night). The courage required: “Nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.” [II.3 n37] (ours: now, Aeneas, there is need of courage, now of a firm heart). Aeneas meeting his father in Elysium receives the Epopteia of Universal Nature, spirit and mind pervading the whole: “Spiritus intus alit” [II.4 ¶21; II.4 ¶22; II.4 n14] (ours: a spirit within nourishes).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), where the author is not named, the drawn sword illustrates the light of reason confronting and dispersing the images in the vital chaos: “Strictamqu Aeneas aciem venientibus offert” [APP ¶165] (ours: Aeneas offers the drawn blade to those coming); Aeneas, the Golden Bough, Tartarus and Elysium are read as stages of the work [APP ¶166; APP ¶168; APP ¶171].

summary: The incombustible moisture in which, according to the Alchemists, the thick fire of life is imprisoned; unpurified, it is Hades.
body: A view of the Alchemists that Atwood endorses: the life is “a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture” [II.3 ¶29]. Unpurified, this moisture is Hades [II.3 ¶29].

summary: Named as Hippocrates' paternal ancestor, honoured with Hercules, a demigod among the Greeks and, for Atwood, modern Mesmerism's only just pride.
body: Atwood names him as Hippocrates' paternal ancestor, honoured together with Hercules, a demigod only among the Greeks, and the only just pride of modern Mesmerism [IV.3 ¶32; IV.3 ¶34; IV.3 ¶36].

summary: The imparted spirit whose reception gives wisdom by awakening a consciousness related to the universal.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the wisdom imparted by the reception of the Afflatus” [APP ¶41]; its reception awakens a consciousness related to the universal.

summary: The spirit, which vivifies and holds together the particles of the matter and is superior to the body in operation; paired with the patient.
body: Atwood calls the spirit “the agent, because it vivifies and holds the particles of the matter together” [I.3 n37], superior to the body in operation. Elsewhere she warns “lest the sin of the agent be multiplied in the patient” [IV.3 ¶56], where the agent is not further defined. See agent and patient.

summary: The active and receptive parties of the work, which act and react on one another progressively and, after Hermetic dissolution, are one identity.
body: Atwood: after Hermetic dissolution “the agent and the patient are one identity” [I.2 ¶48]. The work is progressive action and reaction between them: “The whole work is an action of agent on patient, and the reaction of patient, advancing, on agent.” [APP ¶111] (Appendix, Table Talk, later layer). The work may be protracted “by the indisposition of patients, as by the ignorance of agents” [IV.1 ¶17], terms not further defined there. Compare actives / passives.

summary: Cornelius Agrippa, Trithemius' pupil, author of the Occult Philosophy and the Vanity of the Sciences, cited by Atwood throughout as a witness to self-knowledge, secrecy and the inward Operator.
body:
Listed as Trithemius' pupil among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his three books of *Occult Philosophy* and his *Vanity of the Sciences* (De Vanitate Scientiarum) for the oath of secrecy and the singleness of the subject — “I could tell many tings of this art, if I had not sworn to keep silence” [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n70] — and argues that the *Vanity* is a consummation, not a recantation. From the *Vanity* she also takes the account of Alexander the Great's death by the venom of the waters of the Styx, paralleling Vaughan's [I.1 ¶74, I.1 n94]; knowledge by entering into oneself, with oblivion as impediment: “entering not either into the schools of other philosophers, but into yourself, ye shall know all things” [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n13]; and the praise of the 'asinine condition' of the disciple of Wisdom, which she applies to the Philosophic Subject: “There is no creature, concludes the panegyrist, that is so able to receive divinity as an ass” [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

From the *Occult Philosophy* (Book 3): the soul freed from the senses comprehends all; man is image of God and microcosm — “Whosoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself” [II.1 ¶9, II.1 n4]; and the pure mind laid asleep and brought into its divine nature, which Atwood endorses as alluding to Alchemy: “in us, I say, is the Operator of miracles” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n26]. She says the work expounds diffusely that imaginative impressions linger and pollute the ether of a place [III.4 ¶42].

Other uses: Scripture is no longer read “under the Bark of the Law” [III.3 ¶59]; Scripture is obscure and mystical yet significant (“Clausum est Armarium”) [IV.3 ¶46]; the two natures to be joined (“Pinge duos Angues”) [III.1 ¶50]; within Vaughan's lessons, a heavenly life as condition of communion with superiors [III.4 ¶44]; and his mature conviction that “to know Nothing was the most happy life” [IV.4 ¶27].

Atwood also qualifies him: he knew the First Preparation but not the Solution of the Salt, as his practice at Malines shows, and confessed he could not increase the transmutative virtue [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: Name a cited French source (Mystere de la Croix) gives to the work of repeated cooking until rainbow colours and heavy drops appear.
body: Quoted from the French source *Mystere de la Croix*: the work of repeated cooking, continued until the rainbow colours and heavy drops appear, is so named — “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶18]. The word renders as 'magnetic' (our translation; by: ours). The text here does not itself link it to Atwood's 'magnetic series' [III.3 ¶10].

summary: In Reuchlin, as quoted, the Hebrew name of the Absolute Essence while retracted in darkness and at rest — 'nothing as respects us'.
body: Quoted from Reuchlin: Ain names the Absolute Essence while it is retracted in darkness and at rest, and is glossed by the text itself as “Ain, i.e., to say, Nihil quoad nos; nothing or no entity as respects us” [III.2 ¶10]. It is called nothing not absolutely but relative to us, because “we, being affected with inability in the conception, do judge and imagine of those things which do not appear immediately as if they were not at all” [III.2 ¶10]. Asserted identity: Ain = Nihil quoad nos [III.2 ¶10].

summary: Figure invoked as an image of works that vanish before celestial light.
body: Invoked as an illustration: such works vanish before celestial light like “Aladdin’s rapid castle” [II.3 ¶36].

headword: Alain de l’Isle (Alani Philosophi; Alanai de Insulis)
summary: Alain de l’Isle, author of the Dicta de Lapide and a commentary on Merlin's Prophecies, said to have obtained the Elixir; cited as a case of editors suppressing alchemical testimony.
body: Atwood cites him (as Alani Philosophi, Alanai de Insulis) for his *Dicta de Lapide* and his commentary on the Prophecies of Merlin (*Prophetia Anglicana Merlini*, Francf. 1608). He is said to have obtained the Elixir, and serves as an example of editors suppressing alchemical testimony [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n53, I.1 n54].

summary: Albertus Magnus, a practising alchemist by Atwood's proofs, cited for the first matter, perfect solution as the first rule, the vessel, and man as seat of the highest mineral virtue.
body:
Atwood offers proof that Albert was a practising alchemist who described the first matter and commended alchemy as the best means of inquiry, and an example of renunciation of worldly advantage; she cites *De Mineralibus*, *Libellus de Alchemia*, *Concordanditia Philosophorum de Lapide*, *Secretum Secretorum* and the *Breve Compendium*: “De transmutatione horum corporum metallicorum et mutatione unius in aliud non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶41, I.1 n45, I.1 n46]. He is named with Lully as revering Geber [I.1 ¶32].

First matter: the mercury of the wise is “a watery element, cold and moist, a permanent water” [I.2 ¶29, I.2 n27]; he agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. From the book of Minerals: the highest mineral virtue is in man — “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all, burns more than all glorious in him erect” [II.1 ¶12]; and from *De Minerabilis*, all things may be reduced to gold: “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold, is found in the ultimate alchemical analysis of every existing thing” [III.2 n38].

Solution: “The beginning of the work, says Albertus Magnus, is a perfect solution” — dissolve and recongeal, fix and volatilize [II.3 n2]; “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution”, washing the occult Arcanum ('our brass') until pure [II.2 ¶16, II.2 n15]; “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass”, purified by successive dissolution and coagulation [IV.1 ¶4, IV.1 n2].

Vessel: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]; Norton's verse says “And this sheweth best Albertus Magnus, In his Boke De Mineralibus” on the right figure of vessels [III.4 ¶31].

In quoted verse: Ripley names “Albert, Raymond and Arnolde” as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62]; Norton names “Albertus Magnus, the Black Freere” as lacking understanding of multiplying the Red Stone [I.1 ¶60].

summary: Atwood's later definition: the throwing down of the walls of the harmony-ensphered life, accompanied with noise.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The throwing down of the Walls of this is harmony-ensphered life is the Alchemical solution” [APP ¶50]; it is accompanied with noise. Asserted identity: Alchemical solution = the throwing down of the Walls [APP ¶50].

summary: The Alchemist as agreeing with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, contrasted with modern Alchemists who are mostly silent on their Art's metaphysics.
body: Atwood says the Alchemist agrees with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, while modern Alchemists are mostly silent on the metaphysics of their Art [III.2 ¶46].

summary: The Alchemists as a collective voice Atwood draws on for the Matter, solution, the unclean Instrument, the threefold Law's periods, and the stirring of Motion.
body:
Atwood treats the Alchemists as a body of witness, generally supporting her reading:

- They recommend observing nature for analogy [I.3 n27].
- Their condemnation of the defiled vulgar Matter, and its preparation into the Mercury of the Philosophers, she links to the purification of the Spirit [II.2 ¶16]; their description of the subject — “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” — fits the Common Soul [II.2 ¶18]; their Matter is the Passive Nature: “the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].
- They supply the term dissolve for the trance change (“it ought to be dissolved”), and Black Saturn, the mineral tree, the doves [II.3 n2, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶18].
- Life is a fire imprisoned in aerial moisture (“Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi”); they warn of horrors and phantoms [II.3 ¶29].
- Their saying that there is “nothing of an unclean nature that enters into the composition of the Stone, except One thing” Atwood endorses, explaining at length that the unclean Instrument is necessary because the philosophers are obscure about it [III.1 ¶61].
- They name the three periods of the threefold Law: “called by the Alchemists, for certain accurate reason, Altitude, Latitude and Profundity” [III.3 ¶72].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): their Vulcan is decoded as Motion [APP ¶129]; and the older masters' “when Vulcan appears in the same altar with Minerva the conjunction is ominous” marks the point of passivity at which the Artist must stir up the Motion, which Atwood glosses as the stirred Wisdom-life being taken by self-will [APP ¶82].

summary: Joint witnesses asserting an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena.
body: Cited in support: the Alchemists and Greek physicians assert an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena [IV.4 ¶13].

summary: The Hermetic art: in Atwood's account an antique sacred science of vital chemistry, fermenting and purifying the human spirit by its own Light into regenerated life and relation with God.
body:
**The early account (main text).** Atwood calls it the Hermetic art, to be considered “an antique arifice coeval, for aught we know to the contrary, with the universe itself” [I.1 ¶3]; Egypt's Sacred Art, of which “This Emerald Table, unique and authentic as it may be regarded, is all that remains to us from Egypt of her Sacred Art” [I.1 ¶10], with its practical method in the *Tractatus Aureus*. She suggests it was “perhaps” stigmatized as a Black Art partly from the word Chemia [I.1 ¶5]. Now preserved in archives and despised, it is either “the acme of human folly, or contrariwise, as the recondite perfection of wisdom and causal science” [I.1 ¶76]; “the world has learned to despise alchemy, confounding the genuine doctrine with their sophistical and vile productions” [I.1 ¶53].

It concerns transmutation of metals: per Albert, “non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica”, and he “recommends alchemy as the best and most easy means of rational investigation” [I.1 ¶39]. It has nothing to do with modern chemistry: “No modern art or chemistry, notwithstanding all its surreptitious claims, has any thing in common to do with Alchemy, beyond the borrowed terms” [II.1 ¶5]; it requires the vital force, and philosophers sought it “not so much out of covetousness for gold or silver, but for the knowledge’s sake” [II.1 ¶10]. In it “the nature of things is altogether altered and ultimately reversed” and Final Causes are manifest [III.4 ¶9]. God grants it to few; its records hold the inner sense aloof from the literal, and “the Art will probably continue concealed though many ages still” [III.4 ¶16].

Norton (quoted) calls it “most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶52], holy because found only by grace: “Called this science Holy Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10]. Further verse in the same discussion affirms: “Yet is this science of Alkimy full trew;” [III.4 ¶14].

**Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).** Atwood defines it directly: “Alchemy is an universal art of vital chemistry” [APP ¶6] that ferments, purifies and dissolves the human spirit into new life; “Alchemy is a process of fermenting the vital Spirit in and by its own Light.” [APP ¶27]; “Alchemy is the art of fermenting the human vital spirit” to purify and finally dissolve it, so the principle is reconstructed through regeneration [APP ¶68]. “Alchemy goes beyond nature”, taking her up and advancing her beyond her created state [APP ¶155]. It brings man into relationship with God.

Asserted identities: = Divine Chemistry, “the transmutation of Life” [APP ¶25]; = Holy Alchemy, “called by the Adepts Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29]; = philosophy: “Alchemy is philosophy; it is the philosophy, the seeking of The Sophia in the mind.” [APP ¶183], fully understood only by those working the process.

summary: Emblem-maker whose dolphin wreathed about an anchor ('Festina Lente') Atwood applies to slow trituration.
body: Atwood applies Alciatus' emblem of a dolphin wreathed about an anchor, “Festina Lente”, to slow trituration [IV.1 ¶13].

summary: The vessel, in quoted authorities, through which the spiritualized gold passes and in which the Mercuries are cherished over fire.
body: Two quoted authorities name it. The author of *Lucerna Salis*: “by means of the spirit it passes through the Alembic, its earth remaining black” — said of the spiritualized gold [III.3 ¶32]. Flamel: “cherish them over a fire in thy Alembic”, of the Mercuries [IV.1 ¶41]. Neither passage gives a further gloss; any figurative sense would be inference.

summary: Recipient of Aristotle's avowal that only his pupils would understand the Acaomatic Ethics.
body: Named as the recipient of Aristotle's avowal that only his pupils would understand the Acaomatic Ethics [III.2 ¶40].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited, via the Open Entrance (which a bracketed correction attributes to Philalethes), for the persecution of true adepts.
body: Cited for the *Open Entrance* (*Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palationem*, cap. xiii) to illustrate the persecution of true adepts and the danger of even healing with the medicine: “a continual banishment: deprived of the society of friends and family” [I.1 ¶66, I.1 n73]. A bracketed correction in the text attributes the work to Philalethes.

summary: Group voice cited for the teaching that initiation to the Paternal abode opens all divine paths.
body: Cited in support: initiation to the Paternal abode opens all divine paths [II.4 ¶23].

summary: The Alexandrians, cited for their enthusiasm for the Mysteries and their account of the descent and efflux of matter.
body: Their enthusiasm for the Mysteries is cited as evidence of their high regard [II.2 ¶3]. They explained the descent and efflux of matter, as if knowing the universe by analogy through their own [III.2 ¶40].

summary: 'The Arabian', cited from the Centrum Naturae Concentratum for man as producer of the true fiery water.
body: Cited from *Centrum Naturae Concentratum* in support of man producing the true fiery water: “even thou art he who through the breath and power of the water and earth in thyself, conjoinest the elements” [II.1 ¶14, II.1 n12].

summary: Radical dissolvent of the metals, per Eudoxus a true permanent water staying united with what it dissolves; elsewhere named only among alchemists' goals.
body: Named without explanation in a quoted Faraday Society address listing alchemists' goals: “the philosophers’ stone, the transmutation of metals, the alkahest, and the elixir of life” [I.1 ¶33]. Eudoxus (quoted) gives its meaning: “the great Alcahest, which radically dissolves the metals -- a true permanent water” [IV.3 ¶10], remaining inseparably united with the metals it dissolves and increasing their weight and tincture. Asserted identity: Alcahest = true permanent water [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: What, per Atwood, he possesses who knows Nothing: composed of the whole, he can discern, make and effect the whole.
body: Atwood says he who knows Nothing has the All: “being composed of the whole, he is able to discern, to make, and to effect the whole” [IV.4 ¶27].

summary: Collective witness that knowledge of the Magistery comes rather by Inspiration of Heaven.
body: Cited in support that knowledge of the Magistery comes rather by Inspiration of Heaven: “This truth is acknowledged by all artists” [IV.3 ¶16].

summary: The philosophers just cited, whose combined evidence Atwood says yields the definition of the stone as purified Ethereality.
body: Atwood draws from their combined evidence the definition of the stone as purified Ethereality [I.2 ¶44].

summary: Part of a seven-letter riddle quoted from Hermes, followed by Yda and Liber; not explained.
body: Quoted from Hermes as part of the seven-letter riddle: “for Alpha follows, viz.: Yda and Liber” [I.3 ¶37]. The text gives no explanation here.

summary: Cited for calling the matter a stone.
body: Cited in support of calling the matter a stone: “Si lapis proprium nomen haberet lapis esset nomen ejus” [I.3 n13] (ours: 'If the stone had a proper name, stone would be its name').

equivalences.with: the objective Light, the ether that is above

summary: First of the alchemists' three periods of the threefold Law: the objective Light, the ether above.
body: Atwood names Altitude, with Latitude and Profundity, as the Alchemists' three periods of the threefold Law, and states: “the Altitude is the objective Light, the ether that is above” [III.3 ¶72]. Asserted identity: Altitude = the objective Light, the ether that is above [III.3 ¶72].

summary: Ambrose and Phillip Muller, German writers listed among persecuted adepts.
body: Listed among persecuted adepts and among the German writers, with works cited as *Philippi Mulleri Miracula et Mysteria Medico-Chemica* and Amb. Muller's *Paradeis-Spiegel* [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70, I.1 n78].

summary: Teacher who, Atwood relates, admitted an ass daily to his lectures alongside Origen and Porphyry.
body: Cited as illustration: he admitted an ass daily to his lectures, alongside Origen and Porphyry [III.2 ¶64].

summary: In a quoted Platonic Successor, the impulse toward the First, which the passions impede.
body: Quoted from the Platonic Successor: “the passions alone, which impede our anagogic impulse to the First” [II.4 ¶41]. The text gives no further gloss.

summary: Augustine's third mode of vision, as Atwood reports it: drawn above, beholding intelligible species by pure infusion of light into the understanding.
body: Atwood reports Augustine's third mode of vision: “the third is anagogic, and an intellectual sight, drawn above, by which intelligible species are beheld” [II.4 ¶15]. It is a pure infusion of light into the understanding and occurs in Elysium. Asserted identity: anagogic = intellectual sight [II.4 ¶15].

summary: Called by Atwood one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School; cited for Intellect as separating principle, the ignited Stone as inner Sun, and as an alchemist.
body:
Atwood calls him 'one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School' and cites his lost works as preserved by Simplicius (via Taylor's note to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*) for Intellect's efficient, separating operation: “Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing” [III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶22, III.1 n27]. What he describes as past, internal philosophers describe as present; his “it begins from that which is small to exercise its comprehending power” she applies to starting with a small portion [III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶32]. He “calls it Intellect”, naming the One Thing in consciousness [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶35]; matter is the progeny of mind [III.2 ¶40].

His 'ignited Stone' Atwood identifies with the inner Sun, saying he was discredited through the error that he meant the visible sun [II.3 ¶54]; he identifies the central earth with the Salt of Saturn (“hands loftily”) [II.3 ¶41].

Celebrated as an alchemist, author of the *boke of Conversions Naturall*, praised by Norton as the plainest writer; his metaphysics agrees with Aristotle's [I.1 ¶14, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16]. Within the Ordinal he is cited for “Nemo prima fronte reperitur discretus” [IV.1 ¶26].

headword: ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature
forms: ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature
summary: An unnamed ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature, cited through Khunrath on the divine water.
body: Khunrath cites this author of the *Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature* on the divine water [I.1 ¶20]. The text gives nothing further about the author.

summary: Atwood's name for the experiment of nature that the Inquiry sets out to recover in its causal light.
body: Atwood states the aim of her Inquiry as an attempt to “recover the Ancient Experiment of nature into her Causal Light” [III.4 ¶2]. The record does not define the term any further. The context suggests it names the practical work the book reconstructs, but the text does not say so here.

summary: A group voice that, Atwood says, agrees with the metaphysician by proving the Universal Identity of Nature through experiment.
body: Atwood says the ancient physiologists and alchemists agree with the metaphysician because they prove the Universal Identity of Nature by experiment [II.4 ¶16]. She cites them as support.

summary: A group voice cited as having condemned both inner and material idolatry.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), the ancient prophets are cited as having condemned both inner and material idolatry [APP ¶100].

summary: A group voice whose meaning of metempsychosis Atwood sets against the common, mistaken meaning.
body: Atwood contrasts the meaning the Ancient Schools of Divinity gave to metempsychosis with the common one, which she treats as mistaken [IV.2 ¶18]. She sides with the ancient schools.

summary: Atwood's most frequent group authority, cited throughout as support for the reality, experimental basis and discipline of the Hermetic wisdom and the Mysteries.
body:
Atwood cites “the ancients” almost always as support for her own positions:

- **Reality and experience.** They assert higher realities known through both intellect and experiment [I.2 ¶49]. For them the truth is the same experience in everyone, “one and the same in all, where difference is merged in objective union” [II.2 ¶13]. They held that the worst evil is not seeing one's own evil, and they gave warnings about how the Spirit is to be handled [II.2 ¶14].
- **Preparing the mind.** They warn against passive dreaming in the phantasy. Before contemplation, they require the mind to be cleared and made passive [II.2 ¶22]. They insisted on ways of removing the barriers to the Divine Light. Their Wisdom was gained by discipline, and it goes beyond reason without contradicting it [IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶17].
- **Life and Being.** They held this life to be a lessening of existence [III.2 ¶50]. The “wise ancients” compared a state of Being that verges on annihilation to darkness for the eye [III.2 ¶54].
- **Figures of the union.** Atwood reads the pairs Peleus and Thetis, Earth and Heaven, Bacchus and Ariadne, and Jason and Medea as their prefigurations of the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the marriage, by the ancients so many times prefigured” [III.3 ¶15].
- **The Mysteries.** They are her authority for treating the Mysteries as real inductions. They found their whole philosophy in the vital experiment, and she weighs their philosophy against Physical science [IV.4 ¶5, IV.4 ¶9, IV.4 ¶13].

summary: A name in the book's list of authors, given with the work Opera Omnia Medica.
body: Libavius appears in a list of authors, and footnote n85 gives his *Opera Omnia Medica* [I.1 ¶70, I.1 n85]. The note calls it “A ponderous compilation.” [I.1 n85]. The record says nothing more about how Atwood uses him.

summary: In a quoted adept's words, the subtle spirit conceived when the quintessential nature is opened. It holds the divine act and is a direct beam of Wisdom from God.
body: This is the language of a quoted adept, not Atwood's own words. When the quintessential nature is opened, what is conceived is “the subtle altereity of the angelical spirit in which is the divine act, and immediate beam or Wisdom from God” [II.3 ¶52]. The record gives no plainer meaning.

summary: A treatise cited in a footnote as the source of the Latin sequence of illumination in a philosopher's passage.
body: Footnote n27 cites *Anima Magia Abscond.*, p. 27, as the source of the Latin sequence of illumination in the philosopher's passage, which includes “Eritque in te cum Lumine, Ignis” [IV.2 ¶41, IV.2 n27]. (Our translation: And there shall be in you, with the Light, Fire.)

summary: Atwood's term for the middle soul or center of man or of nature, which she identifies with the medial center.
body: This entry comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer). There Atwood speaks of “the medial center, the anima media”: the middle soul or center of man or of nature [APP ¶147]. According to the record, this center can only be obtained together with its law, which is an impulse toward rectification and regeneration. **Identity:** = medial center [APP ¶147].

summary: The Ethnics' doctrine of the Anima Mundi, which Atwood says differs from Hebrew doctrine only in words.
body: Atwood treats the Ethnics' and Hebrew teachings as one in substance: “the assertions of the Ethnics, about the Anima Mundi, differ very little or nothing in substance from the Hebrew doctrine, but in words only” [I.2 ¶14]. The record does not define the term further.

summary: Atwood's term for the modern discovery that produces Trance and healing effects. She treats it as one name among several for an unknown agency.
body: Atwood presents Animal Magnetism as a modern discovery that produces Trance and healing effects. She treats the name as a provisional label: “Animal Magnetism, or Mesmerism, or Vital Magnetism, or by whatever other term the unknown agency is better expressed” [II.2 ¶6]. **Identities:** = Mesmerism; = Vital Magnetism [II.2 ¶6].

summary: In Eudoxus's account, the Mercury obtained once the King's bath is prepared with the blood of the Innocents. It never loses its virtue if kept well sealed.
body: Eudoxus is the speaker, quoted by Atwood. Once the King's bath has been prepared with the blood of the Innocents, “you will have the animated Mercury of the wise, which never loses its virtue” as long as it is kept in a well-closed vessel [IV.3 ¶10]. The record does not give a plain meaning for these figures.

summary: Named in the Appendix as being Venus and Lune.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Anne Bronte is said to be Venus and Lune [APP ¶175]. The record gives no further context, and it is unclear who is speaking.

summary: The state into which the artist brings all by pressing out the waters of nature's extreme life, after which nature reacts.
body: In Atwood's account, the artist presses out “the waters of her extreme life”, and nature reacts “when the wise artist has brought all into this annihilate condition” [I.2 ¶36]. Apparently this is a stage of the work in which the subject is reduced to the extreme before it revives. The text gives the sequence but no fuller definition.

summary: Atwood's term for the end of Wisdom, a so-called annihilation that leads back into the Nothing that is before all things.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood places the end of Wisdom in “that so-called annihilation bringing back into the Nothing which is before all things” [APP ¶90]. Her “so-called” suggests that she is not using the word in its ordinary sense of destruction.

headword: the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus
forms: the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus
summary: The unnamed author of the Tractatus Aureus, cited as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), this author of the *Tractatus Aureus* (Museum Hermeticum, edit. 1649, p. 45) is cited with approval as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden [APP ¶100].

summary: An unnamed authority quoted as showing the same matter to be the source of blessed waters.
body: An unnamed authority is quoted on the same matter as the source of blessed waters: “Ex mari meo oriuntur nebulae” [II.3 ¶18]. (Our translation: From my sea the mists arise.)

summary: In Aristotle's view as Atwood reports it, the cause that the human Understanding is brought into contact with through mystical exercises and preparations.
body: This is Aristotle's view as Atwood reports it. Through mystical exercises and preparations, “the human Understanding Medium is made to pass into contact with its Antecedent Cause” [II.1 ¶37]. The record does not define the term further.

summary: Atwood's term for the life that comes before outward experience and underlies it. Experience could reveal it if perception were turned inward and the obstacles removed.
body: Atwood argues that if the outward-looking faculty were turned inward and its obstacles removed, “experience might then reveal to us the antecedent life” [II.2 ¶21]. This makes the inward turning of perception a condition of the method. According to the record, the antecedent life is the life prior to and underlying outward experience.

summary: Cited for reference only.
The Alchemists' Antimonial Spirit, rectified by Art and balanced between attraction and repulsion. It alone withstands life's drift toward dissolution.
body: This is the Alchemists' term, cited via Bohme. Their “Antimonial Spirit rectified by Art” [II.1 ¶20] is described as balanced between attraction and repulsion. It is the only thing that resists life's drift toward dissolution.

summary: The adepts' name for the matter of the tincture and for the fire of life. It is not the ordinary mineral, and Basil Valentine calls its preparation the key of Alchemy.
body:
Antimony appears only in quoted voices, mostly Basil Valentine's. Atwood adds a gloss of her own.

- **Not the common substance.** For the adept and Basil Valentine, Antimony names the matter of the tincture. The “oil of this antimony” is “not made of crude melted antimony, such as the apothecaries and merchants sell”, but is drawn from “the true mineral” [II.1 ¶25].
- **Fire of life.** The Paracelsians speak of “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts” [III.1 ¶10]. **Identity:** = fire of life.
- **Key of Alchemy.** Basil Valentine says “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”. It is matured with the corporeal fire of the microcosm [III.1 ¶37]. **Identity:** = stone of Fire: “our stone of Fire (which is Antimony)” [III.1 ¶37].
- **Fixed medicine.** “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases and eradicates them”, but only after all its venomous impurity has been removed [IV.1 ¶40]. Atwood explains this removal as the purging of self-will and other vices from the operator's mind. This reading is hers, and it ties the substance to the operator's own purification.

summary: Named by Atwood among the dark presences at the conjunction. The text does not define it.
body: Atwood names it among the dark presences at the conjunction: “Night, Saturn and the Antimony of the Wise will be present” [III.3 ¶13]. The record does not define it. Compare Antimony.

summary: Cited as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall.
body: Atwood names Antiquity as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall [IV.1 ¶4].

summary: Atwood's name for the cave-like place of descent, which she reads as the heavy, inelastic nether air bordering on the chaos of matter.
body: Atwood describes this place of descent as having air “destitute of elasticity, Aornus, heavy like that of an enclosed cave, and vast” [II.3 ¶18]. She reads it as the heavy lower air bordering on the chaos of matter. The text supports only this physical description. Any further role in the work would be inference.

summary: Invoked by Atwood to show how deeply the truth is hidden: enough to puzzle even Apollo.
body: Atwood says the truth is so wrapped up that it “might puzzle Apollo himself to explicate the whole Enigma” [IV.4 ¶2]. She uses Apollo only as a figure of speech.

summary: Quoted through Vaughan on the Brahmans, whose way of dwelling illustrates the philosophers' habitation.
body: Atwood quotes Apollonius through Vaughan: “I have seen, says Apollonius, the Brahmans of India dwelling on the earth and not on the earth” [II.4 ¶11]. She uses this as an illustration of the philosophers' habitation.

summary: Cited in footnotes, in the Argonautics and Fawkes's translation, as a parallel to the terror caused by Achilles' armour.
body: Two footnotes cite Apollonius Rhodius (Argonaut., Lib. 2; Fawkes’ Apollonius Rhodius Argonautics, Book 1) as a reference or parallel for the terror caused by Achilles' armour: “So the gloomy god/Stood mute with fearto see the golden rode” [III.1 n32, III.1 n35].

summary: The Apostle's scriptural words, which Atwood cites repeatedly to support the nearness of being, transformation, resurrection and the spiritual purification of the operator.
body:
Atwood cites the Apostle as scriptural support, always with approval:

- **Nearness of being** (Act 17:27, 28): “He is not far off from every one of us; for in Him we live, and move, and have our being” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n24].
- **Light to light.** His “and from glory to glory” supports Agrippa's “light to light” [II.4 ¶19].
- **Resurrection** (1 Corinthians 15). This answers how what is destroyed can increase. It covers the law of resurrection, the natural body followed by the spiritual body, and leaven: “that which is sown is not the body that shall be, but mere grain” [III.3 ¶23, III.3 n13, III.3 ¶24, III.3 n17].
- **The veil lifted.** When one turns to the Lord or the Spirit, the veil over the reading of Moses is lifted, “the veil shall be taken away”, and those who behold are transformed [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n38].
- **Spiritual warfare** (2 Corinth. 10:4, 5). The purification of the operator is spiritual, not carnal: “the weapons of this warfare are not carnal, as the Apostle teaches” [IV.1 ¶40, IV.1 n33].
- **Trial by Fire** (1 Corinth. 3:11-17). The one foundation, man as the Temple of God, and “the Fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is” are tied to Atwood's call to press on to Divine Perfection [IV.1 ¶46, IV.1 n41].

summary: Atwood's term for the final stage of the church's mysteries, which was kept most secret.
body: Atwood mentions the church's mysteries, “especially those that relate to the final apotheosis”, as the part kept most secret [II.2 ¶5]. The record does not explain it further.

summary: Author whose accounts of initiation into the mysteries of Isis Atwood uses repeatedly to illustrate the inner light, the goddess (Universal Nature) and the soul's liberation.
body:
Atwood cites Apuleius chiefly as a witness of initiation. From *On the God of Socrates* she takes the inner light experienced when separated from the body: “this knowledge sometimes shines forth with a most rapid coruscation like a bright and clear light in the most profound darkness” [II.3 ¶50, II.3 n54]; his 'midnight Sun' she identifies with the ignited Stone [II.3 ¶54]. The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) likewise uses the midnight sun seen when initiated by Isis to illustrate the coruscation of released light [APP ¶126].

From the *Metamorphoses*, book 11, she draws: the bough connected with the Mercurial caduceus in the procession of Isis initiates [II.3 ¶11, II.3 n6]; the appearance of the goddess (Isis/nature) in the Eleusian Fane and her mandates to the initiate — “Moved by thy prayers, O Lucius! Behold, I am come!” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶17, II.4 n9]; Lucius' praise of the goddess, which Atwood applies to the Universal Nature — “Thou rollest the heavens round the steady poles, dost illuminate the sun, govern the world, and tread on the dark realms of Tartarus.” [II.4 ¶18, II.4 n10]; and Lucius' rosy crown and shedding of the beast's hide as images of the soul's liberation [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n11].

He is listed with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Julian among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27]; he is called to witness by Agrippa [II.1 ¶26]; and Reuchlin's passage cites him to excuse an obscure phrase: “you must pardon, as Apuleius says, the strange expression” [III.2 ¶24]. In I.1 ¶11 he appears as the hypothetical forger of the prophecy, a theory Atwood rejects.

summary: Author of the Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass, cited for being turned into an ass before admission to the mysteries of Isis.
body: Atwood cites the *Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass* of Apuleius of Megara to illustrate that he was turned into an ass before his admission to the mysteries of Isis [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

summary: Treatise in the Mus. Herm. cited for verses on the regeneration (union, dissolution, reunion of spirit, soul and body) and for the triune universal essence.
body:
Atwood quotes translated verses from the *Aquarium Sapientum* (in Mus. Herm., 'The Enigma'): spirit, soul and body in one seat, then dissolution, then reunion in the last heat — “The Spirit is given to the body for a time,” [III.1 ¶51, III.1 ¶52, III.1 n57]. She endorses this as 'the constant doctrine and rule of the regeneration'.

Under the spelling *Aquarium Sepientum* (Mus. Herm., p. 112) it is cited after the birth of Horus to illustrate the triune and fivefold divine-human essence: “Triuna universalis essentia, quae Jehovah appellatur” [IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 n3].

summary: Apparently a region that consciousness must pass through, clear and rational, before entering the Fire World; the text does not define it further.
body: Atwood speaks of consciousness passing “clear and rational from out the Aquaster, enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]; a quoted adept likewise speaks of “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41]. The context suggests a middle region traversed before the Fire World, but the text gives no definition.

summary: Confessed adept whose alchemical treatises Atwood cites for transmutation, deliberate obscurity, secrecy and the sufficiency of Mercury, while criticizing his 'false panegyrists'.
body:
Atwood cites Aquinas (Thesaurus Alchimiae, addressed to brother Reinaldo; Meteorum, lib. iv; De Esse et Essentia; Secreta Alchimiae) as a confessed adept affirming transmutation — “Metalla transmutari possunt unum in aliud” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 n49] — and for his deliberate obscurity and warnings to keep the secret from worldly seekers, which she takes to point to the art's higher theosophical purpose [I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶42, I.1 n50, I.1 n51]. She criticizes his 'false panegyrists'.

From the *Roasrium Abbrev.* (Tract. iii and v) she takes the doctrine that Mercury alone suffices, being the root of gold and silver and working itself: “It is Mercury alone which perfects in our work” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n13].

summary: An Arabian authority (given in the Rosarium as Aristotele Arabus) cited on the Stone: nothing is added, separation only removes superfluities.
body: Via the *Rosarium* (Aristotele Arabus), 'the Arabian' supports the claim that nothing is added in the work: “to which we add nothing different or extract, only in the separation removing superfluities” [I.2 ¶43, I.2 n42]. His 'subtle phrase' on the Stone known and proven is also cited: “Sumatur lais in capitulis notus” [III.2 ¶7].

summary: Apparently a place or vessel in which the two serpents, tied in a love knot, are shut up; the text does not explain it.
body: In a passage from Cornelius Agrippa's 'ingenious disciple', the two serpents are to be bound and enclosed: “tie them in a love knot and shut them up in the Arabian Caraha” [III.1 ¶50]. The context suggests a vessel or enclosure, but the text gives no explanation.

summary: In Vaughan's account, the philosophers' medicine reduced by bodily fermentation to a portable dust.
body: Quoting Vaughan, Atwood records that the philosophers reduced their medicine by bodily fermentation to a dust: “they reduced their medicine to a dust, and this dust is the Arabian Elixir” [IV.3 ¶22] — so the Arabian Elixir = this dust. Unlike the medicine itself it was portable: “This Elixir the philosophers could carry about them” [IV.3 ¶22].

summary: Cited to characterize the 'entertaining' style of the Christian philosophers' promises.
body: Atwood invokes the *Arabian Nights* to illustrate the 'entertaining' style of the Christian philosophers' promises [II.3 ¶34].

summary: Group voice cited for a name of the Matter: Flower of White Salt.
body: The Arabians are cited for a name of the Matter: “Flos Salis Albi” (Flower of White Salt) [III.2 ¶8].

summary: Cited within a Vaughan passage to show that the work does not occupy the operator's attention.
body: In a passage from Vaughan, the *Arcadia* illustrates that the work does not occupy the attention: “a lady may read the Arcadia” [III.4 ¶38].

summary: The secret of the work: the 'great Arcanum' possessed when the tincture rises from the black, identified by Albertus with 'our brass', and wholly revealed to Eirenaeus.
body:
The term appears mostly in quoted voices. A 'more modern experimentalist' says that when the masculine tincture rises from the black “he will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53]. Albertus (spelled 'Mangus') identifies the 'occult Arcanum' with 'our brass', to be washed until pure: “Take, says Albertus Mangus, the occult Arcanum, which is our brass, and wash it that it may be pure and clean” [II.2 ¶16]. Urbigeranus and other Adepts make the Theory of their Arcanum the medium by which the Royal Diadem is extracted; without it dissolution is impossible: “it will be entirely impossible to accomplish without the Theory of their Arcanum” [IV.1 ¶7].

Atwood herself uses it for the whole secret of the work, revealed to Eirenaeus in two and a half years: “the whole Arcanum was revealed to him” [IV.1 ¶17]. In the plural, Eirenaeus speaks of the Chaos “in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43] — the secrets present potentially, not yet actually.

summary: Work supplying the epigraph of IV.1, setting the theme that the arts are bought by labor.
body: The chapter epigraph of IV.1 comes from *Arcanum Ignis Aquae* (Resp. 6): “Dii sudoribus vendunt Artes” [IV.1 ¶1] — the gods sell the arts for sweat (translation ours), setting the theme of labor.

summary: Work cited for a Latin statement on transmuting the salt of blood by urinous ferment.
body: Atwood cites the *Arcanum Liquaris Alkahest* (Resp. 876, 78) in Latin on transmuting the salt of blood: “sanquinis salem per urinaceum fermentum sic transmutari debere” [II.1 ¶21, II.1 n18] — that the salt of blood ought thus to be transmuted by a urinous ferment (translation ours).

summary: Paracelsus' term, which Atwood sets beside the solar plexus as the workshop of the Celestial life, in which the Light lies hidden until drawn out.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the term in apposition to the solar plexus: “the solar plexus, the Archaeus of Paracelsus, is its workshop” [APP ¶32] — the workshop of the Celestial life; so Archaeus = solar plexus there. In the main text she speaks of “the Light, so long hidden and enshrined in the Archaeus” [III.3 ¶71], drawn out by artificial heat and exhalation. Van Helmont, quoted, gives the Archaeus a 'sky' in which ideas from the soul's starry heaven and the spirit of the seven bowels are read: “For in the sky of our Archaeus, aspectual Ideas are deciphered” [III.2 ¶17]. The text does not define the term further.

summary: The order in which all things are causally ranged as originally distributed, seen 'as in a glass' by one who has the Principle.
body: Atwood speaks of “the great Archetypal Law of Light, in which are all things causally ranged” [III.3 ¶39]: the order of things as originally distributed, which the one who possesses the Principle beholds 'as in a glass'. See also Archetype, whose creative mind orders all things by this Law.

summary: The original Light before which the understanding stands to perfect its new-born attributes; perceived, it burns up prior images and is identified with Truth.
body: In the main text, Atwood describes “the understanding vehicle now standing in open presence before its Archetypal Light” [II.4 ¶16], by which it perfects its new-born attributes. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says that this light, once perceived, burns up all prior images, perceives itself alone, “transmuting all that is not combustible into itself” [APP ¶106]; it is both objective and subjective and is identified with Truth: “for it is objective and subjective both; it is Truth” [APP ¶106].

equivalences.with: occult essence of the Intellectual Law

summary: The hidden essence of the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason is only an embryo image.
body: Atwood speaks of “that Archetypal Wisdom which the ancients celebrated as the occult essence of that Law” [II.1 ¶35] — the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason gives only an embryo image. Archetypal Wisdom = the occult essence of the Intellectual Law.

summary: The original of which the self and natural things are images; the creative mind ordering all things causally and the end of the soul's progression.
body:
For Atwood the Archetype is the original of which the self is an image and the end of the soul's progression; it is the creative mind whose Law of Light orders all things causally, “where the Archetype shadows the intellectual spheres” [III.3 ¶39], and in which things are “that which is in the Archetypal mind creatively efficient” [III.3 n27]. In the plural, the Archetypes are the originals of things beheld in nature, which do not truly resemble them: “If indeed things beheld in nature were such as the Archetypes, whence they are derived” [III.2 ¶61]; one established in Intellect is “able through it, as an image, to behold the Archetype” [III.2 ¶66].

In Hermes' account, Poemander asks: “hast thou seen that Archetypal Form, which was before the interminated and infinite beginning?” [III.3 ¶56] — the pattern in which God's Will and Counsel beheld the beautiful world and which it imitated in making this world.

summary: Pythagorean whose fragments Atwood cites on Wisdom as contemplation of first Principles and on right method of investigation as the key to discovery.
body: From a fragment given by Taylor in his Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagorus, Archytas supports Atwood's account of Wisdom, which contemplates the whole and discovers the Principles of Being, leading to a vision of Divinity: “he will have conjoined ends with beginnings” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n34]. He also supports her stress on method — mankind has not known how to investigate: “If you investigate rightly, says Archytas, discovery will be easy for you” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 ¶53].

equivalences.with: aqua alterius naturae (water of another nature)

summary: The philosophic Mercury, the subject of the Art: a water of another nature, a stone and no stone, gold essential but unripe, cleansed and coagulated by its own sulfur.
body:
The term comes almost entirely in quoted voices. Lully calls it a water of another nature: “argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18]; in it the conversion of natures is carried out: “the method of conversion in our Argent vive is the reduction of natures to their first root” [I.2 ¶25]. Arnold: “it is a stone and no stone, in which the whole Art consists, spirit, soul and body” [I.2 ¶29] — volatile, clear, One Thing.

It is identified with the philosophic Mercury (Hermes and the Scholiast): “for that is Mercury which is spoken of concerning the residual earth” [I.3 ¶9]; “this argent vive, then, which is the residuum of the philosophic earth after the separation” [I.3 n9]. Hermes requires two to be mortified together — “it behooves us to mortify two Argent vives together” [I.3 ¶32]; “the Argent vive of Auripigment and the Oriental Argent vive of magnesia” [III.1 ¶43] — not further explained. Eirenaeus: “For Argent Vive is gold essential Only unripe” [III.1 ¶69], which prepared by art gives the secret menstrual.

The Adept, with Atwood, describes its course: “this Argent vive was at first gross, unclean, fugitive, being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” [IV.1 ¶10]; cleansed by Art and coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white, it becomes subtle and penetrative, resolving mineral bodies; “this Argent vive, which is decocted linearly, is generated pontically” [IV.1 ¶11]. In Geber's definition it is the volatile: “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]. In Eirenaeus' projection verse, “Then upon Argent vive cast this with care.” [IV.3 ¶25] — apparently in the place of the 'mercury purged and purified' of ¶20, though the text does not state this. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” [IV.2 ¶35], unexplained.

summary: Classical allusion used to say the philosophic vessels 'speak for themselves'.
body: Atwood illustrates that the philosophic vessels speak for themselves: they, “like the planks of Argo, on occasion, are still oracular” [III.4 ¶32].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Author whose chorus of the Initiated Atwood cites for the privileged light of those who perform acts of piety and justice.
body: From *In Ramis*, Act 1, Atwood cites the chorus to illustrate the privileged light of the initiated, who perform acts of piety and justice: “The sun shines but for us, exclaims the chorus of the Initiated in Aristophanes” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 n7].

summary: Authority (the Stagyrite) cited widely on Wisdom, Intellect, Matter and reduction of metals; Atwood qualifies charges of envy against him but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.
body:
Norton and the adepts criticize Aristotle for envy and veiling; Atwood qualifies this, cites his works (epistles to Alexander on the Philosophers' stone, Secreta Secretorum, book of Meteors) as evidence of hidden knowledge, yet declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher without more evidence [I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, I.1 n22]. Through Ripley's verse the *Book of Meteors* concurs that metals are not transmutable unless reduced to their beginning [I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶6, I.2 n6]; he is cited (n38) for metals reducible to water [III.2 n38].

On Wisdom and Intellect: Wisdom is the highest science, drawn from what is universal in oneself [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n30], the true being of Intellect, small in bulk but surpassing in energy [II.1 n31]; mystical exercises bring the understanding into contact with its cause, and intellect is identical with the intelligible — “True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n32; cf. II.1 ¶44]. He compares Universals to colors needing the sun and calls human reason 'intellect in capacity' [II.1 ¶34]; his 'passive intellect' names the Mundane Spirit first revealed in humanity [II.2 ¶17]; “That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified” [III.1 ¶23, III.1 n30]. The self-perceiving final object “is good, according to the words of the Stagyrite, and the end of spiritual generation” [IV.2 ¶8].

On Matter, 'the logician': “I mean, he says, by Matter, that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity” [III.2 ¶53, III.2 n42]. His triple distinction of heaven [III.2 ¶33, III.2 n32] and his 'perfect world', read as the ethereal [III.2 ¶38]; his abstruse diction illustrates concealment; his criticisms of predecessors — “Parmenides appears to have touched upon the One according to Reason; but Melissus, according to Matter” [III.2 ¶38] — are said to aim at the letter, not the spirit, though he is also blamed for making away with his brethren 'after the manner of the Ottomans' [III.2 ¶36]; his logic is praised in its original intent, later degraded [III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶41, III.2 ¶42, III.2 n37]. From the Ethics: “Ab actionibus procedit speculatio” [IV.1 ¶18]; one deliberates about means, not ends, analyzing back to the first Cause as in a diagram [IV.1 ¶30, IV.1 n25]. 'The Aristotle' is cited for the change of the corruptible into incorruption: “Behold I show you a mystery, says the Aristotle, we shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed” [III.3 ¶27, III.3 n18].

summary: Ancient rites which, Atwood says, refer to the physical secret of regeneration, the god dead and revived being principal in them.
body: Atwood states that “the Arkite Mysteries have reference to the physical secret of the regeneration” [III.3 ¶69]; the god dead and revived is principal in them.

summary: Cited as rites referring to the physical secret of regeneration.
body: Cited by Atwood in support of the claim that these mysteries refer to the physical secret of regeneration [III.3 ¶69]. See the term entry Arkite Mysteries.

summary: Something rectified by Power and Motive 'by an infallible rule'; the text does not explain it.
body: Atwood speaks of Power and Motive that “rectifies the Armed Magnet by an infallible rule” [IV.1 ¶33]. The expression is not explained.

summary: Mystic named in the Appendix as the one who recognizes the depth of the Psalms.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Arndt is named as the one Mystic who recognizes the depth of the Psalms [APP ¶97].

summary: Confessed adept whose Speculum and Rosarium Atwood cites constantly: reduction to first root, the matter as stone and no stone, dissolution of the Stone in its own mercury.
body:
Atwood ranks Arnold di Villa Nova as a confessed adept whose skill, including projections with transmuting powder, is attested by contemporaries [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶43]; he possibly convinced Lully by exhibiting transmutation [I.1 ¶48], though Lully did not receive the mystery from him [IV.1 ¶36]. His *Speculum* gives the basis of the whole theory: “there abides in nature a certain pure matter” [I.2 ¶2]; species are indestructible — “Species non transmutari sed individual specierum” [I.2 ¶5, I.2 n3, I.2 n4] — so the subject must be freed by artificial reduction.

His precept “Converte elementa et quod quaeris invenies” [I.2 ¶22] means reduction of natures to their first root [I.2 ¶25]; Atwood glosses “Convert the elements, says Arnold, and you shall have what you desire” as separating and rejoining in harmonious proportion [I.3 n23]. The matter is a stone and no stone: “Ii is a stone and no stone, spirit, soul, and body” [I.3 n5, I.3 n13, I.3 n17], following whatever is done to it [cf. I.2 ¶29, I.2 n30]. From the *Rosarium*: “The work of philosophers, says Arnold, is to dissolve the Stone in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7, IV.1 n6], to first Matter; the operator needs “three requisites, viz., subtlety of mind, manual skill, and a free will for the operation” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n19].

With Hermes he witnesses that the art must be entrusted by one to another [II.1 ¶25]; verse (versifier not named) cites the Rosary of 'Arnolde of the New Towne' for the claim that none can operate alone: “There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging.” [I.3 n17]. He is also cited for the same testimony [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n100], as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25], with Albert and Raymond in Ripley's verse as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62], with Lully and Artephius as agreeing with the Lucerna Salis on whitening [III.2 ¶5], and within the Ordinal, where the Art belongs to great men so poor men should beware, and the operator should be patient and gentle: “Esto longanimus et suavis” [IV.1 ¶12].

summary: The addressee's term for what Nature wraps herself in to realize her imaginings (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the term as the addressee's own ('what you call'): “She wraps herself about with what you call aromal essences, aromal emanations” [APP ¶122] — Nature clothing herself to realize her imaginings.

summary: In Norton's Ordinal, handicraft, the work of the hands, called Art mechanical; what the Gross Work consists of.
body: A term from Norton's Ordinal, quoted by Atwood: handicraft, “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]. The record says the Gross Work consists of this handicraft. It is equated there with handie crafte.

summary: The Art Atwood calls holy above all arts for aiding devout minds; a remedy of imperfect souls offering means of assimilation, though not itself the cause of salvation.
body: Atwood writes that “The Art of Alchemy is of all Arts distinguished as holt” [IV.4 ¶25] (the spelling is the book's), because it aids devout minds. She adds that “the Art is said to be a remedy of imperfect souls, and offers the means of assimilation” [IV.4 ¶25]. She also holds that the Art is not itself the cause of salvation [IV.4 ¶25].

summary: The ultimate Art, which Atwood says she will not fully expose and which is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.
body: Atwood speaks of discovering, “by a theoretic conduct, the ultimate Art of Life” [IV.2 ¶3]. She does not fully expose this Art; it is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.

summary: A concealed practical art which, with the vessel, the ancients are said to have hidden; Atwood names it without explaining it.
body: Atwood mentions “the concealed vessel or art of vital administration” [II.1 ¶8] among the things the ancients hid. The text does not explain it here; the “or” may present the vessel and the art as alternative names for one concealed thing, or as two things named together; the text does not decide.

summary: The art said by unnamed others to have been first practised in Egypt by Cham, from whom some derive both the name and the art of alchemy.
body: Reporting what others say (not her own claim), Atwood records that in Egypt “it was there that the art of Vulcan was first practiced by Cham, one of the sons of the Patriarch” [I.1 ¶5]; some derive both the name and the art of alchemy from Cham.

summary: Atwood's name for the Art as long called holy, with nothing impure or impious in it.
body: Atwood writes: “These is nothing impure, or of itself impious, in this Art of Wisdom, long distinguished as holy.” [IV.4 ¶24] (wording as in the book). Compare Art of Alchemy, called holy in the next paragraph [IV.4 ¶25].

summary: Author of a celebrated treatise on the philosophers' stone whom Atwood quotes at length on long life, secrecy and the non-literal, cabalistic sense of the art.
body:
Atwood quotes Artephius at length from his celebrated treatise on the philosophers' stone (given in a note as *Artefii Antiquissimi Philosophi de Arte Occulta atque Lapide Philosophorum Liber secretus*) on long life by the quintessence. He says he publishes everything but one point: “I except one thing only, which it is not lawful that I should write, because it can be revealed truly only by God, or by a master” [I.1 ¶27; I.1 ¶36; I.1 n42]. She treats him as a link in alchemy's history as it passed from Asia to Europe [I.1 ¶37].

She cites him with approval to show that the art is cabalistic and must not be read literally: “he that takes the philosophers’ saying according to the outward sense and signification has already lost the clue to Ariadne” [I.1 ¶84; I.1 n108]. Under the spelling Atrephius (*Liber Secretissimus Artefii*) he supports her description of the subject: “a white fume, in substance like to pure silver” [I.2 ¶29; I.2 n28].

With Arnold and Lully he is said to agree with the *Lucerna Salis* description of whitening, as cited earlier “in the Theory” [III.2 ¶5]. As Artefius he is named, with Trevisan and Flammel, among “the sincerest” who passed over the Preparation of Mercury in silence [IV.3 ¶7].

summary: In Geber, a dissolution according to the course of nature; men's ignorance of it made them think gold-making impossible.
body: Quoted from Geber: “the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47]. Because men did not know of this dissolution, they thought gold-making impossible.

summary: The method of the Art, which Atwood says Palingenius divulges in a few lines of verse.
body: Atwood introduces verses of Palingenius as one who “divulges the artificial method in the few following lines” [III.1 ¶26]. The phrase apparently means the method of the Art itself.

summary: The practitioner of the Art, who begins, ends and repeats the experiment, but who, according to the theosophist Atwood quotes, cannot do the work and only prepares the way and the matter.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes the practitioner: “as the Artist begins, ends, and repeats the mysterious experiment” [APP ¶17].

A theosophist she quotes sets limits on the human operator: “the Artist is not to attempt it --- he cannot do it” [IV.3 ¶38]. The Artist only prepares the way and the matter, and must have understanding and faith [IV.3 ¶38]. The two records differ in emphasis: the Artist as active experimenter, and the Artist as one who cannot do the work alone.

summary: An authority (spelled thus in the book) cited for deriving Wisdom from clearness and light.
body: Cited in support of deriving Wisdom from clearness and light: “it is a certain clearness, as being that which renders all things conspicuous” [II.4 ¶26].

summary: In Norton, the astrological ascendant, which should be direct and fiery and, with its Lord, made fortunate for the operation; a common sign suits the work's many repetitions.
body: Quoted from Norton: the operation calls for what “Is a direct and Fiery ascendant” [IV.2 ¶34]. The ascendant and its Lord are to be made fortunate. A common sign suits the many repetitions of the work [IV.2 ¶34].

summary: The prophecy of Egypt's fall in the Asclepian Dialogue; Atwood sees the decline after 640 as something like its fulfilment, only worse than predicted.
