body: Atwood treats the decline after 640 as something like the fulfilment of the Asclepian prophecy, but worse than it predicted [I.1 ¶30]. See Asclepius for the prophecy itself.

summary: The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes, a theosophic Hermetic book; Atwood defends as authentic its prophecy of Egypt's fall and cites it on the magicians' original divine power.
body:
Atwood describes the Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes as a theosophic Hermetic book. It is the source of the prophecy of Egypt's fall: “Oh, Egypt! Egypt! Fables alone shall remain of thy religion” [I.1 ¶7; I.1 ¶10; I.1 n11]. She defends the prophecy as authentic.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she cites the Dialogue, “so called, the 2 nd Book of Hermes, ch. 9”, to support her view that the magicians first drew their power from the Divine Source and later fell into debasement and idolatry [APP ¶5]. See also Asclepian prophecy.

summary: In Khunrath, what the impure body becomes when consumed and blackened; of great worth, the diadem of the body, holding our pigmy.
body: Quoted from Khunrath: the impure body, consumed and blackened, becomes ashes, and these are of great worth: “in them lies our pigmy, conquering and subduing giants” [IV.1 ¶36]. He identifies them with the diadem of the body: “they are the diadem of thy body” [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: Compiler of the Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum, praised by Atwood and cited on secrecy, practical experience, incredulity, the Kelly story and a verse Tablet of Philosophy.
body:
Atwood praises Elias Ashmole's collection, the *Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum* (London 1652). She cites his preface to show secrecy and the need for practical experience, and also cites him on incredulity as a punishment: “I know enough to hold my tongue, but not enough to speak” [I.1 ¶62; I.1 ¶64; I.1 n66].

Ashmole tells the warming-pan story and judges Kelly more profuse than a sober philosopher should be [I.1 ¶66].

From the *Theatrum* (p. 336, *Experience and Philosophy*) she quotes a verse Tablet erected by Philosophy to Experience: “Blessed be thou, Experience!” [III.3 ¶75; III.3 ¶76; III.3 n49]. It speaks of the One Thing, the first Material Mother and the Three Powers in one seat, which the text at III.3 ¶77 glosses as Sulphur, Mercury and Salt.

summary: In Synesius, the soul's consent to its purification; without it the soul lacks every purifying machine, assent being the greatest pledge of reconciliation.
body: Quoted from Synesius: “the soul is deprived of every purifying machine because destitute of assent, which is the greatest pledge of reconciliation” [II.2 ¶13]. The context suggests assent means the soul's own consent to being purified.

summary: In Boehme, what the new man looks into, equated with the geniture; not further explained.
body: Quoted from Boehme: the new man looks into “the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16], which equates it with geniture. The text gives no further explanation.

summary: A fire said to conquer all things and assimilate them to itself; Paracelsus places it in the tincture, and Eudoxus says the Stone is an Astral Fire.
body:
Two quoted authorities use the term. Paracelsus speaks of the fire in the tincture: “an astral fire which conquers all things and changes them into a nature like itself” [I.1 ¶76].

Eudoxus identifies the Stone with it: “Our stone is an Astral Fire” [IV.3 ¶16]. He says it sympathizes with Natural Fire and grows, like a Salamander, in Elementary Fire [IV.3 ¶16].

equivalences.with: internal spiritual Sun; Perpetual Motion of the Wise; Saturnian Salt
midnight Sun of Apuleius; ignited Stone of Anaxagoras
Chariot of Antimony; Armed Magnet of Helvetius; Wheel of Fire

summary: Atwood's name for the internal spiritual Sun gotten and conceived through the work, which she identifies with a series of traditional images.
body:
In her own voice Atwood gives a chain of identities: “This is the true Astrum Solis gotten and conceived, the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52]. So it is the internal spiritual Sun, the Perpetual Motion of the Wise and the Saturnian Salt.

She goes on: “And this we take to be that midnight Sun of Apuleius, the ignited Stone of Anaxagoras” [II.3 ¶54]; and “This is the triumphal Chariot of Antimony, the Armed Magnet of Helvetius turned swiftly about the current axle of life, which is the Wheel of Fire signalized in Ezekiel” [II.3 ¶54].

The records show it as what the work produces within: something gotten and conceived. Every equation here is Atwood's own.

summary: An emblem book whose Latin verses Atwood cites in notes to illustrate the one bird as vulture and crow, the egg analogy and the reddening of the whitened water.
body:
Atwood quotes Latin verses from *Atalanta Fugiens* in her notes as illustrations, not as arguments.

- Emblema xliii shows that the vulture and the crow are one: “Montis in excelso consistit vertice vultur,” [I.3 n12] (ours: On the lofty summit of a mountain stands a vulture).
- Epigramma 8 illustrates the egg analogy: “Est avis in mundo sublimior omnibus, ovum” [I.3 n26] (ours: There is a bird in the world loftier than all, an egg…).
- Emb. xli illustrates the reddening of the whitened water: “Adonis ab apro occuditur, cui Venus occurens tinxit rosas sanquine” [I.3 n54] (ours: Adonis is slain by a boar; Venus, running to him, dyed the roses with blood).

The translations are ours, not the book's.

equivalences.with: furnace having a glass to it

summary: The philosophic furnace in which the matter is decocted with continual fire; Hermes' furnace with a glass, the sealed furnace of the Second Operation, less important than the internal Fire.
body:
A Scholiast calls it “the philosophic furnace called Athanor” [I.3 n57], in which the matter is decocted with continual fire.

Atwood refers to “that Athanor of Hermes before mentioned, or furnace having a glass to it” [II.4 ¶15], “that singular fundamental of his small new world”. She uses it as a comparison for how the Image of Universal Nature is revealed in Elysian intellection.

Eirenaeus subordinates the outer fire to the inner: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. Khunrath names “one theosophic cabalistically sealed furnace of Athanor” [IV.1 ¶36] for the Second Operation.

summary: Author of Du Parfait Amour, which Atwood says shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes; named among the authors of extant treatises on the stone.
body: Atwood says Athenagoras's *Du Parfait Amour* shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes [I.1 ¶29]. She names him with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Zosimus and Archelaus as authors of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

summary: Cited for reference only.
In Vaughan, the material efflux of the soul, which differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.
body: Quoted from Vaughan: “the aura or material efflux of the soul” [III.3 ¶27]. It differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.

summary: The gold-making light of the ferment, into whose substance the ferment transmutes everything.
body: Atwood says the ferment “transmutes all into the substance of its own Aurific Light” [III.1 ¶24].

summary: In Albertus Magnus, the gold-making principle, identified with fire in the life of all things and strongest in man.
body: Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all” [II.1 ¶12]. This equates the aurific principle with fire, and the record adds that it is strongest in man.

summary: A living gold-producing seed, the Light that springs from reason's conscious alliance with the higher Cause; the true form of gold, which the covetous spirit cannot quicken.
body:
Atwood says the seed must be quickened in life, unlike dead metal. The covetous spirit fails at this: “it cannot quicken the aurific seed in life” [III.4 ¶11]. The seed is not further explained in that passage.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she calls it the Light springing from reason's conscious alliance with the higher Cause, which “is the Divine aurific seed and true form of gold.” [APP ¶152]. She also identifies it with the Golden Bough: “That was the Golden Bough which Aeneas carried” [APP ¶152].

summary: The gold-making substance of life, which the will should return to its source and live there rather than possess.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the will fails “for want of returning the aurific substance of life into its source and living there” [APP ¶159]. On her account the will should return this substance to its source, not possess it.

summary: Atwood's gloss: illuminated, by contrariation of its Form.
body: Atwood glosses the word herself: “aurified --- that is, illuminated by contrariation of its Form” [III.2 n38]. Aurified therefore means illuminated (stated).

summary: A kind of sulphur, drawn dry from the fountain by the crowned king; Atwood takes it as the multiplicative virtue of the philosophers' stone and a name for the luminous vital principle.
body:
In the Hermetic passage quoted, the crowned king is described as “drawing from thence the Auripigment dry, without moisture” [I.3 ¶18]. The Hermetic Master's version repeats this: “drawing from thence the Auripigment, dry without moisture” [III.3 ¶17], without defining it.

The same quoted Hermetic material names it among sulphurs: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It also identifies the fat of the brain with it: “and of the brain, which too is auripigment” [I.3 ¶20].

Atwood reads it as “that auripigment of philosophers which is the multiplicative virtue of their stone” [I.3 n22]. According to the readers' record she also treats it as a name for the luminous vital principle (no quote given).

summary: Writer of L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, cited by Atwood critically for treating the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men.
body: Atwood cites the author of *L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, etc.* only to criticize him: he saw the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men, a view Atwood rejects [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n4].

headword: the author of the Filum Ariadne
forms: the author of the Filum Ariadne
summary: Writer of Le Filet d’Aridane, cited in support of the point that the dissolution needs hands, which Nature lacks.
body: Cited (work: *Le Filet d’Aridane*) in support of Atwood’s point that the dissolution requires hands, which Nature lacks: “Nature cannot of herself enter into the dissolution” [IV.1 ¶5; IV.1 n3]. Atwood endorses the citation.

summary: Writer of the Lucerna Salis (cited in Digby’s translation), repeatedly used by Atwood in support of points on the white work, prayer and labour, the gold of the Wise, and fermentation.
body:
Atwood cites the *Lucerna Salis* (footnoted as Digby’s translation / Digby’s *Lucerna Salis*) several times, always in support:

- **White work**: on the whitening of the matter, with the advice “Govern your fire with a great deal of care” [III.2 ¶5; III.2 ¶6; III.2 n7].
- **Study, prayer and labour**: study, meditation and prayer are needed; God grants the art only through instruction and labour, and without prayer obstructs or spoils it: “He does not either grant it immediately to any person, but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n21]. Also cited for many passages to the same effect as Ricardus [III.4 n16].
- **Gold of the Wise**: from the Latin verse *Aurum Sapientum*, the gold of the Wise as pure water, its dissolution and reunion into One inseparable Thing; it declares “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold” [III.3 ¶32; III.3 n22].
- **Fermentation and multiplication** (cap. 8): fermenting with pure gold or silver before projection, purifying the metals, and tenfold multiplication by dissolving and coagulating; “one drachm of gold is sufficient for the fermentation in the red” [IV.3 ¶24; IV.3 n5].

headword: author of the Lumen de Lumine
forms: author of the Lumen de Lumine
summary: Writer of the Lumen de Lumine, cited from its chapter on Matter in support of Atwood’s account of Tenebrae activae beneath sense and imagination.
body: Cited from the chapter on Matter in *Lumen de Lumine* in support of Atwood’s account of the *Tenebrae activae* lying beneath sense and imagination, described as “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13; III.2 n13].

forms: the wise author of the Rosarium
summary: Writer of the Rosarium, cited by Atwood in support of solution, dissolution and patient repetition, and among testimonies to inexhaustible abundance she says are not literally true.
body:
Atwood cites the *Rosarium* (Rosar. Abbrev., Tract ii, De Lapide, in Thet. Chem., vol iii) in support of Solution as the first preparation: subjects of species must be reduced to first matter, with an analogy from glass-making [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n2].

It also supports dissolution, the earthy body of sense made to flow: “Corpora qui vult purgare oportet fluxa facere” [II.3 n2] (ours: whoever would purge bodies must make them fluid).

The “wise author of the Rosarium” (cap. 3) is cited for grinding, cooking and repeating without weariness: “Tere, coque, et reitera, et non te taedeat” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n7].

As “Author of the Rosary” he is cited for an inexhaustible abundance won by industry, patience and one’s own labour, in a passage that continues with Eirenaeus and is footnoted to *Introitus Apertus* cap. 35; Atwood then says this testimony is not literally true [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7].

summary: Unnamed authorities cited in support of the claim that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures.
body: Cited, unnamed, in support of the statement that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures [III.4 ¶25].

summary: In Atwood’s words the first and last defect, leading either to fruitless search in inert matter or, in Mammon’s followers, to abuse of attained power.
body: Atwood calls it “this first and last defect of Avarice” [III.4 ¶4]. It leads either to fruitless searching in inert matter or, among the followers of Mammon, to abuse of the power once attained [III.4 ¶4].

summary: Named by Atwood as demanding notice, with nothing further said.
body: Named as demanding notice; the text says nothing more about him [I.1 ¶35].

summary: Reputed practitioner of transmutation, cited by Atwood on species and the Matter and named among masters who wrote obscurely.
body:
Atwood lists works attributed to him (*de Tinctura Metallorum*, *Porta Elementa*, *de Mineralibus*) and calls him a reputed practitioner of transmutation and magic whose writings are neither lucid nor numerous [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n40]. He is cited, by reference only, as concurring on species [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n5], and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

In Norton’s verse “Avicen” is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the *Ordinal* his *Porta* is cited for balanced feeding of the matter: “Comedas ut bibas, et bibas ut comeda;” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: eat as you drink, and drink as you eat).

summary: Name for the Universal Mercury and the Stone’s active principle, which with fire suffices for the work, reducing bodies to First Matter and reanimating them.
body:
Khunrath (quoted) identifies it: “Azoth, viz., the Universal Mercury” — “which alone with its internal and external fire is sufficient for thee”, transforming itself by fire into what it will, and visible and tangible [I.1 ¶81]. Elsewhere Khunrath presents it as something to be touched and seen, sufficient with internal and external fire for the Stone: “thou shalt see Azoth! The Universal!” [III.3 ¶9].

The Latin formula “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” is given as Hermes’ saying via Norton, without explanation [IV.2 ¶13] (ours: fire and Azoth suffice for thee). In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood repeats it as sufficient for the freed spirit: “ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [APP ¶131].

In IV.3 a cited voice (“continues he”) makes it the Stone’s active principle: “Azoth of our Stone, continues he, reduces bodies to their First Matter and reanimates them with the Universal Form” [IV.3 ¶28]. The vivific Ens is so named because it adheres to bodies, drawing its like into itself by supernatural magnetism: “the Hermetic philosophers have given it the name of azoth, which adheres to bodies” [IV.3 ¶29].

Asserted identities: = Universal Mercury [I.1 ¶81]; = The Universal [III.3 ¶9]; = vivific Ens [IV.3 ¶29].

summary: Named among masters who celebrated the Head Stone and wrote obscurely; his dictum on man as Nature’s servant is accepted by Atwood only for outward seeking.
body:
In Norton’s verse Bacon is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. He is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21], and as having observed the Organon becoming worse than useless [III.2 ¶42].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood uses his lucid style to show that clear language seems mystical when turned to the a priori ground [APP ¶111]. She accepts his dictum “Man is the servant and interpreter of Nature” only for outward seeking and qualifies it: turned within, man can be Nature’s revealer and master [APP ¶120].

summary: Cited as illustration: his ass was clear-sighted and spoke.
body: Used as an illustration: Balaam’s ass was clear-sighted and spoke [III.2 ¶64].

headword: the bards and hallowed sages of Asia Minor
forms: the bards and hallowed sages of Asia Minor
summary: Ancient sages contrasted with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun under which moderns remain blind.
body: Atwood contrasts them with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun, while moderns remain blind [IV.4 ¶28].

summary: Adept called “the monk”, praised by Atwood as the star of his century and among her most-cited authorities on First Matter, Antimony, extraction, and experience before practice.
body:
Atwood praises Basil Valentine as the star of the fifteenth century, credited with a new method for the Red Elixir, and assesses editions and translations of his works (*Chimische Schriften*, *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony*, *Stone of Fire*, *Twelve Keys*) [I.1 ¶59; I.1 ¶61; I.1 n65]. He is listed among genuine seekers against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49], among adepts warning against practice before full understanding, though “Basil’s” receipts also misled literal readers [I.1 ¶86], and as agreeing concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**First Matter.** From *De Prima Materia*: it is like no particular thing, indescribable without experience, one yet three, a third thing: “Corpus anima spiritus in duobus existit” [I.2 ¶31; I.2 ¶32; I.2 ¶42; I.2 n33] (ours: body, soul, spirit exist in two). All metals have one root containing mercury, salt and sulfur: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11; II.1 n8]. His *Stone of Fire* allegory of flight, fall and mountain Atwood reads as displaying the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis; it names what “is the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19; III.2 ¶20; III.2 n20].

**Antimony and extraction.** The true tincture is not common antimony; “how that extraction should be made, is a principal secret in which the whole art of Alchemy consists” [II.1 ¶25]. “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”, done with the microcosm’s corporeal fire [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n42]. Antimony must be freed of venom, which Atwood glosses as purging self-will from the mind; separation is by Fire, Vulcan the sole master: “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n34].

**Experience.** “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” — advice Atwood calls excellent; his celestial part, separating pure from impure by spiritual reason, leads into her turn to spiritual reason [III.1 ¶13; III.1 n10; III.1 n14; III.1 n15]. “more is learned by once seeing the work done, than can be taught by the writing of many pages” [IV.1 ¶2; IV.1 n1]. The winged Matter must be bound and accustomed to flight gradually, lest like Icarus it fly too near the Sun: “permit it not to fly suddenly” [IV.1 ¶15; IV.1 n15].

He also teaches that exterior spirits are intelligent and deceive the unwary, being “endowed with senses and understanding, know Arts, and have in themselves an occult operative life” [II.3 ¶23; II.3 n18]. In the Appendix (later layer) his *Keys* are called the best illustration of the Art as a fermentative process [APP ¶29].

summary: In Eudoxus’ words, the spirits of the bodies, where Sun and Moon wash; the King’s bath, prepared with the blood of the Innocents, in which he is made young.
body: Eudoxus (quoted) identifies the bath with the spirits of the bodies: “the spirits of the bodies are the Bath where the Sun and Moon go to wash themselves” [IV.3 ¶10]. One must “prepare the bath of the King with the blood of the Innocents” [IV.3 ¶10], and “purify, to heal, and to animate the royal bath” [IV.3 ¶16], in which the King is made young again. Asserted identity: = the spirits of the bodies [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: In Atwood’s account, a bath prepared out of the blood of many battles, preceding the rising of the Identical Spirit.
body: Atwood: “So the Bath of Diana is prepared out of the blood of many battles” [III.1 ¶68]; it precedes the rising of the Identical Spirit [III.1 ¶68].

summary: That which is referred to all things and through which they sympathize, inconceivable by ordinary reason, which the soul enters after descent to nonentity.
body: Atwood: Being cannot be conceived by ordinary rational contemplation; “it becomes necessary simply to refer Being to all things, and all things sympathize thereby internally with each other” [III.2 ¶50]. The soul becomes into it after its descent to nonentity, and one is present with it by being present with oneself: “then he is present with true Being, which is everywhere” [III.2 ¶59].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Voice in the Turba Philosophoru, cited by Atwood to explain the paradox of the ‘stone and no stone’.
body: Cited from the *Turba Philosophoru*, Sermo Vigesima (the classic synod of Aristaeus), in support of the paradox of ‘stone and no stone’: “this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone” [I.2 ¶29; I.2 n31].

summary: Phrase of the masters which Atwood applies to the matter’s ripened Life; it is unclear whether it names the green or the purple colour.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood writes: “The purple color is its ripened Life; it is the benedicta viriditas of the masters” [APP ¶119] (ours: blessed greenness). Since the passage joins green and purple, which colour the phrase names is unclear.

summary: Voice cited via Vaughan’s Coelum Terrae in support of solve et coagula, the gross body as vessel, heavenly fire, and work without tools.
body: Cited (footnoted to Mehung in Vaughan’s *Coelum Terrae*, p. 122) in support of solve et coagula, the gross body as the vessel, the heavenly fire, and work without tools: “For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one” [III.3 ¶24; III.3 n14].

headword: the best Greek Authors, historical and philosophic
forms: the best Greek Authors, historical and philosophic
summary: Greek historical and philosophic writers whom Atwood invokes as giving collateral probability to alchemy’s antiquity.
body: Invoked as providing collateral probability for the antiquity of alchemy [I.1 ¶3].

summary: Cited in the Appendix: its protest against idolatry applied to self-made specificating, and Revelation said to rectify man and Nature.
body: Both references are in the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood applies the Bible’s protest against idolatry to unlawful specificating from one’s own mind [APP ¶37]. Revelation rectifies man and Nature; the question of science versus the Bible is left on its own ground [APP ¶161].

summary: Collection whose second edition Atwood notes as containing the Twelve Keys.
body: Its second edition is noted as containing the Twelve Keys [I.1 ¶61].

summary: Twofold conception, which Atwood says must be rejected for Nature to reach Monadic simplicity.
body: Atwood: Nature reaches Monadic simplicity “through the rejection of the Binary” [IV.2 ¶18], “by rejection of her Binary conception” [IV.2 ¶20]. The context suggests it means a twofold conception.

summary: Cited from Siris in support of a universal material called ether, source of air’s vitalizing power.
body: Cited from *Siris* in support of a universal material called ether, the source of the air’s vitalizing power, “a pure invisible fire” [I.2 ¶14].

summary: Cited in the Appendix for Nature being as much God’s voice as Revelation; Atwood agrees, then qualifies that since the fall Nature distorts it.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Nature, as the Bishop of Oxford (Wilberforce) says, is as much the voice of God as Revelation is” [APP ¶161]. Atwood agrees, then qualifies: since the fall Nature distorts that voice [APP ¶161].

summary: Stigmatizing name given to alchemy, perhaps derived from Chemia meaning black matters.
body: Atwood notes that alchemy “has been likewise stigmatized as a Black Art” [I.1 ¶5], perhaps from Chemia taken to mean black matters [I.1 ¶5].

summary: The adepts’ name for the dark nether region and the apparent corruption preceding mystical death and regeneration.
body: Atwood: “It is the Black Saturn of the adepts, and that appearing corruption that precedes the mystical death and regeneration into new life” [II.3 ¶18]; it names the dark nether region. Asserted identities: = lapis niger — “as describing the same ens, they call it lapis niger, vilis, foetens” (ours: black, vile, stinking stone) [II.3 ¶18]; = Urinus Saturni — “Sendivogius calls it Urinus Saturni” [II.3 ¶18].

summary: In Eudoxus’ words, the source of the black, foul, stinking fume whose separation forms the white Stone.
body: Eudoxus (quoted) speaks of “the black, foul, and stinking fume of the Blackest Black” [IV.3 ¶3], whose separation forms the white Stone.

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited for reference only.

Read variously by quoted authorities: in Roger Bacon’s phrase the understanding; in verse from Theat. Chem. Brit. the principal matter of all that increases; in Boehme the fire-and-water union whose warmth is life.
body:
The records give three quoted readings, not reconciled:

- **Roger Bacon**: blood = the understanding: “operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding” [I.1 ¶86].
- **Verse in Theat. Chem. Brit.**: blood contains the three things and the nature of gold, has the proportion of the four elements, and is the principal matter of everything that increases: “For blood is the principle matter of each thing” [II.1 ¶15].
- **Jacob Boehme**: the red fire-form and the thin water-form, “both of which contracting together into one, are converted into Blood”; “the original in the blood, viz., fire, which is its warmth, is life”, and from that warmth the Thin Water of Life proceeds [III.3 ¶24].

summary: In a passage quoted from Eudoxus, a veiled name for the spirits of the bodies, which feed the two Mercuries and prepare the King's bath.
body: Quoted from Eudoxus, who explains the expression himself: “the blood of innocents whose throats are cut; that is to say, the spirits of the bodies” [IV.3 ¶10]. In that passage these spirits feed the two Mercuries and prepare the King's bath. Asserted identity: = the spirits of the bodies [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: A name for the secret product of the work: Khunrath equates it with the gold of the philosophers; the Hunting of the Greene Lyon makes it the King's only food.
body:
**Khunrath** (quoted) names it beside the universal tincture as what he received: “the blood of the Lion, which is the gold of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶81]. Asserted identity: = gold of the philosophers [I.1 ¶81].

**The Hunting of the Greene Lyon** (quoted verse) describes it as the 'secret' drawn off after Lion, Sol and Luna unite and form a skin: “A right good secret withouten any nay: Wych must serve to doe thee good’ For yt ys the Lyons Blood:” [III.1 ¶65]. It is the King's only food, given after he rises from the dead: “And tis as strange that thys Kings food, Can be nothing but thys Lyons Blood;” [III.1 ¶65]; and it is worked with Luna or Sol to prepare the ferments [III.1 ¶65]. Asserted identity: = a right good secret [III.1 ¶65]. A reader noted that the same passage may also call it the King's Father and Mother; this is uncertain.

summary: Author in Ashmole's collection whose Blossoms and Camp of Philosophy Atwood cites for the subject's many names and for the threefold magistery.
body: Atwood counts **Bloomfield's Blossoms** among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64], and names Bloomfield as a witness to rings made of Kelly's gold [I.1 ¶66]. From the **Camp of Philosophy**, book I (in Ashmole), she illustrates the many names of the subject: “It is a privy quintessence; keepe it well in minde” [I.2 ¶41; I.2 n38]. Its Conclusion (in Theatrum Chemicum Brit.) supports her account of the threefold magistery, the Dragon, the blackness and the appearing of Phoebus: “Our magistery is Three, Two, and One” [IV.2 ¶36; IV.2 n25].

summary: In Vaughan's quoted account, the descent or incorporation of the finished Stone cast on molten gold, which abates the gold's strength to fix a projection ratio.
body: Quoted from Vaughan: casting the finished Stone on molten gold so that the gold abates its strength, in order to fix a usable ratio for projection. “This descent or incorporation, some wise authors have called a bodily fermentation” [IV.3 ¶22]. Asserted identity: = descent or incorporation [IV.3 ¶22].

equivalences.with: the sensible and vegetable media of life

summary: In quoted authorities, the hard, dry or dead part of the matter that imprisons the spirit or fire and must be dissolved, rotted and glorified.
body:
Three quoted voices use the term:

- **Eirenaeus**: the hard, dry body in which the fire is imprisoned, rotted by 'our water': “which in the hard and dry body is imprisoned” [III.1 ¶14]. A gloss in the passage (whose voice is unclear) makes it the ethereal body: “by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)” [III.1 ¶14].
- **Eudoxus**: what remains after the Water is distilled off: “the Body remains in the bottom of the vessel, like a dead, black, and dredgy earth” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is not to be despised, and must be wholly dissolved and glorified. He names it Adam: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
- **The Scholiast** (reported by Atwood): “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” [I.3 n38], glossed as “the bodies (i.e., the sensible and vegetable media of life)” [I.3 n38], which must be dissolved into their radical source.

Asserted identities: = ethereal body [III.1 ¶14]; = Adam [IV.3 ¶7]; = the sensible and vegetable media of life [I.3 n38].

summary: Atwood's gloss in the Appendix: the impure natural-born vital spirit.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The body of brass is the impure natural-born vital spirit.” [APP ¶52]. Asserted identity: = impure natural-born vital spirit.

summary: In the quoted Adept, the body which the Preparing Spirit dissolves and cleanses, and from which a tinging spirit is extracted.
body: Quoted from the Adept: the Preparing Spirit “dissolves the body of Light” [IV.1 ¶10], cleansing it, and a tinging spirit is then extracted from it.

summary: Writer Atwood treats as the plainest experiential exponent of the mystery, cited throughout for the Tincture, the Three Principles and divine manifestation, though she judges him theosophical rather than intellectual.
body:
Atwood calls Jacob Boehme the plainest exponent of the mystery from experience, with explicit pointers to the physical basis of magic and the material of the stone, citing the Aurora, Three Principles, Mysterium Magnum, Tree of Life, Turned Eye and Epistles [I.1 ¶68; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n77]. She qualifies this: his revelation is theosophical, not intellectual [I.1 ¶70]. His writings alarmed alchemists by applying alchemy openly to human life [II.1 ¶9].

**The Work.** From the Tract. Aur., Epistles and Forty Questions she takes the white and red stages and the concealment under the Seal of God: “the Work is easy and simple, but the wisdom therein is great and the greatest mystery” [II.1 ¶24; II.1 n20]. Forty Questions 17 gives the core operation, Sol and Luna brought through death at the cross and reconceived: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48; III.1 n53]; Atwood says it comprehends 'the end and beginning of the Sacred Art'. The Three Principles supplies the Antimonial Spirit and the Invisible Mercury: “the agent in the preparation of this spirit, continues Bohme, is the Invisible Mercury” [II.1 ¶20], and the disorder of arterial blood [II.1 ¶21; II.1 n17]; the Generation of the Three Principles gives the creation of a cloud condensed into water: “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. His account of the Tincture, which “is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16], is endorsed as agreeing with the ancient Kabalah [III.2 ¶17]; the Turned Eye gives 'modern testimony' of his illumination: “the gate was opened to me” [III.2 ¶16]. The operator must first “seek God’s love and grace, and resign up themselves to become wholly one with that” [III.1 ¶39]; Atwood qualifies that the divine cannot exactly be given into possession [III.1 ¶40]. On contrition and the Tincture: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24]. He is among Adepts comparing the work to the Creed [IV.3 ¶27].

**Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer): he knew the mystery by experienced in-seeing whereby he became it [APP ¶117]; the deepest writer on ontological subjects, less scientific than the Platonists but more descriptive, awakening, suggestive [APP ¶62]; his three primary forms and doctrine of the Absolute Will read as expressions of conscious experience of the creative mystery [APP ¶65]; surpassing the Neo-Platonists on the Life Center [APP ¶122]. His Law of Divine Manifestation, the order the Hermetic Work imitates: “An Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to introduce the No Thing into Something, that the Will might feel and find and behold itself” [APP ¶73]; cited for the Sulphur, Salt and Mercury nomenclature [APP ¶81]; 'in the Experience' of the uncreated beyond the metaphysicians, though they surpassed him in scientific intuition [APP ¶96]. Also: the Third Principle as medium of perceiving the First, “the sidereal and elementary birth” [APP ¶27]; the Three-fold Life on will begetting a being out of its own image [APP ¶36]; his Mercurius, or spirit of the Sound, for the harmony freed from the lower life [APP ¶49]; Signatura Rerum on knowing things in their roots on entering the Signature, “through the principle in the sound with the voice” [APP ¶63]; with de St Martin, source of 'the Crown', and contrasted with Engelbrecht as penetrating surfaces, his body swallowed up with Light [APP ¶104; APP ¶105]; the bitterness of self-life from which nature shields us, “the bitter anguish of the driving wheel of existence” [APP ¶154].

summary: Atwood's term for the magical bond that everywhere shuts up Nature's Inner Light and principle of perfection, which Nature cannot loosen herself.
body: Atwood speaks of “the bond of coagulation by which her Inner Light and principle of perfection is everywhere shut up” [III.2 ¶61]. Nature cannot loosen this bond by herself [III.2 ¶61]; the context suggests that loosening it is the task of the art.

summary: An enigma which, Atwood reports, the adepts claimed as referring to the occult material of the art.
body: Atwood reports that the adepts claimed the Bononian Enigma as referring to the occult material of the art [I.1 ¶20; I.1 ¶21]. It opens “Nec vir, nec mulier, nec androgyna,” [I.1 n29] (ours: 'Neither man, nor woman, nor androgyne').

summary: Book Atwood quotes as epigraph and illustration: wisdom as water, whiteness, the Radical Essence, and metal mountains melting before the Elect One.
body: Atwood uses the Book of Enoch for epigraph and illustration. Chapter xl.1 heads III.3: “Wisdom is poured forth like water, and glory faileth not before Him for ever.” [III.3 ¶2]. Chapters 46 and 41 illustrate whiteness, “the Ancient of Days, whose head was like wool” [III.2 ¶4; III.2 n6], and the seer's vision of the Radical Essence, winds, clouds and the cloud before creation [III.2 ¶12; III.2 n12]. Section 109, on rain, dew and metal mountains melting before the Elect One, is given without comment: “ye that are capable to comprehend the Elect One” [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n8].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Book whose first chapter Atwood compares with the building of Solomon's Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.
body: Atwood quotes chapter 1, “with the Fiery Letters of the Law, He engraved the empty, and the void, and the obscure mind” [IV.2 ¶33; IV.2 n21], and compares it with the building of Solomon's Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.

summary: Book Atwood praises in the Appendix as the best description of Wisdom as man's exemplar.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood calls it the best description of Wisdom as man's exemplar [APP ¶90]. Cited together with the Poemander, chapter 11, verse 22 illustrates the whole world held before the divine vision, as before one who has the Principle: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

summary: Old sources whose unguents made from fats, hair and similar things are rejected in the passage citing them.
body: Cited critically: the unguents made from fats, hair and the like, “which are written in the books of our fathers” [I.3 ¶53], are rejected.

summary: Modern authority who lauds the Isaacs and, with Homberg and Boyle, held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.
body: Atwood cites Boorhaave for the Isaacs' reputation: he lauds them and seems acquainted with occult science [I.1 ¶58]. With Homberg and Boyle he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

summary: Atwood's gloss: the Philosopher's Stone, made from the Citrine extracted from the Red.
body: Atwood glosses the term in a footnote: “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52], made from the Citrine extracted from the Red. Asserted identity: = Philosopher's Stone.

summary: Modern figure rumoured to have known Philalethes, and named among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.
body: Boyle is rumoured, uncertainly, to have been intimate with Philalethes [I.1 ¶73]. With Homberg and Boerhaave he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

summary: A veiled name in quoted authorities: for Hermes the Art of the permanent water; for Albertus the occult Nature to be washed, dissolved and fixed.
body:
**Hermes** (quoted): “the Art of this permanent water is our brass” [I.3 ¶43]; Democritus draws out the 'Fixed Brass' bodily: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily, writes our Abderite” [I.3 n53].

**Albertus** (quoted) uses it for the occult Nature: “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass” [IV.1 ¶4], which is to be washed pure and clean, then dissolved, distilled, sublimed, calcined and fixed.

Asserted identities: = Art of this permanent water [I.3 ¶43]; = occult Nature [IV.1 ¶4]. See also body of brass, Brazen Body.

summary: In Hermes as quoted, the body to be burned with exceeding great fire, exemplified by Democritus drawing out the 'Fixed Brass'.
body: Quoted from Hermes: “Burn then the Brazen Body with an exceeding great fire” [I.3 ¶42]. Democritus, exemplifying this juncture, draws out the 'Fixed Brass' and works it on the coals [I.3 ¶42].

summary: Atwood's image of the barrier surrounding 'our Heaven' that must be scaled and passed before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.
body: Atwood: “this is that Brazen Wall celebrated by Antiquity, which surrounds our Heaven and must be scaled” [IV.1 ¶4]. It must be passed through before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.

summary: Atwood's gloss: the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit, finally gathered into accord with its first source.
body: Atwood glosses the term: “by the brethren, the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit” [I.3 n50], which are finally gathered into accord with the spirit's first source.

summary: A group voice whose phrase names the only builders who 'erect structures in the air'.
body: The phrase of the Brethren for the only builders who 'erect structures in the air': “Master mason, of Grand Architects” [IV.2 ¶14].

summary: A fraternity which Atwood says agreed about the Matter and found it experimentally; she quotes their letter and the Matter's speeches.
body: Atwood says the Christian brotherhood of the Rosy Cross agreed concerning the Matter, searched Nature experimentally, found it and used it [III.2 ¶60]. A letter circulated under their name gives an allegory of the initiatory passage (mountain, beasts, night, guide, courage): “There is a mountain situated in the midst of the earth or center of the world” [II.3 ¶31; II.3 ¶32]. From the Latin original of the Fraternity, as given in Vaughan's Coelum Terrae, she quotes speeches of the Matter as Goddess (First Matter, Eagle and Lion, five gates) and as Dragon or Mercury: “I am a Goddess for beauty and extraction” [III.3 ¶62; III.3 n45].

summary: In Hermes as quoted, that to which the son is to be joined, called Jupiter and a hidden secret.
body: Quoted from Hermes: “join the son to Buba, which is Jupiter and a hidden secret” [I.3 ¶37]. Asserted identity: = Jupiter.

summary: Boehme's word, glossed in the quoted passage itself as the ground or original foundation.
body: Quoted from Boehme, who glosses it: “the Bysse, or ground or original foundation” [III.2 ¶16]. Asserted identity: = ground or original foundation.

summary: Said of Lully's mind and of the art itself: veiled, full of mysteries, not to be understood according to the letter.
body: Atwood says one must “possess the key of his cabalistic mind” [I.1 ¶48] to understand Lully's obscure alchemical works. Artephius (quoted) applies it to the art: “For is not our art cabalistic” [I.1 ¶84], full of mysteries, not taught openly, not to be understood according to the letter.

summary: Atwood's name for a practice of the time of concealing truth by displacing order, inverting and dispersing repetitions.
body: Atwood blames the displacement of verses from their original order on “the mischievous cabalistic method in vogue at that time” [I.1 ¶64], and traces to it the artifices used to hide the truth, such as inversion of order and dispersed repetition: “A variety of artifices according to the cabalistic method” [I.1 ¶82].

headword: cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience
forms: cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience
summary: Ancient sources whose reported view grounds man's rank in a Divine Reason and latent Faculty of Wisdom; Atwood says it was once proved but is now beyond evidence.
body: Atwood reports their view that man's rank rests on a Divine Reason and a latent Faculty of Wisdom: “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32]. She says this was once proved but is now beyond present evidence [II.1 ¶32].

summary: Figures Atwood names as the god dead and revived among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians.
body: Atwood names Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis and Osiris as instances of the god dead and revived, among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians [III.3 ¶69].

headword: Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus
forms: Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus
summary: Heroes Atwood says passed the same ordeal, their adventures read as records of the soul's struggle with her inner enemies.
body: Atwood names Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules and Orpheus as heroes who passed the same ordeal, and reads their adventures as records of the soul's struggle with her inner enemies [III.3 ¶71].

equivalences.with: extraction of the soul, spirit or body

summary: One of the preparations the vulgar Matter undergoes; Synesius makes calcination a name of the single operation, the same as extracting soul, spirit or body.
body: Quoted from Synesius, calcination is one of the names of the single operation: “to extract the soul, or the spirit, or the body, is nothing else than the aforesaid calcinations” [III.3 ¶60], and these names are used “in regard they signify the operation of Venus” [III.3 ¶60]. Atwood herself lists calcinations among the preparations the vulgar Matter passes through before it becomes the Mercury of the Philosophers: “Hence all those preparations, solutions, calcinations, etc.” [II.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she places it as a step before a reunion into permanent form: “after calcinations there is a reunion” [III.2 ¶64]. The text does not define the operation further.

summary: A king, initiated and converted, cited as author of the Liber Secretorum and as one of the Mahomedan princes agreed concerning the Matter.
body: Atwood cites Calid as a king who was initiated and converted and who wrote treatises, among them the *Liber Secretorum, or Secret of Secrets* [I.1 ¶35]. Later she counts him among “the Mahomedan princes” who agree concerning the Matter, using him as supporting testimony [III.2 ¶60].

summary: Dionysius's name for the primordial cloud, obscure and humanly incomprehensible though visible; called Tenebrae activae by the author of the Lumen de Lumine.
body: A quoted term: Dionysius's name for the primordial cloud, of which it is said “it is obscure and humanly incomprehensible, though visible indeed” and “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13]. It is identified with the Kabalists' term: “The author of the Lumen de Lumine calls it, from the Kabalists, Tenebrae activae” [III.2 ¶13], described as beneath all sense and imagination.

summary: Author whose Hymn to Minerva and Hymn to Apollo Atwood quotes on the purity Divinity requires.
body: Atwood quotes Callimachus's *Hymn to Minerva* in support of the point that Divinity rejects anything mixed: “All mixture of her pure and simple oil” [III.2 ¶64; III.2 ¶65; III.2 n48]. She quotes the *Hymn to Apollo* (in Dodd's version) to illustrate the coming of the God of Light and the purity required to behold him: “Apollo’s eyes endure None but the good, the perfect, and the pure.” [IV.2 ¶37; IV.2 ¶38; IV.2 n26]. In both cases she uses him approvingly as illustration.

summary: Where the conflux of the water below and the ether above takes place, and from which the physical Tetractys springs.
body: Atwood says the meeting of the water below and the ether above happens in a Calx: “the conflux of these two is in a Calx” [III.3 ¶72]; from it the physical Tetractys springs. The term is not further defined.

summary: In a saying of Hermes, that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame, and is corrupted in the heat of the boiling fire.
body: A quoted term from Hermes: that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame — “that which in the heat of the boiling fire is corrupted is Cambar” [I.3 ¶42]. Not further explained.

summary: Author of Antiquities, cited as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins.
body: Atwood cites Camden's *Antiquities* in support, as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins [I.1 ¶47].

summary: Cited for reference only.

equivalences.with: our pigmy / diadem of the body (Khunrath)
dead head; foeces of our sea

summary: The ashes in which the principle of body is preserved and from which the whole life is restored; also an epithet of the Matter.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “what they call the ashes or Caput Mortuum” [APP ¶26] as where the principle of body is preserved; from that one principle the whole life is restored. She reports that Khunrath has other names for it: “Khunrath call it ‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’” [APP ¶26], and tentatively adds “I think he refers to it under the term Duanach” [APP ¶26].

In the main text, quoting Synesius and the New Light, caput mortuum is one of the epithets of the Matter: “O our caput mortuum, or dead head, or foeces of our sea!” [I.2 ¶33].

summary: Atwood's hedged name for Reason investigating her First Source.
body: Atwood names the process she has described, with the hedge 'it would seem', “the Catholic Art of Reason investigating her First Source” [IV.2 ¶21].

summary: What the Hermetic experiment arrives at, passing from either extreme of mind and matter, where external and internal worlds blend.
body: Atwood says the Hermetic experiment, “as passing from whither extreme of Mind and matter, to prove them, it arrives at the Catholic Effect of Life” [IV.4 ¶11]; there the external and internal worlds blend.

summary: For some modern Kabalists, the universal germ before birth, seen as a nebulous cloud; a concentration of Divinity that gives birth to the primitive Ether.
body: A view Atwood reports from some modern Kabalists: the universal germ before its birth appears as a cloud — “This nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo before its birth” [III.2 ¶13] — an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity, giving birth to the primitive Ether.

summary: 'That which is sown' in man: it contains all things and must die before it is quickened.
body: Atwood glosses 'that which is sown' in man: “that which is sown (viz., the catholic germ of his existence” [I.3 n8]. It contains all things and must die before it is quickened.

summary: The universal nature that is the subject of the Art: precious when exalted, defiled and despised in the common world.
body: Atwood: “The same catholic nature, which in its preternatural exaltation appears so very precious” [I.3 n40] is, in the common world, defiled and despised. The context presents it as the subject of the Art.

summary: Something miraculously kindled that kindles the Light of Universal Nature, acting through the three kingdoms and rejoicing most in the Mind of Man.
body: Atwood: “The catholic torch, miraculously kindled, kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]; it acts through the three kingdoms by voluntary assimilation and rejoices most in the Mind of Man. The text does not identify it further.

summary: In the Table Talk, where the individual light of life is lodged, driving adhering evil to the extremities and freeing the threefold life to ascend.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of the time “when the individual light of life is lodged in its causal center” [APP ¶150]: adhering evil is then precipitated to the extremities and the threefold life is freed to ascend.

summary: Knowledge of cause, the only thing that fulfils the Idea of Truth, superior to the exhibition of phenomena.
body: Atwood holds that “neither can anything short of the Causal Discovery fulfill the Idea of Truth” [IV.4 ¶13]; it ranks above the mere exhibition of phenomena, the only doubt being whether it is possible. The adjacent passage speaks of knowledge “leading out from the Causal Fountain into natural effect” [IV.4 ¶12]. See also Causal Knowledge.

summary: The source of all things and of Wisdom, from which riches come and whose emanative splendour the true gods are.
body: Atwood speaks of “riches as from the Causal fountain of all things” [II.4 ¶19], and of the true gods “as an emanative splendour from the Causal Fountain, make manifest in energy its Intellectual Law” [II.4 ¶29]. It is also the source of Wisdom, to be approached by prayer as one applies to a master of an art: “the Causal Fountain for Wisdom, which is His alone and voluntarily to bestow” [III.4 ¶20].

summary: Knowledge of causes, the worthiest part of knowledge, without which external science leaves us no wiser; withheld from the unworthy.
body: Atwood insists the unworthy be kept from it, lest they handle 'the powerful machine of nature' for selfish ends: “these are unfit to be admitted to the Causal Knowledge” [I.3 n10]. Without it external science leaves us no wiser: “what would we be wiser without the Causal knowledge of these things?” [IV.4 ¶29]; and “For the discovery of the Causal Nature is doubtless of all parts of knowledge the worthiest to be sought after” [IV.4 ¶32]. See also Causal Discovery.

summary: The light within a person, which the Art draws forth, fixes and brings to manifestation; nature's Causal Light reached through the Understanding.
body: Atwood identifies it with what is within: “That which is within, viz., the causal light, must be drawn forth by art and fixed” [I.3 n8]. The Art aims to “bring the Causal light to manifestation” [II.1 ¶17], and to recover “the Ancient Experiment of nature into her Causal Light” [III.4 ¶2]. It is reached by rational permeation, “by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20]. The goal includes knowing the First Truth experimentally and being able “to revolve the Causal Light in permanence of intellection” [IV.4 ¶22]. Beyond the identification with 'that which is within', the text does not define it.

summary: In Hermes (Asclepius), something man can both find and effect.
body: Quoting Hermes in the Asclepius: “man should be able not only to find the Causal Nature but to effect it” [III.1 ¶21]. Atwood also calls its discovery the worthiest part of knowledge [IV.4 ¶32] (see Causal Knowledge).

summary: The goal of the ancients' method of ascent, surveyed more or less immediately after gradual assimilation.
body: Atwood describes the ancients' ascent as proceeding by gradual assimilation “to a survey more or less immediate of the Causal Source” [III.2 ¶33].

summary: The truth of causes, as opposed to remote effects, beheld in the apperceptive vision granted to those proved and reproved.
body: Atwood contrasts it with remote effects, speaking of those “who have never glanced even in imagination toward the Causal Truth” [II.1 ¶49]; it is drawn from a deep well. It is what is beheld when Light meets Light, by those proved and reproved “previous to being admitted to the apperceptive vision of the Causal Truth which they describe” [III.2 ¶28].

summary: Four causes — essence, matter, origin of motion, and end — which in the Art pass into one another; cause is not mere antecedence in time.
body: Atwood names four causes: essence (the principle, 'First Why'); matter or subject; that whence motion begins; and “That for the sake of which the inquiry subsists, and the Good which is the end of regeneration” [IV.2 ¶7]. In the Art the First becomes efficient in the Third and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶7]. She rejects attempts to “reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence or juxtaposition in time” [IV.4 ¶15], citing the testimony of instinct, and says this science “exhibits all things in their constructive Causes” [IV.4 ¶22].

equivalences.with: Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life

summary: A place to be entered with prudent motive, from which the mineral radix of the Art is carried away; by Hermetic interpretation, Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life.
body: Atwood gives the Hermetic interpretation: “the Cave of Mercury, which, according to the Hermetic interpretation, is Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life” [III.1 ¶19]. It is to be entered with a prudent motive, and the mineral radix of the Art is carried away from it [III.1 ¶19].

summary: The prior Elements of Life the ancients actually investigated, as opposed to the common elements or abstractions.
body: Atwood says the ancients investigated not the common elements or abstractions but “the prior Elements of Life; which some, openly distinguishing, call the Celestial Elements” [III.2 ¶36].

summary: In the Table Talk, the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, representing the Vegetable Kingdom and seated in the epigastric region.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The Celestial is the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, and represents the Vegetable Kingdom.” [APP ¶32]. It resides in the epigastric region, its workshop the solar plexus; it is identified with the medial life, through which the third life must be born [APP ¶32]. Compare celestial medial life.

summary: In Boehme, the light in which the Tincture is, containing a substance like water which is no water.
body: Quoting Boehme, the Tincture is in the Celestial Light: “And there is in the Celestial Light, continues the same author, a Substance like water which yet is no water” [III.2 ¶16].

summary: The intermediate life preceding the heroic work, which must be cut off, shut up and buried; until it dissolves the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved.
body: Atwood speaks of “the celestial medial life which, in the order of divine rites, precedes the heroic work” [III.1 ¶26]. It must be cut off in its prime, shut up and buried; until “this dissolution of the first medial life” [III.1 ¶28] takes place, the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved. Compare Celestial life, which the Table Talk identifies with the medial life [APP ¶32].

summary: Image of the incessant, repeated purifying labour that clears the wasted field of human life.
body: Atwood's image for the repeated purifying labour of the work, which serves “to clear the wasted field of human life, and harrow it for a more congenial growth” [IV.1 ¶9].

summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai, the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinguished from apparent man.
body: Atwood says the Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” [II.1 ¶40]. Quoting Rabbi Ben Jochai, it is the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinct from apparent man: “on that form in man, which is the Celestial Prototype” [II.1 ¶42]; “no form, no world, could exist before the human prototype” [II.1 ¶42].

summary: A cited figure whose ladder Atwood uses as an image of ascending knowledge and identifies with the magnetic chain.
body: Atwood invokes “Celsus’ ladder” as an image of ascending knowledge [I.1 ¶64]. Later she identifies the magnetic chain with “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54]. The book gives nothing else about Celsus.

summary: In the Table Talk, the center of substantial life which every creature seeks, which each person can find in himself at moments.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “the center of the substantial life which every creature is seeking” [APP ¶113]. She holds that “Every one can find in himself at moments the true center” [APP ¶115], apparently through deep thought, and that the same revelation is given to all who enter it [APP ¶115].

summary: Atwood's paired terms for the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, and the circumference, where being's equilibrium is broken for manifestation.
body: Atwood sets the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, against the circumference, where “the equilibrium of being is broken everywhere at the circumference for manifestation” [II.4 ¶50]. In the illumination she describes, the light spreads outward, “diffusing itself from the freed center outwardly center outwardly until it moved the dark circumference of sense itself” [II.4 ¶54]. The context suggests the work frees the centre so that its light reaches and moves the outer, sensible life. See also centers and circumferences; circulation.

summary: Paired terms Atwood uses in warning that the centers must not be stirred before the circumferences can conceive them.
body: Atwood warns against acting “lest the centers should be stirred up before the circumferences are ready to conceive them” [IV.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the pair further here; compare center / circumference.

summary: That with which the Aqua Philosophica, once conjoined in consciousness, becomes all-powerful.
body: In a footnote Atwood says of the Aqua Philosophica that “being conjoined in consciousness with the central Efficient, it becomes all-powerful” [I.3 n36]. The term is not further defined.

summary: A fire within the will or nature: in the Table Talk, Lucifer's stirring of it burned up the ether; in Vaughan, it stands opposed to the moist natures.
body: Two voices use the term. Quoting Vaughan, the text says that when heat is excessive the moist natures “will stand up against the central fire, and the central fire against them” [III.4 ¶44], producing a division in the Chaos. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of Lucifer's fall as “the stirring up of the central fire in his will” [APP ¶133], which inflamed the vehicle of his life and burned up the ether. Both passages apparently treat the central fire as dangerous when wrongly roused.

summary: The inner force of the Universal Spirit, which repeated operations draw wholly out until it acts forcibly at the circumference.
body: Atwood describes repeated operations upon the Universal Spirit continued “until the central force, wholly drawn out, acts forcibly at the circumference” [IV.3 ¶29]. Compare center / circumference.

summary: That whose whole voluntary force alone can arrest the imaginative flux of freed vitality and compel it to repose.
body: Atwood says that to arrest the imaginative flux of the freed vitality “it need the whole voluntary force of the central magnet” [III.2 ¶24], and that “this alone, which is its proper reason, can compel it to repose” [III.2 ¶24]. The central magnet is thus apparently equated with “its proper reason”, though the referent of “its” is unclear from the passage.

summary: In the Moorish philosopher's words, something man may draw to himself in abundance; not further defined.
body: Quoting the Moorish philosopher, the text speaks of one “who is able to draw to himself the Central Salt of nature in abundance” [II.1 ¶9]. The term is not explained.

summary: The goal towards which consciousness is translated, beneath the sensible medium, by obscuration.
body: Atwood speaks of the need “to translate the consciousness underneath this medium by obscuration, towards the Central Source” [II.3 ¶5]. The context suggests the Central Source is the inward origin reached by withdrawing consciousness beneath the sensible medium.

summary: The voice of the Chaldaic oracles, which Atwood cites repeatedly in support of her account of the fire, the guide and light, and the threefold Art of Reason.
body:
Atwood cites the Chaldaic oracle often, always in support:

- That there are pure demons and that the products of evil matter are useful: “Natura suadet esse demonas puros, et malae materiae germina utilia et bona” [II.3 ¶24] (our translation: nature persuades that there are pure demons, and that the germs of evil matter are useful and good).
- That the practitioner should not heed apparitions: “he apply not his mind to it, nor esteem the voice proceeding thence to be true” [II.3 ¶20].
- On the guide and the promised light: “the mortal, approaching the fire, will have a light from divinity” [II.3 n37].
- In what she calls ‘operative language’, on fire, the intellectual pattern and the Presters of Intellectual Fire: “O how the world hath Intellectual guides inflexible!” [II.4 ¶31].
- As pursuing the same Art of Reason she describes (Monad, Duad, Triad, the Matrix and the Prester of Fire): “For the mind of the Father said that all things be cut into Three” [IV.2 ¶21].

See also Chaldaic Oracles.

summary: A collection of oracles Atwood cites for Latin verse on the life-bearing fire and, in the Table Talk, for the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested.
body: Atwood cites the Oracula Chaldeor for Latin verse on “Vitifer Ignis” and a Centre [IV.1 ¶35]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she uses the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested: “There is room for the image also in the circumlucid place. Every way to the unfashioned soul stretch the reins of fire” [APP ¶96]. Elsewhere in the Table Talk they are only referred to for comparison on the solution (‘Article Hecate, etc.’) [APP ¶50]. See also the Chaldaic oracle.

summary: A quoted term glossed as ‘steel’: the means of extracting ‘our sea water’ and, in Cosmopolite, the partner that conceives with gold.
body: Quoted voices only. In the passage citing Synesius and the New Light, the text speaks of “our chalybs, or steel” [I.2 ¶33], the means by which ‘our sea water’ is extracted; it is otherwise unexplained. In Cosmopolite (quoted via Eudoxus), after gold couples with ‘it’, “the Chalybes conceives and begets a son more glorious than the Father” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not say what the chalybs plainly is, beyond the gloss ‘steel’.

summary: In Eirenaeus, the product of the Dragon–Lodestone conjunction and purgations: ‘our Chaos’, containing all the Arcana in virtue, not yet in act.
body: Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus), the text says that after the conjunction of the Dragon and the Lodestone and the purgations, “Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos, in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43]. So the Chamelion is identified with Chaos [IV.1 ¶43].

summary: The primeval thing, named by several voices; in Atwood it holds the two Principles, which may be dissevered if the internal agent wakes too soon and are to be united to a new Life.
body:
Several voices use the term:

- Khunrath (quoted): when the process is done rightly, “the new Chaos of the Universal Nature” appears unfolded and separated [III.3 ¶9].
- Ovid (quoted): “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” [III.3 ¶45] (our translation: the ancients called me Chaos, for I am a thing of old). In the same paragraph the metropolitan of Memphis gives an account in which the ‘primeval parent’, moved by the breath of Erebus, brought forth Hyle and Eros.
- Vaughan (quoted): when moist natures and central fire are set against each other, “there will be a terrible division in the Chaos” [III.4 ¶44].
- Atwood: if the internal agent wakes too soon there may be “a disseveration in the Chaos, and the two Principles stand up one against the other” [IV.1 ¶15].
- Uncertain voice: “Learn to unite the Principles of our Chaos to a new Life” [IV.2 ¶18], to be regenerated by Water and the Spirit.

The records differ: Khunrath speaks of the Chaos appearing unfolded and separated in the right process, while Vaughan and Atwood warn of a premature division of its Principles. Eirenaeus identifies the Chamelion with ‘our Chaos’ [IV.1 ¶43].

summary: In Vaughan, the nurse of Faith: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.
body: Quoting Vaughan, the text says “as God is the Father, so Charity is the nurse of Faith” [III.4 ¶44]: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.

summary: Mentioned in the Table Talk as being Jupiter and Lune, and as one who ought to have reworked her sister's book.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Charlotte Bronte is said to be Jupiter and Lune and to have ought to rework her sister's book [APP ¶175].

summary: Author of the Breviary of Philosophy, whom Atwood cites on the nested vessels, instructing the potter, and the value of a faithful servant.
body: Atwood cites Charnocke’s Breviary of Philosophy in illustration. From chap. 1, on the nested vessels and the need to instruct the potter: “One within another, it is a pretty feate, The Third without them to guide up the heate” [III.4 ¶33]. From chap. 3 (‘Idem’), on the trouble with indifferent assistants and the worth of a faithful servant [III.4 ¶34–35].

summary: Cited for the tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman, which Atwood uses to illustrate the boastings and beliefs of ignorance.
body: Atwood cites Chaucer’s tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman as illustrating the boastings and beliefs of ignorance about the art [I.1 ¶64].

summary: Unattributed Latin verse on Cheiron, teacher of Achilles, whom Atwood reads as Power and Motive in alliance educating the Heroic Fire.
body: Atwood quotes unattributed Latin verse: “Ille pius Cheiron justissimus omnes Inter Nubigenas et Magni Doctor Achillis.” [IV.1 ¶32] (our translation: that pious Cheiron, most just among all the Cloud-born, and teacher of great Achilles). She identifies Cheiron as Power and Motive in alliance, educating the Heroic Fire [IV.1 ¶33]; this reading is hers.

summary: An old name of Egypt (Cham), from the blackness of its soil according to Plutarch; also a name for the art, which the adept calls too narrow.
body: Reporting Plutarch, the text calls Egypt the art's “mother land, Cham; for so, during a long period, according to Plutarch, was Egypt denominated, or Chemia” [I.1 ¶5], named from the blackness of her soil. Thus Chemia = Egypt = Cham [I.1 ¶5]. Further, “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated, and other black matters” [I.1 ¶5]. Others derive both name and art from Cham [I.1 ¶5]. A footnote cites Suidas: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” [I.1 n8] (our translation: Chimia is the making of gold and silver). Quoting an adept, the text rejects those “who pin also the narrow name of Chemia on a science ancient and infinite” [I.2 ¶8].

summary: Atwood's word for the art in its historical record: chemical books burned, the chemists' divine water, Roman knowledge shown by the lamps.
body: Atwood uses ‘chemical’ and ‘chemists’ of the art itself in her historical survey: books teaching how to make gold and silver were condemned, so that “every chemical book was to be seized and burned together in the public market-place” [I.1 ¶18]; she mentions “a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20] and Roman knowledge of the art shown by the lamps [I.1 ¶20].

summary: In the Table Talk, fantastic forms the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it; all must be destroyed.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes fantastic forms that the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it, and says “These Chimaeras have all to be destroyed” [APP ¶171]. The context suggests these are illusory images to be cleared away in the inward work.

summary: A murky enveloping medium through whose circumference the intellect penetrates to reach the lapsed soul; not further explained.
body: Atwood speaks of the intellect penetrating “the murky circumference of the chloric ether” [II.3 ¶11] to reach the lapsed soul. The term is not further explained.

summary: An unnamed chronicle Atwood cites for the lasting visibility in Paris, as late as 1740, of Flamel's charities and symbols of the art.
body: Atwood cites a chronicle in support of the lasting evidence of Flamel in Paris as late as 1740: “the evidence of his charitable deeds remained and the symbols of the art” [I.1 ¶58].

summary: A chronicle Atwood cites for its praise of Albert at his death.
body: Atwood cites the Chronicon Magnum Belgicum for its praise of Albert at his death: “magnus in magia, major in philosophia, maximus in theologia” [I.1 ¶41] (our translation: great in magic, greater in philosophy, greatest in theology).

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited from De Nat. Deor. on the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things, and from De Legibus on the Initia as a beginning of a life of reason.
body: Atwood cites Cicero, De Nat. Deor., lib. ii, in support of the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things: “coelestis alstissima aethereaque natura” [I.2 ¶16] (our translation: the celestial, highest and ethereal nature). She also cites De Legibus, lib. 2, cap. 14, in support of the Initia as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue and of the hope of immortality [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n6]. She uses him with approval.

summary: The movement of being and, in the work, the rising and falling of the life-principles between heaven and earth by which they are rectified and exalted; the Stone is completed in three.
body:
Atwood uses circulation in two related senses. Of being as a whole: “And all things in that ultimate circulation are diaphanous” [II.4 ¶50], whereas “But in the sensible world the circulation of things is altogether different” [II.4 ¶50], since there it is broken at the circumference (compare center / circumference). The Vital Spirit ascends and descends in ‘successive circulations’ [II.4 ¶50].

In the practical work, circulation is the upward and downward movement of the life-principles between heaven and earth, which rectifies and exalts them: the operator proceeds “by carrying the circulation upward through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20]; the matter is “Thus exalted by a rotary circulation” [IV.2 ¶32]; and the Stone is “completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33].

summary: What encloses the hidden Reason; it must undergo resolution before the Reason can awaken.
body: Atwood says the hidden Reason cannot awaken “without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. The term is not further defined.

summary: The medium by which the hypostatic unit is multiplied throughout life; not further defined.
body: Atwood says the hypostatic unit is multiplied “by the circulatory medium throughout life” [IV.2 ¶37]. The term is not further defined.

summary: Nature's outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, as opposed to the root.
body: Atwood uses *circumference* for nature's outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, in contrast to the root: “For nature at the circumference subsists in this way” [III.4 ¶8].

summary: The outward life of the spirit, terrified at first by the new light and contrasted with its 'central whole'.
body: In Atwood's notes, the *circumferential life* is the outward life of the spirit. The new light at first “causes a terrification of the whole circumferential life” [I.3 n69]. It is set against a central whole, into which the spirit is spoken of as “converting her circumferential manifestations into their central whole conditionedly” [I.3 n65]. The context suggests the outward manifestations are to be drawn back into the centre.

summary: In a passage quoted from Hermes, a stage or substance extracted out of the Red, from which Botri is made.
body: In the passage quoted from Hermes, Citrine is extracted out of the Red, and Botri is made from it: “if it be citrine and nothing else know it will be thy Wisdom” [I.3 ¶41]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: According to Flammel, as reported through Eudoxus, the Mercury used for the Imbibition of the Red.
body: Eudoxus reports Flammel as saying that “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: In the Appendix, the intermediate state through which present life is led into the third life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood describes the clairvoyant life as the intermediate state through which present life passes into the third life: “this present life may be led through the clairvoyant life into it” [APP ¶2]. Compare *common trance*, in which the third life is not known.

summary: Atwood's term for the purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light.
body: Atwood speaks of a purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light: “this clarified hypostasis (shall we not believe in it?), is the stage of all Forms” [III.2 ¶26]. Elsewhere in the same chapter she uses *hypostasis* for the ground that bounds abstract reason; met by the inner light, that ground is the Absolute Identity [III.2 ¶31]. The text does not say that these two uses name the same thing, so both readings are open.

summary: Author of De Raptu Prosepinae, which Atwood quotes to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis.
body: Atwood quotes Claudian's work (spelled *de Paptu Proserpineae* / *De Raptu Prosepinae* in the text) to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis: “Jam furor humanus nostro de pectore sensus Expluit” [II.3 ¶15; II.3 ¶19; II.3 n11; II.3 n14]. She uses him as supporting illustration.

summary: Writer Atwood cites for the books of Hermes and as a witness that the Mysteries were sacred and continued in Christianity.
body: Atwood cites Clemens Alexandrinus as naming in detail the books attributed to Hermes [I.1 ¶7]. She uses him in support of her view of the Mysteries. He called them blessed: “O mysteries truly sacred, O pure light!” He also describes the Greater Mysteries as unveiling nature, with the Lord as hierophant [II.2 ¶3; II.2 ¶5; II.2 n9]. In Part IV, “the Bishop of Alexandria” is cited, with a footnote naming Clemens Alexandrinus, for the view that the Mysteries continued in Christianity, the Lord illuminating the Adepts: “It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.” [IV.2 ¶16; IV.2 n12]. The link to the footnote depends on reading the marker (2) as n12.

summary: Cited to illustrate the art's revival in Egypt, through her earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to her.
body: Atwood mentions Cleopatra when describing the art's revival in Egypt. She cites the earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to Cleopatra, including *Ars auri faciendi* [I.1 ¶18; I.1 n25].

summary: In the poem The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the learned person who will find truth in the work, as against the 'lay'.
body: In the quoted poem *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, the *Clerke* is the learned person who will find truth in the work: “For surely if thow be a Clerke, Thow wilt finde trewth in thys werke:” [III.1 ¶65]. The lay are told to keep counsel and leave off. The narrator says he is “noe Clerke” in science, yet he has laboured in the work.

summary: Something the depraved 'entangled' and climbed by into self-sufficiency; not explained in the text.
body: Atwood says the depraved climbed into self-sufficiency “basely entangling the clue of life” [III.4 ¶4]. The text does not explain the expression further.

summary: A spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose on seeing the Divine Nature; the vision in Hades is allied to it.
body: Atwood describes a spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose when they see the Divine Nature: “For to this spirit the vision in Hades is allied” [II.4 ¶19].

summary: The error of treating the Identity of Being as heaped up or compounded instead of uncompounded.
body: Atwood warns that “the Identity of every Being is something uncompounded, and that the mind should not fall into the error of coacervation” [III.2 ¶52]. Coacervation is thus the error of treating that Identity as heaped up or compounded. Compare *compounded*.
