summary: Fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution; Albertus says the cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur.
body: In the passage quoted from Albertus, coagulation is fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution: “a successive dissolution and coagulation to make the fixed volatile, and volatile fixed” [IV.1 ¶4]. The cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur. Synesius lists *coagulate* among the names of the one operation of coction (see *coction*).

summary: In a passage from Hermes, a coal whose life is fire; extinct, it becomes a dead body and is returned to the water for thirty days.
body: In the passage quoted from Hermes: “The life of the coal is fire, which being extinct, becomes a dead body” [I.3 n22]. The extinct coal is returned to the water for thirty days. The text gives no plain meaning.

equivalences.with: dissolve, calcine, tinge, whiten, renew, bathe, wash, coagulate, imbibe, fix, grind, dry, distill

summary: The cooking or maturing of the matter; Synesius says all the named operations are only names for this single operation.
body:
Coction is the cooking, digesting or maturing of the matter.

- **Atwood** speaks of the elixir obtained “through superior skill and coction in the vegetal life” [I.2 ¶46].
- **Basil Valentine** calls it the boiling and maturing of the stone of Fire with the corporeal fire of the microcosm: “let no man wonder at this coction” [III.1 ¶37].
- **During the severation**, Atwood writes, “a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. The waters decoct the sensual dominant, and the dragons are decocted in their own venom.
- **Synesius** describes a gentle, gradual and long cooking, “the coction of this water”. He treats it as the single operation: dissolve, calcine, tinge, whiten, renew, bathe, wash, coagulate, imbibe, fix, grind, dry and distill “are all one, and signify no more than to decoct nature until such time as she be perfected” [III.3 ¶60].
- **Decoction**, Atwood reports, is what Hermes calls the first part of the work: “the former Hermes calls decoction, which dissolving the matter discharges also its impurities by a proper rule” [I.3 n7]. It reduces the matter until it is close to annihilation and free of every outward form.
- **Zachary** treats the cooking as continuing until it is complete: “donec decoctio compleatur” (ours: until the decoction is completed) [IV.1 ¶9].

summary: Cited for reference only.
In a passage from Hermes, named as one of several substances that are also sulphur.
body: In the passage quoted from Hermes, colcothar is named as a kind of sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20].

summary: In Iamblicus, the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations and pertaining to Illumination.
body: Iamblicus, as quoted, calls the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations, Collective. It pertains to Illumination and “was called Collective, having for its object to gather the mental powers into accord with their leader” [III.4 ¶24]. Compare *Communion of Operation*, the second class.

summary: The stages of colour the work passes through; in Hermes' division of the Water, colour is a third part, a coagulating moisture.
body: The colours are the stages the work must pass through. In Hermes' division of the Water, colour is one third part: “the one third part of which is colour, that is to say --- a coagulating moisture” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast says Hermes divides the colours “into three red spirits and three white, which have their growth all from the same identical water” [I.3 n5].

summary: In Norton's Ordinal, a mixing-in of something, to be avoided.
body: Norton's Ordinal warns: “Beware of Commixtion that nothing miscape.” [IV.1 ¶28]. Commixtion is a mixing-in of something that must be avoided.

equivalences.with: the agent of present-day mesmerizing / photogenic medium / New Imponderable

summary: For Atwood, the agent at work in present-day mesmerism and also the Alchemists' subject-matter: indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will.
body: Atwood identifies the Common Soul with “the identical agent which is spread abroad in the present day mesmerizing, the photogenic medium, our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul”. She says it is “also the subject-matter of the Alchemists aforesaid” [II.2 ¶18]. It is indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will: “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” [II.2 ¶18]. This is a central identity for her method: the mesmeric agent and the alchemical matter are one.

summary: In the Appendix, the entranced life of sleep-walkers, produced by fermenting present life by its similar; the third life is not known in it.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says that fermenting present life by its similar “leads into the common trance, or is entranced” [APP ¶3]. She equates the common trance with “the common entranced life, i.e., the life of the sleep-walkers” [APP ¶2]. The third life is not known in it. Compare *clairvoyant life*.

summary: The connection the work requires; it is disturbed by air currents, and communion with superiors needs a heavenly way of life.
body: Atwood says that “Strong currents of air are well known to disturb communion” [III.4 ¶42]. She also warns that a heavenly way of life is needed, “otherwise thou canst have no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

summary: In Iamblicus, what the second class of prayer pertains to; it effects the bonds of concordant spirits.
body: Iamblicus, as quoted, says that the second class of prayer pertains to a Communion of Operation: “the second, to a Communion of Operation” [III.4 ¶24]. This class effects the bonds of concordant spirits before intellectual alliance. Compare *Collective*.

summary: In Vaughan, what is to be sought where extremes meet; not further defined.
body: Vaughan, as quoted, advises: “where extremes meet, there look for complexions” [III.4 ¶44]. The text does not define the term further.

equivalences.with: mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur (per Geber)

summary: In Eudoxus, the compound the Wise man makes by secret union of the fixed with the volatile; Geber's mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur.
body: Eudoxus says of the compound of Art: “it is the Wise man who makes it by the secret union of the fixed with the volatile” [IV.3 ¶9]. It is always made by the Artist and is not altogether the same in the Second and Third Work. He adds: “Geber defines it, a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9]. Compare *compound of Nature*.

summary: In Eudoxus, the compound treated in the First Key, made by Nature in ways the Artist cannot understand; he only aids her by external things.
body: Eudoxus says: “The first is the compound of Nature, whereof I have spoken in the First Key” [IV.3 ¶9]. Nature makes it in a way the Artist cannot understand, and he only aids her by external things. Compare *compound of Art*.

summary: Atwood's term for the art's matter: one essence containing everything yet separated in each particular, the ground of the magians' elements.
body: Atwood calls the art's matter “the compound simple of this art”. The hen's egg corresponds to it, except in catholicity [I.3 n26]. In Part II she describes it as “an essence all comprehending, yet separated in each particular, by so great an interval from itself” [II.2 ¶19]. She identifies it with the Monster and the Eternal Riddle: “This is the Monster and the Eternal Riddle explained to common sense as suits it, but misunderstood to this day; that Compound Simple”. She also calls it the ground of the elements: “that Compound Simple and ground of the magians’ elements” [II.2 ¶19].

summary: Whatever is mixed or impure; it cannot approach the divine Fire, which destroys and separates it.
body: In a passage drawing on Sendivogius, *compounded* means whatever is mixed or impure: “nothing that is filthy or compounded, or blemished may come near Him” [II.4 ¶39]. The divine Fire destroys and separates what is compounded. It is unclear whether this view is Atwood's own or reported from Sendivogius; the records tag both voices. Compare *coacervation*.

summary: In Iamblichus, contributing causes: the soul's best dispositions and purity, which accompany the work without being its principal cause.
body: Iamblichus, as quoted, names “all the best dispositions of the soul, and also the purity pertaining, as certain concauses” [II.4 ¶31]. They are contributing causes that accompany the work without being its principal cause.

summary: Degrees of concentration through which, Atwood says, the agent is promoted and fortified; she does not explain them further.
body: Atwood speaks of the agent being fortified “when promoted through a second to a third of concentration” [III.4 ¶9]. The text names these degrees but does not explain what each involves.

summary: The receiving medium through which universal principles are conceived; Atwood says nature lacks a true one, and that truth depends on its purity.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “There is no such thing as truth absolute in nature, because she has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]. The receiving medium must be pure and simple if truth is to be conceived: “Thus everything depends on the purity of the receiving power.” [APP ¶43]. See also *conceptive vehicle*.

summary: The vehicle of conception; Atwood blames the ancients' obscure teaching about it for great error, and says the soul may dissolve its own, the parental bond.
body: Atwood says that “the obscure instructions of the ancients concerning the nature of their conceptive vehicle, has caused incalculable error and confusion” [II.1 ¶8]; she does not define it further there. Elsewhere she treats it as the soul's vehicle from conception, which the soul may dissolve, and identifies it with the parental bond: “she may dissolve her own conceptive vehicle, even the parental bond” [II.3 ¶37]. In the Appendix (a later layer) she says nature “has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]; see *conceptive medium*.

summary: In Norton's verses, an agreement or fit between the art and its requisites, numbered as successive Concords (ministers, places, instrument).
body: The term comes chiefly from Norton, quoted by Atwood. He numbers the Concords: “The Second Concord with this Arte is,” [III.4 ¶36] (concerning apt ministers), and “The Fourth Concord is full notable Between this arte and places convenable” [III.4 ¶41]. He also speaks of the fit of the art with its instrument: “Without full concord of arte with hys instrument” [III.4 ¶39]. Atwood herself uses ‘concord’ for the joining of prayer, self-sacrifice and the faculties of the mind [III.4 ¶28].

summary: Cited once, critically: Atwood rejects his sensual system, together with Locke's.
body: Atwood names Condillac only to criticize his sensual system, along with Locke's [II.1 ¶34].

summary: What man can do in the work: prepare the conditions by patient, disciplined labour, without being able to compel the Divine blessing.
body: Atwood: “Man may conditionate: --- ought, by patient labour disciplining, to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20]. The context sets this human preparation against the Divine blessing, which man cannot compel. See *conditionating*.

summary: Placing oneself under conditions in obedience to the Divine Will, as opposed to searching in one's own will alone.
body: Atwood contrasts searching in one's own will alone with proceeding “by conditionating, in obedience to the Divine Will” [IV.4 ¶23]. See *conditionate*.

summary: The mixture or compound of the work; Hermes says the ferment whitens it, and Atwood warns that a premature permanent confection yields an offspring that does not abide.
body: Hermes, quoted by Atwood, says “the ferment whitens the confection” [I.3 ¶58], and protects it from combustion. Atwood uses the word for a permanent fixing that must not come too early: “if any permanent confection is made or suffered to take place beforehand, the immature offspring does not abide” [IV.1 ¶48].

summary: A fitting faculty of sight without which, Atwood says, the research cannot be carried on; she does not define it.
body: Atwood says of the research: “nor can it be prosecuted without a congenial Sight” [IV.4 ¶32]. The text gives no further definition.

equivalences.with: tetraptive (Ripley); fountain of Pythagoras; Divine Tetractys

summary: The union of the principles in the work, in stages, consummated in a final indissoluble Conjunction that generates a more perfect offspring; Atwood equates it with the circulated Form of Gold.
body:
In Atwood's account, conjunction is the union of the principles (in III.3, of Mars and Venus [III.3 ¶11]), during which a spirituous vapour rises; “in the various hours of conjunction” come Darkness, Saturn and the Head of the Crow [III.3 ¶13].

She distinguishes stages: “In the first conjunction the Spirit predominates; in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light” [III.3 ¶30]. The final Conjunction cannot be dissolved and produces an offspring unlike and more perfect than its parents: “that Conjunction will generate a branch of unlike shape to its parents” [III.3 ¶29].

She gives it several names: “This then is the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation --- the true circulated Form of Gold” [III.3 ¶33]; and “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In III.4 the agent goes on “further multiplying in the Conjunction” [III.4 ¶9], and Norton, quoted there, speaks of unions man may not undo without grace: “For God’s conjunctions man my not undoe” [III.4 ¶10]. Atwood also describes a stage at which the work passes beyond human control: “There is a period too, when in conjunction, the Spirit transcends all earthly control” [III.4 ¶20], recreating under the Divine Hand alone.

summary: The inborn spirit of the soul, whose attractive grace subdues the self-willed agent; Julian says the deified soul strengthens it, making it the safety of the whole body.
body:
Atwood says the self-willed agent is subdued and brought to self-mortification because “it is by the attractive grace of the connate spirit” [III.1 ¶63]; the following ‘This Spirit’, which has self-motion and intelligence, very probably refers to the connate spirit (an inference from context).

Julian, quoted by Atwood, says of the deified soul that “she transfuses a certain vigorous strength into her connate spirit” [IV.3 ¶30], which then becomes the cause of safety to the whole body.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes what happens “when the connate spirit is deprived of its understanding spirit” [APP ¶109]: its life flows away until it rallies from a new center by self-realization.

summary: The inner faculty that, through persevering inward search, reveals higher objects of pursuit.
body: Atwood urges inward search “until Conscience reveal to us those higher objects of pursuit, and truer attractions” [IV.3 ¶50]. See also *contrition*, where she places the manifestation of Light in the distress of the sensible nature in the conscience [III.3 ¶24].

summary: The mode of knowing by which, Atwood says, Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation, as opposed to teaching or inference.
body: Atwood says Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation “not by outward teaching or rational inference from effects, but by the Conscious Intuition” [III.3 ¶49].

summary: In Norton's verses, the celestial influence to which the Stone's elements are most obedient during its generation.
body: Norton, quoted by Atwood, says the elements of the Stone during generation “Have most obedience to constellation” [IV.2 ¶34].

summary: Sharing one substance: Atwood says all things, however various, are consubstantial in their Cause.
body: Atwood: “all things, however various in manifestation, are consubstantial in their Cause” [III.2 ¶35].

summary: The burning, wrathful state of the Prester below, which it ceases to be when placed in the supreme Ether.
body: Atwood describes the Prester placed in the supreme Ether as “not burning as below, or wrathful; but vital, calm, transmuting, recreating, and no longer a Consuming Fire” [II.3 ¶56]. ‘Consuming Fire’ thus names its lower, destructive state.

summary: The containing life which must be preserved when the spirit's external forms are dissolved.
body: In a footnote Atwood describes the task as being “to dissolve without destroying the continental life” [I.3 n62]: the spirit's external forms are to be dissolved while the containing life is kept.

summary: The distress of the sensible nature in the conscience, the great darkness in which Light appears; in the Appendix, repeated contritions absorb the sensuous medium.
body:
Atwood says “the Light is made manifest in great darkness, viz., in the contrition or distress of the sensible nature in the conscience” [III.3 ¶24], so identifying contrition with that great darkness. The flinty conscience “feels no contrition, but by the fiery well-tempered steel” [III.3 ¶11]. The word is also applied to the fretting of particles in fermentation.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), contrition is stirred in the surrounding spirit by the growing Light of the Salt, and “reiterative contritions absorbing the sensuous medium” [APP ¶78] change the circulation of the blood.

summary: In Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, the purified soul's turning to associate with its generator: the only way to scientific knowledge of true Being.
body: Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, describes the purified soul's turning toward its generator as the only route to scientific knowledge of true Being, “which cannot be obtained either otherwise or without such a conversion” [II.3 ¶43].

equivalences.with: procession from and return to the One

summary: The reversal of natures, making light things heavy and active passive and the reverse; Atwood calls by this name all diversity proceeding from and returning to the One.
body:
Arnold, quoted by Atwood, tells the seeker to “understand the conversion of the elements, to make light things heavy, and to make spirits no spirits” [I.2 ¶22], and says that “our operation is nothing else than a mutation of natures” [I.2 ¶25], reducing them to their first root.

Atwood gives her own account: “a conversion of the elements in this respect is just to make active passive and passive active” [III.3 ¶29], the occult manifest and the manifest occult. She widens the term to the whole cycle: “all diversities of things are seen to proceed from and return to this only One; which is called a conversion of the elements” [III.3 ¶29].

equivalences.with: variously discussing and meditating many things

summary: In Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, the mental labour that accompanies prayer, so that prayer is not a tempting of God.
body: Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, defines it: “when you incline your mind to this or that, variously discussing and meditating many things, this is cooperation” [III.4 ¶22]. This labour must go with prayer, so that prayer is not ‘a tempting of God’.

equivalences.with: first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art
quintessential virtue of the New Life

summary: The imperishable quintessential virtue of the New Life and first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art, rejected by ignorance and known only to those who have it in themselves.
body:
Atwood identifies the Corner Stone with the foundation and fruit of the work: it “is the Corner Stone or first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶66]; “the New Life thence arises whose quintessential virtue, imperishable and perpetually victorious, is the Corner Stone” [III.1 ¶66]. It is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise, because they alone can know it who have it in themselves” [III.1 ¶66].

It is brought to light by the work in a proper vessel; without this “the ethereal corner stone would never have been brought to light” [II.1 ¶8], and it is raised within the ‘living temple’: “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8]. Atwood calls for “faith to resuscitate the Corner Stone, which ignorance has rejected from immemorial time” [IV.3 ¶37].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), she says “Everything is in the perfected Corner Stone” [APP ¶134], the state in which the whole regenerate life-force is brought up into head-consciousness, and treats the Hermetic Stone as the analogue of the Chief Corner Stone.

summary: The sensual principle, predominant in the mundane conception, which hides the divine original from consciousness.
body: Atwood glosses the word herself: “by the corporeal, i.e., the sensual principle which is predominant in the mundane conception” [III.3 ¶52]. In the passage this principle obscures the divine original from consciousness.

summary: The dissolved body, which a Latin sentence in the text calls a perennial water congealing Mercury.
body: The text gives the Latin “Corpus solutum est aqua perennis congelans Mercurium perpetua congelatione.” [III.3 ¶21], with no translation in the book and no clear speaker. Our rendering: ‘The dissolved body is a perennial water, congealing Mercury with a perpetual congelation.’ The identity of the dissolved body with perennial water rests on this translation, which is ours.

summary: A term Atwood borrows from the Swedenborgians for the relation of the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood relates the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit, and adds: “There is, as the Swedenborgians would say, a correspondence between them.” [APP ¶15].

summary: In Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, the agents wrongly credited with the single combat of dissolution; the real agent is a specific loosening virtue.
body: Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, rejects reliance on Corrosives acting through ‘Second qualities’: “They err, therefore, who ascribe this single combat only to Corrosives” [IV.1 ¶39]. The true agent, he says, is a specific virtue of loosening.

summary: Dissolution, which belongs only to composites; in a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses, artificial corruption especially manifests the underlying subject.
body: In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses: “This therefore Corruption manifests (especially the artificial), for corruption is of that which is composite” [III.2 ¶48]. Corruption, then, is dissolution of what is composite, and the artificial kind reveals the subject beneath.

summary: The sudden flashing of the released light; Atwood calls the life at the center of the lower life, Apollo, coruscant.
body: Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood calls the flashing center of the lower life Apollo: “Apollo is that life, and it is coruscant” [APP ¶49]; setting it free produces harmony. Of the released light she says “it shines forth with a sudden coruscation feeding on the surrounding ether” [APP ¶126].

summary: An authority Atwood cites with approval on reconciling fire and water and, through his allegory of the old man, on purifying the Mercury.
body: Atwood cites Cosmopolite in support on reconciling fire and water: “All things must therefore being purged make Fire and Water to be Friends, which they will easily do in their earth, which had ascended with them.” [IV.3 ¶7]. She also uses his ‘ingenious allegory’ of the old man (Mercury) on purifying the Mercury and the whole magistery: “if you shall give our old man gold and silver to swallow, that he may consume them, and at length he also dying may be burnt” [IV.3 ¶10]. She draws on his naming of the Mercury as water, steel and lodestone, on gold coupling eleven times, and on the Chalybes. She offers all of this as confirmation of the secret of the two mercuries [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: That in and with which, Atwood says, the third life moves.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3].

summary: A publication (new series, No. 13, 1845) that Atwood cites as the source of the English translations of an epitaph.
body: Atwood cites *The Critic*, new series, No. 13 (1845), as the source of the English translations of an epitaph she gives [I.1 ¶22] [I.1 n30]. It is a reference only.

summary: A cited source (Idem, p. 248) used to support the view that Intellect is a God-given sight which mortals lack through generation.
body: Atwood cites Crito (as “Idem, page 248”) in support of the view that Intellect is a sight given by God, which mortals lack through generation: “gave him a sight called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God” [II.1 ¶38] [II.1 n35]. She uses the passage approvingly.

summary: A disciple of Paracelsus whose *Philosophy Reformed* Atwood cites repeatedly and approvingly on the vital spirit in man, the true physician, and what the operator must be.
body:
Atwood names Crollius among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, with Van Helmont, Fludd, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. She notes that *The Philosophy of J. Crollius* carries the Addresses to the Athenians in English [I.1 ¶64]. She lists him as an adept, citing *Philosophy Reformed* in Pinnel's translation [I.1 ¶70] [I.1 n81].

She quotes him with approval on several points:
- **The vital spirit in man.** In *Philosophy Reformed* he holds that the gold-producing vapour is in man: “the same is the generating spirit of all creatures”. He also describes the true physician [II.1 ¶12] [II.1 n9] [II.1 ¶14] [II.1 n13].
- **Fire and the physician.** From *The True Physic*, chap. 1: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated”. Atwood uses this for trial by fire, for the separation made by the natural inbred chemist, and for the physician born of the light of grace [III.1 ¶10] [III.1 n8].
- **Means of the work.** In the Admonitory Preface of Oswald Crollius, great things come from preparation, contemplation, handiwork and grace: “by a holy assiduity of preparations, joining thereto diligent contemplation of natural causes” [III.1 ¶13] [III.1 n12].
- **Who can do the work.** The slothful and profane are unfit: “these Chemical Secrets will never be fingered by those slothful or sottish despisers of them” [IV.1 ¶6] [IV.1 n4].

summary: The passage or condition under which the old life is crucified and a new one germinates: all is sown under it, and the soul must pass under it before regeneration.
body:
Quoting Jacob Boehme, Atwood gives the Cross as what one must enter “in the Fourth Form”, where Sol and Luna are together, in order to seek gold: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48]. Her own gloss speaks of crucifixion: “out of that crucifixion, by reunion of the principles under another law, the new life is elicited” [III.1 ¶49].

In her own voice, “All is sown under the cross and completed in its number” [III.3 ¶13]. Under the cross fire and water fall together and germinate. A reader's translation (ours, not the book's) has true Wisdom coming under it [III.3 ¶14]. She links this to “out of the crucifixion of the cerebral life” [III.3 ¶15].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the soul passes under its Cross before the residuum supplies its regenerate body, and the earth becomes its punctum saliens: “after that the soul has passed under its Cross” [APP ¶110].

The context suggests that the Cross stands for a death of the ordinary, cerebral life. A new life, joined under another law, then comes out of it.

summary: In Hermes as glossed by Atwood, the chief principle of the art: the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state early in the work; one with the vulture.
body:
In a passage of Hermes that Atwood glosses, the Crow is the chief principle of the art. It is the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state, at the early stage where the revived spirit is joined with its solar ferment: “the crow is also in the infancy of that work wherein the revivified spirit is united with its solar ferment” [I.3 n12].

It is identified with the vulture: “The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate” [I.3 n12].

equivalences.with: first manifested resplendence of the vital tincture

summary: Atwood's gloss on Hermes: the first visible resplendence of the vital tincture, the king triumphing over death when the colours appear.
body: Atwood explains the image directly: “By the crowned king, Hermes signifies the first manifested resplendence of the vital tincture” [I.3 n22]. The figure is the king triumphing over death when the colours appear. The meaning is stated by the text.

summary: The transparent state to which all things must be reduced before the Work truly begins.
body: Atwood writes that, before the Work truly begins, “all things are reduced to a crystalline diaphaneity” [IV.1 ¶48]. It apparently names a necessary preliminary state of complete clarity in the matter.

summary: The condition matter has lain under since the fall; the work aims to redeem matter from it.
body: For Atwood, the curse is the condition matter has lain under since the fall, and the aim of the work is to free matter from it: to “deliver matter from the original curse” and “to redeem matter from the curse, and to raise it from the dead” [IV.3 ¶38].

summary: A Church Father whom Atwood cites as taking up the rites of the Mysteries and veiling the church's mysteries in enigmas.
body: Atwood cites St Cyrillus as a Church Father who adopted the rites of the Mysteries. She uses him to support her claim that the church hid its mysteries in enigmas: “except in obscure terms, in such a manner, however, as that the faithful who are initiated may comprehend, and the rest be discouraged” [II.2 ¶3] [II.2 ¶5] [II.2 n9].

headword: D. Fabianus de Monte, S. Severin
forms: D. Fabianus de Monte, S. Severin
summary: Author of *Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione* (Quest. 5), cited in a footnote for a definition of Alchemy.
body: Atwood cites *Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione*, Quest. 5, in a footnote. The words quoted are “Alchimia est ars perspicaci” [I.1 n52] (our rendering: Alchemy is an art for the perceptive). It is a reference only.

summary: A fable Atwood uses to illustrate the hand and fiery art bringing the metallic veins to light, as the hand expresses a thought formed beforehand.
body: Atwood uses the fable as an illustration: “Such were those Dactyli Idaei, literally the Fingers of Mount Ida” [IV.1 ¶34]. They stand for the hand and fiery art that bring the metallic veins to light, in the way the hand expresses a thought already formed.

summary: In a passage of Ricardus, something overthrown by the enigmas; the text does not define it.
body: In a sentence by Ricardus about study wiping away ignorance: “by these enigmas the Dagon is overthrown” [III.4 ¶20]. The text does not define it. The context suggests it stands for the ignorance that study removes.

summary: In Reuchlin as quoted: dark Aleph is the hidden essence, which becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension.
body: Atwood quotes Reuchlin. Dark Aleph is the hidden essence. It becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension: “is dark Aleph converted into light Aleph” [III.2 ¶10].

summary: In Boehme's scheme of the Three Worlds, a procreation or outer birth: a substance expressed from the internal and spiritual worlds.
body: In Boehme's Three Worlds, as Atwood gives them, the dark world is “a procreation or extern birth or, as it were, a substance expressed or spoken forth from the internal and spiritual worlds” [III.2 ¶16]. It is identified with the outer (“extern”) birth.

summary: In a passage of the Master, what the stone brings forth after Light: the clouds, called the mother of all things.
body: In a passage of the Master that Atwood quotes, the stone after the Light “brings forth the clouds, or darkness, which is the mother of all things” [III.1 ¶49]. Darkness is here equated with the clouds.

headword: darkness upon the Abyss (unattributed in the text)
summary: An unattributed image Atwood uses as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light in the hyperphysical work.
body: Atwood uses the image, without naming a source, as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light during the hyperphysical work: “as there was darkness upon the Abyss when the Divine Spirit moved upon the Water’s face” [III.1 ¶60].

summary: Cited, via the 68th Psalm, on the Divine presence driving out what is alien, within Ripley's verse, and among the Hebrew prophets on the Wheel of Fire.
body: Atwood names David with Ezekiel, Moses, Zachariah and the Hebrew prophets in illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. He is cited inside Ripley's verse about the waters passing away: “Abierunt in sicco flumina” [III.1 ¶57] (our rendering: the rivers went away into dry land). In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the 68th Psalm illustrates the alien being driven out when the Divine presence arises: “as wax before the fire” [APP ¶157].

summary: Cited for reference only.

headword: De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet
forms: De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet
summary: A group Atwood praises as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism; she says the science has gone backward since them.
body: Atwood praises De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend and Dupotet as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism. She says the science has gone backward since their time [II.2 ¶6].

summary: A writer cited throughout the Appendix with approval, on numbers, the divine names, regeneration, and the earth as crucible of souls.
body:
All citations fall in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood praises him as having entered the centre of substantial life [APP ¶112–115]. She cites him approvingly on the following points:
- **The Crown.** With Behmen, he is the source of the phrase “the Crown” [APP ¶104].
- **Numbers.** From *Corresp.*, p. 298: “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]. Atwood extends this to outer nature and to scriptural tradition.
- **Correspondence**, letter 30, and *Theos. Correspondence*, p. 117. With Eckhartshausen, he is cited on the change in the circulation of the blood. He is also a reference on The Name speaking in us and on the mineral earth [APP ¶78] [APP ¶88] [APP ¶89].
- **The two Testaments.** From *Theos. Corresp.*, p. 244: their foundation lies “in the true pronunciation of the two great names” [APP ¶98]. Atwood glosses this as the revealed utterance of the life of God in man.
- **The regenerate body.** From *Tableau Naturel*, vol. 2, p. 230 (spelled “Se St Martin” there): “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]. He is cited on the residue of the sensual medium giving body to the regenerate soul.
- **Law and inquiry.** From *Reply*, p. 364, he is cited on a perfect law that works by degrees. His answers to a friend's particular question illustrate universal truth exploding questions, like the Hermetic inquiry [APP ¶112] [APP ¶113] [APP ¶115].

summary: In Norton, clay that has been heavily roasted; ground and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.
body: Norton, quoted by Atwood: “Dead clay is called such a thing, As hath suffered great roasting” [III.4 ¶31]. Ground to powder and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.

summary: In a quoted adept's verse, where the nucleus of Salt lies, to be guarded in holy silence; not explained.
body: A quoted adept, called “the mysterious adeptest”, speaks of Salt “whose nucleus in the Decad guard in holy silence” [III.3 ¶50]. The text does not explain the Decad.

summary: Diarist whose diary Atwood cites as evidence of Kelly's projection and of Kelly possibly revealing the secret to him.
body: Atwood cites Dee's Diary (n74: Sept. 1586) as a source for Kelly's projection and for the possible discovery of the secret: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me, God be thanked.” [I.1 ¶66] [I.1 ¶67] [I.1 n74].

summary: The dead philosophers whose testimony, Atwood says, is the only evidence on which Alchemy can be imagined to be real.
body: Atwood says the testimony of defunct philosophers is the only evidence on which Alchemy may be imagined real [IV.4 ¶12].

summary: In Aristotle as reported by Atwood, the condition reached when the understanding touches its cause; only the duly initiated are capable of it.
body: In Atwood's report of Aristotle, deification is attained by contact of the understanding with its cause. Only the initiated can reach it: “duly initiated and capable of this deification” [II.1 ¶37].

summary: The creative fire the gods manifest through Intellect in Light, borne by Minerva as Phosphor; hidden from man by sensual conception.
body:
In Atwood's account, the gods manifest the Demiurgic Fire through Intellect in Light. “Minerva is sometimes called Phosphor, as being the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [II.4 ¶26]. To Theurgists the gods show a self-visible Fire: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

It is the creative fire borne by Wisdom. Ordinary sense-bound thinking hides it, “that Fire which the sensual conception occultates, and so forcibly restricts, that man does not suspect it even” [III.3 ¶71]. The context suggests it is the hidden fire the method seeks to release.

summary: That with which Theurgic sacrifice seeks to be joined; not further defined.
body: Atwood says Theurgic sacrifice seeks “a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She does not define it further.

summary: A philosopher Atwood treats as an adept of the sacred art: his reduction of matter, the Fable of Proteus, and his pyrographic portrayal of the work.
body:
**Source and standing.** Atwood presents Democritus of Abdera, author of a book of Sacred Physics (*de Arte Sacra*), as treating the Hermetic art and the occult discovery under ancient philosophy. She names him as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶12] [I.1 ¶20] [I.1 n14] [I.1 n20]. Synesius wrote a commentary on him [I.1 ¶27]. Norton's verse lists “Democrit” among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Norton also reports him as naming the Water: “Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient;” [III.3 ¶74].

**The method.** Atwood endorses his proposal, as Bacon reports it, to reduce matter almost to annihilation and so free the spirit [I.2 ¶24]. Through the Fable of Proteus the matter, near annihilation, restores itself by an inbred force [I.3 n7]. The fable also supports binding the matter: “that method of working with nature is the most effectual that makes use of manacles and fetters” [I.3 n37]. He is cited for “Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36]. With Hermes, he repeats the process of the Vital Spirit [II.1 ¶25]. He hints that the changes stop only when Art brings the Matter into the fixity of its Final Cause [III.2 ¶22]. Following Bacon, Atwood calls the Experiment “the Art of Democritus” [III.3 ¶61].

**The Vulcanic action.** The *Flammelli Summula* gathers sayings from him. It shows, in operative language, the burning of the Brazen Body and Venus becoming golden: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily” [I.3 n49] [I.3 n53]. Atwood says he portrays the Vulcanic action “before all, and as it were pyrographically”: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily, instructs this Abderite” [IV.1 ¶43] [IV.1 n40]. She calls him “our Abderite”.

Having seen it, he laughed at other things [IV.4 ¶27].

summary: Atwood's term for 'the whole' that is first not yet animated by its own returning light, later animated and shining from the dark abyss; apparently the whole subject of the work.
body: Atwood uses the name in two linked passages (spelled two ways). First: “For it is the whole Demogogon, as yet not actually animated by contact of his own returning light” [II.3 ¶30]. Later: “For it is the whole Demogorgon, now actually animated, which before was made visible without its subject light” [II.3 ¶52]. There it is ignited and shines from the dark abyss of being as a luciferous wheel. The text does not otherwise define it. The context suggests it names the whole subject of the work before and after its own light returns to it.

summary: Apparitional beings arising from the enclosed vapour of imagination, children of matter at war with the truth-seeking soul; also Hermes' revenging Demon that torments the wicked.
body:
**Atwood's account.** The demons of antiquity are apparitional beings born of a confined vapour of imagination: “all the race of demons, so much celebrated by antiquity, appear to have their origin in a life of this kind, viz., from an included vapor of the imagination” [II.3 ¶22]. They are called the children of matter: “as the progeny of matter, and as having an energetic virtue, but at natural war with the truth-seeking soul” [II.3 ¶24]. They are said to have sense, arts and an operative life, which they use to deceive, and they are given life by desire. The Chaldaic oracle also speaks of “pure demons”.

**Hermes (Poemander).** Among the wicked, the Mind gives way to the Demon: “giving place to the revenging Demon, which, applying unto him the sharpness of fire, tormenteth such a man sensibly” [III.3 ¶57]. When the body dissolves, this Demon receives the “idle manners”.

summary: Cited for reference only.
That toward which even Matter extends, identified with the Good.
body: The text says even Matter is “extended to the desirable, i.e., to the Good” [III.4 ¶28]. It identifies the desirable with the Good. The speaker is unclear from the record.

summary: For Atwood, the longing of the mind for its object, through which the research is ultimately made manifest and which prayer enlarges.
body: Atwood speaks of the inquiry as “a research which is so much wrapped in and about the Desire as to be ultimately made manifest through its means” [III.4 ¶20]. She treats every desire as a kind of prayer, and prayer in turn works “(by enlarging the desire)” [III.4 ¶24]. The record suggests Desire is the motive force of the method: the research depends on it and comes to light through it.

summary: Scriptural book Atwood cites in support of the unfigured form of the Divine Essence.
body: Atwood cites Deuteronomy 4:15, “Take good heed unto yourselves, for ye saw no manner of similitude on the say that the Lord spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n52], to support her point that the Divine Essence is without figure.

summary: In Eudoxus, what the wise make fall upon the earth so that it yields precious fruit; not further explained.
body: Spoken by Eudoxus (quoted): the wise make it fall upon the earth, “knowing how to make the dew of Heaven fall upon it” [IV.3 ¶12], so that it bears precious fruit. The text does not explain the expression further; its plain meaning in the method is unclear.

summary: In Rabbi Ben Jocahi, the dew shaken from the head of the hidden principle, which awakens the dead and nourishes the saints; identified with manna.
body: Quoted from Rabbi Ben Jocahi: “Thy dew is the dew of light” [III.2 ¶3]. This dew falls from the head of the hidden principle, awakens the dead, nourishes the saints and is white as the diamond. It is identified with manna: “It is this which nourishes the most exalted saints, the manna which descends into the field of sacred fruits” [III.2 ¶3].

summary: For Atwood, a figure of the First Matter and refulgent Light: the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature personified, containing all elements of being.
body: Atwood presents Diana as the First Matter and the refulgent Light, personifying the whole Fundamental Nature, inferior and superior together: “she is the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature at once personified, the knot and link of all the elements o being” [III.1 ¶70].

summary: A term in a Proclus passage, named alongside 'our individual reason'; not further defined.
body: Appears in a passage of Proclus (quoted), where the spirit “becomes perfectly everything from which dianoia and our individual reason consist” [II.2 ¶15]. The text gives no further definition; it is apparently a reasoning faculty listed beside individual reason.

summary: Author of de Quintessentia, cited by Atwood for an account of powder of transmutation found in Lully's Westminster cell.
body: Atwood cites E. Dickenson's *de Quintessentia* for the story of powder of transmutation discovered in Lully's cell at Westminster [I.1 ¶47; I.1 n57]. She uses it as reported testimony; the records show no comment from her on it.

summary: John Digby, given as translator of the French edition of Sendivogius' New Light of Alchemy (London 1722), which adds the Treatise on Salt and a Dialogue.
body: Named in a note on Sendivogius' *New Light of Alchemy*, London 1722: Digby translated from the French edition, which adds the Treatise on Salt and an instructive Dialogue [I.1 ¶71; I.1 n91]. Atwood refers to this as Digby's edition.

summary: An operation by which the powder is multiplied, and a measured process required before perfect dissolution and before extraction of the Fixed Salt.
body: Two quoted voices use the term. An adept (quoted) says the white or red powder is multiplied tenfold with each digestion, and “each digestion is made in tenfold shorter time than the preceding” [II.1 ¶25]. Eudoxus (quoted) requires digestion before perfect dissolution in the Second Key, “after a proportioned digestion and putrefaction” [IV.3 ¶5], and before extracting the Fixed Salt in the Third Key, by “a convenient digestion and a slow distillation” [IV.3 ¶7]. In both cases it is a measured, staged operation within the work.

summary: Authority cited by Atwood for the divine darkness, visible yet incomprehensible, and for the True Thing of negative theology.
body: Atwood cites Dionysius in support of the divine darkness, the “caligo divina” [III.2 ¶13], which is visible yet beyond comprehension. She also draws on him for the True Thing of negative theology, whose possession is the happiest life [III.2 ¶15]. She uses him with approval.

summary: Plato's correspondent; Atwood thinks a practical science drew him to Plato.
body: Named as Plato's correspondent. Atwood suggests he was drawn to Plato by a science she believes was practical [I.1 ¶17].

summary: Speaker in the Banquet, cited by Atwood in support of the idea that the wise mind possesses its object within itself.
body: Atwood cites Diotima in the *Banquet* in support of the idea that a wise mind holds its object within itself: “that mind which is become wise needs not to investigate any further” [II.1 ¶37]. She uses the passage with approval.

summary: Critics of Alchemy whose 'learned cavils and clamours' Atwood dismisses.
body: Atwood criticizes the disappointed chemists for their learned cavils and clamours against Alchemy [IV.4 ¶12]. She rejects their view.

summary: Anonymous voice, endorsed by Atwood, who treats material gifts as tokens of the Spirit's love.
body: A quoted disciple says of the Spirit: “then he sends us these things as tokens and pledges of his love” [IV.3 ¶46]. Atwood endorses this reading of material gifts as signs of the Spirit's love.

summary: In Proclus, meeting, union with and direct sight of the Father; not opinion or science but Intellectual Vision; the Paternal Port.
body: Defined by Proclus (quoted): “For discovery is this, --- to meet with him, to be united to Him, and to see Him Himself” [II.4 ¶41]. It is not opinion and not science but Intellectual Vision of the Father or Maker. Proclus equates it with the Paternal Port: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father” [II.4 ¶41].

summary: In Plotinus, the ordinary reasoning into which the soul falls back from Intellect after the divine state.
body: Plotinus (quoted) describes the soul after the divine state as “falling off from Intellect into the discursive energy of reason” [III.2 ¶50]. It names ordinary step-by-step reasoning, a lower condition than Intellect.

summary: The reasoning faculty which, Atwood says, plays no part in discovering and assenting to universal propositions.
body: Atwood says that in discovering universal propositions and assenting to them “there is no use of the discursive faculty or of external facts to witness” [II.1 ¶34]. Knowledge of this kind does not come by reasoning or from outside evidence.

summary: For Atwood, the core operation of the first work: an artificial loosening of the vital bond that dissolves the fixed sensual compact so the spirit can be renovated and perfected.
body:
Atwood treats dissolution as the central operation of the first work. “The beginning of the whole work is a perfect solution” [IV.1 ¶4]: the subject is dissolved in its own blood, or own mercury, to remove superfluities. The dissolution must be total, for “nothing short of dissolution can give it rest” [IV.1 ¶7].

She takes the term from the old doctrine: “We adopt the term dissolve here in accordance with the old doctrine” [II.3 n2]. She applies it to the change in the vital relation during trance, and notes that the Alchemists say the sensible medium ought to be dissolved. She calls it “an artificial dissolution of the vital bond, by means of Alchemy” [I.3 n64]. The philosophic work begins after it, and by it vapour, blackness and death are driven out: “and this by dissolution” [I.3 ¶56].

In the process, “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved, and that which is dissolved is renovated”, and “by Dissolution thou shalt possess a triumphant reward” [II.3 ¶37]. The process is repeated: “the process by which the spirit is carried on from each succeeding dissolution into a more perfect form of being” [I.3 n19]. In the same note Atwood says a radical dissolution of the spirit reveals the evil of original sin, and that dissolution by the water is the key of restoration [I.3 n19].

She also describes it as the breaking-up of the light's body and of the natural-born life, in which the three principles separate: “an eclipsation of the light takes place, and a dissolution of its body” [III.1 ¶53]. The context suggests its cause is vital heat artificially stirred in the blood [III.1 ¶53].

summary: For Atwood, the divided condition reached by 'falling off', in which one ceases to be the Universe.
body: Atwood writes that by falling off, “in becoming dividual, he ceases to be the Universe” [IV.4 ¶27]. It names the separated state opposed to unity with the whole.

summary: Atwood's name for the Art in its higher purposes: working in and with the Universal Spirit, joined with universal theosophy, beyond its mineral uses.
body:
Atwood uses Divine Art as a name for the Art. Boehme gives the “principles of the Divine Art” and a ground of experience for it [I.1 ¶68]. She separates its mineral uses (quickening and perfecting) from “the higher purposes and application of the Divine Art, and universal theosophy” [I.1 ¶42]. It requires a representative of the rebellious Principle: “that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64]. Nearby text speaks of “the Hermetic Art”, but the records do not say the two names are identical [III.1 ¶66].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “the Divine Art works in and with the Universal Spirit” [APP ¶140]. There it brings forth various states of life that offer allurements to the will, and it uses instruments as well as vessels [APP ¶140].

summary: For Atwood, the loosening of the bond between spirit and its bodily media, which Paracelsus speaks of and mesmerism imitates externally.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls mesmeric practice “an imitation of the Divine Art of the separation of which Paracelsus speaks” [APP ¶73]. The Art apparently loosens the bond between spirit and its bodily media; mesmerism imitates it only outwardly.

summary: For Atwood, a state in which, while it lasts, subject and object are not two in consciousness.
body: Atwood writes that “as in the Divine conjunction, whilst it lasts, there are not two things as of subject and object in the consciousness” [III.2 ¶66]. In it, the life that understands and the light understood are one.

summary: For Atwood, an ecstasy kindled in connection with its Source, which draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art.
body: Atwood speaks of “that kindling of Divine Ecstasy, in connection with its Source” [III.1 ¶70]. It draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art. It is apparently the active power that accomplishes the work.

summary: For Atwood, that with which the resigned Spirit is clothed; it qualifies the true Adept and is identified with the material of the Corner-Stone.
body: Atwood says the resigned Spirit is clothed with the Divine Essentiality: “And this Essentiality it is which qualifies the true Adept” [III.3 ¶24]. It also sanctifies the Adept. She identifies it with the material of the Corner-Stone: “It is this material of the Corner-Stone which links reason to Divinity” [III.3 ¶24].

equivalences.with: the first and most beautiful objects

summary: The first and most beautiful objects of Wisdom: undecaying and invariable, with other things beautiful by participating in them.
body: The phrase is Atwood's gloss on Iamblicus (quoted): Wisdom is “conversant with the first and most beautiful objects (i.e., the Divine Exemplars)” [II.1 ¶39]. They do not decay or vary, and other things are beautiful by participating in them.

summary: Addressed by Atwood as the august Mother of all things; at the Substant Unity, Experience is present with Power.
body: Atwood addresses it directly: “And thou august Mother of all things, Divine Experience.” [III.3 ¶79]. She describes the Substant Unity as the place “where Experience is present with Power, and Effect in substance to bear them witness” [III.3 ¶79].

summary: For Atwood, the inner faculty of perception which, purified and strengthened, perceives the truth of all beings.
body: Atwood, citing Plato, speaks of “that divine eye which, as Plato says, is better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶8]. Purified and strengthened, this inner faculty perceives the truth of all beings.

summary: For Atwood, the divine command that blesses the union of Soul and Passive Spirit, in which the sensual dominant is occultated and subdued.
body: Atwood writes that “the Divine Fiat comes mercifully to bless the union” of Soul and Passive Spirit [III.3 ¶10]. In it the sensual dominant is subdued: “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15].

summary: In Iamblicus, what is received in perfect plenitude through the third class of prayer, the final seal of union.
body: Iamblicus (quoted) writes that “through the energy of the third, we receive a perfect plenitude of Divine Fire” [III.4 ¶24]. The third class of prayer is the final seal of union.

summary: For Atwood, the divine seed in man, beheld in a deformed condition under the evils of its birth.
body: Atwood refers to “the divine germ of humanity said to be beheld under the thousand evils of its birth” [II.3 ¶30]. In that state it appears deformed.

summary: Atwood's term for the ground where the Scriptural phrase is seen and proved; there man may work but cannot compel the Divine Blessing.
body: Atwood speaks of what is “as seen and proved on the Divine Ground” [IV.1 ¶40]. On this ground, she says, man may experiment, plough, plant and irrigate, but he cannot compel the Divine Blessing [IV.1 ¶40].

summary: The affirmation in which Life feels itself to Be; Atwood says the Kabalah uses it to signify the Substant Unity of all that is.
body: In Atwood's account, “Life springs forth with motion, feeling itself to Be.” [III.3 ¶79]. She identifies the Divine I Am with the Substant Unity: “in the Divine I Am, is by the Kabalah signified the Substant Unity of all that is” [III.3 ¶79].

summary: What, according to Atwood, those who live profanely and without self-knowledge cannot attain, entertain or think self-actively.
body: Atwood says that those living profanely and without self-knowledge cannot “attain to the Divine Idea; either to entertain or think It self-actively is impossible” [III.3 ¶78].

summary: In Boehme as quoted, that through which all things arose from the Tincture.
body: Quoted from Boehme: “All things are thence arisen through the Divine Imagination” [III.2 ¶16]. The context ties this arising to the Tincture [III.2 ¶16].

summary: Atwood's name for the passive reception of the divine, raised by love, hope and faith, as opposed to self-active comprehension of Deity.
body: Atwood contrasts “the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] with a self-active comprehension of Deity. In this mode the divine is received passively, and the soul is raised by love, hope and faith [II.4 ¶40].

summary: A term Atwood names as the subject of a Rabbi's advice and links to creation out of nothing, but does not define.
body: Atwood refers to advice “concerning the true nature of Divine Inversion” [III.2 ¶31] and connects it with creation out of nothing. The passage does not define the term.

summary: The formless divine light that the initiate sees; Atwood says it is held captive in this life and that it turns the Quintessence into living gold. In the Appendix she calls it the Essence of Gold.
body:
**Quoted (Psellus; the Oracle).** In the Introspection, “the initiated person sees the Divine Light itself without any form or figure” [II.3 ¶46]. The oracle calls this Sacro Sancto [II.3 ¶46], and speaks of it: “When thou seest a Fire without Form” [II.3 ¶47]; this light, the quoted voices say, will not deceive.

**Atwood.** Without this revelation the operator's purpose is blind. She warns against “he who presumes without the revelation of the Divine Light to introduce his own blind purpose” [III.1 ¶38]. The new life “needs only the corroborative virtue of the Divine light which it draws” [III.1 ¶49], and this turns the Quintessence into living gold. ¶40 also mentions a guardian of the Light [III.1 ¶40]. In this life the light is kept behind “the barriers by which the Divine Light is here held in thralldom” [IV.4 ¶17], and the means of the ancients remove those barriers. “When once the Divine Light is loosened in life” [IV.3 ¶39], everything prospers so long as her Rule is kept; the text leaves unclear whether “her” means the Light or Wisdom.

**Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).** Atwood says the Divine Light is hidden in the self-begotten life, which takes the Divine Life for itself instead of serving it. She identifies it with gold: “The Divine Light, the Essence of Gold” [APP ¶70].

summary: In the Appendix, the highest sphere, above the pure Ether, where high Reason dwells, informed by Love and purified by humiliation.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes a scale of spheres: “Above that is the Divine Light region” [APP ¶170]. It lies above the pure Ether and is the dwelling of high Reason, informed by Love and purified by humiliation [APP ¶170].

summary: The real means by which, Atwood says, Theurgists are joined to the Divine nature, as opposed to a mental conception.
body: Atwood insists that the Theurgists' union with the Divine nature is real: “it is indeed by divine Media, and not a mere conception of the mind or metaphysical abstraction” [II.4 ¶31].

summary: Something Atwood says is established from the triune-essence principles she has just set out.
body: After her passage on the triune essence, Atwood writes: “Hence the Divine Monarchy consists, and is established” [IV.2 ¶12]. Its primary principles are those she has just announced there.

summary: An oracular voice Atwood cites as ratifying the Platonic instruction on how to apprehend the Intelligible.
body: Atwood cites the Divine Oracle in support of the Platonic teaching on how to apprehend the Intelligible: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶42]. The citation continues across [II.4 ¶43–48]. She uses it approvingly.

summary: Oracles Atwood cites as teaching that fire obliterates the strains from generation.
body: In a footnote, Atwood cites the divine oracles in support: they teach that fire obliterates the strains from generation [II.3 n40].

summary: The divine source in which contraries always coexist; Atwood says the common elements of Nature hide it and chemistry cannot identify it.
body: Atwood says that “contraries are always consubsistent in the Divine Original” [III.2 ¶60], such as small and great, deficient and exceeding. Elsewhere she writes: “The common elements of Nature obscure their Divine Original” [IV.1 ¶47]. In that context, chemistry cannot identify this source [IV.1 ¶47].

summary: A principle said to have been originally resident in man's life, which ranked him high, reported from cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience.
body: Reporting cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood describes man as ranked high for “a Divine Reason, on occult principle of Causal Efficience, said to be originally resident in his life” [II.1 ¶32]. This passage identifies the Divine Reason with that occult principle of Causal Efficience.

summary: The knowledge whose temple, Atwood says, admits whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing.
body: Atwood says that whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing “is already admitted to the temple of Divine Science, and joins in with the whole conclave” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: What the matter brought into the right condition attracts, and (in the Appendix) what the spirit that has died to all receives.
body: In the main text, the matter is brought into the right condition by action and reaction, so as “to supply the right condition for attracting the Divine Seed” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the spirit dies to everything, even its own identity, and becomes “a simple receptacle and magnet for the Divine Seed” [APP ¶87]. Both passages describe a prepared receiver that draws in the Seed.

summary: In Trismegistus as quoted, the knowledge of the First Cause: a rest of all the senses in which the soul is changed into the Essence of God.
body: Atwood quotes Trismegistus on the First Cause: “the knowledge of it, says Trismegistus, is a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33]. In this state the soul is drawn from the body and changed into the Essence of God [IV.2 ¶33].

summary: In the theosophist as quoted, the pure spirit that nourished the flame-like life of Adam before the fall.
body: The theosophist, as quoted, says that unfallen Adam's flame-like life was “nourished by that pure spirit of the divine substantiality” [IV.3 ¶38].

summary: Atwood's name for the completed work; the returned Instrument gives it its force and integral perfection.
body: Atwood says the returned Instrument makes up “the force and integral perfection of the Divine Superstructure” [III.1 ¶61]. The term apparently names the finished work.

summary: Cited from the Scriptures to support keeping the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy.
body: Atwood cites the Divine Teacher of the Scriptures to justify withholding the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine” [I.3 n10]. She uses it with approval.

summary: Union with the reality that images stand for. Julian, as quoted, says it is achieved only with the help of Divine Works.
body:
**Quoted (Julian).** “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52]. The assistance meant here is Divine Works.

**Atwood.** Divine Union joins the soul not to an image but to the reality that images represent. Afterwards, what was in the mind before returns heightened: “subsequent to the Divine Union, there recurs That also which was in the mind prior to the union, exalted and multiplied” [III.2 ¶66].

equivalences.with: a spirit of the nature of the ether

summary: In Hermolaus Barbarus as quoted, the chemists' celestial water, an ethereal spirit from which potable gold and the philosophers' stone begin.
body: Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus: “There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20]. It is distinct from every other water or liquor, and Democritus and Trismegistus knew it. It is called by other names, “calling it divine water, Scythian latex, &c.” [I.1 ¶20]. He calls it a spirit “which is a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. Potable gold and the philosophers' stone begin from it. If the outside air is kept out, its ether burns forever: “concerning this water; and he devoutly affirms, that the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

summary: In Synesius as quoted, the help without which the Divine union can neither be achieved nor understood.
body: Synesius, as cited, “bears witness to the efficacy of Divine Works” [II.1 ¶52]. Without this help the Divine union is neither effected nor understood [II.1 ¶52].

summary: The Greeks' teaching, which Atwood praises as unequalled in its scientific explanation of the divine source.
body: Atwood praises the Greeks as unequalled in “their doctrine of Wisdom in perspicuity, grace of utterance, and scientific explication of the divine source” [I.1 ¶70].

summary: In Vaughan as quoted, a twofold birth, visible and invisible, without which the Matter cannot be brought to its final purpose.
body: Vaughan, as quoted, speaks “of a double nativity, visible and invisible” [IV.2 ¶35]. Without it the Matter cannot be altered to its final purpose. The passage does not explain the expression further.

summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, a sign to watch for; the passage does not explain it.
body: Eirenaeus, as quoted, names “your signal the Doves of Diana” [III.1 ¶14]. The passage does not say what they are.

summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's gloss for the maternal instinct, through which the light finds the Paternal Life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: the light finds the Paternal Life “through the maternal instinct (the doves of Venus)” [APP ¶167]. Her stated meaning is the maternal instinct.

summary: In Proclus as quoted, what belongs to opinion: uncertain, close to irrational life, and not true discovery.
body: Quoting Proclus, Atwood separates true discovery from what is “not that which is doxastic, or pertaining to opinion” [II.4 ¶41]. Such opinion is uncertain and close to irrational life [II.4 ¶41].

summary: Translator of the Hermetic books into English; Atwood praises the translation.
body: Atwood praises Dr Everard's English translation of the Hermetic books [I.1 ¶7].

summary: For Atwood, the self-willed spirit that came into nature with the fall into generation and appears as the matter's blackness; Hermes, Bloomfield and a French adept, as quoted, describe it differently.
body:
**Atwood.** In her own words: “The dragon is the self-willed spirit” [I.3 n31]. It entered nature through the fall into generation. It lives in water, oily tincture and faeces, and it rises through blackness. It is the matter's blackness at the first ascension. It is poisonous: “like a poisonous dragon it destroys all that it touches” [I.3 n31]. It watches the crevices and shuns the sunbeams. As the internal light rises, the dragon is hidden: it “becomes so occultated in the rising of the internal light to manifestation” [I.3 n43]. The Dragon therefore apparently marks the dark first stage, which gives way as the light appears.

**Quoted (Hermes).** “The Dragon dwells in all the threefold nature, and his houses are the darkness and blackness that is in them” [III.1 ¶61]. In the same passage, the French adept describes two dragons biting each other until they become a Fifth Essence [III.1 ¶61].

**Quoted (Bloomfield).** The Dragon is the first of the three, and it slays and quells the other two: “The first one is the Dragon fell” [IV.2 ¶36].

The sources don't agree on the details. Atwood treats the Dragon as the self-willed spirit and the blackness, Hermes as a principle dwelling in the threefold nature, and Bloomfield as the first of three, which overcomes the others.

summary: In Sendivogius, what the living metals are to be made into in Our Fire; the text does not explain it further.
body: Quoted from Sendivogius: of the living metals “let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21], in connection with Our Fire. The text gives no further explanation.

summary: Atwood's term for the soul that has left nature and its moisture, turns to itself and radiates its own light; Heraclitus calls it the wisest.
body: Atwood describes the soul that has withdrawn from nature and its moisture: turning to itself, it radiates its own light — “then she becomes a dry splendor from exhalation” [II.3 ¶27]. She cites Heraclitus: “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27].

summary: A philosophers' name for the 'living water' that the Stone is; also one of the forms the subject takes in its changes.
body: Quoted from Geber, dry water is the philosophers' name for the living water that the Stone is: “living water, which we have named dry water” [I.2 ¶11] (= living water). Atwood herself lists *aqua sicca* among the forms the subject takes in its mutations — “a stone, a vapor, or an aqua sicca” [I.2 ¶37] — without further explanation.

headword: dry water of the sea of the wise
forms: dry water of the sea of the wise
summary: In Eudoxus, that with which the extracted water is joined by a 'magical union', dissolving it into the viscous mercurial liquor.
body: Quoted from Eudoxus: the extracted water is dissolved into the viscous mercurial liquor “by a magical union of the dry water of the sea of the wise” [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not explain the expression further.

summary: Cited for his English verse rendering (Aeneid, lib. 6) of a Latin passage Atwood quotes.
body: Atwood gives Dryden's English verse from his Aeneid, lib. 6, as a rendering of the Latin quoted in the same paragraph: “Deep forests and impenetrable night Possess the middle space” [II.3 ¶6; II.3 n3].

summary: The generating pair: if the divine Idea brought forth directly in it, the offspring would be imperfect and discordant; in the oracle it sits beside the Monad.
body: Atwood treats the Duad as the generating pair: “For if in the Duad the divine Idea were suffered immediately to bring forth, an imperfect offspring would result” [IV.2 ¶20] — imperfect and discordant through the predominance of either extreme. In the oracle she cites, the Duad stands beside the Monad: “For the Duad sits beside him and glitters with intellectual sections,” [IV.2 ¶22].

summary: Reflective contemplation, which is excluded, together with multitude, when Matter is called 'one so far as one'.
body: Atwood glosses dual contemplation as reflective contemplation (= reflective contemplation): Matter is called one so far as one by “depriving the idea of multitude and dual, i.e., reflective, contemplation” [III.2 ¶52].

summary: Author of the Histoire Hermetique, cited for a skeptic's praise of English Hermetic writers and for Lully material, yet criticized as ignorant of the subject.
body: Atwood cites his Histoire Hermetique several times. As a skeptic's testimony to English Hermetic writing she quotes: “les Anglois n’ecrivent sur la science hermetique avec beaucoup de lumiere et de profondeur” [I.1 ¶72; I.1 n92] (our rendering: the English write on the hermetic science with much light and depth). He is cited in support of the Lully story; his catalogue lists about 200 of Lully's alchemical treatises; and he is a reference for the laws forbidding transmutation [I.1 ¶47; I.1 ¶48; I.1 n58; I.1 n61]. He is also cited (vol. 2) for transmutation stories [I.1 n104]. But Atwood criticizes his Catalogue (tom. iii, Paris, 1762): he reduced the count of authors, was ignorant of the subject, and excluded writers by title rather than matter [I.1 ¶75; I.1 n97].

summary: In the quoted fraternity of the Rosy Cross, one of two mutually devouring yet loving creatures; tortured, it yields tears, and its 'embers' are obtained at the second gate.
body: Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the Eagle is one of two creatures that devour yet love each other; tortured, it weeps — “Torture the Eagle till she weeps” [III.3 ¶63] — and its embers are obtained at the second gate. The text gives no plain meaning.

summary: Group voices cited together as agreeing that the Mysteries were instituted pure and for the noblest ends.
body: Atwood cites them in support of the original purity of the Mysteries: “early Christians concurring with the wisest Ethnics in declaring that they proposed the noblest ends” [II.4 ¶56].

summary: For Atwood, the crucible for souls as well as bodies; in Hermes, 'our earth', the body of spirit and soul, the feminine earth of the masculine.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]; it is that into which power is turned to be made integral, and “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110].

In the quoted Hermes, 'our earth' has sulphur as its fatness; the earth begot between water (spirit) and redness (soul) is the body of both — “the earth begot betwixt them is the substance or body of both” [I.3 n21] (= substance or body of both); “the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶22]; and Magnesia is sown in the Philosophic Earth. Earth is also identified with the residue: “the faeces or earth which remains below” [I.3 ¶23] (= faeces).

equivalences.with: our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense

summary: In the sage's saying 'visit the interior of the earth', Atwood reads the earth as our chaotic sense-life, not soil.
body: Atwood interprets the sage's saying “Visit the interior of the earth rectifying” [II.3 ¶29]: the earth meant is “not the feculent dead soil, but our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense” [II.3 ¶29] (= our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense).

summary: The Hermetists' earth, located within their heaven and named so to distinguish it from the 'feculent dead soil'.
body: Atwood says the Hermetists place their earth within their heaven and “call it magical, the Earth of the Wise, Olympus, Our Earth” [III.2 ¶36] (= magical earth, Olympus, Our Earth), “in order to distinguish from the feculent dead soil” [III.2 ¶36].

summary: In the Benedictine Monk, the vessel containing fire, air and water in the work, glossed as the gross body or composition.
body: Quoted from the Benedictine Monk: fire, air and water are contained “in their earthly vessel, i.e., in their gross body or composition” [III.3 ¶24] (= gross body or composition).

headword: Eastern temples / the priests at Eleusis
summary: Named as the places and celebrants of the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries.
body: Atwood names the Eastern temples and the priests at Eleusis as where the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries were celebrated [II.2 ¶24].

summary: A source cited in footnotes for honoring the physician and for Wisdom's secret being with the Faithful.
body: Cited (Eccles. 8; Idem., 1) in support of honoring the physician and of the saying that Wisdom's secret belongs to the Faithful: “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36; IV.3 n14; IV.3 n15].

summary: Cited (1:6-8) in support of Wisdom as created by God, poured on all his works and given to those who love him.
body: Atwood cites Ecclesiasticus 1:6-8 on Wisdom: “He created her and numbered her, and poured her out upon all his works.” [III.3 ¶48; III.3 n33] — and given to those who love him.

summary: Cited in the Appendix in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterated contritions.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Eckhartshausen is cited in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterative contritions [APP ¶78].

summary: Atwood's term for the active, working cause within the total essence, to be drawn forth, known in co-identity, and related to mind rather than generative life.
body:
Atwood uses the Efficient for the active cause the method seeks to recover. It is to be drawn forth from within: the aim is to “draw forth the true Efficient and to know it in co-identity” [II.3 ¶5]. It lies in the intelligible substance of reason's Law: “For there the true Efficient is to be found, which is not externally developed” [II.3 ¶46]. Knowledge and the efficient rise together: “It is from within that the knowledge springs together with the true efficient” [III.1 ¶40], the two “which are indeed one in principle” [III.1 ¶40] (= knowledge), though distinguished in practice for the sake of offspring. The “Rational Efficient, armed with a bright intelligence” [III.1 ¶47] discovers the evil of its first conception and dissolves the Vital Bond; the text does not explicitly say this is the same as the 'true efficient'.

In the dissolution, “the newly roused Efficient is exceeding wrathful” [III.1 ¶56], reducing the body of Light (Osiris) to vapor. It is universal: there is “not the smallest grain of sand without the Efficient which is in all” [III.2 ¶43], and without it numbers and figures produce nothing substantive. One who mingles with it keeps a remnant of it: “whoever thus becomes One by mingling with the Efficient, will have a remnant of it with himself” [III.2 ¶66]. The Platonic Successor, quoted, calls it the soul's cause: “the soul, being in such a condition, associates with her Efficient” [III.3 ¶26], gaining a similitude of it. Once Mind attains Self Knowledge, “the Efficient proceeds out wards to image its motive in operation” [IV.1 ¶48].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says this life-power is now dislocated downward: “The Efficient must be regained. That is, it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life.” [APP ¶134].

summary: Atwood's name, in the Appendix, for Causality, of which we ordinarily have no experience; contact with universal power initiates regenerate life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates it with Causality: “We know noting of Causality --- i.e., we have no experience of the Efficient Power.” [APP ¶175] (= Causality). The individual mind's contact with power universal initiates regenerate life [APP ¶175].

summary: In Khunrath, something in vegetables that the Stone increases; not further defined.
body: Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone acts on “vegetables, by an increase of their efflorescent spirit” [IV.3 ¶28]. Not further defined.

summary: In Hermes, 'our egg' holds the one disposition sought; the hen's egg is the nearest natural analogue to the art's compound simple.
body: Quoted from Hermes: 'our egg' holds the one disposition sought. The hen's egg, made of four elements, is the closest natural analogue, “which answers in all respects, excepting the catholicity, to the compound simple of this art” [I.3 n26].

summary: Atwood's name for the subject when it is 'nothing': a formless, potential state amid its mutations.
body: Atwood says the subject, among its mutations, is at one stage nothing “but a potential chaos and egg of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37] (= potential chaos).

headword: Egyptian Fable of Isis and Osiris
forms: Egyptian Fable of Isis and Osiris
