summary: Cited to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring, represented by the birth of Horus.
body: Atwood uses the fable to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring; the birth of Horus represents the metaphysical offspring [IV.2 ¶6; IV.2 ¶7; IV.2 ¶11].

headword: Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris
forms: Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris
summary: The mythology Synesius is said to explain with the enigma of the two pairs of eyes.
body: Named as the mythology that Synesius is said to explain by the enigma of the two pairs of eyes [III.1 ¶45].

summary: Cited to illustrate the rebellious Principle depicted in human form with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes.
body: Atwood cites Egyptian relics as depicting the rebellious Principle in human semblance, with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes [III.1 ¶64].

summary: Cited approvingly for teaching self-knowledge and placing the Sphinx before Isis, but in the Appendix criticized as an example of self-willed magic.
body: Atwood cites the Egyptians in support of the precept “that Man should know himself” [II.1 ¶39], meant experimentally and ontologically. They placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, which she reads as Ether guarding Wisdom [III.1 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) they are criticized as an example of the magic of the self-will: their magicians' “enchantments” drew only on their own strength, and so Egypt fell [APP ¶2; APP ¶4; APP ¶5].

summary: In Poemander's account given by Hermes, Intellect, reached when the ascending part is stripped of all operations; above it powers sing praises to God.
body: Quoted from Poemander in Hermes' account: the ascending part, naked of all operations, “cometh to the eighth sphere, which is Intellect” [III.3 ¶57] (= Intellect); above it are powers singing praises to God.

summary: The adept Atwood calls the most celebrated later adept and a 'perfect artist'; she draws heavily on his verse and prose for fire, matter, operations, multiplication and projection.
body:
Atwood presents Eirenaeus Philalethes as the most celebrated later adept, a perfect artist whose identity is unknown, listing works including An Open Entrance to the Shut Palace of the King, Ripley Revived and The Marrow of Alchemy [I.1 ¶73]; he is the 'foregoing' adept with whom Vaughan is confounded [I.1 ¶74]. She qualifies his Ripley Revived as practically explanatory for the initiated but sophistical to beginners [I.1 ¶64; I.1 n67], and quotes him that “our books are made for those who have been or intend to become conversant about the search of nature” [I.2 ¶50; I.2 n50]. He is among adepts warning against practice before full understanding [I.1 ¶86]; “Few, very few, Philalethes said, there were in his day” [II.2 ¶25] who understood the principle.

On the agent: “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45; I.2 n44]; nature's one secret agent — “For she her secret agent doth possess, Which in the universe is only one” [II.2 ¶28; II.2 n19]; “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold” [III.1 ¶13]; “For in our water is our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69; III.1 n73]. He supplies the account of fire, waters, menstruals, regimen and signs [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood finds 'a profound mystery' in “To Saturn, Mars with bond of love is tied,” [III.1 ¶58; III.1 n64]. Other uses: “Separate, says Eiraneaus, the light from the darkness seven times” [I.3 n39]; “Never grudge, then, that thou hast destroyed thye gold” [III.3 ¶22; III.3 n12], glossed as the first fruits of reason; the one key — “That ‘t is a fountain sealed, Which one thing only can unlocke;” [III.3 ¶67; III.3 n46]; the gross understanding's false light — “that darkness I now perceived had a false fore of its own” [III.4 ¶16; III.4 n11].

On practice: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5], distinct from the Second, where Nature works alone [IV.1 ¶11]; two contrary works done apart then reconciled — “For what one doth concoct t’other will drive away;” [IV.1 ¶42; IV.1 n37]; a favored case — “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17; IV.1 n18]. For multiplication and projection: “But one at last ting’d ninety thousand more” [IV.3 ¶25; IV.3 n6]; “you will no longer be able to calculate the strength of the medicine” [IV.3 ¶18; IV.3 ¶20; IV.3 n1] — the text attributes ¶18 to the Author of the Open Entrance and ¶20 to E. Philalethes' Introitus Apertus without stating they are one. He is cited for a universal medicine — “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7] — after which Atwood tells gold-seekers to disregard such testimony. Within the Adept's words he is cited for the menstruum in the sphere of Saturn that can calcine gold, identified with the Salt [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “Take that matter which is gold” [APP ¶89] is glossed as finding the magical earth at one's own center. Whether 'the Cosmopolite Eirenaeus' [III.1 ¶64] is a further source or a co-source of the Lion Hunt poem is unclear.

summary: In Norton, the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator's nativity may contradict.
body: Quoted from Norton: the Election is the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator's own nativity may oppose — “In contrariety of this Election” [IV.2 ¶34].

summary: The name given to chemical affinity, which a reader records as ruled by the three principles.
body: The text identifies it with chemical affinity: “chemical affinity, called Elective Attraction” [II.1 ¶19]. The reader's record adds that this affinity is ruled by the three principles; the voice of the passage is unclear.

summary: Ordinary, sensible fire, which Atwood distinguishes from true fire as a mere effect of an antecedent potency.
body: Atwood sets true fire apart from the fire of common experience, “distinct from that elementary ignition with which we are sensibly familiar” [I.2 ¶15]. Per the reader's record, such ignition is not true fire but only an excitation or effect of the antecedent potency [I.2 ¶15].

summary: The world over which the regenerate soul gains rule and through which it can pass.
body: Atwood speaks of the soul attaining a state “wherein it can rule over the elementary world and pass through it” [IV.4 ¶20]. The context suggests the regenerate soul is meant.

equivalences.with: elements of the Mercury, properties of the universal spirit
four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water
four elements of the Universal Ether

summary: In Hermetic usage not common elements or chemical simples, but properties of the universal spirit in the Mercury; the true element is a spirit of life.
body:
**Atwood's definition.** The elements of the adepts are not bodily substances: “We must not limit, says Paracelsus, an element to a bodily substance or quality” [I.2 ¶26]. Rather, “the elements they speak of, as being introverted and transformed are the elements of the Mercury, properties of the universal spirit”, and “the true element is a spirit of life, and grows in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; the visible is only its receptacle. Water, air, earth and gold are not true elements; of Nature she writes “but Her, the true element, they have never found” [III.3 ¶65], i.e. the chemists. In verse she cites, the four are divided from a first mass: “And from that lump divided I foure sundry elements,” [III.3 ¶76]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Alchemists refer to the four elements of the Universal Ether” [APP ¶69].

**Quoted authorities.** Hermes says the elements are to be taken “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]; Atwood glosses: “The philosophic water then, being divided into four parts or hypostatic relations, they are called elements” [I.3 n5]. The author of The Triumph and the Master speak of their conversion and dissolution: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6]; “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14]. Eudoxus describes the Second Key, which separates the Stone's constituents and converts them in sequence: it “makes Water of Earth, Air of Water, and Fire of Air” [IV.3 ¶5].

**Identities asserted:** elements of the Mercury / properties of the universal spirit; spirit of life [I.2 ¶26]; four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water [I.3 n5]; Nature (“Her”) as the true element [III.3 ¶65]; four elements of the Universal Ether [APP ¶69].

summary: Accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries, cited by Atwood in support of Wisdom as the offspring of a vital experiment into nature.
body: Atwood invokes accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries to support her view that Wisdom is the offspring of a vital experiment into nature [II.1 ¶52].

summary: A figure the Adepts declare already born: a forerunner baptizing with water, foreshowing all things to the wise, born miraculously and before the Divine Light.
body: Atwood reports the saying of the Adepts: “Natus est jam Elias Artista (5); Elias, the artist, is born already” [IV.2 ¶12] (the book's own translation). In the same passage, per the reader's record, he is described as a forerunner who baptizes with water, foreshows all things to the wise, and is born miraculously and prior to the Divine Light [IV.2 ¶12]. The voice is that of the Adepts as quoted.

summary: A spirit said in the Table Talk to be born when the metal bond is broken, whose work is to prepare for something higher.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that when the metal bond is broken “the Elias spirit is born and his work is to prepare for something higher.” [APP ¶139]

summary: The healing, life-prolonging and transmuting product of the Art, named in many reports of adepts and in quoted verse; also used of the soul's immortal fortification.
body:
**Reports of adepts (Atwood).** Artephius, “by the use of the elixir, is reported to have lived throughout the period of a thousand years” [I.1 ¶36]; the phrase “elixir of life” also appears in a quotation in that paragraph. “Alain de l’Isle is said to have obtained the Elixir” [I.1 ¶45]. Paracelsus is mentioned with “the elixir he boasts” [I.1 ¶64], in a sentence about “one who was in the habit of taking a potent spiritual medicine” whose effects worsened with depravity [I.1 ¶64]. Of Seton, “a report was spread about of the Elixir” [I.1 ¶66], in a passage that also speaks of the medicine he gave the sick; Starkey speaks of “the White and Red elixir” [I.1 ¶73]. Vaughan reportedly died “from an overdose of the elixir” [I.1 ¶74]. These records suggest a product that can be taken and that both heals and transmutes, though the passages do not define it.

**Quoted authorities.** Ripley: the separated elements of Mercury, “again commixed by equal weight or proportion, make the elixir complete” [I.2 ¶25]; the purged stone becomes “in whytenes Elixir of great might” [III.1 ¶62]. Bloomfield lists it among names of the privy quintessence: “Our great Elixir most high of price, Our Azot, our Basiliske, and our Adrop, our Cockatrice.” [I.2 ¶41]. Norton: “In this wise Elixir, of whom ye make mencion, Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34], i.e. engendered when celestial and elemental virtues accord.

**Atwood's spiritual use.** The soul, re-entering the body through death, fortifies it “with the elixir of an immortal life” [II.3 ¶39].

**Identities asserted:** Azot, Basiliske, Adrop, Cockatrice and other names (Bloomfield) [I.2 ¶41]; a thing of Second Intention (Norton) [IV.2 ¶34].

summary: Intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment, called vital products, whose exhibition without disclosure of source astonished common chemistry.
body: Atwood treats elixir and gold together as intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment: “Both of which are vital products” [II.4 ¶58]. Exhibited without discovery of their source, they caused much astonishment to common chemistry [II.4 ¶58].

equivalences.with: tincture of many dyes / union of the purified spirit with its course

summary: Light set free from the central essence, said to prolong life and cure disease and moral and physical defects.
body: Atwood: “This is the elixir of Light from the central essence” [I.3 n18]. In the same note it is identified with the tincture of many dyes and with the union of the purified spirit with its course, and is said to prolong life and to cure disease and moral and physical defects [I.3 n18].

summary: A condition of being beyond corporeal life and generation, the place of the third, intellectual vision and the goal of the hidden labours.
body:
For Atwood, Elysium is a state transcending corporeal life and generation, the goal of the hidden labours, and the place of the third, intellectual vision: “this third vision of the light is in Elysium” [II.4 ¶15].

**Identities asserted:** the Islands of the Blessed — “is denominated the Islands of the Blessed; and these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3]; the enclosed garden of Solomon and the Terrestrial Paradise — “This is Elysium, the enclosed garden of Solomon, where God condescends to walk and drink of the sealed fountain; the true Terrestrial Paradise” [II.4 ¶9].

summary: The light reached after passing through the dark region; the object of inquiry and the state into which the liberated soul passes.
body: Atwood says the dark region must be traversed “before inquiry can hope to meet its object in the Elysian light” [II.3 ¶5]. It is the state into which the liberated soul passes; she illustrates with Aeneas “going forth to meet his father in the Elysian fields” [II.4 ¶21], where he receives the Epopteia. See also Elysian Fields.

summary: The doctrine by which the physical universe proceeds from the superstantial Light or will and is extended and corporified by multiplication of the unit.
body:
Atwood presents an essential emanation as Kabalistic doctrine: “according to the doctrine of an essential emanation, the whole physical universe is extended and corporified” [III.2 ¶3], through multiplication of the indeficient unit into its parts under the Law of its own proceeding Light [III.2 ¶3]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) she speaks of “emanation from the superstantial Light or will” and says “The darkness is the emanation” [APP ¶66], the flat and qualitated becoming cubic by multiplication into itself [APP ¶66].

**Identity asserted:** darkness [APP ¶66].

summary: Author of Wuthering Heights, criticized in the Table Talk as a Saturnine mass of power lacking the clearing Jupiter element.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Wuthering Heights is criticized as a Saturnine mass of power in potentiality, wanting the clearing Jupiter element; Emily is called Saturn [APP ¶175].

summary: A mid-point between mind and matter, by which mind is moved into matter.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says: “Emotion is a mid-point between the two” [APP ¶80], i.e. between mind and matter, mind being moved into matter by it.

summary: Cited by Atwood, mainly from his Physics, in support of the soul's exile from the light, concealed harmony manifested by ether, and the twofold order of union and strife.
body: Atwood cites Empedocles approvingly on several points. On our desertion of the best life by turning to externals: “Heaven’s exiles straying from the orb of light.” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 ¶10]. From the Physics, called “a poet”, he illustrates a concealed harmony made manifest by the motion of ether: “Then all the members of the god appeared” [II.4 ¶26–28, II.4 n16]. He also serves as an instance of “the physiologist” who substitutes elements as principles, differing from others in expression only [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶34]. From Physics, cap. 1, she draws support for a twofold intelligible and sensible order, perpetual interchange, and the One formed from the many: “All things in union now thro’ love conspire, And now thro’ strife divulsed are borne along” [III.2 ¶38, III.2 ¶39, III.2 n35].

summary: Used pejoratively of knowledge lacking the experience, gained only by observing remote effects.
body: Atwood: “All our knowledge without the experience is empirical, the result only of observation of remote effects” [IV.4 ¶12].

summary: Something Hermes says is made from the golden matter; not explained in the text.
body: Hermes, quoted: “of them we make the encaustic of which we have written” [I.3 ¶59]; the reference is apparently to the golden matter. The text does not explain the term.

summary: The handling of the work, which has particular turnings in which Eirenaeus says he often erred.
body: Eirenaeus, quoted: “in some particular turnings of the Encheiresis I erred often” [IV.1 ¶17]. The context suggests it means the manual handling or conduct of the work.

summary: A visionary criticized in the Table Talk for lacking education of the intellect and so having little gauge for truth.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Engelbrecht is criticized as a visionary without education of the intellect, with little gauge for truth, who perhaps misconceived the Evester [APP ¶105].

summary: The veiled teaching and its hidden meaning, whose solution comes through desire and labour and opens the mystery of all things.
body: The first class of prayer is described as “seeking a clue whereby it may enter the intelligible profundity of the Enigma” [III.4 ¶24]. Its solution arises from labour and desire, even from attempts “which were not the solution of the Enigma, the solution itself arose” [III.4 ¶22]; unfolding it opens the mystery of all things. The voice of these passages is unclear in the records.

summary: A work cited by Atwood as celebrating the Laelia Aelia as comprehending all.
body: Atwood cites the Enigma as celebrating the Laelia Aelia as comprehending all [I.2 ¶34].

equivalences.with: the darkened essence of his natural understanding (to be penetrated rationally)

summary: The riddle whose solution is to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of one's natural understanding; Mind is its Key.
body:
Atwood glosses the riddle plainly: “to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx; in other words, to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of his natural understanding” [IV.1 ¶48]. And: “For Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48].

**Identity asserted:** the darkened essence of one's natural understanding, to be penetrated rationally [IV.1 ¶48].

summary: A work in Ashmole's Theatrum, cited in support of Nature and Art as parents and a twofold yet indivisible work.
body: Atwood cites the Enigma Philosophicum (Ashmole’s Theatrum, p. 423) in support of Nature and Art as parents of the work, a twofold yet indivisible work, and the fixed fixing the unfixed: “There is no sun but which is twice begot” [III.3 ¶36, III.3 n24].

summary: An entity; in the Table Talk, such an ens is said to underlie the philosophic stone and to be the final term to which the sensual medium is brought.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says “such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone” [APP ¶108], and speaks of the sensual medium “brought to its pivot, to its last ens” [APP ¶110].

summary: An entity of light, the purer conscious ens carried back to God; named with the rejected Corner Stone as what the wise raise.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the purer conscious ens of light” [APP ¶78] carried back to God, and per the reader's record relates it to the excruciated Philosophic Matter and the real Stone [APP ¶78]. In the main text the wise “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8] in the living temple; it is not separately defined there.

summary: The state of being agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, contrary to phantasy; distinguished by the ancients from fanaticism.
body: Olympiodorus, quoted: “when we are agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, and the phantasy intervenes, the enthusiastic energy ceases” [II.2 ¶12]. Atwood notes the ancients drew a line “between enthusiasm and fanaticism” [II.4 ¶29], parallel to that between imaginative vision and the light of the true gods; she does not otherwise define it.

summary: The person in trance, susceptible to imaginative impressions that linger in a place.
body: Atwood: “the entranced Subject is more or less susceptible of all imaginative impressures” [III.4 ¶42], including, per the reader's record, those lingering in the place.

summary: Said of philosophers in a special sense: they withhold the truth only from the ignorant and vicious, not from the just or wise.
body: Hermes, quoted, explains why philosophers withhold truth only from fools and the vicious, not from the just or wise: “For this reason are philosophers said to be envious” [I.3 ¶11]; again, “For this reason are the philosophers said to be envious” [III.4 ¶9].

summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the view that the Mysteries become venerable when believed to be provided for the perfection of human life.
body: Atwood cites Epictetus in support: the Mysteries become venerable when one believes they were provided for the perfection of human life [II.4 ¶57].

summary: An initiate whose account, cited from Apuleius's Metamorphoses Book 11, Atwood uses to illustrate what was done in the Mysteries.
body: Atwood cites, from Apuleius, *Metam.* Book 11, the Epidaurian's first-person account as an initiate's report of what was done in the Mysteries (quoted voice): “I approached the confines of death, and, having trod the threshold of Proserpine, I returned from it” [II.3 ¶45; II.3 n49].

summary: A work quoted from its end in support of the claim that the all-begetting Spirit dwells within us.
body: Cited from the end of the *Epistle to Trithemius* (quoted voice) in support of the view, which Atwood adopts, that the all-begetting Spirit dwells in us: “But the Spirit begetting all doth in us dwell” [II.1 ¶27; II.1 n27].

summary: The final grade of initiation, following telete and muesis, in which initiates are fixed as spectators of the intelligible and shown the Universal Nature and the soul.
body: In Atwood's account (ATWOOD voice), epopteia is the last of three grades of initiation: “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. The record describes it as being fixed as spectators of the intelligible, its content being the revelation of the Universal Nature and of the soul [II.4 ¶23].

summary: In Khunrath's words, the Stone's balancing power by which it drives out suffering and disease of mind and body.
body: Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone “by its own equilibriate virtue expels suffering and every disease whether of mind or body” [IV.3 ¶28]. The context suggests a link with the health described nearby, from Julian, as a symmetry or equilibrium of nature [IV.3 ¶30]; the connection is the reader's comparison, not stated outright.

summary: Cited for his burlesques, which Atwood uses to illustrate the alchemical mania of the age.
body: Atwood mentions Erasmus's burlesques as illustrating the alchemical mania of the age [I.1 ¶64].

summary: In the passage given by the metropolitan of Memphis, Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle and called chief of the Immortals.
body: In the passage quoted from the metropolitan of Memphis (quoted voice), Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle: “the amiable Eros, chief of the Immortals” [III.3 ¶46].

summary: Book of Esdras, cited to show that few attain the work and for the 'outgoings of paradise', identified with the seven mystic mountains.
body: Atwood quotes Esdras (Book 1, cap. 3) to illustrate that few attain the work: “The earth giveth much mould, whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of” [II.2 ¶29; II.2 n20]. She also cites Esdras for the 'outgoings of paradise', which are identified with the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9].

summary: In Eirenaeus, what gold and Mercury are recongealed into, healing all griefs; in Aristotle and Porphyry, separate particular subsistence and one's own Essence to be established in.
body:
The word appears in quoted voices with different senses.

- **Eirenaeus**: gold and Mercury are recongealed “Both to an Essence which all griefs canheal.” [III.1 ¶69].
- **Aristotle** (as quoted): “a separate subsistence as this or that particular thing especially belongs to what we call essence, (that is to say, composition of subject and object is necessarily implied in the idea of true intelligence)” [III.2 ¶53]; in this passage Matter is not essence [III.2 ¶53].
- **Porphyry**: the reader is to be “being established in yourself and in your own Essence” [III.2 ¶59].

These uses are not reconciled in the records.

equivalences.with: true Form or Idea of Gold

summary: What the Stone is made manifest as; identified with the true Form or Idea of Gold (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says the Stone is made manifest as an Essence of Light, “which Essence is the true Form or Idea of Gold” [APP ¶6].

summary: In the Aristotle passage, the intellect to which human reason is subordinate.
body: Quoted from Aristotle: human reason is described as subordinate “on account of its subordination to essential intellect” [II.1 ¶34].

summary: In Porphyry, an essence infinite in power, self-established and self-sufficient, to which nothing can be added and which place or relation would diminish.
body: Atwood quotes Porphyry (spelled here “Prophyry”): “When you have assumed to yourself an Eternal Essence, says Prophyry, infinite in itself according to power” [III.2 ¶59]. Such an essence is self-established and self-sufficient, seeking nothing but itself; nothing can be added to it, and adding place or relation diminishes it; “it is much more sufficient than any perpetually flowing fountain can be conceived to be” [III.2 ¶59].

summary: In the theosophist's account, Adam's leader, which had dominion in him in his Paradisiacal innocency.
body: Quoted from the theosophist: in Adam's Paradisiacal innocency “The Eternal Word was his leader, and had dominion in him” [IV.3 ¶38].

equivalences.with: quintessence of the four principles called elements
omnia in omnibus of the Hermetic Riddle

summary: Atwood's universal subtle medium: an all-pervading perfective essence, vehicle of the world-soul, which, separated and purified, is the matter of the Stone and rises into Light.
body:
**Nature and authorities.** With Homberg, Boerhaave, Boyle and Berkeley, Atwood describes Ether as a distinct, universally diffused substance, sensible only in its mixtures and effects, source and bond of the elements, giving air its vitalizing power: “the occult virtues of the Ether; its all-pervading essence and perfective power” [I.2 ¶12]; one authority calls it “ether, and a pure invisible fire” [I.2 ¶14]. The **Free Ether** (voice of the Greeks) is “freed from the prison of gross matter, and able to work of itself intimately by the virtue of its own included light” [I.2 ¶16]; Euripides calls it Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17]. Ovid's verse gives “liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera, non quicquam terrenae faecis habentum” (ours: liquid and weightless ether, having nothing of earthly dregs) [III.2 ¶37].

**In the Art (ATWOOD).** Separated and purified it is the matter of the Stone: “the Formal Light, by multiplication in its Ethe, is said to produce gold” [I.2 ¶46]; the Stone has “its foundation in the free Ether” [IV.4 ¶2]. Alchemists are “our Oedipus distillers of this Ether” [III.1 ¶13], ending in “the final resurrection of the pure Ether into Light” [III.1 ¶21], “depriving the ether of its wild affections and impressures” [IV.1 ¶4]. Pseudo-alchemists tried “to compress and entice the ether by mangetical disposition” and failed [II.1 ¶6]. Asserted identities: the alchemists' mineral tree [II.3 ¶18]; “that Augean palace” of the multiplied Prester [II.3 ¶56]; “the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; non-being, the “simple Understanding of its ether” [III.3 ¶15].

**In man and cosmos.** “what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5], vehicle of the world-soul. Wholeness comes “from equilibriate circulation in their Ether” [II.4 ¶29]; rites work “by the medium of the passive Ether” [II.4 ¶36]; Intellect rides “secure in its Ether” [IV.1 ¶33]; see also “the liquid crystal of the understanding ether” [III.3 ¶10]. Imaginations can “pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode” [III.4 ¶42]; ether also names the anaesthetic [IV.1 ¶4]. In Boehme the Tincture “stays in its ether” [III.2 ¶16]; in Khunrath's source (voice unclear) ether in the divine water “will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

**Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, later layer).** “The Ether is two-fold: the mundane, which is full of the false forms; the pure, which is not of this world” [APP ¶64]; it is “a quintessence of those very four principles” and “the Quintessence of both worlds” [APP ¶69]; each has “a scrap of that ether shut in at our birth-conception”, “the omnia in omnibus of the Hermetic Riddle” [APP ¶119]; the spirit-man's work “is to move the Ether” [APP ¶139]; of Lucifer, ether is identified with Heaven: “burn up the ether which was Heaven.” [APP ¶133]; “The Ether is the universal extended Matter; the Divine posit everywhere; life.” [APP ¶179].

summary: In the Appendix, the first Ether arising from nature, through which thoughts, images, passions and desires rise to their own sphere, beneath the pure Ether and the Divine Light.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says thoughts, images, passions and desires “all rise up through this first Ether Natural and abide on a sphere of their own above it” [APP ¶170]. Above it lies the pure Ether, related to the moral nature, and then the region of Divine Light [APP ¶170].

summary: The ethereal which art separates from mortal existence, read as Plato's One Whole and Aristotle's perfect world; its estates rise successively, figured in Hesiod's generations.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) reads Plato and Aristotle as pointing to it: “Plato yet more plainly alluding to the Etheral Quintessence, in Timaeus, says, that of four elements the Demiurgus assumed One Whole from wholes” — perfect and free from age and disease; of such descriptions she asks “what other, therefore, should they either mean but the ethereal” [III.2 ¶38]. In the plural, the Ethereal Quintessences are successive estates called forth by the light and heat of the superincumbent mind: “the several estates of the Ethereal Quintessences arising one above another”, figured in Hesiod's generations [III.3 ¶42].

summary: The one being whose relation, action and passion the authors mean by sulfur, mercury, earth, and twofold or third matter.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) says the authors' various names (sulfur, mercury, earth, twofold or third matter) refer to “the magnetic relation, action, and passion of the Ethereal being in itself” [I.2 ¶42].

summary: The subject described by negations (no form, quality, body, reason or bound, but a certain Infinity) in Atwood's discussion of Matter.
body: Continuing her discussion of Matter, Atwood writes: “But since the ethereal element is described by so many ablative characteristics” [III.2 ¶53], namely that it is neither form, quality, body, reason nor bound, but a certain Infinity. The text does not state that the ethereal element is the same as Matter, though the context suggests a close link.

summary: Something passive to intellect as a mirror is to images, subsisting without imagination, felt rather than known; the Passive Nature is said to be of this kind.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) compares it to a mirror: “so is this ethereal glass to intellect, subsisting according to processure and in defect of all imagination” [III.2 ¶60]. It is felt, not known, and the Passive Nature is said to be a thing of this kind [III.2 ¶60].

summary: The moisture that nourishes and educates the Solar Light, set beside Luna as 'Domina Humiditatis'.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “The ethereal humidity nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]; it is set beside Luna, called Domina Humiditatis (ours: mistress of moisture) [IV.1 ¶29].

summary: The Greek counterpart of the alchemists' first matter: the one life-substance divided into three principles in dissolution, which revolves in its First Cause when the Stone is confirmed.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) treats it as the Greek counterpart of the alchemists' first matter: “that ethereal hypostasis we were before discussing” [III.1 ¶3]. In the dissolution, “the ethereal hypostasis is divided against itself and brought to a separation even as these three” principles [III.1 ¶53]. When the Stone is confirmed, rising in rational supremacy over sense and finite reflection, “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62]; that passage does not define it further. See also “filling the Ethereal Hypostasis with acme and power” [II.4 ¶29].

summary: That which, in the Fifth Essence, becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): in the Fifth Essence “the Ethereal Quadrangle becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity” [III.3 ¶32].

summary: The sought spirit, never existing separately on earth but hidden in the beings it sustains; in Synesius, the intermediate nature joining divine and lowest, phantastic until purified by art.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “the ethereal spirit does not subsist of itself, separate or tangibly on earth” [I.2 ¶20], but is hidden and defiled within the beings it sustains. She equates its subjugation with that of the Sphinx: the trial “ends in her subjugation; in other words, the Ethereal Spirit abandons her phantasy” [III.1 ¶20], yielding the clear light of understanding to the trained investigator. Quoting Synesius, it is the intermediate nature between rational and brutal life, corporeal and incorporeal: “it is the medium which conjoins divine natures with the lowest of all” [II.2 ¶10]. It is identified with “the phantastical condition also of the natural understanding essence, before it is purified by art and exalted. This Etherial Spirit” [II.2 ¶10].

summary: The prepared medium in which the seed of gold is planted so as to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the seed of gold must be “planted in its proper ethereal vehicle, well prepared and fallow” to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase [I.3 n40]. Elsewhere the divine unions “tried the ethereal vehicle to its utmost susceptibility” [II.4 ¶40].

summary: The waters on which the displaced sulfur floats while they tear, decoct and soften the sensual dominant.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the displaced sulfur is made “to float upon the ethereal waters, whilst these continue to tear, decoct, and soften the sensual dominant” [III.1 ¶53].

summary: A work cited for Tartarus as the region next beyond Hades.
body: Cited for Tartarus as the next region beyond Hades [II.3 ¶36].

summary: Used in contrast to Christian; not further defined.
body: Used by Atwood in contrast to Christian, “both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]; the text does not define it further.

summary: A group whose Anima Mundi doctrine Atwood says agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine.
body: Atwood says the Ethnics' doctrine of the Anima Mundi agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine [I.2 ¶14].

summary: Speaker of The Six Keys of Eudoxus, which Atwood quotes as practical instruction on the Art until its defective final Keys make her turn elsewhere.
body: Atwood cites Eudoxus's introduction to the Six Keys in support of the view that the difficulty lies in learning the Art from books and that the seeker needs deep knowledge of Nature: “the practice of our Art is the most difficult thing in the world, not in regard to its operation” [IV.2 ¶4]. *The Six Keys of Eudoxus, Opening Into the Most Secret Philosophy* is named in a chapter heading [IV.3 ¶1], which makes him the first-person speaker of the quoted text that follows; Atwood presents it as instruction on the practice [IV.3 ¶10; IV.3 ¶12; IV.3 ¶14; IV.3 ¶16]. She qualifies its usefulness: its last Keys, on Multiplication and Projection, are avowedly defective, “The Keys of Eudoxus open no more” [IV.3 ¶17], so she turns to another source.

summary: Eudoxus as reported in Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride, cited for the myth of Jupiter's grown-together feet freed by Isis, which Atwood reads as an allegory of the Art.
body: Atwood cites Eudoxus in Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride*, for the myth in which Isis frees Jupiter's grown-together feet; she reads it as an allegory of the Art. The interpretation quoted: “the mind and reason of the Supreme God, which in nature is invisible and dwelling in obscurity, by being put in motion becomes known” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n28].

summary: Quoted for Ether called Jove, for the felicity of seeing the Mysteries, and from the Bacchis on death, purification and initiation.
body: Atwood quotes Euripides (quoted voice) in support of her account of Ether as all-nourishing and called Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17; I.2 n16]. To show that the people placed their chief felicity in the Mysteries, she quotes a line spoken by Hercules and one from the *Bacchis*: “I was blessed when I got a sight of the mysteries” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8]. From *Bacchis* she also takes “a dream of death” for the threshold where the Lesser Mysteries end [II.3 ¶36; II.3 n48], and Bacchae verses supporting purification and initiation [II.3 ¶43; II.3 ¶44].

summary: Paracelsus's term, used by Atwood in the Appendix for the dream of its whole afterlife the soul brings into the body, its destiny; God's grace is the Divine evestrum relative to man.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood takes up Paracelsus's term: “the soul comes into this body with the dream of its whole afterlife presented to it” [APP ¶57]. This is its destiny, which moves a will that does not see beyond it. Against it stands “God’s grace (the Divine evestrum, relatively to man)” [APP ¶57], by which, Atwood says, we overcome it.

summary: What the abusers of the art succeeded in inducing before denying the Light its fulfilment; not further defined.
body: Atwood (her own voice) says the abusers of the work denied the Light its fulfilment after “having succeeded in inducing an exalted energy” [III.4 ¶6]. The text does not define the expression further.

headword: the excellent author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone
forms: the excellent author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone
the pious author of the Aquarium
summary: The author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone, cited by Atwood for the spirit-soul-body cycle and for the warning that pride or covetousness makes the art vanish.
body: Atwood cites this author from the Aquarium Sapientum (in the Musaeum Hermeticum) for a Latin enigma illustrating the separation, putrefaction and reunion of spirit, soul and body: “Spiritus ipse datur pro tempore corpori” [I.3 n21] (our rendering: the spirit itself is given to the body for a time). Elsewhere, as “the pious author of the Aquarium”, he supports her point that pride or covetousness after possession makes the art disappear: “this art will vanish from under thy hands” [III.4 ¶7; III.4 n4]. Atwood endorses this warning.

summary: In the verse Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the residue taken away once the matter has grown very dry, before the young Child is lodged in a bright bed.
body: The word occurs in the quoted verse of The Hunting of the Greene Lyon: when the matter has grown very dry, “The excrements be tane away;” [III.1 ¶65], before the young Child is laid in a bright bed. The voice is the quoted poem, not Atwood's own.

summary: The law of Universal nature, whose fountain Atwood names as the Substant Unity.
body: Atwood speaks of the Substant Unity as “the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law” [III.3 ¶79]. The text gives no further definition.

summary: That without which, Atwood says, every plan of improvement is defective; not further defined.
body: Atwood judges “every plan defective without the Exemplary Light” [IV.4 ¶18]. The expression is not further defined in the records.

summary: In Atwood's words, the Logos hidden and slain from the foundation in the fiat of our Identity, occulted in two diametrically reverse poles or principles.
body: Atwood writes that “the exemplary Logos is hidden, --- slain from the foundation in the exterminating fiat of our Identity” [III.3 ¶79]; its occultation lies in two diametrically reverse poles or principles. The text does not define it further.

summary: Atwood's qualifier for Part I's outer view of the progress and theory of alchemy, used in the heading.
body: The word appears in the heading of Part I: “An Exoteric View of the Progress and Theory of Alchemy” [I.1 ¶1]. Its sense is not further explained in the records; the heading apparently marks Part I as the outward, historical treatment.

summary: In the verse Tablet, a personified creative power that framed all things from nothing; in Atwood's prose, the resulting experience of life, third of the alchemical Three.
body: The voice is unclear. In the verse rendering of the Tablet the speaker addresses Experience as a creative power: “That thou art the very same, That didst from nothing all things frame;” [III.3 ¶76], having made the One Thing. In the following prose Atwood speaks of the Matter proved simple in experience and of “the resulting experience of life” [III.3 ¶77] as the third of the alchemical Three. How the personified power and the third principle relate is not stated; the records leave both readings side by side.

summary: An unnamed authority Atwood relies on for man's connection to the fountain of Universal Nature.
body: Atwood appeals to “the experienced” without naming them, on the point of our connection to the fountain of the Universal Nature [II.4 ¶19].

summary: Atwood's word for the practical hermetic work itself, seldom attempted and more rarely completed, through which the ancients found their whole philosophy and the Fathers came into Experience.
body:
In Atwood's own voice the Experiment is the practical work: “That was the Experiment that led our Fathers into Experience” [III.3 ¶61], and experience is the proper test of philosophy. She insists on perseverance for it (“than perseverance for this experiment” [III.4 ¶45]). She explains “why the Divine Experiment has been so seldom attempted and more rarely brought to a legitimate conclusion on this earth” [IV.4 ¶7], and says “In the course of this vital experiment the ancients discovered the whole of the philosophy they teach” [IV.4 ¶9]. She identifies it with a “pyrotechnical induction” of “the quintessence of Universal nature and her fruitful springs” [IV.4 ¶9].

The adjective “experimental” carries the same weight in Part I: Democritus is styled “the father of experimental philosophy” and “Pliny bears witness to the experimental fame of Democritus, and his skill in the occult sciences and practice of them” [I.1 ¶12]; Aristotle “led mankind astray from the path of true experiment” [I.1 ¶16]; the theosophic schools are “based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17], where practical science is set against abstracts. Contrast Atwood's critical use of “experimental philosophy” for modern science [IV.4 ¶30].

summary: The voice cited from the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C., cited for the reversal of death in the work.
body: Atwood cites the title page of the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C. to illustrate the overcoming of death in the work: “O death how art thou vanquished” [I.3 n43].

summary: What the soul has not yet attained while she regards her image objectively and is 'in Hades'.
body: Atwood describes the soul, while she regards her image objectively and is in Hades, as being “before attaining to the experimental knowledge” [II.3 ¶36]. The term is not further defined here; the context suggests a knowing by inward experience as opposed to outward regard.

summary: Atwood's name for modern science following Lord Bacon's 'exterminating chase', which she says labours for selfish aggrandizement.
body: Atwood, in her own voice, criticizes modern science led by Lord Bacon's “exterminating chase”: “experimental philosophy labours for selfish aggrandizement” [IV.4 ¶30].

summary: The practical stage of the art, which follows study of the doctrine.
body: Atwood distinguishes study of the doctrine from what “is afterwards needed for the experimental proof” [III.4 ¶15], that is, the practical stage of the art.

summary: A required means of approaching the secrets of the highest causes, which Atwood compares to Charon's fee.
body: Atwood states: “neither are the secrets of the highest causes approached without a mean of expiation” [III.2 ¶44], comparing it to the fee paid to Charon. What the expiation consists of is not spelled out in the record.

summary: Unnamed interpreters of the Mysteries whose narcotic explanation of initiatory transfiguration Atwood rejects.
body: Atwood reports the expounders' view that “all this splendid delirium and transfiguration in the Mysteries was the effect of narcotic liquors” [II.4 ¶56], and rejects it as common sense acting Procrustes-like.

summary: In the Appendix, the means by which the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes the desire of the lower life “opening up into the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life, by exstasis” [APP ¶97]. The four names given there are apparently treated as equivalent.

summary: Outer and inner reality, which at the completion of the work are seen to blend and confirm each other.
body: Atwood writes that at the completion “the External and Internal Worlds were seen to blend together in confluent harmony” [III.3 ¶82], each confirming the other.

summary: In Eirenaeus, the well-regulated outward heat that alone assists Nature in the Second operation.
body: Quoting Eirenaeus, Atwood gives the Second operation as performed by Nature “by the sole assistance of a well-regulated external fire” [IV.1 ¶11].

summary: Boehme's term for the outward self, which could hardly grasp or express what he had seen inwardly.
body: In a passage Atwood quotes from Boehme, he says of his inward vision: “I could very hardly apprehend the same in my external man” [III.2 ¶16].

summary: A Hermetic writer Atwood lists among Paracelsus's worthy disciples and in the 'golden chain' of Hermetic philosophers who traced the poets' allusions.
body: Faber is listed in a note with the work Opera Medico-Chimica [I.1 ¶70; I.1 n88]. Atwood names him with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Helvetius as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Tollius and Michael Maier in the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers” who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own; she cites them in support [III.1 ¶25]. In an aside on Ripley's method the text remarks: “Faber is so wise that he will not understand him” [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: The fable of Isis feeding Horus with fire, cited to illustrate nourishing the son with fire.
body: Atwood cites the fable in which “she brought forth Horus, even feeding him with fire” [I.3 n41], to illustrate the nourishing of the son with fire.

headword: fable of Mars and Venus taken together by Vulcan
forms: fable of Mars and Venus taken together by Vulcan
summary: The fable cited to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, with fuller explanation deferred.
body: Atwood cites the fable of Mars and Venus caught together by Vulcan to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, promising to explain it later [I.3 n49].

headword: the fable (Typhon, Osiris, Isis; the Egyptian monarch)
forms: the fable (Typhon, Osiris, Isis; the Egyptian monarch)
summary: The Egyptian fable of Typhon, Osiris and Isis, read by Atwood as a figure of the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis and the reconciling of opposites.
body: Atwood reads the fable that “Typhon killed Osiris, his uterine brother, and scattered his members to the four winds” [III.1 ¶53] as illustrating the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis; the hair grown in Ethiopia figures the fire allowed to grow [III.1 ¶56]; and Isis figures the reconciling of the opposites [III.1 ¶63].

headword: the fables (Theseus, Ariadne, Jason, Medea, Hercules, Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses, Minerva, Aeneas, the Sybil)
forms: the fables (Theseus, Ariadne, Jason, Medea, Hercules, Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses, Minerva, Aeneas, the Sybil)
summary: The heroic fables Atwood cites to show that the hero never labours alone but is aided by wise counsel, as the Moon aids the seeking Reason.
body: Atwood draws on the fables of Theseus and Ariadne, Jason and Medea, Hercules and Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses and Minerva, Aeneas and the Sybil to show that the hero never labours alone but is aided by wise counsel, as the Moon or Passive Intelligence aids the seeking Reason [III.1 ¶40].

summary: The intellect which, Atwood says, is not born without Motion, figured by Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan's aid.
body: Atwood writes: “without the instrumentality of Motion, which the lame god personates, the Fabricate Intellect is not born” [IV.1 ¶34]. The figure is Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan's help; Vulcan, the lame god, stands for Motion (stated).

summary: In the cabalistic scriptures and antique schools Atwood reports, a higher faculty latent in man which, revealed, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her source.
body: Reporting the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood speaks of “the germ of a higher faculty or Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32] in man, which, revealed and set alone, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her substratal source. It is identified with “This Being” (“This Being, moreover, or Faculty of Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32]).

summary: The earthy residue of the matter: in Hermes the third from two, from which death is removed; in Sendivogius cast away; in Eudoxus kept and washed, as hiding the Balm of Life.
body: The records come from three quoted authorities, who differ on its handling. In a Hermetic passage it is the third of the three that come from two, the earth that remains below, and death is to be taken away: “death from the faeces” [I.3 ¶23]. Sendivogius has the residue discarded after putrefaction, before the spirit is returned to the water: “the faeces being cast away” [III.3 ¶29]. Eudoxus, by contrast, says the black earthy residue at the bottom of the vessel must not be discarded: “The Balm of Life is hid in these unclean faeces” [IV.3 ¶8]; it is washed with the celestial water until it is no longer black. Whether these describe different stages or different practices is not settled by the records.

summary: Cited for the soul's permanent union with the glorified body, as an analogy for the union of spirits and purified bodies in the work.
body: The doctrine of Faith is invoked as an analogy: as the soul is permanently united with the glorified body, so spirits and purified bodies are joined, and “there shall be no more separation or death” [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: For Atwood, faith is a real ideal conception that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge, not blind credulity; it is a common witness inferring a reality beyond experience, to be directed by reason.
body:
Atwood insists that “The faith we invite is no blind credulity” [III.3 ¶64]. Faith is a real ideal conception, however small, that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge and practical experience. It is a liberty of thought that bears its own evidence. She equates it with the ideal conception: “without faith, without the ideal conception, nothing is or can be proven” [III.3 ¶64].

Later she presents faith as a witness common to all: “we have a witness which believes and infers, a reality beyond present experience” [IV.4 ¶15]. It draws the other faculties after it: “faith is the very attracting loadstone which hope pursues” [IV.4 ¶19], drawing hope, desire and reason. Faith must nevertheless be directed by reason [IV.4 ¶15–19].

summary: In the Table Talk, Atwood treats the Fall as Nature's being taken from the primal source into a will, a fall that was spiritual before it was sensible.
body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes: “Nature has taken from the primal source into a will is the history of the Fall.” [APP ¶48]. The sentence is garbled as printed; apparently the Fall is Nature's being taken from the primal source into a will. She also holds that “the Fall was not at first sensible, but spiritual; the principle of the Fall is a long way back behind its effects” [APP ¶121]. Birth into this life is a continuous image of it [APP ¶121]. See also *feminine principle*, which she calls the cause of the Fall [APP ¶98].

summary: What remains of sense impressions even in trance, which must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity.
body: Atwood (II.2) describes the remnant of sense impressions that persists even in trance as “a false imagination, which it is requisite to destroy” [II.2 ¶10]. It must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity [II.2 ¶10].

summary: An address at the Faraday Society's opening meeting, cited by Atwood as an example of the modern view of alchemists as deluded crucible-brooders, which she criticizes.
body: Atwood cites this address as a sample of the modern view that the alchemists were deluded crucible-brooders, and she criticizes it [I.1 ¶33]. The passage she quotes derives a word from an alchemist's obscure style: “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33].

summary: Cited for reference only.
In the Table Talk, the feminine principle is that which is above, drawing the self-willed source upward by love; it is the cause of the Fall and, advanced, of restoration.
body: Both points come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood identifies the feminine principle with Wisdom and the heart life: “that which is above (the feminine principle, --- Wisdom, --- the heart life)” [APP ¶98]. It draws the self-willed source upward by love, and the self-willed source thereby becomes a passive feminine principle [APP ¶98]. It works both ways: “As the feminine spirit is the cause of the Fall”, so, advanced, it is the cause of restoration [APP ¶98].

summary: The active agent by which one life works on another (or a thing on itself), opening and dissolving it so that a higher life is freed and exalted; Hermes calls it the Key of the philosophers.
body:
**Atwood's usage.** A ferment is a superior power that frees the subject-matter: “being set free by the force of a superior ferment or attraction” [I.2 ¶4]. The Ether is called fermenting, and “the fermented Spirit assimilates the Light throughout” [I.2 ¶8]. It is a thing's own agent of change and converts it into another nature with nothing foreign added. In the Art the Spirit is raised “by its won prepared must or leaven” and gains virtue “in proportion to the virtue which it has acquired in the fermentation” [I.2 ¶48]. The Stone is exalted by fermentation within its own kind, and “every ferment begets its own exaltation” [I.3 n55]. Reason acts as a ferment and “would gather all up, as a ferment” into its Light [III.1 ¶21]. She contrasts “that body which is gold (not a brazen ferment)” [III.1 ¶19]. Sulfur is called the golden ferment, and the rising light keeps “a fermental odor of the body” so that the soul does not depart altogether [III.1 ¶53]. The result depends on the agent: “according to the virtue of the fermenting principle is the result obtained”. The philosophic matter “is purified by successive interchanging of ferments”, as sap becomes wine [IV.1 ¶44, ¶46].

**Hermes** compares the ferment to leaven in dough: “see how the ferment in this case doth change the former natures to another thing” [I.3 ¶58]. It must be kindred, since “there is no ferment otherwise than from a kindred nature” [I.3 ¶58]. It whitens, prevents combustion, holds the tincture and joins bodies, and it is the Key of the philosophers [I.3 ¶58].

**Other voices.** In a note whose voice is unclear, “the inquisitive light once entering as a ferment” meets its proper pole and converts the medium into itself [II.3 n40]. *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* requires that “Which Ferment must be of such a thing, As was the workes begyning;” [III.1 ¶65]. In the poem this means Luna for the white and Sol for the red, each worked alone with the Lion's blood. It is added warm to the Magnet as a fourth part, and continual fermentation multiplies the Medicine [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood's “Rational Ferment” [III.1 ¶66] is a separate term.

**Table Talk (APP, later layer).** Here a ferment is the action of one life on another: “When one life being fermented throws its life to another equally fermented” [APP ¶42]. Seven is “a Rest from the ferment or action of the Vitalizing or Divine principles” [APP ¶69]. The reader is told to “so ferment the whole including spirit of your life that it, the former, opens, corrupts, dissolves” [APP ¶126], and “each fermented spirit advances upon its origin” [APP ¶111]. *Fermented* = elaborated: “perfectly elaborated --- i.e., fermented”, said of the individual Logos that transmutes the whole being [APP ¶101].

summary: In a passage quoted from Aristhenes, that into which the 'least' thing is to be drawn by artifice; the text does not define it.
body: Atwood quotes Aristhenes, who says to “draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26]. The thing to be drawn in is the ‘least’ thing. The passage does not define the term further. See *ferment*.

equivalences.with: the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God (Kabalah)

summary: The core operation in which a life worked by a kindred life dissolves and passes into a higher state; Atwood's best image of the Divine Art and the final cementing of the Stone's union.
body:
**Main text (Atwood).** Fermentation is the subject's artificial progress to perfection: “In its artificial fermentation and progress towards perfection” [I.2 ¶37]. Liquid analogies denote “the fermental principle of the spirit and her distilled quintessence” [I.2 ¶33]. The chapter title names “the spontaneous fermentation which the Vital Spirit undergoes, and the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” [III.1 ¶9]. Modern practice does not push this process to the uttermost [III.1 ¶9]. Atwood distinguishes two kinds: “there is a twofold fermentation --- a spiritual and a bodily” [IV.3 ¶21]. The spiritual kind multiplies the tinctures, and the bodily kind incorporates the medicine into gold or silver. Fermentation is the last operation, in which the Stone's union is finally cemented and its parts agree and relate to the external world: “which union or consummation of its transmutative virtue is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. She asserts an identity with the Kabalah: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God, that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. The Stone is fermented with its own metal (silver for the White, gold for the Red), which Atwood reads as Light [IV.3 ¶27].

**Eudoxus.** His Fifth Key operation is “the Fermentation of the Stone with the perfect body” [IV.3 ¶14]. The Stone is joined, as leaven and through the Spirit, with the Perfect Body, so that the whole becomes a leaven able to multiply.

**Table Talk (APP, later layer).** Here fermentation is the core operation: a life fermented by its similar passes into a further state, and this is repeated over and over. “The word fermentation conveys an idea of the perfecting principle and of the possibility of transmutation beyond any other word”, and “it is the best image of the Divine Art which earthly processes give” [APP ¶27]. One life is worked by another so that both dissolve and are reproduced in a third. Unlike ordinary generation, the result is exalted: “spiritual generation is according to the fermentative law”, an ascending process [APP ¶132].

summary: The power of vital melioration that man possesses whole within himself, for the rectification of Nature's Law.
body: Atwood holds that man has within himself “the whole fermentative virtue, motive, and principle of vital melioration” for the rectification of Nature's Law [IV.4 ¶3].

summary: Proverbial sayings cited in the Table Talk in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, higher or lower.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood cites “Festina lente, Ne quid nimis” in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, whether higher or lower [APP ¶110].

summary: A philosopher named with Kant and Schelling, whose metaphysics Atwood criticizes as falling short of objective realization; in the Table Talk he saw the Absolute ground without experiencing it.
body: In the main text Atwood groups Kant, Fichte and Schelling and criticizes their metaphysics. It ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Fichte broke through into the Absolute ground, seeing it but without experiencing it [APP ¶96]. He appears again in the same list as one who ‘knew it’ [APP ¶117].

summary: Translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes, whose Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander Atwood cites; he explained the art theoretically.
body: Atwood cites Ficinus's Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and the Poimander [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n11]. She calls him the translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes. He explained the art theoretically, and she cites his *Liber de Arte Chemica* (Marsilii Ficini Florent.) [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n68]. He also appears as “Ficinus the Platonist” in a list [I.1 ¶39].

summary: In a quoted monk's continuation of Basil Valentine, something instituted by one who has befriended Vulcan; the text does not explain it.
body: The monk who continues Basil Valentine says that only one who has “firmly contracted friendship with Vulcan, and instituted the Fiery bath of Love” can demonstrate the separation of venom from the Medicine [IV.1 ¶40]. The expression is not explained.

summary: In a recipe quoted from Eirenaeus, an ingredient (four parts) bearing the Magic Steel in its belly, joined to nine parts Lodestone; the text does not explain it.
body: Atwood quotes Eirenaeus: “Take four parts of our Fiery Dragon, which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The Fiery Dragon is to be conjoined to nine parts Lodestone [IV.1 ¶43]. The passage does not explain it.

summary: In Eudoxus, what animates the Water once the faeces are washed free of blackness; it works all the wonders of the Art.
body: Eudoxus says that once the faeces are washed free of blackness, “your Water shall be animated with this Fiery Essence, which works all the wonders of our Art” [IV.3 ¶8].

summary: The trial that reason is artificially constrained not to escape.
body: Atwood speaks of reason “being artificially constrained, lest it should escape the fiery ordeal” [I.3 n50].

summary: What the two warring dragons become when decocted in their own venom; for Atwood, a state beyond the four degrees, neuter from all yet partaking of all.
body: A French adept quoted by Atwood says the two warring dragons, “being decocted totally in their own venom, are turned into a Fifth Essence” [III.1 ¶58]. Atwood describes it as made beyond the four precedent degrees of perfection: “neuter from all, yet partaking of all in perpetuity of union” [III.3 ¶32]. It is embodied but not subject to gross corporeity [III.3 ¶32].

summary: The end or purpose into whose supernatural fixity Art brings the Matter; hidden in ordinary life but manifest in Alchemy.
body:
For Atwood, the Matter's alterations end when it “is brought by Art into the supernatural fixity of its Final Cause” [III.2 ¶22]. Final causes are ends or purposes. They are hidden in ordinary life, but in Alchemy, in act as in effect, “Final Causes are of all things most manifestly revealed” [III.4 ¶9]. The superior power filling the soul is “proximate to the Final Cause” [III.4 ¶6].

In IV.2 a passage of the Master carries a gloss whose voice is unclear: “the boundary of hearts (i.e., the Final Cause)” [IV.2 ¶14]. It enters above the Foliated Sulphur when fire is poured on it. Compare the generated Being, “perceiving itself indeed to be the Final Object of its own First Cause, is good” [IV.2 ¶8]. See also *First Cause*.

summary: The secret, vital fire of the philosophers, distinct from common fire; variously identified with Intellect, the life of man, the essence of life, the sulfur and seed of gold.
body:
**Atwood.** “Our fire” is the philosophers' own fire, “magical, creative, vital” [I.3 n41]. It is most subtle and extremely volatile, and it vivifies, depurates and segregates; it is distinct from common fire. “Some call it the miracle of the world” [I.3 n41]. The True matter is discovered by “no other Fire but that of Intellect” [III.2 ¶62], sublimed and fortified in its efficient source. She takes “the life of man therein circulating to be a pure fire” [IV.4 ¶4], incorporated in an ethereal vapour and containing the Universal Efficient. The method of ascent is “that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) fire is the medium through which the Divine Will conducts Light: “the fire here is our chaotic will in potentiality”, and “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

**Quoted authorities.** For the scholiast, “the essence of life, says the scholiast, is nothing else than a pure, naked, unmingled Fire” [I.3 n22]. It is celestial and generating, not elementary, and it is “the temperate unguent, which is fire” [I.3 ¶24]. Sendivogius says: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]. “It is also in all things indiscernibly.” [II.4 ¶39], moved only by God's will. It bears God's seal and is the death and separation of everything compounded. Eirenaeus urges: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. He identifies it: “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold, says Eirenaeus”, and “this is the seed of gold, involved in many links, and held prisoner, as it were, in a deep dungeon” [III.1 ¶14]. This fire is imprisoned in the hard, dry body and freed by our water, and it appears in the Third Menstrual [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood names Eirenaeus' ‘internal fire of the sulfur of thy water’ as the vital perscrutinator [III.1 ¶13]. Pontanus says: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul, that so thou mayest attain to thy desire; for it is the key of all the philosophers” [III.1 ¶37]. Vaughan writes that “the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing”, yet it holds all the secrets of corruption and generation [III.4 ¶38]. An Adept names “the natural, unnatural, and the supernatural Fires”, which must be lit quickly so that none puts out another; a Fourth supervenes over them [IV.2 ¶11]. Sendivogius also says to “put them into Our Fire and let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21]. See also *Fire of the Wise*.

summary: In the Paracelsian passage Atwood quotes, the life-fire in man, called Antimony by adepts, which does nothing excellent while immured but flows forth as panacea after purgation.
body: In a Paracelsian passage the fire of life is the life-fire in man: “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts, can effect nothing comparatively excellent whilst it is immured” [III.1 ¶10]. Like unlit fuel, it does nothing while immured. After purgation the pure life flows forth as panacea [III.1 ¶10]. The same passage asserts the identity with Antimony.

summary: A fire named in several contexts: what drew the Magians toward nature's central source, what besieges the bound serpents, and that by which the Matter brings forth Orus; it is not defined.
body: Atwood says the Magians were “drawn about the fire of nature, as it were, into communication with her central source” [I.1 ¶39]. Cornelius Agrippa's disciple advises: “Thou must incamp against them with the fire of nature”, meaning against the bound serpents [III.1 ¶50]. The text does not say whether this is the ‘fire of the natural life’ of III.1 ¶43. The Matter brings forth Orus “by the Fire of nature lawfully conceived” [III.3 ¶62]. None of these passages explains the term.

summary: In Sendivogius, the fire of the second operation, different from that of the first.
body: Sendivogius directs the work to be set on “the fire of putrefaction and generation, not on such a one as thou didst in the first operation” [IV.3 ¶21].

summary: In Eudoxus, the secret fire that is the only instrument of sublimation, dissolving the Stone gently into Water; no philosopher has openly revealed it.
body: Eudoxus calls it “the Fire of the Wise, which is the only instrument which can work this sublimation” [IV.3 ¶5]. It dissolves the Stone naturally and without violence into Water. It is the Secret Fire: “No philosopher has ever openly revealed this Secret Fire” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is also called “this Secret Fire, and this powerful agent, which works all the wonders of the Art” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is known by its described characters and by divine gift. Eudoxus also says “the whole compound, is made perfect by the action of our Fire” [IV.3 ¶7], but he does not assert that this is the Fire of the Wise.

summary: In a quoted adept, a spirit rooted in the spiritual fire earth, from which it is fed by a secret influx.
body: The adept Atwood quotes says the Fire Spirit is rooted in the spiritual fire earth and “receives from it a secret influx upon which it feeds” [II.3 ¶41].

summary: The region consciousness enters after the middle region (Atwood) or after the Aquaster (a quoted adept), where invisible things are seen; the text does not define it further.
body: Atwood says that after the middle region, at the dark descent, consciousness “enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]. The adept she quotes places it after the Aquaster: one who has “entered the Fire World, sees what is both invisible and incredible to common men” [II.3 ¶41]. Neither passage defines it further.

summary: Cited in the Table Talk, where Atwood reads graven images as the practical result of self-centering and stopping in finite gifts as idolatry.
body: Both citations come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood interprets graven images (the Second Commandment) as the practical result of self-centering, which violates the First [APP ¶100]. She also cites the commandments for the view that stopping in finite gifts is idolatry [APP ¶135].

summary: The cause of a being's existence, which each has in himself; the top of the ascending series of causes, into which Reason re-enters and the only proper object of seeking.
body:
Atwood places the First Cause at the top of the ascending series of causes, the ‘Final Cause of all’. The lowest effect reverses it: “the last and lowest effect, in which all the attributes of the First Cause are not only deficient but reversed” [III.2 ¶54]. Selfhood is raised into it. In a passage whose voice is unclear, expulsive life draws consciousness away from it: “drawn without to a debilitated consciousness away from its First Cause” [II.1 ¶21]. In IV.2 it is essence, the subsisting as a particular thing. “cause and principle form the First Why” [IV.2 ¶7]. “the speculative Motive of the first Cause is finally produced in reversionary order from the Third” and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶8]. It is the only proper object of seeking. The aim is to “attain to that supremacy of Reason which re-enters to its First Cause” [IV.2 ¶18], and “the consummating knowledge of the First Cause” comes in quietude and cessation of mental energy [IV.2 ¶33]. At the end of the work “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62], and the upright Mind of Man “co-operates with the First Cause” [IV.4 ¶32].

Aristotle, quoted on deliberation, uses the phrase differently: men work back from the proposed end through its media “until they arrive at the first Cause which is discovered in the last place” [IV.1 ¶30].

In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) each being has the cause of its existence in himself. Since Existence is one, knowing it is knowing the cause of all: “the consciousness can be brought into contact with its First Cause” [APP ¶6]. See also *Final Cause*.

summary: What the dissolving water reduces all metals into, glossed as water.
body: Atwood says the dissolving water “reduces them into their first ens, or water”, speaking of all metals [I.3 n12]. The first ens is thus identified with water.

summary: An initial step whose knowledge, together with volatilizing the fixed tincture, admits one to the temple of Divine Science; the text does not explain it.
body: Atwood writes: “He who knows the first entrance” and how to volatilize the fixed tincture is admitted to the temple of Divine Science [IV.4 ¶32]. The text does not explain what the first entrance is.

summary: In Norton's verse, the foundational knowledge required of anyone who hopes 'to come by Lakimie'.
body: Norton, quoted by Atwood, requires of anyone hoping ‘to come by Lakimie’: “He must know hys first filosophie,” [IV.2 ¶5].

summary: Basil Valentine's term for what nature holds concealed, to be sought with one's own eyes and hand as the basis for judging rightly.
body: Spoken by Basil Valentine (“the monk”), as quoted by Atwood: “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” [III.1 ¶13]. The record presents it as something to be sought personally, with one's own eyes and hand, and as the basis for philosophizing with judgment.

summary: In the Platonic Successor's account, the highest principle, beyond all and more ineffable than all, celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe.
body: A view quoted from the Platonic Successor [II.4 ¶41]. The First God is celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe and only last as producing earth, heavens and souls. He is praised “as the God of all gods, the Unity of all unities, and beyond the First Adyta” and “as more ineffable than all silence, and more Unknown than all recondite essence” [II.4 ¶41].

summary: Atwood's term for the original life about whose penetralia consciousness is drawn in Hades, and from whose perpetual motion the nether darkness flows.
body: In Atwood's own voice: consciousness in Hades is drawn about the penetralia of the first life, and the nether darkness is described as “flowing out from the perpetual motion of the first life” [II.3 ¶18].

summary: In Plotinus as quoted, the light shining primarily in itself, at once illuminating and illuminated, and the foundation of every intellect.
body: Quoted from Plotinus [III.2 ¶66]. The First Light shines primarily in itself and “at one and the same time illuminates and is illuminated” [III.2 ¶66]. It is identified with the ground of intellect: “this First Light, which is the foundation of every intellect and primarily knows itself” [III.2 ¶66].

summary: Albertus Magnus's definition: an unctuous subtle humidity forcibly incorporated with a subtle earthy part.
body: Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “the first material of the metals is an unctuous subtle humidity, forcibly incorporated with a subtle terrestreity” [I.2 ¶29].

equivalences.with: union of masculine and feminine spirits
unam substantiam (one substance created by God)
very natural true sperm of the greater world
water of our sea; water of life
That which is prior to all things
flying eagle (the name it bears at first sight)

summary: The one subject of the Art: the common root substance of all natures, not found on earth or among sensible things, reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life.
body:
**Atwood's account.** The First Matter is the common basis to which bodies can be reduced and from which they take new form — “their common basis or mercurial first matter” [I.2 ¶3] — and so the true subject of transmutation; she equates it with the “Universal Subject” [I.2 ¶7] and the “Universal Matter of the adepts”, which ordinary analysis does not discover [I.2 ¶3]. It is not any sensible thing but a middle substance generated from the Universal Spirit's active and passive relations, “the simple generated substance of life and light, immanifestly flowing throughout nature” [I.2 ¶34]; “the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits” [I.2 ¶33]; “Thus obscure, after all, is the true Matter of the Alchemists” [I.2 ¶34]. Albert describes it “with the characteristic minuteness of personal observation” [I.1 ¶39]; Vaughan's Lumen de Lumine gives “an allegorical display of the first matter” [I.1 ¶74]. The alchemists claim for it extreme attributes and miraculous origin, as the Greeks do for the ethereal hypostasis [III.1 ¶3].

**Identities.** It is generated by an emancipation of the Fontal Source, “and this is Diana, and that refulgent Light which eclipses every other light but that of its proper Reason” [III.1 ¶70]. It is “the abyssal Darkness”, brought forth by God as First Matter [III.2 ¶56]; it is not known in energy “but flies from him, indeed, who wishes intently to behold” [III.2 ¶57]. Beyond all things it is “That which is prior to all things” [III.2 ¶66]. Footnoted identities: “very natural true sperm of the greater world”, and Sendivogius's “water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]. Chapter III.3 treats its manifestation and “Information by Light” [III.3 ¶1].

**Quoted voices.** Mylius: God “creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus” (ours: created one substance; this we name the first matter) [III.2 ¶2; also III.2 ¶56]. Basil Valentine: the all-containing water formed into earth by the dryness of its fire and air is “the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19]. Vaughan: “The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape” [II.3 ¶30], calling it the mineral nature; knowing it is discovering “the Sanctuary of Nature” [III.4 ¶44]. The Rosy Cross: “O, most excellent subject! Out of which all things in the world are generated” — poison named “the flying eagle”, and “the Seed of Divine benediction”, hidden from the wicked by its vestures, parent of the philosophical Sun and Moon [III.3 ¶63]. Arnold: the Stone is dissolved “that it may be reduced into its first Matter” [IV.1 ¶7]; Khunrath: the Azoth “reduces bodies to their First Matter” [IV.3 ¶28] and it appears as wet, impure “mud earth” partaking of Adam [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: Mercury, “Our Old Man”, “is the first matter of all metals” [IV.3 ¶10]. Flamel: “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶57].

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** It is not found on earth but reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life. “It is immediately antecedent to the first consciousness” and presents itself “as the extreme of bound and definiteness reverting to non- being” [APP ¶137]; its attributes are transmutable forms, hence seeming contradictions.
