Elsewhere, “the First Mater which is humanly producible” may be unlawfully formed for a finite end [APP ¶37].

equivalences.with: that life which the creatures have

summary: In Paracelsus as quoted, the invisible, intangible life present in all things — the life the creatures have.
body: Quoted from Paracelsus: “This is the First Matter of the elements, which can neither be seen nor felt, and yet is in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; it is “nothing else but that life which the creatures have” [I.2 ¶26].

equivalences.with: Antecedent and Final Cause of all

summary: In Atwood's words, the One with whom one would move and whose Will one would be, at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all.
body: Atwood asks who can “move One with the First Mover, and Be His Will, who is at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all” [III.3 ¶78].

summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, the laborious manual first stage of the work, disposing the matter as first found, contrasted with the Second where Nature works alone.
body: Eirenaeus's term, as quoted: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6], and “nothing can be achieved in the First Operation without sweating and much labor” [IV.1 ¶11]. It concerns disposing the matter as first found and is contrasted with the Second Operation, in which Nature works alone.

summary: In Vaughan as quoted, the first part of the Gross Work, which Agrippa knew and made clear; not described further.
body: Vaughan says Agrippa “knew the First Preparation, and has clearly discovered it” [IV.1 ¶36]. The packet gives no description of the preparation itself.

equivalences.with: secret natural interior Fire of Adepts

summary: Atwood's term for the subject in its first prepared state, which she says is meant by the Lunar Vulcan and is also called Diana.
body: In Atwood's voice: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject”, “which is also called Diana, and the secret natural interior Fire of Adepts” [IV.1 ¶29].

summary: What the theurgically prepared seeker rises to: the most united in nature, its Flower, through which it is Deity.
body: Atwood, following “the doctrine of the ancients”: “if any one wish to discover the First Principle, according to the doctrine of the ancients, he must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. It is described as the most united in nature, its Flower, that through which it is Deity, suspended from its fountain and holding the Universe in sympathetic consent with itself [III.3 ¶59].

equivalences.with: fugitive spirits condensed in the air

summary: Lully's name for the chaotic, monster-shaped spirits, which Atwood explains by the Seed of Spirit found in their purified material extreme.
body: Atwood reports: “But Lully, indeed, calls these chaotic forms first principles” [II.3 ¶30], and calls the first principles of the Art “Spiritus fugitives in aero condensators” (fugitive spirits condensed in the air) [II.3 ¶30]. Atwood explains the name: they are so called because the Seed of Spirit is found in their purified material extreme, not because they are permanent or rational [II.3 ¶30].

summary: Atwood's phrase for the stage of life in which the true Light, as distinct from common light, becomes efficient.
body: Atwood speaks of the true Light, distinct from common light, as “that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30]. Not further explained.

summary: Atwood's term for the origin from which every advance in externals leads man further away.
body: Atwood: “every advance we make in externals leads us further off from the First Source” [IV.4 ¶18].

summary: In Atwood's words, what man may know really and experimentally — the highest privilege he can propose.
body: Atwood presents as man's highest privilege “to know the First Truth of things really and experimentally” [IV.4 ¶22].

summary: What the sought insoluble, transmuting, uniting union requires; voice unclear.
body: Voice unclear in the record: “such a tie cannot be without the first unity” [III.1 ¶50]. The context links creating and transmuting without violence to the first power, wisdom and love.

summary: In the Appendix, the green first stage of life, identified with hope as the first aspiration to progress, whose ripened Life is purple.
body: From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), in Atwood's voice: “The first vegetative life is green, it arises with hope; it is hope” [APP ¶119]; “The purple color is its ripened Life” [APP ¶119].

summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, the work accomplished by assiduity and industry, with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.
body: Eirenaeus: “it is by assiduity and industry that we accomplish the First Work” [IV.1 ¶6], with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.

summary: In the Appendix, the early results of the work: real but not permanent, to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.
body: From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The first-fruits, tough perfectly real, should not be accepted as permanent” [APP ¶74]; they are to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.

summary: In Atwood's account, the third operation: after calcinations, a reunion into a more permanent form of Being.
body: Atwood describes fixation as the operation in which “after calcinations there is a reunion into a more permanent form of Being” [III.2 ¶64].

summary: The two contrary states the work inverts and unites: the fixed made volatile and the volatile fixed, until both reach perfect Fixity.
body: Atwood describes the work as “that which is fixed becoming volatile and the volatile nature fixed” [I.2 ¶20]. In Part IV (voice unclear) “the fixed is made volatile” in the dissolution, wholly so in the Second Operation [IV.1 ¶36], and the fixed must be separated “from the unfixed” [IV.1 ¶40]; fixed Antimony reaches fixed disease [IV.1]. Eudoxus, quoted, makes the compound of Art from the union of the two, which act on each other until they “are volatilized and fixed reciprocally into a perfect Fixity” [IV.3 ¶9].

summary: In the Democritus passage, material drawn out and worked on the coals until it appears Golden.
body: Quoted from Democritus: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily” [IV.1 ¶43], it is worked on the coals until it appears Golden.

summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, silver (for the white) or gold (for the red), melted with the Stone in projection.
body: The Author of the Open Entrance directs “four parts of one of the fixed metals, i.e., silver of it be for the white, or gold if it be for the red” [IV.3 ¶20] to be used with the Stone in projection.

summary: In Eudoxus as quoted, the salt extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, in which Mercury's whole energy consists; the Blood of our Stone.
body: Eudoxus calls it “the Fixed Salt, which is the Blood of our Stone” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, and the whole energy of Mercury consists in it; distilled water “carries up with it a part of this fiery salt” [IV.3 ¶9].

summary: The balsam of nature that preserves bodies (per the Scholiast), and the Philosophers' Stone into which fixed Mercury turns (per The Triumph).
body: Atwood reports the Scholiast's view: “The fixed sulfur of adepts, according to our Scholiast, is the true balsam of nature” [I.3 n61]; “The more anything abounds with this balsam, the longer it lives and is preserved from perishing” [I.3 n61], and the universal medicine is concreted from things rich in it. The author of The Triumph makes the fixed and nourished Mercury become “the fixed Sulphur, which is the Stone of Philosophers” [IV.2 ¶6].

summary: Something fixed which must be rendered volatile and returned free; knowing how admits one to the temple of Divine Science.
body: Atwood speaks of knowing “how to render the fixed tincture of life volatile, and to return it, being free” [IV.4 ¶32] as admission to the temple of Divine Science. Not further explained.

summary: In Bloomfield as quoted, the three ‘persons’ to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.
body: Quoted from Bloomfield: “The Fixt, the Variable, and the Fugitive” [IV.2 ¶36] are three persons to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.

summary: An adept whose own account of finding, preparing and projecting the Stone Atwood quotes at length, and whom she cites repeatedly as an authority on the matter and fire.
body:
Atwood quotes Nicholas Flamel's own account at length as a remarkable, well-known case: the book, its explanation, the preparation, projection and the moral effect of the Stone — “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶56, I.1 ¶57]. Sources named are his Hieroglyphics and Testament; listed writings include La Sommaire Philosophique (in French verse, translated in the Theatrum Chemicum), Le Desir desiree and Le Grand Eclaircissement [I.1 ¶58]. His Summario Philosophico gave extracts from Democritus [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n16]. He is named with Rupicessa, De Meun, Pontanus, Basil Valentine and Ripley among genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

Atwood uses him as an example: though he had matter, fire and furnace from Abraham the Jew, he still wandered three years [III.1 ¶37]. His Summula supports the alchemists' garden, “where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 n4], and the nature of the fire — not coal or wood but “a bright shining fire like the Sun itself, whose heat must neither be excessive, but always of one and the same degree” [IV.1 ¶41, IV.1 n35]. His Second Book is cited for learned discretion [IV.1 ¶29]. He is cited alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7] and speaks “more particularly” on the two Mercuries: “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red”, warning he was himself deceived until the Jew informed him [IV.3 ¶10]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is compared for the macrocosm's image evolved before the mental eye in regeneration [APP ¶55].

equivalences.with: Water that wets not the hands
White Island of Vishnu; Lord of Radha; White Paradise

summary: An Arabian name for the Matter which Atwood says truly designates the substant hypothesis, identified with Magnesia and the water that wets not the hands.
body: In Atwood's voice, by this Arabian name “thus the substant hypothesis is said very truly to be designated” [III.2 ¶8]. She equates it with several names: “the white sand, Quellum, which Van Helmont speaks of”; “this salt is the Water that wets not the hands”; “that identical Magnesia that was exhibited in the Mysteries”; and “the White Island of Vishnu; the Lord of Radha; the White Paradise” [III.2 ¶8].

summary: What the rectified circulation makes manifest, turned back toward its Archetypal Source.
body: Atwood speaks of the operation aiming “to make manifest the Flower of Intellect retrospectively to its Archetypal Source” [IV.2 ¶20]; apparently the fruit of the rectified circulation, directed back to its origin.

summary: In the Divine Oracle Atwood quotes, the faculty with which the Intelligible must be understood.
body: Quoted from the Divine Oracle: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶43]. The passage associates it with an empty mind and a pure turning eye; the text does not define it further.

summary: Named by Atwood, with Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber, as an intelligent and worthy disciple of Paracelsus.
body: Atwood lists Fludd among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, alongside Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. The book says nothing more about him here.

summary: In a Hermes passage, the volatile to be drowned while flying and separated from its rust; Atwood reads the images as about the freed spirit and its soul.
body: Hermes, quoted: “Take the flying volatile and drown it flying” [I.3 ¶16], separating it from its rust. Atwood takes these images to concern the freed spirit and its soul [I.3 ¶16].

summary: In the Master's words, the substance on which the Fire is poured, so that the Final Cause enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted.
body: Quoted from the Master: “when thou shalt pour forth thy Fire upon the Foliated Sulphur” [IV.2 ¶14]. The Final Cause then enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted [IV.2 ¶14].

summary: The source-light in whose evolution the Universal Nature appears white, as all colours united.
body: Atwood: “just so is the Universal Nature, described as appearing in the evolution of her Fontal Light” [III.2 ¶5]. In that evolution the Universal Nature appears white, all colours united.

summary: The source-nature which the reflective faculty craves but cannot reach; those who know it by experience truly understand why God is to be feared.
body: Atwood says that “they only who have become conversant by experience in the Fontal Nature” truly understand why God is to be feared [I.3 n19]. Elsewhere, the reflective faculty is disabled “in the inquiry after that Fontal Nature which, by a necessary criterion, it craves” [II.1 ¶33]. Apparently, then, it is reached by experience rather than by reflection.

summary: The source from which the individual springs as an outbirth; obscured by the sensual principle and rediscovered in regeneration.
body: Atwood describes the individual as an outbirth “from that Fontal Reason whence it springs” [III.3 ¶52]. The sensual principle obscures it; in regeneration it is discovered, rising through self-perceivance with creative attributes and powers [III.3 ¶52].

summary: That whose emancipation produces the First Matter.
body: Atwood calls the First Matter “an emancipation of the Fontal Source” [III.1 ¶70]; it is not further defined here.

summary: Nature's source-spirit, distinct from its manifestation and from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.
body: Atwood distinguishes “the fontal Spirit of nature, apart from its manifestation” [I.2 ¶15] from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.

summary: The specifying, inward agent that matter lacks; joined to matter it begets a seed. Atwood identifies it with Light and with the sulfurs.
body:
Atwood treats Form as what specifies a body: subject-matter is withdrawn from inferior Forms, and “one form being expelled, another may be introduced” [I.2 ¶5]. She calls it an error that “the alchemists extracted from the Form out of these metals to transmute and increase with” [I.2 ¶9].

Form is the inward agent: “This agent is the form that matter wanted” [I.2 ¶45]. Joined to matter, it begets a seed. Its identity is stated outright: “This Form is Light” [I.2 ¶45]. One material takes many specific shapes: “though the material is one throughout, forms are diverse” [I.2 ¶46]. Forms are also called sulfurs: “her forms or sulfurs are perplexed” [I.2 ¶48].

In the practice, putrefaction makes the body “to corrupt and to lose its Form” [IV.1 ¶41]. Conversely, the Universal Element's invisible vapor is compressed “into a tangible Form” [IV.1 ¶47].

equivalences.with: universal principle of increase and perfection

summary: The ray of motive Light, which Atwood calls the alone universal principle of increase and perfection: the transmutative ferment and Stone.
body: Atwood says the chemists tried “to extract the Form of gold” with salt, sulfur, mercury and antimony [I.1 ¶86]. Her own account: “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9], “the alone universal principle of increase and perfection” [IV.4 ¶9]. When it dominates the circulatory system it is made concrete in life, and it is the transmutative ferment and Stone [IV.4 ¶9].

summary: The new, concentric, finally immortal form in which the subject is established when it is rectified at the end of the operations.
body: Atwood says sublimation ends the operations by “establishing her in a new and concentric Form of Light” [II.2 ¶27]. The philosophic matter is finally “rectified into a consummate and immortal Form of Light” [IV.1 ¶46].

summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai's words, quoted by Atwood, the Form of man contains all that is in heaven and earth.
body: Quoted: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42].

summary: What true generation would simply represent; Atwood says nothing in nature is generated so as to represent it alone.
body: Atwood: nothing in nature is generated “simply so as to represent the Formal Agent alone” [III.2 ¶61].

summary: Matter as perceived in the Night of Matter: obscure, vast and infinite.
body: The passage reads: “her perception of the Formless Subject is obscure, and vast, and infinite” [III.2 ¶55]. In the same passage the intellect is “sinking into the Abyssal Subject” [III.2 ¶55]; the two may be the same, but no identity is asserted. Who is speaking is unclear.

summary: In Eirenaeus's verse, a fourfold distilling spring that washes the king and carries him up, also named May-dew and Eve; Atwood's notes speak of a well, not explicitly identified with it.
body:
Atwood describes the crowned king resting over the fountain and drawing auripigment from it. Her notes speak of a well: “the well is, as the catholic spirit of life, inexhaustible” [I.3 n22], with the occult Causality at its center; another note speaks of the deep well from which the philosophic water is drawn: “because the well is deep out of which it is drawn” [I.3 n36]. The text does not explicitly identify the fountain with the well.

Eirenaeus, quoted: “O crystal fountain! Which with fourfold spring Rubs down the valleys with its pearly drops Distilling” [III.1 ¶69]. The fountain washes the king and carries him up. The same verse names it “This our May-dew which our earth doth move To bring forth fruit, which fruit is perfect gold” and “This is our Eve, whom Adam doth so love” [III.1 ¶69].

summary: In Maria's words, what the matter in which the science is most easily found contains most evidently.
body: Maria, quoted: the science is most easily found in “that matter which most evidently contains the four philosophic elements” [I.3 n48].

summary: The philosophers' name for the vapor into which the body of Light is reduced, which condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually.
body: Atwood: the body of Light is reduced to “a mere vapor, called by the philosophers, on account of its origin, the Four Winds” [III.1 ¶56]. The vapor condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually. In the fable, Typhon scatters Osiris's members to the four winds [III.1 ¶56].

summary: A fourth agent, partaking of the aerial fiery element, that comes over the three fires to complete the work.
body: In the Adept's account, “the Fourth, partaking of the aerial fiery element, supervenes for the accomplishment o the work” over the three fires [IV.2 ¶11]. Atwood then speaks of “the form of the Fourth in that Burning Fiery Furnace” [IV.2 ¶12], which she says can be conceived only from what is written. The text does not say these are the same, and a Fourth cause also appears at [IV.2 ¶7–8]; how these readings relate is left open.

summary: Emanated by the Identity after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding: truthful, godlike, the express image of its motive.
body:
Jacob Boehme, quoted: “enter I even to the cross in the Fourth Form, there you have Sol and Luna together” [III.1 ¶48]; he does not explain it further.

Atwood: after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding, the Identity emanates the Fourth Form: “It emanates a Fourth Form, truthful, godlike” [IV.2 ¶18], the express image of its motive. Later she writes: “And the Fourth, as the artist, applies it to the work in the furtherance” [IV.2 ¶32]. The text does not say that this Fourth is the same as the Fourth Form, or as Boehme's.

equivalences.with: Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace

summary: A prophesied coming age, the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace, when the Mother of sciences comes forth and greater things are discovered.
body: Atwood names the “Fourth Monarchy, which is the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace” [IV.3 ¶49]. It is the time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth, and greater things be discovered than have been hitherto in the past monarchies of the world” [IV.3 ¶49].

summary: Author of La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux, a history of the Kabalah Atwood recommends; her source for the Zohar translations she cites.
body: Atwood recommends Franck's *La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux* as a history of the Kabalah, to be read with no less instruction than delight. It is the source of the Zohar translations she cites [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n2; III.2 n3; III.2 n4]. She uses it approvingly, as a supporting source.

summary: What, Atwood says, the alchemists establish on the same substantial foundation as Greek philosophy.
body: Atwood: “In just such a foundation do the Alchemists establish their Free masonry” [III.1 ¶3], meaning the same foundation as Greek philosophy. The term is not explained further.

summary: The spirit released in trance, which can range through its sphere, reveal hidden things and philosophize, though its freedom does not guarantee truth.
body: Atwood speaks of “the intrinsic intelligence and power of the Free Spirit which can expatiate into the whole circumference of its sphere and reveal hidden things” [II.3 ¶4]. This is the spirit released in trance; it can philosophize, but she warns that its freedom does not guarantee truth [II.3 ¶4].

summary: Not motiveless choice but the operative power freed from bondage, whose effects follow the will in full accord: the Almighty Magnet.
body: Atwood: “That was free Will, not the motiveless chimera which human fancy has been prone to coin, but the operative Almighty Magnet” [III.3 ¶71]. Free will is thus the operative power freed from bondage, with effects that follow the will in full accord.

summary: The liberty, in life, into which souls emerge from Lethe and Egyptian darkness.
body: Atwood speaks of souls emerging from Lethe and Egyptian darkness into “the glorious liberty of the Freed Will in life” [III.1 ¶70].

summary: Named by Atwood among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed.
body: Atwood lists Freher among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27], citing him in support of her own view.

summary: An anonymous adept Atwood cites for the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.
body: Atwood quotes the French adept: “the two dragons do bite one another very cruelly” [III.1 ¶58]. She uses the image to show the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.

summary: In Norton's verse, the harder kind of glass, made from clippings of other glasses.
body: Norton, quoted: “The harder stuffe is called Freton, Of clipping of other glasses it come” [III.4 ¶31].

summary: In a passage given in Hermes' voice, the volatile element that flies away, which sulphurs and albuminous bodies hold and detain.
body: Quoted from Hermes: sulphurs and albuminous bodies are said to be those “which hold also and detain the fugitive Ens” [I.3 ¶21]. The context suggests the term means the volatile principle that tends to escape and must be fixed.

summary: In Geber's account, what fills a fanciful soul so that it cannot receive the true intention of natural things.
body: Geber, as quoted by Atwood among the impediments to the Art, says that a fanciful soul, “because there is replete with fumosities, it cannot receive the true intention of natural things” [III.4 ¶3]. Apparently a mental cloudiness that unfits the mind for the work.

summary: An instrument of the work; Atwood says the old writers devised furnaces for every part, many misleadingly, while the true furnace is a little simple shell.
body: Atwood says the old writers devised a furnace for every part of the work, many of them misleadingly, but “The true furnace has been described as a little simple shell” [III.4 ¶38], small enough to be carried in one hand. She notes that “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38], so Athanor is another name for it. She criticizes those who followed Geber's example and described the furnace with a misleading subtlety [III.4 ¶38].

summary: In a quoted adept's account, a transparent salt seen in the waters of the vessel, said to be no different from pumice stone.
body: An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (identified in n26 as Grasseus) describes the waters of the vessel as “full of a certain transparent salt” [III.2 ¶25], and judges “that fusil kind of salt to be not different from pumice stone” [III.2 ¶25]. So the text equates fusil salt with pumice stone. The plain meaning beyond this is not stated.

summary: Named in a passage from Helmont that criticizes measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold, the method of Galen's art.
body: In the Helmont material Atwood cites, physicians are criticized for “being allured with the facility of the art of Galen” [IV.3 ¶34], that is, for measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold. The view is Helmont's; Galen's method is the thing rejected.

summary: Named by Atwood in a contrast: she would as soon have lived in Galileo's days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism.
body: Atwood says she would as soon have lived in Galileo's days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism [III.4 ¶12]. Galileo is used only as this point of comparison.

summary: The alchemists' name for the meadow of Divine Ideas, a place of sweet dew where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated.
body: Atwood says of the meadow of Divine Ideas (the Pratum) that “the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. She describes it in the alchemists' words: “the philosophers have indeed a garden where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9]. In her account it is where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated [II.4 ¶9].

summary: Something that, in Atwood's account, must be dissected and shorn, in parallel with stripping the Orient Animal's skin.
body: Atwood writes that “the whole garment of Light must be dissected, shorn, and the signal of victory be heroically transferred” [III.1 ¶64], in parallel with the stripping of the Orient Animal's skin. Apparently an image for laying open the vital or luminous covering of the subject. The text does not state this meaning directly.

summary: The passage at the beginning of the work through which the great change happens, which Atwood ties to the soul's willed dissolution of her bond to the body.
body: Atwood quotes the adept's cry: “O happy gate of Blackness! Cries the adept, which art the passage to so glorious a change!” [II.3 ¶37]. She equates it with the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics: “That was the way to "precious death", spoken of by the Hebrews and Academics, this the "happy gate of blackness" celebrates by the old adepts” [II.3 ¶37]. She also equates it with the head of Hermes' crow: “the "happy gate of blackness" celebrates by the old adepts, the "head of Hermes’ crow", which is in the beginning of the work” [II.3 ¶37]. In her context it is the soul's willed dissolution of her bond to the body, at the opening of the work. That reading comes from the surrounding passage, not from a stated definition.

summary: The common name, per Atwood, for a stage of dissolution in the work: a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit.
body: Atwood describes a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit, and adds: “This is commonly called the Gate of Putrefaction” [III.1 ¶58]. In context it names the stage of dissolution.

summary: In the Rosy Cross fraternity's account, the five contested stages of the work, from knowledge of the true matter to projection.
body: Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the work is accomplished by “entering in by five litigious gates” [III.3 ¶63]. These are knowledge of the true matter, preparation, fire to maturity, multiplication and projection [III.3 ¶63].

summary: Author of Monde Primitif, whose agricultural interpretation Atwood criticizes.
body: Atwood cites Gebelin's *Monde Primitif* to criticize its agricultural interpretation [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n3].

summary: An authority the adepts rank next after Hermes. Atwood defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils and draws on him throughout for doctrine, the work's impediments and its terms.
body:
**Standing and veiling.** Atwood reports that the adepts rank Geber greatest after Hermes, and she defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils [I.1 ¶31–33; works cited at I.1 n37]. In Norton's verse he is among the masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Ripley's verse calls failed practitioners “as one of Geber’s cooks” [I.1 ¶65]. Read literally, his receipts led seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86]. From the *Summa Perfect.* she quotes his exclusion of the unworthy: “Ye sons of Avarice and Ignorance, cries Geber, and ye of evil manners, avaunt and fly from this science” [III.4 ¶18, III.4 n14]. On the word gibberish, see E0670.

**Doctrine.** Atwood uses him to support these points:
- The work is verified by experiment: “we have searched out and found, and have seen with our eyes and handled with our hands” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n101–102].
- “All is made of Mercury” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n12].
- Metals can be perfected: “In metals,says Geber, is lesser perfection than in animals” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n47].
- Theory must come first: “he who knows the principles and the way of generation, which consists according to the intention of nature, is but a very short way from the completement” [I.3 n2].
- The root lies in the operator: “he has not the true root in him whereon to base his labor and intention” [II.1 ¶11, II.1 n7].
- The work fails through ignorance: “men have thought the confection of fold impossible, because they have not know the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47, II.1 n43].
- The compound of Art is “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9].

She reinterprets his “the thing which perfects in minerals, is the substance of argent vive and sulfur, proportionally commixt in the bowels of clean inspissate earth” [I.2 ¶42, I.2 n39] as relations of the Ethereal being, not literal substances. Elsewhere he is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25] and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**Impediments.** She follows his list of bodily and mental impediments: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3–6, III.4 n1]. She also follows his ranking of the unfit [III.4 ¶12–16]. His “necessary charges” she reinterprets as giving up selfhood [III.4 ¶6]. Geber gives the furnace the name Athanor: “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38]. She faults later writers who copied him in describing it with misleading subtlety.

equivalences.with: artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan

summary: Atwood's name for the method of the work, indicated by the order of her exposition and identified with the artistic fabrication of the Promethean Fire.
body: Atwood says the order of her exposition indirectly indicates “the genealogical method of ascent; even that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. The method is thus identified with the fabrication of the Promethean Fire.

summary: Embodied, born mortal life, into which souls descend and from whose bond and strains they must be freed. It is also the process through which every creature is brought into life.
body:
**Atwood.** Generation is the realm of birth into mortal life. Souls descend into it: “souls descending into the realms of generation” [II.4 ¶7]. They must be freed “from the bond of its earthly geniture” [II.4 ¶3] and redeemed “from the oblivious realms of generation” [II.3 ¶36]. In the work, “those strains are all finally obliterated that accede to the soul from generation” [II.3 n40]. She also uses the word for a process in which each being's central spirit is separated off: “the separation of this is constantly enacted in generation” [III.3 ¶52]. Through that process every creature is brought into life and operation. For her paired saying on generation and dissolution, see E0662.

**Quoted voices.** Crito says Intellect is withheld from every mortal nature in this life, “this however is not deprived by God but by the essence of generation” [II.1 ¶38]. Iamblicus says prayer “expels whatever is prone to generation, and retains nothing of the dregs of mortality” [III.4 ¶24].

summary: Atwood's principle that what generation binds, the inbred evil, only dissolution can unloose.
body: Atwood: “That which generation binds dissolution only can unloose” [IV.4 ¶17]. In context, what generation binds is the inbred evil. See also generation (E0661).

summary: In the later Appendix, the life into which the life-force is now wasted when it should be related to mind.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer of the book. There Atwood says the life-force should be directed to mind: “it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life” [APP ¶134]. In the Aristaeus story, the bees are lost along with “all the faculties of his soul, with the generative life” [APP ¶144].

summary: A power which, drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light, marks the origin of matter for the Platonists. It is alienated and later reunited to mind.
body: Reporting the philosophers' view, the text speaks of the origin of matter “when the generative virtue is drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. In a later passage, whose speaker is unclear, the primary motion of the ebbing life brings it about that “the Generative Virtue, which was alienated, becomes re- united to mind” [III.2 ¶66]. Compare generative life (E0663).

summary: The biblical book, which Atwood cites to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom and to liken the work to the creation of the world.
body: Atwood cites Genesis 2:10, “that land of Havilah where good gold is” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n4], to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom. She cites chapter 1, “And the Spirit of God moved upon the Face of the Waters.” [IV.2 ¶30, IV.2 n19], to liken the work to the creation of the world.

summary: Atwood's term for the real, not imaginary, production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis.
body: Atwood presents the production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis as real rather than imaginary: “but as the true Genesis of Light” [III.2 ¶26].

summary: Cited by Atwood as carrying, in symbol, the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing.
body: Atwood says Gentile Mythology carries in symbol the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing [III.3 ¶69].

summary: Listed by Atwood as a persecuted adept and friend of Fichtuld, author of the Opus mago-Cabbalist.
body: Atwood lists George Von Welling among persecuted adepts and as a friend of Fichtuld [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70]. The footnote gives his work as *Opus mago-Cabbalist* [I.1 n80].

summary: A Latin poem, its author not named here, whose fourth book Atwood quotes for the binding of a shape-changing captive (Proteus) with force and bonds.
body: Atwood quotes the fourth book of the *Georgics* (no author named) on the binding of the shape-changer. The captive held in bonds changes into varied shapes: “Verum,ubi correptum minibus, vinclisque tenebis” [III.2 ¶21, III.2 n21]. Only force and bonds compel it: “vim duram et vincula capto Tende” [III.2 ¶23, III.2 n24], and “Orando flectes: vim duram et vincula capto” [I.3 n37]. The more it turns into all forms, the tighter the bonds must be: “Et, quanto illa magis formas se vertet in omnes,” [I.2 ¶38, I.2 n37].

summary: A word that a quoted Faraday Society address derives from Geber's mysterious style. For Atwood, that style is deliberate veiling.
body: Atwood quotes an address to the Faraday Society that names Geber as the one “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33]. The derivation is the address's own. Atwood's point is that Geber's obscurity was a deliberate veil (see Geber, E0659).

summary: In Norton's verse, the vessel material that keeps spiritual matters from escaping, named as the vessel God gave. Vaughan adds that the glass is one.
body: Norton is quoted: “But other vessels be made of glasse, That spiritual matters should not outpasse” [III.4 ¶31]. Norton's Master identifies glass with the vessel God gave: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶31]. In our translation (by: ours), the Latin reads: if God had not given us the vessel, he would have given us nothing. The better kind of glass is called morning stuffe, and the harder kind Freton [III.4 ¶31]. Vaughan is quoted saying “the glass is one, and no more” [III.4 ¶38].

summary: Named by Atwood as one whose receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice.
body: Atwood says Glauber's receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86].

summary: In a Proclus passage, an energy of the soul that faith surpasses, set beside intelligence and judgment.
body: Proclus is quoted saying faith is “which is then better than every Gnostic energy” [II.4 ¶40]. It is set beside intelligence and judgment. The term is not defined further.

summary: For Atwood, manifestations of the Demiurgic Fire made distinct in Light through Intellect, and the unities of all being. They appear as simple light, not phantasms.
body: Atwood asks: “what are all the gods but manifestations of this same Fire germinating through the projecting energy of Intellect distinct in Light?” [II.4 ¶26]. She also calls them “the genus of the gods, which are the unities of all being” [II.4 ¶29]. In her account each god is an aspect of that Fire. Intellect makes the gods visible and nourishes them. They are an intelligible union and Truth, and they appear as simple light, not as phantasms [II.4 ¶26–29].

summary: In Atwood's usage, the adepts' name for the Soul, meaning its Light, in the second conjunction. It is also the seed that must be destroyed to be multiplied.
body: Atwood gives a stated identity: “in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light; which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. So Gold is the Soul's Light, predominant in the second conjunction. Its formal virtue stays sealed until Mercury penetrates it [III.3 ¶30]. Elsewhere gold must be destroyed as seed in order to be multiplied: “he that saves his gold, that is to say, remains satisfied in the first fruits of his reason” [III.3 ¶22]. Saving one's gold thus means resting content in the first fruits of reason. See also Gold Alchemical (E0676).

summary: In the later Appendix, the first conceived Paternal Light and the metaphysical seed of mineral gold.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “The Gold Alchemical is the first conceived Paternal Light” [APP ¶20], and “it is the seed metaphysical of mineral gold” [APP ¶20]. Compare gold (E0675).

equivalences.with: a certain water clear and pure

summary: In the author of Lucerna Salis, the gold of the Wise is not vulgar gold but a clear, pure water that becomes spiritual.
body: Atwood reports the author of *Lucerna Salis* as declaring “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold; but it is a certain water clear and pure” [III.3 ¶32]. On the packet's reading, this water bears the Lord's lightning, from which all things receive life, and passes through the Alembic; hence, the quoted author says, “this is the reason, continues he, why our gold is become spiritual” [III.3 ¶32]. The gold of the Wise is thus identified with that water (QUOTED: the author of Lucerna Salis).

summary: In a Rosicrucian passage, Gold philosophical is named as the husband of Mercury; the text does not explain it further here.
body: In a passage attributed to the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, Mercury speaks: “my husband is Gold philosophical” [III.3 ¶64]. The text gives no further explanation at this point (QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross).

equivalences.with: Caduceus of Hermes; ferrying Cup of Hercules

summary: The Golden Bough, the offering and talisman by which Aeneas descends; Atwood reads it as a ray of living light, the intellect, and a passport into hidden realms.
body:
Atwood treats the Golden Bough as what the Sybil sends Aeneas to find, “he may discover and bring to her the Golden Bough” [III.1 ¶15], and offers it as a parallel to the hidden object of the work. It is the required propitiation for the descent; literally part of the sacred equipage, “connected with the Mercurial caduceus” [II.3 ¶11], but read by Atwood ontologically as the intellect: “a ray of living light, golden and flexible, the true Brancha Spiritualis of Raymond Lully” [II.3 ¶11].

It is one of the “golden passports” into the hidden realms, and it is the bough, not the tree, that is to be taken, the small portion to start from: “Ramus, non arbor --- The bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken” [III.1 ¶32]. Atwood sets it beside other emblems: “Such was the Caduceus of Hermes --- the Golden Bough, the ferrying Cup of Hercules” [III.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Aeneas passes Tartarus to Elysium “By propitiation, through the offering of the Golden Bough” [APP ¶168], which he is to “take as his talisman to pass through the Infernal Regions to Elysium” [APP ¶171]; there its tree appears identical with Proteus' last transformation [APP ¶171]. All voices are ATWOOD.

Asserted identities: = Brancha Spiritualis [II.3 ¶11]; = Caduceus of Hermes and ferrying Cup of Hercules (set in apposition) [III.1 ¶36].

summary: Something drawn to its native soil that passes through death and darkness, takes root, and blossoms into illuminating light; not explicitly identified.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the Golden Branch as drawn to its native soil, which “through death and darkness enters; and taking root at last, gathers strength to germinate and blossom, as a radiant flower” [II.4 ¶7]. The passage does not explicitly say what the branch is.

summary: In the Table Talk, the purplish outward appearance of the light of Life diffused over the seeker's body in the third life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The Golden Fleece is the outward appearance presented by the light of Life diffused over the body of the seeker in the third life” [APP ¶22]; the appearance is described as of a purplish luster (ATWOOD).

summary: In Basil, the one thing holding mercury, salt and sulphur, knowledge of which gives the root of life; called also a magnet.
body: Quoting Basil (QUOTED: Basil), the text presents the golden seed as the one thing that holds mercury, salt and sulphur; whoever knows it has the root of life. It is equated with a magnet: “this golden seed or magnet” [II.1 ¶11].

summary: The adept's water, found not in wells or depths but in higher places, as ripe Mercury rises.
body: Atwood quotes an adept: “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells, nor in profundities, but in higher places” [III.3 ¶17]; the context connects this with ripe Mercury rising (QUOTED: the adept).

summary: Atwood's name for the central difficulty of the Hermetic Mystery: knowing the Salt and its solution.
body: Having treated the Salt and its solution, Atwood (ATWOOD) declares: “Here then liest the Gordian Knot of the Hermetic Mystery” [IV.1 ¶37]. The knot is thus the crux of the method: knowing the Salt and how it is dissolved.

summary: Cited as carrying the Christian doctrine of fulfillment, which Atwood adds to the other traditions as agreeing with them.
body: Atwood adds “the Christian doctrine of fulfillment” of the Gospel to the other traditions she has surveyed, as agreeing with them in the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

headword: Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ
forms: Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ
summary: The Gospel account of Christ's life, to which, Atwood says, the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work and human redemption.
body: Atwood notes that the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work to the Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ and to human redemption [IV.3 ¶27]; she cites it as illustration.

summary: The divine gift by which alone, according to Norton and Kelly, the Art is found and obtained, rather than by study or will.
body: Two quoted authorities make grace the condition of the science. Norton's *Ordinal* calls it “A singular grace and gift of the Almightye;” and says of the science, “But only by grace, she is holy in her kind.” [III.4 ¶10]; on the packet's reading, the student must be proved able to receive it, and it is needed to undo God's conjunctions (QUOTED: Norton’s Ordinal). Kelly likewise says the Art comes not by reading, sitting still, fancy or will: “But, as I said, by grace it is obtained:” [IV.1 ¶19]; it is to be sought (QUOTED: Kelly). The records do not show Atwood qualifying either view.

summary: The ancients' exact art of growing and subliming the Spirit to higher degrees of concentrated essentiality in successive vessels or forms.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “that exact art of grafting and transplanting which the ancients practiced” [III.1 ¶9]: the Spirit is grown and sublimed to a third, fourth and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality, in as many representative vessels or forms. The horticultural image apparently stands for the stepwise concentration of the Spirit in the method.

summary: In a passage from Stoboeus via Dr Warburton, the next initiation, which affects the mind as death does.
body: In a passage cited from Stoboeus through Dr Warburton (QUOTED: Stoboeus / Dr Warburton), the next initiation, “initiation into the Grand Mysteries” [II.3 ¶37], is said to affect the mind as death does.

summary: Adept reputed author of the Water Stone, said to be Boehme's friend; Atwood cites his eyewitness vessel account and endorses his Stone/Christ analogy.
body:
Atwood lists Grasseus as reputed author of the Water Stone and a personal friend of Boehme [I.1 ¶70]; the note gives titles *Das Wasser-Stein des Weissens*, *Arca Arcano* and *Lillium inter Spina* [I.1 n83]. As J. Grasseus, his *Water Stone of the Wise Men* is said to have been published with the *Aurora* [I.1 ¶64].

Called “an ancient and much esteemed Adeptus”, he supplies (*Theatr. Chem.* 6:294) an eyewitness account of a world in miniature in the vessel: “Within this fabric (i.e., the consecrated vessel), was a certain mass moving circularly” [III.2 ¶25, III.2 n26]. Atwood reads this as the whole Hermetic laboratory.

He is named among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), under the spelling Grsaeus, his *Aquarium* supplies the analogy of the Stone with Christ the Head Corner Stone, which Atwood endorses as a “versimilitude” [APP ¶46].

equivalences.with: vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit

summary: In the Table Talk, inwardly a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit; outwardly its weakened material form, common idolatry.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) gives an inward meaning: “A graven image means a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit” [APP ¶100], one worshipped by the heart. Outwardly, its weakened material form is common idolatry.

summary: St Paul, cited from 1 Corinthians 15:37 to support the teaching that what is sown must die to be quickened and rise in better form.
body: Atwood cites the great Apostle (St Paul), 1 Corinthians 15:37 [III.1 n36], to support the principle that what is sown must die to be quickened and rises in a better form: “thou sowest not that body that shall be” [III.1 ¶30]. She uses the passage approvingly.

summary: The ancients' art, which, Atwood says, Bacon knew nothing of, together with its subject.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says of Bacon that “he knew nothing of their Great Art, or of its subject even, and naturally mistook their hidden ground” [I.2 ¶24].

summary: In the Table Talk, Wisdom, the Universal Will, which dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) glosses the expression herself: “The great Salt Sea (Wisdom, the Universal Will)” [APP ¶94]. It dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will. Asserted identities: = Wisdom; = Universal Will [APP ¶94].

summary: The secret of the art, mentioned in the accounts of Kelly, Dee and Philalethes; the text does not say what it is.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) relates that “the secret of making of the Powder was confided to Kelly some years afterwards by a dying monk” [I.1 ¶67], and quotes Dee: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me” [I.1 ¶67]. Philalethes is said to have possessed “the secret” when young [I.1 ¶73]. These passages do not say what the secret is.

summary: An authority cited within Proclus's passage on the soul's entry into the Adytum of Life.
body: The great theologist is cited within the Proclus passage on the soul's entry into the Adytum of Life [II.4 ¶29]; the text gives no further identification.

summary: The highest reality, unknown because concealed in this life; it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of those who “seek to prove Reality in the Great Unknown --- unknown, because concealed in this life” [II.4 ¶42]. According to the passage, it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.

summary: The totality contained proportionally in every portion of existence; simple, and known by contact and intuition in self-knowledge.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) holds “every portion of existence to be continent and comprehended proportionally of the Great Whole” [III.2 ¶45]. Being simple, “it is simple, and not so much therefore an object of reason as of contact and intuition” [III.2 ¶46]; it is reached in self-knowledge.

summary: Paired terms: man prepares the way of the Greater Good in the Lesser, and the Lesser is blessed by the Greater.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) gives man's task as “to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20], adding that “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater” [III.4 ¶20].

summary: The higher grade of ancient initiation, alone promising assimilation and final contact with the first principle; its doctrine concerned the whole universe.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says assimilation and final contact with the first principle were promised “to those who were initiated in the Greater Mysteries only” [II.2 ¶5]. Citing Clemens Alexandrinus with approval: “The doctrine of the Greater Mysteries, says Clemens Alexandrinus, related to the whole universe” [II.2 ¶5]. Later she says the revelations she has gathered partly describe “the visions, and awful accompaniments which took place in the celebration of the Greater Mysteries” [II.3 ¶49].

summary: In the monk continuing Basil Valentine, two domains each with its Vulcan; the Lesser World's Vulcan amends what the Greater Orb's leaves crude.
body: The monk, continuing Basil Valentine (QUOTED: the monk), says: “Whatsoever the Vulcan in the Greater Orb leaves crude and perfects not, that in the Lesser World must be amended by a certain other Vulcan” [IV.1 ¶40]. Apparently the Lesser World's fire completes what the Greater Orb's leaves imperfect; the text does not gloss either domain further here.

equivalences.with: Earth which is without form and water (its virgin womb)

summary: In a quoted adept, the world whose virgin womb, Earth without form and water, is where Ruach Elohim is made body.
body: A quoted adept (QUOTED: the mysterious adeptest) speaks of “the virgin womb of the greater world, viz., that Earth which is without form and water” [III.3 ¶50], where Ruach Elohim is made body; then “The Son, born into the light of the macrocosm” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage uses “macrocosm”, but the text does not explicitly identify it with the greater world. Asserted identity: its virgin womb = Earth without form and water [III.3 ¶50].

summary: Greek fable of Midas, which Atwood reads in the Table Talk as the will starved in possession of the aurific life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the Grecian fable of Midas to illustrate the will starved in possession of the aurific life [APP ¶159].

headword: Greek and Alexandrian Platonists; mystics of the middle ages; the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
forms: Greek and Alexandrian Platonists; mystics of the middle ages; the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
summary: Groups of writers whose works, Atwood says, give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report.
body: Atwood says the writings of the Greek and Alexandrian Platonists, the mystics of the middle ages and the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report [II.4 ¶56]. She cites them in support.

summary: Cited to support that the subject is least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, and that preparation removes superfluities.
body: Atwood cites the Greek Aristhenes in support of her account of the subject: least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, with preparation removing its superfluities: “Take that which is least, and draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26, II.2 n18].

headword: Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day
forms: Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day
summary: A hymn cited to illustrate the tradition that St John made gold and gems.
body: Atwood cites the Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day to illustrate the tradition of St John making gold and gems: “Qui de virgis fecit aurum Gemmas de lapidibus” [I.1 ¶24, I.1 ¶25]. Translation (ours): Who made gold from rods, gems from stones.

summary: An unnamed Greek authority cited as agreeing with others concerning the Matter of the work; the text does not otherwise identify him.
body: Cited in support: the Greek Divine is said to have agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. The text does not otherwise identify him.

summary: The Greek heroic fables of Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas, which Atwood decodes as figures of the mind's faculties in the work.
body: Atwood decodes these fables: the heroes are those “who represent the Rational Ferment”, while their associates stand for the other faculties of the mind [III.1 ¶66].

summary: Greek philosophers whose course Atwood says guided her in following Nature back to her Initial Source.
body: Cited in support: Atwood says the course of the Greek Ontologists guided her in following Nature to her Initial Source [IV.4 ¶6].

summary: Greek philosophers whose authority Atwood invokes, in part, to ground the inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious.
body: Their authority partly grounds Atwood's inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious [II.2 ¶24].

headword: Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus
forms: Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus
summary: The Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo and Bacchus, cited by Atwood as institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom.
body: Atwood cites these temples as illustration: institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom [IV.3 ¶36].

summary: The Greeks as a collective voice whose doctrine of Wisdom Atwood holds unequalled and whose names and doctrines she repeatedly cites in support of the Hermetic view.
body: Atwood holds up the Greek doctrine of Wisdom as unequalled, promising to discuss it later [I.1 ¶70]. She cites Greek usage repeatedly in support: they name the essence freed from gross matter “the Free Ether” [I.2 ¶16]; they call Intelligible Causes gods [II.4 ¶39]; Isis was “by the Greeks called Myrionymous”, the goddess with a thousand names [III.3 ¶62]. Greek philosophy substantializes mind as the substratal matter of existence, and its ethereal hypostasis parallels the alchemists' first matter [III.1 ¶2, III.1 ¶3]. By contrast, the Greeks kept silent about, or poetized, the physical revealments of the Tartarean realms, out of fear of vulgar curiosity [II.3 ¶34].

headword: the Greeks and eastern sages; Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Peripatetics
summary: The Greek and eastern sages and the philosophical schools (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics) cited together for the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source.
body: Cited in support of the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source, described as “a certain pure and hidden fire” [I.2 ¶12].

equivalences.with: true matters of the Blessed Stone (with the Vitriol of Venus)

summary: In Khunrath's words, a matter that appears with the Vitriol of Venus when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed; together they are the true matters of the Blessed Stone.
body: A term from Khunrath, quoted by Atwood: when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed there appear “the Green Duenech and the Vitriol of Venus, which are the true matters of the Blessed Stone” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

summary: A name for the matter when first sublimed, so called for its strength and crude vitality; central agent of the Hunting of the Greene Lyon and figured also by Khunrath and Ripley.
body:
Atwood: the matter when first sublimed “is called a serpent, dragon, or green lion, on account of its strength and crude vitality” [I.2 ¶40].

In the quoted poem *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* it is the central agent: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” — green for being unripe, not for its colour; and it is not common quicksilver: “For they weene that our Lyon ys Common Quicksilver, but truly they miss:” [III.1 ¶65]. The poem also has it swift, devouring and eclipsing the Sun (turning red to white) yet perfecting him; as Priest it weds Sun and Moon, who were born in its Bed; it supplies the Lion's Blood; and it beguiles most who hunt it [III.1 ¶65].

Khunrath (quoted): “The Green Lion, lurking and concealed, is drawn forth from the Cavern of his Saturnine Hill” by allurements suited to his nature, pierced with a lance, and his blood collected [IV.1 ¶36]; not otherwise explained.

Ripley (quoted) says that fools give the name to vitriol: “vitriall, Which folys doe call the Grene Lyon” [I.1 ¶65]; the passage apparently rejects this vulgar identification without saying what the true Green Lion is.

summary: The preliminary preparation of the matter, before the dissolution, after which the philosophic work proper begins; long, foul, costly and perilous per Norton.
body:
Atwood: “the preliminary preparation of the matter being very generally termed the gross work”, and “The philosophic work is not considered to begin until after the dissolution” [I.3 n56]. Of the many called at first, “few, it will be understood, are chosen to proceed beyond the exigencies of the preliminary Gross Work” [III.4 ¶32]; Norton describes “the needful qualification and numbers of individuals employed about the Gross Work” [III.4 ¶36].

Norton's *Ordinal* (quoted): “For the Gross Worke is foule in her kinde,” [IV.1 ¶25] — a long phase (three years would be a blessed chance), perilous and costly, a handicraft full of possible faults: “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]; once completed it need not be begun again.

Atwood also calls it “this said hyper-physical Gross Work” [IV.1 ¶36], with a First Preparation and a Second part, the Second being one of the Art's greatest subtleties.

summary: The understanding which Atwood says must be properly conceived before any experiments are undertaken.
body: Atwood advises to “leave off experiments until the ground of wisdom is properly conceived” [I.1 ¶86]: understanding must precede practice.

summary: The spirit of growth in children, identified with the vegetable spirit, more phantastic than the animal, allowing free imagination until the circle of life closes.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Children have the growth spirit in them (the vegetable spirit which is more phantastic than the animal)” [APP ¶122]. It allows free imagination until the circle of life closes. Identified with the vegetable spirit.

summary: A figure before whom, the book reports, a transmutation took place in 1620, the gold being coined into medals; cited as evidence for transmutation.
body: Cited in support of the reality of transmutation: one was performed before him in 1620 and the gold coined into medals [I.1 ¶77, I.1 n104].

headword: H. O’Brien, author of the Round Towers
summary: Author of the Round Towers of Ireland, mildly criticized by Atwood for mistaking the White Paradise for his Emerald Home, yet praised as an estimable work.
body: Atwood cites *the Round Towers of Ireland* (chap. 22, p. 327) and mildly criticizes its author for mistaking the White Paradise for his 'Emerald Home' — an exclusiveness she pardons for its enthusiasm — while calling the book 'an estimable work' [III.2 ¶8, III.2 n10].

summary: A figure quoted by Atwood to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise.
body: Quoted to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise: “he had horns coming out of his hand, and there was the hiding of his power” [IV.3 ¶39].

equivalences.with: aerial moisture in its native (unpurified) state

summary: Not fleshly existence but a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries: the dark, image-loving lower world and unpurified aerial moisture of life, the soul's state while her hypostasis remains dark.
body:
In the quoted Sacred Discourse, through downward will or evil agencies “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶14].

Atwood's own reading: Hades is not the corporeal nature or fleshly existence but “a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries, when the consciousness is artificially drawn about the penetralia of its first life”; she equates it with Lethe — “by Hades, or that profound Lethe” [II.3 ¶7]. She describes “Hades dark all over, squalid, delighting in images, unintelligible, precipitous” [II.3 ¶26], where consciousness wrapped by the Mysteries is anxious and perplexed. It is the aerial moisture of life unpurified: “which moisture in its native state, before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason, is that Hades we are treating of, the Purgatory of the wise” [II.3 ¶29]. And “the soul is said to be in Hades all the while that her hypostasis continues in darkness” [II.3 ¶36] — that is, while she regards her image objectively, before experimental knowledge.

Identities: Lethe [II.3 ¶7]; the Purgatory of the wise; the aerial moisture in its native state [II.3 ¶29].

summary: An authority cited on the necessity of the vessel or place, and, in the Appendix, for the noise accompanying the Alchemical solution.
body: With Morien and Albert, Hali supports the necessity of the vessel or place: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Haly is cited as saying the Alchemical solution is accompanied with noise [APP ¶50].

summary: The ancients' more scientific practical art by which, Atwood says, they experimentally entered the temple of Divine Wisdom.
body: Atwood: “a more scientific Handicraft enabled the ancients experimentally to enter” the temple of Divine Wisdom [IV.3 ¶37].

summary: The transverse poles of the Ether, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; in man a natural fire, the fire of the Ether in our life organism.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The hands of the Ether are its transverse poles”, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; “in man a natural fire ---i.e., the fire of the Ether in us, or of our life organism” [APP ¶177].

summary: An adept named among the persecuted, sometimes confused with Philalethes.
body: Named as a persecuted adept, sometimes confused with Philalethes [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73].

summary: The one life we presently live, the animal and rational life, out of three possible lives; the Hermetically regenerated give it up.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “We live in but one life, the head life, but there are three possible lives” [APP ¶45]. We have no right to be efficient in it, and the Hermetically regenerated give it up. Identified as “the Head life or the animal, the rational life” [APP ¶60]. Contrast heart life.

summary: Per a quoted modern exponent, the black, motionless state at the beginning of the work, after three months' circulation.
body: Quoted from “our modern exponent”: “the head of Hermes’ crow is said to be in the beginning of this work” [II.1 ¶23] — the black, motionless state reached after three months' circulation. See also Head of the Crow.

summary: Named by Atwood with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and Obscurity as present in the hours of conjunction; not defined there.
body: Atwood lists it with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and “Obscurity and the Head of the Crow in the various hours of conjunction” [III.3 ¶13]. Not defined in the record; compare head of Hermes’ crow.

summary: The stone whose virtues Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber celebrate, mentioned by Atwood in connection with Reason acting as a ferment.
body: Atwood says Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber were “abundantly celebrating the virtues of their Head Stone” [III.1 ¶21], in a passage on Reason acting as a ferment; the context apparently links the two, though the record does not state the identity.

summary: The consciousness into which the whole force of regenerate life is brought up in the perfected Corner Stone.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the whole force of regenerate life is “brought up into the head-consciousness, what they call in the north” [APP ¶134], in the perfected Corner Stone.

summary: Medicine as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing.
body: Atwood presents the Healing Art as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing: “So the origin, decline, and fall of the Healing Art has been pictured by one of its brightest ornaments” [IV.3 ¶35].

summary: The higher life into which the lower opens: that which is above and attracts, identified with the feminine principle and Wisdom.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the higher life into which the lower opens, “that which is above (the feminine principle, --- Wisdom, --- the heart life)” [APP ¶98], which attracts. She also writes “the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life” [APP ¶97]; whether these are strict synonyms or a series is uncertain from the text. Contrast head life.

summary: In Vaughan's words, the heat the operator applies, which must not exceed the natural proportion; its literal nature is not stated.
body: Vaughan (quoted) warns of the operator's heat: “if thy heat exceeds the natural proportion” [III.4 ¶44]. The record does not say what this heat literally is.

summary: Per Proclus, intellectual contact with the intelligible; Aristotle distinguishes three senses of the word, and the Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven.
body: Proclus (quoted): “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36]. Aristotle distinguishes three senses, including “we are accustomed likewise to call that heaven, which is composed from every natural and sensible body” [III.2 ¶36]. The Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven [III.2 ¶36].

summary: Two principles which Hermes says are to be joined through the Water; Atwood reads them as the two invisible poles of the Spirit.
body: Hermes (quoted): “the Heaven is to be joined mediately with the Earth” [I.3 ¶55], that is, through the Water. Atwood reads the passage as signalizing the two invisible poles of the Spirit [I.3 ¶55].

summary: An expression, in a quoted adept's voice, for the agent and patient of the work, which must be united in friendship and love.
body: Voiced by the Adept Atwood quotes: the Heaven and Earth philosophical are treated as agent and patient, “the Heaven and Earth philosophical, even as agent and patient” [IV.2 ¶30], which must be united in friendship and love. Asserted identity: = agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30].

summary: The Benedictine Monk's own fire, which stirs up the elemental fire; set against coals and common fire.
body: In the words of the Benedictine Monk (quoted): “For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one” [III.3 ¶24]. This fire excites the elemental fire as the matter desires a fitting Form, and is contrasted with coals and common fire [III.3 ¶24].

summary: With 'the fire', one of the two agents of the work, glossed by the scholiast as the external and internal agents of the Hermetic work.
body: A quoted scholiast reads the pair: “By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified, says the scholiast, the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work” [I.3 n16]. The heavenly Flyer (or bird) is thus paired with the fire as one of these agents; the text does not say which of the two is external and which internal.

summary: The Hebrew teaching, which Atwood says differs from the Ethnic Anima Mundi only in words.
body: Atwood compares the Hebrew doctrine with the Ethnic Anima Mundi and finds that it differs from it only in words [I.2 ¶14].

summary: Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis, cited by Atwood in support of absolute Idealism, the fall and reunion of creation, reason over authority, and self-inquiry.
body: Atwood cites the Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis in support of absolute Idealism, of creation's fall and reunion, of reason over authority, and of self-inquiry [II.1 ¶40; II.1 ¶41].

summary: A group voice whose 'precious death' Atwood equates with the gate of blackness.
body: Atwood equates the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics with the gate of blackness [II.3 ¶37].

summary: A modern metaphysician whose doctrine of pure Being Atwood contrasts with the Hermetic way, and whom the Appendix lists among moderns who drew on the Mystics.
body: Atwood quotes “the German philosopher (Hegel)”: “All things, says the German philosopher (Hegel), have their commencement in pure Being” [III.2 ¶30]. She uses this as a contrast: abstraction reaches pure Being, which is equal to non-Being, but only as a void [III.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named among modern metaphysicians who took their starting point from the Mystics [APP ¶96], and appears again in the same list as one who 'saw it' [APP ¶117].

summary: Author to whom the mystical romance Theagenes and Chariclea is attributed; named among writers of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone.
body: The mystical romance *Theagenes and Chariclea* is attributed to Heliodorus, who, the book says, resigned his bishopric of Tricca rather than disavow it [I.1 ¶28; I.1 n34]. He is also named with Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras, Zosimus and Archelaus as an author of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

summary: 'The acute Helvetius', cited by Atwood as a witness of transmutation and of the transcendent Light found at the centre; a worthy disciple of Paracelsus.
body: Atwood names Helvetius with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Faber as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and cites his explicit transmutation story in support [I.1 ¶77]. His 'Armed Magnet' is identified with the Wheel of Fire or inner Sun [II.3 ¶54]. From his *Vitulus Aureus*, 'the acute Helvetius' is cited as testifying to the transcendent Light and to finding the mystery, by experience, at the centre: “that most recreant Beauty can never be blotted out from my mind” [III.1 ¶70; III.1 n74]; how far the cited words are his own is not clear from the passage.

summary: Philosopher Atwood cites repeatedly in support: the dry soul, living the death of others, the principle named fire, and the Well where Truth lies hidden.
body: Atwood says Heraclitus' metaphysics agrees in essentials with Aristotle's [I.1 ¶16], and cites him as supporting that the theurgic media are medicines of imperfect souls [II.2 ¶5]. For the dry, self-turned soul she quotes “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27]; for nox corporis, souls dead to this life and alive in the other, “we live their death and die their life” [II.4 ¶9]. He is cited as naming the principle, according to essence, fire: “have denominated it to be fire” [III.2 ¶35]. The Wisdom is 'that Well of Heraclitus' where Truth lies hidden, 'whence also those philosophic tears' [IV.4 ¶27]. Atwood uses him in support or illustration throughout.

summary: Figure whose cleansing of the Augean Stable figures, in the Appendix, the cleansing of the mineral soul.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Hercules' labour of cleansing the Augean Stable figures the cleansing of the mineral soul [APP ¶71], and his grief for Hylas illustrates the same point as the Iliad [APP ¶109]. In the main text, Hippocrates is said to have been honored by the Athenians with the same gifts as Hercules and Aesculapius [IV.3 ¶34].

summary: Author of De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina, criticized by Atwood for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention.
body: Atwood criticizes Herman Conringius, author of *De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina.*, for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n1].

summary: Author of Probier Stein, listed by Atwood among persecuted adepts.
body: Herman Fichtuld, cited for his *Probier Stein*, is listed among persecuted adepts [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n79].

summary: The adept king credited with the Hermetic writings, whose Golden Treatise Atwood prints and glosses, and a constantly cited authority on the work, its agents and its moral conditions.
body:
Hermes (Trismegistus) is the starting point of the Hermetic story, an adept king credited with the Hermetic writings [I.1 ¶6; I.1 ¶7]; the works imputed to him were translated from Greek into Latin by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. Geber ranks after him, and Artephius learned the art from his books [I.1 ¶31; I.1 ¶36]; Norton's verse lists him among masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

**Golden Treatise (Tract. Aur.).** Introduced as an ancient epitome of the whole Art of doubtful authorship [I.2 ¶50], it is printed in full as the main text of I.3 and glossed in Atwood's notes [I.3 ¶1–¶58]; she calls it a fair, less sophistical example of alchemical writing, yet veiled [I.3 ¶46]. Its key lines: “the work is both with you and about you” [I.3 ¶1]; “the masculine truly is the heaven of the feminine, and the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶15]; “the whole matter I know to be one only thing” [I.3 ¶36]; “that which is born of the crow is the beginning of this Art” [I.3 ¶46]. 'Hermes the King' first declared that Mercury cannot be mortified alone [I.3 n17]. Atwood reinterprets its Water as the ethereal body, not common water [I.2 ¶43; I.2 n41], and cites it throughout: the vessel is the water, “vas philosophorum est aqua eorum” [II.1 ¶8]; “Extract from the ray its shadow and its obscurity” [II.3 ¶27]; two natures mortified together [III.1 ¶43]; “Take, my son, the flying bird and drown it flying” [III.1 ¶53; IV.1 ¶15], where she notes he 'does not speak of it openly' [III.1 n67]; the chain binding the matter [III.2 ¶22]; secrecy toward the vicious [III.4 ¶9]; the science as “the sole gift of the living God” [III.4 ¶20].

**Other works.** The separation precept (cited with the Tract. Aur., the Smaragdine Tablet and the Asclepius), “Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross”, is read as Mind the Separator [III.1 ¶21; III.1 n22]; the Tablet is quoted in full as summary instruction, “That which is above is as that which is below” [IV.2 ¶43]. The Poemander (Pymander) testifies to inward regeneration: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; “Conceive well the Light in thy Mind, and Know It.” [III.3 ¶52]; each principle carries “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. Knowledge of the First Cause is “a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33].

**Practice (IV.3).** He supports the First Key and beheading the Raven [IV.3 ¶3], the Stone as “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶5], keeping the earthy residue [IV.3 ¶7], “The first of all is the water which issueth out of this Stone.” [IV.3 ¶8], and the permanent union of purified bodies and spirits [IV.3 ¶10]. He names the Spirit of Universal nature “a Quintessence” [III.2 ¶36]. Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): the Poemander on the downward-born nature [APP ¶18]; the Golden Treatise cap. 4 [APP ¶51].

**Also cited.** Trismegistus as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶20]; the Stone generated with light and bringing forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30]; furnace and glass making a new world, via Fludd's Mosaica [II.3 ¶52; II.3 n58]; “our Son, as Hermes calls him”, a personification of the intellectual purpose [III.1 ¶36]; equal Spirits, “both need the help of the other” [III.1 ¶41]; the necessity of labor, via Eirenaeus [IV.1 ¶6], and his toil for 'the blessed Lunary of Diana' [III.2 ¶64]; in Norton's verse, the water of crude Mercury [III.3 ¶74] and “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [IV.2 ¶13].

summary: Apparently a name for the Matter, whose many epithets (heaven, water, mercury, salt nitre, sulfur, caput mortuum and others) are said to be those of Hermes' Bird, never at rest.
body: In a passage voiced by Synesius and the New Light, a list of names for the Matter (heaven, water, mercury, salt nitre, sulfur, caput mortuum and others) closes: “And these are the Epithetes of Hermes, his Bird, which is never at rest.” [I.2 ¶33]. The Bird thus apparently stands for the Matter itself.

summary: In the Marrow of Alchemy, the closure of the single glass holding the composition.
body: In verse quoted from the *Marrow of Alchemy*, the single glass holding the composition is closed “which shut With Hermes’ seal, no fear it should be lost” [IV.3 ¶23]. The text does not explain the seal further.

summary: Ancient fragments whose 'soul-stirring syllables', Atwood says, agree in the same divine tradition.
body: Atwood cites the Hermetic and Chaldaic Fragments in support: their 'soul-stirring syllables' agree in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

summary: The art at the centre of the book: the perfecting of the mineral life in man, an operation on the Undetermined Subject, identified with Theurgy and with Alchemy.
body:
Atwood defines the Art as the perfecting of the mineral life in man, typifying the celestial and Divine: “The Art is a question put to Nature respecting the first cause” [APP ¶48] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer). In the main text it is the right disposition and manipulation of the Undetermined Subject through stated operations; riches come to “he that knows the Art, and the expressions, and hath the medium” [II.2 ¶18].
