By it the Matter, having “worked out its own restitution”, is brought into the fixity of its Final Cause [III.2 ¶22]. A passage of uncertain voice makes Art complete what nature cannot, adding supernatural light by graduation, and “leaves the victory to Art” [II.1 ¶25]; in Vaughan it unites a Particular Spirit to the Universal [II.1 ¶25].

History: Democritus' Sacred Physics “treats especially of the Hermetic art, and that occult discovery on which the systems of ancient philosophy appear to have been very uniformly based” [I.1 ¶12]; Bacon stated “the roots of the Hermetic science” while concealing practice [I.1 ¶39]; Flamel's name is honorably connected with it [I.1 ¶56]; Atwood distinguishes “the genuine Hermetic art” from pretenders' follies [I.1 ¶64]. Its ground is “as far out of the road of common thought as if it were tabooed” [I.1 ¶76]. It is cabalistic and veiled, plain in itself but in metaphor: “For is not our art cabalistic” [I.1 ¶84]; the world is ignorant of “the genuine doctrine and Art of Wisdom” [I.1 ¶86].

Identities: = Theurgy and = Art of Divine works: “Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy” [II.2 ¶3], practised in the Mysteries [II.2 ¶2]; = Alchemy, “the most commendable art of Alchemy” [I.1 ¶84]. Labels such as 'the Secret Art', 'the Divine Art' and 'the Great Art' also occur near I.1 ¶39–¶43, but no explicit identity among them is asserted there.

summary: The Art whose province is to resuscitate the buried Source of reason and bring it, through self-knowledge, into living experience.
body: Atwood: “this it is the province of Hermetic Artifice to resuscitate and bring through self-knowledge into the experience of life” [IV.4 ¶20], the thing resuscitated being the buried Source of reason.

summary: The operation that obtains the right recipient, separates pure from impure and subtle from gross, and makes agent and patient one.
body: Atwood: “by the Hermetic dissolution the right recipient is said to be obtained” [I.2 ¶48]; the same operation separates pure from impure and subtle from gross, and makes agent and patient one [I.2 ¶48].

summary: The theory of the art as acquired by reading, which requires the same faculties as the later experimental proof.
body: Atwood says the same faculties are needed “in acquiring the Hermetic doctrine, by perusal, as is afterwards needed for the experimental proof” [III.4 ¶15].

summary: The practical work itself, whose method and true basis Atwood says the passages she has gathered clarify.
body: Atwood presents her cited passages as clarifying matters “with respect to the method and true basis of the Hermetic experiment” [III.1 ¶71].

summary: The means by which ancient fables were interpreted as philosophy.
body: Atwood mentions writers who “explained them by the Hermetic key” [I.1 ¶70], i.e. read ancient fable as philosophy; the passage does not say what the key is.

summary: The agent and patient aspects of the one self-purifying subject; in full advancement, the Sun and Moon philosophical.
body: Atwood: the one self-purifying subject is “in turn agent and patient, which are the Hermetic luminaries; in their full representative advancement, the Sun and Moon philosophical” [II.2 ¶26]. Asserted identities: = agent and patient; = Sun and Moon philosophical [II.2 ¶26].

summary: The voice Atwood cites from the Tract. Aur., cited on the crowned operator, the moral qualifications for Wisdom, and Wisdom as a gift.
body: Quoting the Tract. Aur. (and Ripley Revived), Atwood cites the Hermetic Master on the accomplished operator: “henceforth thou art a Crowned King, resting over the Fountain” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n9]; on the moral qualifications for entry into hidden Wisdom, one must strive “to free himself from the usurpation of vice, and to be good, just, and of sound reason” [III.4 ¶15; III.4 n10]; and on Wisdom as not won by effort: “Wisdom was with thee, says the Hermetic Master; it was not gotten by thy care” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n31]. All are cited in support.

summary: The work and its end, figured as a line that returns into its beginning to form a circle, joined in Eternity rather than in time.
body: Atwood: “This is the work --- this is the Hermetic method and its end” [IV.3 ¶62], figured as “The line returns to form a circle into its’ beginning, and they join not in time, for their union is Eternity.” [IV.3 ¶62]. Asserted identity: = the work [IV.3 ¶62].

summary: The subject of the whole book: a genuine tradition whose nucleus is Life and whose Key is Light, culminating in divine illumination.
body: Atwood defends “the genuine tradition of Hermetic science” against sophists' deceits, holding that public disbelief “are no proofs in philosophy, even if it were without so many witnesses, that the Hermetic mystery is groundless” [I.1 ¶86]. After describing the divine illumination she writes “That was the sum of the Hermetic Mystery” [IV.2 ¶43], the sum being also the ultimate object of the Alchemical Art; what 'that' covers is apparently most directly the illumination of IV.2 ¶39–¶42, but its exact extent is not certain. Finally: “And Life is the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery, and the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: Practitioners of the Hermetic art; a title Atwood withholds from Aristotle and Plato without further evidence that they practised it.
body: Atwood will not grant Aristotle or Plato the title without more evidence that they practised the art, evidence needed “to prove their claim to the title of Hermetic philosophers” [I.1 ¶17]. Practitioners of the Hermetic art are so called [I.1 ¶12].

summary: Experimental inquiry into the Universal Spirit through man; universal, rational and divine knowledge beside which worldly science is relatively vain.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls Hermetic Philosophy experimentation into the Universal Spirit through man, “a development of the art by which a particular spirit (to use Vaughan’s words) is allied to the universal” [APP ¶53]. In the main text it is knowledge described as universal, rational and divine, beside which worldly science is relatively vain, with “the ground of the whole Hermetic philosophy laid out” [I.1 ¶64].

summary: A regular inquisition into life, in which motion is present with interrogation.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Hermetic Process is a regular inquisition into life.” [APP ¶138]; in it motion is present with interrogation.

summary: A riddle Atwood cites to illustrate the circulation of all things in all, and whose ‘omnia in omnibus’ she identifies with the Universal Ether.
body: Atwood cites the Hermetic Riddle to illustrate the circulation by which the Flower of Intellect is manifested back to its Archetypal Source: “The First all things in all gave the First Second all things in all, from the all in the First Second to the Third all” [IV.2 ¶20]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) its “omnia in omnibus” is identified with the Universal Ether [APP ¶119].

summary: Atwood's name for the art the book investigates: an ancient eastern tradition, peculiar and distinct from other philosophy, experimental and practical, embracing physical and moral science.
body:
In Atwood's own voice, the Hermetic tradition is ancient and eastern: “The Hermetic tradition opens early with the morning dawn in the eastern world. All pertaining thereto is romantic and mystical.” [I.1 ¶2]; it survives in dark and enigmatical monuments, emblems and writings. It is not bound to any one creed or class: “men of every religion, time and country and occupation, have been found professing it” [I.1 ¶31].

She treats it as a discipline of its own, “peculiar and distinct from every other branch of philosophy” [III.4 ¶2], requiring a naturally fitted disposition in its student. It is eminently experimental and practical in its consequences, and — with a hedge on its validity — “the Hermetic Science, supposing this indeed to be well founded, would include both in the ample compass of its experiment” [IV.4 ¶11], that is, both physical and moral science.

summary: In a Scholiast quoted by Atwood, the exact sealing of the philosophic vessel's orifices and junctures so no vapour escapes; equated with the lutum Sapientiae.
body: A Scholiast quoted in a footnote describes “how the orifices and junctures of the philosophic vessel must be encircled, so that no breath may go forth” [I.3 n57]. The same note equates the seal with the lutum Sapientiae: “with the lutum Sapientiae, or Hermetic seal” [I.3 n57]. Any plain meaning beyond the closing of the vessel is not given in this record.

summary: In the Appendix, the vehicle of the dead Divine Life within us, and at the same time the death of itself.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The Hermetic sepulcher is the vehicle of the dead Divine Life within us” [APP ¶19], adding that it is at the same time the death of itself.

summary: The single repeated operation that comprises all the named operations (calcination, inceration, fixation, etc.), improving the matter each time; not ordinary chemical sublimation.
body: Atwood explains that Hermetic sublimation is the one operation covering all the named ones — calcination, inceration, fixation and the rest. It is repeated many times, and each repetition changes and improves the matter. She warns against the chemical reading: “This sublimation is not, therefore, exactly to be conceived by analogy with the ordinary chemical process, which is a mere elevation of the subject to the top of the vessel” [I.3 n14].

summary: The body of tradition Atwood says she has run cursorily through in the book.
body: Atwood refers to the Hermetic Tradition as the body of tradition she has run cursorily through [IV.4 ¶10].

summary: A work cited in the Appendix whose latter part illustrates the sacrifice of the first-fruits.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the latter part of The Hermetic Wedding is cited as illustrating the sacrifice of the first-fruits [APP ¶74].

summary: A work Atwood cites in support of the Stone being prepared with the Lunar Vulcan, which she glosses as the first prepared Subject.
body: Atwood cites the Hermetical Triumph in support: it speaks of “the Stone of Philosophers, which is a pure petrification of the Spirit” [IV.1 ¶29], prepared with the Lunar Vulcan, which Atwood glosses as the first prepared Subject.

summary: A group voice cited and endorsed in the Appendix: the Mystery is discovered by artificial dissolution of the natural bond of life and regeneration under a reversed law.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood endorses the Hermeticists' view that the Mystery is discovered by an artificial dissolution of the natural bond of life, and by regeneration under a reversed law [APP ¶7].

summary: In the Appendix, the magnetism of Light according to its own law, that Law being its emanating spirit, called wisdom.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood defines it: “Hermetism is the magnetism of Light according to its own law” [APP ¶47]; that Law is its emanating spirit, called wisdom. Hermetism is thus identified with the magnetism of Light.

summary: An author cited in support of the existence and nature of a divine water of the chemists.
body: Atwood cites Hermolaus Barbarus, in a corollary to Dioscorus or some other work (the text is uncertain), in support of the divine water: “There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20].

summary: Historian cited for recording Egypt's remaining splendour after Cambyses.
body: Atwood names Herodotus as the historian who recorded the splendour that remained in Egypt after Cambyses [I.1 ¶10].

summary: Something of ‘illimitable virtue’ that Power and Motive corrects, educates, tames and directs; not further explained.
body: Atwood speaks of Power and Motive that “corrects and educates the Heroic Fire, tames and directs its illimitable virtue” [IV.1 ¶33]. The text gives no further explanation of the term here.

summary: The intellect whose long labors must all be passed through before the work is complete.
body: Atwood says that before the work is complete there are “all the labors of that Heroic Intellect to be passed through” [II.2 ¶29].

summary: The self-sacrificing will, read in Achilles' ‘vindicative will’, that enters after the loss and stirs the bitter waters to recover the lost kingdom.
body: In her allegorical reading of the Iliad, Atwood writes that after the loss “the Heroic Will enters in, self-sacrificing, and stirs the bitter waters” [III.1 ¶30], to recover the lost kingdom; she connects it with Achilles' vindicative will.

summary: Poet whose theogony Atwood cites as ‘very regular and correct’ when compared with alchemical descriptions, and as accepted by ancient philosophers.
body: Atwood cites Hesiod's theogony (beginning “First of all existed Chaos” [III.3 ¶41]) in support, judging it, when compared with alchemical descriptions, very regular and correct, and noting that ancient philosophers accepted it [III.3 ¶41, III.3 ¶42, III.3 n28]. The Epic Cycle and The Weeks and the Days are also named in connection with him.

summary: Atwood's image for the three offspring or supernal benefits that Life brings forth and sacrifices at each passage from one form of perfection to another.
body: Atwood describes Life bringing forth, at each passage from one form of perfection to another, three offspring or supernal benefits, “as it were three Hesperian Apples of Gold” [III.4 ¶25], which it sacrifices in turn.

summary: That in which the whole mystery is comprehended; the philosophers found them out and increased them.
body: The whole mystery is said to be comprehended in the hidden elements; of the philosophers it is said “they themselves found out these hidden elements, and themselves increased them” [II.1 ¶14]. The voice is unclear from the record. Compare hidden Wisdom, which hides beneath these elements [I.3 ¶25].

summary: In Hermes as quoted, the hidden Wisdom that comprehends all the world's wisdoms; learning the Arts consists in discovering the hidden elements beneath which it hides.
body: Hermes, quoted by Atwood, says: “All the wisdoms of the world, O son, are comprehended in this my hidden Wisdom” [I.3 ¶25]. The learning of the Arts consists in discovering the hidden elements beneath which this Wisdom hides.

summary: The officiant of the inner temple who passed aspirants on; in Clemens Alexandrinus, the Lord himself, who seals and illuminates the adepts in the true mysteries.
body:
In Atwood's own usage the Hierophant is the officiant of the inner temple who passed the aspirants on: “the Hierophant of the inner temple” [II.3 ¶36].

Quoting Clemens Alexandrinus, she gives the term a spiritual sense: “it is the Lord himself who is the hierophant” [II.2 ¶5], who seals and illuminates the adept. The same point recurs from the Bishop of Alexandria: “It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.” [IV.2 ¶16] — in the true mysteries the Lord seals the Adepts and illuminates them.

summary: A group whose atmosphere, Atwood says in the Appendix, opens the depths of St Paul, in contrast to the commentators.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the atmosphere of the higher Mystics is said to open St Paul's depths, in contrast with the commentators [APP ¶118].

summary: Physician named via Pliny as illustrator of medicine; Atwood uses ‘the Night of Hippocrates’ and his figure as the divinely endowed healer to illustrate the Art.
body: Hippocrates is named, after Pliny, as the illustrator of medicine, contemporary with the magic of Democritus [I.1 ¶12]. Atwood uses the expression ‘the Night of Hippocrates’ to name the end of the destructive way [III.2 ¶28]. She also uses him to illustrate the divinely endowed physician who imparts healing to others [IV.3 ¶32, IV.3 ¶34].

summary: Unnamed biographer of Pythagoras, cited as reporting that Pythagoras healed and purified his followers' souls by divine arts.
body: Atwood cites Pythagoras' biographer as reporting that Pythagoras healed and purified the souls of his followers by divine arts [II.2 ¶11].

headword: his ingenious disciple (of Cornelius Agrippa; not named)
forms: his ingenious disciple (of Cornelius Agrippa; not named)
summary: An unnamed disciple of Cornelius Agrippa, cited for ‘more suggestive language’ on the work's sequence and for Agrippa's poverty after his failure.
body: Atwood cites Agrippa's unnamed “ingenious disciple” as expressing, in more suggestive language, the joining, siege and creature sequence of the work: “Take our two serpents, which are to be found everywhere on the face of the earth” [III.1 ¶50]. She cites him again on Agrippa's poverty resulting from his failure: “This was it, adds his disciple, that made his necessities so vigorous and his purse so weak” [IV.1 ¶36].

headword: Histoire Hermetique; Lives of the Adepts; Les Hieroglyphiques de N. Flammel
forms: Histoire Hermetique; Lives of the Adepts; Les Hieroglyphiques de N. Flammel
summary: Cited for reference only.
Painter cited as a contrast: in ordinary arts the maker's moral state does not show in the product, unlike in Alchemy.
body: Atwood uses Holbein as a contrast: “The pictures, of Holbein are not less beautiful for all the covetous spirit that reigned with their conception” [III.4 ¶8]. In ordinary arts the maker's moral state does not appear in the product; in Alchemy, by implication, it does.

summary: Scripture, cited as read by the Kabalists as divine symbols.
body: Atwood cites Holy Writ (the Pentateuch, the Old Testament) as read by the Kabalists as divine symbols [II.1 ¶40, II.1 ¶41].

summary: Poet whose Iliad and Odyssey Atwood reads as allegories of the Art, holding in the Appendix that the Hermetic is the only true key to them.
body:
Atwood reads Homer allegorically throughout. From the thirteenth book of the Odyssey she takes the cave in Ithaca with its two gates — “A lofty gate unfolds on either side” [II.4 ¶5] — as an allegory of descent and ascent [II.4 ¶5, II.4 ¶6, II.4 ¶7]. From the Iliad she reads Achilles' armour, the death of Patroclus, and Achilles' vow and death as an allegory of the Art [III.1 ¶25, III.1 ¶29, III.1 ¶30, III.1 n32, III.1 n35]. From Odyssey book 19 she cites in support that quietude and the cessation of mental energy are needed to receive divinity: “Be silent, repress your intellect, and do not speak.” [IV.2 ¶33, IV.2 n22].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she states that the Hermetic is the only true key to the Iliad and Odyssey [APP ¶157], and identifies Proteus' last subterfuge, his transformation into a tree, with the tree of the Golden Bough, illustrating the elusive Protean life [APP ¶171].

summary: Nature of the same kind, which the perfected Spirit draws everywhere into itself.
body: Atwood describes the perfected Spirit as drawing “the Homogeneal Nature everywhere into itself” [IV.3 ¶29] — apparently, nature of its own kind.

summary: The one uniform substance in nature that is the material basis of Hermetic philosophy and sole principle of transmutation, life, increase and perfection.
body: Atwood posits “the existence of a Homogeneal Subject in nature” [I.2 ¶49]: one uniform substance that is the material basis of Hermetic philosophy and the sole principle of transmutation, life, increase and perfection.

headword: Hone soit qui mal y pense (unattributed)
forms: Hone soit qui mal y pense
summary: An unattributed motto Atwood invokes in support of her point against the charge of impiety.
body: Atwood invokes, in support of her point against the charge of impiety, the unattributed motto “Hone soit qui mal y pense.” [IV.4 ¶24]. Translation (ours): shamed be he who thinks evil of it.

summary: In the later Table Talk, Atwood links the Horizontal with fixation and with 'latitude'.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), speaks of “the fixation by the Horizontal; altitude and latitude” [APP ¶173]. The record suggests Horizontal Magnetism is what effects fixation, set beside 'latitude'. The text gives no fuller definition.

summary: In Apuleius' tale as Atwood cites it, the form Lucius regains with the goddess's help when he sheds the ass's hide.
body: The voice is the quoted Apuleius. The goddess promises Lucius that “by whose assistance you will return to the Human Form” [II.4 ¶17]. Return to the Human Form means shedding the ass's hide.

summary: The human will, which Atwood says has corroborative efficacy when it acts in concert with its Final Cause to fulfil it.
body: Atwood speaks of “the corroborative efficacy of the Human Will, acting in concert with its Final Cause to fulfill it” [III.4 ¶28]. The record gives the Will a supporting power in the work only when it acts in concert with its Final Cause.

summary: Author of Poetry of Science, cited by Atwood as showing that modern science admits the nature of light is unexplained.
body: Atwood cites Hunt's *Poetry of Science* in support of her point that modern science admits it has not explained the nature of light [I.2 ¶47, I.2 n45]. She uses him as a supporting authority.

summary: Lully's name for the subject, a clear compounded water like argent vive; also, in a cited cosmogony, the 'enormous first-born' of Chaos's primeval parent.
body:
Two quoted voices use the term.

Lully names the subject Hyle and describes it: “it is a clear compounded water, most like in substance to argent vive” [I.2 ¶29]. In the readers' summary of the passage it also flows on earth, is generated in every compound from the substance of the air, and is extremely heavy [I.2 ¶29].

In the account Atwood attributes to the metropolitan of Memphis, the primeval parent of Chaos “brought forth her enormous first-born Hyle” [III.3 ¶46].

The records do not say whether the two uses are meant to be the same thing.

summary: A hymn to Mercury, its source not named, that Atwood quotes as illustrating Mercury 'with like allusion'.
body: Atwood quotes a hymn, without naming its source, as illustrating Mercury “with like allusion”: “Hear me, O Mercury, and Son of Maia; the bright expositor of things!” [I.2 ¶36].

summary: The teacher who, Atwood says, taught Synesius the occult truths of the philosophy.
body: Atwood names Hypatia as the person who taught Synesius the occult truths of the philosophy [I.1 ¶27]. That is all the record says about her.

summary: Atwood's word, applied to Democritus' occult researches and to Plato's whole philosophy with its mystic, recondite character.
body: Atwood applies the word to Democritus' occult researches, such as making precious stones (“these and such-like hyperphysical researches” [I.1 ¶12]), and to Plato: “But the whole philosophy of Plato is hyperphysical” [I.1 ¶17]. There it goes with the mystic, recondite character of Plato's philosophy. The text gives no definition.

equivalences.with: radix of the reason that seeks

summary: Atwood's recurring, undefined term, apparently for the substantial ground of a being, which must be dissolved and renewed and is to be redeemed as reason's true objective reality.
body:
The voice throughout is Atwood's. She never defines the word, so its meaning has to be gathered from how she uses it.

**The natural self that must die.** She speaks of “The self-willed hypostasis of nature must die” so that nature's universal being can evolve [I.3 n53]. Elsewhere the condition of new life and of growth into consciousness is “a dissolution of the whole natural born hypostasis” [III.1 ¶50].

**The soul's ground in darkness.** While “her hypostasis continues in darkness” the soul is in Hades. It is “the alone eternal hypostasis to be redeemed from thence”, that is, from the oblivious realms of generation [II.3 ¶36].

**Reason's true object.** Reason's true Hypostasis is her objective reality: “it is her true Hypostasis, for which, as Isis for Osiris, she is constantly seeking, her objective reality in the Great Unknown” [II.3 ¶46]. The 'new world' made with furnace and glass is glossed as “a new hypostasis, and a new stone” [II.3 ¶52]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), once the Chimaeras are destroyed, what remains is “the simple Hypostasis or radix of the reason that seeks” [APP ¶171], so the Hypostasis is equated with the radix (root) of the seeking reason.

**Transformation.** “the whole hypostasis was converted finally through faith into the identity of substant light within” [III.1 ¶11]. At the Soul's return “a new hypostasis is created out of the darkness to abide” [III.3 ¶10].

**Matter and Essence.** She uses the word of the First Matter (“such an hypostasis is in the beginning without all affirmation” [III.2 ¶57]) and of the Eternal Essence perceived intellectually: “an hypostasis unwearied, untamed, and never failing” [III.2 ¶59].

**Adjective forms.** In the Vital Spirit, active and passive power are joined in a 'hypostatic union', and there are “the hypostatic principles of attraction and repulsion and circulation” [III.3 ¶9]. The Initiates' regard of God “was not extraneous but hypostatical, as of like to like” [II.4 ¶40].

The common thread, as these uses suggest, is a substantial ground or root of being: in its natural, self-willed state it must be dissolved, and in its true state it is sought and renewed.

summary: The working of the essences in life, which Atwood says is proved by those who enter experimentally within.
body: Atwood refers to “the hypostatic action and passion of the working essences in life” [IV.4 ¶4]. Those who enter experimentally within prove it. It is not further explained.

summary: The reality the consciousness in Hades is taught to aspire to but cannot find by itself through the darkness.
body: Atwood speaks of “that Hypostatic Reality towards which it is instructed evermore to aspire” [II.3 ¶29]. 'It' is the consciousness in Hades, which cannot find this reality by itself through the darkness.

summary: Body, soul and spirit, taken as three relations of one life, distinguished only as agent, patient and offspring.
body: Atwood identifies “body, soul, and spirit --- the three hypostatic relations” [III.3 ¶67]. They are relations of one life, born one from another and distinguished only as agent, patient and offspring. On transmuting these relations, see hypostatic union.

summary: In the cited Vaughan, the union of celestial nature, aerial spirit and the soul's aura, which are one in substance.
body: The voice is the quoted Vaughan. He names three things, the celestial nature, the aerial spirit and the soul's aura: “These three, being but One substantially, admit of a perfect hypostatic union” [III.3 ¶27]. The Quadrature is achieved “by a transmutation of the hypostatic relations” [III.3 ¶30], which the readers render as an exchange of active and passive. Atwood also speaks in her own voice of a 'hypostatic union' of active and passive power in the Vital Spirit [III.3 ¶9].

summary: That which is triply introverted and multiplied by the circulatory medium throughout life to manifest the magistery.
body: Atwood speaks of the “multiplication of the hypostatic unit by the circulatory medium throughout life” [IV.2 ¶37]. The unit is triply introverted, and its multiplication manifests the magistery. It is not further defined.

summary: The union in which Light overcomes darkness, which Atwood offers as the proper antidote to inbred evil.
body: Atwood speaks of “overcoming darkness by Light in the hypostatical alliance” [IV.4 ¶17]. She presents this as the proper antidote to inbred evil, and does not explain it further.

summary: A Neoplatonist whose Life of Pythagoras and On the Mysteries Atwood cites often and with approval, on Theurgy, prayer, divine union, purification and the Tetractys.
body:
Atwood spells the name Iamblicus, Iamblichus and Jamblicus. She lists him among the Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27]. She also lists him among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9]. He is consistently a supporting authority, and she does not dispute him.

**Life of Pythagoras.** Wisdom “is truly a science which is conversant with the first and most beautiful objects”, objects that do not decay and by participation in which other things are beautiful [II.1 ¶39, II.1 n37]. The uninitiated mind is like “dense thickets, which are full of briars”, and souls must be cleansed before they receive doctrine, as in the dyer analogy [II.2 ¶11, II.2 n12]. Nearby, Theurgic rites follow immutable intellectual canons, and the mundane spirit fashions the soul's powers [II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶15]. Chap. 28 is the source of the verse on the Tetractys: “Whence all our Wisdom springs, and which contains Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root” [III.3 ¶34, III.3 n23].

**On the Mysteries.** Theurgists became partakers in Wisdom “by certain ineffable and sublime media that Theurgists became cognizant partakers in the Wisdom of true Being”, not by contemplation or representation [II.2 ¶3, II.2 n7]. Union comes from divine media and Synthemata, not from intellectual perception, through “the perfect efficacy of ineffable works”. Atwood endorses this [II.4 ¶31, II.4 n23]. The gods give true illuminations, not phantasms: “By no means therefore, says Iamblichus, does Divinity either transform himself into phantasms” [II.4 ¶29, II.4 n20]. He also describes the effect of the divine vision on initiates with the image of fishes [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n12]. Pure Matter, “being connascent with the gods by whom it is imparted, will doubtless be an entire and fit receptacle for the manifestation of Divinity” [III.2 ¶49, III.2 n39]. Theurgists consulted the divine intellect only on the purification, liberation and salvation of life [III.1 ¶12, III.1 n9]. Atwood uses him to judge Hermes' lost books by the surviving Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n9].

**Prayer.** In defending prayer, she writes: “Prayer, according to Iamblicus, was divided into three classes”. She takes from him that prayer is necessary in sacred operations and purifies the soul [III.4 ¶24, III.4 n26].

summary: Icarus and his father, used as an illustration within Basil Valentine's allegory.
body: Icarus and his father Daedelus appear as an illustration within Basil Valentine's allegory [III.2 ¶19]. The record says nothing more.

headword: Idea of the Good, the Pure, and the True
forms: Idea of the Good, the Pure, and the True
summary: The alluring object all inwardly worship, the progeny of Divine Intellect, shining dimly through sense and selfishness as a guide.
body: Atwood writes: “The Idea of the Good, the Pure, and the True is the alluring object which we all innerly worship” [IV.3 ¶52]. She calls it “the progeny of Divine Intellect, immortal and strong --- even Moral beauty”, which equates it with Moral beauty. It “ever shines attractively --- our Polar Star” through the mists of sense and selfishness, though obscurely, and so serves as a guide [IV.3 ¶52].

summary: The ideal measure of excellence, which Atwood says modern literal conceits have stripped bare.
body: Atwood complains of “conceits which have stripped the Ideal Standard of all excellency” [IV.4 ¶29]. The context links these conceits to modern literal readings.

summary: The universal forms of Nature from which essence takes form, and the conceived pattern that the alchemical agent images as the will directs.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood equates “Ideas or the universal forms of Nature” [APP ¶37] and calls them that from which essence receives form.

In the main text, the Idea is the pattern a work images. In the ordinary arts the product remains “to image, not the motive instigatory, but the Idea” [III.4 ¶8]. In Alchemy the agent images what is conceived as the will directs: “to image the conceived Idea” [III.4 ¶9].

summary: A co-operation without which, Atwood says, we can never learn how Nature works; she contrasts it with reasoning from sense.
body: Atwood writes: “nor shall we ever learn, without Identic co-operation, how Nature works” [IV.4 ¶12]. She contrasts it with reasoning based on the senses and does not define it further.

summary: The indestructible substance that survives the dissolution of the whole being: true grain, root of the world, and seed of this world and the next.
body: Atwood describes it as the indestructible substance that survives when the whole being is dissolved. It renews the dissolved parts, and once freed it is Protean and changes colour [III.2 ¶20]. It is “the seed not only of this world but o the next” [III.2 ¶20]. She equates it with the true grain (“adepts have concluded this Identic Salt to be the true grain”) and with the root of the world (“this mystical substance, this root of the world”) [III.2 ¶20].

summary: The source in which the soul, in awe, begins to perceive herself, and into whose consciousness she passes through regeneration.
body: Atwood writes that the soul “begins to perceive itself in that Identic Source” [II.3 ¶37]. In the same paragraph she speaks of “the reminiscent consciousness of her Causal Source” [II.3 ¶37]. This apparently names the same source, into whose consciousness the soul passes through regeneration.

summary: The spirit that rises pure, bright and contrite from its primaeval element when the conflicts end, subject only to its own Law.
body: Atwood writes: “the Identical Spirit arises, pure, bright, and contrite, from its primaeval eleemtn” [III.1 ¶68]. It does so at the end of the conflicts, and afterwards it is subject only to its own Law. The text does not explain the word 'Identical'.

summary: Atwood's term for knowing without separation of subject and object, a state reason enters through regeneration; also used of individual selfhood, which must pass into universal accord.
body:
The voice throughout is Atwood's.

**A state of knowledge.** Once the inner light is fixed and the outer spirit made pliant, reason may “become into that Identity by which the powers of the Universal Nature are made manifest and intrinsically understood” [I.3 n8]. Here subject and object are not separated: the soul knows “but absolutely, in Identity” and becomes consubstantial with what she knows [II.4 ¶42].

**Made in regeneration.** Identity is “made in the regeneration by the reprocedure into experience out of the dissolute void of life when artificially induced” [III.2 ¶16].

**Selfhood.** Atwood also uses the word for individual selfhood. She speaks of “the exterminating fiat of our Identity”, which hides the exemplary Logos [III.3 ¶79]. In the final step, by the energy of faith, “the Identity passes into universal accord” and leaves separable selfhood behind [IV.3 ¶60].

**Ambiguity.** The Wisdom is reached by “the searching and proving of His own Identity” [IV.4 ¶27]. The text leaves unclear whose Identity 'His' refers to.

The two senses, the goal of knowing and the separate self to be transcended, sit side by side in the text.

summary: In the later Table Talk, Atwood's special sense of idolatry: forming the First Matter to a particular end of one's own, or stopping at any finite gift instead of the Universal.
body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) and are in Atwood's voice. In one, idolatry is man specificating and qualitating from his own mind, forming the First Matter for a particular end: “in this consists the true idolatry against which the Bible so strongly protests” [APP ¶37]. In the other, the work offers gifts and finite ends, and “you may stop in any of them; if you do, you commit idolatry.” [APP ¶135]. Stopping there instead of seeking the Universal means the will is creating idols for itself.

summary: The philosophers' fire, which the later Table Talk distinguishes from Vulcan (Motion), the stirrer up of the fire.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says: “Vulcan is not the fire, the ignis Philosophorum, but the stirrer up of the fire.” [APP ¶129]. Vulcan is identified there as Motion. Nothing more is said about the fire itself. (Latin *ignis Philosophorum*: 'fire of the Philosophers', our translation.)

summary: The poem as Atwood quotes it, for mutual aid, for the passing on of healing virtues, and (in Table Talk) for the connate spirit deprived of its understanding spirit.
body:
Atwood uses the Iliad for illustration only.

Book 10 illustrates the mutual aid of two: “By mutual confidence and mutual aid” [III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶46, III.1 n52].

Book 11 illustrates how healing virtues are handed on: “Such as sage Chiron, sire of pharmacy, First taught Achilles, and Achilles thee” [IV.3 ¶33, IV.3 n11].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), the episode after the death of Patroclus illustrates the connate spirit deprived of its understanding spirit [APP ¶109].

summary: In Iamblicus as Atwood cites him, what the first of the three classes of prayer pertains to.
body: The voice is the quoted Iamblicus, as Atwood reports him: “The first, recapitulates our author, pertains to Illumination” [III.4 ¶24]. 'The first' is the first of the three classes of prayer.

summary: The self as likeness of its divine source, which one reflects into for self-knowledge and passes beyond toward the Archetype.
body: Atwood speaks of “that great and miraculous mystery of our Image” [III.3 ¶25]. On the readers' account, the self is a likeness of its divine source and is to be reflected into for self-knowledge. One “passes from himself as an image to the Archetype” [III.3 ¶26].

summary: A title given to man as containing the Universal Reason, and, in the Poemander, to everything that is.
body: As Atwood reports Agrippa, man is called the Image of God because he contains the Universal Reason and corresponds with all levels of creation: “man was said to be the express Image of God, seeing he contains the Universal Reason within himself” [II.1 ¶9]. This equates the Image of God with man. In the Poemander, quoted by Atwood, the term is extended to all things: “For there is nothing which is not the Image of God” [III.3 ¶78], so the divine way proper to the Good meets one everywhere.

summary: A faculty with an elevating power, imaged by the Sphinx's 'winds', through which the phantastic spirit becomes capable of divine assimilation.
body: Atwood speaks of “the elevating power which the imagination possesses” [III.1 ¶6]. She says the Sphinx's 'winds' image this power, and through it the phantastic spirit becomes capable of divine assimilation.

summary: Atwood's phrase for what must be arrested, apparently the Protean succession of forms and colours described just before.
body: Atwood writes: “To arrest this imaginative flux of freed vitality” [III.2 ¶24]. Here 'this' apparently refers back to the Protean succession of forms and colours described just before [III.2 ¶20–22]. The flux is what the work must arrest.

summary: Impressions of the imagination that persist in a place after their act has passed and pollute its ether.
body: Atwood describes imaginative impressures that “even after their act has passed away, hang and pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode” [III.4 ¶42]. Compare the impressures implanted in the Vital Spirit (see impressures).

summary: The faculty that makes apparitions, as in dreams but more intensely.
body: Atwood: “For it is the imaginative spirit which is the maker of these images” [II.3 ¶22]. It produces the apparitions as it does in dreams, but more intensely.

summary: An operation of giving the dried matter 'drink', grinding, sealing and drying, repeated on a schedule; called the secret of the whole work.
body: In *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, quoted by Atwood, Imbibition gives the dried matter 'drink' (the Lion's sweat), followed by grinding, sealing and drying, repeated on a fixed schedule. The poem calls it “The secret of Imbibition never out tould;” and says “Because in it consisteth the whole subtill warke;” [III.1 ¶65]. In Eudoxus, also quoted, Imbibition is an operation named for the Red (with the citrine Mercury). In the Sixth Key it is paired with drying in the cycle of multiplication: “imbibing and drying” [IV.3 ¶16].

summary: The direct operative cause of the work, which Atwood says the alchemists concealed.
body: Atwood asks of the adepts “what was their immediate efficient?” [II.1 ¶47], meaning the direct operative cause of the work, which they concealed. Shortly after she speaks of arts and media “producing the central efficient into conscious being and effect” [II.1 ¶52]. The text does not say that the 'central efficient' and the 'immediate efficient' are the same.

summary: In Roger Bacon, as quoted, the goal that cannot be reached without a sanctified mind, purified soul and union with God.
body: Atwood quotes Roger Bacon: “it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality” [III.3 ¶28] without a sanctified mind, a purified soul and union with God.

summary: Geber's list of mental defects that exclude a person from the Art.
body: Atwood introduces Geber's list: “respecting the Impediments of Mind, the Arabian continues” [III.4 ¶3]. The defects are lack of sagacity, dullness, fantasy, changeability, beast-like blindness, disbelief and love of money. Each excludes a person from the work.

summary: What mesmeric tests identify as the same throughout; not further defined.
body: Atwood says such tests “prove nothing but to identify the same Imponderable through all” [II.2 ¶7]. The text does not define the term further here.

summary: Imaginative impressions implanted in the Vital Spirit by birth into sense, which cloud the spirit and obscure intelligence.
body: Atwood speaks of “imaginative impressures which, by the birth into sense, had become implanted there” [II.2 ¶8], that is, in the Vital Spirit, where they obscure intelligence. They are residual: “their impressure yet remains” [II.2 ¶10]. The spirit may “err amongst the turbulent and shadowy impressures of this of this life’s birth and sphere of accidents” [II.2 ¶14]. Compare imaginative impressures, which pollute a place [III.4 ¶42].

summary: In the Poemander, that which contains all things, being most capacious, swift and powerful.
body: Atwood quotes the Poemander: “Consider that which contains all things” [III.3 ¶78]. It is described thus: “it is most capacious, most swift, and most strong” [III.3 ¶78].

summary: Being without body, whose necessary existence Aristotle demonstrates; glossed as essential being.
body: Atwood refers to Aristotle demonstrating the necessary existence of “incorporeal (i.e., essential) being” [II.1 ¶37]. She glosses incorporeal being as essential being.

summary: In Aliphili, as quoted, the action of the fiery water on fixed gold, reducing it to black earth.
body: Atwood quotes Aliphili: the fiery water “incrudates even the mature, constant, and very fixed, fiery and abiding mass and matter of gold” [II.1 ¶14], reducing it to black earth.

summary: The Matter as formless subject opposed to form, apprehended only by the Indefinite; not to be despised when turned towards things prior.
body: In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses, the Indefinite is the Matter as the formless subject opposed to form. Yet “This Indefinite is not therefore everywhere to be despised” [III.2 ¶49] when it applies itself to things prior, that is, the divine exemplaries and the most excellent life. Plotinus, as quoted, adds that by the principle that like knows like, “the Indefinite also will be apprehended by the Indefinite” [III.2 ¶53]. Reason then passes out into an undefined void of thought. Compare Infinite.

summary: Atwood's account from Norton: provisional instruments are used at first until the determinate ones prove themselves fit by the Spirit.
body: Atwood, giving what she says Norton shows: “indeterminate instruments must be employed in the beginning, until the determinate shall declare themselves as by the Spirit they are proved fit” [III.4 ¶40]. Compare Vaughan's indeterminate agents [III.4 ¶44].

summary: Vaughan's advice to use agents provisionally until a single determinate agent is found.
body: Atwood quotes Vaughan: “Make use of indeterminate agents till thou canst find a determinate one” [III.4 ¶44]. The agents are not further defined. Compare indeterminate / determinate instruments [III.4 ¶40].

headword: individuals of various ages and nations, whose names are renowned in philosophy
forms: individuals of various ages and nations, whose names are renowned in philosophy
summary: Atwood's description of the witnesses gathered in the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience.
body: Atwood uses this phrase for the witnesses she has gathered for the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience [IV.4 ¶2]. She relies on them as support.

summary: The outward method that moves away from the causal source and cannot originate effects (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes something that “the inductive philosophy or method never can arrive at, since it goes further and further out, and finds its strength in remoteness from the causal source” [APP ¶120]. The method cannot originate effects. Compare inductive sciences [III.1 ¶8].

headword: inductive sciences / modern method of experimenting
summary: The modern experimental sciences, which Atwood criticizes because their long-accumulated facts fail to satisfy reason.
body: Atwood criticizes the inductive sciences and the modern method of experimenting. Facts accumulated over ages have not yielded the satisfaction reason requires [III.1 ¶8]. Compare inductive philosophy [APP ¶120].

summary: The lower region of life where the Sulphur lies bound (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of the Sulphur as “bound down in the inferior mineral region of life” [APP ¶125]. Compare Infernal life, which also represents the Mineral Kingdom [APP ¶33].

summary: The voluntary agent in life, representing the Mineral Kingdom and residing in man in the lumbar region (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The Infernal is the voluntary agent in life, and represents the Mineral Kingdom.” [APP ¶33]. In man it resides in the lumbar region. Compare Infernal motive wheel [III.1 ¶60].

summary: The swifter contrary current in the circulation, which surmounts and eclipses the Divine Light.
body: Atwood: “the swifter current of the Infernal motive wheel surmounts and eclipses the Divine Light in the circulation” [III.1 ¶60].

summary: Fashionable faithlessness that denounces whatever is new without rational ground; Atwood calls it perhaps the most absurd obstacle to human advancement.
body: Atwood defines it: “by infidelity, we mean that fashionable kind of faithlessness, which, without rational foundation, denounces everything that is new” [III.4 ¶12]. It also denounces whatever is unfamiliar and believes nothing worthy of belief or veneration. She calls it perhaps the most absurd obstacle to human advancement.

summary: What the Matter is, 'a certain Infinity', which eludes thought as a circumscribing boundary.
body: Atwood says the Matter is “but a certain Infinity” [III.2 ¶53], and that “for the thought, as circumscribing boundary, eludes the Infinite” [III.2 ¶57]. Compare Indefinite [III.2 ¶49, ¶53].

summary: A name for the Mysteries, as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue.
body: Atwood reports the view of the Platonist, Psellus and Cicero that the Mysteries “were truly called Initia, for they were the beginning of a life of reason and virtue” [II.2 ¶4].

summary: The origin to which life is led back from created individuality, described as its return to its First Source.
body: Atwood describes life being led “from the manifest created individuality, back into the Initial germ” [III.3 ¶79]. There it “returns to refund its treasury again its First Source” [III.3 ¶79]. The Initial germ is thus linked to the First Source. Compare Initial Source and Initial Principle.

summary: The first principle on which the whole Hermetic philosophy and occult tradition depend; named variously by the philosophers, and Wisdom or Supreme Crown in the Zohar.
body: Atwood says the whole Hermetic philosophy and every tradition of occult science depend on this principle: “it will be requisite to consider this, their Initial Principle, more particularly” [III.1 ¶3]. She proposes to examine how it may have become known 'in its first arcane descent and emanation'. What 'this' refers back to is not clear from the record. In the Zohar, once it has become manifest, it “is in the Zohar designated by the name of Wisdom, or the Supreme Crown” [III.2 ¶3], and “the divine hypostasis is distinguished by the epithet of Unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. This equates it with Wisdom, the Supreme Crown and the Unknown in the Beginning. Atwood surveys the philosophers: “some saying indeed of the Initial Principle, that it is one and finite, others infinite” [III.2 ¶35]. Some, “as Heraclitus, according to essence, have denominated it to be fire” [III.2 ¶35]. Another, “rather regarding the perfection and origin of the One Thing in consciousness, calls it Intellect” [III.2 ¶35]. Others call it water or earth. She concludes that “the substance alluded to by them all is the same” [III.2 ¶34], with mind and matter consubstantial in it.

summary: Nature's origin, into which she was followed and where she works her own annihilation and survives on her redeemed Light.
body: Atwood speaks of the effort “to follow mysterious Nature through many intricate windings and circumstantial difficulties, into her Initial Source” [IV.4 ¶6]. There Nature voluntarily works her own annihilation and survives upon her redeemed Light. Compare Initial germ [III.3 ¶79].

summary: The Initiated knew the means of the Art and kept silent about them; initiation is admission into the deeper mysteries.
body: Atwood notes “that the Initiated were so profoundly silent upon these means” [II.1 ¶53], meaning the means of the Art. Atwood also quotes Iamblicus and Synesius on initiation as admission into the deeper mysteries. Restoration of the soul is obtained by a few 'as a gift of divinity and initiation'. The uninitiated, “those who have not been purely initiated” [II.2 ¶11], are surrounded by 'dense thickets'. Compare Initia [II.2 ¶4].

summary: An unnamed poet, called “the initiated poet”, whose Metamorphoses Atwood cites for an apt figure of the celestial elements.
body: Atwood cites the initiated poet's *Metamorphoses* as offering an apt figure of the same celestial elements she is discussing: “the arising circulation of Mature from the four concentering winds” [III.2 ¶36]. The text names him only by this description.

headword: the initiated, who celebrated her Mysteries in the Eleusian fane
forms: the initiated, who celebrated her Mysteries in the Eleusian fane
summary: The initiated who celebrated the goddess's Mysteries in the Eleusian fane, cited by Atwood for how they described the multinominal goddess.
body: Atwood invokes the initiated who celebrated the goddess's Mysteries in the Eleusian fane to illustrate the multinominal goddess as they described her [III.3 ¶62].

summary: Nature's principle of perfection, held shut up by the bond of coagulation.
body: Atwood speaks of Nature's “Inner Light and principle of perfection” [III.2 ¶61], identifying the Inner Light with her principle of perfection, which is shut up by the bond of coagulation.

summary: The hidden meaning of the alchemical records, kept apart from their literal sense.
body: Atwood states: “In almost all the records of Alchemy, the inner sense is held aloof from the literal” [III.4 ¶16] — the records' inner meaning is kept apart from what they say on the surface.

summary: In a quoted Hermetic passage, the innermost chamber of life, where the Argent vive is prepared and coagulated.
body: In a footnote quoting Hermes with a Scholiast's comment, the Argent vive is said to be prepared in the innermost chamber: “It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life, and there it is coagulated” [I.3 n9]. The place is glossed as the ‘ultimate axle of each created life’ [I.3 n9]. The voice is the quoted authorities, not Atwood directly.

summary: The trained seeker or operator of the Art, who must learn what, where and how to obey, inquire, will and hope.
body: Atwood refers to “all the care that is taken to train the true Inquisitor” [III.1 ¶38]: the seeker of the Art must be trained in what, where and how to obey, inquire, will and hope.

summary: In the later Table Talk, the enclosing of the lower life, figured by the Walls of Troy and done in a great resonance.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood reads the Walls of Troy as a figure “of the insphering of the lower life; it is done in a great resonance” [APP ¶49] — apparently the enclosing or bounding of the lower life within a sphere.

equivalences.with: Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities

summary: The one unclean thing that enters the Stone, moving the gold to putrefy; evil at first but necessary, it finally gives the work its force and perfection.
body:
Atwood says nothing unclean enters the Stone “except One thing, which is the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy” [III.1 ¶61]; “it is the very grave of the rational light” [III.1 ¶61]. It is evil at first but necessary, and once returned through the natural Alembic it constitutes the force and perfection of the work [III.1 ¶61].

Identities: “it is called by them Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities, etc.” [III.1 ¶61].

summary: The alliance and power man enters by conditioning himself in obedience to the Divine Will.
body: Atwood writes that by conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will “he comes into the integral alliance and power” [IV.4 ¶23].

summary: In ordinary use the power of demonstrative knowing; in its highest sense the purified divine sight that beholds God, separates contraries, and is identified with the true man and the intelligible.
body:
**Two senses.** Atwood distinguishes Intellect in ordinary use — the power by which we know and prove things demonstratively — from its highest sense: a sight “called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God” [II.1 ¶38]. In that sense “True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential” [II.1 ¶37]; mortals lack it through generation. Identities: “the true man, according to Plato and Aristotelians, is this Intellect” [II.1 ¶35]; “that Intellect is the same with the intelligible” [II.1 ¶37].

**Quoted authorities.** Plotinus asks of the gods' beauty, “What else, however, is it but Intellect through which they are such?” [II.4 ¶29]. Atwood, endorsing Synesius and Anaxagoras, makes Intellect the superior separating power: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20], purifying and attenuating that Spirit and extending it to Divinity; and “Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing; but is alone by itself.” [III.1 ¶22]. Its special part is apparently the sequestatrix, though this reading is uncertain.

**In the method.** Drawing on Aristotle and Plotinus: “That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified” [III.1 ¶23]; it gives the soul a sudden Light, and “this Light is from Intellect, and is also It” [III.1 ¶23]. Without its light it suffers “the wanderings and anguish of Intellect so artificially isolated on the plain of Truth” [III.1 ¶28]. It is “the watchful eye of Intellect, well advised and able” that cuts off the sleeping Will [III.1 ¶68]. The Poemander testimony shows “the operative revelation of Intellect” [III.3 ¶59], known by experience.

**Fable readings.** “that court of King Alcinous, to which Ulysses became admitted, is the dominion of Intellect” [IV.1 ¶22], also signified by the Phoeacian ships. The fable conceals “the principiating action of Intellect but the methodical art of the same subtle Antecedent” [IV.2 ¶7] — its bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring.

summary: Aristotle's name, as reported, for human reason: subordinate to essential intellect and perfected only by a new awakening.
body: Atwood reports that Aristotle “denominates human reason, intellect in capacity” [II.1 ¶34]. It is subordinate to essential intellect and reaches its perfection only by a new awakening.

summary: The Intellect from which, Atwood says, the Greeks derived nature mediately, fixing her true Being in the Law of Universals.
body: Atwood says the Greeks “derived nature mediately from a certain Intellect in energy, but without distinction, fixing her true Being in the Law of Universals” [III.2 ¶34].

summary: Intellectual activity in Elysium, whose permanence alone is accompanied by eternity and in which the exemplary Image of Universal Nature is revealed.
body: Atwood writes that “eternity is consubsistent only with the permanence of intellection itself” and that “this is the Intellection in Elysium where the exemplary Image of the Universal Nature also is revealed” [II.4 ¶15].

summary: Illumination proceeding from the Divinity within when the conditions are duly offered; Reason is its temple.
body: Atwood speaks of the “Intellectual Ilumination which proceeds, when the conditions are duly offered, from the Divinity within” [III.1 ¶5], and calls Reason its temple. The book's spelling is “Ilumination”.

summary: Plato's term, as given, for the sudden kindling of a self-nourishing light in the soul; Schelling describes waking from it as from death.
body: Atwood applies the term to Plato's account of a self-nourishing light suddenly kindled in the soul after long converse and a conforming life, “speaking in like manner of the Intellectual Intuition” [II.3 ¶50]. She also quotes Schelling: “We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death” [IV.2 ¶33] — waking into created personality, where He can no longer be known.

summary: The self-evident law of reason (intuition, Universals) that proves and orders ordinary inquiry; abstract to the moderns, nature's efficient force to the ancients.
body: Atwood presents the Intellectual Law as the self-evident law of reason — intuition, Universals — that proves and orders ordinary inquiry. Moderns recognise “that same Law which the former recognizes but as an abstract boundary of thought only, having its object in sensibles” [II.1 ¶35], whereas the ancients treated it as the subject of nature's efficient force. A higher principle (Intellect/Wisdom) “bears the same relation to our Intellectual Law as does this to the reasoning faculty” [II.1 ¶39].

equivalences.with: Caduceus of Hermes; Golden Bough; ferrying Cup of Hercules

summary: The heroic, separable, thrice-refined purpose personified by many heroes and by Hermes' ‘our Son’, which passes through darkness, death and the Stygian waters.
body:
Atwood speaks of “that heroic, separable, triply refined intellectual purpose” [III.1 ¶36], personified by many heroes and passing through darkness, death and the Stygian waters.

Identities [III.1 ¶36]: “This is that prolific Mustard-seed, and Light of divine Faith”; it is “our Son, as Hermes calls him, born a king”; and “Such was the Caduceus of Hermes --- the Golden Bough, the ferrying Cup of Hercules”.

summary: The field whose upper grades are aspired to through labours and dangers.
body: Atwood mentions “those who aspire to the upper grades of Intellectual Science” [II.2 ¶14], who do so through labours and dangers.

summary: In Proclus as quoted, direct intellectual sight: contact with the Intelligible and union with the Demiurgic Intellect, opposed to syllogistic science.
body: Quoting Proclus, Atwood sets Intellectual Vision against syllogistic science: “But it is that which subsists according to Intellectual Vision itself: a contact with the Intelligible, and a union with the Demiurgic Intellect.” [II.4 ¶41]

summary: In Proclus as quoted, what the soul becomes when assimilated as far as possible to the whole intelligible universe.
body: Proclus, quoted, speaks of “the soul thus becoming an Intellectual World” [II.4 ¶41] when it is assimilated as far as possible to the whole intelligible universe.

summary: In a Zohar passage quoted by Atwood, the name Thought takes on becoming Spirit; Life springs forth by Intelligence excruciated.
body: In the Rabbi's account from the Zohar, Thought on becoming Spirit takes this name: “Arrived at this estate, it takes the name of Intelligence” [III.3 ¶78]. In the next paragraph Life springs forth “as by Intelligence excruciated” [III.3 ¶79].

summary: The object of intellectual contact, existing beyond the mind; the higher of the twofold nature, in which it is better for the soul to abide.
body:
Quoted authorities speak here. The Divine Oracle makes the Intelligible the object of intellectual contact, understood with the Flower of the mind but never wholly comprehended: “That thou mayest learn the Intelligible, for it exists beyond the mind.” [II.4 ¶48]. The Platonic Successor speaks of “having transcended the Intelligible” [II.4 ¶41] toward the Ineffable.

Plotinus and Porphyry, quoted: “And since there is a twofold nature, one intelligible and the other sensible, it is better indeed for the soul to abide in the intelligible world” [III.2 ¶50]; one is assimilated to it by being established in one's own essence.

summary: Empedocles' twofold natural procedure, as Atwood reports it: the sensible derived as an image from the intelligible as its exemplar.
body: Atwood reports Empedocles' twofold procedure of nature, “deriving the latter as an image from the former as an exemplar” [III.2 ¶38] — the sensible as image of the intelligible.

summary: The ordered progression, called gods by the Greeks, through which the perfected souls of the Initiated pass before contemplating the Highest Unity.
body: Atwood describes the perfected souls of the Initiated passing through “the whole progression of Intelligible Causes, by the Greeks called gods” [II.4 ¶39] before contemplating the Highest Unity.

summary: An inner agent which, awakened by too great excitation, could cause a disseveration in the Chaos.
body: Atwood warns of excess: “lest by too great excitation the internal agent awakening should cause a disseveration in the Chaos” [IV.1 ¶15].

summary: The adepts' inner fire, essential to the Hermetic work, which alone, purified, perfects it, unlike external or natural fires.
body: Atwood names “that internal fire and vessel of the adepts, so essential to the accomplishment of the Hermetic work” [II.1 ¶6]. She contrasts it with the external coal fire and the fire of the natural life, which only alter: “the internal alone is able, being purified, to perfect the work begun” [III.1 ¶43].

summary: The light within the matter, made manifest as the Dragon is occultated, which once manifest must enter another life and die again.
body: Atwood describes the light within the matter becoming manifest as the Dragon is occultated; once manifest to sense, it must enter another life and die again [I.3 n43, n44]. Related expressions appear nearby — ‘metallic light’, ‘fermenting light’ and the vital light: “The vital light, as we have before explained, is centrally hidden in nature until it is drawn forth” [I.3 n46] — but the text does not explicitly assert they are the same.

headword: Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palationem / Palatio / Introit. Apert.
forms: Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palationem / Palatio / Introit. Apert.
summary: Cited for reference only.
Psellus's term, as cited, for the initiate's inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure, distinguished from the Superinspection.
body: Atwood cites Psellus for the initiate's inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure: “This is the Introspection which Psellus speaks of, as distinguished from the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” [II.3 ¶46].

summary: Inward testing, without which inbred evil cannot truly be discovered.
body: Atwood holds that inbred evil cannot be truly discovered without inward testing: “or even discover it truly without introspective proof” [IV.4 ¶17].

summary: A complete process that must be passed through before the work is perfected; not further defined.
body: Atwood states that “it is not perfected unless the whole introversion is passed through” [III.1 ¶21]. The text here does not define the process further.

summary: Direct, self-evident knowing, which Atwood treats as the evidence and end of all rational proof and the highest human certainty.
body: Atwood's own term for direct, self-evident knowing. She holds that “intuition is the evidence and end of every rational proof” [II.1 ¶33], and that “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. On her account it is the highest certainty open to a human being.

summary: The level of life reached by cutting off the sensuous life; dissolving the sensuous reaches the intuitional, called divine.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “You cut off the sensuous life and get into the intuitional” [APP ¶176]. Dissolving the sensuous life is said to reach the intuitional, which she calls divine. A reader linked it with the “medial life” of [APP ¶182], but that identity is inferred from the parallel, not stated in the text.

summary: The reversal of nature's ordinary order: Atwood calls it our present state, a requirement for perfect manifestation, and reason turning back on itself.
body:
Atwood uses the word in three related ways.

- **Our condition.** In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Our present state is one of inversion.” [APP ¶45]
- **A requirement of the work.** The ordinary order of nature's procedure has to be reversed, and this lies beyond ordinary art and nature: the work proceeds “by a real experimental inversion” [I.2 ¶22], since “the order of natural procedure ought to be introverted for a true and perfect manifestation” [I.2 ¶27].
- **Reason turning back on itself.** Logic “becomes bounded about its own inversion” [III.2 ¶67], while the experiment actually carries the inversion out. Followed strictly, both lead to the First Source [III.2 ¶67].

The text does not say whether these are one process seen from different sides.

equivalences.with: secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature

summary: The true worker of the work, according to a quoted Adept: the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature.
body: A quoted Adept speaks here: “The work is performed by an invisible Artist; for there is a secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature” [IV.2 ¶18]. The invisible Artist is thus identified with the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature, which is the real agent behind the work.

summary: The inner hand of which the outward hand is the image and clothing; it works effects according to what it has attained.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The hand outward is an image of the invisible hand, its clothing” [APP ¶177]. The invisible hand works its effects according to what it has attained.

summary: In Bohme's account, the agent that prepares the Antimonial Spirit, also called the spiritual air of Antimony.
body: Bohme is quoted here. The Invisible Mercury prepares the Antimonial Spirit. It works when condensed in its vehicle, and its operation brings the three principles into harmony [II.1 ¶21]. Identity: “the invisible Universal Mercury, or spiritual air of Antimony” [II.1 ¶21].

headword: The Isaacs (J. I. Hollandus, I. Hollandus)
summary: Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked successfully; Atwood gives their works as references.
body: Atwood names the Isaacs (J. I. Hollandus and I. Hollandus) as Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked the art successfully [I.1 ¶58]. She gives their works, *de Lapide Philosophico* and *Opera Universalia*, as references [I.1 n63].

summary: Cited twice: for the overflowing of the dark power, and for gradual purifying and perfecting.
body:
Atwood cites Isaiah twice.

- Isaiah, Chap. 8, verse 8 illustrates how the dark power overflows at this stage of the work: “He shall overflow the channels, and go over all the banks” [III.1 ¶60, III.1 n65].
- Isaiah 38:13 supports gradual purifying and perfecting: “Line upon line, Precept upon precept” [IV.3 ¶39, IV.3 n19].

equivalences.with: Pessinuntica, Cecropian Minerva, Paphian Venus, Diana Dyctynna, Stygian Proserpine, Ceres, Juno, Bellona, Hecate, Rhamnusia

summary: The goddess Atwood identifies with nature, Minerva, Athena and the Wisdom under inquiry, and the name of the Matter once it becomes intelligent and convertible to every form.
body:
**In Apuleius (quoted).** Isis appears to Lucius and names herself: “call me by my true name, Queen Isis” [II.4 ¶17]. She calls herself nature: “I, who am nature, the parent of all things” [II.4 ¶17]. She is also queen of the elements, the one goddess “whose one divinity the whole orb of the earth venerates under a manifold form, by different rites and a various of appellations” [II.4 ¶17]. Among those appellations are Pessinuntica, Cecropian Minerva, Paphian Venus, Diana Dyctynna, Stygian Proserpine, Ceres, Juno, Bellona, Hecate and Rhamnusia.

**Atwood's identifications.** The Sphinx stood in “the vestibule of Isis, who is the same with Minerva and that Wisdom we are investigating” [III.1 ¶5]. So Isis is equated with Minerva and with the Wisdom that is the subject of the inquiry.

**In the fable and the work.** In the fable, Isis gathers Osiris's scattered members: “but Isis, recollecting, hides them in a chest” [III.1 ¶53]. In the work, the Lunar Vulcan plays her part. It tempers Typhon and reconciles the opposed principles, which then circulate with her in equilibrium [III.1 ¶63]. She is “as Isis in the Mysteries, where she is also called Athena” [III.1 ¶63]. That second name is given “to express that self-motion and intelligence with which this Spirit is endowed” [III.1 ¶63].

**Name of the Matter.** After the process described in [III.3 ¶61], the Matter is endowed with understanding, can be converted into any Form, and is the pre-existent mother of all. “Then she is Isis, the Divine I Am” [III.3 ¶62]. She is also “by the Greeks called Myrionymous, or the goddess with a thousand names” [III.3 ¶62]. Yet “As respects herself, she is Nothing” [III.3 ¶62].

All of these are Atwood's statements except the Apuleius passage, which she quotes.

summary: A pairing Atwood uses to illustrate reason constantly seeking her true Hypostasis.
body: Atwood uses the pair as an image: reason constantly seeks her true Hypostasis “as Isis for Osiris” [II.3 ¶46].

summary: Isis of the old mythology, used to illustrate the divine beauty pursued and the Goddess whose temple is Reason.
body: Atwood brings in Isis of the old mythology to illustrate the divine beauty that is pursued. Isis is the Goddess whose temple is Reason [II.1 ¶50].

summary: In Olympiodorus, a figure for a condition above corporeal life and generation, the same as the Elysian Fields.
body: Olympiodorus is quoted here. The Islands of the Blessed stand for a condition above corporeal life and generation, just as “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He adds that “these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3].

summary: An unattributed saying that the adept then interprets.
body: An unattributed saying, “Man, it is said, was created of the dust of the earth” [I.3 n51], is cited and then interpreted by the adept.

summary: In Hermes, the ferment made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water; it tinges and fixes, and bodies cannot be made pure without it.
body:
Hermes is quoted here. Ixir is the ferment, made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water. It tinges and fixes, and it is that “without which bodies cannot be made pure” [I.3 n63].

Identities stated:
- gold and ferment: “gold, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶58]
- Sericum: “we make of them Sericum, i.e., Ixir” [I.3 ¶59]
- seriacum: “we make seriacum, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶62]
- Elixir, true Ferment: “This is the Elixir, Ixir, or true Ferment tinging and fixing” [I.3 n63]

summary: A Dutchman and elegant classical expositor of Hermetic matters; Atwood counts him in the golden chain of Hermetic philosophers.
body: Atwood calls Tollius a Dutchman and an elegant classical expositor on the same ground [I.1 ¶70]. His works listed are *Tollii Fortuita*, *Manudcutio ad Coelum Chemicum* and *Sapientia Insanies, sive Promissa Chemica* [I.1 n87]. Alongside Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Michael Maier, he belongs to the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers”. These writers traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own, and Atwood cites them in support [III.1 ¶25].

summary: Cited in support of self-renunciation as the way to union.
body: Atwood cites words she attributes to Jacob in support of self-renunciation as the way to union: “Wherefore I abhor myself, cries Jacob” [IV.3 ¶58].

summary: Atwood holds that the Theurgic Art comes nearest to their doctrine of regeneration.
body: Atwood makes a comparison: the Theurgic Art comes nearest to “the perfect doctrine of regeneration preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles” [III.1 ¶11].

summary: The person who told Flammel the truth on this point.
body: The Jew is mentioned as the one who told Flammel the truth on this point [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: An author Atwood lists, with his works.
body: Beccher appears in a list of writers [I.1 ¶70]. His works given are *Physica Subterranea*, *Oedipus Chemicus Aperius Mysteria* and *Laboratorium Chemicum* [I.1 n86].

summary: Job and his book, cited often: his story is a type of the regenerate's sacrifice in faith, and his texts on Wisdom, Leviathan, gold and humbling support Atwood's argument.
body:
Atwood cites Job and the Book of Job often.

- **Job 28, on Wisdom.** Quoted at length to illustrate a contrast. Precious things hidden in the earth are brought to light, but the place of Wisdom is hidden from all living and known to God. For man, “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is Wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n5].
- **Job 41, Leviathan.** Quoted at length right after the account of how Typhon is subdued, with no commentary: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with an hook?” [III.1 ¶63, III.1 n71].
- **Job 31 and 33.** Cited for the accountability of moral evil and the condemnation of trusting in gold: “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [III.4 ¶7, III.4 ¶8, III.4 n5]. Note n6 goes with Adam hiding his iniquity in his bosom [III.4 n6].
- **Job 40:14.** Supports the humbling of the proud, followed by the promise of saving power: “THEN WILL I ALSO CONFESS UNTO THEE THAT THINE OWN RIGHT HAND CAN SAVE” [IV.3 ¶58, IV.3 n27]. The note marker follows the end of the quotation, and the text does not say how far back the citation reaches.
- **An objection answered.** The saying “no one by searching can find out the Almighty to perfection” holds, Atwood says, for a man searching by his own will. It does not hold for one conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will [IV.4 ¶23].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Job's story is “all a type” of the sacrifice in faith made by the Hermetically regenerated [APP ¶60]. His words illustrate the contrast between the perfection of the Law of Light and human defection: “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth Thee; therefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes” [APP ¶90].

summary: Cited as a witness to Arnold's conversion of iron bars into gold at Rome.
body: Atwood cites John Andre as testifying that Arnold turned iron bars into gold at Rome [I.1 ¶43]. The source is *in addit. ad Speculum Rub de crim. Falsi*: “Nostris diebus habuimus magnum” [I.1 n52]. Our rendering, not the book's: In our days we had a great [one].

summary: Abbot of Westminster: a long-labouring seeker, misled by the adepts' enigmas, who found enlightenment by seeking Lully; his Testament supports the Lully story.
body: Atwood presents John Cremer, Abbot of Westminster, as an example. He laboured for a long time, was misled by the adepts' enigmas, and found enlightenment by seeking out Lully [I.1 ¶46]. His *Testament* (*Cremeri Testamentum*) supports the Lully story, and in it Cremer openly condemns the king's breach of faith [I.1 ¶47, I.1 n56].

summary: A practitioner who translated Sendivogius as The New Light of Alchemy, with a preface Atwood calls bold and striking.
body: Atwood names John French as a practitioner who translated Sendivogius (*The New Light of Alchemy*) and wrote a “bold and striking” preface [I.1 ¶71]. *French's Art of Distillation* is also cited [I.1 n90].

summary: Listed among the great spirits; Atwood names him as Agrippa's source for the means and principles of Occult Science.
body: Trithemius is listed among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood says that Abbot Trithemius was Agrippa's source for the means and principles of Occult Science [I.1 ¶64].

summary: The Emperor Julian, cited on vital rectification and on Divine union needing assistance; Atwood counts him among the Alexandrian revival figures.
body:
Julian is one of the Alexandrian revival figures (with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Apuleius) who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge and are quoted later [I.1 ¶27].

- From the *Oration to the Extra-Mundane Mother* (*Julian’s Orations II*), illustrating vital rectification: the purified soul receives Divine Light and strengthens its connate spirit, and disease comes from erroneous motion of the spirit. “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature” [IV.3 ¶30, IV.3 n10].
- The Emperor Julian's arguments, preserved by Cyril, support the view that Divine union needs such assistance: “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 n46].

summary: The Hebrew tradition Atwood cites in support at several points: Boehme's agreement with it, the Divine I Am, union with God as Fermentation, and going forth and returning.
body:
Atwood cites the Kabalah consistently in support:

- Boehme's testimony is said to agree “in all particulars with the most ancient Kabalah and profound experimental divinity” [III.2 ¶17].
- The Kabalah supports the view that in the Divine I Am is signified the Substant Unity of all that is [III.3 ¶79].
- Its union of man with God is identified with Fermentation: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27].
- From *Sephir Jezirah*, cap. 1, going forth and returning, with closed-eye meditation, forms part of the final passage into accord: “Egredere et regredere, et propterea pactum praecisum est” [IV.3 ¶60, IV.3 ¶61, IV.3 n28]. Our rendering, not the book's: Go forth and return, and for this reason the covenant is cut.
- The Hebrew Kabbalah is described as “profound yet simple metaphysics”, “partially transmitted”, and agreeing within the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

headword: Kabalistic commentators and mystics of the middle ages; the Rabbis
summary: The Kabalistic commentators, medieval mystics and Rabbis, who Atwood says reached the same ideas as German metaphysics by ontological experiment.
