body: Atwood cites these figures in support: they hold the same ideas as German metaphysics, but reached them by ontological experiment [III.2 ¶29].

summary: Cited, by way of Blackwell's Mythology, on creation as the Divine Will producing itself into material form.
body: Atwood cites the Kabalistic Interpreter (by way of *Blackwell’s Mythology*, letter 7) for creation as the Divine Will producing itself into form out of inane Identity: “the Divine Will, then alone operating, says the Kabalistic Interpreter, produces itself into a material form and recreation” [III.3 ¶43, III.3 n29].

summary: Kabalistic writers Atwood cites in support on the Quintessence, man as prototype, the Abyss as the Matter, uniting end and beginning, and the Law's hidden soul.
body:
Atwood cites the Kabalists in support at several points:

- They name the pure Quintessence “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light” [I.2 ¶16].
- They raise man up as containing the prototype of creation [II.1 ¶42].
- Their Abyss is identified with the Matter, “styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60].
- From *Liber Jezirah*, cap. 1, the completed work unites end and beginning: “Unite the end to the beginning as the flame is united to the coal” [III.1 ¶50, III.1 n55].
- From the *Zohar*, part 3, fol. 152, verso, a view Atwood endorses: the Law's narrative clothes a sublime mystery, its Soul. “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n39].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Kabalists celebrate the White Light as belonging to the Ancient of Days, the primeval Light [APP ¶157].

summary: Criticized by Atwood: his metaphysics stops short of objective realization and never got past the negative margin of intellectual intuition.
body: Atwood criticizes Kant together with Fichte and Schelling. Their metaphysics ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Kant is criticized for never getting past the negative margin of intellectual intuition [APP ¶96]. He is also said to have “saw that”, but the text does not state what he saw. Apparently it is the preceding point about intellect and the Universal Reason [APP ¶117].

summary: An adept whom Atwood cites as having reportedly possessed the Powder; she judges his book weak and his lavishness blameworthy, but uses his verses on the Art coming by grace.
body: Atwood names Kelly, author of *De Lapide Philosophorum*, as an adept who reportedly possessed the Powder, but she judges his book of little value and criticizes his lavishness [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶67]. Elsewhere she cites Kelly’s verses in Ashmole’s *Theatrum* in support of her view that the Art is not obtained by reading or by will: “by grace it is obtained” [IV.1 ¶19; IV.1 n19].

summary: The decisive secret that opens the Mystery and the Art; also, among the authorities, the name for successive numbered operations of the practice and for explanatory texts.
body:
**Atwood's usage.** For Atwood the Key is what opens the Mystery and alone passes its wards: without it the Mystery can neither be entered nor explained, and with it the Adepts' writings become instructive — “If, however, the Key is wanting, how may we presume to enter” [IV.4 ¶32]. She identifies it with Light: “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]. Even holding it does not guarantee more than entry to the vestibule when the texts are scrambled, “even to those who had already become possessed of the true key” [I.1 ¶82]. The Alchemists “delivered many Keys, whereby, as they say, we may enter into the sanctuary of philosophy”, but these do not unfold the first approach [IV.1 ¶3]. She also calls the six texts she then presents Keys: “The six following Keys, delivered into the safe hand of the intelligent inquirer” [IV.2 ¶45].

**Quoted authorities.** Basil Valentine, with Kirchringius and Madathan, makes the key the decisive secret, opening the first and the last gate, so that missing it ruins the whole course: “this key is the principal part of the whole Art; this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last” [III.1 ¶37]. Eudoxus uses Keys for six successive, numbered operations, each ending at a stated point — the First at the whitening of the Stone, the Second at digestion and putrefaction — and placed within works: “the operation of the Second Key of the First Work is ended” [IV.3 ¶5]. He also speaks of the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Keys, and says that whoever knows the Stone and Our Fire has “the Keys of the Art”; the mercurial liquor is “the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16].

The records thus show two senses: a single decisive secret (Atwood, Basil Valentine), and a sequence of operational stages or texts (Eudoxus; Atwood's six Keys).

summary: Held by the one competent to minister, who opens and no man shuts; Atwood does not explain it further.
body: Atwood says the one competent to minister is “he that hath the Key of David”, who opens and no man shuts [IV.3 ¶39]. The text gives no further explanation. Compare the Appendix's “Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97] (see Key to the Work).

summary: In a passage quoted from Hermes, the ferment's action of whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies.
body: Quoting Hermes, Atwood gives the ferment's action — whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies — and Hermes says “this is the Key of the philosophers and the end of their works” [I.3 ¶58].

summary: In the Master's words, the dissolution of the composition by the power of the Water.
body: In a passage given as the Master's, the dissolution of the composition by the Water is named: “when by the power of the Water the composition is dissolved, it is the Key of the Restoration” [IV.2 ¶14].

equivalences.with: Key of the House of David

summary: In the Appendix, entry into the work or into another life, gained when the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life by exstasis.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the entry into the work, or into another life, is gained from the desire of the lower life opening into the heart life by exstasis. She equates it with the Key of the House of David: “The Key to the Work, or into another life, the Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97].

summary: Something “rejected” that regains “her Head place” only after the labours of the Heroic Intellect; the text does not decode it.
body: Atwood writes of the labours of the Heroic Intellect, which must come “before the rejected Keystone regains her Head place” [II.2 ¶29]. The text does not say plainly what the Keystone is.

summary: A pious German adept, author of the *Ampitheatrum Sapientae Eternae*, whom Atwood treats as a main authority on the Azoth, the Stone's virtues, and the practice.
body:
Atwood lists Henry Khunrath among the German adepts, a pious adept embittered by mistreatment; works named include the *Ampitheat. Sapientiae Eternae* and *Magnesia Catholica* [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n84].

**What she takes from him (endorsed).**
- The Azoth as tangible; he received the universal tincture and healed with it, and argued against self-deception: “I write not fables” [I.1 ¶81; I.1 n106]. He cites an ancient author on the perpetually burning ether: “the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20; I.1 n28].
- The threefold secret, separation, no manual labour, the Azoth, and the colour sequence ending in the glorified Stone: “Seek Three in One, and again seek One in Three, dissolve, congeal” [III.3 ¶9; III.3 n3; III.3 ¶19; III.3 n11].
- The adept's discipline: indefatigable labour at his own expense, learning from error, book interpreting book, note-keeping, constant meditation — “What was wrong taught me what was right” [IV.1 ¶29; IV.1 n24].
- A detailed account of the first act and the Second Operation: “In the first act of the physico-chemical works, explains Khunrath” [IV.1 ¶36; IV.1 n29].
- An epigraph (“Enigma”) on a first-second-third transmission that introduces the threefold order: “Omnia in omnibus primum, omni Tertio traditit” [IV.2 ¶2].
- He is named among Adepts linking the work to the Creed, and is her main authority for the Stone's universal virtues, the Azoth and the fermentation with its metal; rightly conceiving the azoth is half the work. “It is the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27; IV.3 ¶28; IV.3 ¶29; IV.3 n8; IV.3 n9].

**In the Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer): he names the preserved principle of body (Caput Mortuum) “‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’”, and Atwood thinks he also calls it Duanach [APP ¶26]. He teaches that the Art perfects the mineral life and typifies the Divine; with Grsaeus he insists on the Stone/Christ analogy, which Atwood defends as “more than pardonable” [APP ¶44; APP ¶46]. She compares him for Behmen's law: “the Enigma Omia in omnibus” [APP ¶73].

summary: In Maria's words, the soul and spirit: two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body.
body: In a passage quoted from Maria, “Kibric and Zibeth (the soul and spirit)” are “the two fumes which comprise and embrace each other in the two luminaries”; they are two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body [I.3 n67].

summary: A figure for the ruling principle: the Rational Efficient, the soul as man's centre, and the source of the soul's faculties, held captive until it is restored.
body:
**Atwood.** In a note, the crowned speaker chained to his mother, who makes occult matter appear, is explained: “By the king, the Rational Efficient is signified” [I.3 n50]. She observes that the adepts keep his secret and “make little or no mention of the king at all” [II.1 ¶7]. In Part IV the soul's faculties are “engaged voluntarily in the restitution of their King”, “for the sake of him who is their source”, who is otherwise held in “an illegitimate thralldom under all”; he is renewed together with his ‘brethren’ [IV.4 ¶20].

**Sendivogius.** The King is the soul in man, his centre, seated in the vital spirit in the purest blood: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10].

**The Hunting of the Greene Lyon** (quoted). The King is the child of Sun and Moon wedded by the Lion: “And yet thys King was begott by none other, But by Sun and Moone hys owne Sister and Brother.” He is fed on the Lion's Blood, dies (paired with blackness) and rises, and is fed with Luna if white, the Sun if red [III.1 ¶65]. The same sequence calls the matter ‘this young Chylde’ or ‘Child’; the text does not say outright that King and Child are the same.

The readings fit together (rational principle, soul as centre, source of the faculties), but the text does not join them explicitly.

summary: Cited in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710.
body: Atwood cites the king of Prussia in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710 [I.1 ¶77; I.1 n104].

equivalences.with: great Law of Light / universal reason

summary: Glossed by Atwood: Hermes means the great Law of Light or universal reason, impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature.
body: Atwood explains it in a note: “By the King’s seal, Hermes signifies the great Law of Light or universal reason”, which is impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature [I.3 n69].

summary: Correspondent in the *Theos. Correspondence*, cited in the Appendix with approval on the physical problem and the Divine Will, but criticized as a seeker who did not wholly convert into the Light.
body: All citations are in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). From the *Theos. Correspondence*, p. 168, Atwood takes the naming of ‘the physical problem’, making the invisible spirit visible [APP ¶93]. From p. 236 she endorses: “the Divine Will makes use of the human voice as an organ for conducting the Light, through the fire”, glossing the fire as our chaotic will [APP ¶97]. From p. 359, said “for de St Martin”: “there is no true government but a Theocracy”, which she calls a great truth but qualifies. She criticizes Kirchberger himself as an intellectual seeker who did not convert wholly into the Light [APP ¶112; APP ¶114].

summary: Cited for alchemy's antiquity, for a Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies, and for a transmutation story.
body: Atwood cites A. Kircher (*Oedipus Aegyptiacus*; *de Lapide Philos. Dissert.*) in support of alchemy's antiquity, and as the source of the Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n2; I.1 ¶7]. His *Mundus Subterraneus* supplies an explicit transmutation story [I.1 ¶77].

summary: An adept and commentator on Basil Valentine, whose Latin version underlies the only good English Valentine; cited on the key and on prayer in the work.
body: Atwood calls Kirchringius ‘the adept’ and his commentaries ‘useful’ [I.1 ¶27]. His Latin version of Valentine, with its ‘admirable commentary’, is the basis of the only good English translation [I.1 ¶61]. She cites him with approval: the key is the principal part of the Art, and “this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last”; its method is called Manual Operation [III.1 ¶37]. From his *Annotations* on Basil Valentine she takes the efficacy of prayer, both in the work and in solving enigmas: prayer as desire plus cooperation, yielding revelation — “even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed, says Kirchringius” [III.4 ¶22; III.4 n24].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited for reference only.
Author of *des Cieux*, criticized by Atwood for an agricultural interpretation.
body: Atwood criticizes La Pluche (*des Cieux*) for an agricultural interpretation [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n3].

summary: Atwood's term for man himself as the true place of the Hermetic work.
body: Atwood concludes that the work's place is man: “Man then, shall we conclude at length, is the true laboratory of the Hermetic art” [II.1 ¶30]; “Man was the proper laboratory of the whole Art” [IV.4 ¶3].

summary: Cited in support of a prophecy's authenticity, since he mentions it without doubt.
body: Atwood cites Lactantius in support of the prophecy's authenticity, since he mentions it without doubt [I.1 ¶11].

summary: A name for the Matter as latent in and about all things, celebrated by ‘the Enigma’; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood speaks of “the alone Laelia Aelia latent in and about all, which the Enigma celebrates as comprehending all” [I.2 ¶34]. The context suggests a name for the Matter; the text does not explain it further.

headword: Land of Promise of the Wise
forms: Land of Promise of the Wise

equivalences.with: the earth made from the mercurial water

summary: In Eudoxus' words, the fertile earth into which the mercurial water is turned, on which the wise make the dew of Heaven fall.
body: Quoting Eudoxus: the mercurial water is turned into an earth on which the wise make the dew of Heaven fall: “An earth admirable is it for fertility -- the Land of Promise of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶12].

summary: A name for the Matter as liquid, equated by the quoted authorities with the sharp vinegar and blessed water, which the alchemical reduction uncovers.
body: In a passage given from Synesius and the New Light: “this Latex is the sharp vinegar which makes gold a pure spirit, seeing she is even that blessed water which engenders al things” [I.2 ¶33]. The Alchemists seek “such a reducation of nature as shall discover this Latex without destroying her vehicle, but the modal life only” [II.1 ¶47]; this passage does not define it further.

summary: Unattributed Latin maxims that Atwood cites in support: only one who has it can give it, and the end depends on the beginning.
body: “Nemo enim dat id, quod non habet.” (ours: For no one gives what he does not have) supports her point that only one who has it can impart it [II.2 ¶29]. “Sie finis ab origine pendet.” (ours: So the end hangs from the beginning) supports her point that the Motive governs the result [IV.1 ¶45].

summary: The union of Altitude and Profundity at their extreme poles, by which the wheel of Life is turned.
body: Atwood: “Altitude and Profundity, being united at their extreme poles, make Latitude”, and by it the wheel of Life is turned [III.3 ¶72].

summary: Cited for reference only.
The intelligible law of reason or soul, whose revelation is the soul's own self; in the Kabalist's sense, the scriptural Law, whose real substance is its Soul.
body:
**Atwood.** The perfected soul, “percipiently included in the circular necessity of her Law, believes its revelation which is her very self” [II.3 ¶46]. The wisely simple are those “who have subdued their will to the Law of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶55].

**The Kabalist (endorsed by Atwood).** The scriptural Law has an outer story that clothes it: “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law”, and each word cloaks a sublime mystery “under the Bark of the Law”. Its real substance is its Soul: “the Soul, which is the basis of all rest; which is the Law itself” [III.3 ¶59].

summary: What the priests forsook when they tried to wield magic power without it, which led to confusion.
body: Atwood says the priests, “having forsaken the law of conscience, attempted to wield without it the rod of magic power”, which led to confusion [I.1 ¶30].

summary: Behmen's law: an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself; the Hermetic Work follows the same order.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Law of Divine Manifestation is expressed in those striking words of Behmen” — an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself. Atwood says the Hermetic Work follows the same order [APP ¶73].

summary: Where, Atwood says, ‘the strength of sin’ lies; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood: “the strength of sin is in the Law of dual generation” [III.2 ¶62]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: The law that exacts exact retribution (‘eye for an eye’) in the spheres of the work.
body: Atwood: “so does the Law of Justice exact retribution in those spheres”, that is, an eye for an eye [III.4 ¶9].

summary: A law that must move through Love in the will; for the Kabalists, the superstantial law from which the world emanates as an efflux of Mind.
body:
**Atwood** (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer): “there is a law of Light, which must move through Love in the will” and act on the will-moved mind; the mind must be subservient to it or become demoniacal [APP ¶9].

**Hebrew Kabalists** (reported): in their Idealism “the whole world was before their eyes as an efflux of Mind, an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. Compare King's seal, glossed as “the great Law of Light or universal reason” [I.3 n69].

summary: Nature's simple and harmonious law, which baffles the operator who brings his own blind purpose; the moral, physical and organic laws are one at the root.
body: Atwood: “The Law of Nature, being simple and harmoniously framed, will baffle him” — the operator who brings his own blind purpose is baffled and condemned [III.1 ¶38]. The Laws of Nature — “the moral, the physical, and the organic are well reasoned, as in their constitutional consequences, apart from each other” — seem independent at nature's circumference but are one at the root [III.4 ¶8].

summary: The voice of Deuteronomy, cited by Atwood to warn those favoured in the work against presumption and forgetting God in prosperity.
body: Atwood cites the Lawgiver (footnote: Deuteronomy 8:10) on the Israelites' suffering for rebellion and the warning against forgetting God in prosperity: “Beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God” [IV.3 ¶57; IV.3 n26]. She applies it by analogy to those favoured in the work, as a warning against presumption; she endorses it.

summary: The scientific laws of the Art, whose study together with the Hermetic records Atwood makes the needed foundation before any trial.
body: Atwood names the “study of the Hermetic records and scientific Laws of Art” [IV.3 ¶54] as the foundation required before anyone attempts a trial of the work.

headword: the learned Rassbi / the Rabbi; Ben Jochai and his disciples
summary: Rabbinical voices cited by Atwood, with endorsement as Hermetic, for creation from nothing understood as from the primitive non-Being, Wisdom.
body: Atwood cites the learned Rassbi (the Rabbi), Ben Jochai and his disciples in support of creation from nothing as from the primitive non-Being, which is Wisdom: “by non-Being they mean that which is neither conceivable as cause nor as essence, but yet is in fact the Cause of causes” [III.2 ¶31; III.2 ¶32]. She endorses the view as Hermetic. A footnote marker (29) at this point has no footnote in the chunk.

summary: The assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; Atwood also invokes purging out the old leaven.
body: Atwood treats leaven as the assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; bodies are “preserved by the assimilating must or leaven” [III.3 ¶23], which makes must another name for it. The old leaven is to be purged: “Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump” [III.3 ¶23].

summary: In Palingenius' Latin verse, the ethereal stone that the worthiest art fashions, forbidden to the profane and granted to few.
body: In Latin verse quoted from Palingenius, the Lepidem Aetherium is the object of the worthiest art, to be fashioned: “Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium, quem scire profanes Haud quaquam licet” [IV.3 ¶55]. It is forbidden to the profane, sought in vain by the wicked and granted to few. Translation (ours): “Ethereal Stone”; the book gives none.

summary: The first, popular grade of initiation, open to all, revealing only the internal life and ending with the soul on the borders of Tartarus.
body: For Atwood the Lesser Mysteries are the first grade of initiation. In them, it appears, the revelations of the natural spirit's first sphere were passed: “passing these, as it appears, in the Lesser Mysteries” [II.2 ¶8]. It was “the only popular initiation open to all” [II.3 ¶3], revealing only the internal life, a field of natural contemplation without rule. It ended with the soul on the borders of the Stygian lake in view of Tartarus: “And here the Lesser Mysteries ended” [II.3 ¶36].

summary: In the mysterious adeptest's words, the lesser world is the father of the Son, or what the Son is likened to; possibly linked with the microcosm.
body: The mysterious adeptest, quoted by Atwood, says the Son is “consubstantial nevertheless, and like his father the lesser world” [III.3 ¶50]. The phrase may name the lesser world as the Son's father or only liken the Son to it. The same passage calls the Stone “wonderfully salutary to the microcosm in universal triunity” [III.3 ¶50], but the text does not explicitly identify the microcosm with the lesser world. Not defined further.

summary: In Agrippa's words, the drink of forgetfulness that is to be cast out.
body: Agrippa, quoted by Atwood: “Cast out the drink of Lethe” [II.4 ¶19]. Lethe is the drink of forgetfulness.

summary: Atwood calls Life the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery.
body: Atwood: “And Life is the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: A secret binding of natures, paired with their magical dissolution, which Atwood says Bacon discovered; not explained.
body: Atwood credits Bacon with discovering “the secret ligature of natures, and their magical dissolution” [I.1 ¶38]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: The hidden, self-multiplying formal Light that perfects matter, is the Form of Gold and the Key of the Hermetic Mystery, and is to be freed.
body:
**Physical role.** An adept quoted by Atwood says “It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied, for this ascends and descends from the first fountain of multiplication and generation” [I.2 ¶8]; once perfected by art it exalts any body in its kind. Atwood makes it the forming, fermenting agent: “Light is the true fermental principle which perfects the Ether in its proper kind” [I.2 ¶44]; “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45]; “the universal magnet of its own infinite self-multiplicative Light” [I.2 ¶48]. Albertus Magnus (via Becher) calls it “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold” [III.2 n38].

**Hidden and to be freed.** “To find this Light, and to free it from captivity” [III.1 ¶11] was the adepts' aim: “the Central Light and Wisdom was all their aim” [III.1 ¶13]. It is “not common Light, but that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30], latent in every kingdom of nature; Atwood asks, “is not Light the true Aurific Seed” [IV.3 ¶30], and calls it the Stone's own metal, its ferment. “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9]; Nature is to “establish a stable monarchy upon her redeemed Light” [IV.4 ¶6].

**Inner and divine.** All Nature is its Efflux [III.3 ¶78]; Thought emanates it [III.3 ¶79]; recreation is “a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], with “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light” [III.3 ¶80]. The practice develops “by rational inquisition of the Light within” [IV.1 ¶18]; “Some have met the Light sooner, some later” [IV.1 ¶17]; one passes “by a living experience into the Light” [III.4 ¶15]. Quoting Plotinus, the soul receives a sudden Light: “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41]; Atwood also calls the magistery “a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37].

**Key.** “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]; Atwood says “we pretend only to have signalized the Light” [IV.4 ¶2], and that she has shown “the golden ore” of it [IV.4 ¶32]; “for those to whom it is addressed the Light will attract” [IV.4 ¶31]. The selfish “have willfully denied the Light its true fulfillment” [III.4 ¶6]; in its vision the philosophers despised gold and silver [IV.3 ¶26]. In the later Appendix (Table Talk), “It requires Light to throw Light upon Light” [APP ¶118]; it is “the light which comes into every soul born into the world” [APP ¶126].

summary: In the theosophist's words, the other principle in everything, the woman's seed, to be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.
body: The theosophist, quoted by Atwood, names “the woman’s seed the light and love fire” [IV.3 ¶38]: the other principle in every thing, which must be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.

summary: What the quintessences lack, so that they resolve and die (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says quintessences “uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23]. Not further defined.

summary: What Atwood says is discovered by inquiring into the substance and practical evolution of the psychical experience.
body: Atwood: “It is into the substantiality of this and for its practical evolution that we must inquire, if we would discover the true Light of Alchemy” [II.1 ¶47]; the “this” is the psychical experience.

summary: In Boehme's words, the Light needed to understand the Tincture, which nature cannot grasp by its own ability.
body: Boehme, quoted by Atwood: “the understanding and capacity is not in nature’s own ability without the Light of God” [III.2 ¶16]. To those in it the matter is plain: “it is very easy to be understood by those who are in the Light” [III.2 ¶16].

equivalences.with: The light exhibited in the Eleusinian msteries

summary: The light exhibited in the true Eleusinian initiations, which they could kindle and fortify.
body: Atwood: “The light exhibited in the Eleusinian msteries, i.e., in the true initiations as is plainly to be gathered from the sense of the ancients, was the Light of Life” [II.4 ¶56], the light “which these could kindle and fortify” [II.4 ¶56].

summary: In Sendivogius' words, nature's own light, hidden by the body of sense, which when it enlightens someone clears the cloud and penetrates inward things.
body: Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood: “nature, having her proper light, is by the shadowy body of sense, hidden from our eyes” [II.1 ¶10]. When “the light of nature doth enlighten any one, presently the cloud is taken away from before his eyes” [II.1 ¶10]; “so far doth the light of nature penetrate and discover inward things” [II.1 ¶10]. The philosophers see all things in it as in a mirror.

summary: The light that flows into and purifies the aerial moisture and re-enters in the Mysteries; Atwood identifies it with the Sulfur of adepts.
body: Atwood speaks of the aerial moisture “before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason” [II.3 ¶29], and of “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts” [II.3 ¶30]. The ignorant scoffer lacks it, and so “without the Light of Reason, would be least of all able to precipitate its downfall” [IV.3 ¶56].

summary: The light kindled by the catholic torch; not further defined.
body: Atwood says the catholic torch “kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]. Not further defined.

summary: Our present life going forth in a line, which must be taken up into a circle back to its first source (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “Our life goes forth into a line at present, it has to be taken up into a circle” [APP ¶48], that is, back into its first source.

summary: The single uniform course of dissolution throughout the work, in one matter and one vessel, which the Adepts also call Manual.
body: Atwood describes “one linear decoction throughout and dissolution by line” [IV.1 ¶3] and “one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9], in one matter and one vessel. It is “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5]. Not further explained.

summary: In the words of the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, the creature whose blood, joined with the Eagle's tears, is the treasure of the whole earth.
body: In the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, quoted by Atwood, the Lion is the other creature; weakened, it bleeds: “The blood of this Lion incorporated with the tears of the Eagle is the treasure of the whole earth.” [III.3 ¶63]. A green and red lion is drawn from the Dragon's body. Not further explained.

summary: In The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the liquid given to the pure matter at each imbibition.
body: The verse *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, quoted by Atwood: “A portion of your Lyons sweate Must be given it for to eate:” [III.1 ¶65], i.e. at each imbibition of the pure matter. Not further defined; how it relates to the Lion's Blood is unclear.

summary: In Eudoxus' words, the liquor hidden under the Stone that contains all the work needs, which has over a thousand names and is the great Alcahest.
body: Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood: “search the source of the Liquor of the Sages, which contains all that is necessary for the work; it is hidden under the Stone” [IV.3 ¶10]. He calls it “this precious liquor, to which the philosophers have given more than a thousand different names, which is in sum the great Alcahest” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether it is the liquor from which the two Mercuries are made is not stated.

summary: Cited for reference only.
What the Quintessence becomes with the Divine light's virtue: transmuting, multiplicative gold, the concrete form of what is valued in dead metal.
body: Atwood: with the virtue of the Divine light the Quintessence becomes “the living gold of the philosophers, transmuting and multiplicative --- the concrete form of that which in the dead metal we esteem” [III.1 ¶49].

summary: The Light which, Atwood says, became known to Solomon together with the mysteries of universal creation.
body: Atwood says Solomon “celebrates the revelation of that Living Light which became known to him” [III.3 ¶49], together with the mysteries of universal creation.

summary: The inner place, guarded by the adepts' equivocations, where the wise raise the Corner Stone and where desire is addressed from the Divine Light within.
body: Atwood: the adepts' equivocations protect “that living temple wherein alone the wise of all ages have been securely able to raise their rejected Corner Stone” [II.1 ¶8]. Effectual desire is “addressed within the Living Temple from the Divine Light within” [III.4 ¶27]. The context suggests an inner place; it is not further defined.

summary: Author of the Essay, cited by Atwood in support of intuition as the highest certainty, though she criticizes his 'sensual system'.
body: Atwood cites Locke's *Essay* in support of intuition as the highest certainty: “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. She also criticizes Locke's 'sensual system', so her endorsement is partial.

summary: An image of attraction and a cover-name: the enlightened see the point of the philosophers' lodestone; Cosmopolite gives the name to the Mercury.
body: Agrippa and Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood, use it as an image of attraction. Man is to “draw and bring them to himself as a loadstone, iron” [II.1 ¶9]. The enlightened man “can behold the point of our lodestone, answering to each center of the beams” [II.1 ¶10] of the philosophical sun and moon. Eirenaeus (“the same author”) prescribes “conjoin to nine parts of our Lodestone” [IV.1 ¶43] with the Fiery Dragon; not explained. Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite gives the Mercury (Our Old Man) “also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. In a passage of unclear voice, “as steel draws the loadstone and the loadstone in like manner turns toward steel” [IV.2 ¶30] is compared to freed Will and Understanding; our loadstone has Salt at its center, turning to the Pole, and our Magnet shows “that Polar Star which our Magnet exhibits” [IV.2 ¶30].

summary: Used by Atwood of those whom Ripley's Twelve Gates edified; apparently an inner circle of the initiated.
body: Atwood says Ripley's Twelve Gates “little edified any without the Lodge” [I.1 ¶64]. The context suggests the Lodge is an inner circle of the initiated, but the text does not say so; other readings are possible.

summary: The Logos: for Philo, the seal by which the world was framed and of which the soul is an impression; for Atwood (Appendix), each man's fundamental faith and the Crown.
body:
Quoting Philo, Atwood gives the Logos as that “by whom the world was framed”, “the seal after the impression of which everything is made” [II.1 ¶43]; accordingly “the soul of man is an impression of this seal of which the prototype and original characteristic is the everlasting Logos” [II.1 ¶43].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood speaks in her own voice of “his fundamental faith, which is his individual Logos” [APP ¶101]: each man's individual Logos is his fundamental faith, to be fermented until it transmutes his whole being. She also identifies it with the Crown: “The Crown, to use Behmen’s and de St Martin’s phrase, is the Logos.” [APP ¶104].

summary: Lord Bacon, cited repeatedly by Atwood: partly as a witness favourable to the philosophers' stone and the ancients' wisdom, partly criticized for mechanical methods and ignorance of the Great Art.
body:
Atwood uses Lord Bacon both as support and as a foil.

**Support.** He reportedly experimented toward the philosophers' stone and recognized its possibility in the *Advancement of Learning*, without condemning the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. From the same work she takes his advice to regard the early sages with more reverence [III.2 ¶33; III.2 n30]. His Fable of Proteus (*De Sapientia Veterum* / *Wisdom of the Ancient*) supports, via Democritus, the principle of torture and restoration — to “torture and vex it in order to its annihilation” [I.2 ¶23] — and is quoted again with endorsement: matter, forced to extremity, runs through all forms and restores itself; he “lays hold of and works upon matter in the extremest degrees” [III.3 ¶61; III.3 n44], which Atwood glosses as the last exigence of life.

**Criticism.** She faults him for proposing mechanical dissolution and for not knowing the Great Art or its subject [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n19]; his “particular digesters applied to the fire” (*Sylva Sylvarum*; *History of Rarity and Density*) would expel the very nature prized [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n20]. His supposition (*Instauration of the Sciences*) that the understanding is too polluted by the fall to reflect total reason raises a difficulty, since introspection would then be useless [II.2 ¶21; II.2 n17]. Finally she calls him leader of the 'exterminating chase' of experimental philosophy, yet notes he recommended the pursuit of Causes and inquiry after the ancients' hidden Wisdom, 'though he knew it not' [IV.4 ¶30].

summary: Lorenz Oken, praised in the Appendix for treating nature 'in that higher way' and for an apparent inspiration into the science of created nature.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood praises Lorenz Oken (cited in a Ray Society edition, London, 1847) as dealing with nature 'in that higher way' and as best evolving Causal Truth into the outward forms of life [APP ¶31]. Elsewhere she says he appears to have had an inspiration into the science of created nature [APP ¶96].

summary: The generative, fallen life, whose desire, opened upward, yields the Key.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of “the desire of the lower life, the generative, the fallen life” [APP ¶97]; this lower life is thus identified with the generative and the fallen life, and its desire, opened upward, is said to yield the Key.

summary: Lucerna Salis Phil., a verse treatise Atwood quotes on the one universal matter (the Sages' salt), the stone, and its dissolution without corrosive.
body:
Atwood quotes this treatise (also given as *Lucerna Solis*, with a note referring to 'Lucerna Salis, from the Latin verse') in support of several points:

- The one universal matter, called the Sages' salt: “A certain thing is found in the world” [I.2 ¶9; I.2 n10].
- The stone, its growth, the Red Lyon and red Sulfur: “It is a stone and no stone, In which the whole art consists;” [I.2 ¶30; I.2 n32].
- The Stone is to be dissolved after the mind of the wise, “Nullo corrosivo adhibito” [III.2 ¶63; III.2 n46] (ours: 'with no corrosive applied').

Elsewhere Arnold, Lully and Artephius are said to agree with its description of whitening [III.2 ¶5].

summary: One of the ordinary mesmeric phenomena, named alongside prevision and community of sense, will and thought.
body: Atwood lists lucidity among “The ordinary phenomena of lucidity, prevision, community of sense, will, and thought” [II.2 ¶6].

summary: Named in a companion inscription declaring that corpse and sepulcher, contained and container, are the same.
body: A companion inscription under the name Lucius Agatho Priscus is quoted to the effect that contained and container are one: “Both corpse and sepulcher the same!” [III.3 ¶66].

summary: Raymond Lully, a confessed adept Atwood cites very often and with approval on the subject, the agent, secrecy, the inner work and the need for divine revelation.
body:
Atwood treats Lully as a major authority and endorses his testimony throughout.

**Witness to the art.** His own declarations are evidence for the England story; his alchemical writings are obscure but numerous and favourable to the art [I.1 ¶47–48; I.1 ¶76]. In the *Ultimum Testamentum* he is a confessed adept of known Christian zeal, with the story of gold for Edward II: “Converti una vice in aurum 50 millia pondo argenti vivi, plumbi, et stannic.” [I.1 ¶39, ¶46; I.1 n55] (ours: 'I once converted into gold 50,000 pounds of quicksilver, lead and tin'). She calls his *Theoria et Practica* one that “appears to us one of the very best pieces of Alchemical philosophy extant” [I.1 n58]. Norton's verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely [I.1 ¶15]; Ripley's verse names him as an authority, as having determined the science true, and as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [I.2 ¶6; II.1 ¶13; III.1 ¶62], and as one who revered Geber [I.1 ¶32].

**The subject.** An apparent contradiction (*De Arte Magna*) is explained: he denies only to a false position of the art [I.2 ¶7; I.2 n8]. The subject is of another nature and needs human art — “Imo argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18; I.2 n17] (ours: 'indeed our quicksilver is a water of another nature') — Hyle, a clear compounded water, a third thing (*tertium*) [I.2 ¶29, ¶31, ¶42]. He agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; a quoted adept identifies his Lunaria with the authors' mercury [III.2 ¶25]. In the Appendix (a later layer) he supports the claim that nature has no pure conceptive vehicle: “The pure matter of the philosophers is not to be found on earth” [APP ¶43].

**Method.** He teaches patient rational inquiry and intimates Reason as a ferment; the golden bough is read as the subtle intellect: “Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intelligendum res intelligibles” [III.1 ¶13, ¶21; III.1 n26; cf. II.3 ¶11] (ours: 'the intellect, having a subtle nature for understanding intelligible things'). He warns against too strong a fire: “Let the heavenly power or agent be such in the place of generation, or mutation” [III.1 ¶55]. The Mercury “comes not but by help of ingenuity, and the Manual operations of man” [IV.1 ¶5]. First principles appear as cloud-like monstrous spirits, which Atwood reads as known from inner self-inspection [II.3 ¶30]. He adds “a sufficiency of the Divine Favour, and books to open the understanding and give it zest for truth” to Arnold's requisites [III.4 ¶20]; after a tedious common process he performed the Solution in nine days by the secret from God, which only God can reveal [IV.1 ¶36, ¶39]. He also charged strict secrecy [I.3 n15].

summary: Cited for reference only.
In Synesius, two lights made manifest, one fixed and one volatile; when the lower rises upon the upper an incomparable Luminary issues.
body: Quoting Synesius, Atwood records that “there are made manifest two luminaries, the one fixed, the other not” [III.3 ¶60]: one fixed (male, below), the other volatile (above, ever moving). When the lower rises upon the upper, “there then issues forth an incomparable Luminary” [III.3 ¶60].

summary: The agent that takes the principal part when Sol is eclipsed, like Isis in the Mysteries; Atwood says it means the first prepared Subject, the Adepts' secret interior Fire.
body:
Atwood writes that, “Sol being eclipsed, the Lunar Vulcan acts a principal part, as Isis in the Mysteries” [III.1 ¶63].

Later she says the Stone is “prepared by those who trace nature with the assistance of the Lunar Vulcan” and explains: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject” [IV.1 ¶29] — also called Diana and the Adepts' secret interior Fire. As 'Lunar Caustic' it needs outward stimulus: “this same Lunar Caustic is brought into act by an exterior excitation” [IV.1 ¶29]. The identity with the first prepared Subject is stated by Atwood herself.

summary: Lully's term, identified by a quoted adept with the quicksilver that authors call mercury.
body: An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (Grasseus, per n26), quoted by Atwood, holds “that quicksilver, which authors call mercury, to be the same with Lully’s Lunaria” [III.2 ¶25].

summary: What Hermes suffered and toiled to obtain; not otherwise explained in the text.
body: Atwood reports that “to obtain the blessed Lunary of Diana, he had suffered much, and toiled incessantly” [III.2 ¶64], of Hermes. The text does not explain the expression further.

summary: Purificatory rites of the Mysteries by which the soul is liberated into a divine condition.
body: Atwood writes that “by the lustrations in the Mysteries, as they describe, the soul becomes liberated and passes into a divine condition of being” [II.2 ¶9].

summary: Cited for reference only.
An image thrown forth, passive and ephemeral, identified with the downward-born nature and with Eve brought forth by Adam.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes an image thrown forth, macrocosmic, passive and ephemeral for want of consubstantiality; its perfect beauty attracts the soul and, united to it, brings the ideal forth as actual offspring. She identifies it: “The macrocosmic image of the microcosm is the downward-born nature” and “It is the Eve which Adam brought forth” [APP ¶18].

summary: An adept who failed for five years and received the key by revelation; also rebuked by Nature for seeking the Stone without dissolution.
body: Atwood cites Madathan (*Mus. Hermeticum*, Lumen de Lumine) as an example: after failing for five years, he says, “I was entrusted with the Key of Power, by a secret revelation from Almighty God” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n41]. She also quotes Nature rebuking him for trying to make the Stone without dissolution: “Dost thou think, says she, to eat the oysters, crabs, shells and all?” [III.2 ¶61].

summary: A voice quoted from Agrippa supporting the view that reason needs divine illumination.
body: Atwood quotes from Agrippa's Third Book of Occult Philosophy: “All is one soul, says the Magian, but reason, unless it be illuminated, is not free from error” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n29], in support of reason's need for illumination.

summary: Magic: an imputation against Bacon, in Paracelsus a natural secret of separation, the 'service of the gods', and in one passage the inward union of the elements.
body:
The records show several uses:

- **As imputation (Atwood).** Against Bacon “the imputation of magic has seemed ridiculous” [I.1 ¶38]; Atwood suggests that reducing it to natural skill may be as wrong as the old superstition. The medieval adepts are called “Magians, who were drawn about the fire of nature” [I.1 ¶39]. Ashmole “exposes certain principles of magic” [I.1 ¶62], and of Agrippa: “there stood the magician at last” [I.1 ¶64].
- **Paracelsus (quoted).** A natural, not specially divine, secret giving entrance into nature: “if that magic then were natural, certainly it was most wonderful, very excellent for quickness of separation” [I.2 ¶25].
- **Plato; Psellus (quoted).** The magic of Zoroaster, whose use is to perfect the soul by the power of materials; the cited view “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51].
- **Its end (voice unclear).** The elements, unless united through the first love, “will never inward and essentially unite; which is the end and perfection of magic” [III.1 ¶50]. Boehme's phrase “bruise that composed magical body” [III.1 ¶48] describes a body that, bruised, becomes 'magical and hungry after nature'.

summary: The key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus to open the Hermetic garden, said to have been lost by the Masons.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of a magic Key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus “to open the door into the Hermetic garden” [APP ¶100], and says the Masons lost it.

summary: A region in which every desire becomes prolific and embodies itself by the ethereal conception.
body: Atwood writes that “every desire is, in the magic region, made prolific” [IV.4 ¶10], embodying itself by the ethereal conception.

summary: Something the Fiery Dragon carries in its belly, in a passage quoted from Eirenaeus; not explained.
body: Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus, per n37), Atwood mentions the Fiery Dragon “which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The text gives no explanation.

summary: The pure earth found at one's own center that commences Regeneration; also the Matter as an earth containing the recreative fire, the Land of Havilah.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood places the magical earth at one's own center, quoting “nascitur in aere terra magica; in aethere clarificatur” [APP ¶89] (ours: 'the magic earth is born in the air; in the ether it is clarified'). She explains that there “you find that which is in the air or the vegetable life, that pure earth which commences the Regeneration” [APP ¶89], in contrast with the mineral earth of the lower life.

Earlier she calls the Matter “the true magic earth wherein is the recreative fire” [III.2 ¶8] and identifies it with the 'Land of Havilah, where good gold is' [III.2 ¶8].

summary: The dissolution which, with human aid, enables the Spirit to leave its extraneous forms.
body: Atwood writes of the Spirit that “Without the magical solution and human aid to fortify” [III.2 ¶61] it cannot leave its extraneous forms.

equivalences.with: the Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone
a fiery form of Light inspisate

summary: The accomplished work or mastery of the Hermetic art, its goal and product; Atwood calls it a fiery form of Light inspisate and a type of the Christian Creed.
body:
Magistery is the adepts' name for the whole work, its mastery and its product.

**Atwood.** Wisdom guards “her universal magistery from an incapable and dreaming world” [I.1 ¶33], and men were “unable to perfect the same magistery” through the philosophers' obscurity [I.1 ¶36]; the word also appears in Geber's title 'The Sum of the Perfect Magistery' [I.1 ¶33, ¶36]. It is reached by communion with the ruling Spirit of nature [I.3 n19]. Man's virtue within himself to prove the Universal Source “was the foundation of the whole Hermetic magistery”, and “without this knowledge no one can attain to the magistery” [II.1 ¶8] — the knowledge of the vessel. In it the luminaries pass “through many phases from imperfection to perfection in the true magistery” [II.2 ¶26]; only those with “this passport can attain to the Magistery of life” [III.1 ¶13]. She defines it: “Which magistery is a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37], made manifest by triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit. The Adepts claim “their magistery not only corresponds, but is in every deed a type, and promise, and foundation of our Christian Creed” [IV.3 ¶27].

**Quoted authorities.** Flamel: “Having this, I easily accomplished the magistery.” [I.1 ¶57]. Geber: “the completement of matters sought after in our magistery” [I.1 ¶76]. Synesius: the soul is “drawn by our magistery out of its mine” [III.1 ¶70; cf. I.2 ¶33]. Bloomfield: “Our magistery is Three, Two, and One --- The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “the knowledge of our Magistery comes rather by the Inspiration of Heaven” [IV.3 ¶16]. An unattributed verse: “Material of our Magistry a substance insensible.” [III.1 ¶7].

summary: A name for the matter calcined by its proper fire, also called lead of the wise; sown in the Philosophic Earth it dies and corrupts.
body: Atwood says the matter calcined by its proper fire “is called magnesia and lead of the wise” [I.2 ¶40]. A quoted scholiast writes: “our Magnesia, continues he, being sown in the Philosophic Earth, dies and corrupts” [I.3 n21], to conceive itself anew. *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* says the old philosophers described its making at large while concealing how to order it afterwards: “To create Magnesia they made no care, In their Bookes largely to declare;” [III.1 ¶65].

summary: In Atwood's Appendix, a will as center of attraction (two magnets in man are two wills); in the Greene Lyon verse, the fair white part left in the midst.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes that “self becomes the magnet” [APP ¶122] and that “There are two magnets in man, i.e., two wills contending for man” [APP ¶124].

In *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* (quoted), the Magnet is the white part left when the matter separates from its black, light 'vile Erth': “Your magnet in the midst wilbe, Of Collour faire and white trust me;” [III.1 ¶65]; it must show full white, and the ferment is put into it as one fourth part.

summary: Used in Atwood's phrase 'the chain of the magnetic series', which moves when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit.
body: Atwood writes that when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit, “the first link in the chain of the magnetic series moves” [III.3 ¶10]. See also magnetic chain.

equivalences.with: ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster

summary: The continuum from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to the darkness of Matter; the ladder of Celsus and Zoroaster.
body: Atwood describes Matter as lying at “the opposite extreme of the magnetic chain, which is extended a non gradu ad non gradum” [III.2 ¶54] (ours: 'from no degree to no degree'), from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to darkness. She identifies it: “this is that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

summary: Apparently the drawing power by which the gold attracts divine increase; the Stone is likened to an armed magnet.
body: The voice is unclear in the record. The Stone is likened to “an armed magnet included and circulating in a perpetual heaven” [II.1 ¶25]; the context suggests magnetical virtue is the gold's drawing power by which it attracts divine increase.

summary: The prophet whose Elijah prophecy frames Atwood's discussion of Elias the artist.
body: Atwood quotes Malachi 4:5–6, “Behold I will send you Elijah, the prophet” [IV.2 ¶12; IV.2 n4], to frame Elias the artist. The Refiner's-Fire messenger passage (Malachi 3:1–4) closes the section without comment [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n9].

summary: Attribution attached to The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, an allegorical verse account of the whole practice that Atwood gives 'by way of recreation'.
body: Atwood gives *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* 'by way of recreation' [III.1 ¶64] — 'in part', though the text is headed as unabridged — as an allegorical account of the whole practice: Green Lion, Sun and Moon, black/white/red, imbibition, ferment and multiplication [III.1 ¶65]. Its opening explains the name: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” [III.1 ¶65]. She does not comment on it there. The attribution to Malden and the label 'Philalethean Lion Hunt' are uncertain from the records.

summary: In Atwood's account, Mammon is the downward-looking spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work astray.
body: Atwood names Mammon as the spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work: “Mammon led them on; mammon that least erected sprit that fell” [III.4 ¶4]. The phrase pictures it as the least upward-looking spirit.

equivalences.with: working upon matter in the extremist degree

summary: A figure that Bacon, writing on Democritus, glosses as laying hold of matter and working on it to the utmost degree.
body: In Bacon's account of Democritus, quoted in the book, the figure carries its own gloss: “manacles and fetters; i.e., lays hold and works upon matter in the extremist degree” [I.2 ¶23]. The text therefore states the plain meaning: working on matter to the extreme.

summary: Cited for reference only.
A collection cited as containing works by Philalethes and Grasseus.
body: Atwood cites Manget's collection as the place where works by Philalethes and Grasseus are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

summary: An author cited from the Astronomicon to support the view that men hold the world within them and are each a small image of God.
body: Atwood cites Manilius (Astronomicon, lib. 10) in support. He holds that men contain the world within them and are each a small image of God: “Quid mirum noscere mundum” [II.1 ¶29; II.1 n28]. That reading rests on our own translation of the Latin, not one the book gives.

summary: A practical technique of the work that Ashmole's notes allude to; the book does not describe it here.
body: Atwood says Ashmole's notes allude to the manual artifice “without much disguise” [I.1 ¶62]. The passage does not describe the technique itself.

summary: The name for the method of using the key (Kirchringius); for Atwood, the literal handwork needed chiefly in the first work, also called the Linear way.
body: The book quotes Kirchringius on the key and “the method, which is called Manual Operation, by which to use it” [III.1 ¶37]. Speaking in her own voice, Atwood says that in the first work “Manual operation is chiefly required” [IV.1 ¶2]. She treats it as the one way of Purification, “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5], and so equates it with the Linear way. Readers took her to mean literal handwork by the operator, but that sense is an inference from context.

headword: manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works
forms: manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works
summary: A verse eulogy, found in manuscript in a volume of Boehme's works, praising Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom; Atwood accepts it with a qualification.
body: Atwood quotes a manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works. It praises Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom: “In Boehme’s wondrous page we view, Discoverd and revealed anew” [I.1 ¶68]. It names the Eastern Magi, Orpheus, Hermes, Confucius, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Plato, Socrates and Epictetus [I.1 ¶68–¶70]. Atwood accepts its praise only “theosophically, but not intellectually” [I.1 ¶70].

summary: A poet whose verse, Atwood says, divulges the artificial method; she says his name means 'one regenerated'. His Zodiacus Vitae is cited on the Ethereal Stone.
body: Atwood cites Manzoli, called Palingenius, in support. She says his verse divulges the artificial method, quoting “Take this Arcadian slippery lad that’s apt to fly.” [III.1 ¶26]. She also says the name Palingenius means one regenerated [III.1 ¶27]. From the Zodiacus Vitae she cites the art of fashioning the Ethereal Stone: “Invenere artem, qua non ars dignior ulla est, Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium” [IV.3 ¶54; IV.3 n25]. In the readers' account, this art is found only after long trial and cost, is closed to the profane and is granted to few [IV.3 ¶54–¶55].

summary: Author of the Defensio Idearum Operaticium, cited on the impress and on a plant born, dying and reborn in a glass vessel.
body: A footnote quotes Marcus's Defensio Idearum Operaticium on the impress and on a plant that is born, dies and is reborn in a glass vessel: “Quid quaesco dicerunt hi tanti philosophi, si plantam quasi momento nasci in vitreo case viderent” [III.3 n27].

summary: A Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, linked with Democritus at Memphis; Atwood often cites her Practica on the matter, the vessel and the order of the work.
body:
Atwood describes Maria as a Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, associated with Democritus at Memphis, whose treatises are extant [I.1 ¶13; I.1 n20]. She cites Maria repeatedly, mostly in support:

- **Matter:** “this science may be found in all bodies”, most easily in matter that plainly holds the four elements [I.3 n48].
- **Order of the work:** Maria illustrates white before red and the rectification of Kibric and Zibeth, which are soul and spirit and the two fumes at the root of the science. Atwood quotes “Take the white, clear, and dignified herb, says Maria, which grows upon the little mountains” [I.3 n67].
- **The vessel:** a divine secret that cannot be done without and is never openly revealed. “Philosophers have spoken sufficiently of all that is necessary concerning the work, with exception of the vessel” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1].
- **Shortness of the work:** Maria is cited for the work's shortness as the reason philosophers say little about it [II.1 ¶14].
- **The poison:** once resolved, the deadly poison becomes productive. “when this poison is resolved into a subtle water, it coagulates our Mercury into most pure silver” [III.1 ¶61; III.1 n68].
- **Latin verse:** on fixing the fugitive and binding it in three hours, “Gummis cum binis fugitivum figit in imis,” given without comment [IV.2 ¶31; IV.2 n20].

summary: Maria's treatise, cited for the vessel of Hermes as the 'measure of thy fire', placed after the Passive Understanding.
body: Atwood cites the end of the Maria Practica, to support or illustrate the vessel of Hermes as the measure of thy fire, which she places after the Passive Understanding: “Istud est vas Hermetis, quod Stoici occultaverunt” [III.1 ¶40; III.1 n44]. The treatise is cited elsewhere under Maria.

equivalences.with: union of Mind and Universe (Mentis et Universi)

summary: The union of Mind and Universe, in which solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether; ancient mythic marriages prefigure it.
body: For Atwood, the marriage is the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the union supersentient, the nuptials sublime, Mentis et Universi” [III.3 ¶15]. In the readers' summary, solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether, and ancient mythic marriages prefigure this. Her figure for it is “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North” [III.3 ¶15].

summary: A verse treatise cited to illustrate that a small quantity of the composition is sealed in one glass.
body: Atwood quotes a line from Book 3 to illustrate that a small amount of the composition is sealed in one glass: “And it sufficeth in one glasse to put” [IV.3 ¶23; IV.3 n4].

summary: Planetary properties of temperament whose dominance, Atwood says, draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood speaks of “People in whom the Mars and Venus property is dominant” [APP ¶113]. She says that in such people the dominance draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.

summary: The tincture that fixes the light of Venus in manifestation; it rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.
body: Atwood says the light of Venus cannot hold “without the masculine tincture to fix it in manifestation” [I.3 n49]. In the same note she says the tincture rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.

summary: Criticized in the Appendix: they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key, keeping an absurd outward form.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood criticizes the Masons. She says they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key. Their outward form is absurd, she says, and survives only through a secret response of common sense to the original mystery [APP ¶100].

summary: The author of the Tractatus Aureus, quoted on the stone generated with Light and on dissolution by the watery Form.
body:
Atwood quotes the Master's Tractatus Aureus twice:

- **Cap. 3**, after her own gloss on Boehme, on Nature's middle principle: “Our stone comes with Light, and with Light it is generated” [III.1 ¶49; III.1 n54]. The stone is generated with Light and brings forth darkness.
- **Cap. 2**, in support of dissolution by Water, fire on the Foliated Sulphur, the King's Tincture and revival: “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n7].

summary: That whose application moves the first link in the chain of vital causes; also the concealment under which the Adepts kept the three operations.
body: Atwood writes: “The first link in the chain of vital causes moves, as we apply the Master Key.” [III.4 ¶47]. She does not explain the key there. Elsewhere she says the Adepts kept the three operations “reserved strictly under the Master Key of their Dilemma” [IV.2 ¶3], so the term also names their concealment.

summary: Only a Master mason can 'erect structures in the air'; in context this apparently means Mind working by its own reflective energy, too hard for inferior craftsmen.
body: Atwood writes: “it is the work only of a Master mason, of Grand Architects, as the Brethren have it, to erect structures in the air” [IV.2 ¶14]. She equates the Master mason with the Grand Architects of the Brethren and says the task is too onerous for inferior craftsmen. The context suggests the image stands for Mind working by its own reflective energy, but that reading is inferred, not stated.

summary: A group voice whose term “benedicta viriditas” Atwood applies to the green or purple vegetative life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood applies the masters' term “benedicta viriditas” to the green or purple vegetative life [APP ¶119].

summary: What the work is done on: all men have it and live by it, but few can handle it.
body: The material is what the work is done on: all men have it, but few can handle it. Atwood: “because all men have the material and live by it” [III.4 ¶2]. She does not identify the material further in this passage. See also Matter.

summary: Atwood's name for the subject whose development her Kabalistic and Greek concordances are meant to support.
body: Atwood speaks of “the development of this Material of Mind” [III.1 ¶71]. She says the Kabalistic and Greek concordances that follow will support it.

summary: For Psellus, the only means of strengthening the soul's vehicle: perfecting the soul by the power of materials on earth.
body: Atwood quotes Psellus, who calls material Rites the only means of strengthening the soul's vehicle. Their aim is “To initiate or perfect the human soul by the power of materials here on earth” [II.1 ¶51].

summary: The celestial instinct that first conceived the tree of life; it alone reveals the tree and leads into the Paternal light of life.
body: Atwood equates Maternal intelligence with the celestial instinct. She speaks of “the celestial instinct only to reveal; that subtle Maternal; intelligence which originally conceived it” [III.1 ¶34]. This intelligence first conceived the tree of life, alone reveals it, and leads into the Paternal light of life [III.1 ¶34].

summary: An unnamed voice quoted in Latin, praising the Creator's laws and foundations.
body: Atwood quotes the mathematician in Latin, illustrating praise of the Creator's laws and foundations: “En tibi Norma Poli --- ! en divae Libramina Molis!” [II.4 ¶30]. The rendering is our translation, not one the book gives.

summary: Atwood's word for the emanation's passage from flat to cubic, in the phrase 'Mathesis becoming geometric'.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood describes the emanation passing from flat to cubic: “It is Mathesis becoming geometric.” [APP ¶66]. She gives the term no further gloss.

summary: That on which the sulphur must return for any effect to be produced.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood says an effect requires “a return of the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life) on its matrix” [APP ¶183].

equivalences.with: Water of our Sea (by rhetorical question)
Thing itself / our Identity / true Hermetic material

summary: The Hermetic subject: one simple substance under all forms, identified with our Identity, known only in the experience and by the Fire of Intellect, not in nature.
body:
**Atwood's main account.** The Matter is diffused everywhere and partly obtainable anywhere, but the aim is to perfect it. In her words, “there is but One Matter truly qualifiable or capable of qualifying matter to be harmonized in this way” [II.1 ¶20]. It is no common water but “an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting” [III.2 ¶7]. She identifies it with “the Thing itself, which is our Identity. This is the true Hermetic material” [III.2 ¶7]. In the same passage it is the power borne by Cheiron, it is Pan, and by rhetorical question it is the Water of our Sea of the old Alchemists [III.2 ¶7]. The Arabians call it Flos Salis Albi [III.2 ¶8]. Readers note that it first appears in vision in demoniacal forms [III.2 ¶7].

**The philosophers' Matter.** Atwood sets out, apparently with approval, the view of these philosophers. Matter is “the Material Principle which, according to these philosophers, the Divine experience imparts” [III.2 ¶51]. It is one and all, everywhere and nowhere, uncompounded, an Infinity, describable only by negations and apprehended by ablative reasoning and negation: “that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity, nor any one of those things, by which Being is defined” [III.2 ¶53]. It is the last and lowest effect, the inverse of the First Cause, yet “somewhat; and real” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it with the Quintessence of Plato, the Water of Thales, the Non-Being of Parmenides and the Abyss of the Kabalists [III.2 ¶60]. “For in the natural world there is no such Matter to be found” [III.2 ¶61]. Life and the Fire of Intellect discover “the True matter of the adepts” [III.2 ¶62].

**Matter (the One).** “The Matter of all things is One and proved simple in the experience” [III.3 ¶65]. It is Nature, “one and the same Unknown Identity through all” [III.3 ¶65], the true element chemists have never found. As non-being, it arises by severance from real being [III.3 ¶77]. When it is sacrificed in the reunion, it supplies body to the Divine.

**Other voices.** The metropolitan of Memphis says “Matter appeared: and inseparable from it attraction instantly began to operate” [III.3 ¶48]. Vaughan speaks of that without which “the Matter is not alterable as to our final purpose” [IV.2 ¶35], namely the sublimations and double nativity. A passage whose voice is unclear says the Matter must be fed leisurely, cleansed and given wings that are held back: “Cause, therefore, wings to be prepared for the Matter” [IV.1 ¶15].

**Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860). “The Matter is seen with the inner eye” [APP ¶162], with agent and patient alternating. In handling it, it flows from the new-born consciousness through the hands to ferment another life [APP ¶164].

summary: For the prince, what is perfected and corrupted; full knowledge of this is the goal of study.
body: Atwood quotes the prince, who makes the goal of study “a plenary knowledge of the verity of perfecting and corrupting Matter and Form” [III.4 ¶20].

summary: A maxim quoted within Basil's passage, where the praise of the science lies in experience.
body: The maxim “Physician, heal thyself” appears inside a passage Atwood quotes from Basil. There, the praise of the science consists in experience [IV.1 ¶2].

summary: Maker of the perpetual lamp found near Alestes, whose urn inscription Atwood cites as speaking of elements digested by laborious art.
body: Named as the maker of a perpetual lamp found near Alestes [I.1 ¶18]. His urn inscription is cited for its line about elements enclosed and digested by heavy labour: “Namque elementa gravi clausit digesta labore” [I.1 ¶19]. Our rendering (by: ours): for he enclosed the elements, digested with heavy labour. Atwood cites it for its mention of elements digested by laborious art.

summary: In an Indian record Atwood quotes, whatever appears or does not appear in the mind apart from the First Cause: the mind's image or delusion.
body: A term from a quoted Indian record, not Atwood's own: whatever appears or does not appear in the mind, other than the First Cause, is to be known as “the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48]. The gloss “image or delusion” is the text's own.

summary: The meadow of Divine Ideas: the prolific power of life and the grasp of the first efficient causes of life and Forms; the Alchemists call it their garden.
body: Atwood, drawing on Plato, says “the Meadow is the prolific power of life, according to Plato” [II.4 ¶16]; she describes it as the comprehension of the first efficient causes of life and of Forms. She identifies it with the Alchemists' garden: “this meadow of Divine Ideas, or Pratum, as the Oracle denotes it, is a place well known to philosophers; the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. So in her reading the Platonic/Oracular Meadow (Pratum) and the alchemical garden name the same place.

summary: In Hermes as quoted, the third product from the Stone after water and gold, nobler than the water with the faeces.
body: Hermes, as quoted, lists it as the third product from the Stone: “the third is our almost or medial gold which is more noble than the water with the faeces” [I.3 ¶55]. The text does not explain it further.

equivalences.with: exalted spirit (the spirit in this life)

summary: The middle or second life, between the mineral and the higher life, reached by dissolving the sensuous medium, through which the third life is raised and born.
body:
Atwood's term for an intermediate level of life. Most records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).

**In the Appendix.** It is the second life: “Dissolve the sensuous medium and you have the second or medial life.” [APP ¶182]. The third life is born “through the medial or celestial life” [APP ¶35], so it is equated with the celestial life. The exalted spirit is “the spirit in the medial life” [APP ¶15]. When life is drawn inward, “the medial spirit is changed; life is attracted in, instead of out” [APP ¶24]. It sits between the mineral and the higher life; the Salt “must be translated or drawn up into the medial life” [APP ¶77], and the heart centre is “the heart of the celestial medial vegetable life” [APP ¶95]. It is also the life in which we ought to be efficient, so as to be efficient for the divine life above us; Atwood equates this with faith: “efficient in the medial life --- in faith” [APP ¶45].

**In the main text.** In the order of the Mysteries, “Close upon the revealment of the Medial Life then, as we take it, in order of the Mysteries followed the Purificative Rites” [II.2 ¶20]; the passage does not define it. Following the Platonists, the generative virtue forms an “intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. Atwood glosses Enoch's wooden receptacles as this life: “the wooden receptacles (the vegetable or medial life)” [III.2 ¶12].

Whether the II.2 usage means the same as the Appendix's second life is not stated.

summary: The senses' own light, in which they are entranced at the start of the practice.
body: Atwood speaks of “entrancing the senses in their own medial light” [IV.1 ¶3] at the start of the practice. The text gives no further gloss.

summary: The middle region of life into which the hidden Sulphur must be transplanted before it can grow and become manifest.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the Sulphur “has to be drawn forth and transplanted into the medial region before it can grow and become manifest” [APP ¶125], and that something follows “When the medial life draws the hidden central light” [APP ¶125]. The context suggests the medial region is the place of the medial life (see medial life).

summary: A spirit whose forms and properties are extinguished in the fermentation; not further explained.
body: Atwood describes the fermentation as taking place “by an extinguishing of the forms and properties of the Medial Spirit” [III.2 ¶28]. It is not explained further here; compare the Appendix's “medial spirit” that is changed when life is drawn inward (see medial life).

summary: In the Lucerna Salis as quoted, the means by which God grants the art: instruction and the labour of the hands.
body: The author of the Lucerna Salis, as quoted, says God grants the art not immediately “but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20].

summary: The transmuting and healing product of the work, the Stone in its tinging form, whose virtue grows with each dissolution and multiplication.
body:
The medicine is the agent that transmutes metals and also heals. Its strength is spoken of as its height or virtue: “the true height of the medicine” [I.1 ¶66]; “the White medicine of sufficient virtue to convert 120,000 times its weight into the purest silver” [I.1 ¶73], also called a tincture in the same account [I.1 ¶73].

**Quoted authorities.** The Lucerna Solis and the monk of the Rosary make it from the salt of the world and call it one thing: “the medicine is one, in which the whole mystery consists” [I.2 ¶11]; “Of it is made that medicine which will preserve you from all maladies” [I.2 ¶10]. The Scholiast says the bodies are reduced into it, it tinges 10, 100, 1000 parts, and “the oftener the medicine is dissolved, by so much more it increases in virtue” [I.3 n38]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon keeps ferment in the fire “That thy Medicine augment mayst aye;” [III.1 ¶65]. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The third gate is the fire which conduceth to the maturity of the medicine.” [III.3 ¶63]; at the fourth gate it is a universal medicine for all diseases. In IV.3 it is the Stone in working form; diluted in mercury “you will have the medicine, though of an inferior order” [IV.3 ¶20]; Vaughan speaks of “the Stone and magic medicine” and calls it “such a subtle moist fire” that only its proper glass can hold it [IV.3 ¶22].

**Atwood.** Philosophers, “when they have obtained this medicine”, did not care to lengthen their days or parade riches [IV.3 ¶48]. She also reports Heraclitus calling the theurgic media medicines: “Heraclitus calls these medicines, as being the help and remedy of imperfect souls” [II.2 ¶5]; these also healed the body.

summary: A mean or intermediary: the precepts demand one between the two; in the practice, the sensible medium released by entrancing and purified; also any means toward an end.
body:
The word carries several senses.

**A mean between two.** Hermes, as quoted: “for the precepts demand a medium” [I.3 ¶23]; “the temperate unguent, which is fire, is the medium between the faeces and the water” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood repeats “for the precepts demand a medium” [III.1 ¶41] as why the two Spirits need each other. Compare “medium and bond”.

**The sensible medium.** Atwood uses it of the mesmeric agent, the photogenic medium. Quoting an adept, one who has the Art “and hath the medium, will be richer than any other” [II.2 ¶18]; the purified principle becomes “the medium of that holy and sublime experience” [II.2 ¶25]. In regeneration “the sensible medium, which in this present birth is dominant, being made occult” [III.1 ¶50]. It is released by entrancing: “the medium in its natural state is volatile, immanifest, phantastic, irrational, and important” [IV.1 ¶4], so it must be purified; there are “many ways of including the sensible medium” [IV.1 ¶5]. In IV.1 ¶7 the word is also used for the means by which the Royal Diadem is extracted.

**A means toward an end.** Aristotle, as quoted: in deliberation “they consider how and by what Medium it may be obtained” [IV.1 ¶30], tracing media back to the first Cause. Atwood applies this: “That Medium, therefore, which is last in the analysis is first in generation” [IV.1 ¶31]; inquiry ends at the medium immediately in the operator's power, and there the work begins. Zachary, quoted: “Mediums nevertheless are to be employed” [III.4 ¶20] besides prayer.

How far these senses are one in Atwood's mind is not stated.

summary: What Atwood says any increase of the Spirit requires.
body: Atwood: “neither is there any increase of the Spirit, as we have already shown, without a medium and a bond” [III.4 ¶30]. See medium.

summary: Improvement: the natural life needs it, and the operator must have its principles in himself.
body: Atwood speaks of “how much such a life is in need of melioration” [II.2 ¶18], and of those “wanting the very principles of melioration in themselves” [II.2 ¶29], meaning the operator must have these principles within.

summary: Reported via Aristotle as holding the One according to Matter; the view is dismissed as rustic.
