body: Known in the text only through Aristotle's report: Melissus takes the One according to Matter, a view dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

summary: A figure teaching the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than words.
body: Atwood uses the Memphian prophet as the teacher of the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than by words [III.3 ¶44].

summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, one of three menstruals; the freed fire appears visibly in the third, which only one who knows the first two can see.
body: Eirenaeus, as quoted, speaks of three menstruals. The freed fire “appears visibly in our Third Menstrual” [III.1 ¶14], but “he that knows not our two first menstruals is altogether shut out” [III.1 ¶14]. The text does not say what the menstruals are.

summary: What 'that water' must be: drawn out of the sphere of the Moon and rectified until it can calcine gold.
body: In a passage of uncertain voice: “Now that water must be the menstruum of the world” [IV.3 ¶21], “out of the sphere of the Moon so often rectified until it can calcine gold” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is not explained further.

summary: In Eudoxus as quoted, the viscous water into which the secret fire's water dissolves; the beginning, foundation and Key of the Art.
body: Eudoxus, as quoted: the water drawn out by the secret fire, through magical union with the dry water of the sea of the wise, “is dissolved into a viscous water -- into a mercurial liquor” [IV.3 ¶16], “a mercurial liquor, which is the beginning, the foundation, and the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16]. It is thus equated with the viscous water. See Mercury.

summary: In Ripley as quoted, said of mineral and metallic bodies reduced to their beginning; apparently 'turned into mercury'.
body: Ripley, as quoted: “Mineral and metalline may be mercurizate” [I.2 ¶6], said of fusible bodies once reduced to their beginning. The text does not gloss the word; the context suggests made into mercury in the philosophers' sense (see Mercury).

equivalences.with: carbuncle of the Sun; clarified Earth
the workman which is in it already

summary: One of the three principles with Sulphur and Salt; in the philosophers' sense the first matter, a living spirit-water, not common mercury, in which the art begins and ends.
body:
**Not common mercury.** The philosophers never teach that “mercury as mercury specificate, can be changed into gold” [I.2 ¶4]. Their Mercury is the first matter to which bodies are reduced: “reduce the body into water, that is, into mercury” [I.2 ¶5], also called argent vive [I.2 ¶5]; it is the root of gold and silver [I.2 ¶11]; “All is in Mercury which the wise men seek” [I.2 ¶12] (Bacon, Rosarium, Geber, Aquinas, endorsed by Atwood). Atwood: “the Mercury of the philosophers is not found of itself on earth” [I.2 ¶49]; it is “the Universal Spirit or Mercury” [I.2 ¶49], also called Proteus and quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; the preparation includes “multiplying the Mercury by its proper Light” [I.2 ¶39]. Albertus calls it permanent water, unctuous vapour and spirit of body [I.2 ¶29]; Lully calls it Hyle [I.2 ¶29].

**Living agent.** The Scholiast: “philosophic, fiery, vital, running” [I.3 n9]; the art begins and “finishes in the same” [I.3 n55]. The adepts call it “the recreated body of the spirit, passive and pure” and “the earth of the wise” [I.3 n29]. After preparation the vulgar Matter becomes “pure, agile, intelligent, living” [II.2 ¶16]. Atwood: it is “the impure vapor of life” that the sulphuric Spirit putrefies [III.1 ¶24]. The Alchemists say it comes only “by help of ingenuity and industry” [III.1 ¶13]; Lully, by ingenuity and manual operation [IV.1 ¶5]. Boehme, Agrippa and Paracelsus' disciples: “the Mercurial Spirit is everywhere” [II.1 ¶9], though not equally extractable from all. Eiraneaus: separating light from darkness seven times, “the creation of the philosophic mercury will be complete” [I.3 n39]. Eudoxus: its whole energy lies in “the fixed salt of our compound” [IV.3 ¶9].

**Identities.** Atwood: in the first conjunction the Spirit predominates, in the second its Light, “which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. Eirenaeus: “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69], the first matter of metals, a water dry. Grasseus: quicksilver, the same as Lully's Lunaria [III.2 ¶25]. The Rosy Cross Dragon: “I am called of the philosophers Mercury: my husband is Gold philosophical.” [III.3 ¶64], also Egg and Light of nature. Eudoxus: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10], first matter and water of metals, white and red, carrying “in its centre its own Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶12]; “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. Sendivogius: the water into which earth is resolved [IV.3 ¶21]. Atwood names it with the Sal Sepientum [II.4 ¶39], and Behmen's Mercurius as “spirit of the Sound” [APP ¶49, Appendix layer].

**In the work.** The adept: it rises “to her superior habitation” [III.3 ¶17]. The author of The Triumph: it is whitened, citrined and fed “with its own blood” [IV.2 ¶6]; the theosophist says it “doth all this itself” as “the workman which is in it already” [IV.3 ¶38]. The bottomless Mercury of Eirenaeus [III.1 ¶19; APP ¶89] is not decoded. Whether the fixed philosopher's Mercury of III.3 ¶32 is the same as Mercury-as-Spirit is open.

summary: Planetary properties to which perception and intuition belong: clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres, weaker in feeling and realization.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood assigns “perception or intuition, which are the property of Mercury and Jupiter” [APP ¶113]; these are clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres but weaker in feeling and realization.

summary: In the Open Entrance as quoted, what is added, three or four parts to one of Perfect Matter, in Multiplication.
body: The Author of the Open Entrance, as quoted, directs adding “three or four parts at most of the Mercury of the First Work” [IV.3 ¶18] to one part of the Perfect Matter in Multiplication. Not further defined.

summary: Listed among the great spirits; his Prophecies are reported to refer solely to Hermetic arcana, and Norton names him among masters who wrote obscurely.
body: Atwood lists Merlin (given as St Ambrose) among the great spirits, and reports that his Prophecies refer solely to Hermetic arcana [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n54]. Norton's verse names him with Hermes, Rasis, Geber, Avicen, Hortolan, Democrit, Morien, Bacon and Raymond as masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

summary: The modern art that uses the same agent as the Mysteries but for inferior ends; Atwood's first key and Door-keeper to the vestibule of antique science.
body:
Atwood treats Mesmerism as a real but external, preliminary form of the same art. It works with the same agent, but “the object was different and immeasurably superior to those proposed by modern Mesmerism” [II.2 ¶24]. In its preliminary practice “the modern art, called Mesmerism, strikingly accords” with the Mysteries and Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

She ranks it as a beginning only: “This Mesmerism, in respect of our Mystery then, may be regarded as a first key” [III.1 ¶8], one that opens only into the vestibule and shows the labyrinth of life, since its practitioners mesmerize one another without knowing how to amend the Thing. “Mesmerism, as it is mechanically practiced in the present day, is a first step indeed” [IV.3 ¶37] before the temple of Divine Wisdom.

She credits it personally: “We allude to Mesmerism: not ashamed, but grateful to acknowledge the neglected Door-keeper” [III.4 ¶13], “the neglected Door-keeper that gave us first introduction to the vestibule of antique science” [III.4 ¶13]; it relieves suffering and offers the multitude a new guide to knowledge and felicity.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The action of mesmerism is a very external way” [APP ¶73]: by vertical passes it loosens spirit from its corporeal media for the moment, an external imitation of the Divine Art of separation.

summary: Mentioned as reviving belief in an Odic Force, which Atwood does not assume, and as having Aesculapius as its only just pride.
body: Atwood notes that the phenomena of Mesmerism have revived belief in an Odic Force, which she does not assume here [I.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she says Aesculapius is its only just pride [IV.3 ¶36]; whether this is praise or a limitation is unclear. See the main Mesmerism entry.

summary: What the soul is said to be: a mesothesis between two spheres, its ultimate perfection.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the soul: “it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres” [APP ¶178]. The term is not glossed; the context suggests a middle position between two spheres.

summary: Something whose breaking precedes the birth of the Elias spirit; not explained.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “When the metal bond is broken” [APP ¶139], the Elias spirit is born. Not explained further.

summary: What Atwood says the soul's angelic essence is.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The soul’s angelic essence is a metallic humidity.” [APP ¶181]. Not explained further.

summary: The perfection reached in metals, belonging only to the primary evolution of life and distinct from the ultimate Divine association.
body: Atwood speaks of “the metalline perfection, which belongs to the primary evolution of life only” [IV.3 ¶27], and warns against confusing it with the ultimate Divine association.

summary: The metallic root, which appears first in the experimental process and is most easily apportioned.
body: Atwood: “the metalline radix first presents itself in the experimental process” [I.2 ¶49], and it is the most easily apportioned.

equivalences.with: ethereal metals; the Ether’s progressive stages

summary: In the Appendix, Atwood identifies the philosophers' Metals with the ethereal metals, the Ether's progressive stages from lower to higher forms.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood states: “The Metals of the philosophers are the ethereal metals; the Ether’s progressive stages” [APP ¶180]. So the Metals = ethereal metals = the Ether's progressive stages, apparently its processes from lower to higher forms.

summary: Atwood's term for the condition, proved by ancient experience, of passing beyond ordinary consciousness toward deification.
body: Atwood speaks of “Such is the condition and metaphysical alienation which ancient experience sublimely proved, as passing to deification” [II.4 ¶49]. The context suggests a passing beyond this life's consciousness; the text links it directly to deification.

summary: Something to be found and made profitable by joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other.
body: Atwood describes the procedure of joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other: “this is the true way and means by which the metaphysical body of gold will be made profitable” [III.1 ¶50].

summary: That which undergoes abyssal regeneration and contest in the intermediate stages before birth into sense perception, and on which the geometric procedure operates.
body: Atwood speaks of “the abyssal regeneration and contest of the metaphysical Embryo before it is born into the perception by the eye of sense” [III.1 ¶56], placing it in the intermediate stages of the work, before anything becomes visible. Elsewhere she refers to “the geometric method of procedure with the Metaphysical Embryo, through its complex parts” [III.3 ¶37], i.e. the circle–square–triangle–circle procedure; the term is not further defined there.

summary: A small, purified, fire-tested portion that re-enters its native life and transmutes the whole into its own Aurific Light.
body: Atwood: “a small grain of the metaphysical ferment leavens the whole lump” [III.1 ¶24]. In the same paragraph she calls it a graft: “the metaphysical graft, already purified and passed the fire, re-enters to redeem its congenital life” [III.1 ¶24], transmuting it all into its own Aurific Light. Leaven and graft are images used for it here, not separate terms.

summary: The one born in the third vessel, triply covered, represented by the birth of Horus.
body: Atwood, discussing the birth of Horus, writes: “even so is the metaphysical offspring said to be involved” [IV.2 ¶11], i.e. triply covered and born in the third vessel. Compare the 'supernatural offspring' that Intellect begets [IV.2 ¶7].

summary: Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood criticizes for reducing the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence.
body: Atwood rejects their attempt to reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence, saying human instinct opposes it [IV.4 ¶15].

summary: The analysis of the Universal Subject: separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord, displayed in Valentine's allegory.
body: Atwood says that in Valentine's allegory “the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis of the Universal Subject is displayed --- the separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord” [III.2 ¶20]; she also inserts “[viz., in the metaphysico-chemical analysis]” into a quoted passage [III.2 ¶19]. These three phases apparently outline the method as she reads it here.

summary: Atwood's name for the Hermetic science, whose 'Fermentation' she matches with the Kabalah's union with God.
body: Atwood equates the Kabalah's union with God with “that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27].

summary: In the Ancient Schools of Divinity, the human Identity's passage out of animal terrene existence through ethereal elements toward the Reason re-entering its First Cause.
body: Atwood distinguishes the common acceptance of metempsychosis, which she says has bred many errors, from its sense in the Ancient Schools of Divinity: “a transmigrating of the human Identity out of this animal terrene existence through the ethereal elements of its original fundamentals of nature” [IV.2 ¶18], toward the Reason that re-enters its First Cause.

summary: A quoted speaker whose cosmogony (Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit stirring the mass) Atwood uses as illustration, footnoted to Blackwell's Mythology.
body: Atwood quotes him: “And know, consecrated Youth, adds the metropolitan of Memphis” [III.3 ¶46]. His account — Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit's breath stirring the mass, and the separation of congenial from heterogeneous parts — illustrates her reading of the work [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶48]; the source is footnoted to Blackwell's Mythology.

summary: Hermetic writer whom Atwood ranks first among those explaining ancient fable by the Hermetic key, and cites repeatedly for emblems and supporting passages.
body: Atwood ranks Maier first among those who explained ancient fable by the Hermetic key, though he was profoundly guarded [I.1 ¶70, I.1 n89; works named: Symbola Aurea Mensae, Ulysees, Septimana Philosophica]. He detailed the whole allusion of the epitaph [I.1 ¶24; n31 gives Symbola Auriae Mensa]. She lists him among writers giving specimens of the preliminary lessons, citing Atalanta Fugiens, Emblem 18, for the gold/Mercury passage [III.1 ¶13, III.1 n18]. His Emblema 21 supplies the geometric symbol of the procedure (circle, square, triangle, circle) yielding the Stone: “Fac ex mare et foemina circulum; inde quadrangulum” [III.3 ¶31, III.3 n21]; Atwood calls it 'epigrammatically symbolized by Michael Maier' [III.3 ¶37, III.3 ¶38, III.3 n25]. She places him, with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Tollius, in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25]. His Emblems support the affinity of body and spirit and the agriculture analogy: “Naturam natura docet, debellat ut ignem” [I.3 n37, I.3 n40]. His Hierog. Egypt. Graec. supports the stripping of the Orient Animal: “Animal de Oriente pelle sua leonine spoliari debet” [III.1 ¶64, III.1 n72], given in Latin untranslated (ours: 'the Animal of the East must be stripped of its lion's skin'). Atwood uses him throughout with endorsement.

summary: Man as the lesser world, comprehending and representing the whole of the macrocosm; the small world in which the work's mysteries are consummated.
body:
Several voices agree that man is the microcosm. Sendivogius calls it “the lesser world or microcosm” and says “Thou hast in thy body the anatomy of the whole world” [II.1 ¶10]; he also says “man, after the creation of all things, was created into a particular world or microcosm” [II.4 ¶39], on account of the fiery rational soul infused into him. Atwood reports the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience: “man is a perfect microcosm, wherein, as it was said, the great world and all its creatures might be summarily discerned” [II.1 ¶31]; “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32] — while noting this cannot now be proved. In the same context Atwood uses “celeberrimus ille microcosmos et Adam” [II.4 ¶39] (ours: 'that most celebrated microcosm and Adam') alongside the hidden Reason; the referent is unclear.

In her own voice the Microcosm is set against the Great World: it is the scene of “the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation” [III.3 ¶33], and the Archetypal Law is “Perfect in the Microcosmic Unit as in the total Deity of the Great World” [III.3 ¶39]. In the Appendix (later layer): “man, being a microcosm, comprehends and represents the whole and each” of the three Lives, its limbs a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶35]; and “The whole image of the macrocosm is formed, and has consequently its typical representation, in the Microcosm” [APP ¶55].

summary: The pairing of individual and universal: the microcosmic experiment yields knowledge of the macrocosmic Cause, and the microcosm's fire continues where the macrocosm's ends.
body: Atwood: “by the microcosmic experiment into It, the knowledge if the macrocosmic Cause also was derived” [III.1 ¶23] — knowledge of the universal is gained through experiment on the individual. She also speaks of “the corporeal fire of the microcosm” [III.1 ¶37], which takes over where the macrocosm's operative fire ends.

summary: Three centers in man: head (animal rational life), heart (celestial medial vegetable life), and lumbar region (inferior mineral life).
body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “There are three microcosmic centers in man” [APP ¶95] — the head, the eye of the Divine and seat of the animal rational life; the heart, of the celestial medial vegetable life; and the lumbar region, of the inferior mineral life. Compare mineral life.

summary: The inner heaven according to whose magnetic virtue the Spirit displays its properties, and where the rainbow-token of reconciliation appears.
body: Atwood says the Spirit displays its universal properties internally “according to the magnetic virtue, action, and passion of the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.2 ¶16]; this is not further explained. By analogy with the sky after storm, “the same beautiful token of reconciliation is made apparent in the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.3 ¶13], i.e. the rainbow appears there.

summary: The life in the individual, which in its natural state resembles the world's vitality taken into the blood by respiration, and needs melioration.
body: Atwood: “the microcosmic life is not dissimilar from the vitality of the greater world” [II.2 ¶18], which respiration takes into the blood; in its natural state it needs melioration.

summary: The inner re-creation of man, whose basis is the will as fire.
body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood says of the will as fire: “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

summary: The tradition Atwood suggests arose from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.
body: Atwood proposes to show “how the microcosmical tradition arose” [III.3 ¶77]: from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.

summary: Cited as a contrast: one who preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god.
body: Atwood uses Midas as a negative example: he preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god [IV.3 ¶48].

summary: Cited in support: their 'refined enthusiasm' agrees with the same divine tradition.
body: Atwood says the 'refined enthusiasm' of the Middle Age Adeptists agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

summary: The specificative form by which a thing is generated as its own kind; the principle in which Nature contains and separates natures.
body: In the grain analogy Atwood identifies it: “in its middle principle, that is to say, in the specificative form” [I.3 n40] — the form by which a thing is generated as its own kind. Nature is addressed as that “which containest and separatest natures in a middle principle” [I.3 ¶33]; the Master, quoted, has “which containest and separatest all things in a middle principle” [III.1 ¶49]. So = specificative form.

summary: Poet quoted from Paradise Lost to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.
body: Atwood quotes Milton (paradise Lost, 1:676): “That riches grow in hell” [II.3 ¶35, II.3 n41], to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.

summary: The divine in man, identified with God and Poemander; for Atwood the true Separator, the efficient and regimen of the work, and the Key of the Hermetic Enigma.
body:
Quoted Hermetic voice: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; Atwood seeks entrance to “the shut palaces of Mind” [II.1 ¶53]. In Hermes' account Poemander says “I am, quoth he, Poemander, the Mind of the Great Lord” [III.3 ¶52] and “I am that Light, the Mind, they God” [III.3 ¶54]; and “That which, in thee, seeth and heareth the Word of the Lord, and the Mind, the Father, God, differ not one from another” [III.3 ¶54]. Mind is always present, comes into the holy and pure, and is “the Porter and Door-keeper” against evil works [III.3 ¶57]. So, per Poemander, Mind = Poemander = Light = God the Father = Porter and Door-keeper. The Rabbi in the Zohar says the articulate voice proceeding from Spirit “comes from the Mind” [III.3 ¶78].

In her own voice, Atwood: “we observe Mind to be the true Separator, the efficient as well as the regimen of the work” [III.1 ¶21]; nothing foreign enters it. And: “Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48]; “no sooner does it attain to Self Knowledge, by proper inquiry within” than the Efficient acts outward [IV.1 ¶48].

summary: That from which the quintessence is drawn by the magistery; not glossed.
body: Quoted from Synesius / the New Light: the quintessence is “drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]. The term is not glossed; the context shows only that it is that from which the quintessence is drawn.

equivalences.with: third life; lowest life in man
mineral soul; lowest form of life in us

summary: The third and lowest life in man, which the Hermetic Art perfects; it contacts the macrocosmic mineral life and first appears in introspection as a dark vapour.
body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “The third life, the mineral or lowest life in man” [APP ¶59]; “The Vegetable and Animal lives are higher than the mineral life in us.” [APP ¶59]. The Art is “a perfectioning of the third or lowest or the mineral life in man” [APP ¶44]. It brings one into contact with the Macrocosmic mineral life and is first seen by introspection as a dark vapour. Identity: “The mineral soul or the lowest form of life in us” [APP ¶71] — so = mineral soul. Compare microcosmic centers (lumbar region).

equivalences.with: true mater of the Hermetic Art

summary: What is carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury: the root and true matter of the Hermetic Art.
body: Atwood: “the mineral radix and true mater of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶19], carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury. So = the true matter of the Art.

summary: The inner 'secret chamber' guarded by horrors and phantoms.
body: Atwood speaks of horrors and phantoms “guarding the secret chamber of their mineral soul” [II.3 ¶29]. In the Appendix the mineral soul is identified with the lowest form of life in us (see mineral life).

summary: The Spirit that acts without intervention or concealment throughout the work.
body: Atwood: “without intervention or concealment in the ministering Spirit throughout” [III.4 ¶9]. The 'highly effective agent' springing from ourselves, mentioned directly after, apparently refers to it (inferred). Whether 'the Spirit' that some were “compelling the Spirit to their private ends” [III.4 ¶6] is the same is not stated.

summary: In Norton, the assistants who carry on the work, with stated moral and practical qualifications, numbers and conduct.
body: Quoted from Norton: “When ye can finde apt Ministers” [III.4 ¶37]; “Noe Minister is apt to this intent But he is sober, wise, and diligent” [III.4 ¶37]. Norton sets out their qualifications, numbers and conduct.

summary: In Atwood's words, the Word that contains the two catholic natures, the changeable and the immutable.
body: Atwood speaks of “the two catholic natures contained in the mirific Word” [III.2 ¶24]. From the context of her record, these two natures are the changeable and the immutable. The text gives no further definition here.

summary: In the Alchemists' teaching as reported, the part of nature that the reduction destroys, as distinct from her vehicle.
body: This is a view reported from the Alchemists. The modal life is what the reduction destroys, as opposed to nature's vehicle. The context suggests it is her superfluous forms, since nature is said to be addressed “where nature may be addressed in order to the rejection of her superfluous forms” [II.1 ¶47]. That equation is an inference, not the text's own statement.

summary: An unnamed modern adept whom Atwood cites to support her claim that hiding the truth let ignorance spread.
body: Atwood cites an unnamed modern adept in support of her point that concealment spread ignorance: “this bushel being placed over the light, the darkness of it invited ignorance abroad” [I.1 ¶64]. She endorses the view.

summary: Unnamed modern interpreters whom Atwood criticizes for explaining the lights of the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy.
body: Atwood rejects the reading of unnamed modern interpreters (“as some say”) who explain the lights shown in the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy [II.3 ¶49].

summary: Modern metaphysicians, whom the Appendix contrasts with its own view because they make Time a condition of thought.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), modern metaphysicians are set in contrast because they make Time a condition of thought [APP ¶172].

summary: Modern metaphysics, which Atwood contrasts with her own view because it treats mind as only abstract or inferential.
body: Atwood sets modern metaphysics against her own position because it treats mind only as abstract or inferential [III.1 ¶2].

summary: The moderns and empirical chemists, whom Atwood criticizes: their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean.
body: Atwood criticizes the moderns and empirical chemists. Their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean, “as the empirical chemists formerly imagined” [I.2 ¶39; I.2 ¶43].

summary: The fire the matter is to be boiled in, named in Hermes' precept and not explained at that point.
body: Hermes' precept, which Atwood repeats, says: “Put the matter into a moist fire” [I.3 ¶10]. The moist fire is the fire the matter is boiled in. The passage does not explain it: the nature, origin and “artificial excitation” of the philosophic fire are put off until later.

summary: In the Poemander, what the descending darkness turns into: an unspeakably troubled moist nature that gives off smoke, with Light before it.
body: Hermes speaks in the Poemander. The descending darkness changes into “a certain moist nature unspeakably troubled, which yielded a smoke, as from fire” [III.3 ¶53]. It is “that moist nature, that appeareth out of the darkness”, and the Light is before it. When the Word joins Nature, pure fire flies upward out of it [III.3 ¶54].

summary: In Vaughan's warning, natures that rise against the central fire when excess heat provokes them.
body: Vaughan warns that too much heat provokes the moist natures: “thou hast stirred up the wrath of the moist natures, and they will stand up against the central fire” [III.4 ¶44]. This is a caution about managing the fire.

summary: Venus's spirit, to which metalline bodies cling so that it may give them life.
body: In a footnote, Atwood says metalline bodies cling to Venus's moist spirit so that it can give them life: “they gladly adhere to this moist spirit, that it may vivify them” [I.3 n49].

summary: The simple unity to which the Ternary is reduced, Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, and man is reduced in union with God.
body: Atwood treats the Monad as the simple unity at the end of the reduction. The Ternary is reduced, and Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, “to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18]. She also speaks of “the Monadic simplicity of her Element” [IV.2 ¶20]. In the Chaldaic oracle she cites, the (Paternal) Monad generates Two and rules the Triad: “The Monad is enlarged which generates Two,” [IV.2 ¶22]. Discussing the Kabalah, she cites the union it describes, “the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27]. On this reading, reducing man to the Monad and reducing Nature to it seem to be the same aim. The text sets the two passages side by side but does not state that link.

summary: The ordered state in which the renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord under Light.
body: Atwood uses the phrase for the outcome of renewal. The renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord “to testify and maintain the triumphant Monarchy of Light” [IV.4 ¶20].

summary: The monk who wrote the Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv), cited for the teaching that Stone and medicine are one.
body: Atwood cites the monk in his Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv) in support of the teaching that the Stone and the medicine are one, with nothing added or taken away: “The Stone is one” [I.2 ¶11; I.2 n11]. She endorses it.

summary: The monks, whom Atwood criticizes for promoting Agrippa's Vanity as if it were a recantation.
body: Atwood criticizes the monks for promoting Agrippa's Vanity as a recantation [I.1 ¶64].

equivalences.with: ethereal light / passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven

summary: The passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven: in Atwood's account the Passive Intelligence, paired with the Sun, and named by many authorities in veiled forms.
body:
**Atwood's statements.** In Alchemy “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40]. With the Sun, it is one of the pair that “sound the depths together”. Citing Plutarch, she writes that “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason, and to proceed from Wisdom” [III.1 ¶45]. She also reports that Boehme finds Sol and Luna together at the cross.

**Hermes, glossed by Atwood.** “Luna after fifteen days is diminished; and in the third, she is augmented” [I.3 ¶7]. Atwood explains this Luna as “that ethereal light, which is the passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven” [I.3 n7]. Its waning and waxing match the moon's, and the philosopher names it after the moon by analogy. Elsewhere Hermes says: “My own Luna, also, is my light, exceeding every other light” [I.3 ¶37]. This is the Stone's own light, and it is not explained further.

**Other quoted authorities.**
- *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*: the Moon is sister and bride of the Sun, born with him in the Lion's Bed, and with him a parent of the King. Luna holds parallel positions in the poem. She is fed to the Lion with Sol and worked alone with the Lion's blood, “Worke Luna by her selfe alone, With the blood of the Greene Lyon:” [III.1 ¶65], for the white ferment, and she feeds a white King. The passage does not assert that Luna and the Moon are identical.
- Eirenaeus: when the soul imprisoned in Saturn is set free, a shining vapour arises, “A Vapour shining, like pearl orient, Which is our Moon and sparkling Firmament” [III.1 ¶69]. Elsewhere he pairs Sol and Lune as what projection produces: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” [IV.3 ¶25]. The next line says they will prove both gold and silver pure.
- The author of the New Light: “our lune or silver, not common silver” [I.3 n40], which receives the seed of gold.
- Pierce, the Black Monk, names Lune among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].

Asserted identities: Moon = Passive Intelligence [III.1 ¶40]. Luna = the ethereal light or passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven [I.3 n7]. Moon = the shining Vapour and sparkling Firmament (Eirenaeus) [III.1 ¶69]. Lune = silver, not common silver (New Light) [I.3 n40].

summary: In Vaughan, a middle Nature that is placed equally within two elements in the vital heat-operation.
body: Vaughan, as quoted, gives the instruction: “take the Moon of the Firmament, which is a middle Nature” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the vital heat-operation it is placed equally within two elements. He asserts its identity with a middle Nature in the same place.

summary: The author of Centrum Naturae Concentratum, cited for the claim that man is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature.
body: Atwood cites the Moorish philosopher (Centrum Naturae Concentratum) in support of the claim that man himself is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature. The cited passage speaks of what “contains not so great mysteries and excellences as Man reformed by God into his image” [II.1 ¶9; II.1 n3]. She endorses this.

summary: Unnamed observers whose testimony Atwood cites: very few people are naturally suited to the research.
body: Atwood relies on the testimony of more experienced observers that very few people are naturally suited to the research [III.4 ¶2].

headword: the more modern class of adepts
forms: the more modern class of adepts
summary: Later adepts whom Atwood cites for the view that man's life is a fire capable of improvement.
body: Atwood cites the more modern class of adepts in support of the view that man's life is a fire capable of improvement: “a pure, naked, and unmingled fire of infinite capability” [II.1 ¶17].

summary: An unnamed experimentalist cited for the sign of the Arcanum: the masculine tincture rising from the black and uniting with the white spirit.
body: In a footnote, Atwood cites a more modern experimentalist. When the masculine tincture rises from the black and unites with the white spirit, the operator “will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53].

summary: An adept who taught King Calid. Atwood cites him often for the teaching that the matter is taken from man himself, and on the operation.
body:
**Story.** Morienus was the disciple of an adept, Adfar, and later initiated King Calid. Their dialogue is cited as *Morienus Eremita Hierosol. De Transfiguratione Metallorum* [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n38]. Atwood says his biographer's story is too long to extract.

**The matter.** Atwood takes his advice to Calid as pointing to the matter being taken from man: “This matter, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1] and “The thing, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶16; II.1 n15]. She says Sendivogius diverted this hint. Morien also supports her vessel and place doctrine [II.1 ¶8], and he is counted among the authorities who agree about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**The operation.** “Our operation, concludes Morien, is nothing else but extracting water from the earth and returning it again” [IV.1 ¶41; IV.1 n36]. This is an alternating extraction and return of moisture that leads to putrefaction. Atwood then glosses it as action and reaction.

**Other uses.** As cited by Eirenaeus, he warned Calid that many philosophers were overcome by the fatigue of this work [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5]. He supports the teaching that the magistery is God's secret of secrets, entrusted to the prophets: “Scire etiam tibi convenit, O bone rex” (ours: It is fitting also for you to know, O good king) [II.4 ¶39; II.4 n27]. Norton's verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely, “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Atwood uses him mainly as a supporting authority.

summary: The unnamed writer of Morienus's story, which Atwood mentions but finds too long to extract.
body: Atwood mentions that Morienus's biographer tells his story, but she judges it too long to extract [I.1 ¶35].

summary: Putting the matter to death as a necessary step of the work. For Atwood, it is the death of the fiery self-willed agent once it is ripe.
body: Hermes makes mortification necessary, together with generation: “except one understandeth how to mortify and induce generation” [I.3 ¶26]. That is, the matter must be put to death through its proper nature. Atwood applies the term to the fiery, self-willed agent. It grows to its full extent “until the time for his mortification is ripe and ready at hand” [III.1 ¶56]. The connate spirit then finally brings the agent to this death, so it becomes a self-mortification.

summary: The Mosaic Scripture. Some learned writers held it to be the only revealed truth; Atwood would still revere it if all cosmogonies share one divine source.
body: Atwood reports that some learned writers judged that “the Mosaic was the only revealed truth of all” [III.3 ¶42]. She qualifies this view. If all cosmogonies share one divine source, she would still revere Scripture.

summary: A figure whom Atwood cites as one who taught under a veil and whose legitimate power she sets against the Egyptians' enchantments.
body: Like Hermes, Moses gives his instruction under a veil [I.3 n40]. In the Apostle's text she quotes, the Law is read under a veil: “when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart” [III.3 ¶59]. Atwood compares him on the waters: those on which the Spirit of God moved are not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He appears with Ezekiel, David and Zachariah as illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. Boehme names him with the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles as teaching what Boehme finds in his inner book [III.2 ¶16]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Moses' legitimate power under God's law, “might in word and deed”, is set against the Egyptians' enchantments [APP ¶2; APP ¶4].

summary: Philosophers whom Atwood cites in support of the difference between common and natural calcination.
body: Atwood appeals to the most enlightened philosophers in support of the difference between common and natural calcination [IV.3 ¶16].

summary: The great mystery in which, Atwood says, we stand even now.
body: Atwood writes: “And so far we stand even now in the great mystery, in the Mother of all beings” [III.3 ¶52]. The passage does not define the term further.

summary: Something Atwood expects to come forth in the Fourth Monarchy; the text does not define it further.
body: Atwood looks ahead to a time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth” [IV.3 ¶49], in the Fourth Monarchy. The term is not defined further.

summary: The operator's motive, which Atwood calls the true spiritual ferment: everything depends on it, and the Work truly begins only when the right Motive is found.
body: For Atwood, the Motive is decisive: “Everything depends upon the Motive, which is the true spiritual ferment” [IV.1 ¶44]. The result corresponds to the virtue of the Motive, and the Work truly begins only then, since “it is not until the right Motive is discovered” [IV.1 ¶48]. She identifies the Motive with the spiritual ferment [IV.1 ¶44].

summary: An expression Atwood uses once, for the purpose towards which conviction is steeled. The text does not define it further.
body: Atwood speaks of “conviction steeled to the purpose of her Motive Light” [IV.4 ¶19]. The record gives no further definition.

summary: Atwood's term for man's life, set against man seen as the individualized multiplication of a blind will.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “tat Motive Reason which is his life” [II.1 ¶42], so she identifies Motive Reason with man's life. She sets it against man as the individualized multiplication of a blind will [II.1 ¶42].

summary: A Latin motto cited in support of the First Matter as the one substance God created in the beginning.
body: The motto is cited (QUOTED) in support of the First Matter as the single substance God created: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, Creavit unam substantiam, Hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶56]. Our translation, which the book does not give: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. The same sentence also stands as the epigraph credited to Mylius [III.2 ¶2].

summary: Flammel's seven-fold mountain, with a royal herb at its top. Atwood equates it with several other symbols: Esdras's outgoings of paradise, Sendivogius's Planetary Sphere and the Sapphiric Mine's tincture.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes Flammel's seven-fold mountain, at whose top a royal herb is found [II.4 ¶9]. She then equates it with other names: “Those seven mystic mountains, whereupon grow the roses and lilies, are the outgoings of paradise mentioned in Esdras” [II.4 ¶9]. She adds “and the Planetary Sphere of Sendivogius” and “and that most famous tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [II.4 ¶9]. So the text treats these as several names for one thing. It does not state the plain meaning.

summary: In Proclus and the Phaedrus passage, the second grade of vision. It is seeing stable appearances with closed eye, through the pure soul, and comes through silence imparted by faith.
body: This term comes from quoted voices, not from Atwood. In the passage from Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus), muesis is the second grade: “But we view with closed eye, i.e., with the pure soul itself (muoumetha) entire and stable appearances” [II.4 ¶23]. These appearances come through the connective gods [II.4 ¶23]. Proclus (QUOTED) says that “muesis, in short, is neither through intelligence nor judgment, but through the uncial silence imparted by faith” [II.4 ¶40], so faith is named as its cause. The text gives no further definition.

summary: Increasing the finished Stone or Medicine without limit by repeating the same operation: dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Atwood also uses it of frauds' promises and of Light's assimilative virtue.
body:
Most records come from quoted authorities. Several describe it as the stage after the Stone is made, when its virtue is increased.

- Norton speaks of the Red Stone: “Him to increase in multiplication” [I.1 ¶60].
- Paracelsus says the tincture stays “immutable in the multiplication” [I.1 ¶76].
- *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* says the Medicine is increased without restarting the work, best by continual fermentation: “It’s so well Multeplied as with continuall Firmentation:” [III.1 ¶65].
- The fraternity of the Rosy Cross makes it the fourth gate, together with augmentation: “The fourth gate is that of multiplication and augmentation in which proportions and weights are necessary.” Reaching this gate gives a universal medicine [III.3 ¶63].
- Eudoxus makes it the Sixth Key, “the Multiplication of the Stone, by the reiteration of the same operation”, which raises its virtues without limit [IV.3 ¶16].
- The Author of the Open Entrance writes: “It remains only for the work of Multiplication” [IV.3 ¶18]. He describes joining the Stone with Mercury of the First Work, then dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Each round multiplies its virtue and goes faster [IV.3 ¶18].

A footnote of unclear voice describes the same repeated dissolution and coagulation by the water of the medicine's mercury, which raises its tinging virtue. It also says that “the multiplication of its internal form has rubified it” [I.3 n67].

Atwood herself (ATWOOD) uses the word in two other ways. First, frauds cheated merchants out of gold, silver and gems, “which they lost, in vain hope of getting them multiplied” [I.1 ¶55]. Second, she makes multiplying a property of Light alone: “Or what else should possibly transmute or multiply by its own assimilative virtue?” [IV.3 ¶30].

summary: The purely mineral goal to which many gave up their lives. Atwood contrasts it with the art's higher purposes.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes those “sacrificing their whole life’s hope to the multiplication of gold” [I.1 ¶42]. She treats it as a merely mineral aim, set against the higher purposes of the art.

summary: The universal Spirit as it is first consciously revealed in humanity's receptive life. It can receive anything and be converted to anything, and it is equated with Aristotle's passive intellect.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the universal Mundane Spirit, as it is at first consciously revealed in the recipient life of humanity” [II.2 ¶17]. She says it can receive anything and be converted to anything. She equates it with what Aristotle names: “which Aristotle, in his Metaphysics, calls passive intellect” [II.2 ¶17].

summary: Purified or cleansed. The Spirit's mundification must be completed “in both kinds” before the Philosophic Work truly begins.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. In context the word apparently means purified. She also says the Philosophic Work does not truly begin “until the mundification of the Spirit is completed in both kinds” [IV.1 ¶48]. The text does not say what the two kinds are.

summary: The person addressed in an Orphic fragment as “offspring of the bright Silene”.
body: Musaeus appears only as the addressee of the Orphic fragment cited at [II.4 ¶40], where he is called the offspring of the bright Silene.

summary: A term used once for what appeared during the evaporative process of purification. What exactly it refers to is unclear.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “And that such actually appeared to be the Musai, during the evaporative process of purification” [II.3 ¶22]. This comes in connection with the material images seen during that purification. The text does not make clear whether the Musai are those images or something else.

summary: A collection Atwood cites as containing works by Philalethes and the Water Stone.
body: Atwood cites this collection as the place where works by Philalethes and the Water Stone are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

summary: The Greeks' name for the aspirants, whom the Hierophant passed on to the immortal abode.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) gives Mustai as the Greek name for the aspirants: “the aspirants, by the Greeks called Mustai” [II.3 ¶36]. The Hierophant passed them on to the immortal abode [II.3 ¶36].

summary: Norton's master, quoted inside Norton's verse as revealing the secret that the vessel is glass.
body: Inside Norton's verse, his “good Master” is quoted (QUOTED) as revealing that the vessel is glass: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset” [III.4 ¶31]. Our translation, which the book does not give: If God had not given us the vessel, he would have given nothing.

summary: Author cited for the epigraph saying that God created one substance, the first matter.
body: Mylius (QUOTED), *Phil. Reform.*, Pars. VI, Lib. 1, gives the epigraph: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶2]. Our translation: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. Atwood uses it in support of the one First Matter. The same words are cited again as a motto at [III.2 ¶56].

summary: The initiates who, according to the expounders, were given narcotic liquors before the shows.
body: This is the expounders' view (QUOTED: the expounders), which Atwood reports. They say narcotic liquors were given “which were administered to the Mystae before the shows commence” [II.4 ¶56].

summary: The initiates whose inner experience, Atwood says, the Neo-Platonists did not make public.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says: “It was not their practice to declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi” [APP ¶122]. “Their” refers to the Neo-Platonists.

summary: A French treatise Atwood cites in support of the conjunction of Mars and Venus yielding solar sulphur, repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear, and the magnetic work.
body: Atwood cites *Mystere de la Croix*, chap. 13 (spelled 'Mystere de la Crois' in n10), in support of three points. The first is the conjunction of Mars and Venus, which yields a solar sulphur. The second is repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear. The third is that the work is magnetic: “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶11; III.3 n4; III.3 ¶18; III.3 n10]. Our translation: This work is called Magnetic. She uses it as support for her own view.

summary: The ancient initiatory rites, Ethnic and Christian, held at Eleusis and in Eastern temples. Atwood treats them as real, scientific inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.
body:
Atwood (ATWOOD) treats the Mysteries as real and effective, not as ceremony. They were initiatory rites, “both Ethnic and Christian”, that kept a secret apart from ordinary worship: “There was undoubtedly a secret, hanging about these celebrations, both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]. Their object was Ontological Wisdom, and they really obtained it [II.2 ¶5].

She holds that “the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries, celebrated in the Eastern temples and by the priests at Eleusis, were real and efficacious” [II.2 ¶24]. Their stages ran in order: revealment of the Medial Life, Purificative Rites, then final initiations [II.2 ¶24]. They worked a vital change in those who sought wisdom and immortality, and “the conduct of the Mysteries was uniform and entirely scientific” [III.1 ¶9].

In them, apparitions come before divine illumination, “wherein the consciousness, becoming artificially wrapped by the Mysteries” is held in Hades [II.3 ¶29]. She reads the Rosicrucian letter as describing a passage of initiatory progress within them [II.3 ¶29]. A passage of unclear voice speaks of Intellect “descending into the bosom of the Mysteries” when it perceives the Formless Subject [III.2 ¶55].

Historically, “Necessity, at length, compelled an abandonment of the Mysteries” after the fall of Alexandria, along with the banning of Theurgic rites [I.1 ¶30]. Synesius “was careful, however, to protect the mysteries of his religion from vulgar abuse” [I.1 ¶27]. Yet “the Mysteries of Antiquity changed their form only to appear more resplendent when Christianity came to be the prevailing religion” [IV.2 ¶17]. In Christianity they took the form of effectual baptismal regeneration and the Eucharist [IV.2 ¶17].

Atwood asks that the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest be understood “not as mere external ceremonials, pictured scenes of suffering and beatitudes, but as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source” [IV.4 ¶5]. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

summary: The Mysteries cited as a voice. They call Isis Athena, and their mandate forbade telling the revelation to the profane.
body: Atwood cites the Mysteries twice. In them Isis is called Athena, which expresses the Spirit's self-motion and intelligence [III.1 ¶63]. Their mandate forbade passing the revelation on to the profane [III.2 ¶46].

summary: The mysteries and their wise hierophants, cited to show that the mind must leave all images behind to perceive Divinity.
body: Atwood cites the mysteries and the wise hierophants as an illustration. The Aspirant leaves the statues behind to behold the Adytum, and this shows the mind leaving all images; it is “the order in which Divinity is perceived” [III.2 ¶66].

headword: Mysteries celebrated at Eleusis and the rest
forms: Mysteries celebrated at Eleusis and the rest
summary: The Eleusinian and other Mysteries, which Atwood reinterprets as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.
body: Atwood reinterprets the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, not as external ceremonies. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5]. See also Mysteries.

summary: An adept, cited from Khunrath's Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern., who defines the philosopher's stone as embodied Ruach Elohim. Atwood admits such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown.
body: Atwood quotes him: “The philosopher’s stone, says the mysterious adeptest, is Ruach Elohim” [III.3 ¶50]. The note cites Khunrath, *Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern.*, Isag. in fig. [III.3 n35]. He calls the Stone embodied Ruach Elohim, names Salt as its principle and calls it Wisdom [III.3 ¶50]. Atwood uses him in support but admits that such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown [III.3 ¶50].

equivalences.with: transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men

summary: The object of Agrippa's search. The Rosy Cross fraternity calls it the most ancient knowledge, breathed into nature by God's Word, and equates it with the Fire of Life and the Wise men's red gold.
body:
Atwood (ATWOOD) says Agrippa reached his final conviction by “searching and proving the magnitude of the Mystery” [I.1 ¶64].

The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (QUOTED) describes the mystery as the most ancient knowledge, “a knowledge which God Almighty, by his Word, breathed into nature” [III.3 ¶63]. It is given to few, though it lives and moves daily in sight of all [III.3 ¶63]. They equate it with “a miraculous power, the blessed Fire of Life” and with “the transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men” [III.3 ¶63].

summary: The regenerative mystery, of which, Atwood says, the Reformers kept little more than a traditional faith.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says the Reformers kept little of it, “retaining, indeed, little more of the mystery of regeneration than a traditional faith” [I.1 ¶26].

summary: The one analysis that resolves a pot into gold and gold into an indissoluble water. It agrees with hermetic doctrine in both inner and outer senses, and its final stage yields Light.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “For by no other analysis either is a pot resolved into gold, or gold into a water which is indissoluble.” [III.2 n38]. She holds that this analysis agrees with hermetic doctrine in both its internal and external senses, and that its ultimate stage yields Light [III.2 n38].

summary: A topic Atwood deliberately leaves aside at this point. She says it will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject is made manifest.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD): “We omit many things here relating to the mystical death and regeneration” [II.3 ¶56]. She says these will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject has been made manifest.

headword: the mystical problem of the Trinity
forms: the mystical problem of the Trinity
summary: The Trinity's “three in one and one in three”, cited as an analogy for agent, patient and offspring in all created things.
body: A footnote uses the mystical problem of the Trinity, “three in one and one in three”, as an analogy for the agent, patient and offspring found in all created things [I.3 n30]. The voice is not specified.

summary: Cited in the Appendix as foreshadowing the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother”.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the myth of Oedipus is said to foreshadow the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother” [APP ¶73].

summary: The Myths, cited in the Appendix for showing Vulcan as lame. This is explained as halting motion.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Myths are cited for showing Vulcan as lame, which is explained as halting motion [APP ¶129].

summary: A commentator cited by Atwood for his commentary on an enigmatic epitaph, printed in the Theatrum Chemicum.
body: Cited as having commented on the epitaph discussed in the text [I.1 ¶24]; the footnote names his commentary in the Theatrum Chemicum, *Commentariolum in Enigmaticum quoddam Epitaphium Bononiae studiorum* [I.1 n32].

summary: The Name that, Atwood says, we have no business to speak; if it speaks in us, it works its own change.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), insists: “We have no business whatsoever to speak The Name.” [APP ¶88] Her point, as the record gives it, is that it is not for us to utter; if it speaks in us, it works its own change [APP ¶88].

summary: The soul's bond in life, which she must give up, with dread, during the transition.
body: Atwood speaks of the soul about to “relinquish her natal bond in life” [II.3 ¶37]. The record glosses it as the soul's bond in life, which she gives up with dread during the transition.

summary: A figure who, the text says, would not teach Agrippa despite his entreaties.
body: Cited as having refused to teach Agrippa despite his entreaties [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: That through which the impure Instrument is brought and returned; the wording also suggests the Instrument then itself constitutes it.
body: Atwood writes of the Instrument that “when finally brought through the natural Alembic, and returned, it constitutes the natural Alembic” [III.1 ¶61]. Two readings are possible. On one, the natural Alembic is the passage through which the impure Instrument goes and returns. On the other, the Instrument itself becomes the natural Alembic. The repeated phrase may be a printing slip, so the text leaves this open.

summary: The vital fire of the natural life, which when fermented and opened frees the celestial Life and Light; in Eudoxus, the fire the Stone sympathizes with.
body:
**Atwood (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer):** the natural fire is the vital fire of the natural life. Fermented by the same life from another, it is opened and “sets free the celestial Life and Light” [APP ¶38].

**Eudoxus (quoted):** the Stone, an Astral Fire, sympathizes with Natural Fire, and “the igneous spirit of the natural fire is corporified in the substances which are analogous to it” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Stone grows in an 'Elementary Fire' geometrically proportioned to it [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not say that Natural Fire and Elementary Fire are the same.

summary: Geber's term for a natural unfitness for the work, caused by defects of body or of soul.
body: Atwood reports Geber's term for a natural incapacity for the work, caused by bodily defects or defects of soul: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3].

summary: In Crollius, the agent that separates each mystery into its own receptacle and frees the medicine from impure outside elements.
body: Crollius (quoted): “the natural inbred chemist teaches to segregate every mystery into its own reservacle” [III.1 ¶10]. It frees the medicine from impure external elements. The text gives no further definition. The phrase apparently names an inner, natural agent of separation, though what exactly it is stays open.

summary: Man's 'phantasic' Spirit, the vestibule of Reason, which in man matches the Ether in the universe; it is imperfect and its Light is hidden.
body: Atwood: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5]. She calls it 'phantasic' and the vestibule of Reason [III.1 ¶5]. Earlier chapters have shown “the imperfection of the natural Spirit in his world, the occultation of its Light” [III.1 ¶4].

summary: The soul's ordinary, unregenerate state, where no lasting leader rules and passing motives take control.
body: Atwood: “the government of the natural life is oligarchical, almost an anarchy” [II.4 ¶38]. In this state no permanent leader rules and passing motives take control.

summary: Ordinary reason: needed at the threshold but dull and idle in the work, unable to purify the phantastic Spirit; it is the image of the supernatural reason.
body:
Atwood treats natural reason as necessary but only an aid at the threshold. In the work itself it is dull and inoperative [III.1 ¶20–21]. It cannot purify the phantastic Spirit: “But the natural Intellect cannot do this” [III.1 ¶20]. It is the image of the higher faculty: “these things which the natural reason as an image enacts theoretically, this supernatural reason is said to do as an archetype essentially” [III.1 ¶21].

= **iron key**: “as it were an iron key, intended to unlock the golden treasury of light within” [III.1 ¶13].

summary: What the avaricious are afraid to 'interposit'; Atwood glosses this as giving up the life of selfhood and turning the product to a benevolent and truthful end.
body: In the passage from Geber, on the avaricious: “but are afraid to interposit the necessary charges” [III.4 ¶3]. In Geber's wording the failure is covetousness of money. Atwood reinterprets the charges in her own voice: “i.e., to abandon the life of selfhood, and return the product to a benevolent and truthful end” [III.4 ¶6]. Her gloss apparently makes the cost moral and inward rather than financial.

summary: A Lion said to be born of 'her foam' and identified with what the sentence before describes; the exact referent is unclear.
body: Atwood: “and this is that Nemean Lion said to be born of her foam” [IV.1 ¶29]. The Lion is identified with what the sentence before describes. It is unclear from the record what that is, and whose foam is meant.

summary: Philosophers Atwood cites for a hidden Principle of Universal Science and for teaching principles while keeping silent on the Practice.
body:
Atwood cites them as support for a latent Principle of Universal Science that can be known under certain conditions [II.1 ¶39]. They spoke of Principles and of how the mind proceeds while avoiding the Practice; their images stir inward faith [III.2 ¶46].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she qualifies this. They set out principles scientifically and went through long-perfected Initiation, but did not declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi. They kept to psychological investigation, and Behmen surpassed them here [APP ¶122].

summary: A region reached after the first barriers, where one must choose Light; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood mentions “approaching to the Nether confines, to make choice of Light” [IV.1 ¶25]. The region comes after the first barriers. The text does not explain it further.

summary: The moment when extremes are present and Light springs forth out of the abyssal Darkness.
body: Atwood: “extremes are said to be present at the new birth, when Light springs forth to manifestation out of the abyssal Darkness” [III.2 ¶56].

summary: The new beginning that the former life, all but destroyed, draws to itself through a new seed.
body: Atwood describes the former life, nearly annihilated, “which at length, in its extreme exigence, draws a new seed to begin a New Generation” [III.2 ¶28]. The new start comes out of the extreme destruction of the old.

summary: Atwood's name for the agent of mesmerism, which she identifies with the Common Soul.
body: Atwood uses this name for the agent at work in mesmerism and identifies it with the Common Soul: “our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul” [II.2 ¶18].

summary: What arises once the evil of Original Sin is overcome by subtle stratagems; its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone.
body: Atwood: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems, the New Life thence arises” [III.1 ¶66]. Its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone [III.1 ¶66].

summary: The New Light of Alchemy, cited as one of the sources of a summary passage.
body: Cited as one of the sources of the summary passage [I.2 ¶33]; the footnote names it as the *New Light of Alchemy* [I.2 n36].

summary: In Boehme, the regenerate inner seer who looks into the astral birth, as opposed to the external man.
body: Boehme (quoted): “for the new man speculates into the midst of the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16]. The new man is contrasted with the external man, so the context suggests the regenerate inner seer.

summary: Cited as recognizing the possibility and not condemning the tradition; also used once for comparison.
body: Atwood cites Sir Isaac Newton as support: he recognized the possibility and did not condemn the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named for comparison only [APP ¶122].

headword: Night of Hippocrates / Day of Orpheus
forms: Night of Hippocrates / Day of Orpheus
summary: Paired images: the radical destruction leads back to the Night of Hippocrates and on into the Day of Orpheus.
body: Atwood calls the radical destruction “the way of the recedure to the Night of Hippocrates, leading thenceforth into the Day of Orpheus” [III.2 ¶28]. The text does not explain the two terms further. The context suggests a return to darkness that is followed by light.

summary: The state of the mind beholding Matter: it receives the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely, feeling without understanding.
body: The passage opens: “When therefore the mind is in the Night of Matter” [III.2 ¶55]. In this state the mind suffers the reception of the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely; it feels without understanding [III.2 ¶55]. The voice is unclear: the record does not show whether this is Atwood or a cited authority.

summary: An unnamed adept cited for the view that Venus's light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture.
body: Atwood cites this unnamed adept in support. Venus's light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture, though at that stage “the artist is rejoiced, and thinks perhaps his work is finished” [I.3 n49].

headword: a no less subtle than experienced adept
forms: a no less subtle than experienced adept
summary: An unnamed adept cited for water turning into air and back, and for the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver.
body: Atwood cites this unnamed adept to illustrate water turning into air and back again: “the central heat may change the water into air” [I.3 n31]. The adept also gives the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver [I.3 n31].

summary: Used as an illustration of the principle kept safe in the water through destruction, which then renews all things.
body: Atwood uses Noah to illustrate the principle preserved in the water through destruction, which renews all things: “as Noah in the Ark” [III.3 ¶71].

summary: In a quoted poem, the narrator's master, whose deathbed oath is the narrator's reason for veiling the secrets.
body: Inside the quoted poem, the narrator gives his master's deathbed charge as his reason for veiling: “At his death he made me sweare hym to, That all the secrets I schould never undoe” [III.1 ¶65].

summary: Coins struck from Lully's gold, about 10 ducats each, of the finest metal, with a marginal inscription said to mark their miraculous origin.
body: Atwood reports that from Lully's gold “a coinage of the gold was struck in pieces weighing about 10 ducats each, called Nobles of the Rose” [I.1 ¶47]. They were of the finest metal, and their marginal inscription was said to denote their miraculous origin [I.1 ¶47].

summary: In Parmenides, what neither mind nor speech can reach; in Hegel, the empty abstraction of pure Being; for the Kabalists, the primitive non-Being, the Cause of causes.
body:
The text quotes three distinct views.

**Parmenides:** Non-being is what neither mind can see nor speech reveal, “since, as of Being void, ‘Tis not the object of the mental eye” [III.2 ¶14].

**Hegel:** “this pure Being is no other than a pure abstraction, it is a term absolutely negative, which may also in its immediate conception be called non-Being” [III.2 ¶30]. So for Hegel pure Being = non-Being.

**The Kabalists (the Rabbi):** non-Being is not nothing in the ordinary sense. It is not produced “from nothing in the common-sense acceptation of that word; for Being could never be produced from non-Being (deficiently understood), but by non-Being they mean” [III.2 ¶32] something else. It cannot be conceived as cause or essence, “but yet is in fact the Cause of causes: it is that which we call the primitive non-Being; because it is anterior to the universe” [III.2 ¶32]. It is not corporeity: “by it we do not signify corporeity either, but that Principle or Wisdom on which it is founded” [III.2 ¶32]. It holds no distinction. Identities asserted: = Cause of causes; = Principle or Wisdom [III.2 ¶32].

The readings differ: Parmenides calls it unknowable, Hegel calls it an empty abstraction, and the Kabalists call it the Cause of causes and the Principle or Wisdom.

summary: The initial nothingness of all things, which Atwood says Parmenides and others were cited to prove, and at which the soul does not stop but passes into true Being.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “Parmenides and the rest cited to prove the same initial nonentity of all” [III.2 ¶54]. The soul, she continues, “not enduring any longer to stop at nonentity, becomes into true Being” [III.2 ¶55]. Nonentity is thus apparently a stage the soul passes through, not its goal.

summary: Author of the verse Ordinal of Alchemy, an authority Atwood cites throughout and endorses on secrecy, the few chosen, patience, purity, learning and the requisites of the work.
body:
Norton's *Ordinal* is cited throughout the book, almost always in support of Atwood's own positions.

**Secrecy and the few chosen.** From the Proheme Atwood takes the point that masters wrote under coverts, while “Yet Anaxagoras wrote plainest of them all In his boke of Conversions Naturall;” [I.1 ¶14, I.1 n21]. He supports the view that few are chosen and covetousness disqualifies: “Quod inter mille millia, vix subt tres electi” [I.1 ¶40, I.1 n47]; “Scarcely seven men maie this science finde.” — the science being granted to few faithful, lowly men and withheld from proud clerks who then call it fable [III.4 ¶14, III.4 n9]. Secrecy is a duty because “If one evil man had hereof his will, All Christian peace he might easily spill;” [I.3 n15]; the art is a holy gift taught orally under oath to the proven [III.4 ¶9–10, III.4 n8]: “Wherefore old Fathers, conveniently, Called this science Holy Alkimy”.

**Name and profundity.** “For it is most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶49, I.1 n59; cf. I.2 ¶51]. In chap. 1 he also illustrates the universal craze for alchemy, the ruin of hasty seekers and the damage done by a monk's book of false receipts [I.1 ¶49–54].

**Order of the work.** He supports white-before-red: “Till the white medicine be fully wrought;” [I.1 ¶59–64, I.1 n64]; Atwood praises the *Ordinal* as candid and orderly except for the concealed Subject Matter. He notes that the parts are divided among authors: “Every and each of them disclosed but a parte” [I.1 ¶83, I.1 n107]. Verse on the never-wasting Water cites Democrit and Hermes [III.3 ¶73–74, III.3 n48].

**Conditions and practice.** Only those of stable wit finish [III.4 ¶16–17]; the Work begins only after purity: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49, IV.1 n42]; “Greate neede hath he to be a clerke” [IV.2 ¶5, IV.2 n6]. He is the main authority on vessels, ministers, furnaces and places: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶30–41]; Atwood calls his account of the Preparatory Practice naive and “without much envy”. He also supports astrological election and the Elixir as a thing of Second Intention [IV.2 ¶34, IV.2 n23], and advice on servants [IV.1 ¶9].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for the name Holy Alchemy [APP ¶29] and against over-haste: “Haste is the Devil’s part” [APP ¶103].

summary: Norton's verse treatise, cited in IV.1 as the main verse authority on the conduct and hazards of the Gross Work.
body: Cited from chap. 4 (as Ordinal or Norton’s Ordinal) as Atwood's main verse authority on balanced, unhasty feeding of the work, its cost, patience and simmering, the three-year Gross Work, and the Gross Work as a foul, perilous handicraft needing experience, uniformity and able ministers [IV.1 ¶12–28, IV.1 n14, n17, n22, n23]: “Excess of one half quarter of an hour May destroy all”. See also Norton.

summary: In Atwood's usage, that which is before all things, in which the Eternal Will arises and into which Wisdom returns; knowing Nothing means having the All.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes of “bringing back into the Nothing which is before all things” as Wisdom's end; the Eternal Will arises in it [APP ¶90, Appendix, later layer]. Earlier she says: “For he who in such wise knows Nothing --- no one apostate particular --- has the All” [IV.4 ¶27], so knowing Nothing apparently means holding to no separated particular.

summary: “Night of body or corporeal sleep”: a name Atwood reports for the Terrestrial Paradise, where souls are dead to this life and more alive in that.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) identifies it with the Terrestrial Paradise or Elysium: “the true Terrestrial Paradise, which some have called nox corporis, the night of body or corporeal sleep” [II.4 ¶9]. The text glosses the Latin itself. Souls there are dead to this life and more alive in that [II.4 ¶9].

equivalences.with: length, breadth and profundity of Nature

summary: Nature's three dimensions as displayed by the Spirit in her emanative Law.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) calls number, weight and measure the dimensions the Spirit displays in Nature's emanative Law: “For these are the length, and breadth, and profundity of Nature” [III.3 ¶67].

summary: Outwardly mere 'bark' of things; theosophically, the order in which the Divine Law develops in creative operation, known through theurgic art.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]; understood theosophically, numbers are the order of development of the Divine Law in creative operation, known through theurgic art [APP ¶107].

summary: Author cited from Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi and Tractatus de Vero Sale on the mineral spirit, gold's magnetical virtue, and innate heat.
body: Introduced as “another” authority on the power of the pure mineral spirit, which “it will work such an alteration in things of like nature with themselves, that they shall equalize the Philosophical Elixir” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n49] (Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi, ed. Combachius). The *Tractatus de Vero Sale* is footnoted as the source for gold's magnetical virtue and the names Microcosmic Sun and Stone of Fire [II.1 n21]. From the Latin of Combachius Atwood takes that the effective heat is innate, a terrestrial sun, not external: “sed potius solis terrestris innatus calor” [IV.1 ¶43, IV.1 n39]. She cites him in support throughout.

summary: The state of the mental eye when all thought is submerged: a crass, obscure vacuity, called the Original of Life, related to true Being as night to day.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the objectless mental eye, all thought submerged, becoming one with darkness as the eye does: “a crass, obscure vacuity” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it: “that obscure oblivion which is the Original of Life” [III.2 ¶54]. It stands to true Being as night to day [III.2 ¶54].

summary: The art Atwood says Alexandrian Christian Platonists and divines studied and discussed; St John is said to have practised it for healing and making gold, silver and gems.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) reports the Alexandrian Christian Platonists and divines “studying and discussing the Occult Art in their writings”, and that St John is said to have practised it for healing and for making gold, silver and gems [I.1 ¶24].

summary: The hidden discovery on which, Atwood says, the systems of ancient philosophy were uniformly based; the passage does not say what it is.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) refers to “that occult discovery on which the systems of ancient philosophy appear to have been very uniformly based” [I.1 ¶12], without here naming it.

summary: The hidden material of the art, to which the adepts claim the Bononian Enigma exclusively refers.
body: Reported as the adepts' view (QUOTED: the adepts): the Bononian Enigma refers exclusively to “the occult material of their art” [I.1 ¶20].

summary: Atwood's name for the subject of her inquiry, considered in its means and principles, and for the medieval epoch she surveys.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) frames her inquiry around “the means and principles of occult science” [I.1 ¶2] and calls the medieval period “this extraordinary epoch of Occult Science” [I.1 ¶39]. Agrippa received “the means and principles of the Occult Science” from Trithemius, and Ashmole and Boorhaave are said to be acquainted with it [I.1 ¶64].

summary: The hidden Medicine that the Light of Faith discovers when it searches the interior.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says the Light of Faith, searching the interior, discovers “the occult Stone --- the hidden Medicine” [III.1 ¶36], identifying the two.

summary: A supposed 'New Imponderable' suggested by recent experiments and Mesmerism, which Atwood says few believe in and does not assume.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) mentions “the supposition of a New Imponderable, or Odic Force” [I.2 ¶16], suggested by recent experiments and Mesmerism; few believe in it, and she does not assume it in her argument [I.2 ¶16].

summary: Mythic figure Atwood uses as an image of the inquirer who solves the Sphinx's riddle by the Light of true Chemistry and by unhasty, rational self-penetration.
body: Atwood uses Oedipus illustratively. Aided by the Light of true Chemistry, he vanquishes the Metaphysical Monster and enters the Temple of Truth [III.1 ¶4]. His lameness signifies not hastening to solve the Sphinx's riddle [IV.1 ¶13]. The one who rationally penetrates his own natural understanding, “like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx” [IV.1 ¶48].

summary: In a passage given as Hermes', the second of the three that come from two, holding a blackness that must be removed.
body: Voice: QUOTED: Hermes. The oily tincture is second of the three produced from two: “then the oily tincture” [I.3 ¶23]; it holds a blackness to be removed [I.3 ¶23].

summary: 'The learned Dane', author of De Ortu et Progressu Chemiae, cited for alchemy's antiquity, the Lully gold-coin story, transmutation stories and a count of 2500 authors.
body: Atwood cites his *De Ortu et Progressu Chemiae* in support of alchemy's antiquity, calling him “the learned Dane” [I.1 ¶3, I.1 n3]; for the story of Lully and the English gold coins: “Aureas illas Anglorum primum...” [I.1 ¶47, I.1 n57]; and (as Borricius) for counting 2500 authors and for transmutation stories [I.1 ¶75, I.1 n96, I.1 n104].

summary: Traditional maxims Atwood cites in the Appendix on the transmission of spirit and the wisdom of the receiver.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood cites “Ut ventus qui flat, est ille qui dat” [APP ¶41] (ours: as the wind that blows, so is he who gives) for the imparter of spirit as wind, and “Qui capit, ille sapit” (ours: he who receives, he is wise) for the wisdom of the receiver [APP ¶41].
