summary: Collective authority whose definition of the Matter Atwood endorses: bodies are to be turned into vapour, which is the Stone.
body: Atwood cites and endorses the old Alchemists' definition of the Matter: “it is no common water, but an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting” [III.2 ¶7]; bodies are to be turned into vapour, and this is the Stone [III.2 ¶7].

summary: A mythic analogy Atwood uses in the Appendix to illustrate drawing the Salt up into the medial life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Troy in the old analogy is that citadel where Apollo keeps his cattle” [APP ¶77], used to illustrate drawing the Salt up into the medial life; how the image maps onto the operation is not spelled out in the record.

summary: Scripture, cited in the Appendix as founded on revealed utterance, with the New fulfilling the Old's promise and giving another.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood illustrates with the Testaments: both are founded on the revealed utterance; the New fulfils the Old's promise and gives another [APP ¶98].

summary: Authority cited (lib. Concilio, Quest 74) as having praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom.
body: Cited in support: he praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom [I.1 ¶43, I.1 n52].

summary: In Khunrath's words, a fire with which the internal and external fire must be in sympathy; the text does not define it.
body: Voice: QUOTED: Khunrath. The internal and external fire must be “in harmonious sympathy with the Olympic Fire” [III.3 ¶9]. The passage does not say what the Olympic Fire is.

summary: 'The Egyptian Olympiodorus', cited in support on phantasy as an impediment, allegorical readings of Elysium and Tartarus, and reason's rule over the soul.
body: Atwood cites him approvingly. Phantasy opposes divine enthusiasm, and perceiving Universals proves the soul can act without it: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12, II.2 n13]. From his Commentary on the Gorgias she takes an allegorical reading of Hercules' last labour and of the Islands of the Blessed / Elysian Fields as a state above corporeal life: “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He also supports an ethical/physical reading of Tartarus: “souls, in which reason does not preside as a charioteer, are changed according to the subject temperament of the body” [III.2 ¶9, III.2 n11]. He is listed among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].

equivalences.with: God (according to Xenophanes, as reported by Aristotle)

summary: The philosophers' absolute unit, Fountain of all being, implied in every multitude and each part; reported from Xenophanes as God.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says “the One of these philosophers is the Fountain of all being” [III.2 ¶45], implied in every multitude and each part; “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45]. She also reports Xenophanes, via Aristotle (QUOTED), identifying it with God: “looking to the whole heaven, he says, the One is God” [III.2 ¶40].

equivalences.with: subject of the most holy stone of the philosophers

summary: In Agrippa's words, the single thing besides which there is no other, the subject of the most holy stone, of which to speak rashly is sacrilege.
body: Voice: QUOTED: Cornelius Agrippa. He speaks “of the one blessed stone alone, besides which there is no other thing, the subject of the most holy stone of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶64], treating rash speech of it as sacrilege [I.1 ¶64].

summary: The ancient theory of a single vitalizing principle in air and all things, which Atwood says moderns deride because it escapes their analyses.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) notes that “the ancient theory of the One Element has been very much derided” [I.2 ¶14], because the single vitalizing principle in air and all things escapes modern analyses [I.2 ¶14]; her tone implies she does not share the derision.

summary: The single matter of all things in the Beginning, which the process imitates as all diversities come from and return to the One.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD): “as in the Beginning there was said to be one only matter of all things” [III.3 ¶29], so in the process all diversities proceed from and return to the One [III.3 ¶29].

summary: In Proclus' words, the principle found only by becoming assimilated to it, the most united in nature, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent.
body: Voice: QUOTED: Proclus. “if any one wish to discover the One Principle he must become first assimilated to it” [III.2 ¶50]. It is the most united in nature, through which it is Deity, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent [III.2 ¶50].

summary: The single subject from which, after the Smaragdine (Emerald) Table, all things proceed by adaptation; Atwood identifies it with the Identity made in regeneration and, later, with our psychical essence.
body:
The term comes from the Hermetic Table, cited as the Smaragdine, Emerald or Smagardine Table (also as the Smaragdine Tablet of Thrice Great Hermes): it speaks of “for performing the miracles of the One Thing whence all the rest proceed by adaptation” [III.1 ¶41; cf. I.1 ¶9, I.2 ¶48]. The Table as quoted makes the Sun its father, the Moon its mother, the Wind its carrier and the Earth its nurse, and says “This is the father of all perfection and consummation of the whole world.” [IV.2 ¶44]. A quoted master, whom Atwood follows, says “the whole matter I know to be One only Thing” [III.1 ¶21]; in that passage folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are its modes of being.

Boehme, as quoted, says the first something was “a certain cloud or darkness, which was condensed into water”, and that “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. Atwood takes this up herself: “God of nothing created something which was made that one thing in which are all”, and she adds that “this One Thing appears to be nothing less or more than that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16]. For the creature it is the first divine manifestation out of the abyss.

Atwood says that “The same tradition of the manifold powers and preservation of the One Thing runs in symbol” through the Gentile Mythology [III.3 ¶69]. The verses she quotes make it the only key to the sealed Art (“Which one thing only can unlocke; This one things learn to know,” [III.3 ¶68]) and “A mass confused and darkly clad, That in itself, all Nature had”, called “The first Material Mother of all.” [III.3 ¶76]. The verses call it indestructible, easy to find and hard to get.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says plainly: “The One Thing; it is our psychical essence; our nervous system.” [APP ¶176].

summary: An unnamed authority (“says one”) whom Atwood cites in the Table Talk to support her claim that everything depends on the will and the intention.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), an unnamed authority is quoted in support of the point that all depends on the willing and the intention: “That which in the hands of fools is nothing in that of a philosopher becomes to be all in all” [APP ¶35].

summary: Atwood's name for philosophy in the true sense: the knowledge of true Being that was the object of initiation.
body: Atwood equates the two terms directly: “philosophy, that is to say, Ontological Wisdom” [II.2 ¶4]. She calls it “the Wisdom of true Being” [II.2 ¶5]. In that passage it is the knowledge that initiation aimed at.

summary: In Agrippa's phrase, the worker of all wonderful effects, which is located within us.
body: Atwood quotes Agrippa: “in us is the Operator of all wonderful effects” [II.1 ¶26]. The Operator is inward, not an outside agent.

summary: A principle that, once freed, draws the mind's other faculties into its vortex, revels with them until satiated, and is then more easily ensnared.
body: Atwood says the faculties are “drawn away afterwards into the vortex of the Opposive Principle, rapidly attracting them when it is freed” [III.1 ¶66]. It revels with them, becomes satiated and is then more easily ensnared. She illustrates this with Orpheus's tale of Saturn bound in fetters while drunk [III.1 ¶66]. The text does not say outright that this is the same as the ‘rebellious Principle’ of III.1 ¶64.

summary: An oracle of Apollo, taken from Eusebius, used as the epigraph of II.2: the path to Deity is hard, and the Egyptians and other ancient peoples disclosed it.
body: Atwood uses it as an epigraph: “The Path by which to Deity we climb Is arduous, rough, ineffable, sublime;” [II.2 ¶1]. The verses go on to say the path was disclosed by the Egyptians and other ancient peoples.

summary: The oracle given to Amelius, which Atwood quotes to show the place where the soul of Plotinus dwells.
body: Atwood quotes the oracle given to Amelius about where the soul of Great Plotinus is. It describes the place in Latin: “Ubi Amicitia est, ubi cupido visu mollis” [II.4 ¶11, II.4 ¶12] (ours: where Friendship is, where desire is gentle to behold).

summary: Oracular sayings that Atwood cites often, including the Oracula Chaldaica and Zoroastri Oracula, to support her teaching on the soul's ascent, the formless Fire, purification and piety.
body:
Atwood treats the oracles as supporting authorities. One urges the soul to turn upward, away from the image-loving Hades: “Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards” [II.3 ¶26, II.3 n27; footnote cites Zoroastri Oracula, Anima, Corpus, Homo]. Another, from the Oracula Chaldaica, names the true vision as the formless Fire: “When thou seest a Fire without Form, Shining flashingly through the depths of the World, Hear the voice of Fire” [II.3 ¶46–47, II.3 n50]. It is cited again for the Fire as the derivation and dispenser of Fire [II.3 ¶52–53].

The Oracle also gives the name ‘Pratum’ (meadow) to the meadow of Divine Ideas [II.4 ¶9]. It warns about the infinite End of the principle: “Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth” [III.2 ¶15]. The oracles are said to teach that the impure perceptive medium needs ‘alternation and solution’ before it can tell good from evil [II.2 ¶15]. On piety, Atwood writes: “Thus piety is available for all things, as the oracles declare” [III.4 ¶22]. In that passage prayer is piety's chief exercise and is profitable for great undertakings. With Julian, the oracles support the claim that “through purifying ceremonies bodies become worthy of receiving divine assistance and health” [IV.3 ¶30–31, IV.3 n10]. An oracle is also reported to have called Socrates the wisest of mankind because of that Nothing [IV.4 ¶27].

summary: In Clemens Alexandrinus's words as Atwood quotes them, the rites or celebrations of the Mysteries.
body: Atwood quotes Clemens Alexandrinus: “These are the orgies of the Mysteries” [II.2 ¶5]. The word means the Mysteries' rites.

summary: The adepts' figure of an animal that must be skinned by the Hand; in the Table Talk, Atwood explains it as the opposite will clothed in Light.
body:
In III.1, Atwood reports the adepts' saying: “For the Orient Animal must be stripped of his skin, not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. The skin is a lion's skin. The Latin in that passage adds that the animal then enters the great salt sea and comes out again with beauty. The figure is not explained there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood herself gives the meaning: “The ‘orient animal’ means the animal (that is, the opposite) will which is clothed in Light”. She also calls it “the third which rises in opposition to the first” [APP ¶21].

summary: A Hermetic expression quoted from Hermes: two oriental quicksilvers that hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies.
body: Hermes, as quoted, speaks of “the fat of the two oriental quicksilvers, which hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies” [I.3 ¶20]. The text does not explain the expression further.

summary: Named in the story about Ammonius.
body: Origen is named only in the story of Ammonius [III.2 ¶64].

summary: Nature's Original Light: the infallible touchstone by which the capable can tell what is rationally possible.
body: Atwood speaks of Nature's “infallible touchstone of her Original Light” [IV.3 ¶54]. The able use it to discern what is rationally possible.

summary: The state to which bodies must be reduced, by introversion of the generated life, before they can be truly manifested and made permanent.
body: Atwood names as a condition of true manifestation and permanence “the reduction of bodies to their original matter, by introversion of the generated life” [I.2 ¶49].

summary: An evil that is overcome by subtle stratagems, after which the New Life arises.
body: Atwood writes: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems” [III.1 ¶66], after which the New Life arises. The context suggests that the stratagems are those just described for ensnaring the Opposive Principle.

summary: The real power that the types signify; without understanding it and cooperating with it, the types only mimic efficacy.
body: Atwood says the types need “a true understanding and cooperation of that original virtue, apart from which they do but mimic an efficacy” [I.1 ¶26].

summary: An authority whom Atwood cites often for mythic illustrations that she reads hermetically: Pan, the Cave of Mercury, Saturn's fettering, and the Day that follows the Night.
body:
Atwood quotes Orpheus to illustrate Pan as the whole of nature: “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis” [I.2 ¶28, I.2 n26, Orpheus Hymni] (ours: strong, subtle Pan, whole and universal). From the Argonautics she cites prudent entry into the Cave of Mercury (“Mercurii ingedier spuluncam” [III.1 ¶17–18]), which she interprets hermetically. In the same vein, Orpheus is said to have recommended taking the Hermetic material in the cave of Mercury [III.2 ¶7].

She draws on Orpheus for the tale of Saturn, bound in fetters while drunk by his son through a stratagem: “and by the advice of the goddess, too, according to Orpheus, the subtle stratagem was contrived” [III.1 ¶66]. It illustrates how the satiated Opposive Principle is ensnared. She also cites ‘the Day of Orpheus’, which follows the Night [III.2 ¶28].

summary: An emblem work (Emblema LVI) that Atwood cites to support the point that the corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.
body: Atwood cites the Apodosis of Emblema LVI: “Cui scelerum viru mens moribunda tumet” [III.3 ¶11–12, III.3 n5] (ours: whose dying mind swells with the poison of crimes). It supports her point that a corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.

summary: An Orphic fragment that Atwood cites on purity and contemplation of the One, while qualifying its claim that He is never seen by mortal eyes.
body: The fragment opens: “I open a secret to the Initiated, but let the doors be shut.” [II.4 ¶40, II.4 n28]. Atwood uses it in support of purity and contemplation of the One. She qualifies its statement that He is ‘never seen by mortal eyes’: the Initiated, she says, did behold Him.

summary: Cited for the teaching that Pan, of necessity, evolves every property and form out of his central will.
body: Atwood cites the Orphic oracles in support of the teaching that Pan evolves every property and form out of his central will, of necessity [I.2 ¶36].

summary: An unnamed Orphic poet, quoted in Latin, on what blessed Eurotas heard while Phoebus (Apollo) meditated.
body: Atwood quotes the Orphic poet's verse on Apollo contemplating such rivers: “Omnia quae Phoebo quondam meditante beatus Audiit Eurotas” [II.4 ¶13–14] (ours: all that blessed Eurotas once heard while Phoebus meditated).

summary: An Orphic verse cited for the radiant return of Bacchus.
body: The verse shows Bacchus returning “triumphant, and appearing in splendour to mortals” [II.4 ¶54].

summary: The offspring that the Matter brings forth by the Fire of nature, lawfully conceived; Atwood calls it the Philosophic Sun.
body: Atwood says what the Matter brings forth by the lawfully conceived Fire of nature “is Orus, the Philosophic Sun” [III.3 ¶62].

summary: In the fable, the brother whom Typhon kills and scatters; applied to the work, Atwood identifies him with the Divine Light, the foreign body of Light.
body: In the fable, Typhon kills Osiris and scatters his body. Applying it to the work, Atwood identifies Osiris with “the foreign body of Light, which is Osiris” [III.1 ¶56] and “Osiris, i.e., the Divine Light” [III.1 ¶63]. The Efficient reduces this Light to vapor, and it suffers restraint as it passes through the voluntary axle [III.1 ¶56–63].

summary: A Persian sage who, as Atwood reports from Pliny, first brought the Persian spirit into Greece.
body: Citing Pliny, Atwood names Ostanes as the Persian sage who first brought the Persian spirit into Greece [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n13].

summary: Unnamed philosophers reported as teaching that the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon and the Red Mercury the bath of the Sun.
body: The speaker reports others as saying “the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon, and that the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun” [IV.3 ¶10]. The speaker does not dispute this but adds to it.

summary: Earlier masters who, Hermes says, veiled the secret in figures, which he claims he will now open.
body: Hermes, as quoted, says the secrets “are given by our ancestors in figures and types” [I.3 ¶50]. He claims to open them.

summary: The author of The Triumph, cited for listing the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone.
body: This author is cited for a list of the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone. The list begins: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6].

summary: Cited for the view that the Art is perfected by multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether.
body: ‘Our doctors’ are cited in support of the view that the Art's perfection lies in multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether [II.3 ¶56].

summary: In Sendivogius's words, the source of the water and the salt-nitre, holding a river of living water.
body: Sendivogius, as quoted, speaks of “Our Earth in which there is a river of living water” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is the source of the water and the salt-nitre. The text does not define it further.

summary: Christ, cited in the Appendix (Table Talk) for sayings Atwood applies to the Hermetic Art and the Stone.
body: Cited only in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). His words “The wind bloweth where it listeth” are cited as an analogy, Christ the Head Corner Stone is named as the analogue of the Stone, and the regenerated are said to enter his life [APP ¶41, APP ¶46, APP ¶60]. His saying “Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things shall be added unto you” supports Atwood's point that seeking the Universal first is the shortest and truest road in the Hermetic Art [APP ¶134]. His use of the language of David — “I have said ye are gods, if (says our Lord) ye called them gods unto whom the Word of God came” — illustrates powers subordinate to God evolved where the Word comes, with the danger of self-centers [APP ¶100].

summary: Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood sets in contrast: they lamented natural reason's inadequacy but could not free it from dependence on sense.
body: Atwood cites them by way of contrast: they lamented the inadequacy of natural reason but could not free it from its dependence on sense [II.1 ¶32].

summary: An unnamed modern writer whom Atwood cites to confirm and illustrate Hermes' process in terms of the three principles.
body: Atwood cites this unnamed modern exponent as confirming and illustrating Hermes' process in terms of the three principles: “in three months circulation, says he, by digestion, the powder becomes black” [II.1 ¶23].

summary: Cosmopolite's allegorical name for the Mercury, as reported by Eudoxus; apt because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals.
body: Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). He explains that Cosmopolite's allegory — “give our old man gold and silver to swallow” — names the Mercury: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]. The name fits, he says, because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: Eudoxus' name for the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, with the Spirit uniting them, compounded in proportions learned from bread-making.
body: Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). The paste is the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, the Spirit uniting them; it is composed of several matters whose proportions are learned from the analogy of bread-making — “the matters which compose our philosophical paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. Once fermented, all the philosophic confection becomes itself a leaven [IV.3 ¶14].

summary: Sendivogius' term for the philosophers' own gold and silver, called living, as opposed to common gold and silver, called dead.
body: Voice: Sendivogius (quoted). The philosophers' own gold and silver are called living, against common gold and silver, called dead: “take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21]. The text does not positively define them here.

summary: Poet whom Atwood calls an initiated poet and quotes from the Fasti and Metamorphoses on Chaos, the Aether, man's origin and the steep first way.
body: Atwood presents him as an initiated poet, inspired, “as he declares, by that same universal deity of the two-faced Janus” [III.3 ¶44]. From the Fasti she quotes “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” — Chaos as the primeval thing, opening the cosmogony [III.3 ¶45, III.3 n30]. From the Metamorphoses: “Ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo”, illustrating man made from divine seed or from earth holding seeds of heaven [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶47, III.3 n31]; “Haec super imposuit liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera”, placing the dreg-free Aether above the rest and introducing the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶37, III.2 n33]; and “Ardua prima via est”, the steepness of the first way [IV.1 ¶8, IV.1 n11]. (Renderings of the Latin are readers' own, not the book's.) Elsewhere he is named with Virgil, Horace and Vitruvius among Augustan men accused of sorcery, illustrating Rome's limited achievement [I.1 ¶18].

summary: The one universal Nature: in the Orphic hymn the whole that is all elements; for Atwood the Alchemical Pan, one in himself and multitudinous in offspring.
body: In the Orphic hymn Atwood quotes, Pan is “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis; Et totus ignis, aura, terra, sive aqua,” — the beginning and end of all [I.2 ¶28]. Atwood then turns to “the most Ancient Nature”, speaking of it as he: “Yet not in his elementary immanifest diffusion let us invoke the most Ancient Nature”, but as the Hermetic masters found it [I.2 ¶29]. In her own voice the subject is a single being with manifold offspring: “so is it said to be with the Alchemical Pan, who, being but one himself, is in his offspring multitudinous” [I.2 ¶34]; he contains Proteus and evolves all forms from his central will [I.2 ¶34].

summary: What the purged, pure life flows forth as, in a declaration Atwood reports.
body: In an unattributed declaration (“as is declared”), the purged pure life flows forth as “a pure panacea from the god of Light” [III.1 ¶10].

summary: Writer Atwood cites as describing several perpetual lamps.
body: Cited as describing several perpetual lamps [I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶20].

summary: A figure in Democritus' image who appears golden under the fire and is then called such a Venus.
body: Voice: Democritus (quoted). In his image Paphia, under the fire, appears golden, and is then identified with Venus: “Perchance, it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus” [I.3 n53].

summary: A group named in a chapter title, cited for the view that the true medicine and fire of life are bound in man.
body: Named in the chapter title. Atwood cites them in support of the view that the medicine and fire of life (called Antimony) are in man and are freed by purgation: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶1, III.1 ¶10].

summary: Authority Atwood cites often, chiefly on Separation as the Art's primary object and on the tincture, while criticizing his deliberately misleading writings.
body:
Atwood calls him “our doctor” and draws on him chiefly for Separation. From the addresses To the Athenians: “The greatest miracle of all in philosophy is separation”, with the true element as the spirit of life and First Matter of the elements [I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶26, I.2 n21, I.2 n24]; and “Separation is the greatest miracle in philosophy”, the Art's primary object, with free will as friend or foe and the sequestatrix [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n20]. In the Signatura Rerum he describes the tincture's astral fire, signs, and transmuting and medicinal power: “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n99]. He supports whiteness as the simple ground of diversity whereon to recreate: “Omnia in Dei manu alba sunt; is eas tingit ut vult” [III.2 ¶5]; and he is said to agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. With Van Helmont he corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea — “by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit” — though Atwood qualifies this as only a secondary witness [III.3 n27].

She also criticizes him for deliberately misleading writings, names his best works (the three Addresses to the Athenians, Aurora) and discusses his death [I.1 ¶64]. Cited with his Libro de Vita longa, he is compared to Avicenna's ill-directed genius and appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶35, I.1 ¶36, I.1 n41]. His De Natura Rerum was published with French's New Light, 1650 [I.1 ¶71]. He is mentioned as calling Crollius a natural divine, with “salem Paracelsi” in the Latin [II.1 ¶14, II.1 ¶21].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “the Archaeus of Paracelsus” is set in apposition to the solar plexus, workshop of the Celestial life [APP ¶32]; he is the source of “evestrum” for the soul's destiny-dream [APP ¶57] and of the name Evester for the analogical sphere [APP ¶105]; and mesmerism is said to imitate the Divine Art of separation he speaks of [APP ¶73].

summary: Followers of Paracelsus who, Atwood says, applied alchemy to human life and suggested the method and medium of attraction.
body: Cited as having applied alchemy to human life and suggested “the method and medium of attraction” [II.1 ¶9].

summary: Work (author not named in the text) quoted to illustrate Mammon as the downward-looking spirit leading the depraved operators.
body: Atwood quotes it on Mammon, the downward-looking spirit who leads the depraved operators: “for e’en in heaven his looks and thoughts Were always downward bent” [III.4 ¶4, III.4 ¶5, III.4 n2]. The author is not named.

summary: Paris, who preferred Venus to Juno and Minerva, invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) in the Democritus passage.
body: Invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) of the Democritus passage: “Perchance it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus, he did prefer her both to Juno and Minerva” [IV.1 ¶43]. Whether Atwood or the quoted source speaks here is unclear.

summary: Authority whose Non-Being Atwood identifies with the Matter, cited on non-being and the initial nonentity of all.
body: Atwood quotes his Fragments on “Non-being, which nor mind can see”, as a check on intellectual notions along this path [III.2 ¶13, III.2 ¶14, III.2 n14]. Via Aristotle she reports that he touched the One according to Reason and saw more than Xenophanes and Melissus [III.2 ¶40]. He is cited with the rest to prove the initial nonentity of all [III.2 ¶54], and “the Non-Being of Parmenides” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

summary: Vaughan's term for an individual spirit that a certain Art unites to the Universal; distinguished from the divine spirit.
body: Voice: Vaughan (quoted): “a certain Art by which a Particular Spirit may be united to the Universal” [II.1 ¶26]. The Particular Spirit is distinguished from the divine spirit [II.1 ¶26].

summary: The Spirit made passive, into which the supernatural reason infuses itself throughout.
body: Atwood: the supernatural reason works “by pure infusion of Itself to the passified Spirit throughout” [III.1 ¶21].

summary: Aristotle's term, as Atwood reports and adopts it, for an intellect capable of receiving and being converted to all things.
body: Aristotle's term as Atwood reports it (and adopts): the intellect he “calls passive intellect, because capable of receiving and being converted to all” [II.2 ¶17].

summary: The receptive intelligence, identified with the Moon, which, freed by art and in conjunction, answers the Will of her seeking Reason.
body: Atwood: the Passive Intelligence, spoken of as her, once freed by art and set in conjunction, “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason”, finds the way, removes obstacles and passes with him through the abyss [III.1 ¶40]. Identity asserted: “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40].

equivalences.with: the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists

summary: The pure, indeterminate receptive nature that should reflect the Divine Light unrefracted; identified as the Alchemists' Matter.
body: Atwood: “And the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind, pure and indeterminate” [III.2 ¶60], reflecting the Divine Light without refraction or mixed images. Identity asserted: “Such was the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].

summary: The receptive spirit, spoken of as herself, whose returning faith and desire draw the Soul back into itself at the extreme of tribulation.
body: Atwood: at the extreme of tribulation, “the returning faith and desire of the Passive Spirit attracts the Soul again into herself” [III.3 ¶10].

summary: Nature's receptive spirit, enclosed and impure in its ordinary state, made a right recipient by dissolution.
body: Atwood: in its ordinary state “the passive spirit of nature is included and impure” [I.2 ¶48]; dissolution makes it a right recipient [I.2 ¶48].

summary: That which the Vital Spirit's fermentation changes; not further defined.
body: Atwood speaks of “the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” by the Vital Spirit's fermentation [III.1 ¶9]. The text does not define it further.

summary: Understanding gained in transcendental contemplation of herself, which directs the mode of analysis and supplies most of its means.
body: Atwood: “the Passive Understanding gotten in transcendental contemplation of herself” directs the mode of analysis and provides most of its means [III.1 ¶40]. The passage does not explicitly identify it with the Passive Intelligence discussed alongside it.

summary: The first source of life and the last initiation, goal of every step of ascent, whose rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites.
body: Atwood: “the paternal is the first source of life, and the last into which the conscience is initiated” [II.4 ¶25]. It is the goal of all steps of ascent, and its rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites [II.4 ¶25].

summary: In the Chaldaic Oracle, the source from which intellectual notions crop the Flower of Life.
body: Voice: the Chaldaic Oracle (quoted): “Intellectual notions from the Paternal Fountain cropping the Flower of Life” [II.4 ¶32]. Not further explained.

summary: In the Appendix, the fundamental life sought by the light; related expressions Paternal ens and Paternal Spirit dwell in liberty in Elysium.
body: Appendix only (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood speaks of “seeking the Paternal Life, the fundamental life” [APP ¶167]. Related expressions name what dwells there: “where the Paternal ens resides in liberty” [APP ¶168] and “to Elysium, where the Paternal Spirit lives” [APP ¶171]; the text does not state in so many words that these are the same as the Paternal Life.

summary: The soul's original, more central light, antecedent to the Maternal intelligence; identified with the generative light.
body: Atwood calls it “the yet more central, antecedent Paternal, light of life”, into which the Maternal intelligence leads [III.1 ¶34]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) it is the soul's original light, obscured by the vaporous vehicle to bring it into sense, and identified: “the pure paternal light of life --- the generative light” [APP ¶121].

summary: In Proclus as reported by Atwood, the soul's undefiled union with the Father, in which it rests established in him as in a harbour.
body: A term Atwood reports from Proclus: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41]. The image is of “locating the soul in the Father, as in a port” [II.4 ¶41]. So the text itself identifies the Paternal Port with undefiled union with the Father.

summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's name for the seed of this life, which is said to be drawn up.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates the paternal principle with the seed of life: “The seed of this life, the paternal principle, is drawn up.” [APP ¶98]. The text gives no further explanation here.

summary: That which Intellect seeks in the allegory of the descent, according to Atwood.
body: Atwood reads the allegory of the descent as “an inquiry of Intellect after its Paternal Source” [II.3 ¶13]. The context suggests the term names the origin to which Intellect seeks to return. The text does not define it further.

summary: Paired with 'agent': that in which the agent's sin is multiplied and lives on in the 'unhappy offspring'.
body: Atwood uses 'patient' as the counterpart of 'agent'. The records show it as that in which the agent's sin is multiplied, so that “it should survive in the unhappy offspring unto the third or fourth generation” [IV.3 ¶56]. The text does not define the term further here.

summary: In Eudoxus, the leaven needed to ferment the Stone in the Fifth Key.
body: Eudoxus speaks here, quoted by Atwood: “the Perfect Body is a necessary leaven of Our Paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. So the text identifies the Perfect Body with the leaven of Our Paste, the leaven by which the Stone is fermented in the Fifth Key.

summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, the matter joined with the Mercury of the First Work in the Multiplication.
body: This comes from the Author of the Open Entrance, quoted by Atwood. In the Multiplication one is told to “take one part of the Perfect Matter” [IV.3 ¶18] and join it with the Mercury of the First Work. The term is not defined further here.

summary: Whitened water made red by conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit; its Art is called 'our brass'.
body: In a footnote, Atwood gives the reddening of the whitened water: “By a conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit, the albified water is made red” [I.3 n54]. The same note links the Art of the permanent water with 'our brass'.

summary: In the Appendix, the Divine line in all things, which withdraws from sense in mesmerizing, as opposed to the transverse line.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The perpendicular line is the Divine line in all things” [APP ¶13]. In mesmerizing it withdraws from sense. Were it stronger in us than the transverse line, we would no longer be in sense [APP ¶13].

summary: In the Appendix, the magnetism ('altitude') that dissolves the sensuous vehicle, freeing the soul and moving consciousness into another medium.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that Perpendicular Magnetism dissolves the sensuous vehicle and moves consciousness into another medium: “By the former the soul is set free” [APP ¶173]. It is linked with 'altitude'. The context suggests it is set against another, contrasting kind of magnetism.

summary: Ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, which Atwood takes as proof that the Romans knew chemistry and the occult laws of light.
body: Atwood describes ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, kept alight by a pure liquor. She treats them as evidence: “the perpetual lamps best prove, and without offence, that the Romans understood something of chemistry and the occult laws of light” [I.1 ¶18].

summary: Thorough, searching investigation: the means by which reason proves all things, and something the stiff-necked lack.
body: Two voices use the word. Geber, quoted by Atwood, describes the stiff-necked as “void of ingenuity and every sort of perscrutination” [III.4 ¶3]. Atwood herself makes it reason's task: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15]. In her method, then, searching inquiry is required, and its absence disqualifies.

equivalences.with: internal fire of the sulfur of thy water

summary: Hermes' name for the searching inner fire or secret sulfur that stirs up and purifies the matter; Atwood identifies it with the investigating Intellect that works the change.
body:
In a footnote, Atwood, citing Hermes, describes a secret sulfur: “It is the stirrer-up of the whole power and efficacy and purifier of the matter; hence Hermes calls it the Perscrutinator” [I.3 n32]. Hermes calls this temperate unguent or fire 'the Perscrutinator of the water'. Atwood adds that it is what is “eminently distinguishing the Rational Ferment” [I.3 n32].

In III.1 she takes the term inward. It is “that same perscrutinating Intellect which Hermes speaks of” [III.1 ¶21], the searching intellect that brings about the whole change. The sequestration that gives form and essence belongs to it [III.1 ¶21]. She also equates it with Eirenaeus' phrase: “It is this vital perscrutinator, the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water, as Eirenaeus calls it” [III.1 ¶13].

Asserted identities: the secret sulfur [I.3 n32]; the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water [III.1 ¶13]; the perscrutinating Intellect [III.1 ¶21].

headword: Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason
forms: Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason
summary: Heroes Atwood cites together: their labors before reward illustrate the toil needed to gain Wisdom.
body: Atwood names these heroes together. Their labors come before their reward, and she uses this to show the toil required for Wisdom [IV.1 ¶25].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited for reference only.
Author of an epistle addressed to Artaxerxes, cited for its account of Hippocrates' divine nature and healing.
body: Atwood cites an epistle by Petris, the Persian, addressed to Artaxerxes. It tells of Hippocrates' divine nature and healing: “this man is the prince of divine knowledge” [IV.3 ¶32]. See also [IV.3 ¶34]. The footnote points to Helmont, Tumulus Pestis [IV.3 n12]. Atwood uses the epistle as illustration.

summary: Cited for reference only.
In the Appendix, a region passed before entering the world's solution, after which the inner vision is the same for all.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that the inner vision is the same for all “after they have passed the phantasmagoric region” [APP ¶144] and entered the world's solution. The text does not explain the term further.

summary: Figured images produced by the mind's own fancy, or by nature and the demiurgic intellect, as distinct from the gods' true self-manifestation.
body: Atwood separates phantasms from the gods' true self-manifestation. Phantasms are figured images that come from the mind's own fancy, or from nature and the demiurgic intellect. She speaks of the case “if various phantasms are hurled forth before the presence of them” [II.4 ¶29].

summary: The imaginative spirit, the natural vehicle of our life and the vestibule of Reason; confusing and possessive while impure, it can be purified and refined by Intellect.
body:
In II.2 Atwood describes the imaginative spirit in man and animals. While impure it produces a 'phantastic life' and confusion and possession of the mind, and it is likened to the Sphinx: “such is said to be the nature of the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. It can be cleansed: “But the phantastic Spirit may be purified, even in brutes” [II.2 ¶13]. She links it with what Iamblicus calls the mundane spirit: “Thus Iamblicus, speaking of this mundane spirit, says” [II.2 ¶15].

In III.1 she places it in the soul's anatomy: “the Phantastic Spirit, which is the natural vehicle of our life” [III.1 ¶5]. She also links it to the natural intelligent Spirit: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe; and this intelligence, phantasic as it is and drawn without, may be called the vestibule of Reason” [III.1 ¶5].

Synesius, as Atwood quotes him, gives Intellect the work of purifying it: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20]. Intellect thins it and extends it toward Divinity. The text does not say it is the same as the Ethereal Spirit.

Asserted identities: mundane spirit [II.2 ¶15]; natural vehicle of our life [III.1 ¶5]; natural intelligent Spirit [III.1 ¶5].

summary: The imagination: a region of notions and instincts that hinders intellectual conception and, if it prevails, turns the inner life to folly.
body:
Olympiodorus, quoted by Atwood, calls it a hindrance: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12]. He also sets it against enthusiasm.

The ancients, as she reports them, describe “the region of the phantasy, with its notions and instincts” [II.2 ¶22]. Its contents are often more false, fleeting and evil than sense images, and it is dangerous to dwell in passively.

In her own voice, Atwood counts phantasy as a mode of the One Thing, alongside folly and passion: “the phantasy, if suffered to prevail, will convert all to her own folly in the internal life” [III.1 ¶21]. Once phantasy is subdued, the Ethereal Spirit abandons it.

summary: Religious groups Atwood names together in the Appendix as examples of religious self-will in history.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names these groups as historical examples of religious self-will [APP ¶110].

summary: Cited for reference only.
'The Jew Philo', whom Atwood cites for the rational part of man as God's temple and the soul as the impression of the Logos-seal.
body:
Atwood cites Philo in support of two points: that the rational part of man is God's temple, and that the soul bears the impression of the Logos-seal. “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]. The works named in her footnotes are De Praemiis et Poenis, De Nobilitate, De Profugis and De Plantatione Noe [II.1 n39, II.1 n40].

Elsewhere she lists Philo-Judaeus with Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus, Julian and Apuleius. These are Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, and she says she will quote them later [I.1 ¶27].

summary: An unnamed 'philosopher' cited throughout the book for a range of maxims on the work, the soul and illumination, usually in support of Atwood's points.
body:
The phrase 'the philosopher' stands for an unnamed authority at many points. The text does not show that it is always the same person.

- Within Hermes' text, the philosopher is cited for the permanent works [I.3 ¶30] and for the Botri saying: “Botri is made from the Citrine” [I.3 ¶41].
- On the soul, citing Plotinus's Select Works (Taylor, page 387) in a footnote: “When the soul is situated in the body, says the philosopher, she departs from self-contemplation” [II.1 ¶50, II.1 n44]. The point supported is that the purified soul recollects what it forgot.
- “Dimidium facti qui bene coepit habet” [III.1 ¶24], i.e. (ours) a good beginning is half the work.
- On the Night of Matter: “By no means, says the philosopher” [III.2 ¶55]. Here the point is that the mind receives the formless rather than understanding nothing.
- The worker should work faithfully until it be the Divine pleasure to make the work appear [III.3 ¶80].
- On the Gordian Knot: “who is he that is bale to untie it, enquires the philosopher?” [IV.1 ¶37].
- “Labor to know causes” [IV.1 ¶44]. Atwood endorses this as the condition of success.
- On self-preparation, invitation and sudden illumination: “Fit thy roof to thy God in all thou canst” [IV.2 ¶39, IV.2 ¶41].

summary: Genuine seekers of the Stone, as against knaves and sordid chemists; the disciplined, proven person to whom alone Nature gives up her casket.
body: Atwood separates true philosophers from impostors. Experiments went on in secret “both by knaves and philosophers” [I.1 ¶55], and the philosopher stands apart from idlers and 'sordid chemists'. In her account Nature gives her secret only to the qualified: “she will surrender to none but a philosopher, one too that has been disciplined in her schools” [III.4 ¶13]. That is someone tried and proven able to bear the sacred trust.

summary: The adepts as a group, cited for doctrines on the First Matter, gold, and spirit and body; Atwood also notes they are silent on key preparations.
body:
Atwood cites 'the philosophers' as a group for several doctrines:

- The First Matter is sought inwardly: “The First Matter is not to be found on earth, as the philosophers say” [APP ¶137] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer).
- As Hermes reports, they praise gold: “this gold, in relation of other bodies, is as the sun amongst the stars” [I.3 ¶58].
- Spirit and body must be joined for generation: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
- In ancient times they dug out the saving Salt and exalted it by circulating media [IV.4 ¶20].

She also points out their limits. None of them shows how to obtain the two mercuries. They pass over that point 'very slightly' and treat the preparation of Mercury 'in silence'. The Adepts say more about the last operations than about the First, so reading them alone will hardly suffice [IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶16].

summary: Authorities cited within Norton's verse on working 'within locks nyne' and on the importance of a fitting place.
body: These authorities speak inside Norton's verse, which Atwood quotes: “Philosophers said, by their engine, How it should be wrought within locks nyne” [III.4 ¶41]. The passage also stresses how much a fitting place matters for the work.

summary: Not common gold but a living, luminous, purified substance that ripens and perfects other bodies; also the transmuting powder in Van Helmont's projection.
body:
In Van Helmont's account, quoted by Atwood, it is a transmuting powder: he projected “one grain of the philosophers’ gold upon some thousands of grains of boiling quicksilver” [I.1 ¶76]. In Khunrath's words it is identified with “the blood of the Lion, which is the gold of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶81]. It may also be read as the universal tincture; the text leaves this open.

Atwood's own account, drawing on the adepts, makes it a living substance, not metal: “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63]. It has a heavenly complexion, and it ripens and perfects other bodies. Paradoxically “the gold of the wise is more heavy than lead” [I.3 ¶61], and it is made into Ixir with a fiery water.

Asserted identities: living gold, “The gold of the philosophers, or living gold, as they sometimes call their luminous concrete” [I.3 n65]; our earth, “our earth is gold” [I.3 ¶62]; the blood of the Lion [I.1 ¶81].

headword: Philosophers of tyme old / olde Fathers
summary: Earlier authorities criticized inside a quoted poem for describing the making of Magnesia while hiding imbibition.
body: Inside a poem Atwood quotes, the 'Philosophers of tyme old' or 'olde Fathers' are faulted for describing the creation of Magnesia while concealing imbibition: “The secret of Imbibition never out tould;” [III.1 ¶65].

summary: The body of the work, which carries a shadowy darkness with it until it is purified of sensual defilements.
body: Atwood writes in a footnote: “A shadowy darkness passes always along with the philosophic body” [I.3 n21]. The darkness stays with it until the body is purified of sensual defilements.

summary: In Eudoxus, a purely natural calcination of the Stone that sublimes and distills it and increases its radical humidity, unlike destructive common calcination by fire.
body: Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, calls it “a philosophic calcination which is purely natural” [IV.3 ¶16]. He contrasts it with common calcination by violence of fire, which destroys the body: “this philosophical calcination, which sublimes and distills the Stone in calcining it, much augments its humidity” [IV.3 ¶16]. It preserves and increases the Stone's radical humidity.

summary: In Eirenaeus, things whose exact preparation is the first degree of perfection in the Art; not explained further.
body: Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, says: “the exact preparation of the philosophic Eagles may be considered the first degree of perfection in this Art” [IV.1 ¶11]. The text does not explain what the Eagles are.

summary: The process in which Life's substance is wholly transmuted, its threefold property developed and the forms of the Medial Spirit put out, followed by radical destruction and New Generation.
body: Atwood writes: “as Life passes through the philosophic fermentation, its substance is entirely transmuted” [III.2 ¶28]. In this process the threefold property of Life is developed and its heterogeneous parts are divided. The forms of the Medial Spirit are extinguished, and a radical destruction and a New Generation follow [III.2 ¶28].

summary: The field where, in Atwood's figure, the Prototypes of the sacrificial beasts remain feeding and fattening; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood speaks of the sacrificial beasts “whilst their Prototypes remain feeding and fattening in the Philosophic Field” [III.2 ¶44]. The passage gives no further explanation of the expression.

summary: The realm whose powers, Atwood says, are shaken and defiled during the putrefaction.
body: In Atwood's account of the putrefaction, “the powers of the Philosophic Heaven are so wonderfully shaken and defiled” [III.1 ¶58]. The text does not define the Philosophic Heaven further here.

equivalences.with: mens sublimes et mare patens (a mind sublime, and an open sea)
entelechy of body bearing the spirit

summary: The subject of the Hermetic work: hidden in the central motion of mineral life, called by many names, properly the Stone in concrete form, and described as an excruciated ens of Light.
body:
Atwood treats the philosophic matter as the subject of the work. It lies hidden “in the central motion of the mineral life, where the spirit is first coagulated and conceives itself into a concrete form” [I.3 n13]. It has many names: she notes one author who “eloquently identifies the philosophic matter, calling it mens sublimes et mare patens” (a mind sublime, and an open sea) [I.3 n13], and says that “in the concrete form, and for reasons before given in part, it has been properly called the Stone” [I.3 n16].

In Part IV she describes it as “the philosophic matter, drawn in part from the heterogeneous air and defiled breath of vitality” [IV.1 ¶46], which is purified into an immortal Form of Light. She mentions that Basil Valentine goes on to describe it after the passage she quotes (“before proceeding to a description of the Philosophic Matter” [III.2 ¶19]), but that description is not given there.

Quoted voices: in Hermes, the Son bears the Matter, which has a fixed watery form; the Master says “For this Son is the treasury, bearing even (in his hand) the Philosophic Matter” [IV.2 ¶14].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood gives two definitions: “The Philosophic Matter is an excruciated ens of Light”, “alight extracted through anguish from Life” [APP ¶84]; and “The Philosophical matter is the entelechy of body bearing the spirit” [APP ¶178].

Asserted identities: = the Stone [I.3 n16]; = mens sublimes et mare patens [I.3 n13]; = excruciated ens of Light [APP ¶84]; = entelechy of body bearing the spirit [APP ¶178].

summary: In the Appendix, being conversant with the soul in her philosophy: the recreative, or rather separative, process.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood glosses the philosophic process as being “conversant with the soul in her philosophy --- i.e., the recreative, or rather separative, process” [APP ¶181].

summary: A figure in the Art whose will, unlike natural species, is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light; the text does not define it directly.
body: Atwood writes that “the will of the philosophic Proteus is free to be drawn without hindrance” [I.2 ¶48]. Unlike natural species, it is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light. The context apparently ties it to the fermented Vital Spirit, but the passage does not define it.

summary: A Salt discovered in the work, glossed as the voluntary bond; its solution is the Second Work, and knowing it is the secret of the Ancient Sages.
body:
Atwood says that the stated periods of the work are often metaphorical: “the periods are often to be understood metaphorically with respect to the discovery of the philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶17]. She glosses it as the voluntary bond, writing of “the Solution of the Philosophic Salt (i.e., the voluntary bond)” [IV.1 ¶36]. This solution is the Second Work, and “He who knows the Salt and its solution, knows the secret of the Ancient Sages.” [IV.1 ¶37].

Asserted identity: = the voluntary bond [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: The Matter considered as the subject of the work: universal, with perfective virtues, burdened with superfluities, and prepared by slow, gentle, continuous trituration.
body:
Atwood uses the term for the Matter as the subject on which the work is done. She speaks of “the alleged virtue and perfective properties of the Philosophic Subject” [I.2 ¶34], which go beyond ordinary light phenomena, and calls it universal, so that every epithet fits it: “inasmuch as nothing can be said amiss of a Universal Subjet” [I.2 ¶37].

She defers its full treatment, saying the mystical death and regeneration will become clearer “when we come to treat of the manifestation of the Philosophic Subject” [II.3 ¶56]. The ass's qualities are “very applicable and necessary to be found in the Philosophic Subject” [III.2 ¶64] if it is to carry out the Divine behests.

In Part IV the subject is prepared by hand (“Preparation of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶2]). It is burdened with “such a mass of heterogeneous superfluities adhering to our subject” [IV.1 ¶7], and is worked by “the trituration of the Philosophic Subject, which ought to be slow, gentle, and continuous” [IV.1 ¶13].

summary: The vessel of the work, concealed by Hermes, described as having an apparatus of nerves, veins and alembics, and best when it accords with the vessel of nature.
body:
Atwood notes that “Hermes has chosen to conceal the philosophic vessel” [I.3 n48]. The context places the science in all bodies and its preparation in the innermost chamber of life.

Later she describes “the Philosophic Vessel and its multiform distillatory apparatus, of nerves, veins, and alembics” [III.4 ¶30]. The best vessel is “She that concordeth with vessel of nature” [III.4 ¶31]. It is finally constructed and vitrified by the Spirit and is called 'oracular'. The described apparatus apparently suggests a vessel within the living body, but the records do not state this directly.

summary: The one water from which all things grow and into which they dissolve, containing its own sulfur; Hermes' Aqua Philosophica that dissolves the elements.
body:
Atwood speaks of things “which have their growth all from the same identical water, and are resolved into the same again” [I.3 n5]. This water is divided into four relations and contains its own sulfur: “this water or mercury of the adepts has, within itself, its own good sulfur” [I.3 n5].

In the voice of Hermes it is addressed: “O, blessed watery pontic form, that dissolvest the elements” [I.3 ¶27]. Its dissolution of the composition is the key of restoration. Atwood's note on this passage adds: “Great is the reputed virtue of this Aqua Philosophica, which distills itself finally to manifestation by the Art of Life” [I.3 n36]. It cleanses inwardly and itself, and, joined in consciousness with the central Efficient, becomes the key of every magic art. It is learned only by practice.

Asserted identity: = mercury of the adepts [I.3 n5].

summary: The work proper, begun only after right motive and complete purification, with a threefold order of operation concealed by the Adepts and distinct from the preliminary practice.
body:
Zachary, as quoted, advises reading the philosophers and praying “before thou extendest thy Hand to the Philosophic Work” [III.4 ¶20]. An unclear voice equates the work with the practice: “the practice (that is of the ultimate Philosophic Work)” [III.4 ¶44].

Atwood says “few are chosen to proceed with the Philosophic Work” [IV.1 ¶31] out of those who consult on the means. It begins only after the right Motive, complete mundification and crystalline diaphaneity, so that only then can it be said “that the Philosophic Work has been said truly to being” [IV.1 ¶48]. Everything before is preparatory. She supports this with verse: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49].

Part IV.2 is headed “Of the Philosophic or Subtle Work” [IV.2 ¶1]. There Atwood says that “in the Philosophic Work, preceding her, there is a threefold order of legitimate operation” [IV.2 ¶3], which the Adepts concealed. Norton's verse calls it 'this Subtill Werke'.

Asserted identities: = Subtle Work [IV.2 ¶1]; = the practice [III.4 ¶44].

summary: A process out of which the Matter first appears pure and white; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood reports that the Matter comes forth “pure, as they say, and white, out of the philosophical contrition” [I.2 ¶36]. The term is not further explained there.

summary: In the Appendix, the dissolution in which soul and spirit separate from the breathless body, held to it as by a thread until refixation.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “In the Philosophical dissolution of the body, soul and spirit are separate” [APP ¶96]. They remain joined to the breathless body as by a thread until refixation.

summary: A product of the work whose divine virtues wise men admire; things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it.
body: Atwood mentions “the Philosophical Elixir, whose divine virtues wise men so much admire” [I.2 ¶49]. Things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it. Nearby she separately names 'the elixir of the wise' as the result of superior skill and coction in vegetal life [I.2 ¶46]; the text does not say the two are the same.

equivalences.with: an appetition of reason for its antecedent light

summary: Reason's desire for its antecedent light.
body:
Atwood defines philosophy as reason's longing for its source: “philosophy was a desire of this kind, an appetition of reason for its antecedent light” [II.1 ¶44].

Asserted identity: = an appetition of reason for its antecedent light [II.1 ¶44].

summary: A piece in Ashmole's collection that Atwood counts among the most instructive.
body: Atwood lists *Philosophy and Experience* among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64].

summary: In quoted verse, the bright appearance that follows the blackness and its strange colours, and the coming God whom only the pure can endure.
body: The term appears in quoted verse. Bloomfield, as quoted, says that after the blackness and its strange colours, “Then shall Phoebus appear first out” [IV.2 ¶36], signalling the joy to come. In the hymn (Callimachus) Phoebus is the coming God whom only the pure endure: “Bright Phoebus comes and thunders at the gate.” [IV.2 ¶38]. In context this apparently marks the light that follows the dark stage of the work.

summary: Atwood's figure for something with a reviviscent spirit that passed from East to West, apparently alchemy; in a quoted source, the deep red bird that appears after the fire.
body:
Atwood writes that “our Phoenix too bestirred herself, and passed into the West” [I.1 ¶37], around the twelfth century, and gives it a 'reviviscent spirit'. The context suggests the Phoenix here stands for alchemy itself, but this is an inference.

Cornelius Agrippa's ingenious disciple, as quoted, describes the Phoenix that appears after the fire is fortified: “It is a red bird of a most deep color with a shining fiery hue.” [III.1 ¶50]. It is fed with the fire of its father as meat and the ether of its mother as drink.

summary: Medicine as Crollius describes it: a knowledge to be tried by fire, inseparable from pyrotechny, and practised by the physician.
body: Crollius, as quoted, says “the trial of the knowledge of physic is to be made by fire” [III.1 ¶10]. In his account physic cannot be separated from pyrotechny, and it is practised by the 'physician'.

summary: Atwood's two divergent kinds of science, physical (external, sensory, utilitarian) and moral (inward); neither can prove or disprove the other, and the Hermetic Science would include both.
body: Atwood contrasts the two. The Physical sciences rest on an external basis, take the senses as evidence and practical utility as their end. The Moral sciences have their evidence and object within the mind and slight worldly benefits. The two diverge, with “the Spiritual unable to prove itself absolutely, or the Material to disprove the other practically” [IV.4 ¶11]. The Hermetic Science would include both.

summary: Kirchberger's term, endorsed by Atwood: making the invisible spirit visible, by taking the infinite Light-nature into bound through hypostatic multiplication of its image.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood adopts Kirchberger's term. The physical problem is “the making visible the invisible spirit” [APP ¶93]: taking the infinite Light-nature into bound by hypostatic multiplication of its image.

summary: The Art whose 'obstetric hand' assists the Stone's own regenerative self-manifestation.
body: In the words of the mysterious adeptest, the Stone is “made manifest by itself regeneratively by the obstetric hand of the Physico-Chemical Art” [III.3 ¶50]. The Art apparently assists, as a midwife does, a manifestation the Stone accomplishes itself.

summary: A writer whose De Auro Atwood cites to link Alchemy with profound metaphysics and to report a friend making gold and silver in his presence.
body: Picus di Mirandola is named in a list of authorities [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his *de Auro* (*Opus Aureum de Auro*) to support the link of Alchemy with profound metaphysical science [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n69]. She also cites *De Auro* for his testimony that a friend made gold and silver in his presence: “I have seen it and done it myself” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n103]. Atwood uses him as a supporting witness.

summary: A writer on the Elixir in Ashmole's collection whom Atwood cites on the Matter and the Stone, and on the piety needed by the seeker.
body:
Atwood names Pierce the Black Monk among the 'ecclesiastics of different orders' who agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She counts his *Fragment* among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64].

From his verses on the Elixir she quotes a recipe for the Stone with the Water of Might: “In Arsenic sublimed there is a way straight” [III.3 ¶16, III.3 n6]. From the same work in Ashmole's *Theatr.* she takes support for the view that the subject is a seed from a body, not common gold and silver. The seeker must be pious, charitable and prayerful, and covetous men never find it: “Therefore there ys no other waye But to take thee to thy beades and pray:” [III.4 ¶21, III.4 n23]. Atwood cites him in support.

summary: A philosopher Atwood cites widely, for veiled hyperphysical philosophy, self-knowledge, philosophic death, intellectual intuition and the Matter; she declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.
body:
Atwood cites Plato many times, almost always in support.

**Veiled philosophy.** From many dialogues and Epistle II she takes his hyperphysical, veiled philosophy and his dread of writing the truth: “it is a parturition respecting this ingenerated in the soul, from which he who is not liberated will never in reality acquire truth” [I.1 ¶17, I.1 n23]. She suggests the science behind it was practical but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher. She mentions him as translated by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. She also places him in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25].

**Self-knowledge and the Mysteries.** From the *First Alcibiades*: “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n33]; he “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51]. From the *Phaedo*: assimilation through the Greater Mysteries and the divine eye, “better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶5, II.2 ¶8], and philosophic death, “it is the business of philosophers to study how to be dead” [II.3 ¶37]. Wisdom belongs to old age, meaning intuitive Intellect free of imaginative error; he condemns 'two-fold ignorance' [II.2 ¶13].

**Descent and ascent.** “It is necessary that a man should have his right opinion as firm as adamant in him when he descends into Hades” [II.3 ¶12]. He likens the soul's descent into generation to an earthquake [II.3 ¶20], and compares Glaucus deformed by weeds to the viscous soul [II.3 ¶30]. On intuition: “on a sudden a light, as it were a leaping fire, will be enkindled in the soul, and will there itself nourish itself” [II.3 ¶50]. Pure souls see visions “resident in a Pure Light” [II.4 ¶29]. “Plato beautifully unfolds the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] through love, hope and faith. Atwood reads his “there are many more thrysus bearers than Bacchic souls” [II.4 ¶54] as meaning that many have the fire but cannot draw it forth.

**The Matter.** He places earth within heaven: he “calls it the most ancient element within the heaven” [III.2 ¶36]. Matter is grasped “by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53]. The *Timaeus* is read as alluding to the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶38], and “the Quintessence of Plato” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. Via Olympiodorus his Tartarus is read ethically, physically and psychically [III.2 ¶9], and via Proclus the Meadow is the prolific power of life [II.4 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for alchemy being understood only by those “conversant with the soul in her philosophy” [APP ¶181].

summary: Cited for reference only.
A late Platonic writer Atwood cites for Sacred Arts replacing lost revelation, an exhortation to inner stillness, and the soul's ascent from image to Archetype.
body: Atwood cites the Platonic Successor, via Iamblichus on the Mysteries and Taylor's notes, for the view that Sacred Arts replace lost spontaneous revelation: “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53, II.1 n46]. She praises the 'magnificence of thought and diction' of his exhortation to inner stilling and adoration of the First: “Now, if ever, to remove from ourselves multiform knowledge” [II.4 ¶41]. She also cites him on the soul's ascent from image to Archetype and its recovery after falling from the vision of God: “he will again, says the Platonic Successor, be elevated” [III.3 ¶26]. In every case she endorses him.

summary: The later Platonists, whose 'highly elevated philosophy' Atwood says agrees in the same divine tradition.
body: Atwood cites the Platonic successors to show that their 'highly elevated philosophy' agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

summary: Cited by Atwood as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being.
body: Atwood cites Platonic theology as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being [III.2 ¶33].

summary: Paired voices Atwood cites for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or known only as nothing.
body: Atwood cites the Platonist and the Kabalist together for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or is known as nothing [III.2 ¶57].

summary: The Platonic school, cited by Atwood for the whiteness of true Being, the origin of matter, the Epic Cycle as a secret of creation, and the Mysteries as Initia.
body: Atwood cites the Platonists in support: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9], and she draws on their view of the origin of matter [III.2 ¶9]. She reports them as saying that the Epic Cycle includes the true philosophic secret of creation [III.3 ¶42]. 'The Platonist' is cited again for the Mysteries having been called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she contrasts them with Behmen: the Platonists are more scientific and less descriptive [APP ¶62].

summary: Author of the Hist. Nat., whom Atwood cites on Ostanes bringing the Persian spirit to Greece, Democritus' fame and occult practice, and Caligula's failed attempts.
body: Atwood cites Pliny's *Hist. Nat.* (lib. xxx, cap. I; lib. 33, cap. 4) in support of three points: Ostanes brought the Persian spirit to Greece; Democritus was famous for experiment and practised in secret; and Caligula's attempts failed [I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶18, I.1 n13, I.1 n17, I.1 n26]. She quotes: “Plenum miraculi et hoc pariter utrasque artes effloruisse, medicinam dico, magiciemque eadem aetate” (our rendering: this too is full of wonder, that both arts flourished together, medicine, I mean, and magic, in the same age) [I.1 ¶12].

summary: Neoplatonist philosopher Atwood cites heavily in support of inward withdrawal, sudden divine Light, union with the source and pure Matter; the later Appendix qualifies his account of First Matter.
body: Named among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27], and among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9]; Atwood calls him ‘the graceful Plotinus’ [II.1 ¶39]. She cites him in support throughout: on the same doctrine while condemning suicide [II.3 ¶37]; on the soul's participation of Deity, perceiving “that the supplier of life is present” [II.3 ¶46]; on the beauty of the gods seen through Intellect — “All the gods, says Plotinus, are beautiful, and their splendour is intense.” [II.4 ¶29; II.4 n17]; on the sudden arrival of the One: “He comes, says Plotinus, suddenly alone” [II.4 ¶50]. From the Select Works and Ennead 5 she takes the sudden Light of Intellect — “a sudden Light, and this Light is from Intellect, and is also It” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n31] — and approach to the universal subject through an image, a portion of gold [III.1 ¶32; III.1 n37]; and again “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41; IV.2 n28]. With Porphyry he is the source of her summary on the Subject of bodies, analysis and pure divine Matter, that “there should be a Nature primarily vital which is also formless, indestructible and immortal” [III.2 ¶46–49; III.2 n38–39]; n38 says he alludes to the mystical analysis. He supports knowledge of real beings by self-investigation, where “the reality is testified by reminiscence” [III.2 ¶50], and asks how the infinite is conceived — the Indefinite by the Indefinite [III.2 ¶53]; and inward conversion, union with Divine nature, the soul's middle order and the value of its fall from the treatise on the Descent of the Soul: “Often when by an intellectual energy, I am roused from body and converted to myself” [III.2 ¶50; III.2 n41]; union as experimental ingress requires that one “separate body from the man and its defilements” [III.2 ¶66]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is referred to on how pure matter is generated [APP ¶43] but qualified: he gives only the metaphysic of the First Matter's generation, never realized so — “a recessure of reason behind itself into the indefinite intermediate between reason and the Absolute” [APP ¶137].

summary: Author Atwood cites, as ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, on Chemia, the passions as impediments, the Moon and Sun, Typhon's names and the fable's meaning.
body: Atwood cites Plutarch for the etymology of Chemia: Egypt was called Cham/Chemia for its black soil, and “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated” [I.1 ¶5]. From De Iside et Osiride, calling him ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, she takes support for senses and passions as impediments, the rites preparing the aspirant for knowledge of the Supreme Mind: “the souls of men are not able to participate of the Divine nature whilst they are thus encompassed about with senses and passions” [II.1 ¶50; II.1 n45]. He supports the Moon as reason and Wisdom, the Sun as force: “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n49]; he explains that Typhon's names Seth and Bebo import violent restraint, contrariety and subversion [III.1 ¶63]; and he is cited, with the Adepts, as witness to the fable's meaning [IV.2 ¶7].

summary: The soul's subtle vehicle which, when humid and condensed, presents apparitions to the inner sense.
body: Atwood speaks of “our pneumatic vehicle, becoming humid and condensed beneath her heaven” [II.3 ¶22]; in this state it presents apparitions to the inner sense, and the soul looking outward “beholds the shadow and images of her vaporous vehicle” [II.3 ¶27]. Whether the ‘vaporous vehicle’ is the same as the pneumatic vehicle is apparently implied by the context, not stated.

summary: The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus, praised for sublime doctrine and cited as testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect.
body: Atwood praises the Divine Poimander for sublimity of doctrine, though it concerns divine capabilities and regeneration rather than their physical ground [I.1 ¶7]. From book 2 she takes a testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect to which, she says, nothing can be added: “For the sleep of the body was the sober watchfulness of the mind” [III.3 ¶58; III.3 n36]. It supplies language for the real suffering passions cause in the revealed light — they “do force the inwardly placed man to suffer sensibly” [III.3 ¶71]. From book 10, introduced with ‘Yet’ against an impossibility she has stated, it teaches that one must enlarge the self beyond body and time to understand God, self-limitation being the obstacle and knowing, willing and hoping the way: “for the like is intelligible by the like” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n51]. A passage cited with the Book of Wisdom (chap. 11, ver. 22) illustrates the world held before divine vision: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

summary: An unnamed poet quoted for a line on the black soot bringing light and a phrase on the remoteness of the discovery.
body: An unnamed poet supplies a couplet illustrating that the black soot brings light: “Adferet haec Phoebi nigra favilla jubar.” [I.3 n22] (ours: ‘This black ash will bring the radiance of Phoebus’). Another phrase illustrates how remote the discovery is: “reclusa resedet longius” [III.1 ¶13] (ours, roughly: ‘withdrawn, it lies further off’).

summary: Poets in general, whose fables Atwood reads as veils of the vaporous estate, the Intelligible Sun, and receptive versus presumptuous approach.
body: Atwood reads the poets' Pan as a veil for the vaporous estate and its frightening disguises [II.3 ¶20]. Within the Platonic Successor's passage the Sun from which the Intelligible gods proceed is described as “emerging, as the Poets say, from the bosom of the ocean” [II.4 ¶41]. The stories of Actaeon and Endymion illustrate that presumptuous striving repels while sleeping receptivity receives the presence: “to the sleeping Endymion she vouchsafed her willing presence” [III.2 ¶57].

summary: Poets and traditionalists who, by the Walls of Troy built by Apollo's music, meant the insphering of the lower life (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Walls of Troy, said to be built by Apollo's music, are what the poets and traditionalists meant as a figure of the insphering of the lower life [APP ¶49].

summary: A point in the process with no attraction, only indifference to life and death, when the Artist must stir up the Motion.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Alchemists, with Atwood's endorsement, say “there is a point of passivity” [APP ¶82]: a point in the process with no attraction but indifference to both life and death, at which the Artist must stir up the Motion.

summary: The adepts' name for what is entered for the dissolution, ‘the greatest poison’; the root of the Science is also called ‘a deadly poison’.
body: Atwood reports that the adepts call what is entered for the dissolution the greatest poison — “adepts describe it indeed as the greatest poison” [III.1 ¶56] — and that the root of the Science is called deadly: “because the root of this Science is a deadly poison” [III.1 ¶61]. The text does not say outright whether these are the same thing. Resolved into a subtle water, the poison coagulates our Mercury into silver [III.1 ¶56].

summary: In the Adept's loadstone figure, the point toward which the center turns, where the steel's virtue strengthens and the heart of the mercury, a true Fire, lies.
body: Speaking through a quoted Adept: “This center turns naturally towards the Pole where the virtue of the steel is gradually strengthened.” [IV.2 ¶30]; “In this Pole is the heart of the mercury, which is a true Fire” [IV.2 ¶30], in which its Lord rests. The figure is the loadstone and steel; its plain meaning is not stated in the record.

summary: The just weight or proportion in which, per Eirenaeus, the first water is joined to the body.
body: Quoting Eirenaeus: one is “to join it to the body in a just pondus” [III.1 ¶14] — the first water joined to the body in just weight or proportion.

summary: Author Atwood cites as a genuine seeker: he erred two hundred times, held the Fire the unrevealed key, and taught nothing in the subject is discarded.
body: Pontanus's Epistola appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶36; I.1 n41]. He is listed with Rupicessa, De Meun, Flamel, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]. From his Epistle (Theat. Chem.) Atwood takes in support that he erred two hundred times, that the Fire is the unrevealed key found only by profound meditation: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n40]. He also supports that nothing in the subject is to be discarded, superfluities being converted into essence by the Fire: “he who pretends to separate anything from our subject knows nothing of philosophy” [IV.3 ¶7].

summary: Something without which, along with Theurgic assistance, one cannot transcend the consciousness of this life; not explained further here.
body: Atwood writes: “Without the Pontic Medium, without Theurgic assistance we are unable to transcend the consciousness of this life” [II.4 ¶49]. The passage does not explain the term.

summary: The manner in which the Argent vive is generated: by a reciprocal alternation, passing its virtue hand to hand.
