body: Atwood says the Argent vive “is generated pontically, as it were by a reciprocal alternation” [IV.1 ¶11], distributing its advanced virtue by hand to hand. Not otherwise explained.

summary: Eudoxus's name for the viscous liquor thickening under repeated affusion, also called Water of Life and the great Lunaria.
body: Quoting Eudoxus: “the philosophers give this viscous Liquor the name of Pontick Water” [IV.3 ¶9]; the liquor thickens under repeated affusion, and its exuberant ponticity is the character of its virtue. Asserted identities: = Water of Life — “It has been called the Water of Life, because it gives life to the metals” [IV.3 ¶9]; = great Lunaria — “it is properly called the great Lunaria, because of its brightness wherewith it shines” [IV.3 ¶9].

summary: Pope, whose Homer's Iliad Atwood quotes while criticizing his rendering of the heroic tears as ‘unavailing’.
body: Atwood quotes Pope's Iliad, book 18 — “Patroclus dead, Achilles hates to live.” [III.1 ¶29; III.1 n35] — and criticizes him for rendering the heroic tears ‘unavailing’ [III.1 ¶30].

summary: Pope said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it.
body: Atwood reports that Pope John XXII is said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it, illustrating its continued secret pursuit [I.1 ¶55].

summary: Pope's Homer's Odyssey, book 8, read as figuring the dominion of Intellect and the sea barring the goal.
body: Atwood quotes Pope's Odyssey, book 8 — “In wondrous ships self-moved, instinct with mind;” [IV.1 ¶20; IV.1 n20] — reading the Phoeacian ships and Alcinous' court as the dominion of Intellect and the vast sea as the barrier before the goal [IV.1 ¶21–24; IV.1 n21].

summary: Author of Mundorum Explicatoio, quoted for verse on the sphere where God displays himself to himself.
body: Atwood quotes Pordage's Mundorum Explicatoio (p. 320): “Here ‘tis that God himself t’ himself displays” [III.2 ¶18; III.2 n19], illustrating the sphere of divine self-display.

summary: A school Atwood says is not to be undervalued, on the same original track as Boehme.
body: Atwood says the Pordage and Lead school is not to be undervalued, being on the same original track as Boehme [I.1 ¶68].

summary: Neoplatonist whose Auxiliaries to Intelligibles and Cave of the Nymphs Atwood cites on purification, the twofold death, the soul's reunion with its source and pure Matter.
body: Named among the Alexandrian revival figures [I.1 ¶27], the Neoplatonists who dilate on the same ground [II.1 ¶39] and whose writings show the Mysteries [II.2 ¶9], and in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25]. His Auxiliaries supply a chapter motto: “It s necessary that the soul, when purified, should associate with its Generator.” [II.3 ¶2; cf. II.3 ¶43]. A moist spirit binds the soul to images and earth: “If the soul on its departure, says Porphyry, still possesses a spirit turbid from humid exhalations, it then attracts to itself a shadow and becomes heavy” [II.3 ¶27; II.3 n29]; leaving nature makes it a dry splendor. He explains the twofold death, which Atwood glosses — “the other peculiar to philosophers, in which the soul is liberated from the body” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n45]. His Hymn to Plotinus illustrates waking vision: “Nor was the vision like the dreams of sleep, But seen whilst vigilant you brave the deep” [II.3 ¶51; II.3 n57]. The Cave of the Nymphs supports the northern and southern gates as descent into generation and ascent to divinity [II.4 ¶7; II.4 n2]; the self-reflexive vision is “a fountain, not flowing outwardly, but circularly scattering its streams into itself” [II.4 ¶15; II.4 n6]. When discipline is complete “the motions themselves will be dissolved through their proximity to the reasoning power” [II.4 ¶36–37; II.4 n25]. Additions of place or selfhood veil the Eternal Essence; “being established in yourself and in your own Essence, you will be assimilated to the Intelligible Universe” [III.2 ¶59; III.2 n44]. With Plotinus he is co-source of the summary on pure Matter [III.2 ¶46], and ‘the Greek Porphyry’ appears in the Ammonius story [III.2 ¶64].

summary: A product which, like the philosophers' stone, takes its beginning from the divine water (per Hermolaus Barbarus).
body: Quoting Hermolaus Barbarus, the divine water is that “whence potable gold, and the stone of philosophers, takes its beginning” [I.1 ¶20].

summary: The transmuting agent in the Dee/Kelly story, found at Glastonbury and so strong its true height had to be found by trial.
body: In the Dee/Kelly story Atwood relates the finding of “a large quantity of the Powder of Projection in a niche amongst the ruins of Glastonbury Abbey” [I.1 ¶66]; it was so strong (1 upon 272,330) that its ‘true height’ had to be found by trial.

summary: Transmuting powder said by Dickenson to have been found in Lully's cell, enriching the workmen.
body: Per Dickenson, “a certain quantity of the powder of transmutation” [I.1 ¶47] was found in Lully's cell and enriched the workmen.

summary: What secrecy ensured could be discovered only by the long labour of an experienced, upright mind.
body: Atwood says secrecy was kept “that the Power might only be discovered through the long labour of an experienced and upright mind” [III.4 ¶9].

summary: The double capacity figured by Cheiron, who educates the Heroic Fire and rectifies the Armed Magnet.
body: Atwood describes Cheiron “in his double capacity of Power and Motive in alliance” [IV.1 ¶33], educating the Heroic Fire and rectifying the Armed Magnet.

summary: The Light shining in darkness within man, identified with the true Light; an enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple.
body: Atwood: “This therefore is that Power which is hidden in man, the true Light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [II.3 ¶55] — thus = the true Light. It is “An enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple” [II.3 ¶55].

summary: One of three modes of consciousness, with the sensible and perceptive, which conjoined to them makes them efficient (Appendix).
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names three modes: “either in the sensible, the perceptive, or the power life; this last conjoined to the other two makes them efficient” [APP ¶45].

summary: The operative procedure of the Hermetic work, which Atwood seeks to understand rather than exhibit, touching only certain particulars.
body: Atwood distinguishes understanding from exhibiting the operative procedure: “But we are not yet proposing to exhibit the Practice, but only to understand it” [III.1 ¶56]. She sets out impediments and endowments “before we enter on the routine of Practice” [III.4 ¶2], and at the close says she has “suggested certain particulars concerning the Practice at this latter end” [IV.3 ¶54], which may be unfamiliar to the reader.

summary: Cited for reference only.
Mother of Hippocrates, of the race of the Heraclides.
body: Named as Hippocrates' mother, of the race of the Heraclides [IV.3 ¶32].

summary: Desire directed to its object, above all to God for wisdom; it collects the mind and, joined with labour, brings revelation, and esoterically works within the operations themselves.
body:
Atwood treats prayer first in a broad sense: “every desire of the mind is in its kind a prayer and preparative for the acquirement of its object” [III.4 ¶22]. Directed especially to God for wisdom, it collects the mind and, joined with labour (cooperation), brings revelation; “prayer especially, which is its principle exercise, is profitable for great undertakings” [III.4 ¶22]. She then goes further: “But the esoteric ground brings us acquainted with prayer in a far deeper sense” [III.4 ¶22], where prayer works within the operations of the Art; she reports that Iamblicus distinguishes three classes of prayer leading to union and the Divine Fire.

Asserted identities: prayer = the great desire of knowing — “for if you burn with a great desire of knowing them, that is prayer” [III.4 ¶22]; and prayer as the Divine Key — “It likewise is the Divine Key which opens to men the penetralia of Wisdom” [III.4 ¶24]. In the method, prayer thus appears both as the disposing desire of the operator and, in the deeper sense, as an active part of the work (the exact mode of that working is not spelled out in these records).

summary: The Preacher, cited by Atwood for the veiled, pointed nature of wise writings and for the need of a companion in the work.
body: Atwood cites the preacher twice. First, to illustrate the pointed, veiled character of the writings of the wise: “The words of the wise are as goads” [III.4 ¶19]. Second (with the reference Eccels. 4:8,9), in support of her point that the work needs a companion, a medium and a bond, since one alone labours endlessly: “Behold, two are better than one, says the Preacher” [III.4 ¶30; III.4 n27]. In both she uses him approvingly as support for her own position.

summary: The earlier, preliminary part of the practice, handed down inconsistently; Atwood holds that knowing it is insufficient without the ultimate theory.
body: Atwood speaks of the preliminary practice as handed down inconsistently, and insists that mastery of it does not suffice without the ultimate theory: there are “many even with a perfect knowledge of the preliminary work, and having the true Matter in Hand also and means of purification” [IV.2 ¶4] who nevertheless fail.

summary: The preparatory stage of the work: for Flamel, preparing the prime agents, the hardest part; for Atwood, a stage exercising every faculty of the mind, sometimes lasting years.
body:
Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood, makes the preparation of the first principles or prime agents the most difficult part of the work, after which the magistery is easy: “For knowing the preparations of the prime agents, and then literally following the directions in my book, I could not then miss the work if I would.” [I.1 ¶57].

In Atwood's own voice the Preparation is a stage in which no part of the concord may be left out: one must not “deny any faculty of the mind its due exercise in the Preparation” [III.4 ¶28]. She also notes its length: “Years have been employed by some in the Preparation” [IV.1 ¶17]. Whether her Preparation is the same as Flamel's preparation of the prime agents is not stated in these records See also Preparatory Practice and prime agents.

summary: A practice Atwood defers to a later discussion, there to show the value of assistance; Norton describes it.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) postpones discussion of the Preparatory Practice to a later point, where the value of assistance will be clearer: “when we come to speak of the Preparatory Practice which Norton, naively, and without much envy, describes” [III.4 ¶36].

summary: In an adept's account, the spirit that dissolves and cleanses the body of Light and draws from it a second, tinging Spirit.
body: Voice: an adept quoted by Atwood. The Preparing Spirit dissolves and purifies the body of Light and extracts from it a Second, tinging Spirit: “The Preparing Spirit dissolves the body of Light, and cleanses it from the corrupting causes” [IV.1 ¶10].

summary: Zoroaster's term, which Atwood reads as the Fire Spirit of Life, the supernatural centre of every living thing, which the Art sought to multiply and exalt.
body:
An adept quoted by Atwood pairs the Prester with the Sun: “the miraculous conspiracy that is between the Prester and the Sun, the external and internal fire of life, the thing desiring and the thing desired” [II.3 ¶41].

Atwood herself identifies it: “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54] — the identity sustaining all things, the supernatural centre of every living thing. The perfection of the Art was “to multiply the Prester and place him in the most supreme Ether” [II.3 ¶56].

In a Chaldaic oracle she quotes, the Prester is the Flower of glowing Fire drawn from the matter springing from “The Matrix containing all things” [IV.2 ¶28]: “Whence is extracted a Prester the Flower of glowing Fire,” [IV.2 ¶28], flashing into the cavities of the world. The oracle passage is not further explained there.

summary: In Chaldaic oracle language used by Atwood, the powers of intellectual fire to which all things are subject and which follow their First Cause in order.
body: The phrase comes from the Chaldaic Oracle, taken up in Atwood's own discussion (the records do not separate the two voices sharply): “to these Intellectual Presters of Intellectual Fire all things are subservient by the persuasive will of the Father” [II.4 ¶33]; and “the Presters of Intellectual Fire follow in radiant order the will of their First Cause” [II.4 ¶38]. See Prester.

summary: In Flamel's account, the initial agents of the work, whose preparation must be known before the work can succeed.
body: Voice: Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood. The preparation of the prime agents is the key requirement: “knowing the preparations of the prime agents” [I.1 ¶57]. In the same account Flamel apparently uses the phrase in place of first principles, though the identity is not explicitly asserted. See Preparation.

summary: For some modern Kabalists cited by Atwood, the pure attracting vacuum or understanding, born of the concentrated Divinity, that draws the central efficient into will and operation.
body: Voice: some modern Kabalists, reported by Atwood. The primitive Ether is born of the concentrated Divinity like a shower from a cloud, and is identified as “the primitive Ether, which is the pure attracting vacuum, or understanding” [III.2 ¶13], which draws the central efficient to will and operation.

summary: An author cited from the Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection, whom Atwood uses to show that the student must gather the dispersed teaching and test it.
body: Atwood quotes the prince (work given as Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection) in support of her view that the student must collect the dispersed teaching and test it by experiment: “let the sapient artificer, concludes the prince, studiously peruse our books, collecting our dispersed intention” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n15].

summary: In Reuchlin, the second of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word: incorruptible, immutable and always subsistent.
body: Voice: Reuchlin, quoted by Atwood. Of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word, the second is set against the visible, changing nature: “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24].

summary: The beginning or principle of the work, which Atwood identifies with the intention; hard to find because the rational ferment lies hidden in our life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood identifies the principium with the intention: “The difficulty is to find this principium, the intention” [APP ¶35]. The difficulty arises because the rational ferment is hidden in our life.

summary: The one source to which all things, thoughts and actions are resolved and from which every particular can be recomposed; the final term of the soul's ascent.
body: Atwood presents the Principle as the end of the soul's ascent — the ascent rises “afterwards to the Principle of things” [III.3 ¶26] — and as the one source into which all things, thoughts, passions and actions are resolved. Whoever reaches it gains more than possession: “he will not alone have that Principle, and be able to compose and renumerate every former particular out of the same” [III.3 ¶39]. The method apparently involves resolving everything into its source and recomposing from it. See also Principle of things.

summary: For the Hebrew Kabalists, a principle remaining in the life of fallen individuals that will in time restore them to their source in higher perfection.
body: Voice: the Hebrew Kabalists / Rabbis, as Atwood reports them. Even after the fall, “the principle of reunion nevertheless abides in the generated life of individuals” [II.1 ¶41], and in time it will restore them to their source in a higher perfection.

summary: That with which the intellectual energy of the intelligible world keeps perpetual, tranquil contact, and from that contact generates Light.
body: Atwood writes that the intellectual energy of the intelligible world “generates Light through a perpetual tranquil and quiet contact with the Principle of things” [II.4 ¶16]. See Principle, where the same phrase names the final term of the soul's ascent [III.3 ¶26].

summary: A real and efficacious principle that Atwood holds lies latent in human life and can be known only under specified conditions.
body: Atwood asserts “a Principle of Universal Science latent in human life, real and efficacious” [II.1 ¶39], which can be known only under specified conditions.

summary: What the Hermetic names Sulphur, Salt, Mercury and the elements refer to, as opposed to qualities; in Eudoxus, the principles of 'our Mercury' separated in the Third Key.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood states that the Hermetic names — Sulphur, Salt, Mercury, water, air, fire — refer to principles, not qualities, though “in the spirit they become qualities” [APP ¶81].

Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, speaks of the principles of 'our Mercury' (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury), extracted after sublimation and then separated and purified in the Third Key: “the separation and the purification of the Principles of our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶7].

equivalences.with: three leaves of the inner book

summary: In Boehme, the three leaves of the inner book (the image of God) in which he finds all that scripture teaches.
body: Voice: Boehme, quoted by Atwood. The inner book he opened, the image of God, holds everything scripture teaches: “my book hath only three leaves, the same are the Principles of Eternity” [III.2 ¶16].

summary: Inquiry from the inner, causal ground: for Atwood the true method for first truths, which then proves itself a posteriori by its effects.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the a priori method, inquiry from the inner causal ground, against the inductive method: “The a priori method is the true one for the discovery of the first truths” [APP ¶120]. Only the soul's lapse into selfhood hinders it. Once established, “it proceeds to prove itself a posteriori by efficient procedure, as it were by what is commonly called miracle” [APP ¶120]. See a priori ground.

summary: The ancients' philosophical method, contrasted with modern inductive science; long neglected, it is the ground Atwood wants philosophy to return to.
body: Atwood contrasts the ancients' method with modern inductive science and wants philosophy to “return with her instruments to work as formerly on the a priori ground” [III.1 ¶8], a ground long left uncultivated. See a priori.

summary: Author of works on Plato whom Atwood cites often on the Mysteries, initiation, the soul's purification and its union with the One, almost always in support.
body:
Atwood names Proclus among the Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, to be quoted later [I.1 ¶27]. She also lists him among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9], and in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25].

She uses him throughout in support of her own account:
- The mundane or phantastic spirit: “it folds itself about the indivisibility of true intellect (which is in its center)” [II.2 ¶15].
- Why Theseus and Pirithous were detained in Hades, a reading she endorses [II.3 ¶13].
- Deceptive images come before illumination: “In the most holy Mysteries, says he, before the presence of the god, the impulsive forms of certain terrestrial demons appear” [II.3 ¶22; II.3 n17]. She applies the same to the speculation of Wholes. In the Hymn to the Sun, demons keep souls in the body, forgetful of their origin: “Demons who machinate a thousand ills,” [II.3 ¶24; II.3 ¶25].
- Astonishment at the mystic spectacles: “Beauty shining forth astonishes those that behold it, converts the soul to itself” [II.3 ¶50; II.3 n53].
- Hercules' purification, the Elysian fountains and the Meadow as the prolific power of life: “the plain of Truth, he says, is intellectually expanded to intelligible Light” [II.4 ¶3; II.4 ¶16; II.4 n8].
- Grades of initiation and the soul's inward conversion: “there are indeed many steps of ascent, but all of them extend to the Paternal port and the Paternal Initiation” [II.4 ¶23; II.4 ¶29; II.4 n15, n21, n22]. Initiation comes through faith-given silence: “what else than faith is the cause of this ineffable muesis?” [II.4 ¶40; II.4 n29]. The goal: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41].
- The twofold Apollonical Intellect, paralleling Wisdom and Power: “the prophetic power unfolds the simplicity of truth and takes away the variety of that which is false” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n50].
- “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36; III.2 n31].
- To discover the One Principle one must be assimilated to it: “he must raise himself to that which is most united in nature, and to its flower” [III.2 ¶50].
- The god torn, preserved and renewed (Hymn to Minerva): “The heart of Bacchus, swiftly slaughtered king, Was saved in Aether” [III.3 ¶70; III.3 n47].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says he develops the ontological basis of the Iliad [APP ¶157]. She also praises his Commentary on the Timaeus, which treats Time as the image's participation of the Paradigm, against the relational view held by her addressee and by modern metaphysicians [APP ¶172].

equivalences.with: the subjective life, the water that is below

summary: One of the alchemists' three periods, which Atwood identifies with the subjective life, the water below.
body: Atwood names the Profundity as one of the alchemists' three periods and explains it: “the Profundity is the subjective life, the water that is below” [III.3 ¶72].

summary: The final operation: casting the Stone, powder or medicine onto a metal or mercury to tinge or transmute it, which Atwood also extends to 'the imperfect metal of any life'.
body:
Projection is the application of the finished Stone, powder or medicine to a substance to transmute it. In Atwood's historical accounts: Arnold's “wonderful projections he made with the transmuting powder” [I.1 ¶43]; “In Dee’s diary we have the account of Kelly making projection with one small grain” [I.1 ¶66]; “However, I made projection of a part” [I.1 ¶73]. Flamel, after the magistery: “Having attained this, I came now to the Projection; and the first time I made projection, was upon mercury” [I.1 ¶57], turning it to silver, and with the Red Stone to gold. Van Helmont: “I have made projections divers times” [I.1 ¶76], casting a little powder on boiling quicksilver.

Technical conditions: an adept says the medicine must first be fermented with pure gold, or “there would ensue loss and damage in the projection” [I.3 n70]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon says continually fermented medicine grows stronger: “And sure far it will be exalted at the last, And in Projeccion ren full fast:” [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood advises that “it is always best to make projection by degrees until the Stone yields no more tincture” [IV.3 ¶20], onto purified metal. She gives an alternative name: “the final Projection, as the metalline perfectibility of the matter is sometimes called” [IV.3 ¶19].

Some sources limit its importance. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The fifth and last gate is projection.” [III.3 ¶63], which serves only for metals. Eudoxus deliberately leaves “the Projection of the Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16] undescribed, since success does not depend on it.

Atwood also applies the term beyond metals: the Mercury “projected on the imperfect metal of any life, dissolves, drawing away the foundation into itself” [III.3 ¶32].

summary: Mythic figures Atwood uses to picture the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire.
body: Atwood illustrates the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire, which Prometheus received from Vulcan and Minerva disseminated [IV.4 ¶8].

summary: Atwood's image for the goal beyond the sea of sense, which a haven and signal marks direct one to.
body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes that beyond the sea of sense “there is a haven and signal marks to direct where the Promised Land is to be found” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: Prophecies of the Fourth Monarchy that Atwood notes but does not dwell on.
body: Atwood reports prophecies foretelling the Fourth Monarchy — “Many prophecies there are of times to come” [IV.3 ¶49] — but does not tarry on them.

summary: A prophetic voice cited from the Book of Enoch on those who misuse secrets, and in the Ordinal on the feeding of the matter.
body: Atwood cites the prophet (Book of Enoch, cap. 64, sect. 2) in support: those who discover secrets and turn them to ill account are judged — “They have discovered secrets, and these are they who are to be judged” [III.4 ¶6; III.4 n3]. She identifies them with Geber's avaricious. In the Ordinal, as quoted, the prophet's words are cited as a wondrous mention of the feeding of the matter, 'If ye apply it to this intention': “Visitasti terram et inebriasti eam,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: 'Thou hast visited the earth and watered it').

summary: In Atwood's reading, the intellect's congenial life: our lapsed soul, hidden in her dark hypostasis.
body: Atwood glosses Proserpine as the intellect's “own congenial life, which is Proserpine, and that lapsed soul of ours, seated in her dark hypostasis unknown” [II.3 ¶11].

summary: A verse piece, apparently spoken by the Stone, cited by Atwood for the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation.
body: Atwood cites the Prosopopoeia of the Stone (references given as Theatr. Chem., Tome 3, p. 764; Processus Chiica, Carmen Elegans; Vaughan’s magia Adamica) to illustrate the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation: “I am not dead although my spirit’s gone,” [III.1 ¶53; III.1 ¶54; III.1 n59].

summary: In the later Appendix, Atwood's name for the shape-shifting life sought in the work, which she says is very hard to discover.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says “The Protean life is very difficult of discovery” [APP ¶171]. Its last shape, she indicates, is a tree [APP ¶171].

summary: Atwood's figure for the one ever-changing universal entity of life, the subject of the work, identified with Mercury, the quintessence and the mercury of the Philosophers.
body:
Atwood uses Proteus as an image of the one subject in all its changing forms. In Part I she says “For Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36], citing the verse “Etherial, watery, earthy general soul, Immortal Fire! Even all the world is thine And pars of thee, O Proteus, power divine;” [I.2 ¶35]. She equates it with the Mercury and the quintessence: “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37]. In a footnote Proteus is the image of the one agent that is a serpent on earth, a fish in water and a bird in air, “yet is, not withstanding, One throughout the multiformity of nature” [I.3 n55].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) makes the same identification. Proteus is “the one universal entity of life, the omnia in omnibus before manifestation and individuality, the thing of which you may assert everything; Proteus.” [APP ¶138]. All descriptions of the Matter refer to it, and the work is said to be mechanical as well as alchemical, using instruments and vessels. It is also the world's “dissolved essence which is the mercury of the Philosophers, Proteus.” [APP ¶144].

Identities asserted: = Mercury, = quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; = one universal entity of life, = omnia in omnibus [APP ¶138]; = mercury of the Philosophers [APP ¶144].

summary: The field in which an adept cited by Atwood claims to have manual experience.
body: Atwood cites an adept's claim to “his own manual experience in the proto-chemistry of Hermes” [II.1 ¶11]. The packet gives no further explanation. Compare protochemistry and Protochemic Artifice.

summary: The practical art through which, according to Vaughan, the true foundation is found; Atwood sums up its whole performance as solution, sublimation and fixation.
body: In a passage attributed to Vaughan, a knowledge of this art comes before the philosophy of Wisdom: “a knowledge of the Protochemic Artifice; for that by means of this, and this only, the true foundation is discoverable” [II.1 ¶26]. Atwood, in her own voice, reduces it to three operations: “All that is performed in the Proto-chemic artifice may be comprehended in three terms” [III.2 ¶64]. These three terms are solution, sublimation and fixation.

summary: The protochemistry of Hermes, which Atwood says is the ground of Vaughan's discourse on the nature of man.
body: Atwood says that Vaughan's discourse on the nature of man is “grounded on the protochemistry of Hermes” [I.1 ¶74]. The term is not explained there. Compare proto-chemistry of Hermes and Protochemic Artifice.

summary: A biblical book Atwood quotes in support of seeking Wisdom and Self-Knowledge, and which she applies to the Mercury or water of the work.
body: Atwood cites Proverbs ii, 4, 5 in support of the call to Self-Knowledge: “If thou seekest for her as silver, and searchest for wisdom as for hidden treasures” [I.3 n46]. She uses Proverbs 8, introduced “as Solomon says”, for the worth and promises of Wisdom: “I love them that love me, and those that seek me early shall find me” [IV.3 ¶47; IV.3 n21; IV.3 n24]. She applies Proverbs iv, 8, 9 to the Mercury or water, which crowns the one who exalts her: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n8]. In each case Atwood quotes the text approvingly.

summary: Quoted by Atwood in support of the view that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.
body: Atwood quotes the Psalmist with approval: “I called upon the Lord, exclaims the Psalmist, and He heard me out of His holy temple” [III.4 ¶28]. She uses the line to show that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.

summary: Praised in the Appendix for their depth of Divine experience, which Atwood says the Mystics have neglected.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Psalms are praised for their “surpassing depth of Divine experience”, and Atwood says the Mystics have neglected them [APP ¶97].

summary: Commentator on the Chaldaic Oracles whom Atwood cites on material rites, on the Mysteries as Initia, and on apparitions and introspection in the Chaldaic rites.
body: Atwood cites Psellus' commentary on the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the view that the soul is perfected by material rites together with divine illumination: “there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites” [II.1 ¶51]. She cites him again as having said that the Mysteries were called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In Part II, ch. 3 she uses his commentary (footnoted as “Pesllus de Oraculis”) on the apparitions of the Chaldaic rites, superinspection among them, as empty products of the soul's passions: “mere appearances, having no substance, and therefore not signifying anything true” [II.3 ¶20; II.3 n15]. She also contrasts “the Introspection which Psellus speaks of”, the formless Divine Light, with Superinspection in Hades [II.3 ¶46]. In all these places she uses him as support.

summary: Atwood's name for false seekers who followed receipts literally, without theory, in search of gold, as opposed to the true adepts.
body: Atwood sets the pseudo-alchemists against the true adepts. Their motives were “as those of the pseudo-alchemists, on the other hand, were reckless and despicable” [I.1 ¶41]. They took the receipts literally and, with no theory, worked with mineral sulfur, mercury and salt to make gold: “The pseudo-Alchemists dreamed of gold, and impossible transformations” [II.1 ¶6].

summary: The threefold separated essence that equals the whole dissolved compound it comes from; it is known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.
body: Atwood describes the Psychical Quintessence as “being in its own threefold segregated essentiality equal to the whole dissolute compound whence it arises” [III.2 ¶44]. It casts off what is superfluous, and she reads Pythagoras' hecatomb for his theorem as a symbol of its discovery [III.2 ¶44]. Identity asserted: = Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine (“that miraculous Psychical Quintessence, known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.2 ¶44]).

summary: Mentioned only once in the Appendix, where his astronomy is compared with Newton's.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Ptolemy appears only in a comparison between his astronomy and Newton's [APP ¶122].

summary: In the Appendix, the higher Cause of life, which Reason reaches through secondary causes; Atwood also says the earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross.
body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes that “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110], and does not explain this further. Elsewhere she identifies the term with “the higher Cause, the punctum saliens of life” [APP ¶152]. Reason reaches it by way of secondary causes and there consciously finds its own roots. Identity asserted: = higher Cause [APP ¶152].

summary: In Crollius' account, the separated and purified medicine that is to be given to our bodies.
body: Speaking in Crollius' voice, the passage describes separating and purifying the medicine “that the pure crystalline matter may be administered to our bodies” [III.1 ¶10].

summary: The universal matter that subsists about Intelligibles and mediates between causes and their gross effects; the Theurgic Art makes it manifest, and in the Appendix it is the first, passive product of the work.
body:
In Part III Atwood describes “a certain pure matter subsisting about Intelligibles which is universal” [III.2 ¶46]. It is the origin of all vital and corporeal existence. It is hidden but can be made manifest to sense, and the Theurgic Art makes it manifest. It is connascent with the gods and receives Divinity. She also calls it “a certain pure and divine Matter mediately subsisting between primary and secondary causes and their gross effect” [III.2 ¶49].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds that, according to Lully, pure matter is not found on earth, and that “You may find out in Plotinus how that pure matter is generated.” [APP ¶43]. There it is the first product of the work: “a pure matter which is passive, having no power of perfecting itself; it is the attractive power” [APP ¶182]. Identity asserted: = the attractive power [APP ¶182].

summary: The purification of the soul, of which Atwood says Will is the greatest part; for the Paracelsians, the separation of the pure life from impurity, as metal from ore.
body: Atwood says that “Will is the greatest part of purgation” [II.2 ¶13], where purgation means the purification of the soul. In a passage given in the voice of the Paracelsians, purgation separates the pure life from the impure: “by a due purgation, the pure life is separated, as metal from the dark and sordid ore” [III.1 ¶10].

summary: The cleansing of souls, which Servius says the Bacchic rites served and which was a chief benefit of the Mysteries.
body: Atwood quotes Servius on the function of the Bacchic rites: “the sacred rites of Bacchus pertained to the purification of souls” [II.2 ¶5]. In the same paragraph the benefits of the Mysteries are given as “moral enlightenment and purification of life” [II.2 ¶5].

summary: The stage of the Mysteries that follows the revealing of the Medial Life; it restores the rule of reason and frees the inclination from sense before the deeper initiations.
body: Atwood places the Purificative Rites after the revealing of the Medial Life. They were rites “which were designed also to restore the monarchy of reason in the soul” [II.2 ¶20], and they prepare for the final initiations. The deeper mysteries require them, because after them comes “the inclination being already freed from the dominion and all the superficial progeny of sense” [II.3 ¶9].

summary: The agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward; Atwood identifies it with Isis.
body: Atwood describes the purified spirit or intelligence as the agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward. Identity asserted: = Isis (“the purified spirit or intelligence, that is Isis” [III.1 ¶23]).

summary: The decay and death that, according to Atwood, comes before every new form: linked with blackness (the ‘gate of blackness’, the ‘blackness of the night’), in which the matter dies and corrupts before it rises again.
body:
Atwood states that “putrefaction precedes the generation of every new form into existence” [I.3 n42], and links it with the ‘gate of blackness’. In the crow image she explains: “The blackness of the night is the putrefaction of the same” [I.3 n12]. The matching ‘clearness of the day’ is resurrection to a relative purity. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the darkened matter “lives in the putrefaction” [I.3 ¶48], and its dark clouds are changed.

In Part III Atwood applies the term to the decay of the vital vapour under the ferment. More generally, she applies it to the death and corruption that every life passes through before rising better, as a seed does: “Does not the grain putrefy in the moist earth before it springs?” [III.1 ¶30]. Morien, quoted in Part IV, describes the earth as having its water drawn off and returned again and again “until the earth is completely putrefied” [IV.1 ¶41]. The earth is then corrupt, without its Form, and dead for a season.

Identity asserted: = blackness of the night [I.3 n12].

summary: Atwood's name for the vital experiment, through which powers, the regenerative original and temptations were revealed to conscience.
body: Atwood uses the phrase for the vital experiment: “by this pyrotechnical induction, powers were revealed to conscience” [IV.4 ¶9]. What was revealed included the regenerative original and the temptations.

summary: A term Crollius pairs with physic, saying the two cannot be separated, in the context of trial by fire.
body: In a passage given in Crollius' voice, and in the context of trial by fire: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated” [III.1 ¶10].

summary: Greek philosopher whom Atwood cites on Wisdom, on initiatory ordeals and on the Tetractys; she reads his hecatomb symbolically as the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence.
body:
Atwood names Thales and Pythagoras among the early Greek philosophers who sought eastern wisdom, and notes that their writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She cites Pythagoras' definition of Wisdom as “the science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39; II.1 n36]. She also uses him as an example of the long preparations and ordeals required before admission to the deeper mysteries, and of the purifying of disciples' souls [II.2 ¶11].

She reports that Aristotle criticized him for explaining essence by number [III.2 ¶40]. She then reads his hecatomb, offered for the right-angle theorem, as a symbol of the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence [III.2 ¶43; III.2 ¶44]. She identifies the Conjunction with “that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer, spelled “Pythagorus”), his Tetractys is obtained by theurgic multiplication and is the kind of ens that underlies the stone. Atwood calls it “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108]. Throughout, Atwood uses him as support.

summary: Cited in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries bring about assimilation and final contact with the first principle.
body: Atwood cites the Pythagoreans in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries lead to assimilation and final contact with the first principle [II.2 ¶5].

summary: A precept Atwood quotes as a warning to would-be practitioners, alongside ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.
body: Atwood quotes the Pythagoric precept “Neither break a superficies” [IV.3 ¶56] as a warning to would-be practitioners and sets it beside the counsel ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.

summary: Impossible by natural means, Atwood says, but demonstrated supernaturally by transmuting the hypostatic relations; whoever finds it perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature.
body: Atwood writes that “the Quadrature of the Circle was supernaturally demonstrated; which naturally it cannot be” [III.3 ¶30]. It is demonstrated only by transmuting the hypostatic relations. The one who finds it has resolved all things into one Principle and perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature [III.3 ¶30].

summary: In the Appendix, to give something specific quality and form: essence is qualitated by Ideas, and the speech of Mind qualitates in the pure Ether.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: “essence is qualitated, i.e., specificated, and receives form from Ideas” [APP ¶37]. Elsewhere she writes: “The speech of Mind uttered into the pure Ether qualitates and specificates.” [APP ¶64]. Identity asserted: = specificate [APP ¶37].

summary: The elements as they exist at their source; they multiply into distributive powers whose remote subjects are the sensible elements.
body: Atwood describes the source as “making elements there to subsist as qualitative virtues, which, multiplying into being, become distributive powers” [III.2 ¶38]. The remote subjects of these powers are the sensible elements.

summary: In the Adept's words, the fourfold through which the Ternary is reduced; it is identified with the four elements.
body: In a passage given in the voice of an Adept, the instruction is to “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18]. Identity asserted: = four elements (“the Quaternarius, or four elements, as some call them” [IV.2 ¶18]).

summary: Van Helmont's white sand, which Atwood describes as showing itself in a vital soil that no spade or mattock has ever pierced.
body: Atwood describes Van Helmont's Quellum, his white sand, as “manifesting itself forth in a vivid vital soil, which spade or mattock never pierced” [III.2 ¶8].

equivalences.with: Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light
our viscous celestial and glorious soul
arising Spirit of the Universal nature

summary: The essence drawn out by the work: the celestial soul or arising Spirit of universal nature, identified with Mercury, the Elixir of Life, the Free Ether and Lumen Vestimenti.
body:
Atwood treats the Quintessence as no mere speculation: “that elder Quintessence of the magi which they introduce, not as a being of speculation merely, but of experimental science” [I.2 ¶16], obtainable as a compact, tangible essence. In the same passage she reports other names for it: the Kabalists' “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light”, and “the Greeks, the Free Ether, that is to say, freed from the prison of gross matter” [I.2 ¶16].

It is identified with the soul: “the quintessence is no other than our viscous celestial and glorious soul drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]; Synesius is quoted to the same effect, “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70]. It is also “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37], and a name of the whitened stage: “which, whitening, is called milk, dew, quintessence” [I.2 ¶40].

In the method it is the new life elicited from the crucifixion of the old: “which life is a very real and pure Quintessence, the Mercury so much sought after, even the Elixir of Life” [III.1 ¶49]. After seven repetitions comes “the final resurrection of the Quintessence into a permanent form of life” [I.3 n40]. Atwood says Hermes calls by this name “the arising Spirit of the Universal nature which, persisting separately, bounds as it were, by an invisible summit, every corporeal subsistence” [III.2 ¶36]. An adept reads “the dust of the earth” as “the arising quintessence of the universal nature” [I.3 n51].

It must be handled gently: Vaughan calls it “the sweet spirit of Peace, the true eternal Quintessence”, which “will depart from the elements, leaving both of them and thee to confusion” [III.4 ¶44]. A passage of uncertain voice (possibly the author of The Triumph) directs one to “convert and congeal the new-born Quintessence or mercurial water into an incombustible fixed unguent” [IV.2 ¶6]. Artephius credits his long life to “the use of this admirable quintessence” [I.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “As man was the Quintessence of the whole creation, so woman was the Quintessence of man --- the love-spirit was in her” [APP ¶72]; and of the lower spherical quintessences, “these world forms are unstable and, uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23].

summary: Phrase from Hermolaus Barbarus's gloss on the divine water, describing it as of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things.
body: Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus, who glosses the divine water as “a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. The grammar leaves it unclear whether the water is the quintessence of things or only of its nature.

summary: What is found when the elements of the compound creature are divided; further opened, it yields the angelical spirit.
body: In a quoted adept's counsel: “divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; opened further, this nature yields the angelical spirit. Atwood also speaks of the son as the quintessential nature concentrated [I.3 n40].

summary: Author cited as containing allusions that support the story of Lully.
body: Cited by Atwood as containing allusions supporting the Lully story [I.1 ¶47].

summary: Rabbi cited from the Zohar on man as the Celestial Prototype and on the dew of light shaken from the hidden head.
body: Atwood cites the Rabbi (from the Zohar) approvingly for the doctrine of man as Celestial Prototype and image of God: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42; II.1 n38]; he reads 'The Eternal has founded the earth upon his wisdom' as referring to the human prototype. Under the spelling “Rabbi Ben Jocahi” he is cited for the white form of the hidden principle and the dew of light: “From his head he shakes a dew which awakens the dead” [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n4].

summary: Voice of the Zohar cited for Thought as the hidden Principle unfolding into Spirit and articulate voice, which Atwood takes up as her theme.
body: Atwood quotes: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n50]. She takes up this account of Thought unfolding into Spirit or Intelligence and articulate voice as her theme, calling it a 'Magnificent, yet impervious assertion'.

summary: The dissolution the operator enters once self-will and the other vices have been removed from his mind.
body: Atwood requires that self-will and the other vices “be removed from the mind of him who is to enter into the radical dissolution of Life” [IV.1 ¶40].

summary: Something discovered and set free through the adepts' theory once the superfluities are discharged.
body: Atwood speaks of “the medium by which the radical element is discovered and set free to the accomplishment of its inclusive law” [I.3 n4], once the superfluities are discharged. Elsewhere the 'radix' is to appear under the moist fire [I.3 ¶10]; the text does not explicitly link the two.

summary: What the prophet Enoch beheld in the Place to which he was snatched up, paired with the mystical Adamic Soil.
body: Atwood mentions “what he beheld of the Radical Essence, and the manifold glories of that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], of the prophet (Enoch) snatched up to that Place.

summary: In Eudoxus, the body's essential moisture, consumed by common calcination but preserved and increased by philosophic calcination.
body: Quoted from Eudoxus: common calcination “consumes the greatest part of its radical humidity” [IV.3 ¶16], whereas philosophic calcination preserves and increases it. In the Fourth Key the earth is moistened with its own humidity [IV.3 ¶16].

summary: The substance of which metals are uniformly composed, which can be withdrawn from inferior forms and pass into a more perfect form.
body: Atwood equates it with the metals' subject-matter: “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4]; it can be withdrawn from inferior Forms. Under a fermentive test it passes into a more perfect Form: “The radical moisture of the metal likewise, obeying the fermentive virtue of such a test when applied” [III.2 n38]. Khunrath is quoted that the Stone benefits metals “by transference of their radical moisture” [IV.3 ¶28], removing their terrestreity; this is not further defined.

summary: In Sendivogius, what remains after the philosophers' water consumes the gold and silver.
body: Quoted from Sendivogius: what remains ('the tenth part with one part') after the philosophers' water consumes the gold and silver — “this shall be the radical moisture of the metals” [IV.3 ¶21].

summary: The homogeneous root substance of all things, whose homogeneity is the ground of transmutation.
body: Atwood grounds transmutation in “the homogeneity of the radical substance of things” [I.2 ¶3].

summary: In Geber, the true root of the science, found only by a subtly searching mind.
body: Quoted from Geber: those without a subtly searching mind “cannot find the true Radix of this most precious science” [III.4 ¶3].

summary: A connection by which one in this state meets the whole image-world of his sphere; the change to a spiritual body comes by divine rapport.
body: Atwood writes that “each by rapport in this state becomes conversant with the whole phantasmagoric universe of his sphere” [II.3 ¶22], and that one “is changed from an earthly to a spiritual body, by rapport divine” [II.3 ¶29].

summary: The operation which, repeatedly passed through, alters the Vital Spirit and dissolves the whole natural born hypostasis.
body: Atwood: “a true Rational Analysis, which, repeatedly passed through, leads on to a dissolution of the whole natural born hypostasis” [III.1 ¶50]. Elsewhere 'the mode of analysis' is said to be directed by the Passive Understanding [III.1 ¶40]; the text does not explicitly link the two phrases.

summary: That by which the Matter returns in the Freed Will to consciousness and manifests the Supreme Cause.
body: Atwood speaks of the Matter “returning by its Rational Boundary in the Freed Will to consciousness” [III.2 ¶60], so manifesting the Supreme Cause. Not further explained.

summary: The pure aurific seed of Light hidden in ordinary life, represented by Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas; also named Perscrutinator.
body: Atwood names the Rational Ferment (also called Perscrutinator) as something “concerning which it will be our purpose to inquire hereafter” [I.3 n32]. In myth it is represented by heroes; of Cadmus: “identified him with Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas, and the rest, who represent the Rational Ferment;” [III.1 ¶66]; the other faculties of the mind are originally attendant on it. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she explains why the principium is hard to find: “the rational ferment, the pure aurific seed of Light, is hidden in this life of ours” [APP ¶35].

summary: The inbred form according to which the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself.
body: Atwood: the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself “according to the Rational Form inbred” [IV.3 ¶29].

equivalences.with: honey of the bees; aurific seed

summary: The strongest of lights, the One Leader which, discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit to overcome the corporeal; also the aurific seed.
body:
Atwood: “The Rational Light, once discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit” [III.3 ¶23], which then overcomes the corporeal. It is the sole deliverer of the veiled spirit: “there is but One Leader, who should undertake the deliverance; one only, we repeat; he that is allied --- the same Rational Light” [III.4 ¶19]; strengthened in practice, it is raised to the 'allegoric siege of life' and kindled to overcome the stronghold of evil there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): Saturn must be satiated from without with plenty “of the honey of the bees", the aurific seed, the Rational Light” [APP ¶72]; “The Rational Light is the strongest of all lights, and overcomes every other.” [APP ¶168], and once realized all life orders itself round it, constituting re-integration of being. In the inner combat it acts last: deprived of its understanding essence, “the rational intellect goes forth to avenge it and die” [APP ¶153].

summary: Something moved about by the Almighty force, set beside the image of an established monarch whom inferior powers follow.
body: Atwood mentions “the Almighty force that moves about the Rational Magnet” [II.4 ¶38], alongside the image of an established monarch followed by the inferior powers. Not further defined.

equivalences.with: that which is present with himself

summary: In Porphyry, that which is present with a man himself; being present with it, and absent from externals, is presence with true Being.
body: Quoted from Porphyry (spelled 'Prophyry'): one should be “present with that which is present with himself, that is to say, with his rational part” [III.2 ¶59]; such presence, with absence from the external, is presence with true Being.

summary: The way, by reflexive analysis of the analyzer, of penetrating through Nature's Understanding into her Causal Light.
body: Atwood, of reflexive analysis of the analyzer: “this is the way of rational permeation, by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20].

summary: Reason's inquiry that proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true; better called discrimination, and required of the Hermetic Student.
body: Atwood distinguishes it from its mock ally: “Rational skepticism has quite another object and never exhibits itself in the refractory form of its mock ally.” [III.4 ¶15]. It proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true, and is required of the Hermetic Student: “Such skepticism, more properly perhaps called discrimination” [III.4 ¶15].

equivalences.with: the reasons of life and understanding (in Fire)

summary: In Sendivogius, the reasons of life and understanding in fire, infused by God into man, by which alone he differs from other creatures and resembles God.
body: Quoted from Sendivogius: “This soul was of that most pure fire, infused by God into the vital spirit” [II.4 ¶39]; “In it are the reasons of life and understanding, which are distributed in the first infusion of man’s life, and these are called the rational soul” [II.4 ¶39]. By it alone man differs from other creatures and is like God. A Latin line of unclear voice reads “Deus nunquam creavit rem nobiliorem sub coelo praeter animam rationalem” [III.3 ¶81] (ours: God never created a nobler thing under heaven except the rational soul); per this rendering it is ranked against 'our Mercury', but the reading is uncertain.

summary: Voice of the Famma et Confessio, cited to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place.
body: Cited from the Famma et Confessio to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place: “Vidi aliquando Olympicos domos” [II.4 ¶11; II.4 n5] (ours: I once saw the Olympic houses).

summary: The state in which all life moves orderly round the realized Rational Light.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), once the Rational Light is realized and all life orders itself round it: “This constitutes the re- integration of being” [APP ¶168], called there 'the manifestation of the **** in man'.

equivalences.with: Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture

summary: The superior, supernatural ruling principle in man, temple of the Deity, which as ferment gathers all into its Light; called Wisdom, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture.
body:
Atwood makes Reason the rightful ruler of the soul, around which the inferior powers settle; in this life it is hidden and latent. One “will so venerate this Reason” [II.4 ¶36], and she names it: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39]. It is the dwelling of Deity: “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]; “For this Reason is her temple wherein the Eternal Self-existent dwells” [II.1 ¶50]; and “Reason, which is, as it were, the temple of that Intellectual Ilumination” [III.1 ¶5], entered through the phantasic vestibule.

The superior, supernatural Reason (of which natural reason is the image) works as ferment: “this Reason gaining the ascendancy, would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light” [III.1 ¶21], separating false forms and assimilating the inferior life. “It is of this the ancients speak, calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture”; “For it is Light indeed, and an occult splendor of existence transcendentally pure”; it is conceived as “the Intellectual sun” [III.1 ¶21].

It is the one universal faculty consciously distinguishable by itself: “this root of reason which is truly catholic”; “in our mere individual consciousness it is the foundation of all law” [III.1 ¶23]; cut off from its source it is weak and unaware of it. Completed by the work, “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light in the periphery of her fiery essence remains immortal, and is the Mistress of Life” [III.3 ¶80], “leaving reason nothing more to doubt of” [III.3 ¶82].

In practice it is man's “especial prerogative of Reason and rectitude of purpose” [IV.4 ¶12], with “the Reason also, purified and singled out by Art for the encounter” [IV.4 ¶9]. The upright mind submits to the universal Rule, “including all in the catholic perceivance of this Reason”: “let him search for the Root of Reason rationally, and hold by it, and conspire with It” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: A principle with stolen forces provoking conflict in life, whose identical representative the Divine Art requires so those forces can be drawn forth and spent.
body: Atwood describes a rebellious Principle whose 'stolen forces' provoke a bloody conflict in life; the Divine Art requires an identical representative of him so those forces may be drawn forth and spent. Egyptian relics show “innumerable similitudes belonging both to this rebellious Principle and to that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64], depicted in human semblance between foes.

summary: The recipes of mercenary pretenders, which led people into error and crime.
body: Atwood blames mercenary pretenders for error and even “the commitment even of egregious crimes by their receipts” [I.1 ¶64].

summary: In the Appendix, the place where the originals of the true tools are; outward tools only represent these.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of outward tools “they are representatives of these that are in the Recess of Light” [APP ¶100]. The originals of the true tools are thus placed in the Recess of Light; the text gives no further explanation.

summary: A collective witness that Plato cites for the saying about the thrysus-bearers.
body: Plato cites the records of the Mysteries as witness to the saying about the thrysus-bearers [II.4 ¶54].

summary: A metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light, in which the visible springs from the invisible.
body: Atwood: “the recreation was seen to be a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], in which the visible springs from the invisible.

summary: The fire within the magic earth that spontaneously binds its parts, coagulates them and stops their flux.
body: Atwood describes the fire within the magic earth: “this fire binds the parts thereof spontaneously to himself, coagulates them, and stops their flux” [III.2 ¶8]. Arresting the flux of the matter is thus this fire's work.

summary: The force the alchemists claim man has brought into action through rational conditioning.
body: A claim Atwood reports for the Alchemists: “man, by rationally conditionating, has succeeded in developing into action the Recreative Force” [II.1 ¶47]. The text does not define the force further.

summary: The Red, named as the source of the Citrine; its root, the red root, is identified with the Terra Adamica.
body: Atwood names the Red as the source of the Citrine and asserts an identity: “The red root is the Terra Adamica” [I.3 n52].

summary: A product of the Work whose process had been laborious and rarely achieved; Basil Valentine reportedly found a new way to work it.
body: Atwood reports that Basil Valentine found “a new method of working the Red Elixir” [I.1 ¶59]; the process had previously been laborious and rarely achieved. She also cites Norton's lines on the Red Stone as evidence on this point [I.1 ¶60] (see Red Stone).

summary: In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., something possessed, together with pure Mercury, by whoever has the vapour of the subject.
body: In the verses quoted from Lucerna Salis Phil., whoever has the vapour of the subject “Has the gilded splendor of the Red Lyon, The pure and clear Mercury.” [I.2 ¶30]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: In Eudoxus, one of the two Mercuries, identified with the most sharp Vinegar and called by others the bath of the Sun.
body: Eudoxus (quoted) speaks of two Mercuries and identifies one: “the most sharp Vinegar is the Red Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]; he adds that “the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun” [IV.3 ¶10], a name others give it. Asserted identities: = most sharp Vinegar; = bath of the Sun.

summary: In Eudoxus, what is struck upon the Stone so that a clear fountain issues from it.
body: Eudoxus (quoted) directs one to “strike upon it with the Red of Magic Fire” [IV.3 ¶10], whereupon a clear fountain issues from the Stone. The expression is not explained in the text.

summary: What Kelly is believed to have had, whether by secret information or by making it himself.
body: Atwood reports the belief that Kelly “became possessed of the Red Powder by some secret kind of information” [I.1 ¶66], or else made it himself. The text does not state outright that it is the same as the Powder of Projection.

summary: What Ripley tried to putrefy by alternate heat and cold, and which he called his Gold.
body: The text (voice unclear) says Ripley tried to putrefy “this Red Salt which he enviously calls his Gold” [IV.1 ¶36] by alternate heat and cold. Asserted identity: = Gold (Ripley's name for it).

summary: The final perfection of the matter, the form of the Stone that turns mercury into gold; also called phoenix, salamander and royal essence.
body: Nicholas Flamel (quoted) reports: “I made projection of the Red Stone, on a like quantity of mercury” [I.1 ¶57], yielding gold, where the earlier projection had yielded silver. Norton (quoted) says scarcely one in fifteen kingdoms possesses it — “In fifteen kingdoms hath our Red Stone.” — that it is not to be sought until the white medicine is fully wrought, and that it can be increased in multiplication; the passage also has the form “Had not of our Res Stone consideration” [I.1 ¶60]. Atwood cites these lines as evidence about the Red Elixir. In her own voice the Red Stone is the final perfection of the matter: “it is henceforth a phoenix, salamander, their royal essence and Red Stone” [I.2 ¶40]. Asserted identities: = phoenix; = salamander; = royal essence.

summary: In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., the red Sulfur contained in the subject, knowledge of which gives the whole foundation.
body: From the verses quoted from Lucerna Salis Phil.: “And he who knows the red Sulfur which it contains, Has within his power the whole foundation” [I.2 ¶30]. The text does not explain it further.

summary: In Hermes, a redness corrupted with water, held like fire in a live coal, to be purified by repeated withdrawal; called the soul.
body: Hermes (quoted) instructs: “Take, my Son, this redness, corrupted with the water” [I.3 ¶17]; it holds its fire like a live coal and is to be purified by repeated withdrawal. A note identifies it: “the redness is its soul” [I.3 n21], the soul of the passive spirit. Asserted identity: = soul.

summary: In the Appendix, what brings the philosophical dissolution to an end.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the philosophical dissolution that “this continues until the refixation takes place” [APP ¶96].

summary: Exclaimed over as a most mighty and surpassing magic, right after the account of life's return to its source; not defined.
body: Atwood exclaims “Most mighty and surpassing magic of Reflection.” [III.3 ¶79], directly after describing life's return to its source. The term is not defined there.

summary: The inferior nature, i.e. the person engaged in the rite, from whom divine things do not take their principle of energy.
body: The text (voice unclear) glosses the term itself: divine things do not take their principle of energy “from an inferior nature (i.e., to say, from the regardant subject)” [II.4 ¶31]. The regardant subject is the one engaged in the rite. Asserted identity: = inferior nature.

summary: In the Appendix, the life that begins when the individual mind contacts universal power, ferments the sensorium of this life and lives on its decease.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the contact of the individual mind with power universal is its start: “that experience is the initial of the regenerate life” [APP ¶175]. This life ferments the sensorium of the present life and lives upon its decease. See regeneration.

summary: The soul that puts on the Stone as a new body.
body: Atwood says the Stone is what “the regenerate soul puts on as a new body” [IV.4 ¶20]. See regeneration.

summary: In the Moorish philosopher, the wisdom of a man reformed into God's image, by which he possesses all things and unlocks nature's mysteries.
body: The Moorish philosopher (quoted) says the man reformed into God's image “in his regenerate Wisdom possesseth all things, and with this light can unlock the most hidden and recluse mysteries of nature” [II.1 ¶9].

summary: The recreative process, physical and spiritual, by which the vital principle is reconstructed, the natural life dissolved and the Identity made; the process the Hermetic Art serves.
body:
Atwood's term for the process the Art serves. Already in Part I she says the Poimander and Asclepian books “denote rather our divine capabilities and promise of regeneration than the physical ground of either” [I.1 ¶7], that physical ground being treated with the practical method in the Tractatus Aureus; and in early Christianity “the mystery of human regeneration, so zealously proclaimed, was also rationally understood” [I.1 ¶11]. Only by it can an immortal essence “pass into immortality” [II.4 ¶7].

As process: it is the miraculous principle “by which the relationships of the vital elements are exchanged” [III.1 ¶50] — the sensible medium becomes occult and the occult, catholic reason of life becomes manifest. In it is made “that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16], by reprocedure into experience out of an artificially induced dissolute void of life. Upon dissolution of the natural life, “in the regeneration this Reason is said to be discovered” [III.3 ¶52], arising through self-perceivance; the Stone is made manifest regeneratively. It is the physical secret the Mysteries refer to; its first principle: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will” [III.3 ¶77]. It is renewal by Water and the Spirit; “baptismal regeneration was an effectual rite” [IV.2 ¶17], and Christ is brought forth anew as “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. With the fall it is “the ancient doctrine” [IV.3 ¶38], understood only through self-knowledge.

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds: the vital principle is reconstructed “through a regeneration” [APP ¶68] in “the recreative process of the regeneration” [APP ¶55], the macrocosm's image being evolved before the mental eye; the Hermetically regenerated give up the head life. It brings the whole of life into the Sonship: “It is the death to sin with a new birth awakened in us” [APP ¶79]; begun by the pure earth, it is highest when the spirit, dead to its identity, re-arises as the Divine image — “the condition of the highest regeneration” [APP ¶87]. The philosophic birth “is known in Regeneration, individually proven and proving all” [APP ¶108]; regenerate bodies are penetrated with Light, and the regenerate soul receives body from the residuum of the sensual medium. “The mystery is an art revealed to regenerating men, to advance them on to perfection” [APP ¶146]; it gives freedom to realize every volition, later surrendered to the Father's Will, and involves “a drawing of power and life up through the feet” [APP ¶158].

summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, the succession of colours the matter passes through, run through again in each multiplication.
body: The Author of the Open Entrance (quoted) says that in multiplication “every regiment of the colors will in that brief space be passed through” [IV.3 ¶18]: the whole succession of colours recurs, but quickly.

summary: In the Appendix, the wise men's name for the analogical sphere, of only relative truth, valued by Hermetists only for its derived light stripped of phantasmagoric form.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “There is a certain truth in the analogical sphere, but it is only relative. The wise called it the Regio phantastica” [APP ¶105]. For the Hermetists “it was as a pabalum for them, but only when deprived of all phantasmagoric form” [APP ¶105] — valued for the derived light of its essence. Some visionaries “misconceive this Evester, as Paracelsus calls it” [APP ¶105]. Asserted identities: = the analogical sphere; = Evester (Paracelsus's name).

summary: The religion whose pursuit was punished by death once the Mysteries were abandoned, as the Asclepian prophecy foretold.
body: The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes (quoted) prophesies that in a degenerate age “a capital punishment shall be appointed for him who applies himself to the Religion of Intellect” [I.1 ¶10]. Atwood takes up the phrase, in quotation marks, for the time when the Mysteries were abandoned and Theurgic rites proscribed: “a punishment, no less than death, was menaced against him who dared to pursue the "Religion of Intellect"” [I.1 ¶30]; then “tradition and secular delirium had taken place of intellectual enthusiasm, and idle dreams were set up as oracles in the place of Divine inspiration” [I.1 ¶30]. The term is not further defined.

summary: The soul's recovery of what it forgot in embodied life — the awakened recollection of the intellect that the rites produce, sought by Reason in her root of Light.
body: Atwood: the soul “will recollect all those things, the remembrance of which she loses in the present life” [II.1 ¶50]; souls allied to antecedent realities feel it, “thrilling into reminiscence, as of some long past life forgotten” [II.1 ¶53]; it is also the recovery of the ancient experiment. The rites work by “awakening intellect into reminiscence” [II.4 ¶36], but the hidden Reason cannot “be awakened to reminiscence without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. Reason, roused from lethargy, goes “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15].

summary: Author of The Mirific Word and De Arte Cabalistica, whom Atwood cites approvingly for the purified principle, Wisdom as darkness turned to light, and the mirific Word's two natures.
body: Atwood lists John Reuchlin among those who blended alchemy and therapeutics with neoplatonism and cabala [I.1 ¶39]. From The Mirific Word she takes support for the purified principle as medium of divine experience: “Ex natura et divino factum est” [II.2 ¶25] (ours: 'it is made from nature and the divine'; the book's own rendering is not in the packet). From De Arte Cabalistica, third book: “Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.” [III.2 ¶10] (ours: 'there is nothing in the beginning but Wisdom'), with Wisdom as Ain in darkness and the dark Aleph turned to light Aleph. From de Verbo Mirificao: two natures in the mirific Word, the changeable and the immutable — “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24; III.2 n25] — which is said to allude to arresting the flux. She uses him throughout as supporting authority.

summary: The Book of Revelation, which Atwood cites for the competent minister, the Stone with a new name, the white splendour, Wisdom's fruits and the marriage of man and God.
body: Atwood cites Revel. 3:7 for the qualifications of the competent minister: “he that hath the Key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n17]. Chapters 2–3 support the promises of material fruits with Wisdom: “To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the Tree of Life” [IV.3 n22]; the passages at [IV.3 ¶41–45] apparently come from these chapters (the footnote numbering is unclear). Chapters 1:14 and 2:17 illustrate the white appearance of the primeval splendour (the White Stone, the Son of Man): “whose hair was like wool, and white as snow” [III.2 ¶4; III.2 n5]. She also invokes the Stone of the Apocalypse and the Stone with the new name [II.3 ¶52, ¶54]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) the Book of Revelation is said to hint at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79].

summary: In Kirchringius, the sudden arrival of a solution after persistent desire and labour, given only to one who prays with great desire and labour.
body: Kirchringius (quoted): after persistent prayer, desire and labour, “at length, in a moment, the solution will fall in; this is a revelation” [III.4 ¶22]. Asserted identity: = the solution falling in.

headword: Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides
forms: Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides
summary: Atwood's list of generic alchemical book titles, all pointing to the Royal Road once it is found but useless to most modern readers.
body: Atwood lists these generic titles of alchemical books — Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides — to show that all direct to the Royal Road once it is found, yet are useless to most modern readers [III.4 ¶15].

summary: The reviving spirit of the Phoenix from which, Atwood says, Bacon filled his lamp; the text does not explain it further.
body: Atwood speaks of Bacon being able to “fill his lamp from her reviviscent spirit” [I.1 ¶38], the spirit belonging to the Phoenix, which he worked by ascending and descending. The passage leaves the expression unexplained; it apparently names a vivifying principle drawn from the Phoenix, but the text gives no plain meaning.

summary: An Arabian alchemist the book cites for public transmutations, as a master who wrote obscurely, and in the Ordinal for the dietary of the matter.
body: Atwood names Rhasis as an Arabian alchemist famous for public displays of transmutation [I.1 ¶34]. As “Rasis” he appears in Norton's verse among masters (with Hermes, Geber, Avicen, Morien, Bacon, Raymond and others) who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the Ordinal, Rasis is cited as having “set the dietary”: the matter must not eat hastily — “Non tamen comedat res festinanter,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: yet let the thing not eat hastily). He is also named in Eirenaeus' allegory as read by those sitting in darkness [III.4 ¶16].

summary: Cited for reference only.
An adept (Richardi Ang. Libel.) cited to support the view that study of the philosophers' writings must precede practice.
body: Atwood quotes “the adept Ricardus” from Richardi Ang. Libel. cap. 3: “I beg of thee, my son, says the adept Ricardus, to examine the writings of the philosophers” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n16]. She uses him with approval to support her point that study of theory precedes practice and that study overthrows ignorance.

summary: An adept, author of the Twelve Gates, Medulla and verses to King Edward, whom Atwood cites often on the First Matter, solution, putrefaction and concealment, while criticizing the Gates' disorder.
body:
Ripley is one of Atwood's most-cited authorities.

**On concealment and honesty.** His Fifth Gate supports her view that a plain art is veiled to protect it from the unworthy: “In horrid metaphors veiled are an art most plain” [I.1 ¶85; I.1 n111]. In his Epistle to King Edward IV he offers, conditionally, to show his king the Stone's working and argues against wilful deceit: “Never trewly for merke nor for pounde Make yt I common” [I.1 ¶79–80; I.1 n105].

**Against ignorant practice.** His Admonition of Erroneous Experiments illustrates the failures of working on vulgar substances: “But profytt found I right none therein.” [I.1 ¶64–65; I.1 n72]. Via Ashmole he is cited for verses against those who prate “Of Robin Hood, and of his Bow” without practice [I.1 ¶64]. Yet Atwood criticizes the Twelve Gates as disorderly and misleading [I.1 ¶62–63].

**On the Matter.** Stanza 10 of the Epistle supports reduction to the first matter: “Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable” [I.2 ¶5–6; I.2 n7]. The Medulla, cap. i, supports that separation and recombination of Mercury's elements make the elixir: “The elements of Mercury being separated” [I.2 ¶25; I.2 n23]. He calls the First Matter a middle or third thing: “Aquosa substantia sicca reperta” [I.2 ¶31, ¶42] (ours: a watery substance found dry). The Admonition supports that man is the mine of the natural mercury: “Out of hy myner by arte yt most be brought” [II.1 ¶13; II.1 n11]. “The Canon Ripley” is among those agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**On the operation.** The Second and Fifth Gates and Ripley Revived illustrate the vapor running down in the vessel, the sun obscured with waters like Noah's flood, and purgation to a white Elixir: “Ryght so to water minerall reduced ys our gold” [III.1 ¶56–62; III.1 n61, n63, n69]; Atwood glosses his phrase “by Crafte occasionate” [III.1 n69]. The consummating Conjunction is “by Ripley called tetraptive” [III.3 ¶33]. In contrast, his attempt to putrefy his Red Salt by alternate heat and cold is called a “singular” method [IV.1 ¶36].

He is listed among genuine seekers, against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): he warns against haste under the similitude of red poppies [APP ¶103].
