summary: Cited for reference only.
Author of De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae in the Theatrum Chemicum, cited for the antiquity of alchemy.
body: Atwood cites Robert Vallensis's De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae, in the first volume of the Theatrum Chemicum, in support of alchemy's antiquity [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n4]. A further footnote refers to the same work as a source, closing “Haec ille Andaeas” [I.1 n52] (ours: thus that Andaeas).

summary: Atwood's expression for that which is so called because it lies in great obscurity and is hard to reach, surrounded by darkness and clouds.
body: Atwood explains the name herself: “This is the rock in the wilderness,, because in great obscurity and difficult to find the way of” [II.3 ¶30]. It is surrounded by darkness, clouds and exhalations, as though in the bowels of the earth. The text states the reason for the name (obscurity and inaccessibility); what “this” is must be taken from the surrounding passage.

summary: The ‘experimental Friar’, an adept Atwood cites on concealment, the Matter, solution, the operator's purification and the primacy of understanding over experiment.
body:
Atwood treats Roger Bacon as a genuine adept who produced gold; Friar Bacon said he saw and touched the perfect thing transmuting [I.1 ¶76]. His maxim justifies concealing the practice: “truth ought not to be shown to every ribald, for then that would become most vile, which, in the hands of a philosopher, is the most precious of all things” [I.1 ¶38–39; I.1 n43, n44]; conscience led him to withhold his gift. His Libro de Mirab. Natur. Operib. contains extracts from Rhasis and appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶34, ¶36; I.1 n41].

On method, he supports leaving off experiments until understanding is attained: “operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding” [I.1 ¶86; I.1 n112]. Called “the experimental Friar”, he supports that the beginning is dissolving and investigating the philosophic man: “Volo ovum philosophorum dissolvere et partes philosophici hominis investare, nam hoc est initium ad alia” [II.3 ¶5; II.3 n1] (ours: I will dissolve the philosophers' egg and investigate the parts of the philosophic man, for this is the beginning of the rest). The Radix Mundi and Speculum support that subject-matter, not species, is transmuted, and that the first work is Solution: “Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime” [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n1] (ours: species are not transmuted, but the subjects of species best and most properly). The Radix Mundi also supports the operator's moral requirements: “it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality, unless you become sanctified in mind and purified in soul” [III.3 ¶28; III.3 n19].

As “the experimentalist” he is agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; something warned him “from the error of his ways” [IV.4 ¶27]. Norton's verse names “Freer Bacon” with Albertus, and Agrippa followed Friar Bacon's example in proving principles [I.1 ¶60, ¶64].

summary: In quoted authorities, the one root from which all metals and minerals descend, identified with the metallic seed.
body: Quoted from Basil and Geber: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11]. The same passage equates it with the seed: “this metallic seed, or root” [II.1 ¶11]. The record suggests that this root is also the inner basis the operator must find in himself, though that is the context's implication rather than a stated definition.

summary: Atwood's term for the source in which Reason is to seek genuine reminiscence.
body: Atwood says Reason is “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15]. Apparently the same source she elsewhere calls the Root of Reason [IV.4 ¶20], though the text does not equate the two expressly.

summary: The Source and proper object of the rational faculty, buried in the life of sense and resuscitated by Hermetic Artifice; identified with Wisdom and the saving Salt.
body: Atwood: “the proper object of the rational faculty is in its Source, which lies profoundly buried in this life of sense” [IV.4 ¶20]; Hermetic Artifice resuscitates it. She identifies it directly: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20] — so = Wisdom and = saving Salt.

summary: Cited for reference only.
A secret association, known through the Fame and Confession, into which some adepts carried their work for protection.
body: Atwood says some adepts carried their work into a secret association, the Rosicrucian Fraternity of the Fame and Confession, for protection [I.1 ¶66]. She also notes that certain Rosicrucians were alarmed by the books of Agrippa's and Paracelsus' disciples [II.1 ¶9].

summary: A voice cited (Calid in Salmon) for the view that the art belongs to those who understand and cannot be bought or sold.
body: Atwood cites the royal artist, per the footnote from Calid in Salmon, p. 30: “this treasure is not to be bought with money; and as it cannot be bought, so neither can it be sold” [III.4 ¶18; III.4 n13]. She uses it in support: the art is for those who understand.

summary: In Urbigeranus and other adepts, that which is extracted from ‘our Sordid Subject’ by the medium the Arcanum shows.
body: Quoted from Urbigeranus and other Adepts: the Arcanum shows “the medium by which the Royal Diadem may be extracted from our Sordid Subject” [IV.1 ¶7]. The text does not explain the expression further; it apparently names the precious product hidden in the base subject.

summary: In Flammel, the herb found triumphing at the summit of the mountain of the Seven, called mineral, vegetable or saturnine and being ‘either and all’.
body: Quoted from Flammel: at the summit of the mountain of the Seven is “a royal herb triumphing, which some call mineral, some vegetable, some saturnine” [II.4 ¶9]; it is said to be either and all. The text gives no plainer gloss.

summary: Atwood's name for the single path toward which all Hermetic treatises direct once it is found.
body: Atwood says the Hermetic treatises are “all directing on the same Royal Road when this is found” [III.4 ¶15]. The expression is not otherwise defined here.

summary: In a quoted adept, that which moved upon the waters, made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identified with the Stone.
body: Quoted from “the mysterious adeptest”: “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters, the firmament being in the midst” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage has it conceived and made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identifies it with the Stone.

summary: The God-given standard for discerning right from wrong; the superior Reason is called ‘the Reason of our Rule’.
body: The Alchemists' counsel: “Take hold of that Rule which God hath given thee for direction” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood links it to the superior Reason: “the superior virtue of that which is the Reason of our Rule” [III.1 ¶21]. Compare Rule of Reason.

summary: Atwood's term for Reason as guide of the pursuit: under it every step progresses, it alone enters the true Form of Gold, and it proves all things.
body: Atwood: “every step is progressive where the Rule of Reason is pursued” [III.4 ¶11]; of the true Form of Gold, “Reason alone can enter into it” [III.4 ¶11]. Reason's office is inquiry: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15].

summary: Atwood's term for that Spirit, communion with which is the way to the magistery, and whose Law is to be feared and obeyed.
body: Atwood presents “communion with the ruling Spirit of nature” [I.3 n19] as the way to the magistery; its Law is to be feared and obeyed.

summary: An adept named among genuine seekers and cited in support of Basil Valentine's view.
body: Rupecissa is cited as supporting Basil Valentine's view [I.2 ¶31]. As “Rupicessa” he is listed with De Meun, Flamel, John Pontanus, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

summary: The ancients' art practised in the Mysteries, which Atwood connects with Alchemy and Mesmerism and seeks to revive.
body:
Atwood speaks of the ancients' Sacred Art practised in the Mysteries, comparing it with Mesmerism: “if we connect it with the ancients’ Sacred Art” [II.2 ¶7]. She says her chapter aimed “to indicate the connection of the Sacred Art and Alchemy” [II.4 ¶58]. At the close she describes her work as reviving “these lights and relics of the Sacred Art long buried in oblivion” [IV.4 ¶30], and holds that whoever “can understand the language of the philosophers, will understand their Art” [IV.4 ¶32].

The Platonic Successor (quoted) says Jupiter, after spontaneous revelation ceased, “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53] for communication with the gods.

summary: A treatise cited for the labours of Hercules as the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and for the Spirit's sinking when the will inclines downward.
body: Atwood cites the Sacred Discourse in support: the labours of Hercules are the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and when the will inclines downward “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶13–14].

summary: Sacred knowledge and rites which, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified.
body: Atwood: “sacred mysteries, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified by their abuse” [I.1 ¶11] — a ground for the secrecy she defends.

summary: In a quoted adept, the name for the genuine art which fraudulent books blasphemed.
body: Quoted from the adept, on fraudulent writers: “they have blasphemed the Sacred Science, and by their errors have brought contempt on men philosophizing” [I.1 ¶53].

summary: An anonymous voice whose sayings Atwood cites on sense-life, the purified internal fire, and putrefaction.
body: Atwood reads the sage's saying “Visitabis interiora terrae rectificando” [II.3 ¶28–29] (ours: you will visit the interior of the earth by rectifying) as referring to sense-life. Another saying supports the superiority of the purified internal fire: “Si pariat ventum valet auri pondera centum” [III.1 ¶43] (ours: if it brings forth wind, it is worth a hundred weights of gold). Via Ripley Revived, 5th Gate, the sage/adept supports putrefaction as the key, and tincture as coagulated blood: “O happy gate of blackness” [I.3 n42, n43].

summary: The voice of the Book of Enoch, cited to illustrate the guarded mineral soul.
body: Atwood cites the Book of Enoch, chap. 64: 7, 8: “there is an angel standing upon it, and that angel struggles to prevail” [II.3 ¶29; II.3 n32], illustrating the guarded mineral soul.

summary: Author of a two-volume work on the Mysteries whom Atwood criticizes as thorough in research but astronomical and superficial in reading.
body: Atwood cites Sainte Croix's des Mysteres (2 vols, 8vo) and criticizes it: the research is thorough, but the reading of the Mysteries is astronomical and superficial [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n2].

summary: Invoked for their gift of healing, which Atwood notes is absent today.
body: Atwood contrasts the saints and apostles' gift of healing with its absence today, promising the reason in the sequel [III.1 ¶9].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Salt of the Wise (our rendering): Atwood's name for what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened, identified with Mercurius Philosophorum.
body: Atwood: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39] — so = Mercurius Philosophorum. The rendering Salt of the Wise is ours. In context it names what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened.

summary: In quoted adepts, an image of the Stone as born and nourished in fire, enduring it unharmed and curing diseases of men and metals.
body: The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (quoted) says the Eagle and Lion together take on the Salamander's nature, “which, if it remains in the fire without any detriment, cures all the diseases of men and metals” [III.3 ¶63]. Eudoxus (quoted) uses it as an image of the Stone, which “as a true Salamander receives it nativity, is nourished and grows in the Elementary Fire” [IV.3 ¶16].

equivalences.with: most ancient principle of the Stone
menstruum in the sphere of Saturn

summary: One of the three principles (with Sulphur and Mercury); identified by Atwood with Will, Wisdom and the Root of Reason, and by quoted adepts as the most ancient principle of the Stone.
body:
Salt is one of the three principles with Sulphur and Mercury; Atwood lists it third in the series of [III.1 ¶53], in the same position as the body principle and the proceeding substance (how these relate is left open), and the Adept she cites says “yet without Salt no man can attain to this Sacred Science” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius's fable “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56].

**Atwood's identifications.** In the main text she speaks of the Saturnian Salt which, developed to intellect and made erect, subdues all nature, equating it with “the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52], and with “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She calls it “that saving Salt which philosophers were wont anciently to excavate and by so many circulating media to exalt”, identifying it with the Root of Reason and Wisdom: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20].

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** Salt = Will: “There is no true body but Will; it is the principle of the body --- the Salt.” [APP ¶65]. “The Slat is the voluntary substance”, bound in the generative mineral life; drawn up into the medial life, “the Salt thus transplanted becomes Light and grows” [APP ¶77]. “The Salt, the will, opens it secondfold.” [APP ¶182] (the sense of ‘secondfold’ is unclear).

**Quoted voices.** The mysterious adeptest calls it “Salt, that most ancient principle of the Stone” and “The Salt of Saturn, the Universal son of Nature”, “always and everywhere universal through its own fusibility, self-existent in nature”; “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom”; its nucleus in the Decad is to be kept secret; with the Sun, it is that “than which, together with the Sun, nothing is found more useful” [III.3 ¶50]. The Adept speaks of an immortal Salt in the mind's machinery, “that marvelous Salt, which is that menstruum in the sphere of Saturn mentioned by Eirenaeus, which can calcine gold” [IV.2 ¶30]. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

summary: The most abstruse principle of the Stone: deprived of light, the central earth whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe; identified with Demogorgon and the mineral soul.
body: In a passage whose voice is unclear, “The Salt of Saturn, that most abstruse principle of the Stone --- the most ancient Demogorgon” [II.3 ¶41] is said to be deprived of light, the one “whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe, and is the mineral soul” [II.3 ¶41]. It is also the central earth whose Being is Tartarus: “This is the earth, distinguished by Anaxagoras, which abiding durably in the center” [II.3 ¶41]. Compare Salt, where a quoted adept calls the Salt of Saturn the “Universal son of Nature” [III.3 ¶50].

summary: In the Lucerna Solis verse, the Sages' name for the one universal thing containing all nature and Life, extracted from their earth, and not vulgar salt.
body: Quoted from the Lucerna Solis: the one universal thing, present everywhere, containing all nature and all Life and extracted from ‘their earth’, is known only to the Sages: “The band of Sages only have known it, And they call it their salt.” It is explicitly not common salt: “Nor the vulgar salt in any manner, But rather the salt of the world” [I.2 ¶10].

equivalences.with: paternal, maternal, and proceeding ens of life
the active, the passive, and the resulting experience of life
the spirit, the soul, and the body

summary: The three principles of the Adepts: modes of being of one Matter, related as agent, patient and offspring; not the literal substances chemists misapplied.
body:
**Atwood.** Literal chemists failed to extract the Form of gold “by salt, sulfur and mercury, or the three combined with antimony” [I.1 ¶86]. Properly, “The three principles, the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, are merely different as modes of being of the same thing” [I.2 ¶39], exhibited by nature from the Matter's unity after the annihilate condition, as agent, patient and offspring. They are contained in the first matter of metals, a doctrine “of which so much has been spoken and ignorantly misapplied” [I.3 n22]; they are “the paternal, maternal, and proceeding ens of life. And there are the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury of the Adepts” [I.3 n30]; “thou hast in these three principles, says Sendivogius, a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]. Per Vaughan they are hidden intrinsical natures, not literal ‘pot-principles’ [I.3 n30]. At [III.3 ¶77] she names them “the Sulphur and Mercury and Slat, the active and the passive, and the resulting experience of life”: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will”; “the second is of the Humanity, i.e., of the selfhood, prepared and sanctified”; “the result of these two in unison is the Bodily Substance of things thenceforth created” — three powers in one seat. In the mind's machinery she lists “wheel within wheel revolving vitally, Mercury, Sulphur, and an immortal Salt” [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) they are the three principles of the vital force in the blood: “Attraction, Circulation, Repulsion --- the Alchemical Salt, Mercury, Sulphur” [APP ¶24].

**Quoted.** Basil and Crollius: “the mercury, slat and sulfur --- spirit, body and soul --- lie hid together in one thing” [II.1 ¶11]; “there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found in the salt, mercury, and sulfur thereof” [II.1 ¶14]. Eudoxus: they are present, seemingly but not truly united, in the apparently homogeneous Water — “Salt, Sulphur and Mercury --- which are the spirit, the soul, and the body” [IV.3 ¶7]. Note the sources differ on which principle is spirit, soul or body.

summary: In Sendivogius, a substance taken with water from Our Earth, upon which the radical moisture is put.
body: Quoted from Sendivogius: “water and salt-nitre, which comes from Our Earth” [IV.3 ¶21]; the radical moisture is put upon it. Not further explained.

summary: An unnamed author, apparently Eirenaeus (following the n37 verse), cited from Introitus Apertus cap. 7 for an explanation of the whole difficulty.
body: Cited at [IV.1 ¶43] and [IV.1 n38] (Introitus Apertus, cap. 7) for ‘an explanation of the whole difficulty’ — the Fiery Dragon, the Lodestone, purgation, and “Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos”. The note itself names no author; the context suggests Eirenaeus, since ‘the same author’ follows the verse cited at n37.

summary: In Vaughan, the place of Nature's treasures, behind a Door that must be opened through knowledge of the First Matter.
body: Quoted from Vaughan: the Sanctuary of Nature is discovered by knowing the First Matter; “There is nothing between thee and her treasures but the Door: that indeed must be opened.” [III.4 ¶44].

summary: In the Appendix, the self-willed life or Will, which entraps the Light and holds the key to Sulphur's prison.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Saturn or the self-willed life” [APP ¶72], “the selfish Saturnine life in man”, entraps the Light and craves more; it is overcome by satiation and then transmuted [APP ¶72]. “a Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]. As a planetary property, nothing can be felt or realized “without the voluntary dominance of Saturn and Luna” [APP ¶113]. Compare Saturnian Will and Salt of Saturn.

summary: Planetary names used in the Appendix as qualities of character and work: Saturnine dark potentiality cleared by the Jupiter element.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood, judging a work or character: “It is a Saturnine mass of power in mere potentiality; a dark cloud; chaos before Light strikes through it.” and “It wants the Jupiter element to clear it.” [APP ¶175].

headword: Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will
forms: Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will
summary: Something founded on the Matter (as Pan), once circumscribed in Intellect for the manifestation of its Light; not further explained.
body: Atwood says the Matter, as Pan, is “the foundation of the great Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will, which was once circumscribed in Intellect, for the manifestation of its Light” [III.2 ¶7]. Not further explained.

summary: The Will, figured by the drunken Saturn of the verse, which revels without rational restraint through the subordinate faculties until sated and asleep.
body: Atwood reads the drunken Saturn of the verse as the Will: “For the Saturnian Will, being allowed to revel without limitation or rational restraint” through the subordinate faculties, until “his desires are more than satisfied, and, as the image runs, from the effect he sleeps” [III.1 ¶68]. Compare the Appendix account of Saturn as self-willed life overcome by satiation [APP ¶72].

summary: The knowledge the few wise took with them into obscurity.
body: Atwood says the wise preserved their knowledge “by burying themselves with their saving science in profound obscurity” [I.1 ¶30].

summary: Cited for the command to have Salt in ourselves and for the honour of the ass at his triumph.
body: Atwood cites the Savior's order to have Salt in ourselves, “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She also cites the Saviour's choice of the ass ‘on the occasion of his greatest earthly triumph’ to illustrate that animal's honour [III.2 ¶64].

summary: Named by Atwood with Kant and Fichte as falling short of objective realization, though ranked above them; quoted on awakening from Intellectual Intuition.
body: Atwood criticizes Kant, Fichte and Schelling for a metaphysics ending in void non-entity and skepticism, short of objective realization, while ranking Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. She cites him in support of the view that after the intuition only the remembered vision remains, owing to the limits of human reason: “We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death” [IV.2 ¶33]. The Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) mentions him with Fichte by way of contrast [APP ¶96] and in the same list as ones who ‘saw it’ [APP ¶117].

summary: The glossator of the Scholium, Atwood's main and approved commentator in I.3, cited for practical and spiritual readings of the Hermetic text.
body: Atwood cites the Scholiast throughout I.3 with approval (‘our Scholiast’, ‘the wise Scholiast’), taking the Scholium as giving full instructions. He interprets the elements, colours, recipe, Mercury, vulture, mountain, fire and bird, “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]–[I.3 n16]. He locates the work in life — “It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life” [I.3 n48] — and glosses ‘as vinegar makes vinegar’ [I.3 n48–n55]. He supports practical readings of the Athanor and Hermetic seal — “The matter, he says, is to be decocted in the philosophic furnace called Athanor, with a continual fire.” — the treasury of nature in the breast, fixed sulfur as balsam of nature, and the soul of gold as aurific principle [I.3 n57–n67]. He is cited on entering the Spirit (“Thou must enter with thy whole spirit into the center of nature”), the repeated opening of the body, Magnesia, the essence of life as Fire, the Dragon as first blackness, secret sulfur and the rarity of the philosophic water [I.3 n19–n36]; and on the affinity of body and spirit — “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” — dissolution, multiplication and the parents nursed [I.3 n37–n42].

summary: Named only in a phrase borrowed within Vaughan's quotation.
body: Mentioned only within a quotation from Vaughan: “bad news (as the schoolmen phrase it)” [IV.2 ¶35].

summary: Listed by Atwood among the confessed adepts.
body: Named in Atwood's list of confessed adepts [I.1 ¶39].

summary: Cited by Atwood throughout as supporting authority: on Wisdom, blessing from God, purity, the conversion of darkness to light, and as analogue of the Hermetic Work.
body: Atwood cites Scripture as endorsed authority. It promises Wisdom, following Solomon's panegyric, with other such places [II.1 ¶45]; the Scriptures teach a faith bestowing Wisdom, God's sentence on the Serpent (“I will put enmity between thee and the woman”), and promises of Wisdom and material fruits, and are to be read as obscure and mystical [IV.3 ¶37–¶46]. Blessing and increase come from God: “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater”, with ‘Every good gift…’ and ‘God alone giveth the increase’; the talent is taken from him who does not use it [III.4 ¶20]. It supports the conversion of darkness into light: “The night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are all alike to Him” [III.2 ¶10]; number, weight and measure as Nature's three dimensions: “Thou hast disposed all things, in number, weight, and measure.” [III.3 ¶67]; and that the healer must first be healed: “Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in thy field; and afterwards build thy house” [III.1 ¶9, III.1 n7] (the note refers to the Wisdom of Solomon and Proverbs 24), with the beam and mote and ‘Physician, heal thyself’. For purity she cites “He that hath clean hands and a pure heart”, saying she quotes it as apt, ‘proved on the Divine Ground’, not because it is popular [IV.1 ¶39–¶40]. The ancestors found the Word of Life, “which their neglected Scriptures everywhere testify of” [IV.2 ¶43]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Work revealed in Holy Scripture is the analogue of the Hermetic Work, and the Stone of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139].

summary: The Matter in its flowing, moist state, passive to every impression of the light.
body: Atwood: “In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise, passive to all impression and influences of the light” [I.3 n16].

equivalences.with: a ting more precious than the whole world

summary: In Synesius and the New Light, the precious thing congealed in gold and silver and abiding in the sea of the world.
body: Quoted (Synesius; the New Light): the precious thing is “a ting more precious than the whole world; which I plainly tell thee is nothing else than our sea water” [I.2 ¶33]; it is congealed in gold and silver and abides ‘in the sea of the world’.

summary: In Boehme, the concealment set before the true ground of the art to prevent its misuse.
body: Quoted from Boehme: “the Seal of God lieth before it, to conceal the true ground” [II.1 ¶25], so that the art may not be misused.

summary: Greater than the first Adam: the restoration exceeds what was lost.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “for the second Adam is greater than the first” [APP ¶98] — the restoration exceeds what was lost.

summary: In Norton, the character of the Elixir as engendered by the concord of virtues; not further explained.
body: Quoted from Norton: from the concord of virtues “Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34]. Not further explained.

summary: The stage in which Nature alone works, without hands, by regulated external fire; for Atwood, the main reference of the Ordinal's period of years.
body: Eirenaeus: “In the Second, however, Nature alone operates, and without any imposition of hands” [IV.1 ¶11], by well-regulated external fire. Khunrath likewise: after the first act, in one vessel, furnace and fire, body, spirit and soul dissolve and reunite, they “rot of themselves and without manual cooperation, by the sole labors of nature” [IV.1 ¶36]. Atwood says the Ordinal's period of years: “This is meant chiefly in reference to the Second Operation” [IV.1 ¶17], linking it to the discovery of the philosophic Salt. Its relation to the Gross Work is not stated. Compare Second Work.

summary: The Paradisiacal Life, lived under the Cross.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Living in the Second Principle means living the Paradisiacal Life” [APP ¶94]; it is lived under the Cross, the heart life below the extended arms representing it.

summary: In Van helmont, second qualities misleadingly trusted, contrasted with specifical (appropriated) qualities acting only on their proper object.
body: Quoted from Van helmont: those go astray who, “they too much trusting to Second qualities, as being ill secure, do sleep thereupon”, neglect the “specifical qualities, also appropriated ones (which are only extended on their proper object)” [IV.1 ¶39].

summary: In the Adept, a spirit subsisting and tinging in the body, extracted by the Preparing Spirit.
body: Quoted from the Adept: the Preparing Spirit “extracts a Second Spirit subsisting and tinging in the body”, “extracting from it the tinging spirit” [IV.1 ¶10].

summary: The continuation of the First Work, perfecting the new embryo and multiplying its light; for Atwood, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt.
body: Atwood: “the Second Work, which is only, in continuation of the First, to perfect the newly informed embryo and multiply its vivific light” [I.3 n7]. It is one of the Art's greatest subtleties: “By the Second Work we are to understand, therefore, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “The Fourth Key of the Art is the entrance to the Second Work” [IV.3 ¶12], in which the Water is reduced to Earth. Compare Second Operation.

summary: In Eirenaeus, the fire contained in, and identified with, ‘our water’.
body: Quoted from Eirenaeus: “For in our water is our secret fire.” and “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69]; the water is apparently Mercury. Compare secret Fire of the Wise.

summary: The only agent the Art grants for purifying Nature; without knowing it, one fails even with the true matter.
body: In a passage whose voice is unclear (Atwood, or continuing ‘our author of The Triumph’, cited in the next sentence): “the secret Fire of the Wise, which is the only agent granted by Art to purify and dispose Nature to a sacrifice of her last life” [IV.2 ¶6]. Eudoxus: it makes a water that does not wet the hands run out of the dry-looking ‘plant’, and many fail “for want of knowing the secret fire of the wise” even after knowing the true matter [IV.3 ¶16]. The same paragraph names “the Understanding of Our Fire, which is both secret and natural” as one of two things that give the Keys; whether this is the same fire is not stated outright.

summary: In Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, what Argent Vive prepared by art gives: the mother of the Stone, known by several names.
body: Eirenaeus, quoted, says that Argent Vive prepared by art “gives the secret menstrual: The mother of our Stone which is so rare.” [III.1 ¶69] He gives it further names: “Our oil, our unguent, and our marchasite; Which we do name also our fountain bright.” [III.1 ¶69] So, in his verse, secret menstrual = mother of the Stone = oil, unguent, marchasite, fountain bright.

summary: The philosophers' name for what the Art teaches but never teaches openly; in Morieni, the magistery itself, God's secret.
body: Artephius, quoted, rebukes the literal reader: “you, fool, believe we teach the secret of secrets openly” [I.1 ¶84]. Atwood records Secretu Secretorum as a philosophers' name for the same thing, and cites Morieni identifying it with the magistery: “hoc magisterium nihil aliud est, nisi Arcanum et secretum secretorum Dei altissimi et magni” [II.4 ¶39] (our rendering: this magistery is nothing else but the Arcanum and secret of secrets of God most high and great). In Morieni, then, the secret of secrets = the magisterium, God's secret entrusted to the prophets [II.4 ¶39].

summary: What Form (Light) clothed with matter begets, impressing its character on matter; the seed of gold is called the Stone of Fire.
body: Atwood presents seed as what Form, or Light, begets when clothed with matter: “Which clothed with mater doth a seed beget.” [I.2 ¶45] The seed impresses its character on matter; metals arise from metalline seeds out of the Universal Spirit, while vulgar gold lacks seed until art helps it [I.2 ¶45]. An adept, cited by her, identifies the seed of gold with the Stone of Fire: “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44].

summary: In Sendivogius, quoted, that of which man's body is a shadow.
body: Sendivogius, quoted, says “the body of man is a shadow of the seed of nature” [II.1 ¶10].

summary: What is at last found within the purified material extreme of this life, described as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star.
body: Atwood: “within the material extreme of this life, when it is purified, the Seed of Spirit is at last found” [II.3 ¶30]. It is described there as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star [II.3 ¶30].

summary: The active principle whose Will the Passive Intelligence answers and accompanies through the abyss.
body: Atwood speaks of the Passive Intelligence which “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason” [III.1 ¶40]; the seeking Reason is the active partner (spoken of as him), which she accompanies through the abyss.

summary: Cited for reference only.
This life of ours, in which the Divine Light is hidden and which appropriates that Light instead of serving it.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls our life self-begotten, the life in which the Divine Light is hidden: “This life of ours, instead of administering to the Divine Life, appropriates it.” [APP ¶70]

summary: Centers that gifted beings in whom the Word gives power tend to set up; key to the Second Commandment as the result of violating the First.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood warns that “the danger is the tendency in such gifted beings to set up self-centers” [APP ¶100], beings in whom the Word gives power. She treats this as the key to the Second Commandment, as the outcome of violating the First [APP ¶100].

summary: What adulterates vision in the phantastic sphere.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says of vision in the phantastic sphere: “it is self-desire that adulterates” [APP ¶105].

summary: Atwood's name for the Hermetic method itself: inner revelation in a purified soul, the root of alchemical tradition and the narrow way of regeneration.
body:
For Atwood, Self-Knowledge is the Hermetic method: “the Hermetic method of Self-Knowledge” [I.3 n46], which alone enables man to know, understand and possess divine things. She holds “Self-Knowledge to be at the root of all Alchemical tradition” [II.1 ¶30], formerly taken as a way to knowledge of Universal Nature.

It is the object of the inward search whose method she seeks from the ancients: “the true method and conditions of Self- Knowledge” [II.1 ¶46]. She sets it apart from trance or vision and equates it with the true psychical experience: “For it is this, no common trance or day-dream, or any fanatical vision of celestials, that we propose to scrutinize, but the true psychical experience” [II.1 ¶46].

It is among the goods of the higher Mysteries: “the Self-Knowledge and perfection of life and immortality promised” [II.2 ¶7]. Atwood names by it the method of inner revelation in a purified soul, “the narrow way of regeneration into life” [II.4 ¶19]. The Greeks reached “an experimental conception of its reality in the self-knowledge” [III.2 ¶46], i.e. of the reality of the Whole. Its condition is total privation: “Self-knowledge is impossible unless every other knowledge is deprived” [III.2 ¶56].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Self-knowledge is the first contact of consciousness in the ground of life.” [APP ¶137]

summary: That through which the Reason arises, with creative attributes and powers, in regeneration.
body: Atwood says the Reason “arises through the self-perceivance, with creative attributes and powers” [III.3 ¶52]. Whose self is perceived the text does not specify here.

summary: The individual's distinct subsistence as separated, or outborn, from the Fontal Reason.
body: Atwood describes the individual as “a distinct self-spiration, severation, or outbirth, as it were, from that Fontal Reason” [III.3 ¶52]: self-spiration is thus equated with severation and outbirth.

summary: The forbidden regions into which depraved minds climbed by the clue of life.
body: Atwood says depraved minds, given the clue of life, “climbed by it into forbidden regions of self-sufficiency” [III.4 ¶4].

summary: The individual, self-centred will acting for itself rather than under God's law, at war with the Divine Will; to be brought into subjection.
body:
All records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood describes self-will as will acting for itself rather than under God's law: “The magic of the self-will is that which the Egyptians practiced in the days of Moses” [APP ¶2], and power “taken into the self-will and used accordingly it becomes diabolical” [APP ¶4].

When the Wisdom-life is stirred, “what takes it is the self-will” [APP ¶82]; it wars with the Universal Will and, as patient, has its false forms dissolved. Drawn upward by love it becomes passive; acting before its time it destroys: “There is a swiftness in the self-willed magnet working powerfully and to destruction” [APP ¶103]. The Divine purpose is to “bring the self-willed opposition into subjection” [APP ¶104], through man's consent. In religion it distorts: “The action of the self-will on the soul which exaggerates its religious life” [APP ¶110].

It is the principle we are born into: “This war is the war between two principles of the self-will and the Divine Will.” [APP ¶154]

summary: The inner self-will that arrests the entering light; it must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice and is finally subdued by the connate spirit.
body: Atwood describes the light “penetrating to meet the self-willed Identity within, is arrested” [III.1 ¶53]. This Identity must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice, “humiliation of the Selfhood under the exemplary cross of Christ” [III.1 ¶60], and the connate spirit at last subdues it to self-mortification [III.1 ¶60].

summary: The separate, self-centred individual self into which the soul has fallen; it must be dissolved, subverted and abandoned to the Divine Will for regeneration.
body:
Atwood treats selfhood as the separate self that must be undone. Its “dark dominion” [II.3 n2] is dissolved by the magnetic friction of its proper light. Reiterated reflexive analysis serves so that “it may resolve the separable Selfhood” [IV.1 ¶20]; rectification and sublimation are completed “by an actual subversion of the selfhood” [IV.1 ¶47]. The work requires one “to abandon the life of selfhood” [III.4 ¶6], the necessary charges, and return to the Universal by “abandoning the selfhood” [IV.4 ¶27]. Immortality is consummated by “the abandonment of the dual selfhood and its volition to the Divine Will” [IV.3 ¶58]; then “from the separable selfhood, the Identity passes into universal accord” [IV.3 ¶60].

In III.2 (voice unclear) the selfhood is obliterated in the attraction into the First Cause: “as this selfhood likewise is obliterated in the overwhelming attraction, which raises it into the First Cuase” [III.2 ¶56]; and non-being is glossed as the subjective selfhood, whose additions bring poverty [III.2 ¶59].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the soul's fall is “the fall away of it into selfhood, which has defaced the image” [APP ¶120], and the converting light shines on “the darkness of the selfhood on which it shines” [APP ¶114]. The Midas-will holds the life it possesses “holding it as he did the selfhood” [APP ¶159].

forms: the author of the New Light
summary: An adept and author of the New Light of Alchemy, among Atwood's most cited and generally endorsed authorities on the matter, water and practice of the Art.
body:
Atwood names him Michael Sendivogius, author of Novum Lumen Chemicum / The New Light of Alchemy; his imprisonment illustrates persecution, and his book is praised as attractive but deliberately disordered, needing repeated study; some identify him with Philalethes and with Alexander Seton [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶71, I.1 ¶73].

On method of reading: from his Preface, one must read from the possibility of nature, not the words, for “this Art is for the wise, not for the ignorant” [I.1 ¶84]; from his Epilogue, philosophers teach indirectly and contradict on purpose, “it being the custom of philosophers to use them; thou hast need of them” [I.1 ¶84].

On the matter: “Our water is heavenly, not wetting the hands, not of the vulgar, but almost rain water” [I.2 ¶33]; his saying that the matter of metals is twofold Atwood reinterprets as relation within the Ethereal being [I.2 ¶42]. One must seek the hidden thing yielding a moisture “which doth dissolve gold without violence or noise” [I.2 ¶48]. “Vulgar gold Sendivogius compares to a herb without seed” [I.2 ¶49]. The three principles are one substance in triple relation, “a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]; and “our lune or silver, not common silver, is that which receives the seed of the gold” [I.3 n39]. He describes the Water of our Sea, “that water was as white as snow” [III.2 ¶7], “the water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]; and the enigmatic conversion of elements: “who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join a spirit thereto” [III.3 ¶29].

Atwood criticizes him once as diverting readers from Morien's hint [II.1 ¶8], but endorses him on man as microcosm: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10]; on Fire: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]; and on prayer with work: “Pray, says Sendivogius, pray; but work.” [III.4 ¶20]. He also supplies “Urinus Saturni” for the Black Saturn [II.3 ¶18], his Planetary Sphere = the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9], and the fight in which “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56], yielding white milk [III.1 n62]; per n66 he is also the source of the Adept's saying that without Salt no man attains the Science [III.1 n66]. His friends disbelieved that “there was any water in our sea” [III.4 ¶16]. In IV.3, the wary Artist, he teaches spiritual fermentation: “thou takest not common gold or silver, for these are dead; take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21], admitting that his experience stopped there. In the Appendix (later layer) he is cited for the Philosopher who “looks not out on nature with the eyes of common men” [APP ¶67].

summary: Cited, from his Epistola xci, as witness to Democritus' making of artificial precious stones.
body: Atwood cites Seneca (Epistola xci) for Democritus' “his artificial confection of precious stones” [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n18].

summary: Cited for the precept that the volatile must be united with the fixed, which Atwood says deserves attention.
body: Atwood cites Senior's precept on uniting volatile with fixed, “the highest fume should be reduced to the lowest” [IV.3 ¶8], as one which deserves attention.

summary: Sense perception and its beguilements, made the beacon of modern thought; the turbulent sea beyond which the haven lies.
body: Atwood laments that modern thought follows “the beguilements of sense” [IV.4 ¶28] and places the haven “beyond the turbulent sea of sense” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: The medium of sense-consciousness that trance dissolves, beneath which consciousness is later translated.
body: Atwood says trance can “dissolve the sensible medium and convert it to the experience of another life” [II.3 ¶5]; consciousness is afterwards translated beneath it.

summary: What is fixed and must be dissolved in the work.
body: Atwood glosses the alchemical fixed thing as the sensual compact: “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved” [II.3 ¶37].

summary: The dominance of sense-life, identified with the corporeal; softened by the ethereal waters and subdued by Spirit in regeneration.
body: Atwood says the ethereal waters soften the sensual dominant to “make it more fit for the returning reason and understanding to work upon” [III.1 ¶53]. It is subdued “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15], and she identifies it with the corporeal: Spirit “overcomes the corporeal, which is the sensual dominant, in the regeneration” [III.3 ¶23].

summary: What is without a person; it must be made flexible and hidden.
body: Atwood glosses that which is without: “that which is without, viz., the sensual spirit of life must be made flexible and occultated” [I.3 n8].

summary: The principle of sense in the blood, dissolved by magnetizing and reiterated contritions; its residuum supplies body to the regenerate soul.
body: Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood identifies it as “the principle of sense or the sensuous medium in the blood” [APP ¶109], against which the senses are turned. Absorbed by reiterative contritions and dissolved by magnetizing, “it dissolved the sensuous medium and opens the consciousness to the Divine life” [APP ¶91]. Brought to its last ens, “The residuum from this medium supplies body to the regenerate soul” [APP ¶110].

summary: The spirit in the blood through which life acts; taken up into the will, it dies so that new life, the Phoenix, may arise.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood describes the spirit in the blood through which life acts, to be taken up into the will so that new life grows from its death: “Out of the ashes of this present sensuous spirit arises the Phoenix.” [APP ¶91]

summary: In Atwood's modern exponent, what was at first fixed and is dissolved in the blackening.
body: Quoting our modern exponent, Atwood reports that in the blackening “that which at first was fixed, viz., the sentient medium, is dissolved” [II.1 ¶23].

equivalences.with: the ordeals of the Mysteries (decomposition and death of the natural life)

summary: The primary object of the Art: separating pure from impure and subtle from gross, which Atwood takes to be apparently identical with the Mysteries' ordeal of the death of the natural life.
body:
Paracelsus, quoted, held that “separation was the principle and beginning of all generation” [I.2 ¶25], the greatest miracle in philosophy; it is the first half of Ripley's procedure before recombination [I.2 ¶25].

Atwood: “This Separation is indeed the primary object of the Art” [III.1 ¶21], the separating of pure from impure and subtle from gross, done by mind, not mechanical dissolution. She identifies it with the Mysteries: it “appears to be identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries, when the great ordeals are passed through during the decomposition and death of the natural life” [III.1 ¶21].

summary: The true separating agent, whose finding is the greatest difficulty; in Boehme, a divine artist of great subtlety within lovers of the Art.
body: Atwood: “To find the true Separator is described, in fact, as the greatest difficulty” [III.1 ¶32], which she likens to Virgil's hidden tree. Jacob Boehme, quoted, speaks of lovers of the Art “whose Separator is an artist of great subtlety in them” [III.1 ¶39], a divine agent that must not be given into the bestial hand.

summary: In the Adept's words, the seven made when Three and Four unite; the true Sabaoth, the rest of God the creature shall enter.
body: The Adept, quoted: “Three and Four make seven.” [IV.2 ¶18] (the four elements with Unity and Ternarius). He identifies it: “This Sepentary is the true Sabaoth, the rest of God” [IV.2 ¶18], which the creature shall enter.

summary: In a passage quoted from Agrippa, the Sephiroth, glossed as Hochma, are that on which the ass's influence occultly depends.
body: Voice: Agrippa, as quoted. The ass's influence is said to depend occultly on the Sephiroth, glossed in the same breath: “Sephiroth, i.e., Hochma” [III.2 ¶64]. So the text equates Sephiroth with Hochma here; it does not explain either further.

summary: In a passage quoted from Paracelsus, the sequestatrix is that which gives each thing its form and essence; Atwood links it to the special part of Intellect.
body: Paracelsus is quoted: “that is the sequestatrix, which gives to every thing its form and essence” [III.1 ¶21]. In the same passage Atwood seems to call either this sequestatrix or the Separation the special part of Intellect. The text leaves unclear which of the two she means.

summary: Two serpents found everywhere on earth, a living male and a living female, to be understood spiritually and not bodily.
body: Voice: Cornelius Agrippa's ingenious disciple, as quoted. The two serpents are found everywhere on earth: “they are a living male and a living female (understand in relation to the spirit always without all corporeal allusion)” [III.1 ¶50]. The text itself instructs a spiritual reading, without any bodily reference.

summary: Servius, commenting on Virgil, is cited to support the point that the Bacchic rites served to purify souls.
body: Atwood cites Servius's comment on Virgil in support of her point that the Bacchic rites were meant to purify souls: “Libris patris sacra ad purgationem animarum pertinebant” [II.2 ¶5]. A rough rendering (ours, not the book's): the sacred rites of Father Liber pertained to the purification of souls. The claim rests on Atwood's own use of the line, not on our rendering.

summary: Atwood says the great principle of the number seven is a Rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The great principle of the number seven is a Rest” [APP ¶69]. This is a rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.

summary: In Hermes, seven bodies of which gold is first; Atwood reads them as the inferior spheres of vitality in which the soul of gold moves.
body: Atwood cites Hermes: “there are seven bodies --- of which gold is the first, the most perfect, the king of them, and their head” [I.3 ¶58]. In a note she explains what the bodies stand for. The aim is to “perfect all the other seven bodies; i.e., to signify here, according to Hermes, the inferior spheres of vitality in which it moves” [I.3 n65]. So she identifies the seven bodies with the inferior spheres of vitality in which gold's soul moves.

summary: Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, marked by color and quality.
body: Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, distinguished by color and quality. She notes that writers name them differently: “some call them planets, others metals (for the radical life of the spirit is indeed mineral)” [I.3 n47].

summary: The period in which the principles are separated, during which a coction goes on amid flood, eclipse and confusion.
body: Atwood uses severation for the period in which the principles are separated: “during this period of the severation, a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. In her account this period is marked by flood, eclipse and confusion.

summary: A solvent known only to philosophers; Atwood says Cleopatra dissolved her earring in it.
body: Atwood tells how Cleopatra dissolved her earring in “such a sharp vinegar as is only known to philosophers on the ground of nature” [I.1 ¶18]. The text gives it no further identification.

summary: The ‘allegoric’ siege of life, to which the Rational Light is raised and where it overcomes the stronghold of evil.
body: Atwood says the Rational Light “afterwards is raised to the allegoric siege of life” [III.4 ¶19], where it overcomes ‘the stronghold of evil’. The term is not explained further here.

summary: Atwood says an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding to know things in their roots.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding for “the knowledge of things in their roots” [APP ¶63]. The term is not defined further here.

summary: In Norton's Ordinal, the simperings of the Stone must be known until it can no more simper.
body: Voice: Norton's Ordinal, as quoted: “To know the simperings of our Stone, Till it may no more simper do, nor cease,” [IV.1 ¶12]. The verse apparently sets simmering against boiling. This is the reader's inference; the text does not state it.

summary: What Van Helmont was led to perceive in his dream-like vision.
body: Atwood says Van Helmont, in a dream-like vision, was “led along into a perception of the simple element of nature” [III.2 ¶17].

summary: Named as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage that Atwood cites.
body: Atwood names Simplicius as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage she uses [III.1 ¶21]. Nothing more is said of him.

headword: Sir William Jones (translator of an Indian record)
summary: Translator of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1) that Atwood cites: all mental appearances except the First Cause are image or delusion.
body: Atwood cites Sir William Jones's translation of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1, p.241) as giving the same instruction: every mental appearance except the First Cause is image or delusion. The record says: “know that to be the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n51]. She uses it as agreeing with her own position.

summary: In Hermes, a kind of sulphur, identified with lions' and cats' claws.
body: Voice: Hermes, as quoted. Siretz is a sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It is also identified with “the lions' and cats' claws, which is siretz” [I.3 ¶20]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

summary: Those Geber condemns next above the Covetous: they stay ignorant by choice and hinder others; Atwood calls their skepticism the mock ally of rational skepticism.
body: Atwood reports Geber's judgment: “next above the Covetous, Skeptics are condemned by Geber” [III.4 ¶12]. In her account they remain ignorant by choice and hinder others. She adds her own view that modern skeptics only ‘ape’ sound reason, and that their skepticism is the ‘mock ally’ of rational skepticism. She apparently shares Geber's condemnation.

summary: Hermes' Tabula Smaragdina, quoted in full as comprising the working principle and total subject of the art; Atwood calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art.
body:
Atwood quotes the Tablet in full (as the Smaragdine Table, also spelled ‘Smagardine table’, or the Emerald Table). She treats it as containing the working principle and total subject of the art, and calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art. Its key line: “that which is above is as that which is below” [I.1 ¶3; I.1 ¶7–10]. She endorses it and uses it repeatedly:

- As the Emerald Table, to show that agent and patient are one after dissolution, the One Thing: “That which is below is as that which is above” [I.2 ¶48].
- As the Smagardine Table, to show that both the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient must be prepared: “That which is above is as that which is below, and that which is below is as that which is above” [III.1 ¶41].
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), for the point about earth or the residuum: “The power is integral if it be turned into earth” [APP ¶110].

summary: Cited from the Republic, Theaetus and Phaedrus for Wisdom generating truth, for the grades of initiation, and as the one who knew the Nothing that is Wisdom.
body:
Atwood draws on Socrates:

- From the Republic and Theaetus: Wisdom generates truth, perfects imperfect things and calls forth latent Intellections. “Wisdom is generative of truth and intellect” [II.1 ¶37].
- From the Phaedrus, as explained in a passage from Proclus: the ordered grades of initiation. “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. He is also the narrator of Plato's ascent to Intelligible Beauty [II.4 ¶29].
- Atwood identifies the Wisdom with the Nothing that Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27].

She uses all three in support of her own position.

summary: Sol or the Sun: hidden inwardly in the Stone, imprisoned until penetrated by the mercurial Spirit, partner of the Moon, and given to the reduced body as its soul.
body:
Several voices speak of Sol:

- Hermes, as quoted: the Stone's sun and beams lie hidden within it. “My Sol and my beams are most inward and secretly in me” [I.3 ¶37]. Sol is also said to ‘follow’ in the seven letters, but this is not explained.
- Atwood, explaining how Mercury acts on gold: “the formal virtue of Sol is sealed; his sulphur is imprisoned” [III.3 ¶30]. Sol is unaware of himself until the mercurial Spirit penetrates him; then he sends forth his Light.
- Atwood on the Sun as the Moon's partner in the work. Citing Plutarch, she says “the operations of the Sun are seen to resemble those strokes which by mere dint of strength and force bear down all before them” [III.1 ¶45]. In a passage from Boehme, Sol is given to the reduced body as its soul: “give it Sol, viz., the soul” [III.1 ¶48].
- The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, as quoted: the Lion devours and eclipses the bright Sun and brings him to greater perfection. The Sun is the Moon's brother and bridegroom; with her he is parent of the King, and he feeds a red King. “This Lyon maketh the Sun sith [fith] soone To be joined to hys Sister the Moone:” [III.1 ¶65]. ‘Sol’ appears in parallel positions in the same verse, but the text does not state that it is the same as the Sun.
- Pierce, the Black Monk, as quoted, lists Sol among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].
- Eirenaeus, as quoted, pairs Sol and Lune as the products of projection: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” and “Innumerable parts to Sol’s estate.” [IV.3 ¶25]. Their effect will prove ‘both gold and silver pure’.

summary: Atwood equates the Sol principle with the vortex of life, to which Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely in consciousness.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), equates the two: “the vortex of life ---the Sol principle” [APP ¶113]. Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely to it in consciousness.

summary: In Flamel, two Mercuries, one planted in the other, cherished in the Alembic over a constant sun-like fire.
body: Voice: Flamel, as quoted. He speaks of “the Solar and Lunar Mercury, and the plantation of the one in the other” [IV.1 ¶41]. Both are cherished in the Alembic over a constant fire like the sun's. The text does not explain this further.

summary: Light that the ethereal humidity nourishes and educates; set beside Sol as the source of all heat.
body: Atwood says the ethereal humidity “nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]. In the same passage she sets the Solar Light beside Sol as the source of all heat.

summary: In the Mystere de la Croix, a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold, drawn by subtle operations from the vitriol left after Mars and Venus are conjoined.
body: Voice: the Mystere de la Croix, as quoted. After Mars and Venus are conjoined, subtle operations draw from the leftover vitriol “un souphre solaire ou or philosophique vivant” [III.3 ¶11]. Our rendering, not the book's: a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold. The phrasing equates solar sulphur with living philosophic gold.

summary: Atwood equates the Solar Tincture with the Aurific Light.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The Solar Tincture (Tinctura Solaris) is the Aurific Light.” [APP ¶92]. The term is not explained further.

summary: The wise king, cited throughout as a voice on Wisdom: its nature, its gift from above, its increase, and seeing all things in its Spirit.
body:
Atwood often cites Solomon, also called the wise king, in support of her own view of Wisdom:

- Wisdom of Solomon, chap. 7: a panegyric of Wisdom as pure, all-pervading and renewing, entering holy souls. “Wisdom, says the wise king, is more moving than any motion” [II.1 ¶44; II.1 n42].
- Wisdom of Solomon 8: 9: knowledge of creation comes by Conscious Intuition, taught by Wisdom. “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49; III.3 n34].
- Wisdom of Solomon, 21: Wisdom must be given from above, and it preserves the righteous. “Or what man is he, asks Solomon, that can know the counsel of God?” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n18].
- Atwood reads “the fear of God is the beginning of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶37] as the awe of the soul perceiving itself in its source.
- Proverbs iv, 8, 9 illustrates the increase of the fermenting light: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [I.3 n45].
- Proverbs 24, 27 and Eccles. 4: Wisdom joined with strength, and two are better than one. “A wise man is strong, says the wise king, and knowledge increaseth strength” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n51].
- The ‘enclosed garden of Solomon’ and the sealed fountain are identified with Elysium [II.4 ¶9].

Others cite him within passages she quotes:

- Charnocke's verse on the faithful servant: “A good servant, saith Solomon, let him be unto thee, As thine own hearte,in each degree” [III.4 ¶35].
- Eirenaeus, against idleness: “The desire of the idle shall cause him to perish” [IV.1 ¶6].
- Helmont, on the physician as created by the Lord: “Honor the physician with the honor due unto him” [IV.3 ¶34].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Solomon illustrates seeing the nature and virtues of all things in the Spirit of Wisdom [APP ¶67]. He also supports not exceeding the capacity one is given: “Be not righteous overmuch” [APP ¶110].

summary: The dissolving that is the first work and foundation of the art: the body reduced to water or mercury; for Atwood, also the separation of the sensuous medium and a converting comprehension.
body:
Friar Bacon and the Rosarium, as quoted, call Solution the first work: the body is reduced into water, that is, mercury, and “this is called Solution, which is the foundation of the whole art” [I.2 ¶5].

Atwood's own uses:

- She glosses the verb directly: “solve, that is comprehend, it on its own ground” [II.2 ¶15]. The impure perceptive medium needs this: “it needs alternation and solution, as the oracles teach” [II.2 ¶15]. And “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution” [II.2 ¶16].
- On the operation itself: “Solution dissolves and liquifies the included Spirit” [III.2 ¶64].
- Lully dissolved the Philosophic Salt: “he performed the Solution in nine days” [IV.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer):

- Solution is both the answer to a question and a dissolving that enters and converts the enquirer, as light dissolves darkness: “every solution is a convertive process and progress in entity and hypostatic relation” [APP ¶115].
- Past the phantasmagoric region one is to “enter into its solution, i.e., in its dissolved essence” [APP ¶144], the world's dissolved essence.
- “Solution refers to the separation of the sensuous medium itself.” [APP ¶176]. This separation is repeated on the intuitional or medial life to reach the divine.

summary: A formula closing a verse on the fixed and the volatile, linked there to the inversion of fixed and volatile.
body: A verse on the fixed and the volatile closes with this formula: “Solve, Coagula, Fige.” [I.2 ¶21]. Our rendering, not the book's: dissolve, coagulate, fix. The passage ties it to the inversion of fixed and volatile. The voice is unclear from the text.

summary: Unnamed modern Kabalists whom Atwood cites to explain the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether.
body: Atwood cites some modern Kabalists for their explanation of the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether as “an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity” [III.2 ¶13].

summary: In Hermes, the son of king and red daughter, who takes his tincture from the fire and bears the Philosophic Matter: the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified.
body:
Voice: Hermes, as quoted. The son is conceived of the king and the red daughter and takes his tincture from the fire. He is the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified: “this son is himself the treasury, even himself bearing the Philosophic Matter” [I.3 ¶35].

Voice: the Master, as quoted. The Son is dead and then lives: “The Dragon shuns the sunbeams which dart through the crevices, our dead Son lives.” [IV.2 ¶14]. He takes his Tincture from fire and death, comes forth from the Fire, rejoices with his spouse, becomes a warrior in the Fire, and bears the Philosophic Matter. The same passage gives two identities: “Our Son the King” and “For this Son is the treasury” [IV.2 ¶14].

summary: Cited authority (Eccles.) whom Atwood uses to show that Wisdom first tries her follower with fear before revealing her Secret.
body: Cited by Atwood (Eccles. 1:20; 4:17, 18, 28) in support of the point that Wisdom first tries a man with fear and only then reveals her Secret: “at first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n43]. Atwood attributes this to the same intimate experience she is describing, and uses it approvingly.

summary: Cited for reference only.
Basil's name for practitioners of the Art, who all aim at the 'harbor' reached when the Matter's bonds are loosed after its due time.
body: In a passage quoted from Basil, the sons of Art are the practitioners of the Art, whose common goal is the loosing of the Matter's bonds after its due time: “loose its bonds towards which all sons of Art aim to arrive as to their long-desired and sought for harbor” [IV.1 ¶15].

summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, that which alchemy seeks in the mind.
body: Atwood speaks of alchemy as “the seeking of The Sophia in the mind” [APP ¶183] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer). The text gives no further definition here.

summary: Cited by Atwood to illustrate the same point: that life is to be had only there, all other places being full of misery and evil.
body: Cited by Atwood as illustrating the same point as the surrounding passage: “Life only is to be had there, all other places are full of misery and evil” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8].

summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, the soul is the body's ultimate perfection, a mesothesis between two spheres, and in its metalline perfection the philosopher's stone.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The human soul is more than a mere resultant of body; it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres.” [APP ¶178]. Its angelic essence is described as a metallic humidity, and she identifies the perfected soul with the philosopher's stone: “The soul in its metalline perfection is the philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

summary: In Sendivogius as quoted, what man possesses and other creatures, which have only spirit, lack.
body: Sendivogius, as quoted, distinguishes man from other creatures, which “have only spirit and not the soul of Deity” [II.1 ¶10]; man alone has the soul of Deity.

summary: An ingredient in Hermes' recipe, identified with the Meridian Redness and, by the Scholiast, with the true aurific principle that perfects the seven bodies.
body: In Hermes' recipe as quoted, the soul of gold is one ingredient, identified with the Meridian Redness: “the Meridian Redness, that is the soul of gold” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast, who reads the whole recipe as a matter of distillation, explains it as “our soul of gold, writes the Scholiast, which is the true aurific principle” [I.3 n65]: a medium that perfects the seven bodies as the sun perfects sublunary nature.

summary: Works in which, Atwood says, the adepts esoterically credit prayer with efficacy when the mind is lifted up; not further defined.
body: Atwood notes that “adepts are eloquent in their imputations of its efficacy in Spagyric Works, when the mind is lifted up” [III.4 ¶22], referring to prayer. The text does not define Spagyric Works further.

summary: The specific kind of a thing (lead as lead); indestructible and not transmutable, contrasted with the Universal Subject to which transmutation actually relates.
body: Atwood uses species in a special sense: the specific kind of a thing, as lead considered as lead. Species are indestructible, not liable to corruption and not transmutable: “It is not species that they profess to transmute” [I.2 ¶4]. Transmutation instead concerns what underlies them, “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

summary: Contemplation in which, according to Proclus, the same order holds as in the Mysteries: phantasms first, illumination afterwards.
body: Proclus, as quoted, says that “the same method takes place in the speculation of Wholes” [II.3 ¶22] as in the Mysteries: phantasms appear first and illumination comes later.

summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, a seed taken out of a body that contains all things, set against common gold and silver.
body: In verse quoted from Pierce, the Black Monk, the sperme is a seed drawn from a body, set against common gold and silver: “But a sperme owte of a body I take,” [III.4 ¶21]. It contains all: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light, Water and Erth, Fyre and Fryght:” [III.4 ¶21].

summary: Atwood's figure for the Ether, Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries, whose enigma must be fully solved lest she regain dominion over the work.
body:
Atwood says the Egyptians placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, and identifies her with the Ether: “so is that Ether then the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; “Such was the Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries” [III.1 ¶6]. She is the passive counterpart of the inner light: “And she is all things passively which the internal light is impassively.” [III.1 ¶6]. Her animal form with a human face shows a twofold life, and her 'winds' image the elevating power of imagination; the ancients mastered her [III.1 ¶6].

In the practice, the Sphinx is a power that must be fully overcome: if the dissolution is left incomplete before the total solution of her enigma, “the Sphinx should retrieve her dominion unawares and frustrate the work begun” [IV.1 ¶7].

summary: The fabled Sphinx, cited as the barrier at the vestibule admitting only philosophers, whose riddle Oedipus solved.
body: Atwood cites the Sphinx as the barrier at the vestibule that perplexes intruders and admits only philosophers [IV.4 ¶5]. She uses Oedipus' solving of the riddle to illustrate the rational penetration of one's own natural understanding: one who, “like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx” [IV.1 ¶48]. See also the term Sphinx.

summary: Fables cited by Atwood to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being.
body: Atwood cites these fables to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being, with the image of something “carried within the temple upon the back of an ass” [III.2 ¶64].

summary: Atwood's figure for that to which her preceding exposition has served as introduction; not explained.
body: Atwood closes a section: “we conclude our introduction, as it may be called, to the Sphinx’s lair” [III.4 ¶47]. The figure is not explained.

summary: Named by Atwood as a metaphysician who speculated on the same experimental ground.
body: Atwood names Spinoza among metaphysicians and speculators on the same experimental ground [I.1 ¶39]; the text says nothing further about him.

summary: The life-principle of the matter, whose association sums up the Art; in the work it wakes, unifies, builds its own vessel, and (per Eudoxus) is the tie of soul and body, called Eve and Mercury.
body:
**In the work.** The Spirit's removal is the matter's death and its return is its life; it must be kept from escaping the vessel: “In the life and death thereof we work with the spirits” [I.3 ¶49]. The Art is summed up in it: “In a scientific association of the Spirit the Hermetic Art has been said summarily to consist” [I.3 n59]. Atwood also speaks of its superior life, its two invisible poles and its external forms (voice partly unclear in these records).

**Atwood's account.** The Spirit wakes in the congress of allied mind: “the Spirit wakes to consciousness” [III.4 ¶27]; “these diversified parts of the Spirit are in the renascent harmony made one” [III.4 ¶28]. It cannot increase without a medium and a bond. “The Spirit finally constructs its own vessel and vitrifies it” [III.4 ¶32], and it tests the instruments, “as by the Spirit they are proved fit” [III.4 ¶40].

**The Zohar.** The Rabbi in the Zohar, as quoted: “When the Thought begins to develop itself forth, it arrives at that degree when it becomes Spirit.” At this point it is no longer shut up in itself: “Arrived at this estate, it takes the name of Intelligence” [III.3 ¶78].

**Eudoxus.** Joined with body to form the Stone, the Spirit is the soul and body's only tie, “of whom the Spirit is the only tie which works this conjunction”, and is used to wash the earth; “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. It is corporified (turned to earth) in the Fourth Key, and in the Fifth it unites paste and leaven. In the plural, the spirits of the bodies are the Bath and unite permanently with purified bodies: “the spirits desire to be in the cleansed bodies, and having them, they enliven and dwell in them” [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, nature's spirit is all imagination, realizing its imaginings in aromal essences; literal chemists vainly hoped to sublime it with lifeless instruments.
body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The spirit of nature is all imagination, ideality, fancy.” [APP ¶122]. It wraps itself in aromal essences to realize its imaginings. It is a personality in particulars, and “when regarded universally it is the same in the being of the orb soul” [APP ¶122]; it grows more phantastic the more power it is given from the Central Source.

In the main text she criticizes literal chemists who worked with stills and furnaces “in hope by such lifeless instruments to sublime the Spirit of Nature” [I.1 ¶86], implying that such instruments cannot do it.

summary: In the Apostle's words as quoted, the Spirit that brings liberty and changes its beholders into the same image; identified with the Lord.
body: The Apostle, as quoted: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty, and its beholders are changed into the same image, “even as by the Spirit of the Lord” [III.3 ¶59]. It is identified with the Lord: “For the Lord is that Spirit” [III.3 ¶59].

summary: Spirit in its natural state, which Atwood calls degraded and incapable of true intelligence: diseased, falsifying and dulled until clarified.
body: Atwood reports the condemnation of “the Spirit of the natural life as degraded and incapable of true intelligence” [II.2 ¶8], and asks “in what the disease of the Spirit consists” [II.2 ¶9]. In this state the spirit is diseased, falsifying and dulled until it is clarified.

summary: A vindicative power upholding Wisdom's Rule, fulfilling it lovingly but confounding whoever abandons the Divine purpose for private ends.
body: Atwood writes of “the vindicative Spirit of Wisdom for the justification of her Rule” [IV.3 ¶56]. “The Spirit of Wisdom runs lovingly by her own Rule to fulfill it” [IV.3 ¶56], but leaves in confusion whoever turns from the Divine purpose to private ends.

summary: The Spirit's words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.), cited by Atwood in support of steadfastly continuing the labor to its end.
body: Atwood cites the Spirit's words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.) in support of continuing the labor steadfastly to the end: “to fight against the Powers of Darkness requires great force” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n8].

summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, the spiritual man within the natural man, whose work is to move the Ether.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “There is a spirit-man within the natural man” [APP ¶139]; its work is to move the Ether.

summary: In Atwood's Table Talk, promptings from spirits, which give the spirits footing in the life when uttered.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood warns: “To utter from spirit-suggestions is a fearful thing” [APP ¶127], because doing so gives the spirits footing in the life.

summary: The work's two principles, active and receptive: equal Spirits that must both be prepared and allied, each dying in the other so their reunion yields new life.
body: Atwood names the two principles of the work, active and receptive, as equal Spirits that must both be made ready and brought together: “Both therefore have to be prepared --- the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient” [III.1 ¶41]. Each dies in the other, “by death and contrition of the agent in the patient, and vice versa” [III.1 ¶49]. The old life is crucified, and their reunion under another law brings forth the new life.

summary: Fermentation performed by multiplying the tinctures, not by using common gold or silver.
body: Atwood: “The spiritual fermentation is performed by multiplying the tinctures” [IV.3 ¶21], and not with common gold or silver.

summary: Generation under the law that the parent is bettered in the offspring, up to a fourth or fifth generation.
body: Atwood states “the Law especial of spiritual generation that the parent is bettered in the offspring” [III.1 ¶30], up to a fourth or fifth generation.

summary: The one whose constitution and instinct determine how the conditions of the work vary; not further defined.
body: Atwood says that the work's conditions are those “which vary with the constitution and instinct of the spiritual guide” [III.4 ¶42]. The text does not define the spiritual guide further here.

summary: The intellect which natural reason helps bring into self-knowledge, and which then turns back on the outer life to analyze and transform it.
body: Atwood describes natural reason as helping to introduce the spiritual intellect into self-knowledge. Once there, “this latter, returning with power upon the life without, proceeds to analyze and revolutionize” [III.1 ¶13] that outer life 'chemically'. The phrase that follows, 'this vital perscrutinator' (the operating agent of the change), apparently refers to this same intellect.

summary: In St. Paul's words as quoted, the rock that followed the Fathers and gave them spiritual drink, identified with Christ.
body: St. Paul, as quoted, says the Fathers drank spiritual drink: “they drank of that spiritual rock that followed them” and “and that rock was Christ” [III.3 ¶59].

summary: A union that, Atwood says, man can neither cement nor increase by his own power.
body: Atwood says man can “neither cement the spiritual union or give it increase” [III.4 ¶20].

summary: Expression in a passage quoted from Helvetius, whose 'Abyss' is disclosed most inwardly, at the centre where the mystery is found.
body: In a passage Atwood quotes from Helvetius: “There, within most intimately, the Abyss of the Spoagyric artifice is disclosed” [III.1 ¶70]. The text does not explain the expression further.
