summary: Church Father Atwood cites for a work's authenticity, for the Church's adoption of the Mysteries' language and rites, and for three modes of human vision.
body: Atwood cites him as mentioning a certain work without doubting its authenticity, although he judged it “instinctu fallacies spiritus” (ours: by prompting of a deceiving spirit); Atwood attributes that judgment probably to the popular notion and thinks he might later have revised it [I.1 ¶11, I.1 n12]. As St. Augustin he mentions an inextinguishable lamp consecrated to Venus [I.1 ¶18]. She names him among the Church Fathers who adopted the language and rites of the Mysteries, and notes that he quotes many lost Neoplatonist books [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9]. He supports her account of three modes of human vision, the third (anagogic) being placed in Elysium [II.4 ¶15].

summary: The Evangelist, cited by Atwood for the Word as Life and Light, for Christ as the Word of Life manifested, and as a practitioner of the Occult Art.
body: From the first chapter of his Gospel Atwood takes the Word/Light shining in darkness as the same Light: “In Him was Life; and the Life was the Light of men.” [II.3 ¶54, II.3 n60], and also the power to become sons of God [II.3 ¶55]. From the First Epistle she takes Christ as the Word of Life made manifest, the one awaited by prophets and philosophers: “That which was from the Beginning, which they had heard, and seen with their eyes” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n10]. As St John, the Evangelist Apostle, he is cited as practising the Occult Art for the poor, healing and making gold, silver and gems; St Victor's commentary relates the particulars [I.1 ¶24]. See also St John’s Gospel.

summary: The Gospel, cited by Atwood for those to whom the Word of God came being called gods, and for the True Light perfected in the Saviour.
body: Atwood cites chapter 10 for the point that those to whom the Word of God came are called gods, set against unbelief: “thou blasphemest, because I said I am the Son of God” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n37]. She also cites it for the True Light perfected in the Saviour, whose ray cleanses life: “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19, IV.2 n17].

summary: Cited by Atwood to illustrate baptism by Water set against baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire.
body: Atwood cites him to illustrate baptism by Water versus baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire, with the purging of the floor and burning of the chaff: “He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with Fire” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n11].

summary: Cited often by Atwood, chiefly in the Appendix, for the body as temple, the marriage-union of man and God, regeneration, and the purity of the Art.
body:
In the main text Atwood cites 1 Cor. 10:1-4 on the Fathers baptized in cloud and sea, eating spiritual meat and drinking from the spiritual rock, “and that rock was Christ”, without stating its application [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n40]; the Epistle to the Hebrews, for revelation in the Son surpassing every earlier revelation of the Light: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in times past unto the Fathers by the prophets” [IV.2 ¶17, IV.2 n10, IV.2 n13]; and his saying that the impurity lies in the accuser's thought, not in the Art: “to him that esteems a thing unclean, as St Paul says, it is unclean” [IV.4 ¶24].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he supports the body as a temple of the Holy Ghost, its members a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶16]; hints at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79]; and his Epistles are said to be better understood in the atmosphere of the higher Mystics than through professed commentators [APP ¶118]. Atwood reads “the letter killeth” as meaning the living letter of the law is too powerful a test for man's spirit [APP ¶143], and takes “It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption” as the law of regeneration of the anima media, seed of spirit growing to spirit [APP ¶147].

summary: Author of a commentary that, Atwood says, relates the particulars of St John's practice of the Occult Art.
body: Atwood cites a commentary by St Victor as relating the particulars of St John's practice (healing and making gold, silver and gems for the poor) [I.1 ¶24].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Author of Pyrotechny Asserted, cited as testifying that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir and recounting his own wasteful projection.
body: In a footnote Atwood cites Starkey's Pyrotechny Asserted as eyewitness testimony (“I saw”) that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir, together with Starkey's account of his own wasteful projection [I.1 ¶73, I.1 n93].

summary: A name Cosmopolite, as reported by Eudoxus, gives to the Mercury, alongside 'lodestone'.
body: Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite calls the Mercury (Our Old Man) by other names, “to which he gives also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether the term 'Chalybes' is the same name the text does not state.

summary: Preserver of an ancient record that Atwood cites for the conformity between death and initiation into the Grand Mysteries.
body: Atwood cites an ancient record preserved by Stoboeus for the conformity of death and initiation and its stages: “The mind is affected and agitated in death, just as it is in initiation into the Grand Mysteries.” [II.3 ¶37].

equivalences.with: Stone of Fire / seed of gold
feminine of magnesia, hen, white spittle, volatile milk, incombustible ash
Stone with the new name in Revelation
the Hermetic method and its end (the line returning into a circle)
concentrated virtue of the Universal Subject
transmutative ferment / Form of Gold / ray of motive Light

summary: The object and perfected product of the Art: for Atwood, the concentrated, fermented Ether or Light of nature, a real entity of spiritual generation, and the soul in its perfection.
body:
**Atwood's account.** The Stone is the perfective product of the Art, made in and by the universal spirit; “this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone” [I.2 ¶26, I.2 ¶29]. It is the purified, concentrated Ether perfected by its own Light — “their stone is nothing more or less than the pure Ethereality of nature” — and transmutes by assimilating crude life into its own light; she quotes “Lapis noster, hic est ignis, ex igne creatus” (ours: our stone, this is fire, created from fire) [I.2 ¶44], and calls it “this fermented Spirit or Stone” [I.2 ¶48]; the adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44]. It is “one mineral spirit, exalted by fermentation intrinsically in its proper kind” [I.3 n55]; “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52]. Hidden in the interior of the 'earth', it is “the true medicine” [II.3 ¶29]; it comes and is generated with Light, then brings forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30, III.1 ¶49]; its most abstruse principle is the Salt of Saturn (voice unclear) [II.3 ¶41]; the armament contends “for the self-same Stone” [III.1 ¶68], its mother being the secret menstrual (after Eirenaeus) and its Quintessence the soul (after Synesius) [III.1 ¶69]; made in the furnace with 'our glass', it is “a new hypostasis, and a new stone”, “that renowned Terra Maga in aethere clarificata”, and “the Stone with the new name written in the Revelation” [II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54]. What the philosophers found is “this miraculous principle of regeneration” [III.1 ¶50]. Only one unclean thing enters its composition; purged after its darkness it becomes a white Elixir [III.1 ¶61]. It is “a pure petrification of the Spirit” [IV.1 ¶29], the concentrated virtue of the Universal Subject, and “the transmutative ferment” = Form of Gold = ray of motive Light [IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶9]; once fermented it coequals itself to all, “the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶28]. The Hermetic method and its end are “the true Christian Philosopher’s Stone” [IV.3 ¶62]; the regenerate soul puts on its crown of light as a new body [IV.4 ¶20].

In the Appendix (later layer) it is “the efflux of such a life, drawn to a focus and made manifest as a concrete Essence of Light” [APP ¶6]; “a real entity produced by spiritual generation”, “a real ens of light” [APP ¶93]; “a metaphysico-chemical birth” [APP ¶108]; life in its petrified first state, to be taken and fermented [APP ¶132]; analogue of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139]; and “The soul in its perfection is the Christian philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

**Quoted voices.** Geber and the monk of the Rosary: “The Stone is one”; “our Stone is no other than a foetant spirit and living water” [I.2 ¶11]. Hermes: “the concealed Stone of many colours; which is born in one colour” [I.3 ¶13]; composed from four elements [I.3 ¶26]; “the most precious gold without spots”, the Universal Ferment [I.3 ¶60]. The adepts: “a true mineral petrification” [I.3 n13], with many cover names (the feminine of magnesia, the hen, the white spittle, the volatile milk, the incombustible ash) but one epithet, the Philosopher's Stone [I.3 ¶11]. Old Alchemists: “this vapour is the Stone known and proven in the Book of Life” [III.2 ¶7]. Khunrath: a glorified King, “a shining carbuncle” [III.3 ¶19]. The adeptest: it is “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters” [III.3 ¶50]. Maier: “et habebis lapidem philosophorum” (ours: and you will have the philosophers' stone) [III.3 ¶31]. Arnold: dissolve it “in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7]. Norton/Bloomfield: “The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: formed “by the conjunction of the spirit with the body”, “the Sea of the Wise”, “an Astral Fire”, and, after Hermes, “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶3, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶16]. Flamel: perfected, it transmutes metals and removes the root of sin from its maker [I.1 ¶57]. The theosophist: “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38].

**History.** Treatises on it are ascribed to Aristotle, the Alexandrian adepts and Artephius [I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶27]; it was never found when sought “from selfish motives and a blind love of gain” [I.1 ¶39]; Ripley sought it in vain with common substances [I.1 ¶65]; Van Helmont says “I have seen the Stone and handled it” [I.1 ¶76].

summary: Heading under which readers filed an unattributed Latin saying attached to the summary that the Art consists in an association of the Spirit.
body: An unattributed Latin saying, “Ut ventus qui fiat est ille qui dat. --- Qui capit ille sapit.” (ours, roughly: as the wind that blows is the one that gives; who grasps it is wise), is attached to the summary that the Art consists in an association of the Spirit [I.3 n59]. Elsewhere an adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” (see Stone) [I.2 ¶44].

summary: Atwood's name for the product of the work: the perfected lowest life, completed in three circulations and analogous to the Head Stone of the Corner.
body: Atwood says “the Stone of the Wise is the perfected lowest life, its true consummation”, mineral in origin and analogous to Christ the Head Corner Stone [APP ¶46, Appendix layer]. Raised up by the builders while each in turn rejects it, it becomes the Head Stone of the Corner, “as the Stone of the Wise is completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33]. See Stone.

summary: A tale Atwood cites to illustrate that wickedness bars approach to the material of the Art.
body: Atwood cites “the story of an Arabian Magician, who must needs steal a little boy” to illustrate that wickedness bars approach to the material [III.4 ¶6].

summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the view that philosophy was the object of the Eleusinian rites.
body: Atwood cites Strabo in support of philosophy being the object of the Eleusinian rites [II.2 ¶5].

summary: The material the Art works on, never openly declared by the adepts; something the student must find that reciprocates the design, without which the work stays abortive.
body: Atwood calls it “even the common Subject of their Art”, which the adepts never openly declare [I.1 ¶82]. One may be “really conversant with the Subject” [III.4 ¶7]. To begin operations the student needs it: “without a Subject to work with and reciprocate the design it remains abortive” [III.4 ¶29]; she discusses it as 'suitable assistance'. The text does not define it further in these passages.

summary: What unassisted reason fails to grasp, eluding the mind as it pursues it.
body: Atwood says “the Subject Identity slides evermore behind the retardant mind” — reason alone cannot grasp it [II.1 ¶32].

summary: What the work is performed on, constantly concealed by the adepts; also what underlies a species, corruptible and transferable, identified with the metals' radical moisture.
body: Atwood notes that even candid texts such as Norton's Ordinal conceal it: “with the exception of the Subject Matter and certain preliminaries, which are constantly concealed” [I.1 ¶64]. In a second sense it is what underlies a species: not species, “but the Subjects of species rather, since they are corruptible and may be changed”, so it can be freed and transferred to another form [I.2 ¶5]; of the metals she speaks of “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4].

summary: In a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses: what persists through all change of bodies, receiving and reflecting forms; matter subsists according to it.
body: In a summary gathered from Plotinus and Porphyry, endorsed by Atwood, it is distinct from bodies and persists through all their changes: “that which receives the forms and reflects them --- always remains the same” [III.2 ¶47]. Matter is spoken of “according to the subject which is indefinite, because it is note form” [III.2 ¶49].

summary: The soul that suffers when pressed by evil and must be filled by a superior or an inferior power.
body: Atwood asks: “And what will not the subject soul suffer when pressed by so execrable an evil?” — such a soul must be filled by a superior or an inferior power [III.4 ¶6]. The sense of 'subject' here is left open.

summary: In an unattributed saying, the matter pierced by Divine Light, in which the pattern of the universe appears as in a glass.
body: Quoted with 'it is said': when Divine Light pierces their bosom, “the pattern of the whole universe appears in those Subject Waters, as an image in a glass” [III.3 ¶39].

summary: The cause of mesmerism's own effects, which, Atwood says, mesmerism has not investigated.
body: Atwood faults mesmerism for not investigating “the subject-being, the cause of its own effects” [II.2 ¶7].

summary: The product the Alchemists made sublime by an actual subversion of the selfhood.
body: Atwood says that by actual subversion of the selfhood “they made their Sublimate sublime” [IV.1 ¶47].

summary: The raising of the Spirit through degrees of concentrated essentiality; an operation that volatilizes and washes it and separates subtle from gross parts.
body: For Atwood, by grafting and transplanting “a growth and sublimation of the Spirit was effected, even to a third, fourth, and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality” [III.1 ¶9]; “sublimation volatilizes and washes it” [III.2 ¶64]. Vaughan speaks of “a first and second sublimation”, needed for the Matter to be alterable, without explaining them [IV.2 ¶35]. Eudoxus defines it as separating the Elements by “raising up the subtle and pure parts above the thick and terrestrial parts”, and says “Without the sublimation of the Stone, the conversion of the Elements and the extraction of the Principles is impossible” [IV.3 ¶5].

equivalences.with: fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law

summary: The unity of all that is: fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law, and source of miracles and every natural and supernatural increase.
body: Atwood calls it “the Substant Unity of all that is; the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law”, “the source of so many miracles and magical accordances, as of every natural and supernatural increase” [III.3 ¶79].

summary: The extracted product, seminally equal to the whole of its parts; identified with the dry splendour and the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.
body: Atwood speaks of “that Subtendent which is found seminally equal to the whole of the parts whence it is derived”, and identifies it with the dry splendour: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71].

summary: A nature pervading the universe, the All in everything, and alterable by art throughout.
body: Atwood speaks of “a Subtle Nature pervading the universe, which is the All in every thing and susceptible of artificial alteration through all” [IV.4 ¶12].

summary: The fullness Matter and other things reach through desire of the Good, in which they become tranquil, freed from parturitions and natural desire.
body: In a passage whose voice is unclear, things reach this fullness through desire of the Good: “when things have run up so far as to this Sufficience they become tranquil in it”, freed from parturitions and natural desire [III.4 ¶28].

summary: Cited for dating Hermes before the Pharaohs, for defining Chimia, and for the Emperor's burning of Egyptian chemical books.
body: Atwood cites Suidas for placing Hermes before the Pharoahs, about 400 years before Moses, and for his entry on Chemeia: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” (ours: Chimia is the making of gold and silver) [I.1 ¶6, I.1 n6, I.1 n8]. He also supports her account of the Emperor burning chemical books because the Egyptians made gold and silver, which she uses to explain antiquity's silence about the Egyptian Art [I.1 ¶18, I.1 n24].

summary: The sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher's Mercury and causes it to putrefy.
body: Atwood describes the sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher's Mercury and makes it putrefy: “this acute discriminative sulfuric Spirit occasions a putrefaction of the philosopher’s Mercury” [III.1 ¶24].

equivalences.with: this third, this obscure, this radical life
precious ferment, balm of Nature, wonderful unguent
the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries

summary: One of the three principles: the hidden active, luminous ferment or soul of the matter, bound and imprisoned until it is freed, purified and fixed as the seed of gold.
body:
**Atwood.** Sulphur is one of the three principles, with mercury and salt, into which the ethereal hypostasis separates: “the soul, the spirit, and the body principle; the paternal, maternal, and proceeding substance of life; sulfur, mercury, salt” [III.1 ¶53]. It is “The sulfur, which is the soul and golden ferment” [III.1 ¶53]. In the dissolution the oppressive will dislocates it and it floats on the ethereal waters, and “the blackness” comes “from the sulfur” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius's fable Sal mortally wounds Sulfur [III.1 ¶53]. It is the active principle inside the philosophic water, “its own good sulfur, or vital flame”, and tripling it is part of the operator's weights: “to double mercury and triple sulfur” [I.3 n5]. The adepts give the name to light: “light or sulfur, as they call it, is the true form or seed of gold” [I.3 n40]. In the Mysteries it is “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts, causing all this manifold scenery in the disruption of life” [II.3 ¶30]. In Sol it is the inner principle, imprisoned until the mercurial Spirit releases it: “his sulphur is imprisoned, so that he is not aware of it, does not feel or know himself” [III.3 ¶30]. 'Foliated sulphur' [I.3 ¶34] is not explained.

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** “The Sulphur, the pure light of life, is bound down in the inferior mineral region of life” and “Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]; it must be drawn forth and grafted into the medial region to grow. It is “the masculine ferment, the sulphur or divine ferment” [APP ¶182], doubly hidden, to be set free to perfect the passive matter; also “the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life)”, which must return on its matrix [APP ¶183]. “by sulphurs I mean forms” [APP ¶87]; “the impure sulphurs (desires, phantasms)” are the mundane desires in the individual will, to be purified or extirpated [APP ¶94].

**Quoted voices.** Hermes: “the fatness of our earth is sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]; “this sulphur doth tinge and fix, and is the connection of the tinctures” [I.3 ¶21]; “For the unguents are called sulphurs” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood's notes gloss this: “The occult luminous principle of vitalization he calls sulfur, auripigment, etc.” [I.3 n24]; “the philosophic sulfur, or Light” [I.3 n25]; of the adepts, “The purified sulfur, fixed and incombustible, is the generating seed of the universal nature” [I.3 n29]. The Benedictine Monk: “the incombustible sulphur that heats or thickens the coldness and crudities of the quicksilver” until they are one body; Boehme places it in the red fire-form, “which is red, and therein the virtue, viz., sulphur is” [III.3 ¶24]. Eudoxus: the First Key opens “the dark prisons in which the Sulphur is shut up” [IV.3 ¶3]; “the Fire and the Sulphur are hidden in the centre of the Earth” [IV.3 ¶7]; “the precious ferment, the sulphur, that balm of Nature, and wonderful unguent” [IV.3 ¶8]; per Geber, “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]; the body must be dissolved, being “the body in which the Sulphur which coagulates the Mercury is enclosed” [IV.3 ¶12]; the true Mercury yields “the fixed Sulphur and the Universal Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Adept: Argent vive is defiled “being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” but “coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white” [IV.1 ¶10]. Vaughan names “sulphurs simple and compounded” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

summary: A notion the quoted adept dismisses as one of the impostors' fables.
body: The adept quoted by Atwood rejects it: “those imposters who tell you of a sulphur tingens, and I know not what fables” [I.2 ¶8].

summary: In Ripley's Admonition, the 'Sun and Moon' of which our metals are said to be mines; not explained.
body: Ripley's Admonition, quoted by Atwood: “our mettalls be nought ells but miners too, Of our Soon and Moone” [II.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the expression here.

summary: Named in a Sendivogius passage as the source of the 'beams' whose centres the lodestone's point answers; not explained.
body: In a passage of Sendivogius, a parenthetical gloss (speaker unclear) names the beams' source: “viz. of the sun and moon philosophical” [II.1 ¶10]. Not further explained.

summary: The higher work, served by the same bodily members as the natural work, in which a hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “All members that work here for the natural work, work also for the super-essential.” [APP ¶109] Its hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.

summary: Something not to be broken, according to a Pythagoric precept cited as a warning; not explained.
body: Cited as a warning: “Neither break a superficies, as the Pythagoric precept runs” [IV.3 ¶56]. Its meaning is not explained.

summary: In Psellus, the first kind of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, a mere appearance seen by the celebrant and not to be heeded; also a seeing in Hades.
body: Psellus, quoted by Atwood, names two kinds of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, “the first called superinspection, when he who celebrates the divine rites sees a mere apparition” such as light in some form; it is not to be heeded [II.3 ¶20]. Elsewhere he distinguishes “the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” from the Introspection [II.3 ¶46]; not further explained.

summary: Glossed as the Ideas of the Divine Mind, from which things generated below are infused as light.
body: Atwood's bracketed gloss: “the superior stars [i.e., Ideae Divinae Mentis]” [III.2 ¶19] (ours: Ideas of the Divine Mind). Things generated below are infused from them as light.

summary: In Vaughan, the higher and lower orders: superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate; communion with superiors requires a heavenly life.
body: Vaughan, quoted by Atwood: “so superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate” [III.4 ¶44]; without a heavenly life there is “no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

summary: The union in which no faculty of the soul is rejected, all being present under their rightful rule.
body: Atwood answers an objection: “Neither, we reply, is any faculty of the soul repudiated in that supernal alliance” [IV.4 ¶20]; all faculties are present under their rightful rule.

summary: The attraction by which the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself.
body: Atwood: the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself “by a supernatural magnetism” [IV.3 ¶29].

summary: In Eirenaeus, a later work whose commencement he sets apart from the literal labour on things as first found.
body: Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood: “I am not speaking here indeed of the commencement of the Supernatural Work, but of things as we first find them” [IV.1 ¶6].

summary: Used of the latent nature of things implied by intellectual necessity, first in thought though later in time, and of the Kabalists' Law of Light; not defined.
body: Atwood speaks of “a superstantial nature of things implied which, though now latent and succeeding in order of time, is first in thought absolutely” [II.1 ¶34], and of the Kabalists' “an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. The word itself is not defined.

summary: The deep experience of things reached by ascending in thought and then descending.
body: Atwood: by ascending in thought and then descending, one may “hope to penetrate so far as to the superstantial experience of things” [II.1 ¶49].

summary: Named in an objection asking why partaking things do not enjoy its light if true Being is everywhere present; not defined.
body: Named in an objection Atwood reports: if true Being is everywhere present, why do partaking things not enjoy “the light of the so-called superstantial world” [II.2 ¶20]? Not defined.

summary: In Plutarch, the object of the aspirant's knowledge, which the Goddess urges men to seek, dwelling in Reason as in a temple.
body: Plutarch, quoted by Atwood: the aim is “the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Mind, whom the Goddess exhorts them to search after” [II.1 ¶50]; it dwells in Reason as in a temple.

summary: Named for comparison: Engelbrecht lived, like him, in the visionary sphere.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood compares Engelbrecht to Swedenborg as living in the visionary sphere [APP ¶105].

summary: Cited for the idea of “correspondence” between the brain and the spiritual head.
body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood refers to the Swedenborgians' “correspondence” to illustrate the relation between brain and spiritual head [APP ¶15].

summary: The Sybil of Virgil's Aeneid, cited as drawing inspiration from supernal light and as directing Aeneas to the Golden Bough, which Atwood reads as the alchemical Gold.
body: Atwood cites the Sybil as drawing inspiration from rivers of supernal light [II.4 ¶13], and as enjoining peculiar rites and sacrifices to Misenus' remains, compared with those at Patroclus' pile [III.1 ¶25]. From Aeneid lib. 6 she quotes the Sybil's instruction on the Golden Bough, “Alte vestiga oculis: et rite repertum” [III.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶16, III.1 n17] (ours: search on high with the eyes, and when duly found…): it is sought by looking upward and yields only to one whom the fates call. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): the Gold Alchemical is the gold Aeneas was told by the Sybil to find and gather [APP ¶20].

summary: A Sybil figure in Boissard cited for the recreation as a birth of the invisible into the palpable.
body: Atwood cites the Sybil in Boissard in support of the recreation as the birth of the invisible into the palpable: “Verbum invisible fiet palpabile et germinabit ut Radix.” [III.3 ¶79] (ours: The invisible Word will become palpable and will sprout as a Root).

summary: In Atwood's special sense, the true object of philosophy, implicating every science, sought through the categories as a channel for the Divine Intellect's birth into manifestation.
body: Atwood uses the word in a special sense: “That was the syllogism so important to be sought after, which also is according to Aristotle the true object of philosophy” [III.2 ¶42]. It implicates every science and is sought through the categories as a channel for the birth of the Divine Intellect into manifestation.

summary: Cited for reference only.
Bishop-adept and Greek authority whom Atwood cites often and approvingly on the Matter, the phantastic Spirit, the two pairs of eyes, and the practical work.
body:
Atwood names Synesius among authors of extant treatises on the stone (with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Athenagoras, Zosimus, Archelaus) [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34], cites his commentary on Democritus for the work's standing [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n15], and gives him as a bishop-adept who guarded the mysteries and bound initiation by oath [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n35, I.1 n36]. He is a Church Father adopting the Mysteries' rites, and among the Neoplatonists whose writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9].

On the phantastic Spirit: “This Etherial Spirit, he says, is situated on the confines of the rational and brutal life” [II.2 ¶10]; he treats desire, will and assent, the purification of the imaginative soul and the trials of Hercules. Atwood endorses this as 'beautifully suggestive', an account of 'the life that is operated upon' and 'the artifice' [II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14, II.2 n11]. From de Somniis: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20, III.1 n19]; demons are progeny of matter at war with the soul [II.3 ¶24, II.3 n26]. He names the defiled soul “Our viscous soul” [II.3 ¶30]. On Providence: efficacy of Divine Works [II.1 ¶52]; the two pairs of eyes, “this is an enigma indicative of contemplation and action” [III.1 ¶45, III.1 n49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “there are two pairs of eyes; those which are beneath are closed, when those which are above are opened” [APP ¶163].

On the Matter: his treatise closes the verbal instructions with “a clear Light, which fills with true virtue every mind that has once perceived it” [I.2 ¶33, I.2 n36]; 'the Greek saint' gives the summary, which Atwood calls plain words: “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶71]; he agrees with others concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. His True Book gives practical instruction on the one Water, which Atwood calls the Experiment of the Fathers: “labour only for that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals” [III.3 ¶60, III.3 n43].

summary: In Iamblichus, the theurgic aids and media which act of themselves toward divine union and properly excite the Divine will.
body: Iamblichus, quoted by Atwood: “the Synthemata, i.e., the Theurgic aids and media themselves” act of themselves toward divine union, “the things which properly excite the Divine will being the Divine Synthemata themselves” [II.4 ¶31].

summary: With Iris, the appearance of all colours after the darkness; a token of reconciliation.
body: Atwood: after the darkness “all the colours of the world will be apparent; also Iris, God’s messenger, and the tail of the peacock” [III.3 ¶13], a token of reconciliation.

summary: In Van helmont, that whose 'bars and bolts' a specific virtue looses.
body: Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, speaks of “a virtue of loosing the bars and bolts of Tartar” [IV.1 ¶39]. Not further explained.

summary: The region beyond Hades to which initiates were passed, the immortal abode; also called the death of this life and the Being of the central earth.
body: Atwood: Tartarus is the region beyond Hades to which the Hierophant passed initiates, “to its immortal abode: for such was Tartarus, the next beyond Hades” [II.3 ¶36]; she speaks of “the physical revealments of these Tartarean realms” [II.3 ¶34], and of the central earth, “but its Being is Tartarus” [II.3 ¶41]. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Tartarus is the death of this life.” [APP ¶168], passed through by propitiation with the Golden Bough. Olympiodorus, reading Plato's Phaedo, gives it ethically as the place of the soul's trial and “physically, in that it is the wholeness of existence” [III.2 ¶9].

summary: Translator and commentator whose works Atwood uses as sources and praises as most erudite, while faulting his reading of the Mysteries as merely immaterial ceremonies.
body: Atwood relies on Taylor's translations and notes: his rendering of the Asclepian Dialogue and notes in Plotinus' Select Works [I.1 n11, I.1 n12]; his Pausanius notes for the Olympiodorus extract and for Porphyry [II.4 n1, II.4 n6]; Proculus on Euclid and a note to Aristotle's Metaphysics for the Synesius extract and the Anaxagoras passage [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n19]. She praises his Dissertation for setting forth Virgil's Elysian particulars [II.4 ¶16] and for showing the whole Odyssey to be an allegory of the recondite Wisdom of antiquity [IV.1 ¶22], and calls him the 'most erudite translator' who showed Aristotle's strictures misunderstood [III.2 ¶40, III.2 n36, III.2 n38]. She qualifies his Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries: he examined them philosophically but still treated the rites as immaterial ceremonies representing abstract truths [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n5, II.2 n7].

summary: The blessed Water that nature sheds for the world, contemplated in the vestibule of the first Adytum.
body: Atwood: in the vestibule of the first Adytum one contemplates “the Tears of Isis, even that blessed Water which nature sheds divinely for the world” [III.3 ¶3].

summary: An adjective applied to Hercules' arcane labours and to the accomplishments by which initiates' souls are perfected; not defined.
body: Used (speaker unclear) of Hercules: “a part also of the regard of his arcane and telestic labours” [II.4 ¶3]. Atwood uses it of the Initiated, “being made perfect in every telestic accomplishment and virtue” [II.4 ¶39]. The word is not defined.

summary: In a passage from Julian, the art whose pre-eminent power is to impart health, understood as symmetry or equilibrium of nature.
body: Quoted from Julian: “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature, which it is the pre-eminent power of the Telestic art to impart, ordering all things by the unity within” [IV.3 ¶30]. So the art imparts equilibrium by ordering everything through an inner unity.

summary: The first grade of initiation: being initiated, while ascending, by the perfective gods.
body: In Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus): “we are initiated (teleioumetha) in ascending by the perfective gods” [II.4 ¶23]. The record treats this as the first grade of the ascent.

summary: Cited by Atwood as places where bodily healing was widely practised with minor physico-magical arts.
body: Atwood cites the temples of Esculapius to show that bodily healing was widely practised there with the minor physico-magical arts [II.2 ¶5].

summary: Atwood's name for the present age's idol of worldly usefulness, set up by opinion, which even its worshippers feel to be insufficient.
body: Atwood speaks of “that earth-born goddess of temporal Utility, which opinion has set up” [IV.3 ¶50]: the present age's idol of worldly usefulness and advantage. She says even its votaries feel it falls short.

summary: A threefold principle: the thing an offering in the vessel is dedicated to, and the term in the Theosophist's formula for reduction to the Monad.
body:
An ancient Adeptus (Grasseus, n26) speaks of “a holy oblation or present, dedicated to the Ternary” [III.2 ¶25]. The passage does not explain the term.

The Theosophist gives a formula: “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18], that is, reduce it to the Monad by rejecting the Binary. In the same paragraph, at the incarnation the four elements “were united to their eternal Unity and Ternarius” [IV.2 ¶18].

summary: The red root, which the wise sometimes call Magnesia, and Salt once it has been purified.
body: Atwood names Terra Adamica as the red root. She says it is “called sometimes Magnesia by the wise, and Salt after the purification” [I.3 n52]. So it = Magnesia, and = Salt after purification.

summary: The gross, earthy part of metals. It binds their central light and must be purged; the Stone removes it from them.
body: Atwood says metals cannot work “unless they be first purged from their terrestreity” [I.2 ¶49]. Their earthiness overpowers their spirit. In a footnote she says the central light “in metalline bodies is more especially bound on account of their terrestreity” [I.3 n49]. Khunrath, quoted, says the Stone acts on metals by “depriving its terrestreity and foreign oxides” [IV.3 ¶28].

summary: In the Appendix, the sensuous life: it represents the Animal Kingdom and dominates the head in man.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The Terrestrial is the sensuous and represents the Animal Kingdom. In man it is dominating the head.” [APP ¶32]. The reader's record adds that it typifies the highest life man must not aspire to. This point is not in the quoted words.

summary: In Eudoxus, turning the Spirit into earth: the only operation of the Fourth Key, done by boiling.
body: Eudoxus, quoted: “The terrification of the Spirit is the only operation of this work” [IV.3 ¶12]. This is the Fourth Key, and the operation is done by boiling. The same paragraph describes it as the need “to corporify the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12], and as coagulation by the Sulphur. Making the Spirit earthy, giving it a body and coagulating it are apparently one operation.

summary: Cited for reference only.
The fourfold drawn by the Art from three heads. It is identified with the Conjunction and called the source of ever-flowing Nature; such a being was the basis of the philosophic stone.
body:
Atwood calls the Tetractys a fourfold, “drawn from three heads by the obstetric hand of the physico-chemical Art” [III.3 ¶35]. She also calls it “Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root” [III.3 ¶34]. She identifies it with the consummating Conjunction: “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33]. The records also call it indissoluble and the source of wisdom.

She also says “the physical Tetractys springs through the contrite experience into life” [III.3 ¶72]. It springs out of the Calx, with prolific attributes and lasting fruits.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Pythagorus's mystic Tetractys was obtained by the theurgic process of APP ¶107. It is “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108], and such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone.

summary: Early Greek philosopher who sought eastern wisdom. Atwood reads his Water as the Matter itself, not common water.
body: Atwood names Thales, with Pythagoras, among early Greeks who sought eastern wisdom and whose writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She says his water, from which all is generated, is not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He “teaches that all beings have their beginning from water” [III.2 ¶33]. He names the principle after its first material appearance, so he differs from the others only in expression [III.2 ¶34–35]. She identifies “the Water of Thales” with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She reads his deed about inscribing the circle as symbolic, not a plain demonstration [III.2 ¶44].

summary: A work Atwood cites to show that blood is the principal matter of each thing.
body: Atwood cites it for the line “For blood is the principle matter of each thing” [II.1 ¶15, II.1 n14].

summary: A collection Atwood calls “an esteemed work.” She cites it for an annotated Sommaire, for Picus' de Auro, and for the Prosopoiae of the Stone.
body: Atwood calls the Theatrum Chemicum an esteemed work. It contains a translation of the Sommaire with important annotations, and she also cites it for Picus' de Auro [I.1 ¶58, I.1 n69]. From vol. 3, p. 763 she takes the Prosopoiae of the Stone, which she calls instructive and elegant. It begins “Terra mihi corpus, vires mihi praestitit ignis” [III.3 ¶8, III.3 n2], which means: Earth gave me my body, fire gave me my powers (our translation).

summary: Cited for the initiate's perplexity until the conductor opens the vestibule.
body: Quoted in a footnote: “the initiated is seized at first with solicitude and perplexity” [II.3 n37]. This lasts until the conductor opens the vestibule. Atwood uses the passage to support her account of initiation.

summary: In the Appendix, the only true government. Atwood accepts this as a great truth but says it needs a matching surface.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood takes up the claim that theocracy is the only true government (Kirchberger for de St Martin). She endorses it as a great truth, but says it needs a matching surface: “the world’s surface can only be governed by the center from which it is derived --- that is, its king” [APP ¶112].

summary: Science that is everywhere condemned. Atwood says none exists today, because the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.
body: Atwood: “Theoretic science is everywhere condemned; but there is no such thing at this day” [IV.4 ¶28]. Her reason is that the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.

summary: Atwood's word for divine, ultimate knowledge grounded in experiment. She says it opens a wider plane than the theological and contrasts it with the merely intellectual.
body: Atwood calls the subjects of the Poemander and Asclepias “theosophic and ultimate” [I.1 ¶7]: they concern divine capabilities, not physical ground. She hopes to show that “the most famous schools of theosophy have in all ages been based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17]. Of Boehme she says the ancient wisdom was “Revealed anew, it will be observed, theosophically, but not intellectually.” [I.1 ¶70]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Theosophic light opens him at a much wider plane of thought than the Theological.” [APP ¶118]. There she uses the word for the light of the higher Mystics, and also for the doctrine of the Neo-Platonists and Behmen.

summary: A theosophical authority Atwood quotes and endorses. A footnote at one place names him as Khunrath.
body: Atwood quotes the theosophist on the hostile reception that the wrathful outer life gives the new light, and on love's victory over it: “The wrathfulness is mightily exasperated by this appearance of love, says the theosophist” [I.3 n69]. She also uses him, with approval, on Adam and the fall, the two fires, the tincturing of Mercury, the Two Natures, the Mercury as worker and the Artist's role. On this she quotes “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38]. In Amp. Sap. Etern. the Theosophist (footnote: Khunrath) gives the formula “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary, through the rejection of the Binary, to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 n14]. Atwood then explains it.

equivalences.with: the Lord of the Fourth House / the Fourth House

summary: In Norton, the “hidden treasure” of the old clerks, identified with the Fourth House or its Lord.
body: Norton, quoted: “For the Lord of the Fourth House likewise be it done; For that is Thesaurum absconditum of old clerkes” [IV.2 ¶34]. The Latin means “hidden treasure” (our translation). The verse is ambiguous: the treasure may be the Fourth House itself or its Lord.

summary: Unnamed philosophers who supply the mountain allegory. Atwood qualifies them: their promises of gold drew futile public searches.
body: Atwood gives their allegory of the mountain: wind, earthquake, fire, calm, then the tincture. It begins “When you have discovered the mountain, the first miracle that will appear is this” [II.3 ¶33]. She qualifies their use: their promises of gold drew the public into futile searches [II.3 ¶34].

summary: Greek philosophers whose contradictory statements about Matter Atwood explains and defends, comparing them with the Hermetic adepts.
body: These Greeks say contradictory things about Matter: that it is one and all, everywhere and nowhere. Atwood explains and defends these statements and compares them with the Hermetic adepts [III.2 ¶51, III.2 ¶52].

summary: The art of purifying and informing the Mind. Through purification it turns the whole being into inner light and makes the divine Matter manifest in arcane visions.
body:
Atwood says “the Theurgic Art professed a power of purifying and informing the Mind much more beneficial and lasting” than bodily medicine [III.1 ¶11]. By purifying and subduing the passions it turns the whole hypostasis into inner light. Its practitioners consulted the divine intellect only about purification, liberation and the salvation of life [III.1 ¶11].

In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses, the pure divine Matter is shown “by means of the Theurgic Art it is made manifest and imparted through arcane and blessed visions” [III.2 ¶49].

The Alexandrian philosophers practised it, “each professing a genuine knowledge of the Theurgic art, and experimental physics on the Hermetic ground” [I.1 ¶27]. Later, “Theurgic rites, no longer holy, were proscribed” [I.1 ¶30].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says numbers are personally represented in this art, “by which spirit is added to spirit and multiplied as offspring” [APP ¶107].

summary: Ancient rites aimed at the experience of truth, ordered by intellectual canons. Atwood draws on their kinds of invocation to defend prayer.
body: Iamblicus, quoted: “Theurgic rites conspiring to this end were scientifically disposed and early defined by intellectual canons” [II.2 ¶13]. The end is the experience of truth. Atwood draws on “the different kinds of invocation which were employed by the ancients in their celebration of Theurgic rites” [III.4 ¶23] in defending prayer.

summary: Sacrifice whose end is conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect. It goes together with adoration and prayer.
body: Atwood: “the end of Theurgic sacrifice is a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She connects it with adoration and prayer.

summary: In Iamblichus, the soul's union with the Divine nature. Ineffable works and symbols bring it about, not intellectual perception.
body: Iamblichus, quoted: the soul's union with the Divine nature comes about through “the perfect efficacy of ineffable works” and symbols, not through intellectual perception [II.4 ¶31].

summary: In Iamblichus, those to whom the gods show a Fire visible to itself.
body: Iamblichus, quoted: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

summary: Practitioners of theurgy. Proclus is cited saying they place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains.
body: Atwood reports Proclus as saying the Theurgists place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains [II.4 ¶16].

summary: The Greek name for the Hermetic Art. Through it the soul concentrates its vitality, purifies its essence and rises by degrees to knowledge of the First Cause.
body:
Atwood: “Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy” [II.2 ¶3]. So Theurgy = the Hermetic Art. She calls it the practice of the Mysteries. Through it, “through their Theurgic disciplines” [II.2 ¶6], Theurgists shared in the Wisdom of true Being. “The Neoplatonists wrote largely of the Theurgical art” [II.2 ¶9].

Its aim was to concentrate vitality, turn the spiritual eye, purify and analyse the whole essence, and draw out and know the true Efficient: “this was their object and the Art of Theurgy” [II.3 ¶5]. She says this ascent needs those means: “by Theurgic rites, an ascent was made through appropriate media and a gradual assimilation, which without these could not be effected, to the knowledge of the First Cause” [II.4 ¶56]. So whoever seeks the First Principle “must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. That passage does not define the preparation further.

summary: In Jacob Boehme, what proceeds by virtue of the warmth (fire) in the blood.
body: Jacob Boehme, quoted: “in the virtue of the warmth, the Thin Water of Life proceedeth” [III.3 ¶24]. The warmth is the fire in the blood.

summary: Something mesmerists reach without knowing how to alter and amend it. It is not further defined.
body: Atwood says mesmerists reach it, but “without the important knowledge how to alter and amend the Thing” [III.1 ¶8]. The capital letters suggest a technical sense, but the passage does not define it.

summary: In Atwood's Appendix, the lowest of man's lives, in which fallen man now is; it moves with the creative Essence and is to be raised through the medial life.
body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), calls this the lowest of man's lives: “Man is fallen; he is in the third or lowest life” [APP ¶35]. It is “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3]. The records also say that the magic of the self-will exploits its release, that it is reached from present life through the clairvoyant life by repeated fermentation, that it is to be raised through the medial life, and that the seeker in it shows the Golden Fleece. By the order of APP ¶32–35 it apparently corresponds to the Infernal (lumbar, voluntary) life, but the text does not state this identity.

summary: In Boehme's language, as Atwood uses it, the sidereal and elementary birth: the medium of perceiving the First, which lies hidden in its mineral life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood uses Boehme's term: “the Third Principle, i.e., the sidereal and elementary birth, to use Boehme’s language” [APP ¶27]. It “is the medium of perceiving the First, which is hidden in its mineral life” [APP ¶27], and that life is full of defilement and temptation. Earlier Atwood also speaks of the circulation being carried upward “through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20], instead of the Duad generating directly. The text does not identify it further there, and does not say whether this is the same Third Principle.

summary: In Eudoxus's account, the operation of the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order.
body: Eudoxus, quoted, connects the Third work with the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order. He declines to describe it: “I will say nothing in particular of the operation of the Third work” [IV.3 ¶14].

equivalences.with: terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun; triumphal Chariot of Antimony

summary: The finished product of the work, endued with a magnetical virtue that draws divine increase; also called the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun and the Stone of Fire.
body: The finished product: “this gold is endued with a magnetical virtue” [II.1 ¶25] that draws divine increase. The passage gives it other names: “Whence it has been called likewise the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun, the triumphal Chariot of Antimony” [II.1 ¶25], and “this is the Stone of Fire seen in bright lines” [II.1 ¶25]. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or the source she follows is speaking.

summary: A Latin sentence that Norton's verse tells the reader to follow; the text does not say where it comes from.
body: Inside the Norton verse quoted at III.4 ¶17, “this holi letter” is the sentence to follow: “Attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, Disponens omnia suaviter;” [III.4 ¶17] (our rendering: reaching mightily from end to end, ordering all things sweetly). The text does not say who wrote the sentence.

summary: In the Zohar passage Atwood quotes, the Principle of all that is: unknown and shut up in itself at first, then developing and emanating Light; God's creative Thought inverts human thought.
body: The Rabbi in the Zohar, as Atwood quotes him, says: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78]. It develops into Spirit or Intelligence, as “Thought emanating Light” [III.3 ¶79]. Atwood, apparently agreeing, adds that “the Thought which is of God creative is the inversion of our thought” [III.3 ¶78].

summary: In Eudoxus's account, the domains of Nature whose principles and operations the seeker must know.
body: Eudoxus, quoted, says the seeker must know “the operations of Nature in the Three Kinds” [IV.2 ¶4]. The records note that the 'three reigns' of Nature at IV.2 ¶3 may be comparable. The text does not name the Kinds here.

summary: Three domains of nature, which Atwood does not name in these passages; Hermes reputedly found their quintessential perfectibility in their homogeneal unity, and the torch diffuses life through them.
body: Atwood reports that Hermes discovered “the quintessential perfectibility of the three kingdoms in their homogeneal unity” [I.1 ¶6]. Later she says the torch diffuses energy, life and joy “in either if the three kingdoms, as we have shown, by its voluntary assimilation” [IV.4 ¶32], pointing back to an earlier proof. Neither passage names the three. The 'threefold enchantment' entry gives them as animal, vegetable and mineral [IV.4 ¶4].

summary: The principles of the work: Life resolves into them in the philosophic fermentation (Van Helmont's Salt, Sulphur and Mercury), and they are separated and reunited to produce the tincture.
body: In the passage quoting Boehme, “The same Three Principles gradually assume a new life” [II.1 ¶24]. They act in harmony to produce first whiteness and then the tincture, and Boehme speaks of “the mechanical part of the Three Principles” [II.1 ¶25]. Atwood says Life in the philosophic fermentation is “resolved into these three principles, which Van Helmont also calls Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury” [III.2 ¶28]. The author of The Triumph, quoted, speaks of “the separation and the reunion of the Three Principles” [IV.2 ¶6] without naming them. A separate set of three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation) appears at II.1 ¶18; see that entry. The text does not say whether these are the same.

summary: The three principles of motion: attraction, repulsion as its reaction, and circulation arising from their conflict; equilibrium gives a circle, predominance an ellipse.
body: Attraction is the occult first principle of motion, and repulsion is its reaction. “Circulation is the third principle, proceeding from the conflict of the former two” [II.1 ¶18], and it mediates between them. When the two are in equilibrium the motion is a circle; when one predominates it is an ellipse. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or a source is speaking. On bringing the three into equilibrium, see 'threefold secret' [III.3 ¶9].

summary: The worlds Boehme says he knew and saw in himself; the printed passage names the divine angelical or paradisiacal world and the dark world.
body: Boehme, quoted: “I knew and saw in myself all the Three Worlds, viz., first, the divine angelical, or paradisiacal; and then the dark world” [III.2 ¶16]. As printed, the passage does not clearly name the third world.

summary: Atwood's term for how the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are bound together in man's natural Identity; only the animal is developed to consciousness.
body: Atwood says man's animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are “bound together in the threefold enchantment of his natural Identity” [IV.4 ¶4]. Only the animal is developed to consciousness.

summary: The law under which catholic nature necessarily proceeds; its ingress, egress and alternating action make up all the phenomena of the process.
body: Atwood says that nature “operates her proper progress necessitously under the threefold law of life” [I.3 n35]. The ingress, egress and alternating action of this law make up all the phenomena of the process.

summary: In Atwood's Appendix, our life as threefold (sensuous, medial and divine), whose active, passive and resultant principles must each be evolved separately.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “Our life is threefold.” [APP ¶182]. The three are the sensuous, medial and divine lives, and each has its key and its representative. “Each principle of the life --- active, passive, and resultant --- must be produced or evolved separately” [APP ¶183].

summary: The secret of the Art that brings attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond.
body: Atwood: “great care and diligence is needed at this juncture to apply the threefold secret of the Art” [III.3 ¶9]. In context the secret apparently means bringing attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond. See 'Three Principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)'.

summary: That in which Prometheus is fabled to have hidden the stolen fire; Atwood uses 'thrysus bearers' for those who have and perceive the fire but cannot draw it forth.
body: Atwood: “For, in the thrysus, Prometheus is fabled to have concealed the fire he stole from heaven” [II.4 ¶54]. The 'thrysus bearers' are those who “had the fire indeed, and were able even to perceive it, who were without the power to discover and draw it forth to manifestation” [II.4 ¶54]. She sets them against the 'Bacchic souls'.

summary: Cited by Atwood as naming a certain earth as the principle, the most ancient element.
body: Atwood cites Timaeus as one who “mentions a certain earth as antecedent, and the most ancient element” [III.2 ¶35]. She uses this to illustrate a certain earth taken as the principle.

equivalences.with: the soul educed by the death of the first life
a Substance like water which yet is no water

summary: The colouring, transmuting virtue of the work, or what carries it: the red, living soul drawn from the body, which turns imperfect bodies into gold and serves as the medicine of men and metals.
body:
**Transmuting product.** Paracelsus, quoted, calls it “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76]: a heavy red powder with an astral fire that turns imperfect metals into gold better than mined gold, and that is also medicinal. He gives “a true sign of the tincture of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶76]. Atwood describes the tinging power that transmutes imperfect bodies as ending as “a most pure and rubicund tincture of the color of flesh and blood” [I.3 n42]: “our tincture is of blood coagulated, which blood is the boundary or satisfaction of hearts” [I.3 n42]. In the Boehme and Basil Valentine passages it is “a brilliant yellow, red, or purpling tincture” [II.1 ¶24], and “this true tincture of Antimony, which is the medicine of men and metals” [II.1 ¶25]. The Christian philosophers Atwood quotes name as their chief treasure “a certain exalted tincture with which the world, if it served God and were worthy of such gifts, might be tinged and turned into most pure gold” [II.3 ¶33].

**Soul of the body.** In the Hermes material, which Atwood glosses, it is the soul drawn out by the death of the first life: “whence the soul is ediced; which is also the red and living tincture taken from the body” [I.3 n12]. In the end it is “that tincture of many dyes which, being dissolved renews itself, and dying survives itself” [I.3 n18]. Its blackness turns “into the true red” [I.3 ¶43]. The ferment “holds the tincture lest it should fly” [I.3 ¶58], and the quintessence “becomes golden and aurific, communicating its tincture” [I.3 n63].

**Boehme's Tincture.** Boehme, quoted, calls it “a Substance like water which yet is no water, but such a spirit or property: but it burns more like a kindred oil, and is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16]. He also writes: “this Tincture is the source of the material world, and gives to all essences virtue to grow” [III.2 ¶16], and “it is the most hidden thing, and also the most manifest” [III.2 ¶16]. It arises in the light: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24], and its thin water-form “is water, which is the desiring tincture” [III.3 ¶24].

**Atwood's own uses.** Metals must have “their tincture set free in the subtle Origin of all life” [I.2 ¶49]. The philosopher's Mercury is “communicative of tincture” [III.3 ¶32]. Spiritual fermentation multiplies tinctures, while common gold and silver “are not tinctures, but gross compacted bodies” [IV.3 ¶21].

**Other voices.** In Norton's verse the word first means the colouring of glass [I.1 ¶52]. It is also “the tincture of holi Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10], and “He that would seek Tincture most specious Must needly avoid all things wild and vicious.” [IV.1 ¶49; cf. IV.1 ¶16]. In Eirenaeus's verse it is a tincture “of silver fine” [III.3 ¶68]. The Master says of the Son-King: “Then is he transformed in his Tincture.” [IV.2 ¶14]; he takes it from the fire and death and becomes 'of tincture super-excellent'. Eudoxus speaks of “the two mercuries which contain the two tinctures” [IV.3 ¶10] and says the Alcahest increases the metals' tincture. The theosophist describes the dark Mercury as “tinctured” by light and love, so that death becomes triumphing life [IV.3 ¶38]. For the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine, see that entry.

summary: In Eirenaeus's account, what the first water partly extracts from the body, taken as a sign.
body: Eirenaeus, quoted, says that the first water “extracted partly the tincture of Sol” [III.1 ¶14] from the body, and treats this as a sign. The records also note that 'Tincture' is elsewhere a name for Reason, and 'foreign tincture' what Reason grinds out of the inferior life.

equivalences.with: medial receptacle of the newborn light
dry splendour (the Light from the Archaeus)

summary: Atwood's name for the cleansed, prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light; elsewhere, the Light from the Archaeus that comes forth as a dry splendour, identified with the Subtendent.
body: Atwood gives two related identifications. First, it is “the cleansed Augean, the already prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light” [II.4 ¶9]. Second, the Light from the Archaeus “comes forth as a dry splendour, surviving through all. And this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.3 ¶71]. The same passage equates it with the Subtendent: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71]. One passage names a receptacle and the other a light, and the text does not reconcile the two.

summary: Atwood's name for the putrefying stage of the matter, a stronger poison.
body: Atwood says the matter, “which putrefying, becomes a stronger poison, and their venomous toad” [I.2 ¶40]. 'Toad' thus names the putrefying stage.

summary: The ancient book whose counsel Atwood cites to support the adepts' practice of keeping the king's secret close while revealing in part.
body: Atwood cites the book of Tobit for the adepts' concealment of 'the king': it is “to be honorable to reveal the works of the Lord; but good t keep close the secret of a king” [II.1 ¶7]. She endorses this counsel and says she keeps within 'the prophet’s advice' while revealing only in part.

summary: The Golden Treatise ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, which Atwood cites for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy and repeatedly uses for chapter mottoes and supporting passages.
body: Atwood cites it as the Hermetis Trismegisti Tractatus Aureus de Lapidis physici secreto, in seven chapters. She uses it for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n10]. She takes chapter mottoes from it: “Opus vobuscum et apud est, quod intus arripens et permanens in terra vel in mare habere potes.” [II.1 ¶2] (our rendering: roughly, the work is with you and among you, and taking hold of it within you can have it). She also uses “Naturam in primisimitabere in arte, magister.” [III.1 ¶1] (our rendering: first imitate Nature in the art, master). On our tentative rendering of the corrupt Latin of this second motto (not the book's), outer fire only excites, and an inner ethereal agent perfects all. She cites it for the 'Our Mercury' passage: “Our Mercury is philosophic, fiery, vital” [II.1 ¶12, II.1 n10]. She cites the Scholium in support of her view that external fire alters while internal fire perfects: “Que l’art imite la nature” [III.1 ¶42, III.1 n46] (our rendering: that art imitates nature). From cap. 4, “Protégé me et protegam te” [III.1 ¶44, III.1 n48] (our rendering: protect me and I will protect you) illustrates the mutual relation of Sun and Moon; the text does not name the speaker. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the author of the Golden Treatise seems to intermix the steps because he describes different repetitions of the fermentative process [APP ¶17].

summary: Ancient mythological tradition, which Atwood reads as commemorating spectacles of the soul's liberation that Wisdom instituted and art makes natural.
body: Atwood treats myths as spectacles of the soul's liberation that art makes natural. Her examples are the Salamander, Aeneas in Numitius, Pactolus and Midas, Medea and Jason, the Hesperides, Atalanta, Hercules and the Phoenix: “Such are a very few of the games and choice spectacles which tradition commemorates as instituted by Wisdom” [III.1 ¶70].

summary: The mesmeric state, which some writers suggest reveals the temple mysteries; Atwood treats it as a key not yet carried beyond therapy.
body: Atwood reports that some writers “suggest their Trance and its phenomena as a revelation of the temple mysteries” [II.2 ¶6]. She treats the mesmeric trance as a key that has not yet been carried beyond therapeutic use.

summary: The final passage for which contemplation of the indwelling Unity is the last preparation; its theurgic rite involves burying the body except the head.
body: Atwood calls contemplation of the indwelling Unity “the final preparative to translation” [II.4 ¶40]. She speaks of “the theurgic mandates for this translation” [II.4 ¶40], whose rite involves burying the body except the head. Compare 'translation of the consciousness' [APP ¶83].

summary: Atwood's later definition of the whole mystery: consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The whole of this mystery is a translation of the consciousness” [APP ¶83]. She explains that consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.

summary: The conversion of metals into gold or silver; Atwood traces its possibility to a universal subject and reads it as life attracted into the Stone's light, and the Adept equates it with salvation.
body:
**Historical sense.** Atwood uses the word in its historical sense: the conversion of a metal into gold or silver. Rhasis practised it publicly (“on account of the practical displays he made of his transmuting skill” [I.1 ¶34]), and she reports that Avicenna did too. Of another practitioner she writes that “there is reason to believe that he practiced transmutation” [I.1 ¶66]. Parliament and papal bulls forbade it, “forbidding transmutation, on pain of death, and the pursuit of alchemy” [I.1 ¶55]. Aquinas, quoted, holds that “Metals can be transmuted one into another, since they are of one and the same matter” [I.1 ¶42]. He adds that it must be done “transmutare metalla scilicet imperfecta secundum veritatem et non sophistice” [I.1 n50] (our rendering: to transmute, that is, imperfect metals, truly and not by trickery).

**Atwood's theory.** Atwood sets out to investigate “the theoretic ground and matter on which the physical possibility of transmutation rests” [I.1 ¶86]. She explains how the Stone acts: it “transmutes, i.e., attracts the same away from other forms into intimate coalescence with its own assimilative light” [I.2 ¶48]. The adepts, she says, have shown “the principle of Transmutation” to be “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

**Salvation.** The Adept, quoted, says: “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18]. Atwood completes the statement herself: a transmutation “of the component principles of life in the circulation” [IV.2 ¶18].

summary: The ray of Light made concrete in life when it is dominant in the circulatory system; Atwood identifies it with the Philosophic Stone.
body: Atwood says the ray of Light, made concrete in life and dominant in the circulatory system, “is the transmutative ferment --- even the Philosophic Stone” [IV.4 ¶9].

summary: In Atwood's Appendix, the line contrary to the Divine (perpendicular) line; it restores to sense, and the two together form a cross.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the transverse line against the Divine line: it restores to sense: “the transverse line is the contrary; the two united form a cross +” [APP ¶13].

summary: The Tree of Life: its attainment is laborious intellectual work (Van Helmont), and for Atwood it lies hidden and hard to find under the oblivion of natural birth.
body: Van Helmont, as quoted, says that “the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood herself writes that “The tree of life covered over, indeed, with the dark oblivion of this natural outbirth, is latent and difficult to find” [III.1 ¶34]. According to the reader's record, she adds there that it is revealed only by celestial instinct, and that its bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken.

summary: Trevisan (Trevisanus), cited by Atwood for long, fruitless labour before success and for his image of the fixed watery Form as a marvellous fountain.
body: Atwood cites Trevisan as an example of one who worked in vain for over half a century until he found the separated Light [III.1 ¶37]. She also names him alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7]. In the footnotes, Trevisanus (spelled there “Berhard Trevisan”) is cited from his *Opusculum*. Atwood uses him to illustrate the fixed watery Form, his marvellous fountain, “shining like silver and of caerulean clearness” [I.3 n38, I.3 n39].

summary: In the quoted Chaldaic oracle, the threefold that shines throughout the world under the Monad's rule, in which Virtue, Wisdom and Verity appear.
body: The voice here is the Chaldaic oracle, quoted by Atwood: “For in the whole world shineth the Triad over which the Monad rules.” [IV.2 ¶22]. The oracle goes on: “And there appeared in it (the triad) Virtue, Wisdom, and multscient Verity;” [IV.2 ¶24]. The reader's record adds that all things serve its three Principles.

summary: A threefold turning inward which, together with multiplication of the hypostatic unit, makes the magistery manifest.
body: Atwood says the magistery is “made manifest by a triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit” [IV.2 ¶37]. The text does not explain the expression further. Reading it as a threefold turning inward follows the wording and is not a definition the book gives.

summary: Triptolemus appears only in a simile: Hippocrates spread Aesculapius's remedies as Triptolemus spread the seed of Ceres.
body: Atwood's only use of Triptolemus is in a simile. Hippocrates dispersed the succours of Aesculapius as Triptolemus dispersed the seed of Ceres [IV.3 ¶32].

summary: Grinding, used figuratively for the continual, slow and gentle working of the Philosophic Subject, which dissolves the subject's innate defects.
body: Atwood uses the word figuratively, marking it with “as it were”. The aim is “by a continual mechanic trituration, as it were, to dissolve and ultimately obliterate its innate defects” [IV.1 ¶5]. She applies the point “especially to the trituration of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶13]. The record for that passage says this working should be slow, gentle and continuous. The context suggests that the word stands for the continual working of the subject, not for literal grinding.

summary: Cited for reference only.
In the Appendix, Atwood's term for Theosophy on its physical side, as opposed to the alchemy the world has sought without finding.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Alchemy (not that which the world has run after without finding) is related to Theosophy on its physical side” [APP ¶78]. According to the reader's record, she describes it there as a change in the circulatory system of the blood wrought by reiterative contritions.

headword: A True and Faithful Relation of what passed for many years between Dr John Dee and some Spirits
forms: A True and Faithful Relation of what passed for many years between Dr John Dee and some Spirits
summary: Cited for reference only.
The Platonists, as Atwood reports, declared true Being to be white.
body: Atwood reports a view of the Platonists: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9].

summary: The genuine art, as distinct from “clouds of sophistry”, whose Light and virtue helped the ancients.
body: Atwood speaks of “that Light and virtue of true Chemistry, by which the ancients were assisted” [III.1 ¶4]. The reader's record says she sets this genuine art apart from clouds of sophistry.

equivalences.with: the great and miraculous mystery of the world

summary: In Aliphili's words, an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which alone dissolves gold into black earth; called the great and miraculous mystery of the world.
body: The voice here is Aliphili, as quoted. The reader's record gives his account: an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which dissolves gold into black earth, and nothing else does this. Aliphili names it “the great and miraculous mystery of the world; that is the true fiery water” [II.1 ¶14]. This gives the identity: true fiery water = the great and miraculous mystery of the world [II.1 ¶14].

summary: The real object of Alchemy's golden promise; avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it.
body: Atwood contrasts the true Form of Gold with the dead metal: “neither will be found to be the true Form of Gold” [III.4 ¶11]. According to the reader's record, she makes it the real object of Alchemy's golden promise there. Avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it. The text does not define it further here.

summary: Apparently the real being or substance of oneself, which self-contemplation with an unpurified spirit cannot discern.
body: Atwood warns that if we contemplate ourselves with an unpurified spirit, “we shall not there discern the true hypostasis” [II.2 ¶14]. The reading as the real being or substance of oneself is inferred from this context, not stated.

summary: The identity in nature that the pseudo-alchemists failed to divine, which would otherwise have to be sought through all creatures by experiment.
body: Atwood says the pseudo-alchemists worked “without rightly divining the true Identity of nature” [II.1 ¶6]. Without the one subject that contains all, one would have “to search out the identity through all creatures and minerals, by way of experiment” [II.1 ¶9].

equivalences.with: the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself

summary: The proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself, which the wise mind holds within itself; the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.
body: Atwood glosses the term herself: “(since it possesses the true Intelligible); that is to say, the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself” [II.1 ¶37]. This gives the identity: the true Intelligible = the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself [II.1 ¶37]. According to the reader's record, the wise mind holds it within itself, and the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.

summary: That on whose discovery the success of the experiment depends; it is present more or less in every mind, though not clearly discernible in all.
body: Atwood says that success “depends on the discovery of the true Intention” [IV.3 ¶54]. According to the reader's record, she adds that it is involved more or less in every mind, though it cannot be clearly distinguished in all.

summary: In the Appendix, the mind's experimental contact with mystery, in which the mind consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Knowledge is experimental contact of mind with mystery” [APP ¶75]. According to the reader's record, the mind there consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle, with an efflux of life.

summary: The Light needed before practice; hidden and imprisoned within, it is called the fountain of Universal Nature, and is perfected in the Saviour.
body:
Atwood uses the term in three passages.

- **Needed before practice.** Those who failed worked “without the true Light or heeding their injunctions” [I.1 ¶86]. It is not explained there.
- **Hidden within.** She speaks of “the true light shut up as in a prison, the fountain of Universal Nature” [II.1 ¶49]. This gives the identity: true light = the fountain of Universal Nature. According to the record, the senses' outward attraction keeps this light apart from understanding.
- **In the Saviour.** She quotes “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19]. According to the record, the Light is perfected in the Saviour, and one ray of it cleanses our life.

The text does not say outright that these three uses are one and the same.

summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai's words, man as distinct from the man who appears here.
body: The voice here is Rabbi Ben Jochai, as quoted: “But we must distinguish the true man from him who is here apparent” [II.1 ¶42].

summary: The material and proper Subject of the Work, hidden under countless names; finding it is called a great point.
body: The passage says: “It is a great point to find out the True Matter and proper Subject of this work” [IV.2 ¶6]. This gives the identity: True Matter = proper Subject of this work. According to the reader's record, it is hidden under countless names and is not named here. The voice is unclear. It may be Atwood, or she may be continuing a cited author, since the next sentence reads “adds our author of The Triumph”.

summary: In the Paracelsians' view, a medicine bound in man like milk in a hard nut, which must be freed from impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.
body: Atwood reports the Paracelsian view: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶10]. According to the reader's record, it is held there like milk in a hard nut. It must be freed from its impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.

summary: That which the Art restores to its original rule by hiding the opposing principle; not otherwise defined.
body: The Art is said to work “to restore the true rector to his original rule” [II.1 ¶21]. According to the reader's record, it does this by hiding the opposing principle. The voice is unclear, and the text does not define the term further.

summary: In the Appendix, the identity of knower and known, of subject with object.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Science is the contact identical of the thing knowing with the thing known, subject with object.” [APP ¶171]
