summary: In Eirenaeus, the means by which the purged Mercury is vivified; not explained further.
body: The voice here is Eirenaeus, as quoted. Of the purged Mercury he says: “And with true sulfur it can vivify” [III.1 ¶69]. The text does not explain the term further.

summary: In Paracelsus, the matter of the metals, which brings everything into its due form.
body: The voice here is Paracelsus, as quoted: “The truphat, or matter of the metals” [I.2 ¶25]. This gives the identity: truphat = matter of the metals. According to the reader's record, it brings everything into its due form.

summary: In the Appendix, Light in its own ether: the Divine Wisdom made visible to itself.
body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “Truth is, as it were, Light in its own ether, the Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous” [APP ¶171]. This gives the identity: Truth = Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous.

summary: Atwood's name for the Chaldaic oracles (Oracula Chaldaica), which she cites on piety, the fiery mind, and the soul's way of return.
body: Atwood cites the truth-telling Oracle from the *Oracula Chaldaica* in II.3. She uses it in support of these points: piety and the fiery mind preserve the body; the soul's way of return; the warning against stooping down; and the soul clasping God. One line she quotes is “If thou extend the fiery mind to the work of piety,” [II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶38, II.3 ¶40, II.3 ¶42, II.3 n46, II.3 n47]. She cites it with approval.

summary: The Turba, whose maxim that all the wise seek is in Mercury serves as a chapter epigraph and is taken up again in the text.
body: Atwood quotes the *Turba* (Ecercit. 1) as the epigraph of chapter I.2: “Est in Mercurio quicquid quaerunt Sapientes” [I.2 ¶1]. In modern English (our translation): whatever the Wise seek is in Mercury. She takes the maxim up again in [I.2 ¶12].

summary: In the theosophist's words, a heavenly and an earthly matter, to be reduced to one as they were at the beginning.
body: The voice here is the theosophist, as quoted: “That Two Natures be reduced to One, as they were at the beginning.” [IV.3 ¶38]. According to the reader's record, the two are a heavenly and an earthly matter.

summary: Two principles that stand against each other if the Chaos is split apart too early; not named here.
body: Atwood warns that if the Chaos is split apart too early, “the two Principles stand up one against the other, before the intended mastery is secure” [IV.1 ¶15]. She does not name the two Principles here.

summary: In Plato, as quoted, an ignorance that does not know it is ignorant and therefore has no desire to emerge.
body: The voice here is Plato, as quoted. He describes an ignorance “which being ignorant that it is ignorant has no desire to emerge” [II.2 ¶13].

summary: Porphyry's distinction, reported by Atwood, between common death, freeing the body from the soul, and philosophic death, freeing the soul from the body.
body: Reported from Porphyry: “there is, says he, a twofold death” [II.3 ¶37] — the common death, in which the body is freed from the soul, and the philosophic death, in which the soul is freed from the body. The voice is Porphyry's as cited by Atwood.

summary: Apostolic ordinances or material signs, such as water, oil, salt and light, which Atwood says signified real efficacies but later became a source of dissension.
body: Atwood says that in apostolic practice “certain ordinances and elementary types, as of water, oil, salt and light, signified some real and notable efficacies” [I.1 ¶26]. She also calls them material signs, and says that “these very shadows and types of doctrines” became a source of dissension [I.1 ¶26].

equivalences.with: the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy; Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities

summary: In the Osiris fable, the brother who kills and scatters Osiris; applied to the work, the wrathful fire or Efficient of dissolution, and the unclean Instrument that putrefies the gold.
body:
In Atwood's reading of the fable, Typhon is Osiris's uterine brother, who kills and scatters him. Applied to the work, he is the wrathful fire or Efficient of the dissolution, and also a name for the unclean Instrument that moves the gold to putrefy. Isis gradually enthrals him [III.1 ¶63].

Asserted identities:
- The adepts' names: “Adepts call him the Green Lion, Typhon, Firedrake”. And “or during the mortification, he is their venomous Black Toad” [III.1 ¶56].
- As the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy: “it is called by them Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities, etc.” [III.1 ¶61].
- “they gave to Typhon, in this predicament, the name of Seth, Bebo” [III.1 ¶63]. These names import “a certain violent, forcible restraint, contrariety, and subversion” [III.1 ¶63].

Atwood presents these as the adepts' names, set out in her own exposition.

summary: The state reached by passing through reason and beyond every bound, which Atwood identifies with the Infinity of Life.
body: Atwood describes it as the state reached by passing through reason beyond every bound: “that kind of ultimate ignorance, which is the Infinity of Life” [III.2 ¶54]. She equates it with the Infinity of Life.

summary: An unattributed saying that Atwood cites to show the promise that God may be found, though he remains hidden.
body: Atwood cites “Seek and ye shall find, knock and it shall be opened unto you” without attribution [II.1 ¶26]. She uses it to illustrate the promise that God may be found, though he remains hidden.

summary: An unattributed declaration that Atwood introduces with “as is declared”, cited in support of the purged life flowing forth as a panacea.
body: Introduced only with “as is declared”, the phrase “a pure panacea from the god of Light” [III.1 ¶10] supports Atwood's point that the purged life flows forth as a panacea.

summary: An unattributed saying, introduced with “as we are abundantly instructed”, cited in support of dissolving the Vital Spirit's natural bind.
body: Atwood introduces it only with “as we are abundantly instructed”: “Flesh and blood cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, neither doth corruption inherit corruption” [III.2 ¶62]. She cites it in support of dissolving the natural bind of the Vital Spirit. The text gives no attribution.

summary: Unattributed English and Latin couplets that Atwood cites about Art advancing nature, the descent to the Paternal, and finding without seeking.
body:
Atwood cites three couplets without attribution:
- On the descent undertaken to reach the Paternal: “To find the Hero, for whose only sake We sought the dark abodes and crossed the bitter lake.” [II.4 ¶24].
- In Latin, on finding that comes without seeking: “Quaeres multum et non invenies; Fortasse invneies cumnon quaeres.” [III.2 ¶58]. Our rendering (by: ours): You will seek much and not find; perhaps you will find when you do not seek.
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), in support of alchemy advancing nature beyond her created state: “Art, then, what nature left in hand doth take, And out of one a twofold work doth make.” [APP ¶156].

summary: An unattributed Latin tag, “Visitabis interiore terrae”, appended to the Appendix's account of successive dissolutions.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the tag “Visitabis interiore terrae, etc.” [APP ¶182] is appended to the account of successive dissolutions. Our rendering (by: ours): You will visit the interior of the earth. It is given as a reference only, without comment.

summary: Unattributed Latin verses that Atwood cites to illustrate the ascent, return to the archetypal world, illumination, the four principles and knowledge of God.
body:
Atwood cites many Latin verses without attribution (all renderings below are ours):
- “Non levis adscensus, si quis petat ardua, sudor” (no light toil is the ascent, if one seeks the heights), on the toil of the ascent [II.2 ¶30].
- “Ille deum vitam accipiet, divisque videbit” (he shall receive the life of the gods, and shall see [among] the gods), on attaining the life of the gods [II.4 ¶51].
- “Tunc ire ad mundum archetypum saepe atque redire” (then to go often to the archetypal world and return), on repeated going to and returning from the archetypal world [II.4 ¶53, II.4 ¶54].
- “Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.” (If you, my God, illumine me, my darkness becomes light), on darkness made light [III.2 ¶11].
- “Mundum mente gerens, similique in imagine formas” (bearing the world in mind, and forming [it] in a like image), on the world being formed after a supernal exemplar held in mind. It carries footnote (27) [III.3 ¶39, III.3 ¶40].
- “Janua clausa est, vah quae lamentabilis haec vox;” (the door is shut, alas, what a lamentable cry), on the shut door that hands cannot force [IV.1 ¶38].
- “Primus dicatur in quo sensus dominatur.” (let that be called first in which sense rules), on the four principles and their relations, graded against the senses [IV.2 ¶10].
- “Nec Sentire Deum nisi qui pars ipse Dei sit.” (nor does any perceive God unless he himself be part of God), in support of the point that only what is part of God perceives God [IV.2 ¶42].
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas” (happy he who could know the causes of things). There it is called a grand declaration of a deep Hermetic truth: the light of life, lodged in its causal center, frees the threefold life [APP ¶148, APP ¶149, APP ¶150].

summary: An unattributed Latin maxim, “Ne tu augeas fatum”, that Atwood renders “Enlarge not thy destiny” as a warning to the would-be practitioner.
body: Atwood cites “Ne tu augeas fatum” [IV.3 ¶56] with the English “Enlarge not thy destiny” (by: book). She uses it to warn the would-be practitioner against presumption.

summary: Unattributed quotations that Atwood uses for the dreamlike nature of human beings and to name the magic earth.
body: Atwood quotes “such stuff as dreams are made of” [III.2 ¶7] to illustrate the dreamlike nature of human beings, set against the real discovery of the Matter. She also quotes “Land of Havilah, where good gold is” [III.2 ¶8] to identify the magic earth.

summary: Unattributed sayings that Atwood cites about the fear of God as the beginning of wisdom and about the seeker giving up his riches.
body: In a footnote, Atwood cites “The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy is understanding” [I.3 n19]. It supports the admonition to fear God, which she says is proved in alchemy. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “The ransom of a man’s life are his riches” [APP ¶158] supports the point that the seeker gives up the riches set before him.

summary: An unattributed scriptural phrase cited in the Appendix to support the point that the Fall accords with a purpose of greater restoration.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the phrase “eternal purpose, purposed in Christ Jesus, our Lord” [APP ¶98] supports the view that the Fall accords with a purpose of greater restoration.

summary: Unattributed English verses that Atwood cites about alchemy's concrete evidence, the invisible matter, the divine mover, Saturn bound, the working-place, perseverance and the reign of Mind.
body:
Atwood cites many verses without attribution:
- The evidence of alchemy was concrete, not “vaguely opinable, But clean, experimental and determinable” [I.1 ¶78].
- The heavenly bodies proclaim a divine mover: “"The Hand that moves us is divine".” [II.4 ¶30].
- The material of the Magistry is invisible and insensible: “A nature to search out which is invisible,” [III.1 ¶7].
- “Saturn, with honey of the bees produced, Sunk in ebriety; fast bind the god.” [III.1 ¶67, III.1 ¶68]. Atwood glosses this as Intellect cutting off the sated Saturnian Will.
- The need for a fitting working-place: “It is a grace - To finde a fitting working-place.” [III.4 ¶43].
- Persevering, with the completed work kept in mind as aim and model: “Begin today, nor end till evil sink In its due grave” [IV.3 ¶51].
- The hoped-for reign of Mind and man's second birth: “Then shall the reign of Mind commence on earth” [IV.3 ¶52, IV.3 ¶53].
- The divine faculty is confined from birth, yet light can enter: “The beams pour in, and truth and skill may couch the blind.” [IV.4 ¶16].

summary: An unattributed verse about Helius, cited to illustrate the descent to the realm of night and the ancestors, which leads into the discussion of Aeneas.
body: The verse “To Erebus he went, and the sad realms of night” [II.4 ¶19, II.4 ¶20] is cited without attribution. It concerns Helius and illustrates the descent to the realm of night and the ancestors, leading into Atwood's discussion of Aeneas.

summary: An unattributed verse on Proteus that Atwood cites to illustrate the one omniform subject.
body: Atwood cites a verse on Proteus, “Etherial, watery, earthy general soul, Immortal Fire!” [I.2 ¶34, I.2 ¶35], without attribution. She uses it to illustrate the one omniform subject.

headword: unattributed words: 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom'
forms: unattributed words: 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom'
the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom
summary: An unattributed saying whose meaning, the Appendix says, becomes clear on contact with universal power, the initial of regenerate life.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the words “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom” [APP ¶175] are said to become clear in meaning on contact with universal power, the initial of regenerate life.

summary: The human understanding, taken as an essence to be purified, whose occult Causality can be developed to consciousness.
body: Atwood speaks of “purifying the human Understanding Essence, and developing to consciousness its occult Causality” [II.2 ¶22]. In her usage it is the human understanding, considered as an essence that must be purified and that holds a hidden causality able to become conscious.

summary: The light that, Atwood says, the Divine Law takes from the spirit while it is in full vigour, so as to give it a motive.
body: Atwood says the Divine Law deprives the spirit “when in full vigor of its Understanding Light” [III.1 ¶28]. She says this is done to give the spirit a motive.

summary: The human understanding, which mystical exercises and preparations bring into contact with its Antecedent Cause, in a view Atwood reports from Aristotle.
body: In a view Atwood reports from Aristotle, mystical exercises and preparations bring it about that “the human Understanding Medium is made to pass into contact with its Antecedent Cause” [II.1 ¶37].

summary: The higher spirit that, once false imagination is destroyed, can superinduce Divinity, rise above nature, and be inducted by the Mysteries to its Source.
body: In Atwood's voice, false imagination must be destroyed “before the understanding spirit can superinduce Divinity” [II.2 ¶10]. The trials go on “till the Understanding Spirit rises superior to the dominion of nature” [II.2 ¶13]. The Mysteries were “real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source” [IV.4 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), a graven image is “carved into the understanding spirit which conceives it by the desire of life” [APP ¶100]. There it is also that of which the connate spirit may be deprived.

summary: What is nourished and educated in the Elysian state as the embryo life unfolds.
body: Atwood speaks of “the nourishment and education of the understanding vehicle” [II.4 ¶16]. This takes place in the Elysian state as the embryo life unfolds.

summary: Atwood's name for the subject of the Hermetic art, referred to as “her”, which the art takes where nature leaves it and then disposes and manipulates.
body: Atwood calls the subject of the art “this our Undetermined Subject” and refers to it as “her”. The art takes it where nature leaves it and undertakes “the right disposition and manipulation of this our Undetermined Subject” [II.2 ¶27].

summary: In Hermes as Atwood cites him, the temperate unguent is fire, and unguents are called sulphurs. The true unguent is occult, buried in the matter's own body, and extracted without combustion.
body:
These are Hermes's words as Atwood cites them. “The temperate unguent, which is fire” [I.3 ¶24] is the medium between faeces and water and the Perscrutinator of the water. “For the unguents are called sulphurs” [I.3 ¶24], because fire, oil and sulphur are closely akin. So unguent = fire = sulphurs.

The true unguent is “the occult and buried unguent” [I.3 ¶54]. It lies in the matter's own body and is the Form of all other unguents. It has no apparent preparation and is extracted without combustion. It is distinct from unguents made of fats, hair and the like. Hermes also says “the ointments which contain the tincture coagulate the tincture, coagulate the fugitive and adorn the sulphurs” [I.3 ¶54].

summary: The condition in which alone, Atwood says, immortality is consummated; also the joining of the line's end with its beginning, which is Eternity rather than time.
body: Atwood writes that “immortality is only to be consummated in union” [IV.3 ¶58]. On the joining of the line's end with its beginning, she says: “they join not in time, for their union is Eternity” [IV.3 ¶62]. So union = Eternity.

summary: Apparently the soul's last remaining unity, about which it rallies as it draws back from nonentity.
body: The soul, drawing back from nonentity, is described as “rallying about her last deserted Unit” [III.2 ¶55]. Apparently this is the soul's last remaining unity. The voice of the passage is unclear.

summary: The inseparable unity at which the reiterated analysis finally arrives.
body: Atwood says the reiterated analysis goes on “until it arrives at the inseparable Unit of Truth” [IV.1 ¶20].

summary: The whole, identified with the Kingdom of God, which must be sought before any finite end, and into which one returns by abandoning selfhood.
body: Atwood speaks of “returning again, however, into the Universal and abandoning the selfhood” [IV.4 ¶27]. The Universal is the whole: one ceases to be it by becoming dividual and returns into it by giving up selfhood. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), it must be sought before any finite end, and it is equated with the Kingdom of God: “before you seek the Universal --- the Kingdom of God” [APP ¶135].

summary: The occult being in nature on whose assumption, Atwood says, the whole of Hermetic theory and practice proceeds.
body: Atwood states that “the whole of the Hermetic theory and practice proceeds upon the assumption of a certain Universal Being in nature, which is occult” [I.2 ¶26].

summary: In the Appendix, Atwood names the Universal Center as consciousness's own true Source and the source of all things.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood speaks of consciousness drawn centrally coming to know “its own true Source, which is the Universal Center and source of all things” [APP ¶6]. So the Universal Center is identified with that true Source.

summary: What the adepts found to be in the fire of man's life; the text does not define it further.
body: Atwood reports that the adepts found “the Universal Efficient was in this fire” [IV.4 ¶4], the fire being man's life. She presents this with approval. The passage does not define the term further.

summary: What the Alchemists set out to rectify: an invisible vapor they compressed into a tangible Form, as distinct from the common elements of chemistry.
body: Atwood says the Alchemists aimed “to rectify the Universal Element, and compress its invisible vapor into a tangible Form” [IV.1 ¶47]. She sets this against the common elements of chemistry. In her account, then, the Universal Element starts as invisible and vaporous and the art gives it bodily form.

summary: In Khunrath's account, that with which the Azoth reanimates bodies that have been reduced to First Matter.
body: Quoting Khunrath, the text says the Azoth takes bodies reduced to First Matter and “reanimates them with the Universal Form” [IV.3 ¶28]. The Universal Form is therefore what gives those dissolved bodies new life.

summary: What appears in the mind during the work; the impress seen in the vessel serves as a secondary witness that confirms it.
body: In a footnote Atwood speaks of “this appearance of the Universal Idea in the mind” [III.3 n27], comparing it with the pattern seen in the Subject Waters. She treats the impress seen in the vessel as a secondary witness that confirms it. On this account the main evidence is in the mind, and what shows in the vessel only corroborates it.

summary: The one identity in which all things are identical, so every assertion of it is true; body, soul and spirit are born in it.
body: Atwood writes: “All is identical --- need we repeat it? --- in the Universal Identity, and every possible assertion of it will be true” [III.3 ¶67]. She also says body, soul and spirit are born in this identity. Readers listed “Unknown Identity” and “Identity” as variants, but the packet does not show them as forms of this headword.

summary: What the physiologists and alchemists are said to have proved by experiment, on ontological ground.
body: Atwood reports that the physiologists and alchemists “were said to prove the Universal Identity of Nature on the ontological ground” [II.4 ¶16]. In other words, they are said to have proved it experimentally. She gives this as a report (“were said”).

summary: The law under which fulfilment comes once the outer and inner worlds agree.
body: Atwood says that once the outer and inner worlds agree, the result is “a fulfillment under the Universal Law” [III.3 ¶82].

headword: Universal Law of Light in Nature
forms: Universal Law of Light in Nature
summary: The law that, according to Atwood, the philosophers' Stone shows at every stage: its origin, its development and its artificial preparation.
body: Atwood writes that “their Stone exhibits, alike in its origin, development and artificial preparation throughout, the Universal Law of Light in Nature” [IV.3 ¶27]. On this account the making of the Stone follows the same law of light that runs through nature.

summary: In the Appendix, matter that can be obtained at the focus of any of the three microcosmic centers.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “The universal matter is obtainable at the focus of either center.” [APP ¶95]. The centers meant are the three microcosmic centers.

summary: A medicine, described by several cited authorities, that preserves health and cures all diseases, and that comes from the true Mercury of the philosophers.
body:
Three cited authorities speak of it. None of these passages is in Atwood's own voice.

- **The Scholiast:** “the universal medicine is concreted” from things full of the balsam of nature. It preserves health and roots out diseases [I.3 n61].
- **Eudoxus:** the true Mercury of the philosophers is what “will give you the fixed Sulphur and the Universal Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16]. The same passage also speaks of “the medicine of the Third order” and “the three medicines”.
- **Eirenaeus:** the accomplished artist would have “a universal medicine, moreover, capable of curing all diseases” [IV.3 ¶26].

summary: The medium at work in mesmerism. Mesmerists use it as it naturally comes, while the ancients dissolved it further.
body: Atwood treats the Universal Medium as what operates in mesmerism. It can be improved, can rise or sink, and has a right determination. She notes that the mesmerists take it as they find it: “as respects the Universal Medium, they even, who believe in such a thing, take it as it presents itself naturally” [II.2 ¶7]. The ancients, by contrast, worked “to dissolve the medium more entirely” [II.2 ¶8]. The contrast suggests that she sees further dissolution of this medium as part of the ancient method that modern mesmerism lacks.

summary: The life-giving substance that all beings live in without knowing it. It is hidden in natural generation and is to be known from within.
body: Atwood speaks of those who seek “to know intrinsical within themselves the substance of that Universal Nature in which they, with all beings in common, as it were, unconsciously live” [I.3 n8]. She says this nature is hidden in natural generation and must be known from within. She also applies Apuleius' praise of Isis to it: “All which is readily admissible of the Universal Nature” [II.4 ¶19]. Here Universal Nature is the life-supplying source that we are drawn out of and that keeps us in being, and it is revealed in the Epopteia.

summary: What Nature carries sealed in her own vessel through dissolution to resurrection. It is the third of three hypostatic relations, “the All in all”.
body: Atwood speaks of Nature's vessel, “in which she bears her Universal Offspring, hermetically sealed” [III.3 ¶65], from dissolution through to resurrection. She also names it as the third hypostatic relation alongside agent and patient: “that universal offspring which is the All in all, without foreign admixture” [III.3 ¶67].

summary: The reason that man holds within himself. The ancients magnified it, and it answers the sceptical individual intellect when that intellect is humble.
body: Quoting Agrippa, the text says man “contains the Universal Reason within himself” [II.1 ¶9], and that this makes him God's image. In her own voice, Atwood refers to “the Universal Reason so magnified and its ethereal vehicle” [II.1 ¶32] by the ancients, and admits it offers the senses very little evidence. In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) she writes: “The Universal Reason condescends to answer it when not self-seeking and too proud to know.” [APP ¶116]. The “it” is the individual, sceptical intellect.

summary: The science Lully is said to have come to late in life. It is also the state, together with integrity, to which the central work restores the mind.
body: Atwood writes: “Raymond Lully is supposed to have become acquainted with Arnold, and the Universal Science, late in life” [I.1 ¶46]. The context is Lully's turn to alchemy, but the text does not say outright that the Universal Science is alchemy. Elsewhere she says the central work “restores the human mind to integrity and universal science” [IV.4 ¶17].

summary: The soul hidden within Nature, which can be called her temple. The Ether is its vestibule or vehicle.
body: Atwood speaks of “the universal soul of the world, which is occultly suspended in Nature, and may be called her temple” [III.1 ¶5]. So it is identified with Nature's temple [III.1 ¶5]. She describes the Ether as its vestibule or vehicle.

summary: What man, through the virtue within him, could prove and magnify. According to Atwood, doing so was the foundation of the magistery.
body: Atwood says man “nor yet surmises the virtue that is in him, to prove and magnify the Universal Source” [II.1 ¶8]. She presents proving and magnifying this Source as the foundation of the magistery.

summary: The common source of the First Matter, metals and all things. It is a passive middle substance present everywhere in nature, which art can collect, rectify and perfect.
body:
Atwood speaks of the Universal Spirit throughout the book.

**Source and identities**
- The First Matter is generated by “active and passive relations of the Universal Spirit” [I.2 ¶31]. In its common state the Spirit is, “as the Spirit is in nature, said to be everywhere” [I.2 ¶40].
- It is the common source of metals and of all things: “from metalline seeds out of the Universal Spirit or Mercury” [I.2 ¶49]. This identifies it with Mercury.
- She adds that “without this spirit growth is impossible, or transmutation or increase” [I.2 ¶49].

**Nature**
- “the properties of the Universal Spirit are abstrusely included in all existence” [I.3 n4]. They can be understood only through the Spirit's own inner analysis and “introverted light”. The “central experience” within it cannot be found without God [I.3 n4].
- “this Universal Spirit is described as a middle substance --- passive, undetermined, susceptible of conversion and all extremes” [II.2 ¶26]. That is why art can perfect it.

**In the work**
- She speaks of “the Universal Spirit, which has been so often fermented, rectified, and recalcined” [IV.3 ¶29], until its central force acts at the circumference. The passage leaves open whether the Spirit is the common origin of the vivific Ens and of what the Ens assimilates, or is the Ens itself.

**Appendix** (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer)
- “The Universal Spirit is in one form the Principle of all growth” [APP ¶4]. It can be collected and brought to bear on a germ.
- The Hermetic Philosophy experiments into this Spirit through man, because “you must have the Universal developed in you before you can understand the Universal” [APP ¶65].

summary: The spirit by which light can be multiplied; knowledge of it applied in the mineral kingdom produced gold. It is the subject of Vaughan's Anima Magia Abscondita.
body: Atwood refers to the “miraculous multiplicability of light by the universal spirit of nature” [I.1 ¶38]. She says that knowledge of this spirit, applied in the mineral kingdom, produced gold. She also names it as the subject of Vaughan's Anima Magia Abscondita: “the universal spirit of nature, with its strange, abstruse, and miraculous ascent and descent” [I.1 ¶74]. The text does not explain this ascent and descent.

summary: The one subject of the Hermetic art and the foundation of its experiment, identified with the first matter. It exists in nature, can be nourished in Man, and its concentrated virtue is the Stone.
body:
According to the alchemists, the contradictory epitaphs describe “the properties of their universal subject” [I.1 ¶24]. Atwood puts off explaining this until later.

In her own voice:
- She identifies it with the first matter: “their Universal Subject or first matter” [I.2 ¶7].
- “this Universal Subject is the alleged foundation of the whole Hermetic experiment” [I.2 ¶8]. It is both what is transmuted and, once freed into its proper essentiality, what transmutes.
- Some pseudo-alchemists caught “glimpses of the Universal Subject” [II.1 ¶6] and still failed.
- The art's analysis is “the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis of the Universal Subject” [III.2 ¶20].
- It is the one subject underlying all Species, and transmutation concerns it: “there is a Universal Subject in nature, and that Subject is susceptible of nourishment in Man” [IV.4 ¶10]. Its concentrated virtue is the Stone.

summary: In the Appendix, the power the mind becomes related to when it enters the third life, so that it can act out that power's will.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says that the mind entering the third life becomes “related to the Universal Vitalizing Power, and so can act Its will” [APP ¶3].

summary: In the Appendix, the agent of the Work, at war with the self-will. It dissolves the false forms and reproduces the faculties transmuted. It is identified with the great Salt Sea and Wisdom.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The Universal Will being represented as agent dissolves the false forms in the self-will represented as patient.” [APP ¶94]. It destroys the faculties and false forms and then reproduces them transmuted. She identifies it as “The great Salt Sea (Wisdom, the Universal Will)” [APP ¶94]. In plain terms, the agent–patient language of the Work is here read as the universal will acting on the individual self-will.

summary: General truths present in the mind independently of the senses. Atwood offers them as evidence of a higher reality and as grounds for her inquiry.
body: Atwood says “this subsistence of Universals in the human mind deserves to be profoundly considered” [II.1 ¶34]. She cites “the independent evidence of Universals in the human intellect” [II.1 ¶39] as proof of a higher kind of evidence and of a latent superstantial nature. On her account, the fact that the soul perceives universals shows it can act without phantasy, and “they reveal in us a necessity of Being beyond present experience” [II.2 ¶13]. This helps her introduce the Idea of Wisdom. Later she gives “the natural subsistence of Universals in the human mind” [IV.4 ¶14] as a ground of probability for the inquiry.

summary: In the Zohar's account, the divine hypostasis before it is manifested: hidden in the Infinite, unknown while the point of Light remains subjective. It has several names, including the Ancient of Days.
body: The text cites the Zohar here; this is not Atwood's own voice. The divine is described as hidden in the Infinite, without mind, figure or Being, and: “whilst the point of Light remains within subjective and inseparate, he is unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. Even when seen, “under this form by which he is seen, he remains still unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. The same passage gives his names: “in this sense he is called the Ancient of Days, the White Head, the Old Man by excellence, the Mystery of Mysteries” [III.2 ¶3].

summary: An unnamed voice, cited with “Alchemy has been declared”, that supports Atwood's view of Alchemy as the way to enter and discover Truth.
body: Atwood cites an unnamed declaration calling Alchemy “the only true glass of the mind” [IV.4 ¶12]. She uses it to support her view that Alchemy is the way to enter and discover Truth.

summary: An unnamed source, cited with “as it is narrated”, that supports the claim that by the Divine Will man has the mind and manual skill to bring about all things.
body: Atwood cites an unnamed narration (“as it is narrated”) to support the claim that, by the Divine Will, man has mind and manual efficacy to effect all things [IV.4 ¶3].

summary: An unnamed speaker, introduced with “he ... who said”, whose saying supports the idea that the search for Wisdom starts by setting the mind in motion.
body: Atwood quotes an unnamed speaker: “the first step of philosophy is to set the mind a-going” [III.1 ¶8]. She uses it to support the idea that the search for Wisdom starts by setting the mind in motion.

summary: In the Appendix, the region where the Ideas are, which the spirit in the medial life sees as its azure sky.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood places the Ideas in “the Upper Ether, where the Ideas are” [APP ¶15]. To the spirit in the medial life it appears as its azure sky.

headword: Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret
forms: Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret
summary: Urbigeranus, author of the Hermetic Secret, cited for calling the labor a labor of Hercules that cannot be done without the Theory of the Arcanum.
body:
Atwood cites Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret, for two points [IV.1 ¶7]:
- He calls the labor a labor of Hercules.
- Along with “these Adepts”, he holds that it is impossible without the Theory of their Arcanum.

She uses him to support how difficult the work is and that it depends on theory.

summary: Vaughan's term, as quoted, for the working strength of the finished Stone, which casting it on gold serves to qualify.
body: A term in a passage Atwood quotes from Vaughan: the Stone, once made, is cast on gold “to qualify the utensive power of it when it was made” [IV.3 ¶22]. The context suggests it means the medicine's working strength, which this bodily fermentation tempers.

summary: Named a worthy disciple of Paracelsus; Atwood cites him often as eyewitness of the Stone and on the labour, the Hand, the operator and the physician.
body:
Named with Crollius, Fludd, Helvetius and Faber among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64].

**Witness of the Stone.** From his *Book of Eternal Life* and *Ortus Med.*, Atwood cites his eyewitness account of projection on quicksilver yielding gold, with powder received from the stranger Butler: “I have seen the Stone and handled it” [I.1 ¶76; I.1 n98]. She also reports his cures of some 10,000 people yearly without diminishing his medicine [IV.3 ¶35].

**On the work.** From the *Oreatrike* she takes that “the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research” [III.1 ¶13; III.1 n13]; the white sand Quellum in a vital soil never pierced [III.2 ¶8; III.2 n9]; another favoured individual led to perceive the simple element of nature — “I saw, as in a dream, the whole face of the earth” [III.2 ¶17; III.2 n18]; the requirements of the operator and the specific, not corrosive, dissolving virtue — “Not every messenger, says Van helmont, approacheth to the mine of Sontes” [IV.1 ¶39; IV.1 n30]; and the Hand as the soul's instrument, “The Hand, says Van Helmont, is the instrument of instruments”, with learners bidden to buy coals and fire and labour as philosophers did [IV.1 ¶5; IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n3; IV.1 n9]. *Imago Mentis* and *Tree of Life* are cited for the three principles into which Life is resolved, “Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury” [III.2 ¶28; III.2 n27].

**On medicine.** From *Tumulus Pestis* she cites the requirements of the God-chosen physician (“But a physician chosen by God”) and medicine's decline through ambition and gain, calling him “one of its brightest ornaments” [IV.3 ¶34; IV.3 ¶35; IV.3 n12; IV.3 n13].

**Qualifications.** With Paracelsus he corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea (“by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit”), but Atwood treats this as only a secondary witness [III.3 n27]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer) he is said to speak of the White Light as the Quellem “in a very superficial way” [APP ¶157].

headword: the Van Helmonts, father and son
forms: the Van Helmonts, father and son
summary: The Van Helmonts, father and son, listed by Atwood among the adepts, with de Ortu Medicinae and Paradoxes cited.
body: Listed among the adepts, with *de Ortu Medicinae* and *Paradoxes* cited in the note [I.1 ¶70; I.1 n82].

equivalences.with: the material principle in the conception

summary: The material principle in conception, which obscures the generative light to bring it into sense and must be wholly evaporated before truth appears.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood says: “The vaporous vehicle is the material principle in the conception” [APP ¶121]. It obscures the paternal generative light so as to bring it into sense, and “The whole of the self-included vaporous vehicle of the soul must be evaporated before any truth is evolved.” [APP ¶121]

summary: Thomas Vaughan, 'an English Adept', a much-cited modern authority on the First Matter, the Light, the fire, the furnace and the operator's discipline.
body:
**Who, per the book.** Thomas Vaughan translated and commented on the Rosicrucian *Fame and Confession*, with preface and appendix, and is sometimes confused with Philalethes [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶73]. Atwood praises him as showing the Art of vital perfectibility most clearly of English authors, gives his pseudonym Eugenius Philalethes, lists his works (*Magia Adamica*, *Coelum Terrae*, *Anthroposophia Theomagica*, *Anima Magia Abscondita*, *Euphrates*, *Lumen de Lumine*) and reports his death by overdose of the elixir [I.1 ¶74]. She calls him “an English Adept, neither antique nor envious” [III.4 ¶44]; “So wrote Vaughan in 1650” [III.1 ¶9].

**Matter and Light.** As “a modern authority” he defines “the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits” [I.2 ¶33; I.2 n34]; it changes form under nature's fire: “The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape” [II.3 ¶30]; he describes it as an eyewitness: “A fat mineral nature it was, he says, bright like pearls, and transparent like crystal” [III.2 n43]. “It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied”, nothing being borrowed from gold or silver [I.2 ¶8]. Atwood says he “has well described” the Hypostatic Metamorphoses: “These three, being but One substantially, admit of a perfect hypostatic union” [III.3 ¶27].

**Method.** Outward study can only “lick the shell” [III.1 ¶8]; theory precedes practice: “be sure to add reason to thy experience, and to employ thy mind as well as thy hands” [III.1 ¶9]; yet “nature is not moved by theory alone, but by sagacious Handicraft and human assistance” [IV.1 ¶5]. Seekers must “change their abstractions into extractions” [II.1 ¶26]. The furnace is small and simple, women fitter than men [III.4 ¶38]; “the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing” [III.4 ¶38]; of one heat-operation “whose method is vital and far more mysterious than all other” [IV.1 ¶41]. The second part of the Gross Work is “one of the greatest subtleties of the Art” [IV.1 ¶36]. Further operations are withheld [IV.2 ¶35]; “this dust is the Arabian Elixir” [IV.3 ¶22]. His lessons on self-examination, moderate heat, charity, piety, solitude and perseverance are quoted at length and offered in conclusion of the rest [III.4 ¶44]. He is also cited for uniting the particular spirit to the universal [II.1 ¶26; APP ¶53]; for the triplicity as hidden intrinsical natures, “not of kitchen-stuff, those three pot-principles of water, oil, and earth” [I.3 n30]; for the 'father' of the Seed, “a certain inviolable mass” [II.3 ¶30; II.3 n35]; for uniting heaven and earth in the 'little new world' [II.3 ¶52]; for the garden, “the rendezvous of all spirits, where Ideas as they descend from above, are conceived and incorporated” [II.4 ¶9]; for Hyanthe's tears as the shed Water [III.3 ¶4]; for Agrippa's failure at the second part of the Gross Work [IV.1 ¶36]; and, in *Magia Adamica*, for an early Christian mission to China spreading faith by healing [I.1 ¶26].

**Appendix (later layer).** Every seeker “wanders awhile in the region of Chimaeras” [APP ¶171]; he “very elegantly depicts the play of that ether” [APP ¶105].

summary: The growth-causing spirit, predominant in the vegetable kingdom.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood says: “The Vegetable spirit is the growth-causing spirit” [APP ¶54], predominant in the vegetable kingdom.

summary: The medium or vehicle of the mind and soul: clear-seeing when purified, terrene when sensual, strengthened by material Rites, and joined by the soul in its ascent.
body:
Atwood speaks of “the primary and proper vehicle of the mind, when it is in a wise and purified condition, is attenuated and clear seeing” [II.2 ¶15]; when the mind is sensual it is terrene, and unpurified “our vehicle disports herself oftentimes in many mingling forms” [II.2 ¶14]. In the purified ascent “the soul, coalescing with its vehicle, transcends free from corporeal hindrance into the elysian light” [II.4 ¶19].

In II.1 the voice is unclear: the vehicle is what is preserved in nature during the reduction [II.1 ¶47], and “there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites” [II.1 ¶51].

summary: In Atwood's reading, Venus personifies the central light of nature, a moist spirit that begets light, liquefies bodies and vivifies metalline bodies.
body: A passage spoken in Venus's voice: “Now saith Venus: I beget light, nor is the darkness of my nature” [I.3 ¶39]; she liquefies bodies and extracts their substance. Atwood glosses: “Venus personifies the central light of nature” [I.3 n49], a moist spirit vivifying metalline bodies.

summary: Atwood's name for the true principle of the Divine Art: a divine ray or Power issuing from the will of the divinized.
body: Atwood states: “This vertical separated Light then we take henceforth to be the true alternative principle in the Divine Art” [III.1 ¶37], a principle about which the alchemists are very wary. It is a divine ray issuing from the will of the divinized: “it is no common light that enters into Divinity, but a congenial ray; a Power” [III.1 ¶37].

summary: The concealed container in which the Matter is concocted; Atwood calls it internal and a divine secret, and Hermes calls it the philosophers' water.
body:
Atwood: “the master presupposes not only a knowledge of the Matter, but of the Vessel also in which it is scientifically concocted” [I.3 n22]; a pure vessel contains the ascending waters. She speaks of “that internal fire and vessel of the adepts” [II.1 ¶6], and says the vessel alone is excepted: “with exception of the vessel; which is a divine secret, hidden from idolators” [II.1 ¶8]. Hermes's Latin identifies it: “vas philosophorum est aqua eorum” [II.1 ¶8] (ours: the vessel of the philosophers is their water). She also writes of “this only vessel for its elaboration” [II.1 ¶17]; the context there apparently points to the human circulatory system, but this is an inference.

Norton's *Ordinal* is quoted: “Use one manner of vessel in matter and in shape” [IV.1 ¶28]. At IV.2 three vessels of decreasing opacity are described — “the First indeed may be considered to be opaque, the Second less so, and the Third still less so” — the third holding the one to be born, likened to an embryo's triple covering; in Norton both medicines share one vessel until all quick things are dead, then vessels change [IV.2 ¶11]. Who speaks the three-vessel account is unclear.

summary: The forecourt before the temple: in man the phantasic intelligence before Reason, in the universe the Ether before the world-soul; mesmerism opens into it.
body: Atwood's image: what stands before the temple. In man the phantasic intelligence “may be called the vestibule of Reason” [III.1 ¶5]; in the universe the Ether stands before the world-soul [III.1 ¶5]. Mesmerism reaches only this far, “opening into the vestibule” [III.1 ¶8].

summary: Author of Elements de Psycologie (Paris 1836), cited as having used intuitive certainty to shake the sensual system of Locke and Condillac.
body: Cited with approval: he used the truth of intuitive certainty to shake the sensual system of Locke and Condillac [II.1 ¶34; II.1 n29].

summary: Poet whom Atwood reads as an initiate: Aeneid 6 and the Georgics allegorize the Mysteries, the First Matter and the vital transmutation.
body:
**Initiate and allegorist.** Atwood reads Aeneas's descent in *Aeneid* 6 as an allegory of the Mysteries and holds Virgil initiated: the Sibyl's warning (“Facilis descensus Averni”), the golden bough, cave, reception and “king in hell” [II.3 ¶6–¶19; II.3 n4, n5, n12, n13]. The passage from Tartarus to the Elysian Fields (“Devenere locos laetos, et amoena vireta”) and the Eridanus as a flow of spirit are read as the unfolding of the embryo life [II.4 ¶7; II.4 ¶8; II.4 ¶16; II.4 n3]. Misenus's rites, the hidden tree and Golden Bough (“Hunc tegit omnis Lucus et obscures claudunt convallibus umbrae”) and the mother's birds as guides illustrate the method; she denies he was a servile imitator of Homer [III.1 ¶25–¶35; III.1 n33, n39]. “Spiritus intus alit” illustrates the spirit nourishing heaven, earth and stars [I.2 ¶12; I.2 n14]. His praise of the land (“Salve Magna Parens frugum Saturnia Tellus Magna virum!”) is applied to the vision, though he referred them to his native soul, as the text has it [III.2 ¶27; III.2 ¶28]; “vast, endless, horrible” illustrates the vacuity of the Original of Life [III.2 ¶54]. The site of his Bees, excluding evil associates, figures the right working-place [III.4 ¶42].

**Other.** His death is compared to Vaughan's [I.1 ¶74]; with Ovid, Horace and Vitruvius he was among Augustan men accused of sorcery [I.1 ¶18].

**Appendix (later layer).** Proteus's binding alludes to the First Matter's changing forms; Aristaeus's lost bees are the soul's faculties; the Golden Bough is the aurific seed; the *Georgics* allegorize celestial and spiritual agriculture [APP ¶141; APP ¶144; APP ¶152; APP ¶157]; the Aristaeus myth bears on the Vital transmutation in an advanced stage (“Quis deus hac musae quis nobis extudet artem?”) [APP ¶173].

summary: In Norton, operative power of four kinds — formal, instrumental, proper and special, material — from which an infused virtue results.
body: Norton, as quoted, distinguishes four virtues: formal of the orb, instrumental of the eighth sphere, proper and special of the planet, and material of the elements; “The virtue infused resulteth of them all” [IV.2 ¶34].

summary: Synesius's term, cited by Atwood, for the soul circulating amid her Adamical defilements, which Plato likens to the deformed Glaucus.
body: Atwood cites the expression from Synesius: “Our viscous soul, as Synesius calls it, circulating in the midst of all her Adamical defilements” [II.3 ¶30]; Plato compares such a soul to the deformed Glaucus [II.3 ¶30].

summary: The lower visionary stage tied to the co-nascent spirit, whose figured images come from the mind's own fancy.
body: Atwood describes a lower visionary stage tied to the co-nascent spirit and endured without much disturbing ordinary life; its images are “such as the mind before beheld in Hades from its own self-shadowing creative fancy” [II.4 ¶29].

summary: The agencies of life which, with their effects, are submitted to subtle analysis and pure synthesis in seeking the Word of Life.
body: Atwood names the search for the Word of Life a “subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects” [IV.2 ¶43].

summary: The adepts' analysis of bodies by which they found man's life to be a pure fire in an ethereal vapour.
body: Atwood cites “adepts well-skilled, as they profess, in the vital analysis of bodies” [IV.4 ¶4], who by it discovered that man's life is a pure fire in an ethereal vapour; not further explained.

summary: The impure atmosphere around each individual life, seen by clairvoyants, where thoughts and desires are imaged; purifying it is the Mystery's aim.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood describes the atmosphere surrounding each individual life, perceived by clairvoyants: “all the thoughts and desires of life are imaged there” [APP ¶73]. Its density or lightness makes men dark or bright, and purifying it is the aim of the Mystery [APP ¶73].

summary: What the Rational Efficient proceeds to dissolve; not further defined.
body: Atwood says of the Rational Efficient that “it proceeds even to a dissolution of the Vital Bond” [III.1 ¶47].

summary: Kirchringius's name for laborious operations amid which the adepts prayed.
body: Quoted from Kirchringius: “even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed” [III.4 ¶22]. Not further defined.

summary: Atwood's name for the ancient experimental work on life, the vital alteration of the Mysteries, whose progress discloses powers and secrets of nature.
body: Atwood's name for the process sketched through the Mysteries in connection with the Sacred Art and Alchemy: “In the progress of this Vital Experiment, it may not be difficult to imagine that powers would be disclosed and particular secrets of nature in the substance of her Whole.” [II.4 ¶58] Part III opens by examining its Method and Principles before the practice: “Let us examine yet further into the Method of this Vital Experiment” [III.1 ¶4].

summary: The force without which no real transformation occurs; it passes between fermented lives by transmission from agent to patient.
body: Atwood says no real transformation is achieved “unless the vital force be present and in action” [II.1 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer) it is the life passed between fermented lives, progressing by transmission from agent to patient: “That is the law of progression of the Vital force” [APP ¶42].

summary: A young discovery, not yet a science, pursued by patiently gathering outward facts.
body: Atwood: “the discovery of Vital Magnetism is young, and has had no time to grow up into a science” [III.1 ¶8]; it proceeds by gathering outward facts.

summary: What the purified intelligence dissolves in order to open the occult source.
body: Atwood says the purified intelligence, “by dissolving the vital medium, opens the occult source” [III.1 ¶23]. Not further defined.

summary: The perfecting of life, of which the one Art is the medium.
body: Atwood calls the Art “the one Art and medium of vital perfectibility” [I.1 ¶74], in her praise of Vaughan.

summary: Principles of life that subsist even in their extreme separation by Art.
body: Atwood speaks of the “marvelous subsistence of the Vital Principles in their extreme separation by Art” [III.3 ¶9].

summary: The first stage of the Hermetic Practice, commonly called the Gross Work: purifying the medium of wild affections and defects by dissolution, by the Manual or Linear way.
body: The heading of IV.1 identifies it: “Of the Vital Purification, Commonly Called the Gross Work” [IV.1 ¶1]. It purifies the medium of its wild affections and innate defects by dissolution; the adepts “proceeded at once scientifically to purify” [IV.1 ¶4], and “for the Purification we read but of one way, called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5].

summary: That to which the adepts made experimental ingress, thereby discovering within themselves the catholic original of nature.
body: Atwood says the adepts, “by an experimental ingress, as they acknowledge, to the Vital Radix, have discovered the catholic original of nature, intellectual and material” [III.2 ¶28].

summary: Light's greatest and most permanent benefit to man, distinct from its outward use as medicine.
body: Atwood says Light benefits man as a medicine, “but above all, and most permanently, in the vital rectification” [IV.3 ¶30]. It is not defined, but illustrated by Julian's account of the purified soul strengthening her connate spirit.

summary: Man's life-spirit, impure by birth, which the alchemical work purifies, dissolves, ferments and circulates until it is promoted to perfection and ends in the Principle of things.
body:
For Atwood the Vital Spirit is the subject the work acts on. It is promoted by the art “from one form of being into another” through many stages to perfection [I.2 ¶48]. It must be segregated from the defilements and sense-impressions implanted by birth: the aim is “to segregate the Vital Spirit away from those defilements and imaginative impressures” [II.2 ¶8], and the ancients began by “purifying the Vital Spirit in its proper Light” [II.2 ¶24].

After the first preliminaries “the object was to produce an alteration in the Vital Spirit” by Rational Analysis [III.1 ¶50]; yet “Nothing is done radically to meliorate the Vital Spirit” without a motive, which comes from its being deprived of its Understanding Light [III.1 ¶28]. It undergoes a “spontaneous fermentation” that changes the Passive Subject, and by grafting and transplanting could be grown and sublimed by degrees [III.1 ¶9]. Its dissolution and the alienation of its natural bind discover the True matter [III.2 ¶62]. Purified “through sacrifice of all foreign attractions”, it revolves about its center with active and passive power united [III.3 ¶3]; it may lawfully “descend and ascend in successive circulations” until it ends in the Principle of things [II.4 ¶52]. Atwood says that, it would seem, the whole secret “consists in the sanquinary circulation of the Vital Spirit” under a threefold Law [III.3 ¶72]. In the colour process one works with it, and “This Spirit is so full of life” that adding more renews a failed stage [II.1 ¶25].

Sendivogius places the soul “in the vital spirit in the purest blood” [II.1 ¶10]; an unattributed passage calls it “the vital spirit of the arterial blood”, where the three principles are unequally composed and opposition ceases in the blackening [II.1 ¶21].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says it is “in the Universal as well as in the individual” [APP ¶28], that “the human vital spirit” is what Alchemy ferments and purifies [APP ¶68], and that it “always is in chaos, i.e., always coming to be, never is, and whilst in this life wants the rebirth” [APP ¶165].

summary: The transmutation of life; Atwood says the Aristaeus myth bears on it in an advanced stage.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood says the Aristaeus myth “bears altogether on the Vital transmutation in an advanced stage” [APP ¶173].

summary: Vital power, which Atwood says is capable of illimitable artificial increase.
body: Atwood speaks of “the illimitable powers and artificial increase of vitalization”, conceivable to those who apply a fragment of the same virtue benevolently [IV.3 ¶35].

equivalences.with: true matters of the Blessed Stone (with the Green Duenech)

summary: In Khunrath, named with the Green Duenech as the true matters of the Blessed Stone.
body: Khunrath (quoted) names “the Green Duenech and the Vitriol of Venus, which are the true matters of the Blessed Stone” [IV.1 ¶36].

summary: The life-giving essence of the Stone, of the same origin as what it assimilates, the Universal Spirit; called azoth by the Hermetic philosophers.
body: Atwood: “this powerful vivific Ens is of the same origin as that which it assimilates --- viz., the Universal Spirit”, and it draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself [IV.3 ¶29]. Identified with azoth: “the Hermetic philosophers have given it the name of azoth, which adheres to bodies” [IV.3 ¶29].

headword: the Voice at our Lord's baptism; our Lord's prayer
forms: the Voice at our Lord's baptism
summary: The Voice at our Lord's baptism and our Lord's prayer, which Atwood cites in the Table Talk to illustrate the Name speaking and working its change.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood cites the Voice and Christ's prayer (“Father, glorify thy Name”; “Now is my soul troubled”) to illustrate the Name speaking and working its change, and Christ needing new strength by its utterance: “How I have both glorified my Name and I will glorify it again” [APP ¶88].

summary: The only way, Atwood reports it taught, to become partaker of the Divinity one aspires to; also the means by which the torch promotes things to their utmost strength.
body: Atwood reports the teaching that “no otherwise can we be made partakers, it is taught, but by a voluntary assimilation” [III.4 ¶20]. Of the torch's action she writes: “by its voluntary assimilation, increasing and promoting things to their utmost boundary of strength” [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: That through which Osiris, the Divine Light, passes in the regeneration, suffering Typhon's restraint and subversion.
body: Atwood says Osiris (the Divine Light) “suffers in passing through the voluntary axle in the regeneration”, undergoing Typhon's restraint, contrariety and subversion [III.1 ¶63]. The expression is not further explained.

summary: That in which, Atwood says, the central hidden light is hidden.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “the central hidden light (there’s the mystery) is hidden in the voluntary contrariation” [APP ¶125]. The sentence is broken; it appears to link this to Saturn or the Will.

summary: The agent applied to obliterate the defilements of the Universal Element, first in a series with gentleness, beneficence and justice.
body: Atwood: “By applying the proper voluntary corrosive they teach to obliterate its defilements”, i.e. those of the Universal Element; it stands first in a series followed by gentleness, beneficence and justice [IV.1 ¶47].

summary: Something drawn upward into intellectual reminiscence once the vital medium is dissolved; Wisdom's lost Efficient recovered in the Light of life.
body: Atwood says the dissolution of the vital medium “draws the Voluntary Efficient upward into intellectual reminescence” [III.1 ¶23], and speaks of “Wisdom recovering her lost Efficient in the Light of life” [III.1 ¶36]. The term is not further defined.

summary: In Atwood's reading, Motion: the lame god who stirs up the fire, instrument of the mind; also the fire of the work, which destroys and maintains life.
body:
Atwood identifies Vulcan with Motion, “which the lame god personates” [IV.1 ¶34]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) she states: “The Vulcan of the Alchemists is Motion.” He is lame because motion in this life is halting and never returns into its own principle, and “Vulcan is not the fire, the ignis Philosophorum, but the stirrer up of the fire.” [APP ¶129]. Further: “The Vulcan or Faber is the instrument of the motive agent --- the mind.” [APP ¶130].

In the monk's words, “Fire only can effect that, and Vulcan is the sole and only master of all these”: sole separator of good from evil and pure from impure; a Vulcan acts in the Greater Orb and a certain other Vulcan in the Lesser World [IV.1 ¶40]. Vulcan also stands for the fire of the work: “Which Vulcanic action, to destroy life and to maintain it”, and “placing it again upon the coals, stir Vulcan into it” [IV.1 ¶43].

summary: The alchemists' Matter as first known: full of heterogeneous qualities, fallen from its sphere and defiled, needing preparations, solutions and calcinations.
body: Reported as the alchemists' view: the Matter as first found is “full of heterogeneous qualities and notions, as a subject fallen from its sphere and defiled”, and so needs preparations, solutions and calcinations [II.2 ¶16].

summary: Per the Scholiast, the newborn quintessential spirit or Proteus: the first sublimed quintessence not yet perfected by art, the same as the crow in a different estate.
body: Atwood reports the Scholiast: “The vulture, according to our Scholiast, is the new born quintessential spirit or Proteus” [I.3 n11]. It is the Spirit of life in its active, devouring state: “The vulture is the first sublimed quintessence not yet perfected by art” [I.3 n12]. Identified with the crow: “The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate” [I.3 n12].

summary: An orrery cited as the model of the orrery explanation of the lights of the Mysteries, which Atwood rejects.
body: Atwood invokes Walker’s or Lloyd’s Eidouranion to contrast with, and reject, the explanation of the lights shown in the Mysteries as an orrery-like display [II.3 ¶49].

summary: Author of the Divine Legation, whom Atwood criticizes for treating the Mysteries as political fraud but uses on the golden bough and as translator of Stoboeus.
body: Atwood criticizes Warburton for seeing the Mysteries as political fraud and calls his notions obsolete; the Divine Legation, vol. 1, is also cited as a reference [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n1, II.2 n8]. His account of the institution she calls absurd, citing his phrase “a mere illuminated image, which the priest had purified” [II.4 ¶29]. Yet she draws on him where he supports her: the golden bough was literally part of the sacred equipage, and Aeneid VI alludes to the Mysteries [II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶13, II.3 n10]. She also uses his translation of the Stoboeus passage, which she calls well rendered (Divine Legation 1:342) [II.3 ¶37, II.3 n42].

summary: Intricate structures constructed by and for the Key, for it alone to pass through.
body: Atwood: “those mirific wards which were constructed by it, and for it to pass through, and for it alone” [IV.4 ¶32].

equivalences.with: ethereal body of life and light
wine, water of life, vinegar, oil
reducer of the soul to its body
Stilla roris, Lac Virginis, Elixir, Aqua Vitae, Azoth, Prima Materia Lapis et Rebis
Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient (Democrit)

summary: The philosophers' Water: not common water but the ethereal body of life and light, altered and corporified by art; the middle nature, mercurial quintessence and first matter, under many names.
body:
**Atwood's account.** The philosophers' water is not common water but “a certain tortured water, having suffered alteration by art and becomes corporified”; “it is the ethereal body of life and light which they profess to have discovered”, heavenly and not wetting the hands [I.2 ¶43]. Into it gold and metals are reduced in the analysis: “all metals, likewise, may be reduced into water, that is, into their first pure matter” [III.2 n38], and “the water, being incorruptible, will require no analogous process” [III.2 ¶48]. The Water of the Adepts is “the miraculous product of the spiritual poles of mind in sublime conjunction at their source”, a regenerate body made manifest by the physico-chemical art: “this was their Stilla roris, Lac Virginis, Elixir, Aqua Vitae, Azoth, Prima Materia Lapis et Rebis” [III.3 ¶73]; “in this water, when destruction has done its worst with the elements of life, the principle of all is artificially preserved” [III.3 ¶71]. Verse quoted with it equates it with Democrit's “Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient” and Hermes' “water of crude Mercury” [III.3 ¶74]. The meadows “bear water which is the symbol of vivification”, one of the “material rewards of initiation” she defers [II.4 ¶16].

**Hermes.** “The water spoken of by Hermes is the passive spirit” [I.3 n21]; “the water was first in the air, then in the earth” [I.3 ¶19]; yet in the Stone “this, however, is not water in its true form, but fire” [I.3 ¶26]. It is “the middle nature, which is the Water” joining Heaven and Earth [I.3 ¶55]; “The water alluded to is the mercurial quintessence”, born “in a humid and vaprous consistency” and golden when informed by the central light [I.3 n63].

**Eirenaeus.** The fire is freed “by the mediation of our water”, and “the first water will work on the body till it hath opened the pores and extracted partly the tincture of Sol” [III.1 ¶14]; the text does not say whether these two waters are the same.

**Synesius.** “that Water is the most sharp vinegar, which makes gold to be a pure spirit”, “that Blessed Nature which engenders all things” [III.1 ¶70]; the sole object of labour, “that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals”, to be decocted gently [III.3 ¶60].

**Boehme.** Desiring fire takes the Light's virtue and “maketh it an essence, viz., Water” [III.3 ¶24].

**Eudoxus.** “Our Water is a living Spring which comes out of the Stone by a natural miracle of our philosophy.” [IV.3 ¶8]. It is “the soul and the spirit” [IV.3 ¶7], called wine, water of life, vinegar or oil “according to the different degrees of Preparation”, “properly called the Vinegar of the Wise”, the “Divine Liquor”, and “the reducer of the soul to its body” [IV.3 ¶8]. Boiling turns it into Earth, the Mercury of the Wise carrying its own Sulphur: “it is this which reduces our Water into Earth”, and as earth it “shall obtain all the virtues which the philosophers attribute to it” [IV.3 ¶12].

summary: In the Adept's teaching, the two principles present in all things that regenerate and perform the whole work.
body: The Adept (quoted) says of Water and Spirit: “These two are in all things” and “The two former principles perform all.” The Spirit uses the water to purge and wash its body [IV.2 ¶18].

summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, the water with which sublimed arsenic and calcined mercury are ground, carrying life and light into them.
body: Pierce, the Black Monk (quoted): sublimed arsenic and calcined mercury are ground with “the Water of Myght, Which beareth ingression of Lyfe and Light” [III.3 ¶16].

summary: Sendivogius's name for a water that does not wet the hands, white as snow, which he calls the Water of Life.
body: Sendivogius (quoted) speaks of those who “call the Water of our Sea, the Water of Life, not wetting the hands”, and says “that water was as white as snow” [III.2 ¶7].

summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, that which makes the marriage; not explained.
body: Pierce, the Black Monk (quoted): “But the Water of the Wood, maketh the marriage.” [III.4 ¶21]. Not explained further.

equivalences.with: the fountain which Berhard Trevisan mentions

summary: The fixed watery form of the philosophic matter, a mature state that frames the royal elements; in the Master's words, the blessed form that dissolves the Elements.
body: Atwood: “The fixed watery Form of the philosophic matter” is a more mature state of one praised earlier, creatrix of the royal elements, drawing to itself the rubified light of its internal agent; “this is the fountain which Berhard Trevisan mentions” [I.3 n39]. The Master (quoted): “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!”; with it a sulphurous Form is taken up and mixed with Acetum, “with this watery soul” [IV.2 ¶14].

summary: Cited for reference only.
The true philosophic proportions of the work; Hermes says they are the two third waters of the divided Water.
body: Hermes (quoted): “the two third waters are the Weights of the Wise” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast's note glosses them as “the true philosophic proportions called also by Hermes the Weights of the Wise” [I.3 n6].

summary: That upon which deviating profane persons may be broken; not explained.
body: Atwood says deviating profane persons may “become broken necessitiously upon the Wheel of Life” [III.4 ¶9]. Not explained further.

summary: The two forms of the Stone, fermented respectively with pure silver and with fine gold.
body: Unattributed: the Stone is fermented “with pure silver for the White, and with Red for fine Gold” [IV.3 ¶29]. Not further explained here.

summary: In an adept's words, the resting point enjoyed when the colours appear and the king has triumphed over death.
body: An adept (quoted): “Here thou mayest rest and wait, and enjoy the glory of thy white elixir”, once the colours appear and the king has triumphed over death [I.3 n22].

summary: The light revealed beneath the influx of the Holy Spirit when the Divine presence arises; Van Helmont's Quellem, the primeval Light.
body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood says it is revealed beneath the influx of the Holy Spirit when the Divine presence arises: “that wonderful White Light which Van Helmont speaks of, though in a very superficial way, as the Quellem”, belonging “to the Ancient of Days, i.e., the primeval Light.” [APP ¶157].

summary: In Norton, one of the two medicines, White and Red, which share one vessel and working at first.
body: Norton (quoted): the White and Red medicines share one vessel and working at first, and seeking further is useless “Till the white medicine be fully wrought.” [IV.2 ¶13].

summary: In Eudoxus, one of the two Mercuries, identified with the Lunaria and called by others the bath of the Moon.
body: Eudoxus (quoted): “The Lunaria is the White Mercury”, and “the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon” [IV.3 ¶10].

summary: In verses quoted from Norton, the White Stone found through patient labor after true teaching; the white medicine must be fully wrought before the Red is sought.
body: Norton's verse (quoted, not Atwood's own words) says many patient wise men “Found our White Stone with exercise;” after true teaching, and cautions that the Red should not be sought “Till the white medicine be fully wrought;” [I.1 ¶60]. The White Stone thus apparently marks a stage completed before the red work.

summary: In Eudoxus's account, the white sulphur separated by whitening the foul black faeces in the first work; identified with the Sal Amoniac of the Wise and their Chaste Diana.
body: Quoted from Eudoxus: in the first work the foul black faeces are whitened and the white sulphur separated [IV.3 ¶9]. He identifies it as “the white sulphur, which is the Sal Amoniac of the Wise” and as “the Sal Amoniac of the Wise, and their Chaste Diana, who washes herself in the bath” [IV.3 ¶9].

summary: In a passage from a more modern experimentalist, the white spirit with which the masculine tincture comes out of the black darkness in union.
body: Quoted from an unnamed “more modern experimentalist” in a footnote: the masculine tincture comes “out of the black darkness together in union with the white virginal spirit” [I.3 n53].

summary: The stage at which the matter is snow-white and the elixir is perfect as to the white; Norton ties it to making the Moon fortunate.
body: The author of the Lucerna Salis (quoted) describes the matter become snow-white: “Then is your elixir perfect as to the white work” [III.2 ¶5]; the Latin reads “Et tum confectum est elixir ad album” [III.2 ¶6]. Norton (quoted) directs: “For the white Worke make fortunate the Moone” [IV.2 ¶34]; the text does not explain this further.

summary: In Sendivogius, the Whites and Reds with which ignorant montebanks deceived almost the whole world.
body: Sendivogius (quoted) complains of pretenders who “have with their Whites and Reds deceived almost the whole world” [I.1 ¶84]. The expression is not explained there; the context suggests false white and red products of the work.

summary: In Atwood's own voice, chiefly in the later Appendix, Will is the only true substance and foundation of everything, the binding and unbinding power, and the greatest power of purgation.
body:
Atwood's own statements; most come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). There she holds that “for Will has substance, nay, is the only substance” and that “it is the Universal Loadstone of Existence” [APP ¶8]; in higher states it moves from its own center, its efflux is chaotic and must be taken up by an external mind [APP ¶8]. “Will creates an image, not a being.”; passing into desire for that image, it unites with it into a being; Will is the only true body [APP ¶36]. “All in the beginning is Will; it is the foundation of everything, and is everything” [APP ¶86]: all is held potentially in it; it subsists in one will, then two, exists in the third, and then becomes self-assertion. “Weight is the analogue of Will.” [APP ¶123]; it binds and unbinds — “that which Will has bound, Will only can unbind” — and is identified with Saturn: “a Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key” [APP ¶125]. Two wills contend for the soul, and vacuity of self-will gives spirits a footing [APP ¶123–125].

In the main text Atwood states that “Will is the greatest power of purgation” [IV.1 ¶31], and that “no mortal can communicate it to another unless the Divine Will be with him” [IV.1 ¶39] — the Divine Will must be conciliated.

summary: Two separated principles which, once freed, attract one another like steel and loadstone.
body: Speaker unclear: the text speaks of “the separated principles of Will and Understanding in their freed state” [IV.2 ¶30], which attract each other as steel and loadstone.

summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's name for the vital power, at a certain time seated in the lumbar region and sent back.
body: Appendix (later layer), Atwood's voice: “the power, the vital or willing-power” [APP ¶11], at a certain time seated in the lumbar region and sent back.

summary: In Khunrath, the thick, black substance of the first act, called the Blood of the Earth and identified with the Red of Lully.
body: Khunrath (quoted) describes it in the first act as “thick, dense, and black, blacker than black” [IV.1 ¶36]. It is “the Wine which the Wise have called the Blood of the Earth”, “which likewise is the Red of Lully” [IV.1 ¶36]; it is called Red for its tincture, the color of its virtue.

equivalences.with: Law of Light; its emanating spirit
the science of truth which is in all beings
the good, the fair, and the blessed Eternity
the standard of truth in a rectified intellect
the breath of the power of God
Intellect diving intuitively without imaginative error

summary: The object of Atwood's inquiry: the ancient internal Wisdom, the true being of Intellect and self-knowledge, identified with Salt, the substance of the Stone, and the Root of Reason.
body:
Mostly Atwood's own voice. Wisdom is “that Wisdom we are investigating”, identified with Isis and Minerva [III.1 ¶5]; by its Light nature's universal efficient is revealed [III.1 ¶3]. It is the highest faculty: “The term Intellect, as it is here taken in its highest sense, is synonymous with Wisdom” [II.1 ¶39]; “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37]; it is “not conversant with a certain definite existing thing but simply with all things” [II.1 ¶37]. Ancient science's theme was “the standard of truth in a rectified intellect”, Wisdom being “an affirmative operative hypostasis, informing, invigorating, and sustaining all things” [II.1 ¶44] and “the offspring of a vital experiment into nature” [II.1 ¶52]. Hermes (as cited) calls it “the good, the fair, and the blessed Eternity” [II.1 ¶43]. It is “not worldly” [II.2 ¶13], intuitive Intellect without imaginative error.

For the method, Atwood ties it to the Stone: Wisdom “was the worthy object of all Hermetic Philosophy, and the miraculous substance of its transmutative Stone”, and “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom” [III.3 ¶50]; “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20]. From Ecclesiasticus and Solomon (quoted): “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49]. It is “the vehicle of the Catholic Reason in Identity, the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [III.3 ¶71].

Moral conditions: “No impure leaven (need we repeat it?) can enter into Wisdom” [III.4 ¶7]; the covetous flee “Wisdom’s fiery ordeal” [III.4 ¶11]. “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36]; it is given by God “and send thy Holy Spirit from above” [IV.3 ¶39], the gift of perfecting the work [IV.3 ¶48]. It is “a thing acquired, the reward only of peculiar and arduous discipline” [IV.4 ¶17], “above science, art, and every other kind of faith”, the Well of Heraclitus and the Nothing Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27]; yet “the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared from amongst men” [IV.4 ¶28].

Quoted views: Asclepius Trallianus calls it “a certain clearness” [II.4 ¶26]; Reuchlin: “Nothing is in the beginning but Wisdom, or Sapience”, called Ain by the Hebrews [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi says none can tell “in what manner she is contained in non-Being” [III.2 ¶32]. In the Appendix (later layer) it is “a pure exemplar from the first Light or Life, showing man what he ought to be” [APP ¶90], the great Salt Sea or Universal Will [APP ¶94], and the Law of Light's emanating spirit [APP ¶47].

Further asserted identities: Intellect and Divination [II.1 ¶35]; the intelligible essence [II.1 ¶37]; Pythagoras's “science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39]; “the breath of the power of God” [II.1 ¶44]; “the fear of the Lord” [III.1 ¶8]; Understanding [IV.3 ¶47]; Reuchlin's Three Persons in Divinity [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi's Principle [III.2 ¶32]. With Sendivogius, God inspires his Wisdom into philosophers [II.4 ¶39]; Atwood also personifies her as a bride the philosophers wooed, bringing a dowry of creative light [IV.4 ¶10].

summary: Anonymous adepts whose unanimous view Atwood reports: that their work may be likened to the creation of the world.
body: Atwood reports, with approval, the Wise's view that “their work may be likened to the creation of the world” [IV.2 ¶30].

summary: The adepts as a group, cited by Atwood for their warnings that none succeed without right intention and God's blessing, and that their records are two-edged.
body: Atwood endorses their declarations that none attain the Art without right intention and God's blessing and that the pursuit is dangerous to the ill-informed: “As the adepts indeed foretold, their records have proved like a curious two-edged instrument” [III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶16].

summary: An unnamed adept cited as warning that Pluto's Palace exposed with Minerva's Artifice, or Vulcan with her at the Altar, is an ominous association.
body: Cited by Atwood: when Pluto's Palace is exposed with Minerva's Artifice, or Vulcan stands with her at the Altar, “the Association is ominous” [IV.1 ¶34].

summary: The adepts whose enigmas, fables, parables and maxims, Atwood says, all tend to one discovery and must be studied with the Key.
