body: Atwood, with approval, says their enigmas, fables, parables and maxims all tend to one discovery and are to be studied with the Key [IV.4 ¶32].

summary: In Eudoxus, the operator who lends Nature a hand for her compound and himself makes the compound of Art.
body: Eudoxus (quoted): Nature's compound is helped by the Artist, but of the compound of Art “it is always the Artist who makes it”, “it is the Wise man who makes it” [IV.3 ¶9].

headword: the wise poet, in his Georgics
forms: the wise poet, in his Georgics
summary: An unnamed poet whose Georgics Atwood cites for the repeated labor of ploughing and clearing the field.
body: Cited by Atwood for teaching, in the Georgics, the repeated labor of ploughing and clearing the field [IV.1 ¶9]; the context suggests an image for the repeated operations of the work.

summary: In the Poemander of Hermes, the holy Word issuing from the Light or Mind, joining itself to Nature and moving the elements; the Son of God.
body: Hermes (Poemander, quoted): “Then from that Light a certain holy Word joined itself unto Nature” [III.3 ¶53], drawing the fire upward and moving earth and water; “that bright and lightful Word from the Mind is the Son of God” [III.3 ¶54]. God's Will took it in making the world.

summary: What, Atwood says, the ancestors sought and experimentally found through subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects.
body: Atwood: “the Word of Life would seem to have been sought after by our ancestors, and experimentally found” [IV.2 ¶43], by subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects.

summary: In the Appendix, words by which the Initiated moved one another on, found only in the subjective life and lost by the Masons.
body: Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “The Initiated moved one another on by words of power.”; these are words “which are only to be found by seeking them in the subjective, the fundamental life” [APP ¶100]. The Masons have lost them.

summary: In Eudoxus, the three closely analogous works of the Art, each repeating dissolution, removal of blackness, whitening and vivifying.
body: Eudoxus (quoted): “the operations of the three works have a great deal of analogy one to another” [IV.3 ¶3]; each repeats dissolution, removal of blackness, whitening and vivifying, and the philosophers deliberately confuse them.

summary: In the theosophist's teaching, one of two principles in everything, predominant in outward nature since the fall and to be subdued as servant to the light.
body: The theosophist (quoted): every thing has two principles, of which the wrath fire has predominated in outward nature since the fall and must be subdued to serve the light. “The serpent’s sting is the wrath fire” [IV.3 ¶38].

summary: Writers whom Atwood credits with rightly linking Trance to the temple mysteries but faults for going no further than therapy.
body: Atwood qualifies them: they rightly connect Trance with the temple mysteries but do not go beyond its therapeutic use [II.2 ¶6].

summary: Reported through Aristotle as first to introduce the doctrine that the One is God, and dismissed there as rustic.
body: As reported via Aristotle, Xenophanes first introduced the doctrine that “the One is God” and was dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

summary: Author of an Opusculum whom Atwood cites on long searching for the key, on prayer before the Work, and on one method, matter and vessel.
body: Atwood cites Zachary's Opusculum as another example of long searching for the key [III.1 ¶37, III.1 n42]. With approval, she cites him that one should read the philosophers and pray, yet use means: “for no one ever acquired this art by chance, but by prayer rather than by other means” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n17]. Against many furnaces and vessels: “there is indeed but one way of working, in one matter, one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9, IV.1 n12].

summary: Cited by Atwood for the ether as plastic, generating fire, and, within Vaughan's lessons, for listening much and speaking little.
body: Atwood cites Zeno for the ether as an artful generating fire: “Ignem esse artificiosum, ad gignendum progredientem via” [I.2 ¶16] (ours: that fire is artful, proceeding methodically to generate). Within Vaughan's lessons he is quoted: “Nature gave us one tongue and two ears, that we might hear much and speak little” [III.4 ¶44].

summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the absolute unit as the ground of Being.
body: Atwood cites him in support: “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45].

summary: A work Atwood cites on the formless Divinity, the Initial Principle as Wisdom manifesting by a point of Light, and the celestial prototype in humanity.
body: Atwood cites the Zohar in support: Divinity has no form before descent into creation, so no image may represent Him [II.3 ¶48, II.3 n52]; the Initial Principle is Wisdom or the Supreme Crown, the Unknown who manifests — “he begins by producing a point” — with its white appearance [III.2 ¶3, III.2 n3, III.2 n4]. The Liber Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” and shows the covert fire in Holy Writ [II.1 ¶40].

summary: Cited for reference only.
Cited by Atwood for magic as the service of the gods, for the Prester as Fire Spirit of Life, and for the ladder reaching from Tartarus to Heaven.
body: His magic is described as the service of the gods [II.1 ¶51]. Atwood identifies with the Stone or Salt “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54]. She identifies with the magnetic chain “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

summary: Oracles used as a chapter epigraph exhorting the reader to the Light.
body: Used as the chapter epigraph: “It behooves thee to hasten to the Light, and to the beams of the Father” [II.4 ¶2].

summary: An Egyptian reputed a great practitioner, named among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone.
body: Named as an Egyptian reputed a great practitioner [I.1 ¶29], and listed with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras and Archelaus among authors of extant treatises on the stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].
